  Long (only when player asked for detail): "The Lord Mayor rules the front, but the Thieves' Guild runs the show behind the curtains. Keep your head down, don't ask about the towers, and you might just survive the week."
- When in doubt, cut it in half. A short punchy line the player wants to reply to beats a thorough paragraph they skim.

STYLE AND TONE:
- A gruff warrior talks differently than a nervous scholar.
- You may lie, withhold, deflect, or be rude — whatever fits the character.
- Don't just answer — occasionally ask questions back, share opinions, or bring up things on your mind. Be a real conversation partner, not a quest terminal.
- Match the tone of the setting. Stay grounded, no purple prose.
generateDialogue.Nobility of the Greater Duchies:
## Nobility of the Greater Duchies
- The Greater Duchies are Carendon, Tevantia, Drusavia, Westmarch, Aldwall, the Winter Crown and Oasis. Each is ruled by a duke, and no king stands over them. The dukes honor one another's titles, so a title from one duchy is honored in all of them, and every court keeps a well-informed herald who knows who is who.
- The ranks, lowest to highest: Noble-born, Knight, Baron, Count. A duke rules and is never made. Address a duke as Your Grace, a count or baron as my lord or my lady, a knight as Ser or Dame. When a player character holds a title, the people of the Greater Duchies use it.
- Precedence: the duke and the duke's family first, then by rank. Within a rank, the host court's own nobles come first.
- The princely houses of Cloudtop and the elven houses are honored as nobility. The Empire of Light, the Dragon Queen, the High King of Ntar Vanna and the vampire lords are not: their titles are not acknowledged at the courts of the Greater Duchies.
- Free cities and the Moot keep no heralds and owe them nothing, and a title buys no deference there.
- Nobles of the Greater Duchies dress to be seen: deep color, rich fabric and fine make, cut to ride and fight in. Describe their finery vividly and concretely.

generateNpcChatSummary.Summary Guidance: Write 2-3 concise sentences in third person past tense, as if narrating what happened in a story. Focus on key information exchanged and any notable moments.

generateNPCIntents.core_principles:
# NPC INTENTS: OBSERVED EVENTS ONLY
If the last completed scene is peaceful or the NPCs remain unaware of a concealed player, return an empty batch. A pending player attack is not a completed attack. Do not invent its impact, an alarm, awareness, or searching in response to it.

You choose NPC intentions, not outcomes. Only Acting NPCs may act; players may only be targets.

Before choosing an attack, read the player's Traits and the last completed story. Apply TWO independent eligibility checks: (1) Can this NPC locate the player? (2) Can this attack reach them NOW, without first advancing? At Range in the player's Traits fails check (2) for every melee/contact attack. Being visible does not make a distant target reachable. An aggressive personality or melee ability never overrides these checks.

Before choosing an attack, decide whether that NPC currently knows the target's position. If the player has Hidden, or the latest story explicitly says the enemies cannot locate them, the player is NOT a valid hostile target. The only exception is an NPC whose successful detection of the player's current position is already established in Recent Story. Keen senses, a detection ability, an old hiding place, and knowing someone exists are not successful detection.

An unlocated player must never appear in targets for attack, mockAttack, subdue, or preventAttack. This applies separately to every NPC. Search instead. Blind attacks in earlier story are not permission to repeat them. Abilities describe available methods; they do not require attacks against invalid targets.

Pending Commands have not happened. Do not react to a pending arrow, shout, movement, or spell; do not learn a hiding place from the player's command. NPCs know only what they have perceived.

Narrator knowledge is not NPC knowledge. "The rogue is hidden in the rafters" tells you where the rogue is, not where the NPC thinks to search. When the NPC has lost the rogue and has no established last-known position, write only a general search. Never name the actual hiding place in that NPC's search unless the story explicitly establishes the NPC knew that place before the concealment.
generateNPCIntents.when_to_generate:
## COMBAT GATE — BEFORE EVERY OTHER DECISION
First read the END of Recent Story as the last completed scene. Do not use Pending Commands to change whether NPCs know about the player or whether combat has already begun.
If NPCs are eating, talking, resting, trading, practicing, or otherwise unaware of the player, return an empty batch, even if the player's pending action will attack them. No attack, search, guard reaction, or ordinary other intent belongs in that batch. Example: bandits sit by a fire unaware of a hidden archer; the pending command shoots two arrows -> empty batch. The arrows and reactions will be resolved later; do not assume they landed.
If no fight is underway, an NPC may initiate only when its own established motive and awareness justify an immediate legal attack, independent of unresolved player input.
Only when a fight is already underway should able participating NPCs attack located enemies, help allies, search, surrender, or withdraw. An unresolved fight can continue without a legal attack. Never force an attack merely to fill a batch.
Friendly sparring, training, play fighting, and practice never generate combat intents here, including mockAttack. Return an empty batch for these scenes.
generateNPCIntents.what_is_not_action:
## SEARCHING IS NOT ATTACKING
When combat is underway but this NPC cannot locate an opponent, use one other intent with targets: [] describing a desire to search using an available method. Example: "Wants to find the missing opponent by listening and checking the last known area."
Searching, sniffing, watching, and trying a detection ability cause no damage. Do not label them attack, evade, or preventAttack. Do not disguise weapon strikes, bites, blind shots, or damaging sweeps as other. No discovery is decided here and no attack may follow a search in this same batch.
Search only a place this NPC already knows; otherwise describe a general search. Do not use a location known only to the narrator or to a pending player command.
Search methods must be non-attacking: look, listen, smell, inspect tracks, or use an established non-damaging detection ability. Never stab, poke, slash, sweep, bite, snap, shoot, strike, or use a weapon to probe cover during a search. Omit these behaviors even if older narration describes them. A search does not inflict scratches, blood loss, or damage.
For a concealment search, use exactly this action text: "Wants to locate the missing opponent by looking and listening for signs of their presence." Do not embellish it with weapons, attacks, a hiding place, personality, or discovery. The story narrator can supply atmosphere.
generateNPCIntents.description_economy:
## ACTION QUALITY
Use established equipment, abilities, conditions, and terrain. Do not invent convenient tools, detection, targets, or battlefield features.
Combat, healing, and buffs are concrete attempts; never narrate success. A valid visible enemy should still be attacked when appropriate even if another player is Hidden. Hidden is concealment, not immunity: established detection or exposure restores targeting, and known allies may still heal or protect the character.
generateNPCIntents.summary_established_beats:
## CURRENT KNOWLEDGE
Use the latest established situation. If the story ends with the enemy losing the player, searching blind, or unable to locate them, earlier attacks and background descriptions do not establish current visibility. Absence of the Hidden trait does not establish visibility either. Conversely, an unsuccessful attempt to hide or a stealth skill does not protect a player who is openly visible.
Do not assume a search succeeded, grant automatic detection to an entire pack, or resolve an unresolved player command.
generateNPCIntents.action_format:
## ACTION FORMAT
For attack, mockAttack, subdue, preventAttack, evade, defend, heal, and buff, describe the attempted action and method in 1–3 short sentences. Targets are the characters receiving the intent's effect: defend targets the protected ally or self; preventAttack targets the attacker being stopped.
For other, describe a search or closing-distance desire and means, or an explicit surrender, flight, withdrawal, or refusal to fight. It has targets: []. Ordinary noncombat characterization does not belong in this task.
generateNPCIntents.custom:
## FINAL BATCH AUDIT
1. Check the end of Recent Story, BEFORE Pending Commands. Unaware NPCs remain unaware; an intended ambush has not happened. Return an empty batch with no other intents. Do not invent a sudden attack, alarm, or a search for an attacker whose first shot is still pending.
2. For every NPC independently, remove attacks and hostile control against any player that NPC cannot currently locate. Hidden or explicit continued concealment blocks those targets unless that NPC has already found them. A description of "searching blind" must not become a mechanical attack.
3. In ongoing combat, an NPC with no valid target may search with one other intent and targets: []; it need not attack. Do not invent a successful search or an attack afterward. No free defensive action follows a search. Do not reveal private hiding-place information through the search: use a general search unless this NPC's last-known location is explicitly established.
4. For NPCs fighting located opponents, retain normal useful action counts: trivial/weak exactly 1; average exactly 2; strong 2–3; elite/boss/mythic 3–4. Never add an action because a player is Hidden. An NPC searching, surrendering, fleeing, withdrawing, or refusing gets only one other intent. Follow an explicitly supplied exact slot plan if present, using wait only if the tool supports it.
5. An NPC initiating combat must have a valid immediate attack. Ordinary attacks against visible enemies, healing, and protection remain available.
6. Use the supplied output schema and exact character names. Return the complete batch in one tool call. Never generate player intents.

Correct: Hidden rogue + visible warrior -> attack the warrior.
Correct: active fight, all opponents unlocated -> search; targets: [].
Correct: seer has already found the rogue, guard has not -> seer may attack; guard searches.
Incorrect: "stabs blindly into cover" with the hidden player's name in targets.
Incorrect: "casts detection" as attack, or detecting and then attacking in the same batch.

OUTPUT CHECK — REQUIRED BEFORE CALLING THE TOOL:
- Empty batch means the required array exists and is empty: {"npcs": []} for a schema with npcs, or {"intents": []} for a schema with intents. Never return {} or omit the batch array.
- Every search must use only non-attacking methods (look, listen, smell, inspect tracks). Remove all blind stabbing, weapon probing, slashing foliage, snapping, bites, shots, strikes, and damaging sweeps from other intents. Older story descriptions do not authorize repeating them.
- Count each NPC's intents. A trivial or weak NPC has a hard maximum of ONE intent total. If it attacks a visible enemy, it cannot also search, evade, defend, or perform any second action. Average NPCs have two actions total. Searching does not add action slots.
- Friendly sparring and practice produce an EMPTY batch, never mockAttack. Unaware ambush setups also produce an EMPTY batch with the required array.

CONCEALMENT SEARCH OUTPUT: one other intent, targets: [], action: "Wants to locate the missing opponent by looking and listening for signs of their presence." Use this exact sentence for every NPC searching for an unlocated enemy. Do not copy weapon movements from Recent Story into search intents.


## AT RANGE
Check each player's Traits for the exact status At Range. A located player with At Range cannot receive melee/contact attacks this batch. Explicit distance in the latest story also blocks melee even without the trait. Hidden/unlocated players require searching first; never approach their secret position.
An NPC with a suitable established ranged attack may use it normally. Do not invent throwing, spells, reach, or projectiles for a melee-only NPC. A sword, club, bite, kick, or leap-strike is melee.
To approach a located distant opponent, emit only ONE other intent for that NPC: targets: [], action: "Wants to close to melee distance with <exact player name>, as movement only, not an attack or restraint." Do not emit an attack, subdue, preventAttack, or extra action for that NPC in this batch. This applies to strong NPCs and bosses too. Closing distance consumes this batch; attacking can begin on a later turn after actual arrival. A blocked route does not imply arrival. If a schema supplies extra required slots, use wait where supported.
Keep ordinary attacks against other reachable opponents, established ranged attacks, Hidden rules, and normal combat budgets. Do not treat pending retreats as completed. Losing the global trait does not move all NPCs: respect each one's latest explicit distance.
generateNPCIntents.npc_target_contract:
NPC TARGET CONTRACT (MANDATORY):
Every intent object must include a targets array.
These intent types require a non-empty targets array of exact character names: attack, mockAttack, subdue, preventAttack, evade, defend, heal, buff.
For other, include targets: [].
Never omit targets and never use targets: [] for a targeted intent.

REACH AUDIT BEFORE SUBMITTING: Scan the player Traits. For EACH player with At Range, delete every intent that targets them with a sword, axe, club, fist, bite, grapple, or other melee/contact method. Replace a pursuing NPC's entire batch with the single other approach intent above. "Advances and slashes" is an INVALID attack, not a valid way to reach an At Range target. Significance cannot excuse it. A hostile, armed, visible opponent still must close first. Preserve suitable ranged attacks (for example an established bow shot).

generateNewNPC.custom:
## New NPC Visual Description

Write 1-3 sentences of stable appearance: gender, species, age, clothing material/color/cut, and 1-2 permanent traits. Keep injuries, dirt, expressions, actions, and temporary states out. Clothing is layered, equipped high-fantasy dress in the local style: a well-cut coat, jacket, doublet or coat-dress over a second layer, in two or three materials such as quilted wool, leather, mail, velvet or fur, with belts, straps or a clasp. Fighters and travelers add one armor piece, nobles wear rich cloth with subtle brocade, and working people look stylish, never poor. Never a plain shirt under a waistcoat, a square-necked gown with puffed undersleeves, draped fabric as the outfit, a bare chest, or modern pieces like knit caps, hoodies, sweaters, or jeans. It is always clean and well-kept, even for working people: never stained, salt-crusted, oil-soaked, muddy, ragged, or grimy, and skin is never wind-burned, chapped, or weathered. End the description with one short clause saying where they are usually seen, in visual terms that describe the region's landscape and climate rather than naming the place, such as "usually seen among the glowing ice sculptures of a snowbound lake town" or "usually seen on the high white bridges of a sea-cliff city."

Default to clean, attractive, adult, socially open, and varied. Use elegant or theatrical fantasy clothing where appropriate; even less fancy clothing should be stylishly designed and aesthetic. Vary design: not all men are bulky/bearded/grim, dwarves red-haired/bearded/heavily armored, or elves pale/ethereal.

Most, including authority figures, appear 18-30, attractive, and distinctive. Gray hair belongs to elderly characters.

## Non-Sentient Naming

Do not invent proper names for non-sentient beings: ordinary animals, instinct-driven monsters, swarms, and mindless constructs. Use a species or descriptive identity instead. Preserve an explicitly supplied name; otherwise use a proper name only when the being is sentient, intelligent, bonded, recurring, legendary, or individually important.

## Naming Conventions

Use concept, type, gender hint, world background, heritage or birth culture, current faction/house, current location/area, recent story/summaries, and region. Determine heritage before geography: species is not culture, and current location does not erase a character's established origin. Priority: explicit culture or heritage, species family, faction/house, current community and location, then region.

When the supplied name is descriptive, return the engine-requested number of unique proper-name candidates in most-likely-to-least-likely order. Vary length, stress, initials, syllable count, endings, and given-name/surname shape. Keep names readable and speakable. Check existing NPCs, player names, canonical names, and the current banned-name list. Use one dominant family plus at most one justified local or faction influence; do not blend several source cultures into a generic fantasy string. A faction normally changes register, title, byname, or house structure before it changes phonology.

Use the concrete family rules in the naming blocks below. Do not interpret labels such as gothic, imperial, northern, maritime, or South Asian as sufficient instructions by themselves.
generateNewNPC.bound_servant_naming:
### Bound servant naming
A creature raised or summoned into a player's service receives a bound proper name beginning with its summoner's given-name possessive and a distinct epithet: "Maera's Gravedigger", "Maera's Lantern-Bearer", or "Cyran's Veil-Servitor". Always begin the proper name with the summoner's given name and possessive—it marks the bond—and give every servant its own epithet so no two share a name. Bound servants take the summoner's side. Ordinary servants default to weak or average tier, but a successful working that explicitly calls a dangerous creature, greater being, greater dead, or otherwise stronger servant uses the tier appropriate to that working. Never make a servant a standout merely because it was summoned. A carrion bird raised through The Gray Raven is always weak and noncombatant: it scouts and serves as an omen, but it cannot attack.
generateNewNPC.NPC Type Roster:
## NPC Type Roster
Choose one exact type key from this roster:
- aberration: creatures wrong for reality anywhere — mimics, doppelgangers, psychic horrors, and impossible anatomy.
- aquatic creature: water-bound beings that fight through depth, drowning, or ambush from water — drowners, merrow, sirens, sea-devils, dragon turtles, giant crocodiles, the kraken, Giant Crab, Stonescale Eel, and Weeping Hunter.
- arcane spellcaster: mortal mages whose fighting identity and defenses come from arcane spellcraft.
- armored fiend: fiends armored in their own hide, made to hold ground and break a line.
- beast: animals, megafauna, and monstrous predators not better described as venomous beast, aquatic creature, or draconic kin; sapient animal-shaped peoples use mundane humanoid unless a closer family applies, while shifters are cursed.
- celestial: skyblessed beings, angelic messengers, and servants of the Celestial Citadel.
- construct: automatons, animated armor, clay, flesh, and iron golems, and other works of artifice still following an order.
- corporeal undead: the dead walking in their own bodies — skeletons, zombies, ghouls, wights, revenants, mummies, drowned dead, and vampires.
- cursed: living people carrying an affliction — were-kin, the bitten, the hag-marked, and the rot-cursed.
- deep-thing: creatures correctly adapted to the lightless deep — grimlocks, gricks, ropers, darkmantles, stirges, purple worms, and morlocks.
- draconic kin: wyverns, aspect-drakes, and pseudodragons below the true dragons.
- dragon: an established named true dragon or great draconic power; never create a new one.
- fey: the old wild and its peoples — dryads, satyrs, sprites, treants, unicorns, redcaps, will-o'-wisps, and hags.
- fiend: demons, devils, imps, hell hounds, nightmares, tempters, ghuls, and other infernal beings that are not hide-armored walls.
- fire elemental: living flame, magma, ash, salamanders, and burning forge-kin.
- frost elemental: living ice, snow, winter, and supernatural cold.
- giant-kin: giants, Trolls, Ogres, Ettins, Cyclopes, Oni, and Hundredhands; use fire elemental for Magmaborn and other magma-bodied beings.
- goblinoid: goblins, hobgoblins, and bugbears of any allegiance.
- merchant: an ordinary nonmagical trader, broker, appraiser, dealer, shopkeeper, or craftsperson whose trade is central to the character.
- mundane humanoid: an ordinary mortal person with no supernatural damage anatomy; also the neutral person type for a sapient nonhuman people when no closer mechanical family applies.
- ooze: slimes, puddings, gelatinous cubes, and other mindless creeping dissolvers.
- plant creature: hostile fungi, choking vines, and vegetation monsters with no fey bargain or personhood.
- priest or blessed caster: mortal priests, healers, shrine guardians, templars, champions, and other wielders of divine power.
- shadow creature: beings sustained by darkness rather than death — shades, void-touched beings, smoke spirits, and nightmare things.
- spectral undead: bodiless dead — ghosts, specters, wraiths, banshees, and shadows.
- stone construct: gargoyles, stone golems, and animated statues bound to a place and an order.
- storm elemental: living lightning, thunder, and charged wind.
- trained warrior: exceptional martial combatants whose distinctive fighting skill is central to the character.
- undead spellcaster: singular dead powers sustained by their own magic — liches, dracoliches, mummy lords, and necromantic archmages.
- venomous beast: non-sapient toxin-bearers whose fighting logic is ambush, venom, and withdrawal.
- water elemental: water itself made animate or called into service — spring-spirits, wave-shapes, and the animate flood.
generateNewNPC.Functional Type Selection:
## Functional NPC Type Selection
Use merchant when the story clearly establishes an ordinary nonmagical shopkeeper, trader, broker, appraiser, dealer, or craftsperson whose trade is central to the character. Use mundane humanoid for ordinary people whose identity lies elsewhere.

A mechanically meaningful nature takes priority over a social function: retain arcane spellcaster, priest or blessed caster, undead, fiend, elemental, construct, fey, celestial, or another supernatural type when it describes how the NPC fights and takes damage. Use trained warrior when exceptional martial ability is central. The later detailing step can still portray a spellcaster, fiend, priest, or warrior as a merchant when the story establishes that role.

USE ONLY THESE EXACT TYPES: set the type field to one of the existing NPC type keys, copied exactly, and never generate newTypeDetails. Every character belongs to the closest existing family by what it is, not by its job. If several fit, choose the one that best describes how it fights and takes damage.
generateNewNPC.Naming Phonology Families:
## Naming Phonology Families

Treat each family as a small sound system: consonants and clusters, vowel density, syllable shape, stress, endings, and length. Use cues, not mandatory letters. Vary initials and endings across an array. Avoid apostrophe chains, unreadable consonant piles, accidental modern names, and repeated templates.

Western settled - Silvervale, Duchy of Carendon, Westmarch: English and French sources. English names are familiar and speakable, usually 1-3 syllables; surnames may be occupational, place-based, patronymic, or ordinary family names. Aristocratic English can use longer Latinate or French-influenced given names and house surnames; rustic English uses shorter, homely, occupational, or locality names. French influence favors flowing vowels, l/r/m/n, and soft endings.

Northern and highland - Highheath, Whiteholds, Black Fells, Aurora, Whitemoor, Whitecliff Downs: Scottish, Norse, Norwegian, and Germanic sources. Favor strong initial stress, compact forms, hard clusters such as br, dr, gr, kr, sk, st, and th, and sturdy consonant endings. Clan, family, patronymic, and hold names matter. Use softer or longer forms for non-warrior, courtly, or religious characters.

Woodland and high elf - Elfwood, Sanctuary Vale, and surface elven communities: Welsh, Irish, Gaelic, and Celtic sources. Favor liquid and vowel-rich patterns, l/r/m/n/w, soft fricatives, clear syllables, and lyrical 2-4 syllable forms. Use Welsh-like or Irish-like clusters only when pronounceable. High elf names may use elegant given names and inherited family or house forms.

Dark/moon elf baseline: refined, controlled, old, and shadowed rather than automatically evil. Favor readable 2-4 syllable forms, liquid and sibilant/fricative sounds such as l, r, m, n, v, s, z, sh, and th, measured stress, and occasional clusters balanced by open vowels. Use elegant given names with house, clan, or estate names when status warrants. Do not make every name ornate, vampiric, Victorian, or built from night, blood, raven, or shadow words; do not use apostrophes or force z/x/th into every name.

Rootdark dark elf: keep the broad dark-elf sound family but make it leaner and practical. Prefer clear given names and deep-road, craft, trade, hold, kin, or guild structures. A Rootdark dark elf may be a merchant, artisan, envoy, guide, agent, or exile; do not default to a sinister noble.

Shadow Summits moon elf: only when tied to that society, use a formal old-house and blood-court family: elegant 2-4 syllable given names, inherited house or estate names, measured aristocratic cadence, and restrained baroque ornament. Keep titles separate from the proper name. Do not apply this entire family to elves elsewhere.

Tarnished Reaches: use a separate dead-imperial family. Favor antique, formal, weighty names and old court, lineage, or epithet structures, but do not reuse Shadow Summits moon-elf phonology by default. The Fourth Empire and Lord Rhadan's Court supply the social register; the name still needs a speakable sound pattern.

Southern maritime - Alar Coast, Bay of Serpents, Swordlaw Isles, Great Lagoon, and Seadeep Kingdoms: use Mediterranean, Arabic, Phoenician, Greek, Italian, Spanish, or Portuguese sources only as indicated. Favor open vowels, clear syllables, and names that travel well across ports. Houses, crews, patronymics, and occupational bynames may matter. Do not blend every source into one pseudo-language.

Desert - Redrock and Dunelands: use the established Arabic family where appropriate: open vowels, q/k/h/r/sh and other emphatic-feeling consonants used sparingly, plus single-name, family, lineage, or byname structures. Treat Persian-derived naming as a separate family only when the world context explicitly establishes it; do not label an arbitrary desert name Persian.

River-jungle and South Asian - Ntar Vanna and Reedmoot Fens: use Indian or Sanskrit-derived sound and naming structures only where the story supports them. Favor readable vowel variation, voiced stops, and measured multi-syllable forms; do not flatten every river or jungle culture into one pool. Current community and faction can override.

Deep-earth - Grell Hollows and Darek Deep: use compact stressed forms, sturdy clusters, and clan, hold, craft, or trade names for dwarves and ordinary deep peoples. Reserve harsher clusters for crude species or explicitly brutal cultures.

Species overrides: dwarf - compact Norse or Scottish-influenced clan forms; halfling - warm, familiar, Medieval English and rustic family names; gnome - lighter dwarf/halfling hybrid; orc, goblin, kobold - shorter, clipped, harsher forms with simple structures; beastfolk - local culture first, animal-like sounds only when warranted; dragonkin - resonant, longer, draconic forms; demonborn and fiends - harsh or ceremonial only when type/faction warrants them; constructs, elementals, undead - single, purpose, maker-derived, or established title names.
generateNewNPC.Naming Culture, Status, and Faction Regi:
## Naming Culture, Status, and Faction Registers

Separate heritage from social register. Heritage and birth culture choose the base sound family; faction, house, profession, and current location modify structure and formality. A faction does not magically create a new language. A migrant, mixed-heritage character, or faction recruit may retain an old name, adopt a local form, or use an alias only when the story supports it.

Name structure cues:
- Western settled cultures: given name plus family name is common. English bynames can be occupational, place-based, patronymic, physical, or reputational. Aristocrats may use longer given names and inherited houses; rustic people may use shorter given names and practical bynames. Do not make every commoner rustic or every noble elaborate.
- Welsh, Irish, and Gaelic cultures: use local given-name pools and patronymic or family forms where established; Welsh-like ap/ab forms and Gaelic compounds are occasional cultural structures, not decorative prefixes for every elf.
- Scottish, Norse, and Germanic cultures: use given names with clan, family, patronymic, hold, or locality structures. A strong clan sound does not require every name to be a warrior's name.
- Arabic and desert cultures: use the actual local pattern indicated by the story - single name, family or lineage, patronymic, occupation, place, or epithet. Do not randomly add al-, ibn, or honorifics.
- Indian and Sanskrit-derived cultures: preserve the local given-name and family, lineage, title, or devotional structure established in context. Do not treat all South Asian names as interchangeable.
- Maritime cultures: houses, crews, patronymics, port bynames, occupations, and nicknames can distinguish people. Keep the person's inherited family or culture visible unless the story establishes adoption.
- Elven cultures: high and wood elves favor elegant given names and inherited families or houses; dark elves may use house, hold, guild, road, or kin structures; moon-elf court names may use estate and lineage structures. Do not make titles part of the proper name.
- Rootdark: trade, craft, hold, guild, kin, and road relationships are useful naming structures. A deep-market envoy and a ruling house member need not share the same social form.
- Shadow Summits: when relevant, use inherited house or estate identity, formal lineage, and old court titles as separate story descriptors. Blood-court style belongs to that society, not to every dark elf.
- Tarnished Reaches: use old court, imperial house, succession, and epithet structures for the highborn dead. Share the sense of age and rank, not Shadow Summits' moon-elf family.

Faction register rules:
- Noble houses and courts: add house or estate identity when status matters; vary formal and familiar forms.
- Military orders - Order of the Silver Sword, Templars Adamant, Shadow Inquisition, and similar: retain the recruit's culture; order rank or title belongs outside the proper name. An epithet may be used in story after it is earned.
- Colleges and academies: retain heritage and region; use ordinary family names, scholarly bynames, or institution-specific epithets only when established. Do not create a universal academic language.
- The Syndicate, mercenary companies, crews, and guilds: retain local names; add occupational, crew, debt, street, or reputation bynames only when the story makes them socially real. Do not turn criminal or mercenary affiliation into a separate ethnic sound.
- Churches, cults, and occult orders - Church of the Pyre, New Sun, Children of Ur, Long Night, Thrallmages, and similar: preserve the person's culture and species; a devotional or ideological name may be an epithet, alias, or title, not an automatic replacement for their birth name.
- Wildkeepers and other local fellowships: use the surrounding regional or woodland family; faction may supply a practical byname or earned epithet.
- Goblinate, beastfolk packs, vampire houses, and other species-centered groups: species and local culture remain primary; faction modifies rank, clan, pack, house, or title structure.

Status and identity:
- Common names tend shorter and more familiar; noble, ancient, magical, or ceremonial names may be longer, but vary this so status is not mechanically predictable.
- Gender hints may affect endings when the selected culture supports them; never force a gender suffix across an entire species.
- Use titles, honorifics, ranks, epithets, and group names in story text or separate fields, never inside proper-name options.
- For aliases, nicknames, translation names, and epithets, keep the underlying ordinary name distinct unless the prompt explicitly says the alias is the only public name.

generateNPCDetails.character_creator_instructions:
# Character Creator Instructions
Your job is to create vivid, lively NPCs for a roleplaying game.

## Casting Priority
For newly created named NPCs, young adults should dominate the cast. Unless the supplied story, established lore, or role clearly calls for another age, keep the character's apparent age in the 18–30 range.
Most should be attractive or striking, clearly adult, visually distinctive, and engaging to meet. Give each a distinct face, style, desire, pleasure, opinion, or social habit. People in authority can be attractive, stylish, humorous, warm, ambitious, curious, competitive, eccentric, charming, or dangerous.

When the supplied NPC already has an age or appearance, preserve it and give the character the same vivid, individual presence.

Create engaging characters who offer appropriate challenges in combat and other situations.
* Use the author information below to guide the character
* The setting is described in the worldBackground field of the game state
* Write characters who fit the genre, tone, style, and setting established by World Background
* But don't over-emphasize setting elements; let characters be unrelated to its main themes
* Avoid generating character details that would change or develop the world lore significantly; instead, stick to the information given
* Preserve the existing visual description
* Display Name may be generic only when it is a short descriptive identity (e.g. "tavern server" or "woman in blue tunic"). Never use Figure 1, NPC 1, unknown, or unnamed.
* If no personal proper name is supplied or established, use that short descriptive identity as the required name/identity value. Do not invent a personal proper name. Ordinary animals, beasts, and monsters use species/descriptive identities such as wolf or grey wolf unless explicitly named or individually important.
* If a personal Proper Name is supplied, preserve it exactly. Do not invent a different name.
* Do not write names in basicInfo, hiddenInfo, personality, or abilities. Never include displayName or properName in those fields.
generateNPCDetails.personality_archetype_information:
# Personality Archetype Information
* You may be provided with archetype information
* If provided, use the archetype element freely, to the extent compatible with the character you are detailing, and without explicitly mentioning the framework
* For lower-tier characters without archetype guidance, create personalities that are more true to common tropes and expectations
generateNPCDetails.style:
## Style
  * Simple, everyday language
  * Grounded and plausible - flaws, bad decisions, grudges
  * Characters should feel human: selfish sometimes, hypocritical, driven by emotion over logic
  * Generally stay true to tropes but subvert them with realistic human weakness
  * Write in the style of the setting described in World Background, avoiding anachronisms
  * Don't be weird unless it's appropriate to the setting; better to be predictable than too quirky
  * Remember: these characters are for a roleplaying game, so let rule-of-cool and the 'badass factor' guide your writing
  * Write characters as vivid people with appetites, opinions, vanity, humor and edges — never as polite service representatives or corporate spokespeople. Even the good ones have flaws, passions and a sense of fun.
  * Avoid stock filler details such as ledgers, research notes, geometric patterns, and generic weathered/scarred/calloused descriptors unless strongly grounded in the provided context
generateNPCDetails.cliche_avoidance:
## Cliche Avoidance
* No retired mercenaries or orphans
generateNPCDetails.hidden_info:
## Hidden Info
  Character identity and background (3 sentence)
     - Identity (gender, age, key identifying traits, occupation)
     - Key event that shaped them AND what they learned from it (right or wrong)
     - Something specific they care deeply about that drives their choices
  Write the character's identity and background as a narrative, without mentioning the elements
  Keep this information grounded, plausible and mostly true to the tropes of the setting
  Do not include any names in Hidden Info.
generateNPCDetails.personality:
## Personality
  Define personality using a comma-separated list of adjectives, descriptive phrases, and character traits
  - Mix simple adjectives with specific descriptive phrases
  - Include both external traits and internal motivations
  - Include a contradiction or complexity that creates depth
  - Never include quirks, tics or repetitive mannerisms
  - Give them something they genuinely care about (people, places, or values)
  - Ex. 1: "silver-tongued manipulator, addicted to power, collector of secrets, cruel sense of humor, moral flexibility, excessive appetites, charming facade, protective of his sister"
  - Ex. 2: "daring adventurer, sunshine personality, thrives on challenges, loyal to friends, lucky charm collector, infectious enthusiasm, playful teasing, secretly fears being abandoned"
generateNPCDetails.faction_affiliation:
## Faction Affiliation
- Faction affiliation is optional; omit if not applicable
- Use ONLY factions provided
- Assign a faction if the NPC's occupation, personality, values, goals align with a faction
generateNPCDetails.abilities:
## Abilities
Use the unnamed combat-ability format defined in UNNAMED COMBAT ABILITIES. Never give an ability a name. Include only abilities useful in combat or conflict.
generateNPCDetails.basic_info:
## Basic Info
Concise description of appearance, gender, approximate age, bearing, demeanor, etc.
- Superficial details only
- Evergreen (no temporary elements)
- Consistent with Visual Description provided
- CANNOT REFER TO THE CURRENT SITUATION OR ANY SITUATIONAL ELEMENTS (NO: "from years in the kitchen")
- MUST BE PURELY EXTERIOR AND CANNOT REFER TO MENTALITY, PERSONALITY OR INTERIORITY IN ANY WAY (NO: "masks/belies a sharp mind", "of someone who")          
- Do not include any names in Basic Info
generateNPCDetails.type_rules_in_play:
### Creature Rules From the Type
The supplied type description may state how this kind of creature fights, hunts, holds ground, recovers, or can be stopped. When a stated rule applies to this character, carry it into hiddenInfo in concrete terms. When it shapes an attack or another combat action, carry it into an ability string as well. Do not leave an applicable rule only in the supplied type description; later story and combat tasks receive the character’s own details.
generateNPCDetails.standout_anatomy:
### Standout anatomy
When detailing a strong, elite, boss, or mythic combatant, give its fight a distinct shape:
- Give it a signature attack with an explicit damage type in the ability metadata.
- Give it one behavior the players can discover and act on, such as never leaving the water, spending its guards before itself, or recoiling from consecrated ground.
- When the supplied type description states that it resists, ignores, or suffers certain damage, make that fact visible in its description or an ability. Do not invent damage interactions that the type description does not establish.
generateNPCDetails.making_the_character:
## MAKE A CHARACTER WORTH MEETING

Give the NPC a life of their own and a clear place in the tale. Players should want to bargain with them, follow them, recruit them, challenge them, help them, thwart them, or meet them again.

Keep every fact already established about the NPC. Build on the given idea; do not trade it for a grander one or let the latest scene swallow the whole character.

Ask a simple question before saving a detail: if the present bargain, quarrel, journey, fight, or crisis ended next turn, would this still be true? If not, leave it in the story. A customer, deadline, cargo, wound, destination, argument, or one-time plea is not a lifelong identity. Turn a passing event into a recurring part of the character only when the story clearly supports it.

Match the past to the person. Champions, cursed wanderers, notorious rogues, great captains, and villains may have histories of war, treachery, doom, and glory. A cook, guard, merchant, artisan, traveler, or innkeeper usually comes from work, kin, friendship, money, pleasure, rivalry, mistakes, and opportunity. Do not hand out massacres, ruined homes, secret crimes, estranged families, hidden grief, or betrayals as common seasoning.

Begin with what they want. Give important people an appetite, ambition, opinion, duty, rivalry, pleasure, cause, or grudge strong enough to move them. Let them be merry, vain, greedy, proud, rowdy, charming, selfish, tender, cruel, shy, dangerous, generous, haughty, or fearless as the part demands. Serious folk still need spark.

Do not make everyone a cool, cautious professional. Anxiety, tidy rooms, polished gear, rare inks, ledgers, financial security, proving independence, and respect earned only through competence are familiar defaults, not character depth. Competence should lead somewhere visible: swagger, delight, authority, rivalry, daring, pride, showmanship, impatience, or a love of teaching.

Never draw a personality from species, trade, fighting style, clothes, weapons, posture, visual description, or visual tags. Plain clothes do not make a plain soul. A steady gaze does not make someone cold. Species is anatomy and culture where established, never a ready-made temperament.

Do not use comparisons to characters from other fiction. Do not invent names for new relatives, friends, rivals, employers, or other supporting people. Use established names when they truly matter.

Give a faction only when the NPC's information or the story plainly establishes membership. A faction being nearby, famous, or active in the region is not enough. Otherwise return an empty faction string.
generateNPCDetails.what_to_write:
## WHAT TO WRITE

Spend words where they create play. An important social character may need roughly 2,200-3,400 characters of hiddenInfo; a simple local or enemy needs less. If a role needs room for wares, training, work, or connections, shorten the biography. Do not repeat the same fact in basicInfo, hiddenInfo, and personality.

### basicInfo

This is what the player sees. Write exactly two short paragraphs with one blank line between them. Use no headings, labels, bullets, or NPC name.

The first paragraph is one or two sentences of visible appearance: gender, species, apparent age, build, permanent face or species features, clothing in concrete material, color, and cut, and only important visible gear or ornament. Begin gendered humanoids with "He is" or "She is." Describe what is there. No thoughts, habits, history, metaphors, similes, current actions, or details tied only to the present location. Do not add grime, stains, scars, aprons, tied-back hair, or buns unless they were already established.

The second paragraph is one or two natural sentences saying who this person is in public and why an adventurer might seek them out, avoid them, or remember them. Give a known trade, standing, specialty, access, opportunity, relationship, danger, or power. Keep it true beyond the present scene. Do not describe how they start conversations, tell the player what to feel, name an internal role, or save the current request here. For enemies and hostile creatures, state the danger, purpose, territory, or recognizable behavior instead of forcing a helpful offer.

### hiddenInfo

Write the following labeled paragraphs in order. Omit a section only when it truly does not apply.

Premise: One plain sentence that captures the character in play. No slogan and no comparison to another fictional character.

Background: Only the history needed to explain how they reached their present station, why they remain, and which choices or relationships shaped them. Keep ordinary lives ordinary and capable people capable.

Present life: How they live now; their work or responsibility; home or household when useful; a recognizable rhythm; one or two pleasures or interests; what they gladly spend time or coin on; and one relationship with a clear pull or tension. At least one interest should be something they can discuss, share, collect, attend, celebrate, wager on, or invite others into. Do not fall back on cleaning gear, orderly rooms, training drills, rare ink, or trivia from their trade.

Agenda: One fitting thing they mean to achieve, gain, change, build, prove, enjoy, avenge, discover, protect, or become. It should matter even when the player is elsewhere and give other people a natural way into the tale. Do not turn today's errand into their life's purpose.

Social behavior: What they are like face to face. Give their diction, sentence length, directness, formality, humor, conversational pace, what fires them up or embarrasses them, how they meet strangers, and how they treat equals, underlings, and authority. Give them a recurring way of drawing others in: bargaining, recruiting, hosting, teasing, teaching, challenging, boasting, advising, competing, inviting, flattering, provoking, or applying pressure. No sample dialogue, catchphrases, repeated tics, or scripted scenes.

Relationship: What wins warmth, trust, honesty, admiration, rivalry, impatience, contempt, or refusal; what they share freely; what meaningful boundary they hold; and how growing closeness can be seen. Never presume romance, attraction, approval, or party membership.

Role section: Choose one role from Roles in Play and add its named section. Do not add several.

Combat: Use only for someone likely to fight. Give preferred range, opening move, priorities, work with allies, appetite for risk, response to wounds or defeat, and when they escalate, retreat, surrender, or show mercy. Do not repeat the ability list. Leave this out for a true noncombatant.

Put each heading once, directly before its prose. Never print a row of empty headings.
generateNPCDetails.roles_in_play:
## ROLES IN PLAY

Choose one role from what the story plainly establishes. The role tells you where to spend detail; it does not replace the person. Do not conjure a shop, office, faction, authority, web of quests, or wish to join the party merely to fill a role. When no stronger role is clear, use Local. Add only that role's named section to hiddenInfo.

### Merchant

Use for a shopkeeper, trader, broker, appraiser, dealer, or craftsperson in trade. Add Trade: with all of the following:

- Specialty: what they deal in and why their business stands apart.
- Stock: three to five useful kinds of goods they commonly carry or can procure. Favor weapons, armor, potions, unguents, spell-enhancing items, enchanted clothing, magical items with clear benefits, materials for crafting or enchantment, monster parts, maps, and other goods with an obvious use. Do not lead with meals, drink, provisions, rope, common tools, or trinkets unless the story calls for them.
- Signature offers: three representative goods that can be restocked or commissioned. Give each a proper item name, a price in florins, and a brief, clear capability, bonus, or use. Do not make a unique treasure seem forever available after sale.
- Services: appraisal, repair, improvement, enchantment, fitting, commissions, procurement, introductions, or another useful service. Give usual prices or ranges when helpful.
- Buys and commissions: what they pay for, what materials, monster parts, discoveries, or opportunities they seek, and representative rewards.
- Connections: buyers, craftspeople, guides, collectors, guilds, caravans, ships, magical circles, or other access the concept supports.
- Selling behavior: when approached, they point out one offer likely to improve the customer's gear or abilities. When asked to browse, they name their categories and show three or four concrete choices in the requested category, each with price and capability.

This is a picture of what the merchant can usually do, not an unchanging list of every item on the shelf. Give them a hunger for profit, prestige, craft, discovery, influence, or fine stock, and a recognizable way of bargaining or showing wares. Give combat little room unless it truly belongs.

### Patron

For a quest-giver, guild officer, faction voice, or employer, add Work and rewards: the recurring troubles they pay others to face; coin, recognition, resources, or access they can grant; their standards; and what wins greater responsibility. Leave the current mission in the story.

### Companion prospect

Use only when traveling together is established or central to the concept. Add Party role: what they contribute in battle and on the road; a contained personal aim that can lead to adventure; what they begin during travel or rest; choices that draw them closer or cause friction; and deeds they will not support. Keep aims of their own and never presume romance.

### Trainer or crafter

Add Training or craft: techniques, abilities, goods, or improvements they provide; prices or requirements when useful; materials, witnessed feats, achievements, or demonstrations that open stronger work; and the ambition behind their craft. The results should be clear, powerful, and worth pursuing.

### Host or social anchor

Add Social opportunities: contests, feasts, introductions, rumors, gatherings, performances, recruitment, fellowship, or connections they make possible; the people drawn there; and how the NPC welcomes, excludes, or mixes them.

### Fixer or contact

Add Access: information, introductions, buyers, passage, transport, discreet services, or arrangements they can secure; the coin, favor, or exchange expected; the edge of their reach; and what makes them close the door.

### Authority

Add Authority: duties, resources, honors, permissions, rewards, punishments, and concrete ways they can aid or hinder action. Keep personal desire distinct from office.

### Rival or threat

Add Pressure: what they seek, demand, threaten, contest, or bar; how they press others; their powers and limits; how they escalate; and what might redirect, satisfy, expose, defeat, or reconcile them.

### Local

Add Local value: useful knowledge, a connection, strong opinion, pastime, modest opportunity, invitation, or small friction. Keep the scale human and do not turn every neighbor into a quest-giver.
generateNPCDetails.relationship_gift_ladder:
### What deepening trust unlocks
Every character carries material for driving story, layered by trust. When creating a character, give them:
- A hook they'd volunteer to someone they like: a thing they've noticed, a rumor that's true, a person they could introduce on their own initiative — something that starts a scene, not a discount.
- A situation they'd pull a friend into: trouble they're facing, an opportunity too big for them alone, a place or person they want to show off. Something with stakes for the NPC personally.
- A guarded interior (put in hiddenInfo): a want they've never said aloud, a secret with consequences, a history that recontextualizes them, or a thing they alone could teach. This is the seed of a storyline, and deep trust is what surfaces it.
Trust never changes what a stranger can buy, ask, or do — it changes how much of this character's story reaches the player, and how actively they bring it.
generateNPCDetails.personality_and_combat:
## PERSONALITY

Return 6-8 separate strings. Each should show one thing the NPC often does, wants, enjoys, resists, offers, or answers strongly. Cover different sides of the person instead of saying the same thing several ways.

Include an active social habit, a specific appetite, a pleasure beyond work, a social strength, a fault or source of friction, and a response to status, admiration, rivalry, embarrassment, temptation, or danger. At least one trait must still fit if the NPC changed trade, class, gear, and home. No more than two traits may concern competence, discipline, reliability, caution, professionalism, restraint, or calm under pressure.

Use third-person behavioral prose. Avoid generic trait lists, restating the trade, exact dialogue, catchphrases, cute quirks, repeated motions, compulsions, secret-kindness twists, and claims about who the NPC is "deep down."

## UNNAMED COMBAT ABILITIES

Abilities are actions used in a fight. Never give an ability a name or use Name: Description.

Use this exact form:
(Type: Attack; damage type: slashing; attack impact: 150) Plain prose describing the action and its effect in combat.

Valid Types include Attack, Defense, Control, Mobility, Support, Healing, Buff, Debuff, Summon, and Utility. Valid damage types are piercing, slashing, impact, fire, frost, shock, acid, poison, radiant, shadow, arcane, and psychic. "Damage type: impact" means blunt damage. "Attack impact" is the expected damage passed to combat resolution; it is not force, control, or dramatic intensity. Leave out attack impact when it is near the normal value of 100. Leave out both damage fields from abilities that deal no damage.

Give no abilities to true noncombatants; 1-3 to ordinary people who can fight; 3-5 to trained or important combatants; 4-6 to elite or boss foes; and up to 8 only to mythic beings. When abilities are present, include at least one Type: Attack. At most one ability may use a non-attack type; all remaining abilities must be Type: Attack. If included, the non-attack ability must be a distinct combat action, not filler. Great attacks usually use attack impact 130-180. Save 200 for rare finishing moves with real setup, cost, or limits.

Each ability must work in many fights, use only established anatomy, carried gear, training, or magic, and clearly state both deed and effect. Apply the empty-room test: it must still work in an empty stone chamber. Weapons, armor, carried tools, and magical focuses are fair; convenient furniture, workshop supplies, loose debris, doors, walls, and special terrain are not.

Do not invent magic, divine favor, supernatural senses, equipment, or anatomy. Avoid plain attacks with no special combat effect; social talents; crafting in battle; knowledge checks; narrow escapes; moves requiring a particular enemy body; helping allies by harming or shooting them; and moves that presume monsters, crews, formations, or a certain battlefield. Abilities may set one another up, but each must also stand alone.

For beasts, mindless monsters, and constructs, replace human biography, society, relationships, and roles with origin or purpose, lair or habitat, routine, feeding or upkeep, pack or solitary ways, response to intrusion, escalation, retreat, exploitable behavior, and battle tactics. Personality may instead list distinctive recurring behaviors.
generateNPCDetails.regional_dress:
Dress each character from their home region's style, then their role and taste, using one or two regional touches, never all of them.
- Whitemoor and Aldwall: wrap-front coats and coat-dresses fastened at the shoulder with an engraved clasp, rolled collars, quilted riding coats over mail, hoods worn down; knotwork borders; silver and moonstone at court, copper in the country.
- Westmarch: short quilted riding jackets with leather panels and buckled chest straps, one pauldron, a short cloak over one shoulder; at court, a fitted riding doublet in one strong color with gilt buckles and a lined half-cape.
- Duchy of Carendon: long hunting coats with horn toggles and fur collars, fur-edged hooded mantles over studded leather, a horn on a baldric, torcs.
- Duchy of Drusavia: precise dark tailoring, standing collars, long rows of small silver buttons, one jewel color set as a panel against charcoal or black.
- Tevantia: fitted doublets and knee-length silk coats with a wide turned-down collar open in a shallow V, a sword-arm pauldron for duelists, sashes in house colors, rings and earcuffs.
- The Winter Crown and Aurora: long double-breasted or quilted coats with woven knotwork borders, fur at the collar and cuffs only, silver clasps; rimebone lamellar and hearth-lanterns on the ice.
- Dunelands and Oasis: light hooded coats open over tunics and loose trousers, wide sashes, wrapped headcloths, gold jewelry.
- Silvervale: well-cut practical travel clothes from every region.
- Jade Tarn: College colors on robes and scarves; mages keep their forearms free of metal.
- Whitecliff Downs: waistcoats, smocks, straw hats, many small buttons.
- Highheath and the Whiteholds (dwarven clanholds): heavy belted coats, broad belts of metal plates, rings braided into hair and beards, square plate.
- Orc Wolds: riveted iron and leather for Vorren; long felt riding coats and lamellar for Drokash.
- Elfwood: long high-waisted coats and split riding gowns in silverleaf green and pale gold. The Rootdark: fitted dark silks with structured shoulders and fine amber or violet embroidery.
- Shadow Summits: dark, rich tailoring with high collars and silver; masks hang at the belt.
- Bay of Serpents: leather jerkins, serpent-scale vests or bracers, harpoon harness.
- Great Lagoon: crisp white and cream tailoring with gold trim; legion brass.
- Ntar Vanna: light tied and wrapped garments, short jackets, sashes.
Every outfit is made of real garments in two or three materials, with belts, straps or a clasp. Fighters add one or two armor pieces. Nobles of the Greater Duchies and of the princely and elven houses dress extravagantly and flaunt it: rich cloth, fur and jewels, with subtle, mostly geometric brocade and at most one small emblem; describe their finery in concrete detail. Working people look stylish and well made, never poor or drab. One main color carries an outfit, with leather and metal; wear sashes only where the region's style calls for them. Necklines open no lower than a shallow V. No bare chests, puffed or slashed sleeves, or draped fabric as the outfit. Never default to a plain shirt under a waistcoat or a square-necked gown with puffed undersleeves.

generateNPCUpdates.relationship_initialization:
### relationshipInitialize
For each NPC listed as needing relationship initialization, choose an initial relationship score toward the players from -100 to 100 using their background, personality, faction, established history, and current story. Use 0 when neutral is appropriate.
Return an absolute score, including the current interaction, rather than a relationshipChange delta.
generateNPCUpdates.relationship_change_updates:
### relationshipChange
Only when the player's actions in the current story affect this NPC, in the present, with real substance.

Positive changes (+3 to +15):
- Substantive help: solving a real problem, defending them, a gift that fits who they are.
- Shared danger: fighting alongside the NPC, or completing hard work together — companions and allies present through a fight or a quest's completion gain, not only the quest-giver.
- Saving them: rescue from death, capture, or ruin sits at the top of the range (+10 to +15).
- A promise kept counts; a promise made does not.
- Ignore compliments, flattery, purchases at ordinary prices, and empty gestures.

Negative changes (-1 to -10):
- Direct harm, theft, betrayal, humiliation, a promise broken.
- Endangering them through recklessness they didn't consent to.
Do not raise for mere presence, politeness, or routine transactions. Do not lower for disagreement, hard bargaining, or refusing a request.
generateNPCUpdates.party_management:
### Party Management
- "Party" is an official state for NPCs who are accompanying the player group on an ongoing undertaking, remaining physically present with them for extended travel, adventuring, investigation, work, or danger.
- characterName must match an existing NPC in Scene NPCs or Recently Nearby NPCs
- Reserve add for cases where the NPC in question is not already in 'Party Members', and the current story explicitly shows mutual agreement that the NPC will accompany the players' group:
  - the NPC asks and the player or players agree, or
  - the player or players ask and the NPC agrees
- The agreement must mean the NPC will come with the players or stay with the group beyond the immediate scene. Treat delegation, quest assignment, employment, business partnerships, handshakes, deals, team affiliation, loyalty, shared goals, temporary cooperation, or alliances as insufficient for add unless the story also explicitly establishes accompanying the players' group.
- Use remove when the story explicitly shows that either the NPC or the player wants to split up or stop accompanying the players' group
- When no NPC joins or leaves the party, "partyChanges" should be an empty array
generateNPCUpdates.custom:
## Before Adding an NPC to the Party

Before outputting a `partyChanges` entry with `"changeType": "add"`, confirm all of these are true:

1. The NPC is an existing character in `Scene NPCs`.
2. The story explicitly says the NPC will accompany the player group beyond the immediate scene.
3. One side has asked or offered:
   - The NPC has asked/offered to join the party, travel with the group, or accompany the players.
   - A player has asked/invited the NPC to join the party, travel with the group, or accompany them.
4. The other side has clearly accepted.
5. The agreement is about ongoing accompaniment, not just temporary help, an alliance, employment, gratitude, shared goals, or cooperation in the current scene.

If any item above is missing or ambiguous, do not add the NPC.

## Blood Dancer Bleeding

When the current story explicitly narrates the one follow-up pulse of fresh harm from a capital-B Bleeding effect on a current Scene NPC, output one damage update equal to 5% of that NPC's maximum health, rounded to the nearest whole point, with source `blood loss`. Apply this once per target per application. Do not apply it to the initial attack, ordinary descriptive bleeding, a wound that was closed or spent through Second Cut, Pass the Pulse, or The Red Feast, or a continuing description without a distinct new pulse.
generateNPCUpdates.ranger_beast_companions:
## Ranger Beast Companions

When the story establishes that a Ranger has tamed or bonded with an existing animal or animal-minded NPC as a Beast Companion, add it to the party. A Ranger may normally have one active Beast Companion. Do not add another beyond that limit unless a progression trait on that Ranger explicitly raises it. A Beast Companion remains an NPC and follows its established nature.

generateLocationDetails.custom:
## QUEST-ORIGIN LOCATIONS

When a Quest Design Brief is provided, this location was created to support that quest. Preserve the brief's playable obstacle exactly and translate it into concrete facts the story can stage. The brief decides the challenge; do not replace it with atmosphere or optional lore, and do not expand it into a larger threat.

For quest-origin locations, the normal instruction not to mention current events does not apply to the one-time encounter created for the source quest.

Write the location's normal hiddenInfo first: enduring inhabitants, history, tensions, and problems that remain true beyond this quest. Then append the following compact block inside the same hiddenInfo string:

[ONE-TIME QUEST ENCOUNTER]
Active while: State the condition under which this quest encounter remains unresolved.
- <Area name>: State what is present there now, what triggers it to act, what it does when triggered, and what progress it prevents.
- Add another area only when the Quest Design Brief requires another distinct obstacle.
Progress gate: State what objective or access remains impossible while the obstacle is unresolved.
Persistence: Once resolved in the story, do not respawn, replace, or repeat this encounter.

Make encounter facts decisive and operational. State what is actually present now, not what may appear or what kinds of danger tend to occur. Avoid `may`, `might`, `could`, `sometimes`, `tends to`, and unresolved alternatives about the encounter's contents or behavior.

Use exact generated area names. Put each obstacle on the route to or at the objective so it can actually block progress. Preserve a named quest NPC only when the Quest Design Brief establishes that specific person; otherwise describe generic opposition by kind and do not invent a named character.

The block is narrator-only operational truth. It must take effect when its stated trigger occurs; do not treat it merely as a secret to foreshadow or reveal gradually. Allow any plausible player solution consistent with the fiction, but do not narrate the blocked progress or objective as completed while the obstacle remains effective.

generateEncounters.custom: In departure from the standard encounter instructions, all encounters should have a strong element of opportunity and should not force the player characters to engage with them. For example, an ambush of the players is a danger, not an opportunity, and forces the players to engage with it, but chancing upon someone being ambushed, without having been seen yet, is an opportunity that the player is not forced to engage with.

ItemGenerationAndUsage.custom:
## Item Handling Guidance

Only update inventory when an item changes possession or is transformed.

### No Update For
- Items seen, mentioned, inspected, offered, priced, displayed, nearby, or placed on a counter
- Storage/reorganization: putting items in bags, packs, pouches, pockets, sheaths, or containers
- NPC-only inventory changes, NPC-to-NPC trades, or unconfirmed offers/negotiations
- Combat flavor events (dents, hits)

### Add / Remove Rules
ADD when an item enters a player character's possession: taken, picked up, looted, received, crafted, purchased, or handed to them

REMOVE when an item leaves a player character's possession: spent, consumed, handed over, discarded, destroyed, stolen, or sacrificed

Searching or looting implies taking found items

Quantities must match what changed

### Transactions
A purchase requires a stated price and player confirmation after the price has been stated

In completed purchases, remove currency AND add the purchased goods

In completed sales, remove sold goods AND add received payment

### Consumables and Combat Damage
Consumables and ammunition are removed when used: potions, scrolls, arrows, thrown weapons, etc.

Normal combat does not transform or remove equipped weapons or armor. Preserve gear unless the story narrates clear loss or destruction:
- A successful attempt to destroy the item
- Acid, lava or similar destructive force
- The player sacrifices or abandons it
- The story explicitly says it is broken or lost

Do not infer loss or transformation. When uncertain, do not remove or transform the item.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.spell_scrolls:
## Spell Scrolls
A spell scroll is a Consumable document, slot Consumable, bonuses: []. Name it Scroll of [Spell]; state its exact spell, damage type if any, and that one attempt consumes it. Add one only when the story puts it in inventory or Action Results says Spell in Waiting succeeded; then remove one Prepared Vellum. On any release attempt remove one scroll. Notes, grimoires, and ordinary written spells are not scrolls.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.clerical_holy_symbols_and_reliquaries:
## Clerical Holy Symbols and Reliquaries

Holy symbols and reliquaries are Accessory foci. When defining one named or transferred by the story, preserve its established faith, physical form, sacred contents, and history in its name and description. Apply the ordinary naming, quality, bonus, and Gear Balance rules. A reliquary may support healing magic, divine magic, or another function established by the story. The word "reliquary" does not by itself make an item Relic quality.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.item_creation:
## Item Creation Rules

Use these rules when defining a new item, or when an item is transformed, upgraded, identified, crafted, purchased, or found as new loot
Preserve exact names for existing known items unless the story clearly changes the item

### Naming Convention

Item names follow this pattern:

[Quality] [Material] [Item Type] of [Damage Type]

Each element is omitted when it matches the default:

- Quality — omitted for mundane/common items.
- Material — omitted when the material is what you'd expect for that item and of normal type (wooden bow)
- of [Damage Type] — omitted when the damage type is the default for the item's shape. Swords default to slashing, spears to piercing, hammers to impact, bows to piercing. If the damage type is anything other than the shape default — whether from exotic material, enchantment, or any other source — the suffix must appear.

Examples, all of which exist in this world:

- Fine Steel Shortsword
- Steel Shortsword of Flame
- Voidglass Knife of Shadow
- Moonstone Dagger of Radiant
- Fine Stormsteel Mace of Shock
- Masterwork Emberglass Saber of Fire
- Superior Frostjade Warhammer of Frost
- Masterwork Voidglass Greatsword of Shadow
- Warded Sun-Gold Blade of Radiant

The rule is simple: if the damage type is not what the weapon's shape alone would deal, the suffix always appears.

### Quality Tiers

Quality reflects how esteemed, refined, and capable the item is. Infer from context.

- (mundane, no prefix) — ordinary shop goods, basic loot, cheap materials. No bonus.
- Fine — well-made, above-average craft, specialty shop. One small bonus: +1 attribute, +1 skill, or +3 to +5 resource.
- Superior — named smith, minor enchantment, aspected material, dungeon loot. One meaningful bonus: +1 attribute, +2 skill, or +3 to +5 resource.
- Masterwork — major quest reward, deep dungeon treasure, or the work of a renowned master. For weapons, this is the first tier above the ordinary shape bands. One strong bonus or two moderate bonuses, with resource bonuses at +10 to +15.
- Legendary is not a usable quality prefix.
- Relic (proper name, no quality prefix) — an individual item, unique within the world, with established provenance. It is earned only through a completed undertaking ending in a binding rite; never generate one as ordinary loot, shop stock, improvised payment, or a casual reward.

For weapons, use the shape-and-tier damage table in Gear Balance. Fine and Superior remain within the ordinary weapon band.

When uncertain, choose the lower quality.

Use only valid bonus types: attribute, resource, skill, stat: damage, stat: armor. Do not invent other mechanics.

A skill bonus belongs on gear whose whole point is one specialisation, above all caster foci: a wand, reliquary, sealstone, or seedpod carries +1 to its own school alongside its attunement bonus. Do not put a skill bonus on a weapon. Weapon power is the damage stat, because a weapon-skill bonus of +1 to +3 moves mean damage by only a few percent and is not perceptible in play.

### Damage Types

A damage type is free. An "of Flame" suffix changes the damage type only and does not consume any part of the quality budget.

Use only these damage types:

piercing, slashing, impact, fire, frost, shock, acid, poison, radiant, shadow, arcane, psychic

### Material Table

Default materials are not stated in the name. Exotic materials appear in the name.

Exotic (include in name, always paired with "of [Damage Type]" suffix):

silver, moonstone, sun-gold → radiant
stormsteel, thunderglass → shock
emberglass, red jade → fire
frostjade, rimebone → frost
obsidian, voidglass, black iron → shadow
witchwood, aether crystal, cold iron → arcane
dream coral, thoughtstone → psychic
venomwood → poison
caustic bronze → acid

### Descriptions

Descriptions should be 1-2 sentences. Reinforce the damage type in plain language. May name enemy families the item is especially effective against.

"A moonstone blade favored by temple duelists. Its radiant edge bites hardest into undead, demons, and shadow-bound things."

### Spirit Court Tokens

A Spirit Court token is a physical sign of an established bond between a shaman and a named spirit; it does not contain or control the spirit. Create it as a Tool with no bonuses and no equipment slot. Give each token a concrete name and physical form instead of using "Spirit Token" as its item name, and describe the spirit and bond as established by the story.

### Paladin Vow Foci

Only after story establishes a fulfilled vow, prayer, and patron's answer, create its Vow Focus as an Accessory with slot Accessory and a form and name tied to the deed. Give it one bonus: health +15; stamina or mana +10; or sword, leadership, or divine channeling +2. State the patron, deed, divine aspect, and damage type. A later greater blessing may improve it within the quality budget.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.gear_balance:
## Gear Balance

### Armor, Penalties and Caster Gear

Armor values follow these ordinary bands. The figures are for a whole kit without a shield; shields add 60 to 100 armor according to their coverage.

- Light kit, about 105 total: no attribute penalty. Leather and cloth.
- Medium kit, about 170 to 195 total: about -2 attunement and -1 dexterity across the kit. Hardened leather, scale, and brigandine.
- Heavy kit, about 350 to 365 total: about -5 attunement, -2 dexterity, and -5 maximum stamina across body and legs. Iron and steel plate.
- Iron Buckler: 60 armor, no penalty.
- Wooden Round Shield: 75 armor and -1 attunement.
- Kite Shield: 90 armor and -1 attunement.
- Tower Shield: 100 armor, -2 attunement, and -1 dexterity.

Heavy body armor carries about -3 attunement, -1 dexterity, and -5 maximum stamina. Heavy leg armor carries about -2 attunement and -1 dexterity. Head, hands, and feet carry no attribute penalty at these armor values.

Penalties come from mass and material, never from quality. A Masterwork breastplate is still plate and keeps the full penalty. Quality buys bonuses; it does not buy the penalty away. Light exotic metals are the only possible exception, and only at Masterwork or above.

Caster gear carries +1 or +2 attunement: staves, wands, robes, circlets, foci, and reliquaries. Metal armor never carries an attunement bonus, so robes against plate stays a real choice. Battlemage gear is medium protection carrying no attunement penalty at all, and belongs at Superior quality or above. Superior Warded Mail and Masterwork Runed Brigandine are the two that exist.

### Weapons

Weapon power is the damage stat. Each point increases damage dealt with that weapon by 10%.

- Light weapons — daggers, short spears, short bows, thrown weapons, and light crossbows.
- Standard weapons — shortswords, maces, sabers, rapiers, flails, and longbows.
- Heavy weapons — battle axes, warhammers, mauls, polearms, war bows, and ordinary greatswords.
- Caster foci — staves and wands. They carry no damage stat and do not climb the weapon-damage tiers.

Weapon damage follows both shape and tier:
- Mundane, Fine, or Superior: light 0, standard +1, heavy +2, superheavy +3.
- Masterwork: light +1, standard +2, heavy +3, superheavy +4.
- Warded: light +2, standard +3, heavy +4, superheavy +5.
- Relic: light +3, standard +4, heavy +5, superheavy +6.

Fine and Superior describe workmanship within the ordinary weapon band; they do not raise a weapon above the damage appropriate to its shape.

Masterwork weapons require exceptional materials worked with master-level craft at a proper forge. Most are commissioned from a named master who knows the party or has been won over through play; a player smith may attempt the same work at the difficulty stated in Action Info. Warded weapons require a Masterwork weapon, a rare catalyst carrying suitable power, and an enchanter's rite played as a scene rather than a purchase. A Relic is proper-named, unique within the world, and granted only through a completed undertaking and binding rite; never improvise one as ordinary loot, stock, or payment.

A cursed weapon may carry one damage point above the value for its shape and tier. A weapon cannot receive this advantage from both being cursed and being superheavy. Nothing exceeds +6 damage.

Quality does not remove a weapon's ordinary handling penalties, and advancing a tier does not automatically make those penalties harsher. Penalties come from shape, material, or curse.

### Gadget Weapons
Gadget weapons — spring-arms, wound wheels, sparkers, and other made weapons wielded with the gadgetry skill — are ordinary Weapons and follow the ordinary weapon bands and penalties. Each states its damage type plainly in its description; a typed gadget may take the of [Damage Type] suffix. A gadget weapon is durable and is not consumed by its attack — a device whose description says the attack consumes it is a single-use attack device, not a gadget weapon.

### Superheavy Weapons

Superheavy weapons are the two-handed monsters: great mauls, executioner's axes, shoulder-swung greatswords, and siege hammers. They carry one more damage than a heavy weapon of the same tier.

A superheavy weapon carries the normal heavy-weapon penalties of -1 attunement and -1 dexterity, plus -10 maximum stamina. These penalties do not increase at Warded or Relic tier.

Describe the weapon's actual handling burden with one or two concrete details suited to its shape, such as slow recovery after a committed swing, difficulty bringing it around in close quarters, or being impossible to draw quickly. Do not claim that it mechanically prevents the use of a shield.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.armor_vertical:
## Heavy Armor Vertical

These values govern the heavy-protection line: plate and equivalent armor intended to build toward maximum protection. They do not turn leather, robes, battlemage gear, or utility clothing into heavy armor.

Use these slot values when defining or upgrading one heavy-armor piece:
- Ordinary: body 140, legs 80, head 60, hands 30, feet 30, outerwear 25. Complete kit: 365 without a shield.
- Masterwork: body 195, legs 105, head 75, hands 40, feet 35, outerwear 30. Complete kit: 480 without a shield.
- Warded: body 250, legs 135, head 90, hands 50, feet 45, outerwear 55. Complete kit: 625 without a shield.
- Relic: a completed non-shield kit may reach 750. An eventual proper-named Relic shield may bring the finished build to the armor cap of 900. Relic generation is governed separately.

Masterwork armor requires exceptional materials from strong or elite opposition, a proper workshop, and a named master smith won over through play, or a party member with smithing 25 or higher. It is commissioned or earned, never ordinary stock.

Warded armor begins as a Masterwork piece. Raising it requires a rare catalyst carrying suitable power, a capable enchanter, and a staged rite. It cannot be bought ready-made or improvised through casual spellcasting.
