Tier does not automatically increase an armor piece's penalties. Penalties come from its mass, coverage, and material. Body and legs carry the heavy kit's attribute and resource penalties. Head, hands, and feet carry no attribute penalties at these values.

Battlemage gear remains a separate medium-protection line with no attunement penalty. Superior Warded Mail and Masterwork Runed Brigandine remain valid examples and do not receive heavy-armor tier values.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.cursed_gear:
## Cursed Gear

A cursed weapon may carry one damage point above the value for its shape and tier only when it also carries at least -25 health and all ordinary weapon penalties. It cannot also receive the superheavy increase, and nothing exceeds +6 damage.

Give a cursed item a three-to-four-sentence description:
1. Establish its physical form and a concrete origin connected to the world.
2. Describe how its equipped boon and penalty appear on the bearer.
3. Give it one named power with an immediate, exceptional, stageable effect.
4. State the repeatable physical manifestation of that power and the concrete appetite, loyalty, cycle, or bodily price revealed through it.

The named power should resolve in the current action or turn.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.blueprints_and_components:
## Blueprints and Components

Blueprints use category Tool, no equipped slot, and bonuses: []. A blueprint names one exact output and states the minimum skill, toolkit, ordinary components, and any special material required. It is retained after construction.

Only when Action Results says construction succeeds and the player carries the blueprint and stated materials, remove one of each stated consumable material and add one output item. Retain the blueprint and toolkit. A failed attempt retains its materials unless Action Results explicitly says something was destroyed. Never infer missing supplies.

Blueprints may be found, bought, reverse-engineered, or drafted. Drafting an original blueprint is an attempt with the relevant craft skill and must describe a plausible design within the character's established knowledge. A blueprint records a design; it does not supply materials or make an impossible device possible.

Mechanical Components are category Consumable, slot Consumable, and bonuses: []. They supply the ordinary physical workings of traps and modest mechanisms but never replace a special payload, rare material, or aspected material.

On a successful use of Everything Has Parts against an established broken mundane item or substantial heap of discarded manufactured scrap, add exactly one Mechanical Components. If the source was a named carried item, remove one of that item; otherwise the story must establish the scene source being expended. Without a valid source, add nothing.

Typed traps and single-use attack devices use category Consumable, slot Consumable, and bonuses: []. A typed example takes the of [Damage Type] suffix and describes the concrete mechanism or material that produces that damage. A trap states what triggers it and that it strikes once before being spent; an attack device states that the attack consumes it. The authored examples are retrieval anchors, not a closed list.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.device_ability_inventory:
## Device Ability Inventory
When Teeth Underfoot is actually performed, remove exactly one named carried trap whether its attack hits or misses.

When Between Two Footfalls actually constructs and springs a trap, remove the complete materials named by its carried blueprint, retain the blueprint and toolkit, and do not add the finished trap to inventory because it is spent in the same action. If construction never occurs, retain the materials.

When The Third Measure is actually performed, remove exactly one named input consumable, never one per target. If the ability is impossible or the input is never used, retain it.

One More Working uses remnants already spent earlier in the scene and causes no inventory update. The Room Was Ready likewise causes no new inventory removal when its trap was already spent from inventory during preparation.
ItemGenerationAndUsage.item_supply_balance:
## Item Supply Balance

### Potions

Restorative potions use these families and values. State the value in the item description as well as the name.

- Stamina Draught: +15 stamina. Greater Stamina Draught: +30 stamina.
- Mana Philter: +15 mana. Greater Mana Philter: +30 mana.
- Healing Potion: +30 to +40 health.

For a restorative with no family name, estimate a lower value.

### Loot Can Answer Damage Walls

When the story establishes loot, a commission, or merchant stock meant to answer a resistance or immunity the party has encountered, define it as a concrete key to that wall—especially a weapon with an explicit of [Damage Type] suffix. Strong, elite, and boss trophies may be defined as materials suitable for crafting or trade toward such gear. Do not invent a drop merely because a wall was encountered; define only items the story actually awards, offers, or establishes.

### Typed Ammunition, Weapon Oils, and Unguents

Typed ammunition uses category Consumable, slot Consumable, and bonuses: []. It may use an exotic material and takes an of [Damage Type] suffix, using of Radiance for radiant ammunition. The suffix is the entire mechanic.

Weapon oils, venoms, etchants, extracts, and unguents use category Consumable, slot Consumable, and bonuses: []. They can be used to coat a plain weapon and give it an exotic damage type for one attack. Never give one an of [Damage Type] suffix; name it for its substance and state its damage type plainly in the description. When one is used to coat a weapon, one unit is consumed whether the attack hits or misses, and its effect applies only to that attack.

### Protective Ward Charms

Protective ward charms use category Consumable, slot Consumable, and bonuses: []. Use only the four existing types: Ember Charm for fire, Rime Charm for frost, Dawn Charm for shadow, and Bitterleaf Charm for poison.

Each charm raises one personal ward and is consumed when used. These charms are rite-made and scarce, never routine low-cost stock. When offered for sale, they cost 120 to 200 florins. Do not create charms for other damage types without a matching ward trait and trigger system.

summarization.custom:
Write a concise, factual summary of the supplied story. Summarize important events, consequences, relationships, established motives, feelings, knowledge, and unresolved matters. Record these only when the story establishes them; never invent or infer them.

Record concrete social outcomes: agreed prices and terms, debts, promises and oaths, names and aliases, secrets and lies, gifts, rescues, thefts, insults, and changes in allegiance or standing. For a secret or lie, record who said what to whom; call it false only when the story establishes that. Preserve exact wording only for oaths, passwords, riddles, and terms likely to be checked later. Paraphrase everything else.

Record questions, goals, vows, doubts, warnings, and expectations only when a named character expresses them through dialogue or action. For anything not witnessed by everyone, name the audience: “alone with the smith,” “overheard by one guard,” or “unseen.” If the audience is unclear, do not guess.

When condensing summaries:

- Preserve deals, debts, oaths, names and aliases, unanswered questions, vows and goals, and events that change standing.
- If a later input explicitly resolves an earlier question, vow, debt, or threat, replace the earlier item with the resolved outcome.
- Keep the latest state once. Cut travel, description, repetition, and fights with no lasting consequence.
summarization.wizard_spell_research:
## Wizard Spell Research

When a Wizard explicitly records or chooses to pursue a magical principle they successfully identified, preserve the source, the specific usable principle, and what the character understood. Preserve a declared unfinished spell experiment until it succeeds, fails decisively, or is abandoned. When The Unwritten Spell successfully produces a learned spell, replace the open experiment with the completed spell's name and effect. Do not record research merely because the character saw unfamiliar magic.
summarization.sorcerous_awakenings:
## Sorcerous Origins and Awakened Powers

For each Sorcerer, preserve the origin of their inborn magic when established. If it remains unknown, do not invent an answer. Preserve a recurring visible tell only when background or story establishes it as recurring. When No One Taught You This fully succeeds, retain the learned power's name and effect. Do not record ordinary spellcasting or one-time visual details.
summarization.warlock_pact_clauses:
## Warlock Pacts and Clauses

For each Warlock, preserve the patron or answering form, established sign and means of contact, the standing pact's original exchange, accepted clauses and their exact prices, limits, or services, unaccepted offers clearly marked as offers, outstanding obligations, completed or broken terms and their established consequences, concrete leverage, and powers actually granted. Never turn a suggestion, threat, implication, or unanswered demand into an accepted obligation. When a clause is resolved, replace the open term with its outcome but preserve any lasting power or consequence. Do not record every ordinary use of pact power.
summarization.craft_principles:
## Craft Principles

When a character explicitly records or chooses to pursue a craft principle they found, preserve its source, the concrete principle, and what they mean to make with it. Preserve a declared unfinished trial until it succeeds, fails decisively, or is abandoned. When Trial Piece produces a learned technique, replace the open trial with the technique's name and what it makes. Do not record a principle merely because the character handled an unfamiliar material.

generateLearnedAbilities.custom:
# Do not generate an ability when:

- The character used an existing skill or ability
- The character fought well in combat
- The character did something they already have the skills to do
- The character combined two things they can already do
- The character observed, studied, read, or watched someone else do something
- The proposed ability is a narrower or situational version of something in worldAbilityNames or existingAbilityNames - check the lists
- The character had a conversation, made a plan, gave a speech, told a story, remembered something, or had an emotional moment
- The character picked up, bought, found, or was given an item. Items are not abilities. Do not name abilities after items
- The character simply used magic.  These are skill uses, not new abilities, unless the story describes a fundamentally new magical technique being invented or bestowed.
- The event was routine, expected, or something the character has done before. Abilities come from singular breakthroughs, not repeated competence.

# Only propose an ability when:
- the story contains a clear, specific, unrepeatable moment: 
  - direct supernatural transformation
  - a teacher completing instruction in a named technique
  - absorption of power from an artifact or entity
  - or a genuine first-time improvisation that produced a result the character's existing skills cannot explain.

# How to Name Abilities
- Give abilities lore- and setting appropriate fantasy names. Do NOT use technical, engineering, science, or modern terminology unless the story expressly supports it.

Remember:
When in doubt, return an empty list. Most turns should return an empty list. Never duplicate existing stills or abilities.
generateLearnedAbilities.psionic_techniques:
## Psionic Techniques

When a character with the Psionicist trait explicitly uses the available Open the Mind ability and the current story shows the first fully successful performance of a new psionic technique drawn from something witnessed, studied, or practiced, propose exactly one learned ability preserving that technique. This is the narrow exception to the general prohibitions on generating an ability from deliberate study or the use of an existing skill or ability.

Preserve only the technique the story shows succeeding. Give it a setting-appropriate fantasy name and describe what the character can do. Do not broaden its targets, scale, duration, or uses beyond the successful attempt; match its power to the character's current level and psionics skill. Direct mental attacks deal psychic damage; physical attacks use the damage type of the object or force. Open the Mind does not grant permission to perform feats that require a separate explicit license.

Do not generate a technique for observation or study alone, a failed or mixed attempt, ordinary psionics use, or repeating a known technique. Reject duplicates of authored or already learned abilities, narrower variants, pure increases in force, combinations with no genuinely new result, and techniques whose purpose is to create or modify abilities.
generateLearnedAbilities.wizard_spell_design:
## Wizard Spell Design

When a character with the Wizard trait explicitly uses the available The Unwritten Spell ability and the current story shows the first fully successful casting of a spell they deliberately constructed from a specific magical principle established through prior study, propose exactly one learned ability that preserves that spell. This is the narrow exception to the general prohibitions on generating an ability from deliberate study or the use of an existing ability.

Preserve only the concrete spell the story shows succeeding. Give it a setting-appropriate fantasy name and describe its visible immediate effect. If it attacks, state one allowed damage type supported by the completed spell. Do not broaden its targets, scale, duration, or uses beyond the successful casting; match its power to the character's current level and magical skill.

Do not generate a spell for witnessing magic, identifying a principle, finding or reading a formula, planning an experiment, a failed or mixed casting, or an ordinary use of a magic skill. Reject duplicates, narrower variants, pure increases in force, combinations with no genuinely new result, and spells whose purpose is to create or modify abilities. Never copy power that depends on another class's patron, spirit, divinity, bloodline, bodily discipline, item, or relationship; preserve only a formal magical principle the Wizard actually turned into a successful spell.
generateLearnedAbilities.sorcerous_awakening:
## Sorcerous Awakening

When a character with the Sorcerer trait explicitly uses the available No One Taught You This ability and the current story shows the first fully successful use of a magical power they have never used before, propose exactly one learned ability that preserves that power. This is the narrow exception to the general prohibitions on generating an ability from the use of an existing skill or ability.

Preserve only the concrete power the story shows succeeding. Give it a setting-appropriate fantasy name and describe its visible immediate effect. It may resemble other magic, but it must arise from the character's own inborn power rather than being learned by imitation. If it attacks, state one allowed damage type supported by the successful use. Do not broaden its targets, scale, duration, or uses beyond what succeeded; match its power to the character's current level and the existing magic skill that governs the effect.

Do not generate an awakened power for ordinary spellcasting, a failed or mixed attempt, or merely witnessing or studying outside magic. Reject duplicates, narrower variants, pure increases in force, attempts to reproduce another class's patron, spirit, divinity, bodily discipline, or item-bound power, and powers whose purpose is to create or modify abilities.
generateLearnedAbilities.warlock_pact_clauses:
## Warlock Pact Clauses

When a character with the Warlock trait explicitly accepts a new pact clause and the current story shows the patron visibly acknowledging the agreement and actually granting a distinct power, propose exactly one learned ability that preserves the grant. The power may be granted at once against an accepted obligation or after an agreed service is complete, but acceptance or completed service without the patron's actual grant is not enough.

Preserve only the immediate power the story shows being granted, in the patron's established nature and style. Give it a setting-appropriate fantasy name and describe its visible effect. If it attacks, state one allowed damage type supported by the patron and the grant. Do not broaden its targets, scale, duration, or uses beyond the agreed clause; match its power to the character's current level and relevant existing magic skill. Ordinary use of the learned power carries no fresh price unless the agreed clause explicitly established one.

Do not generate an ability for an offer, negotiation, omen, threat, unanswered demand, price paid without a grant, service completed without a grant, ordinary use of existing pact power, possession of a token, or power merely witnessed in a patron, servant, or enemy. Reject duplicates, narrower variants, pure increases in force, and grants whose purpose is to create or modify abilities.
generateLearnedAbilities.monastic_forms:
## Monastic Forms

When a character with the Monk trait completes a teacher's instruction in a distinct Form, or achieves a first-time feat of bodily command during a consequential ordeal, propose exactly one learned ability that preserves the perfected feat. Prefix its name with "Form: ". The Monk trait is a broad license to attempt the impossible; do not treat a specific perfected Form as a duplicate of that license.

A Form is one immediate technique performed through the monk's own body. Give it a concrete fantasy name and describe what visibly obeys: weight leaves or gathers, flesh or bone hardens or loosens, sight yields to hearing or touch, breath or blood stills, or movements fall into exact measure. It may reach through a held object or another body only when the completed instruction or breakthrough explicitly established that reach. An attack deals impact damage unless the story established another allowed damage type.

Match the Form's reach to the character's current Will rank. With no Will rank or at Novice, it commands one part or property of the monk's own body for one immediate feat. An Adept may join two bodily commands in one sequence or carry one through a held object. An Expert may sustain a deeper command through extreme harm or opposition. A Master may combine several commands or reach another living body by touch. A specific authored ability may establish a narrower exception.

Do not generate a Form for ordinary success, repetition, observation alone, practice without stakes, merely finding, buying, or reading a teaching, or merely combining actions already known.
generateLearnedAbilities.ranger_named_shots:
## Ranger Named Shots

When a Ranger first fully succeeds at a deliberately attempted archery feat under genuine danger that changes a shot's path or timing beyond ordinary archery, propose exactly one learned ability preserving that exact Shot. Completed instruction in a named Shot may do the same. This is a narrow exception to the general prohibition on generating abilities from use of an existing skill.

Do not generate one for ordinary accuracy, range, damage, multiple targets, called shots, critical hits, or use of an existing ability. Later breakthroughs may become more ambitious as the Ranger's level rises, but each Shot remains one immediate technique.
generateLearnedAbilities.berserker_fury_deeds:
## Berserker Fury Deeds

When a character with the Berserker trait currently has Fury, Deep Fury, or Unbroken Fury and first fully succeeds under genuine danger at a deliberately attempted immediate feat of strength, endurance, or momentum beyond ordinary mortal ability, propose exactly one learned ability preserving that Fury Deed. Completed instruction in a named Fury Deed may establish the attempt, but propose the ability only after the character performs it successfully while Fury is active. This is a narrow exception to the general prohibitions on generating abilities from physical skill use or fighting well.

Preserve the concrete feat the story shows succeeding. Give it a setting-appropriate fantasy name and describe one visible, immediate act of physical discipline. It may break, lift, throw, carry, withstand, or drive through one concrete opponent, obstacle, or force. It is never magic, a passive benefit, or a sustained state. If it attacks, use the held weapon's damage type, or impact when no weapon determines one. Do not broaden the feat beyond the successful deed; match its scale to the character's current level and the Fury tier that carried it.

Do not generate a Fury Deed for an ordinary attack, high damage, taking damage, merely surviving a fight, entering or ending Fury, passive endurance, a feat already inside an existing skill's ordinary ladder, or success produced by an existing ability. In particular, use of Break the Line, Hurl the Unliftable, Worldbreaker, or another existing ability never generates a new Deed. Reject duplicates, narrower variants, and pure increases in force.
generateLearnedAbilities.druid_remembered_shapes:
## Druid Remembered Shapes

When a character with the Druid trait explicitly uses the available No Shape Forgotten ability and the current story shows their first fully successful transformation into a specific living creature they previously pursued, tended, faced in danger, or closely observed, propose exactly one learned ability preserving that named shape. This is the narrow exception to the general prohibitions on generating abilities from observation, shape shifting, transformation, or the use of an existing ability.

Prefix the ability name with "Shape: ". Preserve only the whole body the story shows the Druid successfully taking. Describe its visible form and only the size, movement, senses, natural weapons, and bodily capabilities established by that transformation. The learned ability is a reliable return to that shape, not permission to separate its features into unrelated powers. If the shape attacks, state one allowed damage type supported by its body. Match its scale and capabilities to the character's current level, shape shifting skill, and the successful transformation.

The shape never grants the creature's memories, knowledge, learned skills, equipment, social identity, authority, spellcasting, or a power the transformed body did not visibly demonstrate. Preserve a supernatural bodily feature only when the successful transformation itself displayed it; never infer the creature's entire NPC or type description. The ordinary limitations in the shape shifting skill still apply while wearing the form.

Do not generate a shape for observation or study alone, finding a corpse or body part, a failed or mixed transformation, ordinary shape shifting without No Shape Forgotten, taking a familiar or already learned shape, or using Greatshape, Wear the Wild, or another existing ability. Reject duplicates and narrower variants. Propose only one learned shape even when the scene contains several creatures or transformations.
generateLearnedAbilities.crafting_techniques:
## Crafting Techniques

When a character explicitly uses the available Trial Piece ability and the current story shows the first fully successful making of a new thing, or of a known thing by a new method, built on a specific craft principle the character found earlier, propose exactly one learned ability that preserves that technique. A principle is one concrete fact about making: how a material behaves, how a finished piece was put together, a master's method seen at work, or a use for part of a creature's body. A master's completed instruction in a named craft secret may be preserved the same way. This is the narrow exception to the general prohibitions on generating an ability from deliberate study, from using an existing skill or ability, or from combining things the character can already do.

Prefix the name with "Secret: " and name it for the method or the material in plain craft words. Describe the one kind of thing it makes, the materials it uses, and the tools or workshop it needs. It either improves one exact kind of making or permits one making that no known method allows; it is never a general craft skill. Keep every requirement the successful making had: weapons and armor still need a proper workshop, traps and devices still need their materials, and nothing is made without its materials. Match its reach to the craft skill used and the character's current level.

Do not generate a technique for ordinary crafting, a recipe or method found, bought, or read, a plan, a failed or mixed attempt, or a repeat of a known technique. Reject duplicates of authored or learned abilities and narrower variants. Reject techniques whose only gain is higher quality, a larger bonus, more output, less time, or less material. A technique never raises a quality tier or loosens what a tier requires: Masterwork still needs exceptional material and master-level work, Warded still needs a rite and a rare catalyst, and no technique makes a Relic. Reject ward charms and any charm that turns harm aside, scrolls, armor that sheds its weight penalty, and anything whose purpose is to create or modify abilities.
generateLearnedAbilities.class_discoveries:
## Class Discoveries

When a character explicitly uses one of these available abilities and the current story shows its first fully successful use, propose exactly one learned ability that preserves what succeeded, with its name prefixed as shown: Make It Mine (Fighter), "Technique: " for a fighting move seen from a master or a foe; Worked It Out (Rogue), "Trick: " for a trick, con, or bit of lockwork of the character's own devising; Answer the Oath (Paladin), "Invocation: " for the power the patron answered a fulfilled vow with; A New Movement (Blood Dancer), "Dance: " for the new movement of the blood-dance; Make a Song of It (Bard), "Song: " for the performance and its concrete effect; Ask in Need (Cleric), "Rite: " for the rite the god answered with; Let a Spirit In (Shaman), "Spirit: " for the spirit's power as it moved through the character. This is the narrow exception to the general prohibitions on generating an ability from deliberate study, from using an existing skill or ability, or from combining things the character can already do.

Describe what the character does in one or two concrete sentences, then state its effect plainly as one to three of: an attack at a stated impact against one foe or up to three, defending the character or one ally, stopping one foe's attack, subduing one foe, healing one target for a stated percent of maximum health (at most 60%), or +N on one kind of attempt. Match its power to the character's current level and the skill used: about impact 150 early on, 200 by the middle levels, and 250 to 300 from level 20.

Do not generate one for a failed or mixed attempt, a plan, a repeat, or something only watched. Reject duplicates and narrower variants of existing abilities, pure increases in power, and anything that affects the whole party, lasts beyond the action, depends on turn order, timing, the kind of target, or whether the target is aware, dodges attacks, or creates or modifies abilities.

generateNPCIntent.custom:
# LARION — PLAYING A SINGLE CHARACTER

Adapted from the narrator's out-of-combat NPC direction. That guidance told the narrator how to
puppet people; this task hands the job to the person themselves.

## WHAT YOU WANT RIGHT NOW

Before anything else, know what this character is after in this moment: to finish work, protect
their standing, learn something, make a sale, avoid embarrassment, enjoy themselves, preserve a
secret, pursue an attraction, escape an obligation, or be left alone.

Responding to the party is part of your situation, not the whole of your existence. Let what you
want shape what you say and do — including wanting them gone.

## DO SOMETHING WHILE YOU TALK

You are in the middle of a life. Work, eat, drink, pack, mend, count, shop, handle stock, attend
to someone, keep an eye on a door. Talking is rarely the only thing happening.

Vary it. Do not repeat the same piece of business every turn.

If this character has already delayed a promised arrival, finish it now instead of asking the player to wait again.

## STRANGERS ARE NOT THREATS BY DEFAULT

Do not open suspicious or hostile toward people who have done nothing. Warmth, curiosity, shyness,
enthusiasm, attraction, awkwardness, vanity, greed, boredom, cruelty and humour are all valid
first reactions. Choose the one this character would actually have.

Held hostility is different: if you already have a reason to distrust these people, keep it.

## ANSWER THE MOVE THEY ACTUALLY MADE

Meet humour, flirtation, kindness, rudeness, threats and disrespect the way this character would
meet them. A persuasive argument can move you without erasing your values or your self-interest —
you can be convinced and still want what you wanted.

## SHOW YOUR TRADE, DO NOT RECITE IT

If you keep a shop, run a guild desk, guard a gate or hold an office, show it through what you do:
handle the stock, name a useful item, quote a price in florins, mention the commission you owe,
turn someone away, send them to the right person.

Do not announce your role, list your inventory, or read out a catalogue. You are not a menu, and
you are not obliged to hand out work — most people with a job are not quest-givers.

## DO NOT MANUFACTURE PRESSURE

Do not act in order to force the player's hand, inject urgency, or start a plot. If the honest
answer to this moment is a short exchange and going back to your work, that is the answer.

Say your piece and stop. Where the conversation goes next is theirs to decide, not yours to
pre-empt.

Larion.name: Larion
Larion.basicInfo: Larion is the physical world of the living — its lands, seas, and skies, and everything that walks under the sun. Its continents span tundra and desert, jungle and grassland, and civilizations have risen and fallen across them, leaving ruins and relics behind. In the present age, realms of varying size and power hold an uneasy balance, while vast stretches of wilderness remain unexplored. Its people range from ordinary folk living quiet lives to those who wield arcane power or serve the gods. Creatures both kindly and monstrous dwell in the wild places between settled lands.

The Shadelands.name: The Shadelands
The Shadelands.basicInfo: The Shadelands is the plane of the dead: a grey country where restless spirits linger. Most of the dead pass on and are gone. Those who will not — too angry, too proud, too bound by things unfinished — stay, and sour, and turn to haunts and hungering dead. The dead shape the grey to their will: a weak shade raises a thin, formless mist, a strong one a vivid world held by its rage or grief or longing — a hall lit warm as the night it died, a garden in impossible bloom. The Shadelands presses against Larion wherever the dead break through. When a haunting will not rest, when the dead keep rising, the root of it runs down to here.

The Underworld.name: The Underworld
The Underworld.basicInfo: The Underworld is the dark beneath the world: endless caverns and tunnels running under every land, threaded through the ruins of empires that fell in ages past and were buried where they stood. Little light reaches here that someone did not bring or make. Underground peoples have raised fortresses called deepholds among the dead cities, and many have no love for the surface. The old world keeps its wealth in the walls — relics and lost work, left for those bold enough to come down for it.

Aurora.name: Aurora
Aurora.basicInfo: Aurora is the frozen top of the world: white plains and glassy ridges under a sky that burns with colored light. It was warm once, the home of the Northrealm, a seafaring kingdom the cold killed. Its people, the snowlanders, now hold out in Warmwater Township, a hot-spring town of lamplit houses and glowing ice sculptures, where the Northrealm's exiled ducal house, the Winter Crown, keeps its court and means to retake the old capital of Northport. A cult called the Long Night chokes the springs that keep the towns alive. On the ice live frost giants, white bearfolk, drakes and the frozen dead, and the glaciers keep sunken ships and older wonders for the bold.

Black Fells.name: Black Fells
Black Fells.basicInfo: The Black Fells are a smoking volcanic peninsula ruled by the Greater Goblinate, the goblin war-state that serves the Dragon Queen. Its capital, Smoketown, is a roaring forge-city built over ancient ruins, where the furnaces never go out and firelances boom in celebration every evening. Out on the lava-fields the Church of the Pyre brews dragonfire, the foundries build the fire-weapons it fuels, and raider fleets bring plunder home to Loot Landing. Useful outsiders can find work here, but spies are burned. Fire-drakes hunt the badlands, Fire Mountain at the northern cape is held by the Goblinate and the Pyre, and only Dun Teine Watch, a dwarf fortress in the snows at the peninsula's southern end, still holds out.

Shadow Summits.name: Shadow Summits
Shadow Summits.basicInfo: The Shadow Summits are cold alpine valleys and black pine slopes under mountains so steep that whole towns pass half the year in shadow. Moon-elf vampire lords rule here from baroque palaces, few in number and immensely powerful, taking blood as tax from prosperous subjects who keep their homes, crafts, and old loyalties under the price. The Summits are beautiful, wealthy, and dangerous: a refuge for the cursed and hunted, a courtly land of masks and old bargains, and a high wilderness where strigoi — the vampire-dead, gone mindless and hungry — haunt the passes and ghouls out of the old silver mines raid the outlying farms.

Highheath.name: Highheath
Highheath.basicInfo: Highheath is open heath-and-crag country of stone roads, upland pasture, rocky hills, caves, and giantborn cattle-steads. At its heart stands Dun Solas, the free cave-city, with the rival dwarf clans of Stonewall and Stormhammer holding the country around it. The clans share old trade, old grudges, and the stormsteel craft that made the region famous. The roads are lively with merchants, miners, clan business, border feuds, and travelers moving between the holds and the wider world.

Whiteholds.name: Whiteholds
Whiteholds.basicInfo: The Whiteholds are white mountain country of dwarf clanholds, glacier roads, high lochs, and halls cut deep under the peaks. At their center, Deepgate has grown around the crater where Stonehome, the old shared capital of the dwarf kings, collapsed into the depths. Delvers descend from there after lost halls, old treasures, and the Darek Deep below. Clan Deepfire digs and forges from volcanic depths, while Clan Icerune carves rune-ice and keeps buried dangers sealed. Greathearth, a neutral hillside village with a great common hall and famous cloudhorn goats, is where the high roads meet. Around them lie a grave-town, a selkie fishing village, ogre-held ruins and dangerous passes, and every argument comes back to what should be recovered and what should stay buried.

Orc Wolds.name: Orc Wolds
Orc Wolds.basicInfo: The Orc Wolds are open grass and iron hills, broken by stone tors and the flat-topped mesa the clans hold sacred. This is orc country: no king, no walls, and no border anyone respects but the orcs themselves. Two great clans dominate the Wold — Vorren, settled iron-builders, and Drokash, roving riders — rivals in everything except holding the land. Raiders press from the west, yetis and frost drakes from the cold north, and war-bands from the south; season after season, the clans throw them back.

Wild Grass Sea.name: Wild Grass Sea
Wild Grass Sea.basicInfo: The Wild Grass Sea is a vast expanse of tall grass and open sky, broken by rocky tors like islands and rivers whose banks are the only clear ground for miles. This is beastfolk country — boarfolk, wolfkin, lionkin, serpentfolk, catkin, and dozens more — each people holding its own ground by its own customs. They are not one nation, and old rivalries run deep, but one law unites them: no kings. At the Moot, the peoples gather under sacred truce to trade, argue, and settle the grass for a season.

Alar Coast.name: Alar Coast
Alar Coast.basicInfo: The Alar Coast is hot sand desert running down to the sea, dunes in the interior and a broad green delta in the southwest where the Emerald River reaches the coast. A generation ago the dragon Nuur-Suthra took the wreck of a fallen sky-citadel in the Redrock coastal hills to the north as its lair, and the Church of the Pyre rose to serve it — demanding tribute of the coast in the dragon's name. The city of Serendipity pays: it stands rich on the delta, keeps the greatest market in the southern deserts, and lives under the Church's rule and its Red-cowl soldiers. Many refused, and burned for it. Their survivors fled into the deep desert, and from there the Desert Tribes raid the tribute roads and shelter all who flee the flame.

Elfwood.name: Elfwood
Elfwood.basicInfo: Elfwood is the high elves' realm at the ancient heart of the Everwood, a land of high elven cities woven through silverleaf trees, green roads, clear streams, and ruins half-swallowed by moss and bloom. It is one of the most beautiful lands in Larion, old in a way human kingdoms can barely measure, and its people keep arts of living wood, song, and wardcraft found nowhere else. Beneath that beauty runs the old wound of the Kindred War: dark elves below in the Rootdark, high elves above in the canopy, and a single crossing between them, at Ilunethel, where a fragile peace still holds.

Sanctuary Vale.name: Sanctuary Vale
Sanctuary Vale.basicInfo: Sanctuary Vale is deep forest country around the walled city of Sanctuary, the one place in this part of the wood where outsiders are allowed to live. The city stands by old agreement: stone walls raised by its founders, elven wards woven into them, and the forest held back only so far. Inside the walls, Sanctuary is crowded, loud, and bright; beyond them, the trees close in around abandoned works, hidden paths, old ruins, and powers that never agreed the city should be here.

Whitecliff Downs.name: Whitecliff Downs
Whitecliff Downs.basicInfo: Whitecliff Downs is gentle halfling country of chalk hills, sea-cliffs, orchards, market roads, kitchen gardens, and small shrines. Its villages are ordinary in the best sense: busy with fairs, meals, gossip, work, family feuds, and neighbors who know one another too well. The Downs are famous for good food, good ale, herbcraft, and the kind of hospitality that becomes everyone's business by breakfast. Beyond the halfling hills lie the crafters of Forge-town, the satyrs' wine-grove at Vilitara, two rival gentry estates on the river, and a monster market on the Carendon border. It is a quiet land, but not an empty one; old blessings, hidden paths, and small dangers lie just past the garden gate.

Silvervale.name: Silvervale
Silvervale.basicInfo: Silvervale is the green heartland around Ardan's Watch, the free city where the Silverflow meets the Great North and the League of Adventurers keeps its headquarters. It is a country of fields, river towns, markets, old roads, and settled farms, safer than most of Larion but not without danger. Ardan's Watch stands at the center of the old road network and the ancient portals that still reach across the world, making Silvervale the place where travelers, merchants, and adventurers from every region cross paths before choosing a road outward.

Duchy of Drusavia.name: Duchy of Drusavia
Duchy of Drusavia.basicInfo: The Duchy of Drusavia is old, green hill country of forested slopes and rich farming dales under weather that runs to mist and low cloud, with the fog lying in the valley bottoms of a morning. It is a settled, prosperous land of villages, mills, and old estates — and it is haunted. Two hundred years ago its people overthrew the vampire lords who ruled them, in the war Drusavians call the Liberation. The dead of that bad age rise in the dales by night, while the Templars Adamant and the Shadow Inquisition disagree on whether the answer is to seal the dead away or enter their country and fight them at the source. No one travels after dark.

Duchy of Carendon.name: Duchy of Carendon
Duchy of Carendon.basicInfo: Carendon is an old, prosperous duchy of forested hills, low mountains, rivers, walled towns, and hunting estates grown rich on timber, fur, and game. It is gracious country, all old families and older castles, but the woods press close and breed things soldiers cannot handle: beasts too large, too cunning, or too strange to leave alone. Carendon's peace depends on keeping those monsters culled. This is the seat of the Order of the Silver Sword, the Silverblades, who hunt with radiant metal that bites what ordinary steel cannot.

Westmarch.name: Westmarch
Westmarch.basicInfo: Westmarch is rich farmland and river-vale country around Marrenford, the great crossing where House Corwin holds the roads, bridges, and river trade. To the north lie the orc lands; to the west, the Everwood. The old Greatwall runs along the hills between them, begun after ancient victories and never finished. Orc reavers still come down from the north, elf renegades still raid from the trees, and the Riders and Rangers of House Corwin still ride out to answer.

Jade Tarn.name: Jade Tarn
Jade Tarn.basicInfo: Jade Tarn is rolling green farm country in the heart of Larion, gathered around a small lake of vivid jade-green water crowded with wooded islands. Orchards and pasture slope down to reed-beds and willow shores. Beyond the farms rise the dark pine slopes of Cold Kell Mountain and a wedge of red, broken badlands. The weather is mild and wet: soft rain, warm summers, and mist on the water most mornings. Tarnholme Academy of the Arcane, the great school of magic, stands on the islands in the middle of the lake, and young mages come from all over Larion to study there. The villages along the shore make their living supplying the school.

Whitemoor.name: Whitemoor
Whitemoor.basicInfo: Whitemoor is a country of open moor and drowned fen where the dead do not stay buried. Three old kingdoms of the realm of Fethloren once held it; two lie drowned out in the fen, and the third survives as Aldwall, the Shining City, the one walled town still standing, whose stone glows by night and holds the dead at bay, built of pale dwarf-stone no one can match now. Its duke holds the town, and above it the Knights Vigilant keep their cliff-fortress — a sworn order of radiant arms who ride out against the moor's dead. The barrows of an older age cover the dry heath, and the drowned crowns sit full of grave-gold under the still water, for those hard enough to take it from the dead that guard it.

Dunelands.name: Dunelands
Dunelands.basicInfo: The Dunelands are a vast desert under a white and merciless sun, where dunes run to the horizon and the wind reshapes the land overnight. At its heart, deep springs feed Oasis, the palm-green white city in a country of sand, stone, and bone. Beyond the water stand the pyramids of the old Sun Kings, still rich with buried gold and whatever was set to guard it. Tomb-crews cross the heat to dig, and the desert takes its share. Djinnborn, jackalkin, desert elves, and other desert peoples crowd Oasis and work the caravan roads, keeping old customs and making hard bargains under the long sun, while a cult called the New Sun holds the waystation at Hillwatch and means to wake the dead kings.

Redrock.name: Redrock
Redrock.basicInfo: Redrock is red badland country: deep canyons, wind-carved mesas, burned cities, and a hard sun, rising northward into cool peaks above the clouds. It was rich once, before demons came and its people burned their own cities in the magic that drove them back. The land never recovered. The low places still smolder, and demons claw up after dark, so travelers race the sun to the next barred door. Danger is worst on the canyon floors, among ruins, raider-held cities, and old burn-scars; high above, where the air is cool and thin, the cities are safer and their people live well.

Great Lagoon.name: Great Lagoon
Great Lagoon.basicInfo: The Great Lagoon is a country of tidal shallows and reed-marsh on the southern coast, and the seat of the Empire of Light, whose citizens call themselves Solarians. Its capital, Caranthoria, stands on ground reclaimed from the lagoon beside the drowned capital of the old Empyrean Empire, and over the city floats the Eye of God, an enormous citadel of gold-bright brass tethered in the sky. The empire takes citizens of every people and hires soldiers of every kind, and it is the strongest and most dangerous power in the south. West of the city its war grinds into the deep fens, where the marsh belongs to the lizardfolk dragon-kingdom of the Reedmoot Fens.

Reedmoot Fens.name: Reedmoot Fens
Reedmoot Fens.basicInfo: The Reedmoot Fens are a vast saltwater marsh peninsula — reed-flats, mangrove, black water, and drowned ruins under a low wet sky. The Fens once traded with the world; now they are closed. A dragon rose from the brood-mounds within living memory, the lizardfolk clans united behind her as the dragon-kingdom, and the dragon-kingdom kills or takes any outsider found in its territory. Only the eastern strip stays open ground, where the free village of Reedmoot holds its wall against the fen and the heronfolk keep their roosts in the Stiltwood. On the north coast the Syndicate's smuggling port, Port Lucre, trades by the dragon's leave.

Ntar Vanna.name: Ntar Vanna
Ntar Vanna.basicInfo: Ntar Vanna is the great river jungle of the southern world, built along the Saranadi as it runs from the deep interior to the sea. The river is the only road through it, and the farther upriver you go, the wilder the country gets. This is hot, rainy, misted land where trees rise like towers, undergrowth swallows roads in days, and beasts grow larger than anything in the outer world. Many proud peoples share the river and no crown rules them all: demonborn at the great port-city of the mouth, monkeyfolk, elephantfolk, serpentkin, frogkin, and others holding their own stretches upriver, trading, feuding, and bargaining as the river carries everything between them.

Swordlaw Isles.name: Swordlaw Isles
Swordlaw Isles.basicInfo: The Swordlaw Isles are a scatter of green islands in a warm southern sea, strung together by the colossal stone bridges left behind by a fallen empire — mile-long spans that vault from isle to isle, half-sunk where the sea has taken them. Tevantia, the dueling city of the four great houses, holds the bridged heart of the isles under its Duke. Beyond it lie Gavarra, the gambling city where any coin is welcome; Beggarsbridge, the lawless market built on a bridge; and Freehaven, the pirate port. The other isles are lawless, home to freebooters and wreckers, and quarrels there are settled by the Swordlaw: steel decides, and the winner's word stands.

Bay of Serpents.name: Bay of Serpents
Bay of Serpents.basicInfo: The Bay of Serpents is a warm southern sea of bright water, green islands, white beaches, and reefs like sunken gardens. The southern shipping lanes cross here, and so do the richest monster waters in Larion: sea serpents, leviathans, krakens, and sea-trolls. Coriva, the great hunting port, grew rich killing the monsters that threaten the lanes; its hunters are celebrities, and its craftsmen turn scale, bone, oil, and hide into goods known across the coast. The same waters hold merfolk lagoon-villages, floating raft-towns, and drakerider isles where sea-drakes carry riders over open water.

Seadeep Kingdoms.name: Seadeep Kingdoms
Seadeep Kingdoms.basicInfo: The Seadeep Kingdoms are open ocean over drowned country — the storm-dark southern sea where Orichala, greatest city of the old empire, sank in a single night, and where the kingdoms of the drowned rule everything beneath the surface. Ships may cross if they keep moving. Stop to take what the sea has claimed, set foot on the drowned places, or pry at the wrecks, and the kingdoms answer from below. Sailors cross Seadeep water without stopping, and count themselves lucky to have crossed it.

Grell Hollows.name: Grell Hollows
Grell Hollows.basicInfo: The Grell Hollows are broad limestone caverns beneath Silvervale, close enough to the surface that daylight falls through sinkholes and broken shafts. The Flood buried the old cities of the Fourth Empire here, leaving paved streets, public squares, statues, and grand halls open to the dark. The Hollows take their name from the Grell, a mythical kobold empire that current clans claim as their birthright; the squatters below raid the surface and feud over the ruins, imperial salvage, and whose grandiose host or legion owns which dead district.
Grell Hollows.hiddenInfo:
The true ruins are Fourth Empire ruins buried by the Flood. Ardan's Watch stands above one of the old entry points; the Delvers' Lift descends from the Basement to The Scrabble. The current kobolds are squatters, not descendants proven to have built the ruins. They have claimed the name Grell for a mythical kobold empire and insist the old city is theirs by birthright. They wear and hoard imperial salvage that does not fit them — oversized armor, too-large weapons, and broken regalia strapped into place — and treat any delver as a trespasser in their empire. Rival kobold hosts and family holds feud constantly; that division is why their raids remain dangerous but containable. They are hostile to Ardan's Watch and periodically raid upward, but this is not an open war. Do not place Grell kobolds as ordinary residents in the city or make them a tolerated surface faction.

The Scrabble is the League's working foothold and quest hub, not a safe settlement. The Imperial Baths are warm, overgrown, contested ruins. The Imperial Shrine to Avarice and its black water are held only around the shore. The Flooded Forum and Imperial Arsenal are deeper unknown sites. Use the region's creatures and kobold roles only when a scene calls for danger; quiet camps, negotiations, and salvage work remain possible.

Darek Deep.name: Darek Deep
Darek Deep.basicInfo: The Darek Deep is a dead subterranean city far below Deepgate, built by the vanished dareks, pale dwarf-like elders who left behind halls of stone and iron, dead machines, and treasure beyond counting. Their constructs still move in the dark, soulstones burning inside them, guarding posts for masters long gone. Crews descend the great shaft for black iron, construct parts, soulstones, and other salvage of a lost age. The upper halls are picked over and quieter; deeper down, the guardians still keep faith with the dead, and morlocks haunt the dark between.

Tarnished Reaches.name: Tarnished Reaches
Tarnished Reaches.basicInfo: The Tarnished Reaches are a province of the Shadelands, the grey country of the dead, where the land takes shape from the memories of those who refuse to pass on. Here linger the highborn dead of the Fourth Empire, the cruel dominion that ruled before Larion: lords and kings too proud to cross the last river and forget. Their dreamed worlds of baroque palaces, fallen capitals, and ruined courts crumble under a starless sky, proud and cruel even in death. At their heart stands Lord Rhadan's Court, the one fixed and guarded place in the Reaches, and the Black Tower's only safe foothold.

The Rootdark.name: The Rootdark
The Rootdark.basicInfo: The Rootdark is the dark-elf realm beneath the Elfwood: a vast cavern-country lit by the Root-sky, glowing roots that hang amber to violet across the dark. At its heart stands Maanvalta, the dark-elf capital, built around the World-root where it descends into the World-spring. Beyond the capital, tunnel-roads run out under the forest and far beyond, carrying dark-elf trade and agents into the wider world, and soldiers keep watch at their gates. It is beautiful, wealthy, and dangerous: a whole underworld kingdom beneath the forest, open to bold surfacers at its gates and lethal to fools who wander from the road.

Ice Sea Northwest.name: Ice Sea Northwest
Ice Sea Northwest.basicInfo: The Ice Sea north-west of Aurora is pack ice the year round, floes grinding together over black water. Nothing lives on it that does not come up from below or fly in from the coast. Ships that winter here do not come out; their hulls stand in the ice where they stopped, and what was aboard them is still aboard.

Ice Sea North.name: Ice Sea North
Ice Sea North.basicInfo: North of Aurora the sea freezes solid against the volcanic shore of the Black Fells, ash greying the floes. Snowlander hunters cross the fast ice after seal and white bear when the leads close, and turn back when they open. The dead walk out here too, further from lamplight than anywhere a person should stand.

Ice Sea Northeast.name: Ice Sea Northeast
Ice Sea Northeast.basicInfo: East of the Black Fells the sea takes the mountain's leavings: cinder rafts, floating pumice, and floes stained grey with ash. The water is warm enough in places to stay open all winter, and goblin crews come out from the forge-towns to dredge the shallows for metal the mountain threw into the sea.

Ice Sea East.name: Ice Sea East
Ice Sea East.basicInfo: The far north-eastern ocean, deep and nearly empty. There is no coast within reach, only drifting floes. Few crews come this far, and the ones who do keep watch on the ice, because rimewyrms grown huge in the open water hunt under the floes and burst up beneath anything that stops.

Ice Sea West.name: Ice Sea West
Ice Sea West.basicInfo: West of Aurora the sound never fully clears. On its northwest shore, where a glacier has come down over the old harbor, stands Northport, the dead capital of the Northrealm. Its ships are still at their moorings, frozen into the sea. Everything the kingdom owned is there, preserved, and guarded by the draugr who froze with it.

Nightfjord Fells.name: Nightfjord Fells
Nightfjord Fells.basicInfo: The eastern fall of the Shadow Summits: black pine spurs and terraced shelves cut into grey cliff, dropping to fjord water. A few moon-elf vampire lords hold the shelves as their valleys, far from their peers. Their blood-tithed subjects farm the terraces, and the lords' watchers mark anyone on the road down to the water.

Fjord Sea.name: Fjord Sea
Fjord Sea.basicInfo: Cold water pushing inland between the pine headlands below the Shadow Summits. The vampire lords take their tax from anything that anchors in their inlets. Crews that must pass do it in daylight and do not stop, because after dark the Crimson Company's boats come out to collect.

Glassmilk Marches.name: Glassmilk Marches
Glassmilk Marches.basicInfo: East of the Whiteholds the glaciers spill out into moraine country: grey ridges, braided meltwater channels, and two milky lochs that never warm. Dwarven delvers work the moraine for what the ice brings down out of the lost halls, camping rough and moving as the channels shift. The ice gives up old things as well as ore, among them dwarven dead frozen in it for ages, and some of those rise and walk when the ice lets them go.

Glass Sea.name: Glass Sea
Glass Sea.basicInfo: The sea off the glacier country runs milk-pale where meltwater clouds it, and grounded bergs sit in the shallows all summer. Dwarven crews work the gravel shore for what the ice carries down out of the Whiteholds, and the ice carries down old dwarven goods as well as stone.

Tarn Sea.name: Tarn Sea
Tarn Sea.basicInfo: The bay east of Jade Tarn, jade-green over sand and reed bank, warm and shallow and busy with small craft. Tarnholme students come out to the skerries to work magic where the Jade Tarn's wild magic thins enough to be safe to work. It is the friendliest water in Larion, which in Larion means only that most people come back.

Wardcoast.name: Wardcoast
Wardcoast.basicInfo: Wardcoast is where the Everwood comes down to the sea: old woodland thinning to heath and pasture, grey cliffs, and small sheltered coves where a boat can land. Weathered elven ward-stones stand along the clifftops, old work of the high elves' wardcraft. The coves are the only way into the deep wood that does not pass a gate, which is why smugglers know them.

Redrock Sea.name: Redrock Sea
Redrock Sea.basicInfo: Where the burned canyon country meets the sea, the cliffs are rust-red and a canyon of fused black glass runs down through the coastal hills to the shore. This is the Slagrun, cut by the Celestial Citadel of Alar when the old sky-fortress fell burning. The wreck lies at the canyon's head, broken into a mountain and still burning day and night, and the dragon Nuur-Suthra lairs in its depths. The Church of the Pyre holds the wreck holy and keeps a watch at its gate. Its Red-cowl patrols sweep the glass for looters, and desert folk pick brass, ornament and voidglass from the wreckage anyway.

West Sea.name: West Sea
West Sea.basicInfo: Cold grey-green water under the chalk sea-cliffs of the Downs. Halfling boats work the skerries for crab and line-fish and are home by dark. It is ordinary sea, in the best sense.

Alar Sea.name: Alar Sea
Alar Sea.basicInfo: Hot water south of the Alar delta, turquoise over reef and deep blue further out. This is the southern shipping lane, and the Church of the Pyre taxes it from Serendipity. Reefs here are littered with the timbers of caravans that tried the sea instead of the tribute roads.

Fen Sea.name: Fen Sea
Fen Sea.basicInfo: Brackish water outside the Reedmoot Fens, mangrove islets and mud banks under a low sky. The lizardfolk kingdom claims it and enforces the claim. Drowned ruins stand in the shallows from when the Fens still traded, and the brood-mounds are not far inland.

Serpent Sea.name: Serpent Sea
Serpent Sea.basicInfo: The Serpent Sea is the open water east of the Bay of Serpents: clear turquoise over reef, green islands, white beaches, and no port of its own. Coriva's hunting ships follow the serpents out here when the Bay's runs are thin, and come back heavy or not at all. The bones on the reefs are the ones that got away from somebody.

South Sea West.name: South Sea West
South Sea West.basicInfo: Warm open ocean in the far south-west, empty enough that a green atoll is an event. Crews blown out this far navigate by the atoll and are grateful for it. Below the surface the kingdoms of the drowned begin, and they do not regard the surface as anyone's.

Vanna Sea.name: Vanna Sea
Vanna Sea.basicInfo: Where the Saranadi comes out of the jungle it pushes silt far into the sea, and the delta bars shift with every flood. River boats refit where they can on the bars before the open water. Everything upriver comes through here, and so do the outsized jungle beasts that follow it down.

South Sea.name: South Sea
South Sea.basicInfo: Warm archipelago water below the Swordlaw Isles, turquoise over sand. One of the fallen empire's colossal bridge spans runs out from the isles and stops in deep water, its piers standing alone. Freebooters use them as marks. The Swordlaw does not reach out here.

South Sea East.name: South Sea East
South Sea East.basicInfo: The storm-dark sea east of drowned Orichala, greatest city of the Empyrean Empire, which went down in a single night. Ships may cross if they keep moving; the drowned permit passage and nothing else, and prying anything loose from wreck or shoal is not permitted.

Grey Gables.name: Grey Gables
Grey Gables.basicInfo: Grey Gables is a fine pale-stone townhouse on Wren Lane, a quiet street opening onto Ducal Square in Drusavia. Three steep slate gables rise above tall gothic windows and a wine-red door. A projecting music-room bay overlooks the lane, and a small walled garden shelters a pear tree and a supper table. Warm hearths, old walnut furniture, and comfortable guest rooms make it a welcoming city home.
Grey Gables.hiddenInfo:
Formerly the home of a retired court musician, Grey Gables is a furnished ducal house granted for recognized service. Its household allowance covers ordinary costs and upkeep. Private bedrooms and two attic guest rooms accommodate residents and invited companions.

Sabine Brisac keeps the household, receives visitors in the Hearth Room and brings friends together for meals and conversation. Her introductions and candid advice connect the house to other households in Drusavia. She has her own accommodation, friendships and commitments.

The Hearth Room hosts shared meals; the Music Room provides space for cards, private conversation and small recitals. Friends gather for supper beneath the pear tree or meet quietly in the upstairs rooms. Candles, daylight and living hearths light the house, and the household keeps the hearth burning through the night in Drusavian custom.

The Hearth Room.description: A carved limestone hearth warms a comfortable dining room with dark walnut paneling, a worn rug, a sideboard and a table with mismatched upholstered chairs. Three matching gothic window lights and a glazed garden door look toward the pear tree. The kitchen adjoins the room, and the stair rises to the music room and bedrooms. Candles and firelight catch the framed paintings.

The Music Room.description: Tall leaded windows in a projecting bay overlook the lane and nearby slate roofs. A polished keyboard instrument and a lute stand ready for music; comfortable chairs gather around a small card table beside a pale-stone hearth. Bound music and books fill low shelves. The room welcomes private conversation and small recitals, with the bedrooms reached from the adjoining landing.

The Owner’s Bedroom.description: A private upstairs bedchamber overlooks the pear garden and city roofs. A small hearth warms a cushioned window seat and two chairs, offering somewhere to receive a close friend away from the shared rooms. A carved walnut bed, writing desk, wardrobe, and washstand leave space for personal belongings. The adjoining landing leads to two attic guest bedrooms.

The Pear Garden.description: A small enclosed garden shelters a mature pear tree, flowers along pale-stone walls, and a table with room for supper among friends. A simple iron gate opens onto Wren Lane, beside a glazed door back into the house. Windows glow above the garden after dusk.

Larkdale.name: Larkdale
Larkdale.basicInfo:
Larkdale is a sheltered Drusavian dale of apple orchards, grazing meadows and pale-stone cottages beneath wooded hills. A gothic manor stands on a low rise above the village, its steep slate roofs and square stair tower visible through the valley mist. Tall windows overlook a sheltered terrace, and orchard paths lead down to a brook crossed by a stone bridge.

The furnished hall offers comfortable rooms for a household and its guests, a library, space for suppers and dancing, and stables for riding through the dale. In the village, visitors find an inn, everyday provisions and neighbors gathering for meals, market days and seasonal celebrations. Rain darkens the stone and gathers on the orchard leaves; hearths and candlelit windows give the house and cottages their warmth.
Larkdale.hiddenInfo:
Larkdale is an established ducal estate granted for court service. Its farms and orchards support ordinary household staffing, supplies, upkeep and horses. Private apartments accommodate the manor’s owners and their invited companions; shared grants provide named shares and separate rooms. Village families retain their own homes, trades, customs and livelihoods.

Solange Cresson owns her orchard and cottage independently of the manor. She grows restorative fruit, works enchantments into living wood and hosts lively suppers beneath the trees. Sir Aubin Tressac serves as the estate’s knight and master-at-arms, trains its watch and accompanies expeditions with his hearthfire sword. He keeps company in the Riding Yard and enjoys dancing and tournament talk.

Meals, music and dancing fill the Great Hall, while readers and visiting company gather in the Library and Gallery. The Orchard Terrace hosts outdoor suppers. Riding lessons and returning expeditions bring residents and stable staff together in the yard. Village fairs, cider pressing and seasonal meals draw guests to the green and inn.

Household staff tend ordinary affairs during the owners’ travels. Larger celebrations and changes to shared spaces are arranged among the people concerned. Village shops and the inn serve residents and travelers independently of the manor. Inhabited cottages and the manor keep their living hearths through the night, with candles and daylight providing the remaining light.

The Great Hall.description: A tall, timber-roofed hall opens from the terrace through heavy oak doors. Pointed windows light pale stone walls, dark oak paneling and a broad hearth carved with branches and small birds. A long dining table occupies one side; cushioned benches and movable chairs leave room near the hearth for conversation, music or dancing. A side door leads to the kitchens and household rooms, while an oak stair rises toward the library and private apartments. Cloaks hang in the entrance passage, with space beneath them for muddy boots.

The Library and Gallery.description: Dark oak bookshelves line a long upper room beneath a carved timber ceiling. Tall leaded windows overlook the orchards and village, with deep window seats for reading. Books of history, poetry and travel share the shelves with maps of Drusavia and music for the household’s instruments. A writing table stands beside a smaller hearth; upholstered chairs and a card table fill its warmer corner. A short picture gallery along the inner wall connects the hall stair to the private apartments.

The Private Apartments.description:
An upper landing opens onto a private bedchamber, a small sitting room, and separate guest bedrooms. The sitting room offers a quiet place for breakfast, correspondence, or conversation with invited company away from the hall.

In the principal chamber, burgundy curtains surround a carved oak bed, and two comfortable chairs face the hearth. A desk, wardrobe, washstand, and window seat leave room for personal belongings. Leaded windows overlook the orchard roofs and hills.

The Orchard Terrace.description: Broad stone steps descend from the manor’s sheltered terrace into a lawn edged with apple trees and old orchard walls. Beneath a shallow stone loggia, a long supper table and wooden chairs overlook the dale; benches stand beside beds of herbs, climbing roses and dark ivy. Gravel paths wind beneath the orchard trees. From the wall, the brook and its little stone bridge are visible below.

The Riding Yard.description:
Slate-roofed stables face a sheltered cobbled yard, with a sand enclosure for riding lessons and practice. Residents, visiting riders, and stable staff gather here to choose mounts, compare horses, and prepare for outings. Returning parties linger to discuss the ride while their horses are tended.

A covered bench beside the tack room offers somewhere to watch lessons or talk out of the rain. Saddles, bridles, brushes, and blankets fill the working rooms; a mounting block stands beneath an open arch.

Larkdale Village.description: Pale-stone cottages with steep slate roofs gather beside a clear brook and a low arched bridge. An inn faces the small green, its common room warmed by a broad hearth and its covered porch looking toward the water. A bakehouse, provision shop and farrier serve residents and passing riders; a roofed cider press stands beside the orchard store. On market days, stalls fill the green with produce, bread and household goods.

Moonbloom Woods.name: Moonbloom Woods
Moonbloom Woods.basicInfo: An old oak-and-chestnut wood in Whitecliff Downs, famous for the moonbloom truffles beneath its roots. Pale chalk banks rise between the trees, and narrow paths wind through fern-filled hollows.
Moonbloom Woods.hiddenInfo:
The kobolds from nearby Whitehill Kobold Warren regard moonbloom truffles as disgusting but know what halflings will pay for them. They dig around old harvesting holes, follow foragers, steal baskets, and sell their finds back to the villages. Their best customers are wealthy halflings unwilling to come into the woods themselves.

The finest moonblooms lie deep beneath undisturbed roots. Trained truffle-hogs can scent them where the kobolds find nothing.

The woodland crews are ordinary kobold scavengers concerned with food, money, and their own skins. They bluff, bargain, set crude snares, and attempt theft. They would rather escape with a basket than fight over it.

The Basket Path.description: A winding path enters the wood between chalk banks and spreading chestnuts. Stumps serve as resting places for foragers and stands for anyone selling their finds. Shallow digging holes surround the nearest trees; smaller tracks leave the path and follow it through the ferns.

The Chalk Hollow.description: White chalk shows through the roots along a steep-sided hollow. Fallen branches bridge a muddy runnel, and narrow ledges skirt its banks. Oak roots twist through the exposed earth, with small burrows and abandoned digging holes between them.

The Old Oaks.description: Great oaks spread their branches over soft leaf mould and deep beds of moss. Their roots form ridges, pockets, and low arches across the ground.

Ardan's Watch.name: Ardan's Watch
Ardan's Watch.basicInfo: Ardan's Watch is a prosperous, cosmopolitan city at the meeting of the Silverflow and Great North rivers, named for Ardan, the ancient hero who founded it. At its heart stands the Watchtower, an ancient elderstone tower and the seat of the League of Adventurers, from which roads and portals reach out across Larion. The city is a free state, governed by the Council of Champions — retired adventurers raised by merit rather than birth.
Ardan's Watch.hiddenInfo:
The Lord Mayor runs the city day to day; the Council of Champions sets its course, and the City Guard answers to the Council. The League governs Ardan's Watch directly, but holds no authority beyond it — elsewhere it works by trust, contracts, and being useful enough that rulers ask its advice. From the Watchtower it tracks trouble across Larion and points adventurers toward whichever road needs them. Older elderstone spires stand among the roofs, repurposed or sealed.
The city is the most mixed place in Larion: humans, elves, dwarves, halflings, orcs, dragonkin, demonborn, catkin, ratkin, and every other people of Larion live, trade, and adventure here side by side, from champions and crews to merchants, scholars, and neighbors, with imps thickest in the Basement below. Horns, wings, tusks, tails, and stranger marks draw less notice here than a bad debt.
Old Town belongs to the Thieves' Guild, and they are thieves in the ordinary way: they pick pockets, fence stolen goods, run the dice rooms and the pit, and smuggle. They keep an honor code — they hold their own turf, and they do not deal in bodies or prey on the helpless. The Syndicate keeps no such code, and wants the Basement: the buried market is the city's richest artery, and the Guild will not sell. The Guard enters Old Town carefully, by an old understanding.
Below Old Town lies the Basement, the city's lantern-strung buried market and pleasure district. From the Basement, the Delvers' Lift drops to Grell Hollows in the Underworld: adventurers ride down to delve the kobold-claimed imperial ruins, and the kobolds raid up out of the dark.
The Delvers' Lift is the only way down from Ardan's Watch into Grell Hollows: reach it by going through Old Town into the Basement, then ride it to The Scrabble.
Outside the walls, the Field of Valor lies west, the City of Ancestors northwest, Gallows Wood north on the High Road, and Muckside across the river.

Thousandlights Market.description: Just inside the gates, Ardan's Watch opens into Thousandlights Market: an old colosseum rebuilt into a permanent market of stalls, shops, balconies, and lantern-strung arches. At its heart is the Hearthfire, a great stone firepit with common benches where food and drink come from the surrounding stalls and a stranger who eats once is rarely a stranger by the time they leave. Outfitters, map-sellers, smithies, armorers, shield-schools, charm peddlers, and bootmakers crowd the outer ring. Ardan's statue stands near the market mouth, one bronze foot worn smooth by centuries of hands touching it for luck. The Watchtower rises above the market arches, and new adventurers spill into Thousandlights at all hours.

The Bargain Hoard.description: A deep stall built into one of the old colosseum's vaulted arches, its counter cut from a single slab of dark wood and its back wall shelved to the ceiling. Sef Pellanor's stock is arranged like a hoard rather than a shop: armour and blades racked by weight, potions in a locked case, and the few pieces worth real coin kept behind the counter where he can reach them without turning his back.

Watchtower - League Hall.description: The Watchtower's ground floor: a bright League hall lined with stained glass of famous adventurers. Long tables fill the center where crews form up, veterans compare routes, and young Coppers measure each other before their first outings. A Silvervale map and changing boards occupy one wall, while Tobiah Finch, the hall master, keeps a table in view where newcomers get their pins, introductions, and directions. Champions and high-ranked crews pass through on their own business. Doors lead through to the Training Yard, and stairs climb to the Map Room and the Portal Hall above. Adventurers arrive, return, train, argue, and find their footing here.

Watchtower - Training Yard.description: A quiet elderstone chamber set aside for combat training. Broad worn rings divide the floor, with chalked boundaries, low ward-lines, weapon racks, and target frames set into the walls. A few simple magical practice figures stand in recessed alcoves, their jointed bodies dull until called to motion. The open ground is large enough for a party to test movement, attacks, defenses, and control without an audience.

Watchtower - Map Room.description: A high floor of the Watchtower with tall windows looking over Thousandlights, the rivers, and the roads out of Ardan's Watch. The walls hold working maps of Silvervale, the Duchy of Drusavia and its city Drusavia, Carendon, Jade Tarn and Tarnholme Academy, Westmarch and Marrenford, Whitecliff Downs and Hillhome, Whitemoor and Aldwall, Redrock and the Citadel of the Pact, and the wider roads beyond. Boards around the walls gather copied letters, pins, route-markers, missing caravans, monster signs, grave-news, border rumors, and chapterhouse reports, so adventurers can read the shape of trouble before choosing which road to take. In one corner, under a window, the halfling author Fenimore Tully keeps a crowded desk stacked with copies of his guide to the guilds.

Watchtower - Portal Hall.description: The top hall of the Watchtower, ringed with elderstone daises keyed to named destinations. Lit daises are realms and institutions that keep a portal here and work with the League. Anyone may walk up and pay the toll; League members pay less. Destinations: Tarnholme Academy of the Arcane at Jade Tarn, Castle Harstone in Carendon, the Black Tower in Drusavia, and the Citadel of the Pact in Redrock.

The Way of Coin.description: The commercial spine of the city: banks, countinghouses, jewelers, auction rooms, guild offices, and merchant houses with painted doors and guarded ledgers. Flamboyant merchant-princes hold parties no one important misses. Some are merely rich. Some are Syndicate money wearing better gloves.

The Sacred Way.description: A long terrace of temples, shrines, holy houses, enchanters, alchemists, charmwrights, reagent sellers, and sellers of blessed gear. Priests bless oaths, hear trouble, sell charms and consecrated oil, and prepare radiant tools for work among the dead. The House of First Light, chief temple of the Lady of Hope and seat of the Order of the Dawn, keeps the sacred fire from which fallen shrines throughout Larion are rekindled. The great domed Two Rivers Bathhouse stands here too, fed by the city's rivers. Funeral processions for the wealthy pass along the Sacred Way toward the City of Ancestors, stopping at the Shrine of the Grey Lady.

Mercy House.description: The Lady of Mercy's infirmary on the Sacred Way, where adventurers carried in from bad jobs are patched up to go again. Bright wards and a surgery hall fill the ground floor, a chapel above lifts curses and cleanses poisons, and Mercy's Runners set out from here to bring back crews that did not come home. Healing and cures are offered to anyone who comes through the door.

The Dry Cistern.description: A dry old cistern beneath the Basement, reached through a locked grate in the back kitchen of Hadrik's cookhouse. The vaulted brick chamber still shows its old waterline and holds enough sleeping space for a small crew, shelves and hooks for cloaks and gear, a scarred table, and a cooking hearth. It is the safehouse of a Thieves' Guild Hand that is down to two members and looking for more.

The Crooked Cellar.description: A hidden den beneath a shuttered Old Town tenement, reached through a false wine rack and a complicated lock. The low brick vault is a new crew's workroom: a planning table, practice locks bolted to one wall, cots in the corners, and a hearth whose smoke disappears into a forgotten flue. Its only mapped way out is back up into Old Town.

The High City.description: The grandest district, built on rising ground with views across the rivers and the plains beyond. Noble houses with exotic gardens, embassies from every region of the worlds, and the Lord Mayor's Palace at the summit.

Champion's Row.description: A row of grand townhouses overlooking the rivers from the High City's edge. Each belongs to a Champion of Larion. At the head of the row stands the Temple of Champions, a vast domed chamber. Within it, the sealed Council Chamber where the Council of Champions sits and Ardan's tomb lies.

The Hippogriff Roost.description: A roost on the old city wall between the Sacred Way and Old Town, where House Edevane of Greenmeadow keeps a handful of trained hippogriffs for the League. Open perches, feed pens, and a broad launch terrace look out over the rooftops. League couriers and Mercy's Runners take off from here when someone needs reaching fast.

Old Town.description: Old Town is a cramped, noisy riverfront neighborhood of old tenements, warehouses, pawnshops, dice rooms, low taverns, fences, and alleys that know everyone's business. The Thieves' Guild claims it, and the Guard avoids it. Muckside's broken silhouette shows across the river whenever the lanes open to the water. Here and there, stairs go down to the Basement.

The Basement.description: Lantern-strung vaults below Old Town: stalls under old arches, smoke from cookfires, music through stone, pit-crowds shouting, fences arguing over salvage, imps hawking goods, and Thieves' Guild enforcers keeping the peace. Delvers, rogues, gamblers, and buyers move between the Imp-orium, the Overburden, the Fist & Flagon, and the Delvers' Lift.
