The Imp-orium.description: A loud, chaotic market where imps sell bootleg charms, fenced rings, dubious potions, counterfeit relics, and small finds from Grell Hollows. Buyers come here for cheap tools, questionable magic, rumors, and objects whose stories are usually better than their proof.

The Overburden.description: The wholesale end of the delver economy: assay tables, salvage auctions, crew postings, repair benches, locked cages for things still moving, and Guild counters where claims are recorded. Loot from Grell Hollows is weighed here, argued over here, and turned into coin or new expeditions here. The salvage-smiths behind the repair benches rent forge, anvil, and bench time by the hour to anyone who pays.

The Fist & Flagon.description: A Basement tavern with a fighting pit sunk in the common room. Pit nights draw bruisers, gamblers, guild runners, delvers, and adventurers looking for contacts. The reigning champion drinks free, settles arguments badly, and hears challenges beside the rail.

The Delvers' Lift.description: An old freight-winch shaft rebuilt into a groaning platform lift. It lowers crews, lanterns, rope, packframes, and salvage gear into the dark, then raises loot, injured delvers, and things that should have stayed below. The Lift goes down to the Scrabble in Grell Hollows.

Bellwether's Land Office.description: A small, bright land office off the Way of Coin, its bow window filled with painted views of town houses, farms and manors for sale, each with its price lettered underneath. Inside are a polished counter, two good chairs for buyers, a shelf of rolled deeds, and a framed list of the city's finer houses the agent has sold.

Muckside.name: Muckside
Muckside.basicInfo: A condemned district across the river from Ardan's Watch proper. Old warehouses and dockhouses list at bad angles where the ground has slowly given way beneath them. Most have partially collapsed. The city wrote it off generations ago rather than shore it up. No one lives here by choice — squatters, outcasts, and gang crews claim the sturdier ruins and fight over what's left. The bridges from the city side are unofficial crossings, rotting timber and rope.
Muckside.hiddenInfo:
No Watch patrols cross the river. The district polices itself, badly. Squatter camps and a few small gangs claim the sturdier buildings — they answer to the Thieves' Guild loosely if at all. Violence is common but small-scale. Most people here just want to be left alone and will be wary but not hostile to outsiders unless provoked. Ratkin are common here — more than anywhere else in the city.

Beneath the ruins is a foundation layer called the Muckwarren, and below that, sealed plague crypts from a long-ago epidemic. Strong local taboo forbids entering the crypts — even the gangs won't go near. The bridges to Ardan's Watch are the only lifeline. Old Town's gangs treat Muckside as overflow territory.

The Dregs.description: A muddy clearing ringed by leaning warehouse shells, the closest thing Muckside has to a town square. Fire pits mark where squatter camps have staked their ground. Across the river, Ardan's Watch rises clean and lit — close enough to hear the bells.

The Still Standing.description: A squat dockhouse that earned its name by not falling down. The ground floor is a tavern — one long room, a tapped barrel, benches made from old cargo pallets. The crowd is Muckside locals: squatters, gang runners, people between worse places. Not welcoming, but not looking for trouble with strangers who buy a round.

The Junkheap.description: An open-air market in a rubble-strewn yard where sellers lay out goods on tarps and blankets. Dented armor, mismatched boots, lockpick sets, unmarked bottles. No one asks where anything came from. Prices are negotiable and so are the weights.

The Muckwarren.description: The old foundation layer beneath Muckside, reached through cracked cellar floors and half-collapsed stairwells. Low ceilings, standing water, the sound of the river filtering through the walls. Smuggler caches and fugitive camps in the drier chambers. The passage deeper — toward the plague crypts — is marked with old warnings scratched into the stone.

The Plague Crypts.description: Sealed chambers where Muckside's dead were entombed during an epidemic rather than carried across the river to the City of Ancestors. The old seals are iron-banded stone, marked with faded ward-signs. The air is dead and dry. Niches line the walls, still occupied. No one from Muckside comes here willingly.

The Hall of Skulls.description: The deepest chamber beneath Muckside. A vast crypt with a vaulted ceiling held up by pillars of stacked stone sarcophagi. The dead here are old — older than the epidemic, older than the district above.

Clachmore Village.name: Clachmore Village
Clachmore Village.basicInfo: A giantborn village in a broad mountain valley, where the Stone-Born clan raises highland cattle renowned throughout the region. The giantborn here claim descent from the first giants, who shaped the mountains when the world was young. They settle disputes through wrestling and feats of strength, take their honor deadly seriously, and throw celebrations that shake the valley walls. Their annual cattle drive to the summer pastures is a highland tradition.
Clachmore Village.hiddenInfo: The Stone-Born are gentle enough in peace but carry the first giants' fire in their blood - insult their honor and you'll face a challenge that ends in broken bones or worse. The chief, a big-voiced old giantborn, has led the clan for thirty years and still wins most wrestling matches despite his age. His daughter wants to prove herself by driving cattle through disputed clan territory this summer, which could either earn her legend-status or start a feud. The village needs steady work done - fences mended, predators driven off, cattle retrieved from places too small for giantborn to reach - and they pay fairly in coin, cattle, or favors. They remember debts and grudges alike for generations.

The Drove Road.description: A wide track worn by generations of cattle and the massive feet of their herders, winding down into a green valley ringed by peaks. Clachmore spreads across the valley floor ahead - stone longhouses sized for folk half again as tall as humans, cattle pens stretching toward the river, smoke rising from a dozen chimneys. The lowing of cattle carries on the wind. A standing stone marks the village boundary, carved with the clan's bull-head sigil.

The Village Green.description: An open common at the village's heart where the Stone-Born gather for contests, celebrations, and moots. A ring of standing stones marks the wrestling ground - the grass inside worn to bare earth by generations of grappling. Lifting stones of graduated weights line one edge, the heaviest a boulder that supposedly only three giantborn have ever raised. The chief's longhouse dominates the north side. The Horned Hall tavern anchors the south, its doors sized for giantborn but with a smaller entrance cut alongside for ordinary visitors.

The Bull Pens.description: Massive stone enclosures where the clan's prize bulls are kept separate from the main herds. These animals are enormous - shaggy, horned, and ill-tempered with strangers. The Stone-Born speak to them like old friends. A giantborn youth tends the pens and knows each bull's lineage back seven generations. Beyond the pens, the valley opens into grazing lands where the main herds dot the hillsides, watched by herders with dogs and long crooks.

Ronansay Village.name: Ronansay Village
Ronansay Village.basicInfo: A fishing village on the shore of Loch Rona where selkies live among humans. Some folk here can take seal form - it's simply how things are, governed by old customs outsiders find confusing. The village has strict traditions about the loch: what can be taken, when, and how to behave toward the seal-folk without giving offense. The fishing is excellent, and the welcome warm if you mind your manners.
Ronansay Village.hiddenInfo: A great loch-serpent, grey and slow and older than the village, lives in the deepest water of Loch Rona. It is not cruel. The selkies have kept peace with it for generations by giving it the first share of every season's catch, and in return it leaves their boats alone. The village elder leads Ronansay and speaks for both the land-bound and the seal-folk; she knows the loch better than anyone living. Recently the loch has grown restless - fish swimming in strange patterns, seals gathering on rocks at odd hours - because the serpent is hungry. A hard winter thinned the herring runs, the share has come up short two seasons running, and the serpent has begun taking nets, boats and seals to make up the difference. The selkies are ashamed that the share failed on their watch and keep it from outsiders they do not yet trust. They need help from someone who can go where seals cannot: into the serpent's den in the caves above the waterline, to bring it an offering it will accept or to drive it off.

The Shore Road.description: A path winding down through heather and gorse to the loch shore, where Ronansay village clusters around a natural harbor. Stone cottages with turf roofs. Fishing boats drawn up on the shingle. Nets drying on wooden frames. Seals watch from rocks offshore with eyes that seem too knowing.

The Harbor.description: The village center, where the fishing boats launch and return. Folk mend nets, gut fish, and trade gossip in a dialect thick with old words. Some of them have a grey sheen to their skin and dark eyes that don't quite track like human eyes. The Selkie's Rest inn sits at the harbor's edge, its common room warm and its fish stew legendary. The elder's cottage overlooks the water from the hill above.

The Seal Rocks.description: A cluster of rocks jutting from the loch a short swim from shore, where seals gather at dawn and dusk. Some villagers swim out to join them; others watch from the beach. The water here is deep and cold and clear.

Tethwell Hotsprings.name: Tethwell Hotsprings
Tethwell Hotsprings.basicInfo: A village built around hotsprings that never freeze, where folk from across the highlands come to soak wounds, ease old bones, and conduct business. The Tethwell family has maintained the springs for twelve generations and enforces an absolute rule: disputes stay outside. The hot water eases wounds and old bones, and nobody leaves without hearing half the highlands' news.
Tethwell Hotsprings.hiddenInfo: The Tethwell family's authority is backed by every major clan - violating the peace here means making enemies of everyone. The family matriarch is seventy years old, sharp as broken glass, and knows secrets about half the thanes in the highlands from conversations overheard in the steam. She never trades in blackmail, which is why everyone trusts her. The springs themselves run hot from volcanic activity deep below.

The Steam Road.description: A path climbing through alpine meadows toward wisps of steam rising from the rocks ahead. The air grows warmer as the village comes into view - stone buildings clustered around pools that shimmer with heat. Snow melts in a wide circle around Tethwell; the ground itself is warm.

The Welcome House.description: The main building where visitors are received. The Tethwell family runs things from here. A great room serves meals and drink - nothing fancy, but hot and plentiful. Sleeping quarters range from common dormitories to private rooms for those who pay extra. The family's matriarch holds court by the fire most evenings, listening more than she speaks.

The Pools.description: A series of natural pools at different temperatures, from pleasantly warm to nearly scalding.

Rathcairn.name: Rathcairn
Rathcairn.basicInfo: A dwarven town in the white peaks, set above a great barrow-field where the dead of the mountain holds have been laid in honored stone for ages. The folk here are gravecrafters — the masons who carve the tomb-stones, the wrights who cut the barrow-seals, and the ward-priests who speak the rites that keep a dwarf at rest under the mountain. Their craft is failing. The dead are rising in the barrows, more than the town can put back down, and Rathcairn has begun to call for any hand willing to do the grim work.
Rathcairn.hiddenInfo:
Rathcairn is a town built around death done properly. The gravecrafters are masons and priests, not scholars — they cut the stone, seal the barrows, and keep the old rites that lay a dwarf to rest and hold them there. The dead of the white holds have been brought here for burial for as long as anyone remembers, and the barrow-field below the town is generations deep. The work is a craft and a sacred duty both, and the folk who do it are warm, plain, and grieving, because lately they are losing.

The mountain's dead are no longer resting. The barrows that held quiet for ages have begun to stir, and wights are rising in the grave-field faster than the gravecrafters can seal them back down. The ward-priests know the cause: the fall of Stonehome. Everyone who died when the capital dropped into the dark went down without rites, and every delve at Deepgate disturbs their bones. There are more unrested dead in the mountains now than there have ever been, and so many restless dead so close wake the old dead in the barrows faster than the rites can hold them. Rathcairn is overwhelmed: the only folk with the craft to put the risen dead back to rest, and far too many doing exactly the work their craft exists to prevent.

IMPORTANT: the risen dead of the barrow-field default to hostile and attack the living that disturb their ground. These are dwarven barrow-wights — the honored dead gone wrong, not the work of any necromancer — cold and strong and clad in the grave-arms they were buried with. They guard the barrows where they were laid and rise against intruders, and what is set to rest stays at rest only when the barrow is sealed again by the proper craft. Putting them down is a mercy owed as much as a danger faced; the gravecrafters reckon it the kindest work there is.

The barrows hold the grave-goods the dead were laid with — old dwarven arms and armor, ornaments, and grave-silver, finely made and ancient, though there is a weight to taking what was buried with the honored dead, and the gravecrafters mark who does. Someone who learns the sealing-craft and proves themselves can rise among the gravecrafters as one trusted to lay the dead to rest.

The Lych Gate.description: The town's entrance, a stone gate carved with the marks of the dead and the wards that ring the burial-ground. Rathcairn rises beyond it — low, solid stone buildings of grey mountain rock, the masons' yards stacked with half-cut tomb-stones, smoke rising from the priests' hall. Below the town the land falls away into the barrow-field, a vast slope of turfed mounds and standing stones stretching down into the snow. Some of the nearer mounds stand broken open, their seal-stones cracked and toppled.

The Town.description: The heart of Rathcairn, a cluster of stone halls and workshops around a central yard. The masons' workshops stand open to the cold, half-carved gravestones and barrow-seals waiting on the benches, chisels and mallets racked along the walls. The ward-priests' hall fronts the yard, its doors carved with rites, and a warm inn backs onto it where the gravecrafters take their meals and their grief. A worn path leads down out of the town toward the barrow-field below.

The Barrow-Field.description: A vast slope of burial-mounds below the town, generations deep — turfed barrows and standing stones marching down into the snowbound rock, the oldest and grandest mounds set lowest and furthest out. Seal-stones stand carved at every barrow-mouth, and many of them are cracked, heaved aside, or toppled, the dark openings beneath them gaping into the mounds. Grave-arms lie scattered in the churned snow where the dead have risen and walked. The field runs down and away into the cold, the furthest barrows lost in the white.

Rocky Gorge.name: Rocky Gorge
Rocky Gorge.basicInfo: A narrow mountain gorge with steep rocky walls and scattered clearings, located along one of the lesser-used highland passes. The area is known to harbor mountain trolls and other dangerous creatures, making it a hazardous route for unwary travelers.
Rocky Gorge.hiddenInfo: Mountain trolls lair in the upper caves and hunt the gorge at night. Travelers who move through by day and don't linger usually pass unmolested—the trolls are lazy and prefer easier prey. The route saves two days over the main pass, which is why desperate or impatient travelers still risk it. Local clans reckon the gorge not worth the blood it would cost and won't send warriors to clear it.

The Gorge Mouth.description: The pass narrows between sheer granite walls, the road reduced to a rocky track barely wide enough for a cart. Old landslide debris litters the ground. The walls climb high enough to cut direct sunlight, leaving the gorge in shadow.

The Narrows.description: The gorge squeezes tighter through boulder-choked clearings connected by passages barely two men wide. Caves and crevices pock the walls. Abandoned camps dot the clearings—some old, others left in haste.

Fire Mountain.name: Fire Mountain
Fire Mountain.basicInfo: The smoking peak at the northern cape of the peninsula. A recent eruption split the mountainside and laid bare doors of black stone buried since the elder ages—and the doors stand broken open from within. The Greater Goblinate garrisons the mountain's exterior and the Church of the Pyre keeps rites at the breach. No one climbs here without the Goblinate's leave, and the Pyre's convoys of relics and prisoners go up the mountain under guard.
Fire Mountain.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Fire Mountain is the most heavily guarded and most dangerous ground on the peninsula. The exterior is held by elite Goblinate troops and Church of the Pyre archpriests who treat any unauthorized approach as an enemy assault. Deeper in, a thing of blue fire wards the deep door and destroys all who are not the Dragon Queen's servants.

The mountain is a binding-works wrapped around a fire-breach in its heart. Ward-chambers, runic seals, and silent mechanisms hold the breach shut, laid over the colossal halls of an older age—giant-cut stone sized for beings three times a man's height, pillars carved with victories no one can read. That thing of blue fire is an arch-djinn, bound long ago by Suleyvan the Sealer to keep the deep door. The guardian no longer keeps everyone out. Its watch is corrupted: it admits the Dragon Queen's servants and destroys everyone else, the seal turned into a gate. The doors of the breach stand broken open from within, and the mountain leaks heat and fire-things up through its halls—the eruption that split it was the Queen's power pressing through from below.

The Church works the breach to open the door the rest of the way. It sends standing demands down the Iron Road for what its rites require—relics of the elder ages, rare reagents, seal-touched objects, prisoners of particular descriptions—and convoys deliver them under escort to the garrison.

At the bottom of the mountain is the dormant gate: a lake of magma that is also a door, ringed with the heaped plunder of a dozen kingdoms, arranged and waiting for an arrival. The Dragon Queen, Atravoraxis, waits on the far side of it. She is absent by default and comes through only when the long work of the main quest turns the key; until then the prepared hall stands ready for someone who has not yet come.

The Queen's Door.description: A Goblinate siege-camp ringing the breach high on the mountainside: palisades, watch-platforms, and barrack-tents pitched on the ash-slope, with elite troops and Pyre archpriests holding the approaches. Convoys are unloaded here under guard, their crates stacked and tallied. The split doors of the Fissure loom above the camp, smoke pouring from the gap.

The Fissure.description: The rent in the mountainside where the eruption tore it open: a chasm of broken black rock venting smoke and heat, and within it two doors of black stone forty feet high, cracked apart and hanging from their hinges. The doors were forced from the inside, the stone around their frames shattered outward. A passage leads down through the broken doorway into the dark of the mountain.
paths: The Halls of the Mountain King

The Halls of the Mountain King.description: Vast halls cut by giants in an age beyond memory, the ceilings lost in shadow, every doorway and stair built for beings three times a man's height. Colossal pillars carry carved friezes of forgotten victories. Over all of it, finer and far later, runs dwarven seal-work—runes and bindings chased across the elder stone. Wide ways lead deeper and down.

The Wards.description: The binding-works the dwarven wardens raised in the mountain's depths: a complex of ward-chambers, runic seal-rings set into floor and wall, and silent mechanisms whose purpose is half-forgotten. Heat bleeds up through the stone, and the seal-light has guttered or gone dark in places. At the heart of the works stands the chamber of the deep door, where a watcher of blue fire keeps its corrupted guard. A final descent opens beyond it.
paths: The Halls of the Mountain King

The Magma Portal Sanctum.description: The lowest hall of the mountain, a great vaulted chamber built around a lake of molten rock that glows and seethes in the dark. The plunder of a dozen kingdoms is arranged around the lake—heaped gold, arms, regalia, and treasures without number, set out as if for an arrival. The magma's surface is the dormant gate, still and waiting. Heat fills the chamber to the edge of bearing.

Clanhold Deepfire.name: Clanhold Deepfire
Clanhold Deepfire.basicInfo: A forge-city built into the caldera of a volcanic vent in the white peaks, where Clan Deepfire has bent the mountain's fire to their craft. Lava channels light the streets and feed the forges, and the city's smiths and miners are the boldest in the Whiteholds — the ones who dig deepest, forge hottest, and take what the mountain is loath to give.
Clanhold Deepfire.hiddenInfo:
Clan Deepfire are the delvers, and their creed is heat, hunger, and the deep vein. They believe the mountain's wealth is meant to be taken by those bold enough to go down for it, that fire is the tool that opens stone and the spirit that drives a dwarf onward, and that caution is the comfort of clans with nothing left to win. They are proud, ambitious, acquisitive, and brave past the edge of sense. Their forges work emberglass and fire-craft no other hold can equal, and their miners cut deeper than any sane dwarf would.

The clan's wealth and pride run on the deep, which is also their unspoken shame. Their deepest delve, chasing a rich vein, broke into old sealed workings beneath the kingdom not long before Stonehome fell into the dark. Deepfire holds, loudly, that the delve was no sin and the fall was not their doing — that the seals failed because they were rotten, that the dead of Stonehome dug their own graves through neglect, not Deepfire's daring. They will not say aloud, even among themselves, that it was their vein that ran toward the dark. The clan that blames them is Icerune, and the grudge between them is a wound that does not close.

Deepfire is split on the gold rush at Deepgate, but the loudest voices welcome it. The delvers swarming the pit are kindred spirits to them — bold folk braving the deep for what it holds — and the clan profits handsomely supplying them with fire-arms and forge-work. The cautious among them mutter that the Deep should never have been opened, but they are outvoted by those who say the deep was always meant to be braved.

The thane of Deepfire is ancient even for a dwarf, kept hale past his years by a lifetime breathing the volcanic heat, and he remembers the kingdom whole. He drove the clan's ambitions for a century and he will not hear that the great delve was a mistake. The clan's forges can work metals no other smiths can handle, and emberglass comes off their fires by the crate.

The deepest cuts, toward the vent, show emberglass in the rock.

The Lava Terrace.description: The heart of Deepfire's street-life, a broad district of homes and halls stepped down the caldera's inner wall on natural stone shelves, linked by bridges and stairs over the glowing lava channels below. The lava-light never fades, throwing warm orange across the carved stone faces of the buildings. The Cooled Cup tavern anchors the terrace, its doors thrown wide, its common room loud with smiths and miners come off the forges — famous across the white peaks for ale cooled deep in the rock, a rare luxury this near the fire. Stalls and shopfronts crowd the terrace-road, selling fire-craft and forge-work, and the talk runs as hot as the channels.

The Forge-Market.description: A bustling market terrace where Deepfire's work changes hands — blades and armor and tools laid out on stone counters, the orange shimmer of emberglass among the steel, traders come up from the lower holds to buy fire-craft found nowhere else. Apprentices run errands between the stalls and the forges, and the masters who sell here are proud, particular, and glad enough of custom. Bridges arch off over the lava channels toward the residential shelves, and the great forge-hall glows at the district's end.

The Lavaworks.description: The great forge-hall at the city's heart, built around a channeled lava flow that gives endless heat. Smiths' stations are ranged in rings around the molten core, the most skilled closest to the fire, and the din of hammers never stops. Finished work cools on the racks — blades, armor, tools of rare make, the orange shimmer of emberglass among the steel. Apprentices haul coal and water through the heat-haze while journeymen work the great bellows.

Cinderwing Eyries.description: A high warm gallery above the lava channels, open to the caldera's rising heat and strung with chains, perches, and little stone nesting-cups. Here Deepfire handlers raise cinderwings: small winged fire-salamanders, bright-eyed and coal-scaled, that glide on the heat rising from the channels and curl around a favored dwarf's shoulders like living embers. They are clever, vain, and loyal once bonded, useful for carrying sparks, finding warm seams, and warning of bad air in the deep cuts. Young cinderwings flit through the rafters and snap at thrown coal-beetles while handlers teach patient visitors how not to get singed.

Clanhold Stormhammer.name: Clanhold Stormhammer
Clanhold Stormhammer.basicInfo: An ancient stronghold of vast fitted megaliths atop a storm-wracked crag, seat of Clan Stormhammer, where lightning is forever stabbing down at the peak and the dwarves have learned to forge with it. The Stormhammer dwarves are hammerdwarves — they charge, they hit first, and they hold that anything worth doing is worth doing at a dead run with a warhammer. They draw the storm down into their forges to make stormsteel, the lightning-charged metal that shatters armor and stone.
Clanhold Stormhammer.hiddenInfo:
Clan Stormhammer are the hammerdwarves, and their creed fits on the head of a maul: hit it harder. They charge where others hold, swing where others guard, and trust that a hard enough blow ends a fight before a shieldwall has finished forming up. The clan runs hot and loud and proud, all swagger and big laughter and bigger boasts, and a Stormhammer would rather lose spectacularly than win by standing still.

The storm is the clan's craft and their glory. Lightning strikes the crag without cease, and the Stormhammer smiths long ago learned to draw it down into the forge and beat it into the metal — stormsteel, blue-sheened and humming, that cracks plate and stone like nothing else and answers a maul-blow with a peal of thunder. Their war-smiths call the storm down into the steel with rites of hammer and spark, and a Stormhammer thunder-hammer is a clan treasure handed down through maul-lineages, each with a name and a tally of skulls. Stormsteel is the clan's wealth and Highheath's wonder, and they sell it dear and brag about it free.

The great rivalry is with Clan Stonewall, and most of it is glorious sport — rustled rams, ruined feasts, kill-counts tallied on every joint hunt, and a grudge-roll of insults four hundred years deep. Stormhammer thinks Stonewall are timid wall-huggers who have mistaken hiding behind a board for valor, and loses no chance to say so, especially loudly and especially at feasts. But one wound is not sport. At Varric's Span, a generation back, a joint muster against a troll-horde broke: Stormhammer charged the horde ahead of the line, and Stonewall's wall held fast and did not break to reach them, and the charge was cut off and butchered on the bridge. Stonewall says the charge doomed itself by breaking discipline. Stormhammer holds that the wall stood there and watched their kin die rather than risk the line, and they will never forgive it, and they do not joke about that day, because the dead on the bridge were theirs.

The thane rules the hold, a huge, grinning, thunder-voiced warrior-smith with a famous stormhammer and a laugh that carries over the forges, who has never once backed down from a fight or a wager.

The Thunder-Court.description: The stronghold's great open court, a vast floor of fitted megalithic stone ringed by towering giant-cut walls, open to the storm-dark sky where lightning forks down at the iron rods raised along the battlements. This is where the clan gathers, drills its charges, and throws its roaring feasts, and the ground is scorched in places where the storm has struck close. The Flash and Boom tavern opens off the court, doors flung wide and common room thundering, and across the way the great forge-hall glows blue and gold, its noise rolling out across the stone.

The Flash and Boom.description: The clan's tavern, a riot of noise and firelight built into the old giant-stone, where off-shift smiths and warriors drink, boast, and arm-wrestle hard enough to crack the tables. The house brew is a fierce storm-ale served in tankards of blue-sheened stormsteel that prickle the lip, and the place takes its name from the game the clan plays with the storm: when the lightning flashes you drink, and when the thunder cracks you stop, and whoever's downed the most between the flash and the boom wins the round — a close strike is a mercy and a far one can drown a dwarf. The talk between rounds is all of the day's forging, the last great hunt, and exactly how soft Clan Stonewall has become, and a stranger who can hold their ale and their boasts is welcome at any table.

The Stormforge.description: The clan's great forge-hall, where the storm is made into steel — conductor-rods run down through the ceiling to the anvils, and when the lightning strikes the crag above, it comes down the rods in a crack of thunder and a wash of blue light, and the smiths beat the charge into the metal in the moment it lands. Stormsteel work cools blue-sheened and faintly humming on the racks — maul-heads, axe-blades, plate that crackles to the touch. War-smiths work the storm-rites at the central anvil, and the hall rings with hammer-fall and thunder.

The High Battlements.description: The stronghold's towering walls and wall-walks, giant-built and massive, raised along the crag's edge with great iron rods standing up from the parapets to catch the strikes. From up here the storm-wracked peaks roll away on every side, the country far below laid open, and the lightning comes down close enough to raise the hair on your arms. The stonework is colossal and old, fitted by hands far larger than a dwarf's, and the marks of the clan are carved over the giant-work that came before.

Clanhold Icerune.name: Clanhold Icerune
Clanhold Icerune.basicInfo: A fortress-city carved into the heart of a great glacier in the white peaks, where Clan Icerune works rune and cold into walls that the worst things in the world cannot break. They are the runeguard of the Whiteholds — the clan that seals the buried dangers shut and stands the watch at every door that must stay closed. Their rune-graved ice turns blades, holds back monsters, and binds what should never walk, and their warriors and ward-priests are the ones who go where something has gotten loose and put it back behind a wall.
Clanhold Icerune.hiddenInfo:
Clan Icerune are the runeguard, and their creed is that some things must stay shut and someone has to be strong enough to keep them so. They hold that the deep places hold horrors meant to stay buried, that the old prohibitions were written in blood for good reason, and that cold is the discipline that holds a thing in its place — and they back that creed with rune-ice that stops an axe-blow cold and walls that a charging monster breaks its skull against. They are proud, unbending, and fearless in the way of folk who have seen what gets out when a seal fails. Their ward-craft binds the restless dead, holds the deep horrors behind stone and ice, and is sought across the mountains wherever something must be kept shut for good.

The clan's pride and their grief are the same stone: the seal that failed. Icerune ward-craft held the old prohibitions on the buried Darek workings for ages, until the night Stonehome fell into the dark — and the seals that should have held it were Icerune's. The clan holds, fiercely, that the wards were sound and the fault lay elsewhere: that Clan Deepfire's reckless delve drove a vein straight into the dark and doomed the kingdom, that no ward ever made could stand against dwarves digging toward damnation from the other side. They will not say aloud, even among themselves, that their wards failed on the one night that mattered most. The clan they blame is Deepfire, and the grudge between them is a wound that does not close.

Icerune is united on the gold rush at Deepgate, and united against it. To them the delvers swarming the pit are fools tearing open the very thing the runeguard spent an age keeping shut, and every haul dragged up from the Darek dark is one more horror loose in the world. The clan wants the Deep sealed again and the sacrilege ended, and chafes that it cannot simply wall the pit and be done — not with a delver-city grown around its mouth and the clans forbidden from open war. 

The thane of Icerune carries the weight of the failed seal as her own, though she was not yet thane the night it broke. She has spent her years since making certain no ward of hers will ever give, and she sends her runeguard out to seal what gets loose with a cold resolve that does not bend.

The Ice-Hall.description: The clan's great hall, carved deep in the glacier where the living rock meets the ice, its walls dark stone veined with quartz and graven with protective runes that catch the firelight. Many hearths blaze along its length — warmth is sacred here, hard-won against the cold, and never let to fail. Long tables seat the clan for meals and ale strong enough to strip paint, and furs and war-banners hang from the walls between racks of rune-marked arms.

The Rune-Market.description: A market hall carved into the ice and stone where Icerune's craft changes hands — rune-graved arms and armor, ward-stones, sealing-work, and cold-craft sought from across the peaks. The walls are sculpted ice, clear and blue and graven with runes that hold the glacier back, and braziers burn between the stalls without ever melting them. Traders come up from the lower holds for ward-work found nowhere else, and the ward-smiths who sell here are exacting and proud of it. Passages of carved ice lead deeper toward the warding hall and the clan's chambers.

The Warding Hall.description: The clan's great work-hall, a vast chamber where the rune-ice is cut and the seals are made, the walls themselves a masterwork of warding that holds back the weight and cold of the glacier overhead. Ward-priests and rune-smiths work at long benches over slabs of clear ice and graven stone, cutting the runes that turn blades and bind monsters. Finished seals and rune-marked arms stand racked along the walls, and a great test-wall of rune-ice stands at the hall's end, scarred and gouged where the clan proves its work against blade and beast.

The Rimewatch Roost.description: A high vaulted chamber of blue glacier-ice where the runeguard keep their rime-owls — pale, silent birds perched in carved ice-hollows up the walls and along the rune-graved beams, watching the hall below with wide pale eyes. The runeguard raise the owls from the egg and bond them young, and a bonded owl rides a runeguard's shoulder out to the seals and the dark places, for a rime-owl sees clean through glacier-gloom and feels the strain on a ward before any dwarf can — it goes still and stares, or gives a low call, when a seal is pressed or something unseen draws near. Ice-perches and roosting-hollows ring the chamber, and owlkeepers move among the young birds.

Whitefang Hold.name: Whitefang Hold
Whitefang Hold.basicInfo: A frost giant stronghold in the highest peaks of the north, a hollowed mountain held by a people three times the height of a man. It is reached only by the North Wind Pass, one of the most brutal roads in the world, where the wind comes off the peaks hard enough to put a traveler on the ground.
Whitefang Hold.hiddenInfo:
The frost giants of Whitefang Hold are a wild people of the high ice, proud, loud, and old in their ways, and the cold that killed the Northrealm is nothing to them — they were always here and always will be. They live as they always have: feasting, boasting, hunting, and settling rank by who can out-do, out-fight, and out-tell the rest. They are not a marauding horde; they are neighbors, on their own terms, dangerous chiefly to those who give them reason or bore them.

The giants and the ice drakes of the White Wyrmspire are locked in an old feud that neither side will end. Young giants prove themselves by climbing the Wyrmspire and stealing a drake's egg; the drakes answer by raiding the giants' herds and hunting their stragglers. It costs lives both ways, every generation, and both peoples seem to want it that way. A party seen near drake eggs may be taken for giants poaching the proof of manhood — or hired by giants too canny to make the climb themselves.

IMPORTANT: The giants are not hostile by default, but they are perilous to anyone who fails their measure. They respect courage, endurance, and a good story, and they despise cowardice and flattery. A smallfolk who impresses them — by daring, by strength, by a tale well told, by surviving something — is fed, housed, and may find the giants will do things for them that no coin could buy. A smallfolk who bores them, lies to them, or shows weakness is, at best, pelted off the mountain. The jarl rules the hold, and his favor is worth more than any door.

North Wind Pass.description: A high mountain road through a notch in the peaks, where blizzards rage more often than not and the wind funnels through hard enough to knock a traveler flat. Sheer rock to either side, deep snow underfoot, and no shelter the length of it. The only way through is forward.

The White Gate.description: The entrance to the hold — a rough-hewn opening in the mountainside, wide enough for three giants to pass abreast. No doors, no portcullis. High ledges flank the opening on both sides, set with stacked boulders, and sentries watch from them, deciding whether those who approach are worth announcing or worth pelting.

The Jarl's Hall.description: A vast cavern where the giants gather, its ceiling lost in the dark above. Fire-pits blaze along the floor, throwing heat and shadow across stone slabs heaped with food and drink. The giants feast here, bellowing songs and challenges the length of the hall. The high seat stands at the far end, raised above the rest.

The War Grounds.description: An open plateau behind the hold where the giants train, wrestle, and settle disputes — though to an outsider's eye the line between sport, contest, and a real fight is hard to find. The ground is bare rock and packed snow, worn down by heavy use. Trophies and trophy-poles from hunts and raids stand driven into the frozen earth.

The White Wyrmspire.name: The White Wyrmspire
The White Wyrmspire.basicInfo: A lone peak in the high north where ice drakes have nested since before the Northrealm. The drakes are enormous, ancient, and territorial, and they suffer no trespass. Hunters climb anyway, because drake bone, scale, and eggs are worth more than most people see in a lifetime, and a single rimebone haul buys a whole winter.
The White Wyrmspire.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The ice drakes default hostile to anything on their peak and do not parley. They are not beasts but cunning, patient hunters with long memories. The eldest, the White Eye, has outwitted giant raiding parties for generations and remembers the faces of those who flee. Drakes glide down silent from the high ledges, strike, and climb out of reach to wait; they will harry a party for hours rather than commit to a losing fight, and they hold grudges across seasons.

The frost giants of Whitefang Hold and the drakes are locked in an old feud: young giants prove themselves by stealing drake eggs, the drakes answer by raiding the giants' herds, and neither side will stop. A party seen taking eggs may be mistaken for giants, or used by them.

Rimebone, the old drake bone frozen into the ice of the peak, is the prize: like frostjade, it is worked into weapons that strike with killing cold and are carried against fire-things. Drake scale armors against cold, and a single egg is worth a fortune to giants, collectors, and worse. The eggs sit in the nesting shelf; the oldest and richest remains lie in the White Eye's lair near the summit, where the cold is past natural and the climb back down is the hard part.

The Approaches.description: The lower slopes, where the mountain narrows toward its peak. Open rock and wind-packed snow with little cover and a long fall on the outward side. Sheltered overhangs along the climb are wide enough to shelter a camp, screened from the wind and from the ledges above.

The Nesting Grounds.description: A broad windswept shelf high on the peak. Nests of packed ice and stone, each the span of a wagon, cradle eggs the size of ale-barrels. The ledges above overlook the shelf on three sides, and old bone lies thick between the nests. The only cover is the nests themselves. Some of the old bone between the nests is rimebone, frozen into the ice.

The White Eye's Lair.description: A deep cave near the summit. The entrance passage tightens to a crawl, then opens into a high vault of blue-white ice. Frozen spoil is set into the walls and floor — arms, bone, and the leavings of old kills, locked in the ice. A single way in and out.

The Crevasse.name: The Crevasse
The Crevasse.basicInfo: A great glacier in the high north, split clean down the middle, with the ruins of a white-stone city standing in the walls of the chasm — towers and halls part-crushed by the ice, part-exposed. The architecture matches nothing else in Larion, and no living people claim it. What can be carried out of it sells for a fortune to those who collect such things, which is reason enough for some to climb down.
The Crevasse.hiddenInfo:
The white city was raised by a people older than the Northrealm, older than the oldest stories of the nanukin, and nothing the dwarves have recorded names them. The builders are still here, and they do not welcome visitors.

IMPORTANT: The city's dead and its guardians default hostile to intruders who go deep, and they do not parley. Its old rulers remain as ice-mummies — the desiccated, frost-preserved dead in their halls, cold and patient and slow to rouse, but relentless once they do. They command the coldstone constructs: figures of the same white stone as the city, carved and bound by the builders, which stand motionless until the mummies wake them and then move to defend the halls. The constructs are the muscle; the mummies are the will behind them. Disturbing the deep chambers wakes both.

The white-stone relics of the city — devices, ornaments, and worked pieces of the builders' craft — are the prize, and the deepest and richest of them lie in the White Hall with the mummy-lords that keep them. The relics do not always behave: some are inert, some are not, and which is which is not always plain until carried.

The Rim.description: The lip of the chasm, where the glacier splits in two. The gap runs for miles and drops hundreds of feet. Below, white towers and broken walls jut from both ice faces at angles, half-encased, half-clear. The only ways down are rope and a long, exposed climb against the ice.

The Crevasse Floor.description: The bottom of the chasm, between two walls of glacier shot through with buried white stone. Fallen masonry and sheared blocks of ice litter the ground, with intact sections of the city standing among them. The light is blue and dim, filtered down through the ice overhead. Sound is close and muffled here.

The White Hall.description: A great structure part-exposed in the ice wall, entered through a gap where the glacier has sheared it open. Within, a vaulted hall of white stone stands cracked but whole, its floor smooth and its columns sized larger than a hall for men would need. Figures of white stone stand among the columns. The cold deepens toward the back, where the hall runs into unbroken ice.

Fort Redclaw.name: Fort Redclaw
Fort Redclaw.basicInfo: An ice-fort in the high north, carved from glacier and packed snow by the claws of the white bearfolk who hold it — the nanukin, a towering people of the cold, sheathed in white fur and armored for war. Fort Redclaw is the seat of the Redclaw line, who keep this stretch of the ice for the nanukin kingdom of the far north. Walls of packed ice stand thick enough to turn a battering-ram, and the tunnels run wide enough for an armored bearfolk to pass at the shoulder.
Fort Redclaw.hiddenInfo:
The white bearfolk (nanukin) of Fort Redclaw were never broken by the cold the way the snowlanders were. The freeze that killed the Northrealm is, to them, only the weather of home — they were always a people of the high ice and they live well in it. They hold the fort as a garrison of the nanukin kingdom of the far north, maintaining the line's claim on the southern ranges, and they regard the human survivors clinging to their warm springs with something between pity and bafflement.

They are not hostile to outsiders. They are pragmatic and direct: they tolerate visitors who are useful or interesting, trade and share what they know, and hire capable smallfolk for work that wants someone smaller or quicker than a bearfolk. They have no patience for flattery or empty words. Everything here runs on dominance and respect, and respect is bought with deeds — a hard task done, a strong hand in a contest, courage shown rather than claimed. A stranger who proves themselves rises in their regard from tolerated, to trusted, to one the chief will hear; a stranger who wastes their time does not.

Chief Redclaw rules from the great hall, where the Ice Throne is hacked from a single block of glacier. Each chief carves a new throne with their own claws on taking command, and the old thrones are broken, so the seat in the hall is always the work of the one who sits it.

The Ice Road.description: A track across open glacier toward a white mass that barely shows against the white land behind it — the fort is hard to make out until you are close on it. Armored nanukin sentries watch from the walls, tall and pale and unhurried.

The Gate.description: A passage cut through walls of packed ice many feet thick, the surfaces scored deep with the claw-marks of their making. The way is wide and high — built to the scale of armored bearfolk, who stand guard to either side, a head taller than a tall man and broad as a door.

The Great Hall.description: The fort's central chamber, carved from solid glacial ice. The Ice Throne stands at the far end — a rough seat hewn from a single block, still bearing the claw-marks of the chief who cut it. Fire-pits burn down the length of the hall, and the nanukin gather here to eat, drink, argue, and settle matters by strength.

The Dens.description: Tunnels branching off the great hall into sleeping chambers carved from the ice, wide and low. The nanukin den in groups for warmth, armor and weapons stacked within reach.

The Yard.description: An open space behind the fort where the nanukin train and contest — grappling, charging, running formations in their armor. The ground is packed ice, worn smooth and rutted by heavy use. Trophies of past raids and hunts stand on poles driven into the frozen ground.

Dun Solas.name: Dun Solas
Dun Solas.basicInfo: A dwarven city in a vast cavern lit by the Eye, a great circular opening in the ceiling far above. At the cavern's bottom lies Lake Two-Waters, fed by underground rivers and by Skyriver, a waterfall pouring down through the Eye. From the lake the walls curve up and away in tiered ring-roads, each lined with beautiful stonework facades cut from the living rock. The terrace farms grow rare mushrooms and lichens famed in brewing and alchemy, and the city is renowned for fine metalwork and mechanisms so delicate they seem alive. It is a Free City, beholden to no clan, busy and prosperous and welcoming to those who respect its ways.
Dun Solas.hiddenInfo:
Dun Solas is the heart of trade, coin, and crime in Highheath and it stays free by keeping its two great neighbors at each other's throats just gently enough. Clan Stonewall and Clan Stormhammer both keep kin-halls and factors in the city, and both are openly working to own it without being seen to own it — chasing council seats, trade-shares, contracts, marriages brokered for advantage, and the question of whose law runs on which ring. The merchant council that governs the city survives by keeping the two from open feuding.

A generation back a Stonewall–Stormhammer wedding meant to seal the peace turned at the feast — a pointed toast, an old word about Varric's Span — and within an hour the whole city had picked a side and a wedding had become a festival had become a five-ring, lake-to-summit dwarf melee that took three days to burn out and nearly made the council close the Iris, the great metal shutter over the Eye, to stop it.

The Trade Guild is the city's competent neutral institution and the surest way for a clanless adventurer to make a name. The Guild keeps the overland roads safe — the passes, the caravans, the high country where the trade runs — and solves the city's own troubles: theft rings, contract fraud, a clan faction reaching too far, a fixer rigging a contest, a fence moving rustled cattle. The Guild also holds the only sanctioned passage to the deep roads beneath the city and guards who goes down.

Beneath the honest city run the Undervaults, where the Syndicate keeps the dark side of every trade above — smuggling past the clan tolls, fixing council contracts, and moving soulstones, gems with a soul trapped inside, down from Deepgate in the Whiteholds to their buyers. Renegade and exiled dwarves, oath-broke factors, and clan castoffs do the work nobody clean will touch.

In crisis the city seals itself by closing the Iris, a great mechanism of metal plates that slides across the Eye.

Edge of the Eye.description: A broad stone platform high on the cavern wall, ringing the topside aperture of the Eye where it opens to the sky. The Waterdrop's pulley-lifts descend from here into the city below, and the great metal plates of the Iris stand ready around the opening's rim. The Long Stair spirals down the inside of the cavern wall alongside the lifts, little used by choice.

Lakebottom.description: The lowest tier, where the Waterdrop lifts come down to land at stone piers reaching into Lake Two-Waters. Skyriver Waterfall thunders down from the Eye far overhead, throwing mist across the water. From here the whole city rises in carved rings — Lakebottom, the Market Ring, the Craft Ring, the Farm Ring, the High Ring. Fishing boats bob at the piers and dwarves swim in the cold water year-round. A rope-ferry crosses to an island at the lake's center, staircases wind up to the Market Ring, and the Wetted Whistle inn dominates the shore.

Market Ring.description: The second tier, a continuous curved street of shop-fronts cut into the cavern wall, busy at every hour, goods on stone counters and hanging from iron hooks. Lodging houses and money-changers cater to traders from across Highheath. Two halls face each other across the ring-road, larger and prouder than the shops between them — one flying Stonewall's colors, one Stormhammer's.

The Wetted Whistle.description: A sprawling tavern built into the cavern wall at Lakebottom, its front terrace half out over the water, perpetually loud and perpetually full. The Trade Guild owns it and runs its business from the upper floors. A work-board by the door is crowded with postings from the city and the surface roads — lift crews being shaken down, valuable Craft Ring work stolen to order, false clan tolls, crooked factors, and caravan routes being bled. The hardest road notices carry blunt warnings; anything pointing toward troll-held Varric's Span is work for a proven crew, not a casual first outing. Crews form at the tables, deals are struck over ale, and veterans tell newcomers which jobs will pay and which will kill them.

Trade Guild Headquarters.description: The upper floors of the Wetted Whistle, reached by a guarded stair behind the bar. Offices where Guild factors negotiate contracts, weigh shipments, and take the measure of those looking for work. Maps of the high roads and the passes cover the walls, marked with where the trade runs and where it has been bled — the troll-bridges at Varric's Span, Clan Bighorn's tor on the Crookback, the contested glens. A heavy iron door at the back opens onto the only sanctioned passage to the deep roads, and the Guild itself is the lock on it.

Craft Ring.description: The third tier, where workshops cut deep into the rock — lens-grinders, lantern-makers, locksmiths, and the famous mechanism-wrights whose work seems almost alive. Apprentices run errands between masters, and the craftspeople are proud, particular, and not to be rushed for anyone's coin. Finished pieces gleam in shop-windows; the sound of fine tools never stops.

Farm Ring.description: The fourth tier, terraced beds of mushrooms, lichens, and mosses grown in careful rows, thriving in the light that filters down from the Eye. The rare growths here feed the city's brewing and alchemy trades. Children from the lower rings are sent up when they get underfoot, and the tiers are quiet but for the drip of water and the tread of tenders.

High Ring.description: The uppermost tier, carved just below the rough cavern ceiling, where old families and wealthy merchants live above the noise of the lower rings. The view takes in the whole city — the descending rings, the lake far below, Skyriver's endless fall through the mist.

The Warm Pools.description: An open-air bathhouse fed by lake water heated over vents, pools steaming at every temperature from warm to scalding. Old Dun Solas opinion holds that warm water weakens the constitution, so the clientele runs to outlanders, the elderly, and young dwarves pretending they only came ironically. Benches and low tables ring the pools.

Lake Isle.description: A large island at the center of Lake Two-Waters, reached by rope-ferry. Colorful cave mushrooms form a canopy over moss and lichen, and old shrines that predate the city stand among them. Dwarves come here to commune with their ancestors, walk among the mushrooms, or escape the bustle of the rings.

The League Chapterhouse.description: A broad hall cut into the stone of the Market Ring, with an open balcony above Lake Two-Waters. Highland maps hang between giant shields, broken troll weapons, and climbing gear left by returning expeditions. Dwarves, giantborn, and travelers from the lowlands gather around heavy tables.

Dun Beithir.name: Dun Beithir
Dun Beithir.basicInfo: A snowlander fishing village on a frozen lake shore, built around an ancient stone broch that has stood against the sea-wind since before the cold came. The folk here are ice-fishers, cutting the frozen lake for their catch, and hunters of the beithir — the great serpents of these waters — which they take together as a whole village. Dwarves of the north keep a presence here too, smithing and trading, drawn by the serpent-bone and the cold-country goods that pass through the harbor.
Dun Beithir.hiddenInfo:
Dun Beithir is a safe and welcoming place, hard-used and warm-hearted — one of the snowlander footholds the cold has not yet taken, where a stranger off the ice can find a fire, a meal, and work. The villagers are ice-fishers first: they live by the holes they cut in the frozen lake and the lampfish they haul up for oil to burn through the long dark. They are also serpent-hunters, and the beithir-hunt is the whole community's work — when one is sighted, every able hand has a part, on the harpoons, the lines, the ice, or the butchery, and a successful kill feeds and supplies the village for a season.

The dwarves here are mostly of the northern holds, prospect-crews and traders who came up for the cold materials and stayed to work them. They smith beithir bone and the rarer rimebone into gear that answers the things of the cold, buy serpent-oil and hide for the southern trade, and keep their own hall by the harbor. Snowlander and dwarf get on plainly here, in the way of people who need each other's trade and each other's backs against the same sea.

The beithir is hunted offshore, out on and under the frozen lake, and is not a danger within the village. IMPORTANT: a beithir is a great cold sea-serpent, and out on the ice it defaults hostile and lethal — it strikes from below, smashing up through the frozen surface, takes prey or hunters off the ice, and submerges to circle and come again. The hunt is dangerous work and not every hand comes back from it. Beithir hide, the great fangs, and rendered serpent-oil are the village's wealth and its trade.

The Broch.description: The ancient round tower at the village's heart, drystone walls thick enough to laugh at the wind, a fire always burning in its great round room. The villagers gather here — fishers, hunters, and the dwarves of the harbor-hall among them — to eat, drink, mend nets and gear, and settle the village's business. Carved housewardens watch out from the lintels, facing the cold.

The Ice-Harbor.description: The working coast below the broch, where the lake lies frozen out past sight and the village's boats sit hauled up on the ice, useless until a thaw that rarely comes. Fishing-holes are cut and tended across the near ice, racks of split fish and hung nets stand along the shore, and the long frames and winches of the serpent-hunt wait beside the butchery-sheds. The dwarves' harbor-hall stands at the water's edge, smoke rising from its forge.

The Cutting Ice.description: The frozen lake itself, out beyond the harbor, a flat white expanse cut with fishing-holes and scored by the drag-marks of past hauls. The ice groans and shifts underfoot, and dark water shows where it has been cut or broken. There is no cover here and a long way back to shore.

Greathearth.name: Greathearth
Greathearth.basicInfo: Greathearth is a large hillside village where the high roads of the Whiteholds meet on neutral territory between clans. Houses, inns, and terraces climb a sheltered slope around the Greathearth, an immense communal hall where residents and travelers eat, trade, perform, and find lodging. Above the village, Mercy's Refuge is a shrine of the Lady of Mercy where priests and druids care for wounded magical creatures. Greathearth is famous for its cloudhorns, large pale mountain goats whose extraordinary footing carries riders and baggage over paths no horse could climb.
Greathearth.hiddenInfo:
Most of Greathearth's permanent residents are human or dwarf, with humans slightly more numerous. Gnome and giantborn households also live here, along with several minotaur families whose arrival lies beyond any record the village has kept. The minotaurs have different trades and allegiances, and no one local treats their presence as remarkable.

Greathearth belongs to no clan. House Merovar is a human noble family entrusted with the surrounding hillside and the safer approaches under a grant from the old dwarf kings. The family maintains Merovar House above the village, supports Mercy's Refuge, and hosts nobles, wealthy travelers, celebrated riders, and distinguished healers. It neither governs the clans nor controls the Refuge.

The Greathearth is the village's common hall and its everyday center. Residents and travelers share its tables, kitchens, entertainment, and inexpensive guest galleries. More prosperous visitors use the discreet inns and private rooms of the Guest Lanes, and Greathearth has a wide reputation as a place where people arrange meetings, begin affairs, renew old attachments, or encounter someone far from the company in which they are usually seen.

Mercy's Refuge shelters wounded magical creatures brought down from the peaks or carried here by travelers. Its priests provide sanctuary and healing, while druids understand unfamiliar bodies and behavior, guide rehabilitation, and determine when a creature can safely return to the wild. The patients change with the story and may include griffons, mountain drakes, owlbears, giant birds, elementals, or stranger creatures. Those well enough to tolerate company may be exercised through the village or on the high pastures under a druid's care.

Cloudhorns are large pale mountain goats with broad backs, sweeping horns, and extraordinary footing. They carry riders and baggage over slopes, ledges, and broken paths that horses cannot manage. They are intelligent, stubborn, and prone to challenging one another by butting horns; an unattended cloudhorn may climb stairs, walls, roofs, or outdoor tables simply because they are there.

Greathearth's outfitters are known for making useful equipment for unusual bodies and creatures. They fit armor and clothing around horns, wings, tails, uncommon limbs, or great size; make saddles, harnesses, barding, and protective gear for mounts and companions; and sell restorative potions, antidotes, charms, ordinary weapons, and travel gear.

Wealthy patrons compete to sponsor the Refuge's most impressive patients and attend their release, sometimes caring more for association with a rare creature than for the work itself. A few residents have gone further. Recovering creatures are sometimes stolen from the Refuge and sold alive to collectors, fighting pits, or magical experimenters. A small corrupt ring identifies valuable patients, supplies sedatives, opens private routes through the hillside, and hides them in guesthouses or covered transport before they leave Greathearth.

The Sun Terrace.description: A broad south-facing terrace below the Greathearth serves as the village's principal arrival and open market. Merchants and vendors sell weapons, armor, charms, potions, clothing, cloudhorn tack, prepared food, and goods brought over the high roads among outdoor tables and grassy banks. The terrace overlooks the lower valleys and ridge after ridge of white mountain. Villagers gather here for meals, music, games, dancing, and cloudhorn races on the sloping ground below.

The Greathearth.description: The immense stone-and-timber hall at the center of the village rises through two open galleries around a broad stone hearth. Long tables fill the main floor, several kitchens serve food through open arches, and a low platform hosts musicians, dancers, storytellers, and informal contests. Hearthfolds—hot folded bread filled with sharp cloudhorn cheese and savory or sweet additions—are served throughout the day. The upper galleries provide simple lodging and look down over the crowded hall.

The Guest Lanes.description: Steep lanes of handsome houses and small inns climb between the Greathearth and Merovar House. The Seven Landings offers lively rooms on several levels, while the Far Lantern is quieter and more private. Many prosperous residents also take paying boarders. Because buildings open onto different streets above and below, private stairs, garden doors, and a few deliberately concealed entrances allow guests to come and go discreetly.

The Outfitters' Row.description: A compact row of workshops serving travelers, unusual peoples, mounts, and animal companions. Armorers and clothiers fit equipment around horns, tails, wings, uncommon limbs, and great size. Saddlers make cloudhorn tack, barding, harness, and gear for stranger mounts, while healers and charm-sellers stock restorative potions, antidotes, medicines, and protective charms alongside ordinary weapons and travel equipment.

Mercy's Refuge.description: A shrine of the Lady of Mercy occupies several green shelves above the village. A stone chapel and treatment hall open onto sheltered paddocks, enclosed caves, recovery pools, and a broad flight yard. Priests and druids care for wounded magical creatures here and prepare them to return to the wild. Patients safe enough to leave their enclosures may exercise on the surrounding paths under close guidance.

The Cloudhorn Yard.description: Terraced stables and open pens stand beside the mountain road. Large pale cloudhorns pick their way over stone steps, mounting blocks, rails, and low roofs while handlers fit saddles or separate animals determined to butt one another. Riders, guides, and pack animals can be hired here, and young locals practice on the steep training paths above the yard.

The High Pastures.description: Open grass and heather rise above the village toward broken mountain slopes. Cloudhorn herds graze across the hillside, and marked paths lead between sheltered folds, lookout rocks, and the quieter outer grounds of Mercy's Refuge. Druids sometimes bring recovering creatures here to walk, fly, graze, or test their strength away from the crowded streets.

Merovar House.description: The home of House Merovar stands on a wooded shelf above Greathearth, an elegant stone-and-timber manor with broad windows, terraced gardens, guest wings, and its own cloudhorn stable. The family receives noble visitors, wealthy travelers, healers, riders, and patrons of Mercy's Refuge. Public dinners and creature-release celebrations open parts of the house, while the family rooms and private guest suites remain closely kept.

Gallows Wood.name: Gallows Wood
Gallows Wood.basicInfo: An old forest north of Ardan's Watch named for its history of banditry, kidnapping for ransom, and other lawlessness. The High Road runs through it, carrying all the overland trade between Ardan's Watch and Highheath to the north. The trees grow close and thick over the road. It is the most dangerous stretch of the northern road, and travelers go through it in numbers when they can.
Gallows Wood.hiddenInfo: Gallows Wood is the bad stretch of the High Road between Ardan's Watch and Highheath. It is the route north, so what happens here matters to trade in both directions. The forest is dense and broken, with good cover off the road. It is the kind of country where road-trouble takes hold.

South Gallows Wood.description: Where the High Road enters Gallows Wood from the south, on the Ardan's Watch side. The road is open here and the wood begins.

The Darkest Mile.description: The middle of the wood, where the trees close thickest over the High Road. The road narrows and the cover comes right up to its edge. This is where visibility is lowest, and the road is most dangerous.

North Gallows Wood.description: Where the High Road enters Gallows Wood from the north, on the Highheath side.

The Old Holdfast.description: An abandoned stone fortress in the trees off the High Road. It is largely collapsed, though sections of it are still in good enough repair to provide shelter.

The Crossroads Inn.name: The Crossroads Inn
The Crossroads Inn.basicInfo: A busy inn on the High Road around a day's journey to the north of Ardan's Watch near the southern end of Gallows Wood. The inn complex is surrounded by a wooden palisade fence with front and back gates. In addition to the main inn building, which stands two stories tall, a stable and barn complete the property.

The Yard.description: The front courtyard inside the palisade gates where carriages unload passengers and cargo. Worn ruts in the dirt show the heavy traffic this inn receives from merchant caravans and messengers.

Stables.description: A wooden stable building with stalls for a dozen horses, space for storing carriages, and a hayloft above.

Taproom.description: The inn's main common room with long tables for dining, a large fireplace, and a bar where the innkeeper serves ale and wine. Stairs lead up to the guest rooms while doors connect to the kitchen and front yard.

The Royal Chamber.description: The inn's supposedly finest guest room on the second floor. Despite its grand name, the room suffers from a leaking roof, drafty windows, and thin walls that offer little privacy from the taproom noise below.

Deepgate.name: Deepgate
Deepgate.basicInfo: A boomtown sprawled around the great crater in the white peaks where Stonehome, the dwarves' shared capital, fell into the dark. At the crater's bottom gapes the mouth of the Darek Deep — the buried halls of the dareks, the old dwarves of the deep, full of ancient treasure and the constructs that still guard it. Adventurers come from across Larion to delve the fallen city and the dead halls beneath it, and a lawless rush-town has grown around the rim to outfit them, buy their hauls, and bury the ones who don't come back.
Deepgate.hiddenInfo:
Deepgate is a delver-city built on a grave. Stonehome was the seasonal capital both clans shared, and when its seals failed it dropped whole into the dark, empty but for its dead, opening into the Darek Deep below — the buried halls of the dareks. It was sacrilege, for ages, to seek the Darek dark. Now it is torn wide open, and a gold rush has swarmed the crater: crews, sellswords, tinkers, wizards, and fortune-hunters of every species, all here to plunder the dead city and the darek halls beneath. The town is loud, rough, and rich, and no single authority holds it.

The prize underneath is the kingdom itself. Stonehome's throne-hall lies down in the dark now, and whoever reclaims it reclaims the crown neither clan will yield. So both clans keep a presence on the rim and grind at each other in the open: Clan Deepfire half-backs the rush, the delvers being kindred spirits and the trade rich, holding that the deep was always meant to be braved; Clan Icerune wants the Deep sealed again and the sacrilege ended, and seethes that they cannot simply wall a pit with a whole city grown around its mouth. Neither will yield the throne to the other and neither can take it, so they circle, deal, and undercut one another while the crater fills with strangers.

The Syndicate has come for the Deep in force. The High Men, the crime-lords who rule the Syndicate, have named the Darek dark their highest prize, and they do not need open war with dwarf clans to take it — they have coin enough to simply buy the rush. They fund crews, fence Darek salvage, and corner the trade in soulstones coming up the pit, and their hand in Deepgate is Greloq's Company, the richest and most hated delving outfit on the rim, who hold the Old Keep above the town and get to the best finds first by every dirty means there is.

The Deep gives nothing freely — the darek constructs still guard the halls, the morlocks press up from below, and now and then a construct climbs the pit on its own. The town's rhythm is the delve: gear up, form a crew, go down, fight for what you find, and haul it back up to sell. The Deep End is where it all happens — crews form there, deals are struck, and the veterans who lived through a delve tell you which halls will kill you.

The Rimside Market.description: Where the road ends and Deepgate begins, a sprawl of stalls and counters ringing the lip of the great crater, the fallen city's broken towers just visible tilting into the dark far below. The trade is Darek salvage and the gear to win it — black iron blades, construct-shell bracers, ward-stones, soulstones sealed in lead cases, and stranger finds that change by the day — sold by hawkers shouting over one another. Tinkers pull apart darek mechanisms at their benches. Two stone halls face each other across the market's width, one flying Deepfire's colors and one Icerune's. Adventurers, sellswords, and folk of half the species in Larion crowd the rim.

The Deep End.description: The delvers' tavern, built right on the lip of the crater, one whole side open to the drop where a rail lets a drinker lean out and watch the cages go down and come up. Rooms upstairs, hot food, cold drink, and someone always playing something loud over the din of a hundred crews. The veterans who have lived through a delve hold court at the good tables, and the green and the desperate buy them drinks for what they know. The tavern runs its own hoist down into the crater, a private cage for those who can pay.

The Old Keep.description: A stone keep on the high ground above the town, the only proper building in a place thrown up from timber — some old mountain watchtower, long abandoned and now seized and held. Greloq's Company flies its flag from the tower, and light spills from every window after dark while the rest of Deepgate sleeps. Hard-eyed crews in the best gear on the rim come and go from its gates, and the townsfolk give the place a wide berth and speak of it low.

The Pit-Stair.description: The mouth of the crater, where the descent into the dark begins — a ring of hoist-towers and heavy winches around the rim, cages and rope-stairs running down past the broken, tilted halls of fallen Stonehome toward the Darek Deep below. Crews check their weapons and ward-charms at the head of the descent, and a worn shrine-post stands at the lip where the going-down touch it for luck. Far down through the gap, the dead city's stonework gives way to older, stranger work, and the cold breathes up out of the deep.

The Dauvigne Preserve.name: The Dauvigne Preserve
The Dauvigne Preserve.basicInfo: The Dauvigne Preserve is a private hunting forest belonging to the wealthy House Dauvigne, enclosed by a low stone wall and kept by gamekeepers. Oak and ash shade the riding trails, and hunting blinds overlook clearings stocked with deer. The Dauvignes have hunted here for generations.
The Dauvigne Preserve.hiddenInfo: Something is hunting the hunters in the preserve. The gamekeepers have heard strange sounds from the deep covert — calls that sound like men shouting for help, and the gamekeepers who went to find the source did not come back. The hunter is a leucrotta, a stag-bodied predator that mimics voices it has heard, here the voices of the men it has already killed; it lairs in a cave in the ravine with their bones and gear. The managed forest near the gate is safe enough; the wild growth around the ravine is not.

The Preserve Gate.description: A stone arch in the boundary wall where the road enters the forest. A gamekeeper's cottage sits beside it, tools and snares on the porch. The main riding trail leads north under the canopy.

The Riding Trails.description: Paths wide enough for horses, winding through managed woodland. Undergrowth cleared, sightlines good. Hunting blinds and feeding stations at intervals.

The Deep Covert.description: Where the managed forest turns wild. Trees crowd together, brush chokes the trails, game paths replace riding tracks. Boar and deer shelter here, and the calls come from somewhere deeper still.

The Ravine.description: A rocky gulch cutting through the preserve's heart. Fallen trees span the gap, and a stream threads the bottom past cave mouths and stony overhangs. No horse can pass here. Whatever has been calling in the covert lairs somewhere in this broken ground.

Fallsmeet.name: Fallsmeet
Fallsmeet.basicInfo: Fallsmeet is a prosperous walled village in a green Drusavian dale, built where two upland streams plunge past a rocky spur and meet below Castle Twinfall. Its Open Games draw competitors, patrons, and visitors from across Larion for martial, magical, and athletic contests. Craftspeople sell fine equipment, local households back new talent, and the taverns fill with rivals and friends.
Fallsmeet.hiddenInfo:
Since the Liberation ended the vampire lords' rule in Drusavia, Fallsmeet has accepted House Avarre as its ruling family. The house's claim rests on both the adventurer couple at its root and its enduring compact with the dragonkin households whose forebears were held as the old lord's guards and hound-handlers. Those households now hold land, workshops, Games offices, and commands in the village watch.

Most residents are human or dragonkin, with established dwarf and gnome households among them. Dwarves are prominent among Fallsmeet's smiths, stoneworkers, competitors, and weapons judges. Gnomes are common among its alchemists, performers, and Games officials.

The Open Games hold martial, magical, and athletic contests on the riverside grounds and across nearby meadows, woods, slopes, and streams. Competitors face one another and the terrain in duels, races, archery matches, magical trials, and team contests. New competitors enter their first trial as the Uncolored, without an announced title, patron, or public history. Afterward, local workshops, taverns, households, and clubs may offer their colors, equipment, training, or sponsorship. House Avarre provides judges and maintains the grounds but never sponsors competitors or wagers on them.

Twinfall Hounds are enormous living dogs, bred long ago by the old lord's handlers to hunt the dead. They can track living and spectral quarry through darkness, fog, and lesser concealment, but Fallsmeet raises them as affectionate watch, rescue, and tracking animals. Dragonkin kennel families maintain the oldest lines.

Colonies of intelligent mistbats—great cave bats clever enough to learn complex signals and carry a lightly equipped rider—live in the high caves above the falls. Trained mistbats carry riders, rescue slings, messages, and light lines across the ravines.

Fallsmeet closes its gates before dark. Twinfall Hounds patrol the walls, while mistbat riders search for travelers caught in the hills.

The Meeting Waters.description: The two streams reunite beneath a many-arched stone bridge inside Fallsmeet’s lower wall. The lower gate, village road, and riverside paths meet beside grassy banks, broad steps, and a calm pool. From the bridge, the village terraces rise toward Castle Twinfall between the two falls; the White Wheel stands over one bank and the Open Grounds spread along the river below.

The Open Grounds.description: The Open Grounds occupy a broad riverside green inside Fallsmeet’s lower wall, with permanent stone galleries rising along one side. Duels, archery matches, magical trials, and team contests fill the grounds, while races and other trials extend into the nearby meadows, woods, slopes, and streams. Officials announce each contest’s victory conditions and stop sanctioned bouts at surrender, incapacity, or the declared result. The grounds are a recognized venue of the Grand Arena Circuit.
