The White Wheel.description: The White Wheel is a lively riverside tavern beneath Fallsmeet’s waterfalls, with broad windows, a crowded common room, and terraces overlooking the water. Competitors, craftspeople, patrons, handlers, and young villagers gather for good food, drinks, games, and wagers. An upper terrace looks toward Castle Twinfall between the two falls.

The Workshop Terraces.description: Stepped streets of workshops climb from the Open Grounds toward the castle road. Smiths, armorers, bowyers, fletchers, alchemists, and focus-makers sell useful equipment, accept commissions, repair damaged gear, and display work tested in the Games. Sponsors maintain fitting rooms and public tables where competitors can discuss colors, equipment, training, and terms.

The Watermills.description: Stone watermills stand along channels below the Workshop Terraces. Water from the falls turns great wheels that power forge hammers, grinding wheels, and bellows. Smiths shape weapons and armor, sharpen blades, and finish useful metalwork in the open workshops. Finished goods are laid out for buyers beside work awaiting collection.

Castle Twinfall.description: Castle Twinfall crowns the rocky spur between the two ravines. Dark walls from the vampire lord's fortress support pale rebuilt wings, steep slate roofs, timber galleries, gardens, and broad terraces. Visitors enter a high public hall where old black stone meets the rebuilt castle: banners hang above a broad stair and gallery, long tables receive petitioners and competitors, and tall windows look toward the falls. The guest halls open for important Games occasions, while the family apartments, upper gardens, and oldest foundations remain guarded.

The Houndyard.description: Stone kennels, exercise yards, and a sloping training meadow stand inside the upper gate. Twinfall Hounds are enormous black or smoke-grey dogs with pale reflective eyes and breath that mists even in warm air. Their handlers train them for tracking, rescue, wall patrols, and Games trials, and the yard keeps scent courses, climbing obstacles, grooming stalls, and a quiet enclosure where young hounds meet unfamiliar people.

The Mistbat Roosts.description: Deep caves and broad launch ledges open in the wooded heights above the falls. Harness rooms, rescue litters, and stores of riding gear occupy the lower caverns, while the mistbats roost farther within. Handlers train with individual bats from the launch ledges before attempting the ravines, and access beyond the working chambers requires their permission.

The Closed Court.description: A circular black-stone arena lies beneath the oldest foundations of Castle Twinfall. Iron gates open from narrow holding passages onto a sand-covered floor. A raised dais and shuttered gallery overlook the arena, while a steep passage climbs toward the Workshop Terraces.

The Shuttered Gallery.description: A private stone gallery occupies one side of the Closed Court. Screened outer arches look across the roofs of Fallsmeet, while narrow viewing shutters on the opposite wall open onto the arena below. Worn benches, curtained alcoves, a serving room, and a stair into the competitors' passage remain behind them. Concealed lamps can light the court while leaving its observers in shadow.

Marrenford.name: Marrenford
Marrenford.basicInfo: A prosperous market town at the great ford on the River Marren, seat of House Corwin, and hub of trade between the elven, orc, dwarf and human lands. On the hill overlooking the town rise the stout towers and bright pennants of Castle Westvigil, where the ruling house keeps open court. The town is home to the Westmarch Rangers and Westmarch Riders, which keep the peace on the dangerous northern and western borders. The Marrenmere, the sacred lake beside the town, draws pilgrims to the statue of Ithunya, goddess of harvest and earned wishes.
Marrenford.hiddenInfo:
House Corwin rules: an old, proud, land-rich family, beloved and overextended. Duke Edmund Corwin manages a grand inheritance on a shrinking purse — the castle, the Greatwall, the bounties, the levies, and the feasts, all maintained out of noble pride past what the treasury can bear. The house keeps open court and pays honestly for service.

The population is human-led. Half-orcs and half-elves are among the younger generation — children of the peace the war-kings' victories made possible. Dwarf traders come up from Highheath on the eastern road, halflings work the farms and market stalls, and the occasional wood elf ranger passes through from Sanctuary Vale.

Two loose companies share the frontier work: the Westmarch Rangers patrol the western forest and river crossings, while the Westmarch Riders patrol the northern hills and man the Greatwall. Both actively seek recruits and offer work to non-members.

Across the Marrenmere on the far shore stands the long, low stone Ancestral Hall, where the war-dead are honored and oaths sworn to the heroic memory.

Marrenmere Market.description: A broad, busy market square facing the Marrenmere. An armorer sells frontier-grade steel, working shields, and riding gear. An apothecary keeps healing draughts, poultices, antidotes, and field supplies. A general outfitter stocks rations, rope, torches, camp kit, and everything needed for a few days in rough country. A factor near the hiring post buys pelts, salvage, reaver steel, and whatever else comes back from the borders — few questions asked. Folk gather at the water's edge to drink and talk.

The Temple of Ithunya.description: A stone temple beside the Marrenmere, kept by priests of Ithunya. Healers mend what an apothecary cannot — wounds, sickness, poison, and curses. They teach the healing arts to those with the gift. The temple sells ward-charms, blessed steel, and sanctified water drawn from the Mere. Priests will bless a party before a dangerous ride, remove hexes, consult on the restless dead, and perform rites — oaths, marriages, and funeral honors for fallen companions. Pilgrims make wishes at the lakeside shrine, and the devout say Ithunya answers the worthy in small ways.

The Elfstone Tavern.description: The oldest inn in Marrenford, beside the lake. One whole wall is a single slab of pale elder stone — the Truthstone, on which oaths are said to be unbreakable. Rival rangers and Riders crowd the common room alongside bounty-hunters, traders, and half-orcs. Challenge games are common, boasts are settled by bouts (sparring must be taken outside), and the loser buys the round, though those who wish to drink in peace are left to do so. By custom, an oath sworn on the Truthstone binds noble and commoner alike, and both come to swear.

Castle Westvigil.description: In the great hall of Castle Westvigil, Duke Corwin hears petitions, settles disputes between villages, and receives reports from the Rangers and Riders. Maps of the region show the latest border markings and known trouble. Those who distinguish themselves in the house's service earn a seat at the duke's table and the kind of work that doesn't go on the public board. A Morcroft knight is usually present at court. Duke Corwin's herald, Aldo, receives the castle's guests and keeps its muster.

The Rangers' Lodge.description: A timber lodge on the town's western edge, home to the Westmarch Rangers. Maps of the forest borderlands pinned to the beams, tracking dogs in the yard. The Rangers know who raids from the Deadfall Gulleys, where the elf renegade camps shift with the season, and which fords the Syndicate uses to move contraband out of Sanctuary Vale. They post scouting and tracking work on their own board, separate from the castle's, and take volunteers who prove they can move quietly in deep forest. A Ranger veteran with the patience for it will teach tracking, fieldcraft, and bowmanship.

The Riders' Hall.description: A stone hall and stable-yard on the town's northern side, where the Westmarch Riders muster. Horses, arms, saddlebags, and a posting board with the latest from the hill patrols and the Greatwall watch. When the border beacons light along the northern hills, the Riders mount here and ride. A Rider sergeant teaches horsemanship, mounted lance-work, and hill-country patrol to anyone who can stay in the saddle.

The Marrenmere Pavilion.description: A pavilion of carved timber and bright pennants on the shore of the Marrenmere, open-sided to the lake, where House Corwin and the Westmarch gentry pass their days: feasts and picnics, music and dancing, archery and riding contests on the green, swimming, fishing and boat-races on the lake.

The Mere House.description: A small two-story whitewashed stone house on the Marrenmere shore, with a blue timber balcony and steps down to a little landing. Two bedrooms stand above a sitting room with a hearth and a table for shared suppers. A boathouse is shared with the neighboring cottage; friends gather by the water for swimming, fishing and meals after a journey. Castle Westvigil and the market are within walking distance.

Gavarra.name: Gavarra
Gavarra.basicInfo: Gavarra is the City of Fortune, a terraced island that climbs in tiers of gambling halls and pleasure-houses toward tall towers that glow blue over the sea at night. The Five Houses, Gavarra's great gambling houses, run the play: games of chance, games of skill, fights and races. Coin spends the same here whatever flag it came under, so everyone's money is welcome, and the Houses compete for all of it.
Gavarra.hiddenInfo:
The towers that light Gavarra are old Empyrean storm-towers that draw the lightning off the sea-storms; their caught light glows blue over the whole island after dark and feeds the bound stormlight in its halls.

Gavarra lives by one rule that needs no enforcing: money is welcome here, and no one asks where it came from. A pirate's plunder, a privateer's prize-share, and an honest merchant's profit all buy the same chips and the same wine, which is why a city of gamblers stays neutral in a sea of flags — taking sides would cost custom, and custom is everything. The Five Houses compete for the play and answer to no one above them; there is no lord of Gavarra, only five Masters who would each like to be.

The city's order is kept by the Surety, the Houses' shared guard. They protect Gavarra's prosperity, not its people: cheats, brawlers, and anyone who threatens a paying guest on the floor are dealt with hard and quietly, and a gambler is under his House's protection while his coin is good.

All debts are honored, and the Houses see to it. A player who loses past his purse signs over a marker — a ship's papers, a deed, a claim, a pledged heirloom — and the House holds it against payment. The Houses' vaults are full of such markers, and a great deal of work in Gavarra is someone trying to recover what the tables took: buy it back, win it back, or get it out of a House vault by less honest means. Things lost at Gavarra are not gone, only held, and held well.

Gavarra welcomes any guest with coin and turns cold the instant the coin or the conduct runs out. The Houses scheme against each other constantly — poaching champions, fixing odds, courting high rollers.

The stakes worth crossing the city for sit at the high tables of the Tower of Fortune: deeds to ships and islands, a rival's marker, charts, and relics no honest market would sell. The Gilded Cage and the Slick are the spectacle and the second economy — fortunes wagered on a fight or a race, and a fighter who survives enough bouts wins a House's sponsorship.

The Promenade.description: The broad middle terrace and the city's public heart, an avenue of gambling halls, dicing-pits, and taverns climbing the island in tiers. The towers above cast a shifting blue glow. Stairs and ramps run up toward the private Houses on the heights and down toward the harbor and the racing course.

Brightlights.description: An open-air rooftop bar high on the Promenade, the city laid out glowing below and the storm-towers near above. A bound lightning-spirit shifts color and brightness through the railings and glassware to match the music. Deep chairs, low tables, and a long bar make it a place to drink, talk, and be seen between the tables.

The Tower of Fortune.description: The grandest of the Five Houses, a tall hall of marble and dark wood rising over the Promenade and glowing blue at its height. The ground floor is open play; the stairs climb past richer and quieter rooms to the high tables at the top, where the city's serious money sits.

The Gilded Cage.description: A multi-story ring of galleries built around a great ornate iron cage, where armed bouts, unarmed matches, and fights against penned beasts are staged for the wagering crowd. The galleries climb from the pit-rail to private boxes near the roof. Weapon racks, holding pens, and a fighters' under-gallery ring the cage floor. Its declared championship is recognized on the Grand Arena Circuit, with the Five Houses competing to sponsor proven fighters.

The Slick.description: The harbor racing course at the foot of the city, a marked sea-circuit of buoys and channels run by riders mounted on broad storm-rays. Tiered stands and bookmakers' stalls line the shore, and contact between riders is legal and expected. The crowd's roar carries up the terraces.

Crescent Bay Isle.name: Crescent Bay Isle
Crescent Bay Isle.basicInfo: An island curved around a warm, glass-clear lagoon — the one truly gentle water in the bay, sheltered by a reef-mouth nothing big can pass. A village of whitewashed stone lines the crescent shore, and the merfolk village glows beneath the surface across the lagoon, shell-roofed, its lanterns lighting the water at night. Merfolk and surfacers have lived here as one town for generations, and people come from across the bay just to swim in water where nothing is hunting them.
Crescent Bay Isle.hiddenInfo:
The lagoon is the village's life and its playground. Merfolk teach visitors to swim, dive the shallow reefs, and hold their breath like locals — children of both peoples grow up in the water together, and some families have intermarried; their half-mer children are equally at home on land or below. The village's great games are the lagoon relays, swimmer to runner to swimmer, merfolk against surfacers, half the field laughing too hard to finish. In the evenings the merfolk sing in the water, and the sound carries through the whole lagoon.

Merfolk tend pearl-gardens in the lagoon's deep middle. Pearls are the village's one export and its gift-currency — being given one means you are trusted here, and everyone knows it.

The village's fiercest dispute is whose fish stew is better, surfacers' or merfolk's. A formal contest is held every year and has never once been settled, because the judges are hopelessly partisan and proud of it.

Visitors are welcomed warmly, fed, taught, and gossiped about. The village asks little except that the lagoon's gentleness be kept — it is the one water in the bay where nothing is hunted.

The Lagoon.description: Warm, glass-clear water inside the reef-mouth, coral gardens bright below and the pearl-beds glinting in the deep middle. Swimmers, merfolk, and children of both peoples share the water; the merfolk village shows shell-roofed on the lagoon floor.

The Anchorage.description: The village tavern, built half on shore and half over the water, with a saltwater pool in its floor where merfolk float at the tables' edge. The long joint table seats both peoples, and the evening songs carry in from the lagoon.

The Shore Village.description: Whitewashed stone houses along the crescent strand, low docks built at wading height, and market stalls standing in the shallows so sellers and buyers meet at the waterline.

Earthsky Island.name: Earthsky Island
Earthsky Island.basicInfo: Earthsky is a volcanic island famous for its glassworkers, who turn its mineral-rich black sand into everything from common bottles to enchanted mirrors. At dusk the islanders light thousands of handmade glass lanterns until the whole island glows, a constellation of earthbound stars that ships can see from miles out across the dark water.
Earthsky Island.hiddenInfo:
Earthsky is a quiet, prosperous island and one of the few easy places in the Swordlaw sea — no flag flies here, no crew holds it, and people come down to it between voyages to rest, spend, and be no one for a while. It lives by glass. The black volcanic sand yields glass of unusual clarity and strength, and the common trade in bottles, panes, and vessels is only the floor of it. The real money is in the magical work: enchanted mirrors that show a shapeshifter's true face or break an illusion, spirit-bottles that trap ethereal things, scrying orbs, and glass blades and arrowheads keen enough to matter. A buyer who wants such work comes to Earthsky for it.

The island is welcoming to outsiders and runs on a few warm customs rather than any law. The lantern-lighting at dusk is the heart of it: flame passed wick to wick across the island until it glows. A dark house on Earthsky is an empty one, and a visitor is given a lantern of his own before he leaves — the islanders hold that no one should sail away from Earthsky unlit.

Goods here are the glasswork itself: fine bottles and mirrors, spirit-bottles and scrying orbs, glass weapons, and made-to-order enchanted pieces from the master enchanters on Glassworks Row. Loot is the same trade — a spirit-bottle worth a fortune to the right buyer, a true-seeing mirror, a glass blade.

Black Sand Beach.description: The island's dark volcanic harbor, a long strand of black sand under terraced hills. Glass lanterns in colored clusters hang on iron frames along the shore and the jetties, unlit and clear by day, catching the sun. Fishing boats and traders tie up here, and the heat of the forges carries down from the slopes above.

Glassworks Row.description: A terraced hillside of glassworks climbing the volcanic slope, furnaces glowing in their mouths and racks of cooling glass stacked along the terraces. The common works sit at the lower end, turning out bottles and panes; the higher terraces hold the enchanters' workshops, where mirrors, spirit-bottles, and finer pieces are shaped. Paths run down to the beach and up to the island's central square.

Second Sky Square.description: The island's heart, a wide terraced square strung with thousands of glass lanterns on iron frames overhead. By day they hang clear and unlit; at dusk the lantern-lighting fills the square and the whole island with colored light. The Fallen Star tavern stands at one side, its windows full of lanternlight, the warm social house of the island.

Confluence.name: Confluence
Confluence.basicInfo: A floating city where the ocean currents meet, made of hundreds of boats, barges, and rafts lashed together in loose clusters with channels of open water between them. The currents bring rich fishing and calm warm seas, and the sea-peoples followed: every seafolk species in the bay moors here alongside humans and halflings. Nobody founded Confluence, nobody governs it, and nobody here answers to captain, house, or crown — the currents feed the city, and its people own nothing but their boats and like it that way.
Confluence.hiddenInfo:
Confluence is what the sea's peoples made when they wanted no masters. The currents feed anyone with a net, so there are no shares to owe, no house's cut, no rent on water. A boat is a whole estate: nobody is richer than their hull, nobody can be evicted, and any dispute can be settled by untying and drifting to a friendlier cluster. The people are loud, unhurried, unimpressed by anyone's name, and generous the way people are when the sea restocks them daily.

Every seafolk people is at home here and landfolk are the guests. Sealion-folk are loud and physical — they swim the channels and bark when they laugh. Shark-folk are quiet, sharp-eyed, and run the best fish stalls. Sea-turtle folk moor their great shell-boats at the rim, and the oldest of their elders has been moored here longer than anyone can prove — slow to speak and worth the wait. Frogkin crouch on every surface, and merfolk live as much in the water beneath the city as on it, surfacing alongside new boats to trade gossip before the lines are tied. Nobody cares where you're from — the currents brought you, same as everyone.

Anything the sea gives can be bought or sold here, deck to deck, with no weigh-house and no house's cut. Seafolk hunters sell monster parts cheap — venom gland, serpent oil, kraken ink, hides — and merfolk sell water-charms: small enchantments to hold your breath longer, keep your feet on a wet deck, or feel something big passing beneath you. Boats sell off gear when they need coin, so good harpoons and the odd fine blade turn up on any given day. Pilots, divers, and merfolk guides hire out from the Raft, and passage can be found to anywhere the currents run.

Everything that happens on the bay is known at Confluence first. Crews and seafolk pass through daily from every water, and the talk on the Big Raft carries the whole bay's news: where the serpents are running, which crew hasn't come home, who's been asking after whom. The news is free the way weather is free — you just have to sit in it.

No one's writ runs here and no one can hold ground in a city with no ground, so people meet at Confluence who can meet nowhere else. Grudges are left at the tie-line: fighting here means fighting on somebody's boat, and every boat has an owner watching.

A boat is how you belong, and hands are how you start. The city runs on volunteered work — hauling at the lashings when clusters re-tie, passing lines when weather turns — and hauling beside someone is how strangers become names. Meals happen on open decks, and being waved onto one is the invitation that counts; every seafolk people keeps the same custom of feeding a stranger.

The Lashings.description: The city itself: hulls of every size and people lashed in clusters, channel-water between them, plank-bridges and jump-gaps linking deck to deck. Shell-boats stand at the rim, and merfolk surface in the lanes.

The Catch.description: A broad cluster of platforms and boat-decks where the day's fishing is sold, cooked, and eaten. Shark-folk gut, frogkin fry, turtle-folk serve stew. The freshest food in the Bay, and everyone here will say so.

The Big Raft.description: A big flat barge under a canvas awning — barrels of drink, no seating plan, and room made for whoever arrives. Sealion-folk take up twice the space, and merfolk float alongside with drinks at the barge's edge.

Tevantia.name: Tevantia
Tevantia.basicInfo: Tevantia is the City of a Thousand Bridges: white towers on sea-cliffs above the Swordlaw sea, high bridges strung between its isles, and sails and wind everywhere, from the great windmills on the cliff-tops to the sail-lifts gliding between the towers. It is the richest and proudest city of the Swordlaw sea, and its nobility is the most flamboyant in Larion: four great houses in their own colors, who settle matters of the heart and of honor with the sword.
Tevantia.hiddenInfo:
Tevantia is a city of a thousand bridges, many too narrow for two people to pass, and its nobility has made giving way on them law: under the Right of Precedence, a refusal to yield can be answered with a challenge and a duel.

The city runs on the wind: windmills on the cliff-tops drive its lifts, pumps, and mills, and sail-lifts carry people between the harbor, the bridges, and the towers.

Four great houses rule its society, Montrose, Marenne, Ravissant, and Levantine, competing for precedence, marriages, pride, and love. Their heads elect the Duke for life; the current Duke is old, the next election is coming, and every house is courting alliances before the Grand Tournament decides who stands highest. The nobility dresses more extravagantly than anyone in Larion: towering collars, jeweled sword-hilts, and capes in house colors.

The Duke names the city's troubles in proclamations posted at the Ducal Palace gate on Golden Row, and the great houses compete to see each one answered in their name, openly courting capable heroes to fight under their banners. Among themselves the houses settle quarrels only in the open: by formal duel, in the Tournament, at the regatta, and in the salons.

Anyone can rise here by the sword: a capable stranger can be hired as a house's blade, sworn as its champion in the house's Great Hall on Golden Row, and, by winning the Grand Tournament, named First Blade of Tevantia. The Two Swords is where champions are matched to causes, and the League keeps its chapterhouse by the harbor.

Tevantia Harbor.description: The busy harbor at the foot of Tevantia's white sea-cliffs, where ships of every flag crowd the wharves and sail-lifts climb the cliff-face toward the city above. The harbor-plaza is a permanent open market of armorers, alchemists, mapsellers, and food-stalls, loud with gulls and criers, and the harbor's sailors, racers, and regatta crowds make it the liveliest place in the lower city.

The Thousand Bridges.description: The bridges strung between Tevantia's isles and towers, high above the sea: broad bridge-plazas ringed with carved railings, with circles marked in their flagstones for dueling, and narrow spans where two people meeting cannot both pass and one must yield. Wind-harps sing from the railings, sail-lifts glide between the arches, and the nobility promenades here to see and be seen. A broad span leads to Highbridge House, a townhouse above a public arcade of shops.

The Windworks.description: The great windmills along the cliff-tops of Tevantia, their sails turning against the sky, and the central station where the sail-lifts gather and depart. Gears, cables, and wind-vanes crowd every roofline, and the wind-wrights who build and tune them work in lofts full of models, sails, and half-finished wind-gliders.

The Amphitheater.description: A massive ancient stone arena on the cliffs, its tiered seats rising over a broad sand floor open to the sky and the sea wind, where the great houses settle disputes through their champions before the city and where the Grand Tournament is fought. Old mechanisms beneath the floor can flood the arena for staged sea-fights. Champions' galleries and the house boxes, hung in house colors, ring the combat ground, and its championship is recognized on the Grand Arena Circuit.

Golden Row.description: The towers of the great houses on Tevantia's highest cliffs, each flying its house colors and linked to the others by its own bridges, with the golden-domed Ducal Palace at the head. Each house's palace opens off the Row, and the Duke's proclamations are posted at the Ducal Palace gate.

The Two Swords.description: A famous duelists' tavern above the harbor, its walls hung with crossed swords taken from celebrated duels and the motto 'what two swords decide is law' carved over the hearth. A long common room of dark wood and good drink draws champions, heirs, duelists, and adventurers alike, with quieter back rooms for talk that wants no audience. A marked floor stands ready for any challenge the patrons care to settle in form. By custom, anyone who carries a blade drinks here as an equal, highborn or not.

Tevantia League Chapterhouse.description: The League house in Tevantia, a stone hall above the harbor. Sea-wise crews, monster-hunters, duelists, and trouble-solvers trade word over long tables. A contract-board faces the room, backed by Swordlaw charts, and the local guildmaster keeps a scarred table where crews claim work, tell what happened, and earn standing before witnesses.

The Palace of Mirrors.description: A glittering cliff-top palace of mirrored halls and crystal chandeliers, where the four houses hold their salons, concerts, card parties and balls. Every mirror doubles the silk and jewels, every duelist checks their profile, and everyone watches everyone else in the glass. Courtships, rivalries and scandals are made here, and every house keeps its own salon in its colors. Its grounds retain the Windward Gardens: a hedge maze, a fountain pavilion, and open terraces above the sea where sky-duelists circle overhead.

The Undercliff Caves.description: A network of sea-caves in the cliffs beneath Tevantia, reached by a tide-stair cut down from the harbor. Green water surges through arched caverns and flooded passages that open and close with the tide, the walls glitter with wet stone and shell, and the deepest caverns are pitch dark and cold. The drowned come up through these caves on the black tides, and deep below, past the flooded passages, is the drowned hold: a vast cavern of green water where they keep the people they have taken, bound in nets and slowly changing, with drowned guards swimming the water around them.

The Black Palace.description: The ruined seat of the house that started the Burning of Tevantia, three centuries dead: a great scorched palace of black stone on its own isle, reached by a single cracked bridge that few dare cross. Its towers are charred shells, its gates hang open, and on some nights pale fire moves behind its windows. The burning dead of its fallen house walk its halls.

Montrose Palace - Great Hall.description: The great hall of House Montrose, the oldest house of Tevantia and the Duke's own, beside the Ducal Palace at the head of Golden Row: a long crimson-and-gold hall hung with ancestral banners, a gallery of famous duelists' swords along one wall, a great carved hearth, and at its head an empty carved chair kept ready for the next Duke from the house. The house receives guests, hears petitions, and takes on heroes and champions here, and its sword-school fences in the grand classical style on the marked floor beneath the banners.

Montrose Palace - Champions' Tower.description: The tall crimson tower of House Montrose's sworn champions, rising over the sea from the palace's seaward side: winding stairs, snug rooms with balconies and wind-harps tuned to the house, an armory of polished blades, and a house servant on every landing who knows the city's gossip.

Marenne Palace - Great Hall.description: The sea-palace of House Marenne, built half out over the water beneath the cliffs of Golden Row: a great hall of sea-green stone and pearl whose floor is thick clear glass over the open sea, with pools along its sides that open straight into the waves, where Marenne swimmers come and go. The house receives guests and takes on heroes and champions here, and its sword-school fences in a fluid, flowing style on the glass.

Marenne Palace - Champions' Tower.description: A pale tower rising from the sea-palace's rocks, its rooms open to the sea air and the sound of the waves, with a private pool at its foot that opens to the sea and a salt-washed balcony for each of House Marenne's sworn champions.

Ravissant Palace - Great Hall.description: The newest palace on Golden Row, and the most dazzling: a mirrored hall of violet silk and silver under crystal chandeliers, with a gallery of paintings of the house's recent victories and a raised floor where House Ravissant stages duels and displays for invited crowds. The house receives guests and takes on heroes and champions here, and its sword-school teaches bravura fencing on the raised floor.

Ravissant Palace - Champions' Tower.description: A slender violet-and-silver tower beside the Ravissant palace, its rooms like jewel-boxes, lined with mirrors, silk, and gilt, where House Ravissant's sworn champions live in more luxury than they know what to do with.

Levantine Palace - Great Hall.description: The wind-palace of House Levantine on the windward edge of Golden Row: a great hall of white stone whose tall arches stand open to the sky and the sea wind, with wind-harps singing along its walls, racks of wind-gliders, and gleaming models of the Windworks' machines. The house receives guests and takes on heroes and champions here, and its sword-school trains leaping and turning on the open floor at the arches' edge and on the high bridges.

Levantine Palace - Champions' Tower.description: A white tower of House Levantine's sworn champions, its top a glider-launch into the sea wind, its rooms airy and bright with sky-blue hangings and the constant song of the tower's own wind-harps.

Ducal Palace - Gilded Hall.description: The great reception hall of the Ducal Palace, all gold leaf, sea-light and painted ceilings, where Tevantia comes to be seen. Petitioners wait on the Duke's business, the great houses trade news and favors, musicians play in the galleries, challenges are named and wagers laid, and anyone who wishes to be received by the Duke is announced by the Duke's herald, Rosalba.

The Sea Balcony.description:
A broad stone balcony along the seaward side of Tevantia’s Ducal Palace, shaded by cream awnings and overlooking the harbor, high bridges, and sail-lifts. Wind-harps sound along the balustrade. Breakfast tables, cushioned chairs, and a card table draw the household’s resident knights and visiting guests out of their rooms. They trade news, argue over duels, and invite one another into the day’s plans.

Private suites open off the adjoining arcade, each with a comfortable bed, writing table, weapons stand, lockable chest, and space to receive friends. Knights granted lodging by Tevantia’s court keep their assigned suite while away adventuring and may leave possessions there. Household staff remember returning residents, ask after their travels, and pass on messages and invitations. Friends may visit; a resident’s private room is entered by invitation.

Court visitors sometimes join breakfast, bringing news, introductions or invitations from other duchies. Residents also gather here without court business: sharing supper, playing cards, or watching ships come into harbor. When someone returns after a long absence, their neighbors want to hear where they have been.

The Drowned City of Orichala.name: The Drowned City of Orichala
The Drowned City of Orichala.basicInfo: Orichala was the greatest city of the Empyrean Empire, and the sea swallowed it in a single night. Not all the way: its towers still stand out of the water, and beneath them the drowned city goes down into the deep kingdoms' waters. The drowned and the sea's creatures fiercely repel any surfacer who lands there. At the city's heart, the crown of a colossal glass dome breaks the surface, and inside it, they say, the dragon of the deep kingdoms keeps her court.
The Drowned City of Orichala.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Orichala is hostile ground. The drowned — once surface folk, remade for the water — garrison the standing city and attack any landing. They fight in bands of six to twelve, surfacing from the flooded streets, striking from the water side and pulling back into it when pressed.

Ophialtha, the dragon of the deep kingdoms, is sea-bound: she cannot leave the water, and no dry ground in Orichala is ever in her reach — only her servants'. She does not stir for fighting in the standing city. Entering the Dome of All Worlds brings her: she comes to the Queen's Lake for anything that disturbs it.

The Dome of All Worlds was the city's great wonder: a colossal sealed habitat holding living specimens from every land the empire ruled. It sank with the city and trapped its air, and its old magic still keeps the air good and the habitat alive. Centuries feral, its creatures answer to nothing: rock-apes in the high tiers, terror-birds running the grass shelf, a grown-monstrous crocodile in the channels, and bright venomous things in the green. Ophialtha enters through the sea-breach in the great lake and rules the Dome as her court — a queen of the deep presiding over a little world of the surface.

The Rooftop Shallows.description: The city's edge, where the drowned streets first break the surface: a reef of rooftops, balconies, and upper colonnades standing out of the sea, with open water in the streets between them. Boats can moor against the ledges. The dry crossings run rooftop to rooftop over gaps of dark water, and the towers' upper floors give high ground the water cannot reach. The city rises tilted toward its heart, where the curve of a great glass dome stands out of the sea.

The Sunken Ways.description: The half-drowned mid-city between the outer rooftops and the dome. The water shallows street by street — chest, waist, knee — and the ways run over causeways of rubble, fallen columns, and flooded avenues between towers still standing to their full height, doorways gaping dark above the waterline. Open water stands deep in the sunken plazas. Ahead, the dome's crown fills the sky, split by a great breach well above the waterline, reachable by a climb up its glass-and-bronze ribs.

The Dome of All Worlds.description: Inside the breach, a whole living country falls away below in vast tiers — forest, grassland, reed-marsh — under a shell of glowing glass that lights it all like a pale day. Below the waterline the glass turns black where the sea presses against it from outside. Old stairs and terraces descend tier to tier through the overgrowth, and channels of open water cut between the gardens gone wild, all running down to a great lake at the heart of it.

The Queen's Lake.description: The lake at the bottom of the Dome, ringed by a shore of white stone built in the wonder's first days. The water is broad, deep, and dark, and somewhere below it a breach opens to the ocean outside. Drowned trophies stand along the shore — ships' figureheads, statues, thrones — arranged facing the water.

Beggarsbridge.name: Beggarsbridge
Beggarsbridge.basicInfo: Beggarsbridge is an anarchic shantytown built on and beneath an ancient mile-long stone bridge spanning the water between two of the larger isles. Anything can be bought or sold here — it is the one market in the Swordlaw sea with no law, no questions, and no door shut to a buyer with coin. Houses and stalls of every description cling to the span and hang under it on stilts and ropes above the canal.
Beggarsbridge.hiddenInfo:
No authority holds Beggarsbridge. It is the region's open market for everything the law forbids elsewhere.

The Syndicate has a heavy presence here, and the man who runs their trade here is Mardrek Venn.

Humans, ratkin, and frogkin live thickest, with fishfolk and other water-folk in the lower levels that flood with the tide, swimming up through doorways the dry-folk never use. Below everything, in the canal under the bridge, the Guttermouths wait — eels grown long and bold on what the bridge drops through its gaps and spillways, which is where inconvenient things tend to go.

Beggarsbridge runs on the unwritten rules: pay your debts, never look weak, and do not bring another isle's quarrel onto the span. A stranger who keeps those is left to do business; one who looks like easy money, or like trouble from somewhere else, finds himself tossed into the canal - or worse. Work here is the criminal trade itself — fencing, smuggling, hiring muscle and killers, buying what is banned, and the jobs Venn hands out to people who do not ask questions.

Anything is for sale on the bridge. The Midmarket stalls carry good steel and pirate iron — cutlasses, boarding-axes, crossbows — alongside salvaged and ship-stripped armor, leathers and brigandines and the odd fine breastplate off a captain. Deeper in, the trade turns to poisons and venoms, alchemical reagents and spell ingredients, scavenged Empyrean relics and charms of doubtful provenance, scrolls and grimoires fenced from dead mages, forged papers, and stolen aspected gear nobody can sell openly — a moonstone blade, a stormsteel cutlass, a witchwood wand — turning up here with no questions about where it came from. Services are traded as readily as goods: mercenaries and killers for hire, smugglers and pilots who know the dark channels, forgers, fixers, and crews willing to take the job no honest crew will. Quality runs the full range, from cheap stall-goods to genuine masterwork plundered off the rich, and a sharp buyer can find an heirloom piece here that a lawful city would never let go.

The Midmarket.description: The bridge's widest section, where the span broadens into a permanent open market roofed over with sailcloth and salvaged timber. Stalls and stacked crates crowd the stone in a maze of narrow ways, and the goods on offer run from ship's rope and tar to things kept under the counter. The stonework rises in great arches overhead, and the sea is visible far below through gaps in the deck. Stairs and ladders drop away toward the levels hanging beneath the bridge.

The Waterline Inn.description: A tall rowdy tavern built into the side of the bridge on two levels. The upper floor is a sailors' common room of long tables and recruiting-corners, loud at all hours. The lower floor sits at the waterline and floods at high tide, its far doorways opening straight onto the canal, so that water-folk come and go by swimming up from below. Drink, hire, and rumor move on both floors.

Venn's Exchange.description: A sprawling fortified shopfront dug into the bridge's stonework behind reinforced doors, where the serious trade is done out of sight of the market. Counting-rooms, locked storerooms, and a forger's bench fill the deep interior, and the back ways connect to the levels below the bridge. This is the bridge's true money-floor.

The Underhang.description: The world beneath the span — a hanging warren of stilted platforms, rope walks, and shacks lashed to the bridge's underside just above the high-tide line. The stone arches close overhead and the canal runs black below, fed by spillway gaps that drop refuse straight into the water. The lowest platforms are slick and half-rotten.

The Bronze Wreck.name: The Bronze Wreck
The Bronze Wreck.basicInfo: An ancient Empyrean warship broken on a shallow reef, big as a fortress — bronze-clad hulls, castles, and tilted decks standing dry above the tide. It is known as a part-time squat of the Sea-Kings, a sharkfolk raider band out of the southern sea. Ships that pass near the reef are attacked, and crews that fight are killed.
The Bronze Wreck.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Sea-Kings are hostile by default — angry, spiteful, and hungry. They attack ships and salvagers on sight, kill, sink, steal, and kidnap. They hold prisoners for ransom. Before killing a victim they loudly proclaim that anything in the sea belongs to them by rights.

The Sea-Kings are grey-hided and shark-toothed, and they work themselves into a frenzy at blood in the water — a wounded man overboard turns a fight into a feeding. They fight from the water and the rigging: boarding over the rails from below, harpoon-lines to drag targets off the decks and into the sea, nets in the shallows. They taunt, they gloat, and they eat what they kill. They are not always at the wreck — bands go out raiding for days — and when an organized force comes against them in strength, they slip into the water and are gone, then return when it leaves.

Prisoners are held in the barred cabins of the stern castle. The Sea-Kings' plunder piles in the bow vaults: stolen cargo, seized salvage, ransom-coin, and what the salvage crews never finished stripping — Empyrean bronze fittings and intact ancient weapons.

The Reef Shallows.description: The reef at low water, wadeable and boat-passable, the wreck rising ahead like a bronze hill. Broken hull-plates and stripped fittings litter the coral.

The Broken Decks.description: Tilted weather decks and fallen masts, open to the sky. Stairs and rigging climb toward the stern castle; the bow vaults open forward.

The Stern Castle.description: The highest, driest quarter of the wreck, its bronze walls intact. Barred cabins line the inner passages, and the high deck commands the whole reef.

The Bow Vaults.description: Forward holds above the tide-line, half-stripped, shelved with cargo and stacked fittings.

Wolfpack Lodge.name: Wolfpack Lodge
Wolfpack Lodge.basicInfo: A fortified warrior lodge of massive rough-hewn timber, raised on the open Wold within reach of the Gods-Anvil. Home of the Wolfpack, an orc-founded company of hunters, fighters, shamans, scouts, healers, beast handlers, berserkers, and beast-bonded champions who take the hunts and battles too great for ordinary warriors. The compound is both home and training ground. It is open to any people who master themselves, stand by their companions, and defend the Wold against those who would conquer it.
Wolfpack Lodge.hiddenInfo:
Rowdy, competitive, intense, and reverent all at once. Sparring never stops, feats of strength are celebrated loudly, and the walls are hung with the trophies of slain monsters. The Wolfpack is a warrior society first and a mercenary company second: it takes gold, but its loyalty is to the pack and to the Wold, and it will not take work that harms either.

The Wolfpack's standing is earned in public. An outsider may enter as a Trial-Hunter and attempt one witnessed proving deed. Success earns a pack clasp and recognition as a Packmate. Three further recognized pack deeds earn the name Proven Hunter. A Proven Hunter may choose to seek a beast-spirit at the Spirit Hearth; if hunter and spirit both accept the bond, the hunter becomes Beast-Bonded. Four serious recognized deeds after the bond may earn recognition as a Pack-Captain trusted to lead lodge contracts and other packmates. The singular Pack-Leader governs the lodge; Pack-Captains do not replace that office.

The heart of the lodge is its spirit-tradition. Proven Hunters may meet a beast-spirit at the Spirit Hearth and borrow its senses, protection, and physical nature. Wolf is traditional, but bear, boar, great cat, raptor, serpent, and stranger Wold beasts may answer. The bond is voluntary and mutual, never assigned merely from a hunter's class or ancestry. Fury is a respected discipline here, but neither Berserker training nor Fury is required for membership, advancement, or the bond. The Spirit Cellar is not where bonds are made: it is a place of containment for those who lose themselves to fury or an uncontrolled shape.

The lodge knows the dark mirror of its own craft. The Wrath-Speakers took battle-fury and gave it to demons for raw, ruinous power. The Wolfpack despises them as everything its discipline is meant to prevent, and gladly takes contracts against them and the Oathbreakers they serve.

The Wolfpack hires out for coin and for cause. Hunts against dangerous beasts, war against raiders and Oathbreakers, rescue, escort, and muster when the Wolds are pressed all count as pack work when they protect people, companions, or the land. Recognition comes through named deeds reported before the Great Lodge, not paperwork.

The Palisade Gate.description: The sole entrance to the compound, heavy timber gates set in walls of sharpened logs. Watchtowers flank the entry, manned by archers.

The Training Grounds.description: A broad, muddy central yard of sparring circles and wooden practice dummies, the hub of the lodge's daily life. Warriors of every kind train here, duel for standing, and keep their gear; the ground connects every building in the compound.

The Great Lodge.description: A massive longhouse that serves as mess hall, sleeping quarters, and meeting place, a central fire-pit burning at its heart. Contracts are posted here, and it is the lodge's social hub—drinking, gambling, boasting, and the trading of rumor and news from across the Wold.

The Iron Forge.description: An open-air smithy for repairing heavy armor and sharpening oversized weapons, built for durability over beauty. A place for trade, repair, and the crafting of the heavy gear the pack's shock troops favor.

The Beast Kennels.description: Enclosures housing the great war-wolves that fight alongside the pack. Handlers train and bond with the animals here, and recruits learn to fight beside a beast before any are deemed ready to bond with a spirit.

The Spirit Hearth.description: A round, open-roofed shrine of standing stones behind the training yard, centered on a low fire fed with herbs, carved tokens, and offerings brought from across the Wolds. Wolfpack shamans keep watch but do not command what answers. Proven Hunters come here voluntarily to seek a beast-spirit whose nature accords with their own; the rite succeeds only when hunter and spirit both accept the bond.

The Pack-Leader's Hall.description: A separated section at the back of the Great Lodge reserved for the pack-leader and the lodge's elders. It holds maps of the region, the company's treasury, and the records of its contracts. The negotiations for major campaigns and the choosing of who is ready for the beast-bond happen here.

The Spirit Cellar.description: A stone basement beneath the Pack-Leader's Hall, walled in reinforced iron cages and heavy chains bolted to the rock. Here a member who has lost control of the fury or the beast-bond is held until it passes, and here too the worst rule-breakers are confined. The deepest cells are built to hold something far stronger than a man.

The Red Chantry.name: The Red Chantry
The Red Chantry.basicInfo: The Red Chantry is a fortified manor on the moor and the home of the Bloodhunters, an order of duelists and blood-mages who hunt the dead. They live finely and fight with antique blades and old blood-magic, and they take in any who would learn the craft and take up the cause.
The Red Chantry.hiddenInfo:
The Bloodhunters are blood-mages and duelists who hunt the moor's dead: the war-dead, the barrow-wights, the drowned courts, and the Deathless, the dale gentry who turned to necromancy and ride as death-knights. The Knights Vigilant scorn them in public for trafficking with blood-magic, and call on them in private when the clean sword is not enough.

Their magic turns blood and life against death: tracking the dead by the traces they leave in their victims, warding the mind against a dead thing's compulsion, and marking undead flesh so it cannot knit and heal. The art costs the user a little of himself each time, a slow corruption every hunter carries and bears as a point of pride.

They welcome anyone with the nerve and the skill, and the way in is the work: a guest who proves useful is taught the blade and the blood-arts, a proven hand is sworn to the order, and the sworn rise by the dead they put down. They train, arm, and send hunters out under contract. The chapter master's study above the hall holds the order's records, its richest bounties, and the Black Book that names every hunter who has fallen.

IMPORTANT: the Chantry is gracious to guests and deadly to enemies, not hostile by default. They are fiercely proud of their honor and their charter, and they turn on anyone who threatens the order, exposes its dealings, or means it harm. A hunter who takes too much of the curse falls, and a fallen Bloodhunter, whose blood-arts serve necromancy as readily as they fight it, is just what the Deathless want, so the Chantry hunts its own fallen quietly, before word can spread, and sends its best after any member who turns.

The Courtyard.description: An elegant fortified manor behind tall iron gates worked with silver, a manicured garden and a fountain within the walls. The gate is warded, and the dead and the tainted cannot pass it. Beyond the garden the manor's doors stand open onto the hall, and a stone dueling-ring lies off to one side.

The Grand Hall.description: A lavish vaulted hall hung with velvet and old steel, a great map of the moor and its graves spread on a central table. A long hearth and deep chairs stand at one end, wine set out on the sideboards. A stair climbs to the chapter master's study above, and doors lead off to the dueling-ring and down to the cellars.

The Duelist's Ring.description: A circular stone platform for fencing and drill, ringed by benches and racks of antique blades. A workbench along one side holds tools for etching runes into steel and mixing the order's alchemy. Doors connect to the courtyard and the hall.

The Undercroft.description: A warded stone cellar beneath the manor, its chambers set apart for teaching the blood-arts and for cleansing corruption from those who have taken too much. Deeper in, rune-carved cells stand ready for captured dead and, now and then, for one of the order's own. The way down is the hall stair.

Garden.name: Garden
Garden.basicInfo: A wood elf village spread across clearings in the deep Everwood, where homes of stone and wood stand among towering trees. Gardens grow beside wildflowers along the banks of a river that feeds a clear lake. Halflings, humans, and gnomes live here alongside the wood elves.
Garden.hiddenInfo:
The wood elves of Garden say the settlement dates to the Kindred War, when those who would become wood elves refused to fight their brethren. A legendary figure called He Who Walks Beside is said to have guided them to this safe place and then perished in its defense. In his memory, wood elves mark births, arrivals, and deaths by repeating his last words: 'May you walk in beauty.'

Garden has no leaders. Decisions happen by talk at the Hearth until everyone agrees or gives up, and the wood elves consider this the height of wisdom. They are certain they were right to walk away from the war — they pity Canopy its politics and Vigil Gorge its glory.

The place runs on its regulars more than any rule. An elder holds court at the Hearth and settles quarrels by outlasting them. The halflings have annexed the best sun-patches on the Green and boast about what they can coax out of cold soil. And the rangers — the finest in the Everwood, and quietly the only ones in Garden who pay attention to the world outside it — bring the news, escort the travelers, and carry a private, affectionate exasperation at how relaxed everyone else gets to be. They know the deep forest better than anyone alive and are the best source of word on beasts on the move and renegades on the forest paths.

The Trackless Way.description: One minute, forest. The next, the trees widen, light softens, running water burbles. A tended herb bed here, a woodpile stacked neatly against a trunk there. As if out of nowhere, cottages with smoke rising from them. No one can say exactly where the forest ends and Garden begins.

The Hearth.description: The gathering place at Garden's center, where an ancient oak shades long tables and stone fire pits. Meals are communal and everyone is welcome, including the stranger who arrived an hour ago and is already being argued at. An elder usually holds the head of the table, settling disputes by talking until the parties forget what they were fighting about. A small shrine to the Lady of the Hearth stands where the oak's roots break the surface, tended with wildflowers; nearby, a carved stone bench marks a shrine to the Lord of the Open Hand.

The Green.description: Garden plots and orchards spread between the trees - vegetables, herbs, berry bushes, medicinal plants, some cultivated, some wild. The halflings have claimed the best sun-patches and grow things that have no business surviving this far north, a fact they will explain to anyone who slows down enough to be caught. The healers work here too, drying herbs on racks and brewing tinctures in an open-air workshop.

Lakeside.description: A clearing where the river opens into a still lake. The water is clear to the bottom, cool and bright. Smooth rocks line the shore. Wood elves swim here at every opportunity, and consider anyone who won't a little tragic.

The Lodge.description: A long timber hall where Garden's rangers gear up before heading out. Bows and traveling cloaks hang from pegs. A map of the region covers one wall, marked with sightings and warnings. The rangers are Garden's connection to the world beyond - they bring news, escort travelers, and deal with whatever the forest sends, while the rest of the village gets to pretend the world beyond is someone else's concern.

Roothold.description: A grove of ancient trees where the eldest wood elves teach whoever wants to learn, for as long as they want to learn it - druidic arts, old magic, herbcraft, the speech of birds, the patterns of weather, the slow deep knowledge of the forest. A few carved benches. A fire circle.

Newgarden.description: A clearing at Garden's edge where a few homes stand and space remains for more. Someone is always halfway through building something, unhurriedly.

The Ashfield.name: The Ashfield
The Ashfield.basicInfo: A stretch of blighted ground where nothing grows right. The trees are blackened but alive, the soil is warm to the touch, and ash falls like snow from a sky that's clear everywhere else. A great battle of the Kindred War was fought here, and elves of both kindreds hold it cursed ground, forbidden to enter.
The Ashfield.hiddenInfo:
Hundreds of elves died here by fire-magic, and the ground remembers. The ash that falls is no natural ash; it is a magical echo of the battle, repeating without end. Fire-magic runs strong here and all other magic falters, which is why the Church of the Pyre has claimed the place as holy ground. The Pyre preaches that the rotten old world must be burned away, and to them a battlefield that still burns an age later is altar and proof at once. Their rites here are slowly making the blight worse, widening the dead ground year by year, and if they are left to finish, the burning could spread across a great stretch of the Everwood.

The elven taboo is deeply felt — both high elves and dark elves lost kin here, and both peoples' histories record the battle as a shame. That makes the field impossible to garrison permanently. The Pyre knows this and trades on it. The cultists do not live here; they rotate in for their rites and withdraw into the forest or underground, and their camps are built to be abandoned in an hour. When the High Wardens break taboo to sweep the field, they find cold fire-pits and scorched circles and no one to punish. The cultists always come back.

The Ashfall.description: Where the blight begins. Healthy forest gives way to blackened trunks and warm ground over a few dozen paces. Ash drifts down from nowhere. The air tastes of smoke. The blackened trees still living here have grown for an age around the battle's magic, and their wood is witchwood.

The Burning Ground.description: The battlefield's heart, where the earth is bare and cracked and warm enough to feel through boot soles.

The Scar Pit.description: A crater at the field's center where the killing blow of the battle landed.

Whitehill Kobold Warren.name: Whitehill Kobold Warren
Whitehill Kobold Warren.basicInfo: A network of tunnels and crude fortifications dug into a rocky hillside. Kobolds have infested this place for generations, but recently they've become organized — patrols, watch-posts, even a gate.
Whitehill Kobold Warren.hiddenInfo: A goblin expeditionary squad from the Greater Goblinate has taken command of the warren, 'recruiting' the local kobolds into the empire's service. The goblin captain sees the warren as a forward outpost — a foothold in Whitecliff Downs far from Goblinate territory. The kobolds are split: some welcome the weapons, training, and sense of purpose; others resent taking orders from outsiders who treat them as expendable labor. The captain has also been sending kobold scouts to map the Downs' trade roads — so that a Goblinate raiding party can one day strike the Downs' villages and markets for plunder and prisoners. The whole operation is small enough to go unnoticed for now, which is exactly how the Goblinate prefers to work.

The Warren Gate.description: The hillside approach, where the ground is pocked with small holes and loose rock. Crude snare traps and pit traps line the obvious paths. A reinforced gate — new, and better-built than anything kobolds usually manage — blocks the main tunnel entrance.

The Workings.description: The warren's main hub — a tangle of low tunnels opening into a central cavern where kobolds eat, sleep, and squabble. Goblin-issue crates are stacked against one wall. A crude banner of the Greater Goblinate hangs over the captain's alcove, which is the only space with a proper door.

The Deep Dig.description: The newest tunnels, where kobolds dig under goblin direction. Shored with timber — another new addition. The air is bad and the tunnels branch in several directions.

Sanctuary.name: Sanctuary
Sanctuary.basicInfo: The one great city of the deep Everwood, and the only place in it where outsiders may live. Sanctuary stands by the Pact of Sanctuary, the old agreement that lets a walled city exist in the high elves' wood - its stone raised by its founders, its wards woven by the elves, neither permitted without the other. There is no room to spread inside the walls, so the city climbs and delves, packed tight and loud, every quarter stacked on the last. The wood presses close on every side.
Sanctuary.hiddenInfo:
Sanctuary governs itself through a city council, by the high elves' leave under the Pact. The city watch keeps the peace within the walls; the high elves' wardens keep it beyond them, in the wood.

Every people of Larion has a foothold here, because Sanctuary is the one place in the Everwood that will have them. Dwarves hold the Underhalls below and work the forges; halflings terrace the Greenwarren; humans run the canals. High elves come and go as the wood's masters but keep no quarter of their own. The lower lanes are as mixed as any in Larion - gnome artificers, foxkin and ratkin traders, demonborn and the odd minotaur, wood elves passing through.

The city runs hot and close. With every people of Larion stacked atop the last and no ground to spare, the quarters bicker like neighbors over a shared wall - whose festival has the canal this week, whose forge-smoke is fouling whose terrace, whose guild had the dock first. It is a proud city for all that, and a generous one in its rough way: a stranger who pulls their weight is a neighbor by the second week, and a stranger who doesn't is talked about in four languages. Newcomers arrive daily off the forest roads, and Sanctuary finds room, because finding room is the one thing it has always had to do.

Pact Square.description: The great square at the city's heart. Council Hall and the Watch Tower stand over the high end; the rest is market, packed wall to wall and stacked up the surrounding tenements. At the center stands the Pact, carved into a tall stone — the agreement that lets the city be, with the day's proclamations and bounties nailed to the post below it where a herald reads them out. An herbalist sells salves, spell ingredients, and charms. A row of stocks stands under the Watch Tower, whatever petty offenders the watch has taken left in them for the crowd. Food-stalls crowd the gaps.

The Shrine of Mother Mayreth.description: A small freestanding shrine wedged between tenements off Pact Square. Inside, the centerpiece of the vaulted chamber is a masterwork wooden statue of Mother Mayreth, depicted as a beautiful half-elf woman with a shepherd's crook. In her day, Mayreth, a cleric of the Lady of Mercy, uncovered a plot to kidnap poor girls of the city. Her followers have sought to put an end to the ongoing abductions ever since. The walls are hung with carved plaques left in thanks by the families of girls brought safely back. A Keeper tends the shrine and takes word of any gone missing, organizing the search for the newly lost and efforts to catch those responsible.

Canal Square.description: Where the canals converge around a broad stone plaza, the water as crowded as the streets - gondolas and flat barges nosing for room, polemen cursing each other in three tongues. Merchants in bright cloth haggle from the boats while warehouses and trading offices line the quays. The water threads on into the lower city from here, the only way through some of the packed quarters where there is no longer room for a street.

The Floating World.description: A grand tavern-barge drifting the canals, its musicians and callers inviting the city aboard. Lanterns sway from silk canopies over a deck packed with drinkers off every quay. Below deck are private cabins, hired by the hour for talk that the open deck is too loud and too public to hold.

Goldmount.description: A low hill above the canals, lined with the gated tower-compounds of Sanctuary's great merchant Houses. Behind iron and private guards, the estates hold everything their owners need to avoid mixing with the crowd below - their own gardens, their own water, their own quiet.

The Last Stand Tavern.description: Built into Westgate Tower, where the city's defenders held the line in the Kindred War. Trophies from legendary kills hang beneath the Great Bell, which still rings when something tests the wards out in the wood. The best tables face the windows over the Everwood, and the drinkers who take them are the ones who go out into it - hunters, rangers, and other adventurers.

Forge Row.description: A narrow street of smithies and armories sloping toward the heavy clan-carved doors of the Underhalls, the ring of hammers steady from before dawn. Dwarven smiths and gnome tinkers work the fronts side by side, and the goods on show run from plain steel to the work the wood demands - cold iron, hammered without fire, the grey metal whose touch the fey cannot abide.

The Greenwarren.description: A winding maze of halfling terrace-mounds, each level joined to the next by paths and shortcuts only locals know. Behind the round doors lie trading offices, snug taverns, and the produce markets that feed half the city. It is the one quarter that feels unhurried, and the halflings will tell you at length that it is also the only civilized one.

The Underhalls.description: The dwarven quarter beneath the city: stone halls, clan holdings, and taverns serving dwarven ale far from the noise above. The clans handle their own disputes down here and answer to the council only when they choose to. Deeper passages wind down past the clan-holds toward the workings where the cold iron is cut.

Grave Street.description: Where the quarters meet and the watch rarely steps: a tangle of tenements, ill-frequented taverns, and back-alley dealing.

The Char.description: A whole block gutted by fire and left to rot, its streets barricaded at both ends and the Watch posted to turn people back. Shadows of the fire's dead haunt its cellars, and a pack of hell hounds, the beasts that started the blaze, dens in the embers at its heart; the sounds that carry out after dark keep the neighboring lanes empty till morning.

The League Chapterhouse.description: A tall, narrow house overlooking Canal Square, its open shutters admitting the noise of boats and street vendors. Adventurers of many peoples crowd the downstairs tables, while a wooden gallery holds maps, trophies, and notices from across the Everwood. Muddy boots and drying cloaks gather by the door.

Hillhome.name: Hillhome
Hillhome.basicInfo: Hillhome is a halfling village built into the gentle hills of Whitecliff Downs, where round doors and grass roofs peek from every slope and gardens fill the dells between them. Children and dogs run loose, neighbors call across the lanes, doors stand open, and not knowing someone's name is downright rude.
Hillhome.hiddenInfo:
Hillhome is halfling-majority, with humans and elves settled in among the old families. Large households and friendly feuds run the village: Mossbottoms against Sweetmeads, Honeycutts against Tickbottoms, Greenbottles against everyone, most of it played out in gossip, fair-boasts, songs, and the occasional thrown pie.

The sharp feud is Balewood against Goldspoon. The Goldspoons own the mill-rights, lend hard coin, and have been trying to buy the Balewoods' Saucy Chicken for thirty years. The village watches every move and discusses it as public sport.

The Newmoon Fair is Hillhome's great event: pies, ale, archery, sheep-shearing, singing, gossip, and family pride. Beyond the village, the Truffle-Woods supply the moonbloom truffles that make Hillhome's pies and stews famous across the Downs.

Hill Street.description: The main lane, winding between grass-roofed hills with round doors, round windows, flower boxes, and kitchen gardens on every slope. Neighbors lean in doorways, children cut across the path, and every errand becomes a conversation.

Hearthhome.description: A cozy hill-home on Hill Street with a bright blue door, flower boxes, a warm living room, a study nook facing the village, a cool cellar, and a small herb garden. The hearth is the heart of the house.

The Saucy Chicken Tavern.description: The Balewood family tavern and Hillhome's evening heart: low rafters, mismatched tables, copper pots over the hearth, songs after supper, and Pernilla Balewood's famous truffle-pies coming hot from the kitchen.

Manu's Blacksmith Shop.description: A stout forge built against a hillside, its living quarters dug into the hill behind. Manu Morganstone works under a wide-eaved roof among tools, harness, mended kettles, farm gear, and the occasional sword.

Bark and Dandy's Home.description: A modest hill-home off Hill Street with a crooked round door, a rarely tidy common room, and a garden planted with more enthusiasm than planning. A lopsided shed stands out back among the vegetables.

Goldspoon Manor.description: The only double-hill home in the Downs, with gold-painted doors, stained-glass windows, imported koi in the pond, and a lacquered iron gate watched by servants. A spoon rampant over wheat is carved above the door.

Greenbottle's Goods.description: The village general store, built out of a hill-home parlor knocked through into a shopfront. Tobin Greenbottle stacks it low-ceiling to floor with flour, salt, candles, twine, preserves, boots, blankets, herbs, and small luxuries.

The Fairground.description: A wide grassy meadow at the village's south edge, ringed by oaks and centered on the Festival Oak. Booth-frames are stacked nearby until the Newmoon Fair turns the field into pavilions, ribbons, contest rings, pie-tables, and family rivalries. Paths branch toward Mossfoot Brook, Honeycutt's hillside apiary, and Marra Withergleam's herb cottage without making them part of the village proper.

The Sleeping Bear Inn.description: A welcoming inn half-buried in the hillside where Hill Street meets the fair meadow. Rosie Butterworth keeps a huge hearth, good meals, a stocked cellar, and the travelers' gossip that reaches Hillhome before the rest of the village hears it.

Knothole.description: The village's dubious lower slope: smaller hill-homes, crooked doors, weedy gardens, unlabeled bottles, stoop-talk, and goods nobody asks too closely about. Respectable Hillhome clucks its tongue and buys the mead anyway.

The Truffle-Woods.name: The Truffle-Woods
The Truffle-Woods.basicInfo: The wooded slopes above Hillhome where the village's truffle-hogs forage. Old oaks and chestnuts, mossy roots, brambles and bracken. Halfling foragers have walked the same paths here for generations, and the woods feel safe enough — at least the parts close to the village.
The Truffle-Woods.hiddenInfo: Hillhome's foragers tend the oak-and-chestnut woods above the village, keeping paths clear and guarding their best truffle grounds. Tinytrolls have nested in the bracken and steal from foragers.

The Forager's Path.description: A well-worn footpath leading into the woods, where halfling truffle-hunters have walked for generations. The trees thicken as you climb. Old oaks with mossy roots, bracken to the knee

The Truffle Patches.description: Where the truffles grow, if you know how to look — under the old oaks, in the soft earth between root and root. Halfling truffle-hogs have been working this ground for so long the soil itself smells faintly of moonbloom in the right season.

The Bramble Hollow.description: A low dell choked with thorn-brambles, where the path forks and most halflings turn back. The brambles are tall and thick enough to scratch through cloth. Beyond the hollow, the woods grow older and quieter.

Canopy.name: Canopy
Canopy.basicInfo: The high elven capital, built among colossal silverleaf trees with the ancient First Tree at its heart. The city rises in tiers connected by winding staircases carved into the trunks. Outsiders are welcome at the lower levels, and the upper reaches are elven domain — open to those who earn the climb.
Canopy.hiddenInfo:
The Council of Elf-Lords governs the Everwood from the high branches of the First Tree. They are divided on the dark elf question: hawks want the Sundering enforced more harshly and have been gaining ground of late, doves seek reconciliation, and a weary majority holds to containment and vigilance. The High Wardens, who enforce high elven law throughout the forest, answer directly to the Council.

The elf renegades who raid the human and orc frontiers are the hawks' radicals, gone further than the Council will openly sanction. Canopy disowns them and does not hunt them as hard as its angry neighbors would like — to the high elves they are an embarrassment to be managed slowly, and the high elves do everything slowly.

Canopy is the orienting point for anyone with forest business: the High Wardens at the Warden Hall know where the trouble is and who to send. Elves at the lower levels are long accustomed to outsiders and many find them amusing — particularly their fear of heights, which elves consider endearing, since an elf moves through the high city with effortless grace and would never be so clumsy as to fall. Outsiders who show courage, usefulness, or genuine respect for elven ways are welcome. Those who cause trouble are simply escorted down and out.

Greenshade.description: The ground level of Canopy, where the silverleaf trunks rise like pillars and the light filters down green-gold through the city above. A market fills the spaces between the great trees - elven craftwork, forest goods, food stalls serving honeycakes and smoked game. Lodging houses cater to visitors. The staircases begin here, winding up the trunks into the branches.

The Silver Bough.description: A tavern and inn built where three silverleaf trunks grow close together, their branches forming a natural platform a hundred feet up. The common room wraps around all three trunks, open-sided. The drinks are excellent. The company is better - off-duty High Wardens, traders up from Greenshade, elven artisans, and the occasional outsider who's earned a regular seat. The best source of news and rumor in the city.

The Warden Hall.description: Headquarters of the High Wardens, built around a massive branch of the First Tree. Armories, planning chambers, quarters for Wardens between assignments. A board posts the forest's current troubles - beasts on the move, the elf renegades harrying the human and orc borders, the open crossing into the dark elf underworld at Ilunethel and what passes through it, the burned ground in the east. The incursion reports out of the deep run worst in the valleys near Vigil Gorge.

The Academy of Greenshaping.description: Where the high elves study their two oldest arts: greenshaping, the magic of growing and persuading living wood that raised the city itself, and the wardcraft that binds and protects it. Chambers grown from living trees house libraries of pressed-leaf books, workshops where saplings are coaxed into walls and stairs, and quiet gardens for the slow work of warding. High elf students spend decades here before they are reckoned merely competent. Outsider mages of genuine talent can petition for a guest residency - the masters are selective, but the art grows nowhere else in Larion.

The High Boughs.description: Three hundred feet up, where the noble houses keep their estates among the upper branches. The architecture is less built than shaped - walls of living bark, floors of woven branch, windows shaped gaps between them. The Council of Elf-Lords meets in a chamber grown from the First Tree itself. The lords here are old beyond counting, and among such company there is always one quietly weighing the long road to Eanleana, the Final City, where elves who have wearied of their years go to an honorable end.

The Crown.description: The top of the canopy, where you step out of the leaves onto a platform above the world. An endless sea of green stretches in every direction, unbroken to the horizon. Wind moves through the treetops in slow waves. Druids tend a small sacred space here, but mostly the Crown is just the view - and the knowledge that the forest below holds more than any lifetime could explore.

Web.name: Web
Web.basicInfo: A colony of giant spiders in the high canopy where a vast web stretches between ancient trees like a second forest above the forest floor. The Spinners — intelligent, horse-sized spiders — are known for trading their legendarily strong silk threads to those able to navigate their often alien ways.
Web.hiddenInfo: Spinners cannot speak; their communication is telepathic impression: images, emotions, senses. They understand speech but respond in projections. They're deeply curious about other minds, but have often been wrongly accused of kidnapping and murder of forest folk, even though their ways forbid preying on sentient species. Their silk is the finest textile in the Everwood — light, strong, and fire-resistant. They trade it for things they find beautiful or interesting, which is unpredictable and often makes little sense to non-Spinners. Spinner territory is clearly marked with boundary-webs. Those who cross uninvited get captured and brought to the Span to be inspected by the Weavespeaker, the colony's eldest, and the only Spinner who can project something close to language — full sentences rather than impressionistic flashes.

The Edge.description: Where the boundary-webs begin — shimmering lines of silk strung between trees at every height, catching light like dew. The webs aren't sticky but they vibrate at a touch, announcing visitors.

The Spokes.description: The main habitable area — a network of silk platforms stretched between tree trunks a hundred feet up, strong enough to hold a dozen people, swaying gently. The silk is translucent in daylight and faintly luminous at night. Spinners move freely across vertical and horizontal surfaces.

The Hub.description: An enclosed silk chamber where the Weavespeaker receives visitors.

Vigil Gorge.name: Vigil Gorge
Vigil Gorge.basicInfo: A high elven fortress-city built into a gorge of silver-white adamant stone. Waterfalls pour through the chasm in sheets of mist and thunder. But step through the Gorge Gate and the fortress reveals a green valley along the river, warm and sheltered, where gardens and orchards grow beneath the high walls. The Legion of the Vigil garrisons the fortress and guards the Everwood.
Vigil Gorge.hiddenInfo:
The folk of Vigil Gorge believe Canopy has grown soft, too taken with trade and politics, and has forgotten why the Sundering was made. They see themselves as the true defenders of elvenkind and the Everwood. The Legion recruits outsiders and treats them as equals once they've proven themselves — a radical stance by high elven standards. New recruits drill hard but are welcomed into a brotherhood. Veterans who settle in the valley raise families, tend gardens, and answer the horn when it sounds.

Secretly, the Legion conducts raids into the dark elf tunnel network. The Sundering's terms forbid both sides from entering each other's territory. Vigil Gorge has stopped respecting this bargain. They hit dark elf outposts and collapse tunnels; the dark elves retaliate; and this quiet war has been escalating for decades.
