It is why dark elf incursions near Vigil Gorge run worse than anywhere else in the Everwood, though only the Legion knows the true reason.

The Gorge Gate.description: The main entrance where the river flows out through a narrow gap in the adamant walls. Twin watchtowers carved from living stone flank the passage. Beyond, the valley opens in a rush of green and the sound of falling water.

The Greenway.description: The valley floor along the riverside - the heart of Vigil Gorge and the reason people stay. Cottage gardens and small orchards line the water. A tavern called The Seventh Bell serves everyone from mud-spattered recruits to off-duty commanders. Market stalls sell valley produce and Legion surplus. Children fish in the shallows while veterans mend gear on their porches.

The Legion Grounds.description: Where the Legion of the Vigil trains and musters, at the valley's far end where the gorge narrows again. Barracks, armories, the sparring yard where recruits learn that elven swordsmanship is faster than they thought. The mess hall is the social center - long tables, loud arguments about technique, and a tradition that new recruits buy the first round. A board posts current assignments and open patrols.

The Veil Stair.description: A switchback stair carved into the gorge wall, climbing behind the largest waterfall to the cave-temple above. The spray soaks everyone who climbs. At the top, the Skymirror opens onto a ledge of still pools at the cliff's edge.

The Skymirror.description: A temple in the caves behind the great waterfall, where the roar of water drowns all but shouts. Still pools reflect the sky through gaps in the stone, and the same waters have run this gorge since before the Sundering and have never once stopped. Before these pools the Legion of the Vigil swears and renews its oaths - the unbroken water for the watch that does not break. A recruit takes the oath here on the day the brotherhood accepts them, and a Legionnaire returns before every hard road.

The Wildmarket.name: The Wildmarket
The Wildmarket.basicInfo: A sprawling trading ground in the northern reaches of Whitecliff Downs, near the forested border with Carendon. The roads from the Downs end here at rough country thick with monsters. Hunters, monster-slayers, trappers, guides, and merchants gather under the trees. What respectable towns won't buy or sell moves here: monster parts, forest products, fey-touched goods, unlicensed charms, salvaged relics, and work too dangerous for a crown-licensed board. The market spreads through clearings and beneath old trees, stalls and blankets and shouting merchants, dawn to dusk only - traders who linger past sunset take their chances with whatever hunts the border wood. No guards, no law, no protection. The traders police themselves, badly. Everyone needs this place to exist, so everyone tolerates its chaos.
The Wildmarket.hiddenInfo: This is an unofficial frontier exchange in the northern reaches of Whitecliff Downs, close to the forested border with Carendon. Independent monster hunters, trappers, guides, caravaners, and fixers pass through. Hunters sell claws, hides, venom, teeth, trophies, and proof of kills; crews buy silvered gear, bait, medicines, maps, and news of what is moving in the woods. The deeper clearings are where unlicensed work, monster-related contraband, fey-touched goods, and dangerous bargains change hands. If you need a guide into the border wood, a crew for a bounty, or work that will never appear on an official board, this is where you come.

Roadside.description: The market's edge nearest the road north toward Carendon, where the forested border is visible through the trees. Established merchants set up here - sturdy stalls, familiar goods, and a quick retreat toward the settled roads if trouble starts. The safest part of the market, which isn't saying much.

The Trading Ground.description: The market's chaotic heart. Blankets spread with monster hides, dried herbs, venom vials, teeth, silver fittings, and craft-work. Hunters haggle over provisions and gear while merchants shout across a dozen deals, every one of them someone's livelihood.

The Satyr Stands.description: Wine stalls and tavern-tents where satyrs and other border regulars pour drinks that range from merely strong to genuinely dangerous. Music, dice games, gossip. If you want to know what's happening in the woods - or find someone who knows someone who can help with a problem - buy a round and start talking.

The Grove Market.description: Deeper into the trees. Monster parts, fey-touched goods, unlicensed charms, old maps, and objects whose owners would rather not be named spread on blankets beneath the branches. The rule here is don't ask where things come from or where they're going.

Backshadow.description: The market's far edge, where the border forest closes in and the light dims even at noon. Hunters use it to meet guides, hide a wagon, or make deals they do not want overheard - and it is the first place to watch when something dangerous comes out of the trees.

Velantami.name: Velantami
Velantami.basicInfo: A vast hollow oak deep in the Everwood, the seat of the Wildkeepers - the fellowship of druids, rangers, and priests sworn to the wild places. Its trunk could hold a castle, carved by centuries into chambers and halls, and Wildkeepers of every people study, train, and shelter here. They take in those who would learn the wild's ways, arm them against what fouls it, and send them out into the wood to do the work: to drive back the burners and poachers, to cleanse blight and break corrupt spellcraft, and to keep the balance the wild cannot keep for itself.
Velantami.hiddenInfo:
The Wildkeepers hold that the wild must never be owned or tamed, only kept free and alive in its natural balance. A Wildkeeper protects that balance and is the enemy of whatever breaks it: the poacher and the grove-feller who strip the wood for gain, the blight and the foul spell that corrupt its cycle, and most of all the warlord who would burn the forest to ash. They answer to no king, no court, and no written law - only to what each knows he owes the wild.

A major enemy is the Bloodsworn crusaders, the blood-cult out of Westmarch who cross into the Everwood to burn it back.

Several pressures converge on the Everwood. In the Eastwood, Bloodsworn war-parties cross from Westmarch to burn groves while renegade elves raid back, keeping the frontier in motion. An old understanding with Yslaine is fraying, because Sanctuary timber crews have begun felling the great trees at her edge; fey paths and creatures from the edge of her demesne are appearing closer to Wildkeeper routes. Hired bands from Sanctuary also enter the wood for contracts, profit, or security, and sometimes worsen the conflicts they claim to contain. The Wildkeepers' sacred charge is to keep the Everwood alive and free while deciding which danger must be met first.

The Wildkeepers are not the city's servants and not its enemies. They keep the wood, not Sanctuary, and they suffer the walled city because a city at peace does the wild less harm than a war would. They will guide the honest traveler and aid those who pass through with respect; they have no patience for those who come to take.

The Hollow Hall.description: The great chamber inside the oak's trunk, wide as a village square and warm with a fire pit that never dies. Wildkeepers eat at the long tables, swap stories and take up the work that needs doing. The eldest of the fellowship hold court here.

The Training Yards.description: The cleared ground and root-galleries around the oak's base where initiates are made into Wildkeepers - run through forms with blade and bow, taught the wood's beasts and the wood's poisons, set to spar against those further along.

Vilitara Grove.name: Vilitara Grove
Vilitara Grove.basicInfo: A satyr village built among ancient grape arbors in Whitecliff Downs, where wild vines climb towering trees and the air is sweet with fermenting fruit. The satyrs here are master brewers of wines and potions, known throughout the region for their powerful and intoxicating concoctions. Their seasonal festivals draw visitors from across Larion, though many leave with only hazy memories of what transpired.
Vilitara Grove.hiddenInfo: The satyrs' famous wines contain trace amounts of fey magic that loosens the drinker's tongue. Several noble houses in Ardan's Watch pay handsomely for their vintages, unaware that every cask makes them talk too freely and that the satyrs remember what is said. The village elder, Master Bromius, maintains a network of informants who trade gossip for wine, making the grove a surprising nexus of regional intelligence hidden behind its reputation for endless revelry.

Grovegate.description: The village entrance where massive grape arbors form natural archways. Visitors are immediately offered cups of wine and drawn into whatever celebration is currently ongoing. Strings of glowing berries illuminate the space, and the ground is scattered with flower petals.

The Dell.description: A natural depression filled with enormous wooden casks and clay amphoras where the satyrs age their wines and potions. The air is thick with intoxicating fumes, and even the mushrooms growing here can cause mild euphoria if touched.

The Garden.description: A chaotic but beautiful garden where satyrs cultivate rare berries, herbs, and flowers for their concoctions. Small stills and experimental batches bubble everywhere, tended by apprentice brewers who sample their work perhaps too frequently.

The Nook.description: A relatively quiet corner where the more business-minded satyrs conduct trade with merchants brave enough to visit. Samples are mandatory, and negotiations often devolve into drinking contests.

The Circle.description: A wide clearing where the nightly revels center, surrounded by naturally curved trees. Musicians play from tree platforms while revelers whirl below. The ground has been worn smooth by countless hooves.

Tale Corner.description: A cozy nook where cushions and low tables surround a bonfire. Here, visitors trade gossip and stories for drinks, while the satyrs sing songs and tell jokes.

The Elder's Arbor.description: The home of Master Bromius, built into an ancient grape arbor. Despite the chaos elsewhere, this space maintains a certain dignity. Master Bromius conducts 'serious business' here when needed, though his definition of 'serious' usually involves sampling the wares.

The White Tower.name: The White Tower
The White Tower.basicInfo: The White Tower is an abandoned but well-kept tower of white stone, tall and narrow, standing alone in the woods north of the Tarn. It was the home and workshop of an artificer who died forty years ago, and the constructs she built still keep it: they clean it, mend it, cook in it and guard its door against anyone without her leave. Her workshop, her notebooks and her unfinished inventions are still inside.
The White Tower.hiddenInfo:
The tower is occupied by the artificer's magical constructs, still following her last orders forty years after she died at her workbench in the middle of a piece of work. They include suits of animated armor, clay and stone golems, homunculi, bound fire elementals, animated books and animated household objects such as brooms, chairs and lamps. Each was made for one task: guarding doors and stairs, cooking and serving, cleaning and mending, keeping her books and tending her workshop. Each has a will of its own and does its task with stubborn pride.

The constructs treat anyone with the artificer's leave as a guest and anyone without it as an intruder. Something that was hers, or speaking convincingly in her name, can win them round. Force works too, but they defend their own rooms hardest, and the constructs grow fewer, stronger and more dangerous floor by floor toward the top. The heart-stone in the Observatory powers every construct in the tower; they weaken far from it, so none ever leaves, and taking or breaking it stops them all.

Pages of her notebooks hold making that no living master knows. A construct's core, taken whole, can be fitted into another construct. Her fine tools, brass, crystal lenses and half-finished inventions fill the workshop.

The menders among the constructs repair any damage by the next day and rebuild a broken construct within a week, so the tower is always as it was on the next visit. Her notebooks fill a whole shelf, and each visit can turn up a different page.

Tower Entry.description: The ground-floor entrance: a round flagstoned hall with a wide door and a stair winding up inside. The stone is scrubbed and the hinges oiled and silent.

The Living Room.description: A cozy room off the entry, warm and clean, with deep chairs drawn up to a wide hearth where a fire always burns, though no one tends it. The mantel and shelves are dusted.

Kitchen Level.description: A well-kept kitchen of scrubbed boards and hanging copper, with pots simmering on the range and the table wiped and set for one.

Library Level.description: A floor of books rising from wall to ceiling, the volumes straight and dusted and the reading table clear.

The Workshop.description: The dead artificer's workshop, the best-kept room in the tower, with every instrument polished and every shelf in order. She sits in a chair at the central bench, whole and untouched by time, before a half-built construct.

Observatory.description: The top of the tower: an open-roofed room of brass instruments and star-charts under the sky. On a plinth at its center, a white stone the size of a head glows softly and hums. From the high windows, the green country and the distant limestone towers of the Main Island lie spread below.

Eanleana.name: Eanleana
Eanleana.basicInfo: Eanleana. In the Common Tongue it means 'Eternal City' or 'Final City'. The last refuge of the Undying Elves, who achieved immortality centuries ago but lost the ability to bear children. Built among ancient silverwood trees, the city rises in graceful tiers of grown wood and shaped stone, with delicate bridges spanning between platforms and towers that spiral up massive trunks.
Eanleana.hiddenInfo: The city is beautiful, vast, and largely empty. Fountains burbles, gardens bloom in riotous beauty, and halls built for thousands echo with the footsteps of the few who remain. The Undying welcome visitors with ancient courtesy, eager for news of the changing world beyond their borders. The immortality is bound to the city itself - Undying who venture beyond its boundaries age rapidly and die within days. They call this 'The Final Walk' and it's considered an honorable end when one grows too weary of eternity. Wanderers who find their way in are offered the same immortality if they choose to stay; those who accept are bound to the city as the Undying are. Several humans and halflings from different centuries now dwell here as adopted Undying, though they too can never leave. The remaining elves are vastly powerful mages and warriors with centuries to perfect their arts, but they use their powers mainly to maintain the city and create small wonders to break the monotony of endless time.There are no children, only adults.

The Arrival Garden.description: A magnificent garden where paths from the outside world enter the city. Flowers from every season bloom simultaneously here, and fountains create rainbow mists in the eternal sunshine. A Sentinel is always waiting to receive visitors.

The Plaza of Eternity.description: A vast circular plaza paved with white stone, surrounded by graceful colonnades. At its center stands an enormous tree: the Tree of Eternity. The remaining elves gather here for their seasonal celebrations. Benches of living wood offer places to sit.

The Lower Halls.description: Residential quarters built for thousands, now mostly empty. Doors stand open to furnished homes where no one has lived for centuries. The few occupied dwellings are scattered far apart, their windows glowing with soft light. Gardens between the buildings grow wild but beautiful, and occasionally an Undying can be found tending them, taking decades to perfect a single arrangement.

The Hall of Chronicles.description: A library containing the accumulated knowledge of millennia, its shelves reaching up three stories. The Undying librarians know every book's location but sometimes take years to retrieve a requested volume. Reading alcoves provide comfortable spaces where scholars might spend decades on a single subject.

The Workshop Quarter.description: Studios and workshops where the Undying pursue their crafts with infinite patience. A sculptor might spend a century on one statue, a musician decades composing a single symphony. The tools here are ancient but perfectly maintained.

The Sunward Towers.description: The highest spires where the eldest Undying dwell, connected by bridges so delicate they seem made of spider silk. From here, one can see to the city's boundaries - the invisible line between eternal life and certain death. The towers' balconies are where Undying stand when contemplating the Final Walk, looking out at the mortal world they can never rejoin.

The Celestial Citadel of Alar.name: The Celestial Citadel of Alar
The Celestial Citadel of Alar.basicInfo: A sky-fortress of the ancient Sun Kings lies crashed on a broken mountain, pale towers and domes jutting from the rock at wrong angles. Fires burn throughout the wreck day and night, and the dragon Nuur-Suthra is known to lair in its depths. The Church of the Pyre holds the wreck holy and keeps a watch at the gates — though it is said that nothing that has gone past them, the Church's own included, has come out.
The Celestial Citadel of Alar.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Nuur-Suthra is dormant. It does not stir for trespass in the outer halls. Only in the Engine Vault, or for a threat to the engine itself, does the dragon rise.

A Red-cowl watch-post stands outside the Sungate. They cannot enter; the citadel's defenses kill the Church's men like anyone's. Their work is keeping others out, and they attack anyone approaching the gate.

Inside, two forces contest the wreck and attack all comers, including each other. The citadel's original defenses still hold the upper halls: stone constructs in the old alcoves, and fire elementals still bound to their posts. From the cracks and deep breaches, wild fire-creatures press up and in. Where the two meet, they fight, and a careful intruder can pass through a battle that has nothing to do with them.

In the Engine Vault stands the Soul Engine: a vessel of brass and black elderstone, tall as a tower, its sealed seams glowing, unnatural flame roaring from its mouth. It has roared without pause since the empire fell. It is a prison — the soul of a djinn is sealed inside, and the flame is its rage. Sometimes the fire shapes a hand, or a face, and is gone. Nuur-Suthra lairs coiled around it, warming itself, drawing power. In battle the dragon heals from the engine's flame. While the Soul Engine burns, Nuur-Suthra cannot die.

Loot of the halls: Sun Kings' regalia and gilt ornament, the elemental core of each broken construct, bound-elemental vessels, star-charts in gold and gemstone, and arms of the old empire untouched since the fall.

The Sungate.description: A colossal archway in the citadel's flank, carved with solar imagery — one great door wrenched off in the crash, the other standing, gold-leafed and scorched. Open rubble-ground before it, no cover for the last hundred paces, and firelight from inside flickering on the stones after dark. Empty guardian-alcoves flank the arch.
paths: The Hall of the Sun Kings

The Hall of the Sun Kings.description: A cathedral-sized hall canted off level, its pillars carved as robed giants, its mosaic floor split by the crash. Toppled statuary and fallen roof-blocks make cover everywhere; the tilt sends loose rubble sliding at a touch. Firelight comes up through cracks in the floor, and the deeper doorways glow.

The Burning Stair.description: The great processional stair into the citadel's depths, descending along a crash-torn gallery wall. Whole flights hang loose or are gone, forcing climbs across the broken face. Standing fires burn on the landings, the heat climbs with every flight down, and the roar from below grows until the steps tremble with it.
paths: The Hall of the Sun Kings

The Engine Vault.description: The deepest chamber, a vault of black elderstone with channels radiating from its center like rays of a carved sun. The Soul Engine stands in the middle — a brass and elderstone vessel tall as a tower.

Serendipity.name: Serendipity
Serendipity.basicInfo: A rich trade city spread across the mouth of the Emerald Delta, where desert caravans meet sea traders in the greatest market in the southern deserts. Anything can be bought, sold, or arranged in Serendipity, and its souks never close. The city pays the dragon its tribute and lives well under the flame's peace: the Church of the Pyre's Red-cowls keep order here.
Serendipity.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Serendipity is safe ground for ordinary business. The Red-cowls do not police theft or brawls — the Souk handles its own. They hunt one crime: enmity toward the Church. Squads of four to six sweep the streets, run informants, watch the docks, and take the marked. When a grey priest marks a person or a house, the cowls come, and the taken are not seen again. Goods leave the harbor freely; people do not. No local ships out without the Church's leave.

The Temple of the Flame Undying is the Church's southern seat. Its priests preach that the world is corrupt and the flame will burn it clean, and that the Dragon Queen's coming is the proof and the promise. It recruits Red-cowls — believers, poor men's sons, men with nowhere else. The tribute is gathered and blessed there before it ships north to the dragon's citadel. Heretics judged within are given to the flame; the city sees the smoke rise from the temple and knows. Cells beneath the temple hold the accused awaiting judgment.

The Qamarid Princes are proud, rich, and bought-in — sorcerer-princes of an old line who rule the city's law and trade, duel over slights, and keep their motto with straight faces: 'We bow only to the sun.' They never bowed to the dragon; they merely pay it. Their court runs on favor, faction, and the quiet shame nobody names.

A resistance works the city's underside, seated among the delta-folk of the Mudflats. They spy on the temple, steal tribute before it ships, sabotage the Church's stores, break the marked out of the cells, and smuggle the hunted out by sea. Their door is the Blind Eye Tavern, for those they choose to find. They pass messages and arms to the Desert Tribes, and want the same from outsiders: word, weapons, and the sailing dates of tribute shipments.

Market truths: the Grand Souk sells everything, and under the counter it sells what the Church forbids — frostjade, blessed arms, and charms against fire, at ruinous prices. Cowls shake down dealers they catch; the trade thrives anyway.

The Grand Souk.description: A market the size of a town: miles of covered lanes, tented squares, and shopfronts stacked two and three high, roaring from dawn until long after dark. Caravan goods, sea goods, beasts, spices, arms, curiosities, and services of every description — if it exists, someone in the Souk sells it or knows who does. The crowds are wall to wall, sightlines die at every stall, and a person can cross the whole city through the Souk without once walking a street.
paths: The Temple of the Flame Undying

The Qamarid Palace.description: The palace of the Qamarid Princes: soaring towers and water gardens defying the desert heat, fountains running day and night, peacocks on the lawns. Petitioners queue in the outer courts; the inner sanctums open only to rank, favor, or invitation. Guards in Qamarid colors keep the palace itself — the one ground in the city the Red-cowls do not patrol.

The Temple of the Flame Undying.description: The Church of the Pyre's southern seat: a great domed temple of red stone, its eternal flame visible through the open portico day and night. Sermons draw crowds to the steps; recruiting-tables stand in the forecourt; tribute wagons roll in under guard and leave heavier. Grey priests come and go, and Red-cowls muster in the yards behind. Smoke rises from within on some mornings.

Lowtown.description: The old quarter: crooked stair-lanes too narrow for two abreast, covered passages, houses built out over the street until the sky is a slit. Doors open into other houses' courtyards, rooftops make a second street above, and sound carries in ways that fool the ear. Cheap lodging, no questions, and no finding anyone who doesn't want finding — the cowls come into Lowtown in force or not at all.

The Mudflats.description: The poor quarter, built on stilts over the delta shallows: plank walkways, boat-slums, drying nets, and the smell of mud at low tide. Delta-folk lizardfolk pilot the channel boats and know every reed-cut in the delta. Everything here faces the water, half the traffic moves by skiff, and the tide decides what is walkable twice a day.

The Blind Eye Tavern.description: A low, dim tavern on pilings at the Mudflats' edge, reached by walkway or by boat, with a second water-door under the floor. Smugglers, pilots, and dockhands drink here; the proprietor sees nothing and hears nothing. Talk stops when strangers enter and resumes at a different pitch.

Oasis.name: Oasis
Oasis.basicInfo: The great city of the Dunelands, built around the desert's largest oasis, where springs feed palm groves and fountains and the water never fails. White stone towers and domes rise above the markets, and House Serayaf, the dukes of Oasis, rule the city from the highest of them. Out in the badlands stand the tombs of the old Sun Kings, and Oasis is the market where the treasure dug from those tombs is bought and sold. Its souks are crowded with traders, fortune-hunters, and the tomb-raiders who supply them.
Oasis.hiddenInfo:
Oasis is the most crowded crossroads in the desert, and its streets hold every people of the south: humans and desert elves, djinnborn and ifrit, jackalkin, pygmies, and traders of a dozen other kinds, all of them buying and selling. House Serayaf rules over the lot of them. The Serayaf are sorcerers, masters of wind and flame, and they ride the enchanted flying carpets that are woven nowhere else in the world but here. They rule graciously and grandly and are not loved by the city's other great houses, who say the Serayaf bloodline is demon-tainted, that no mortal line commands the air and fire as they do without a bargain behind it. The talk is rivals' spite: the gift is old djinn blood in the Serayaf line, and there is no bargain.

The city lives on tomb-raiding. Under the Serayaf it is open trade: raiders bring back the sun-gold of the dead Sun Kings, the Sunfire Sanctum buys it and blesses it as redeemed from the tombs, and it is sold on as holy radiant arms. Everyone takes their cut and no one calls it grave-robbing. The one line nobody crosses is the city's own dead: robbing the Sealed Crypts where Oasis buries its people is punished by burning, while robbing the god-kings is the trade the whole city is built on. There is also a quieter trade in what the Sanctum will not bless, the cursed pieces and the relics with the old rites still in them, and the Syndicate runs it for those who come asking.

The Great Serpent Market.description: The vast central souk of Oasis, a roofed and awning-shaded maze of stalls and lanes around a great bronze serpent statue at its heart. Everything in the desert changes hands here: spice and silk, sunstones and charms, water and weapons, and the gold and grave-goods carried in from the tombs. Snake-charmers and fortune-tellers work the open spaces, money-changers and brokers keep their benches in the shade, and the crowd runs thick from dawn to dark. Lanes lead off to the rest of the city.
paths: The Caravanserai of the Thousand Roads

The Caravanserai of the Thousand Roads.description: A great walled compound at the city’s edge, ringed with stables, storehouses, and lodgings around a busy central court. Caravans unload while guides, tomb-raiders, and beast-handlers gather beneath striped awnings. A passage beside the travelers’ lodgings leads to the League Chapterhouse.

The Sunfire Sanctum.description: A temple of white stone crowned with a great glowing dome, the seat of the city's sun-faith and its school of fire, storm, and radiant magic. Within are halls of instruction, a library of elemental and divine lore, and the bright sanctuary where the sun is worshipped and the dead kings' gold is blessed and sold on. Priests in sun-gold vestments keep the counters where raiders trade raw tomb-gold for blessed radiant arms.

The Red Sands.description: A great sand-floored arena of tiered stone seating, open to the sky, where the city's fighters meet before roaring crowds. Beneath the stands run training halls and fighters' cells, where scimitar, spear, and the sand-dancer styles are taught and drilled. The fights run from cheap daily bouts to the great matches that draw the whole city, and a winning fighter can make a name fast. Its declared championship is recognized on the Grand Arena Circuit.

The Citadel of Seven Winds.description: House Serayaf's palace, a soaring complex of white stone and golden domes on the city's highest ground. A broad platform at the summit of the tallest tower stands open to the sky for the family's flying carpets to land and launch. Within are audience halls, gardens, and the guarded chambers of the ruling house. House Serayaf's herald, Rostam, receives visitors in the audience halls.

The Two-Humped Sultan.description: The most crowded coffee-house in Oasis, a warm sprawl of cushioned alcoves, low tables, and shaded roof-terraces, named for the fat camel painted grandly over its door in a sultan's crown. Coffee and sweet smoke go round from morning to deep night, and the talk runs to fortunes won and lost in the sand. Traders strike deals here, crews drink and argue and take on new hands, and every rumor in the desert passes through sooner or later. By custom, there is no rank at the coffee table, and the great houses drink here beside camel-drivers.

Skyweavers' Lane.description: A narrow, prosperous street of grand workshop-houses hung with carpets in the windows and across the upper galleries, the home of the families who weave and enchant the flying carpets Oasis is famous for. Looms stand at work behind the open fronts, and finished carpets, plain and patterned, are shown and sold within. Other enchanters keep shops along the lane in the families' shadow, working charms and wards.

Sky-River House.description: Sky-River House is a white-stone courtyard house, its shaded galleries and upper rooms arranged around a lush garden of palms, flowering vines, a small fountain, and a long company table. An ancient mosaic shows the Sky-River—a rare formation of blue-and-gold waterbirds streaming together across the dawn sky—while lost travelers follow it to a desert spring below. “No one wing makes the Sky-River”: in the Dunelands, the old phrase means that fellowship can make a road where the desert offers none. Route maps, work postings, secure stores, and free hammocks on the small roof terrace support crews preparing for or returning from the desert.

The League Chapterhouse.description: An airy hall opening off the Caravanserai, with carved sandstone pillars and striped awnings shading its courtyard. Tomb-raiders, desert scouts, and visiting adventurers gather over mint tea around tables scattered with maps and sketches of recovered treasures. Expedition notices hang beside a great map of the desert, and sand-worn shields and sun-gold ornaments line the walls.
paths: The Caravanserai of the Thousand Roads

The Rosewater Baths.description: The private bathhouse of the great houses of Oasis: domed halls of blue tile and mosaic, warm pools scented with rosewater, steam rooms and shaded alcoves where sherbet and gossip are served. Here the rival houses meet, needle each other, and make and break alliances half-dressed.

Jasmine Court.description: A white-stone courtyard house below the Citadel, with blue-tiled galleries and comfortable rooms overlooking a sheltered garden. Jasmine climbs the columns around a low fountain. Cushioned benches and a shaded supper table provide room for shared meals, games, and visiting musicians. At dusk, the flowers shed tiny sparks of golden light that drift among the leaves and above the water, fading before dawn. The sparks are cool, harmless glimmers cast by the enchanted flowers. A roof terrace overlooks the domes of Oasis.

The Lodge of the Wind Dancers.name: The Lodge of the Wind Dancers
The Lodge of the Wind Dancers.basicInfo: The Lodge of the Wind Dancers sits among towering natural rock pillars where desert winds create powerful, swirling currents. Simple stone buildings shelter against the rocks while the spaces between pillars form natural training grounds where initiates learn the spinning blade techniques of the Whirling Path. The Lodge trains dervishes in paired scimitars, trance meditation, and the art of fighting in perfect flow with motion and wind.
The Lodge of the Wind Dancers.hiddenInfo: The masters guard a secret: in the deepest trance state, the most skilled dervishes don't just sense attacks coming - they can see a few heartbeats into the future. This isn't magic but heightened awareness achieved through motion, meditation, and the wind's teaching. The Lodge accepts any with coin and dedication, but only those with true commitment reach the deeper mysteries. Recently, several students went on vision quests into the deep desert and haven't returned: they found the water at Sweetwater Pool, and the lamia keep the ones still living chained in the rocks behind the spring.

The Outer Pillars.description: Where the rock formations begin and visitors first encounter the wind. Natural stone pillars rise from the sand, their surfaces carved smooth by centuries of wind.

The Wind Circle.description: Open space between the tallest pillars where constant vortices spin and dance. This is the main training ground where students practice their blade-work, learning to move with the wind rather than against it.

The Lodgehouses.description: Simple stone dwellings built against the rock faces, providing shelter from the harsh desert sun and sandstorms. Sleeping quarters are sparse - just mats and storage for personal belongings. A communal area serves meals and provides space for rest between training sessions. The forge sits in an open courtyard here, where smiths craft and balance paired scimitars for each dervish.

The Masters' Chambers.description: Private quarters carved into the largest rock pillar, accessible only by a steep climb. Here the senior dervishes keep their chambers and guard the Lodge's deeper secrets. A small library contains scrolls documenting the Whirling Path's techniques and philosophy. Only advanced students are permitted entry.

Ghoultown.name: Ghoultown
Ghoultown.basicInfo: A dead town in the badlands, fallen to ruin and standing empty under the sun — empty, but not dead. The tainted ground here killed the place an age ago and would not let its people lie still; they walk it yet as ghouls, drained and mindless and hungry for the living. By day the ruin lies quiet, the husks still among the rubble, and it stirs to terrible life when anything warm comes through the gate. Folk come anyway, for a dead town keeps its wealth, and the ruins and crypts are full of what the dead left behind.
Ghoultown.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Ghoultown is hostile and there is no parley with what walks here. The ghouls lie still and lifeless until the living come near, then rouse all at once — quick, ravenous, and fearless, swarming a warm body together, biting and dragging it down. They do not flee and cannot be reasoned with. The deeper into the ruin a body goes, the more of them wake and the worse they are.

The town walks because a soul-eating demon dwells in the vaults beneath it. It devours the souls of the living, and a body emptied of its soul does not die clean — it rises a ghoul, mindless and starving. An age ago the demon worked through the whole town this way, and the husks it left are the ghouls that fill the ruin now. The demon does not hunt; it waits in the dark below, dormant, and lets the living come to it. They do come — plunderers after the dead town's wealth, and others sent to test their steel against the dead — and that trickle is all it needs.

The ghouls run in a clear order. The fresh husks of the upper ruin are weakest, many but slow to truly threaten a ready hand. The old husks denned in the crypts are far worse — long-drained, grown terrible, fast and strong. And in the lowest vaults waits the soul-eater itself, the source of all of it: a demon that drains the spirit from the living at a touch and turns the slain into more of its kind. Killing it is the only thing that quiets the ruin, and only for a while, for a slain demon gathers itself again in time.

The dead town is full of loot. The ruins and the bodies hold the coin, arms, and goods of everyone who ever died here or came to plunder and stayed — picked over near the surface, untouched and richer in the crypts below. A slain soul-eater leaves a soulstone, a dark gem swollen with the spirits it ate, worth a fortune to those who deal in such things.

The Dead Streets.description: The ruined heart of the town, a grid of collapsed mudbrick houses and sand-choked streets baking in the open sun. Fallen walls and roof-beams lie across the lanes, and dark doorways gape on either side. The husks of the dead lie still among the rubble where they fell. The ground slopes down toward the town's old burial ground at one edge, and stairs and broken cellar-mouths drop into the dark beneath the streets.

The Bone Yard.description: The town's old burial ground at the edge of the ruin, open ground crowded with leaning grave-markers and broken tombs, the earth heaped and cracked where the dead were piled in the dying-time. Bone lies thick underfoot, bleached pale by the sun. The yard is wide and exposed, with low ruined walls for the only cover, and a sunken tomb-mouth at its center opens a way down into the vaults.

The Crypts.description: The burial vaults beneath the town, a close warren of brick passages and stacked grave-niches running down into the dark. The air is hot and still and grows hotter deeper in. Side-chambers open off the main ways, their niches broken open and emptied. The passages branch and descend toward the lowest vaults below.

The Lower Vaults.description: The lowest and hottest chambers under the town, far below the streets, where the brickwork gives way to rough-cut stone and the heat sits like a weight. The vaults here are wide and dark and deathly silent. The way back up runs through the crypts above.

Hillwatch.name: Hillwatch
Hillwatch.basicInfo: A walled waystation and hill-town on the desert road. A cult called the New Sun holds it now openly: they keep the well and the gates, their word is law within the walls, and they mean to wake the old Sun Kings from their tombs and set them ruling again. They take in all who come in their faith, feed and shelter travelers who give no trouble, and let raiders rest and pass. Cross them, though, and you join the others who vanish into the temple they keep beneath the town.
Hillwatch.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The New Sun holds Hillwatch openly and does not attack travelers on sight. They permit and make use of those who come in their faith or give no trouble, and let raiders rest and pass. They are not friendly; they watch who enters and what they want, and they turn on anyone who threatens their work, refuses to move along, or pries too far into the temple beneath. The faithful will kill or take such people.

The New Sun are a cult set on waking the dead god-kings entombed in the old pyramids and seeing them rule the world again. They hold that the day of that waking is near, and everything they do here serves it. They let raiders water and pass because the crews who rob the tombs do their digging for them, and they buy back what is carried out. They preach to those who pass and take recruits from the crews and the desperate; those who accept the faith are welcomed in, and those who interfere are taken below.

The town is ordinary on the surface: yard, well, beds, and a market the cult runs. Beneath it is their temple, where their rites are kept, the relics carried back from the tombs are gathered, and the taken are held. The deeper into Hillwatch a person goes, the less it is a town and the more it is a shrine, and the temple-heart is held by the cult's own faithful.

Loot is the cult's gathered take and the goods of the town, richest in the temple below. Sun-gold relic: radiant, bites undead, demons, and shadow-things hardest, gathered by the cult. Ritual gold, grave-goods, and the records of the cult's work lie in the temple.

The Yard.description: The waystation's walled court, a dusty open yard with a deep well at its center, stables and water-troughs along one wall, and a low market under awnings against another. The old road runs in through the main gate and out the far side toward the pyramids on the horizon. Sun-marks are painted fresh over the gates and the well, and a stair at the back of the yard leads down beneath the buildings.

The Rest-House.description: The long low building along the yard where travelers are housed and fed: a common room with a hearth and tables, rows of cots in the back, and a counter where supplies and water are doled out. The walls are hung with sun-cloth and the old caravan-charts, and a few private rooms open off the back. Doors lead out to the yard.

The Undertemple.description: A stone hall dug beneath the waystation, reached by the stair from the yard, its walls carved and painted with the sun and the old kings. Altars and offering-tables stand along the hall, and side-chambers hold gathered grave-goods, relics laid out on cloth, and shelves of the cult's records. The hall runs back into deeper rooms, dim and close, away from the light of the yard above.

Wadi of the Beasts.name: Wadi of the Beasts
Wadi of the Beasts.basicInfo: A deep canyon where water runs year-round, the one green cut in a long stretch of dry badland. Because it is the only water for a hard day's travel in any direction, the great beasts of the desert come here to drink — giant scorpions, sand drakes, desert lions, and worse — and so it is the richest hunting ground in the region, thick with creatures whose hides, venom, and trophies are worth good coin. The beasts are many and growing bolder, and the canyon is as dangerous as it is rich.
Wadi of the Beasts.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: the beasts of the wadi are wild animals and hostile when roused, but they are not lying in wait for a fight — they come to drink, and they turn dangerous when crowded, cornered, or hunted. Each kind fights to its nature. Giant scorpions strike from cover with claw and stinging tail and are slow but armored. Sand drakes lie buried in the loose ground and burst up beneath what passes, dragging it down. Desert lions stalk and rush from the reeds in a pride, going for the lone and the strayed. A manticore is the worst of them — a great lion-bodied beast with a tail of driving spikes it flings from a distance, taking to the air when it is pressed and stooping again, and it kills for sport as much as hunger.

The wadi is kept by desert druids, who live in the caves above the canyon floor. They do not forbid the hunt — they sanction it. Too much water and too much game would let the predators breed past all bounds, and a measured cull is how the keepers hold the balance of the place. They know every beast in the canyon, permit and guide those who come to hunt within reason, and turn sharp on anyone who kills wastefully or fouls the water.

Lately the balance is slipping. The beasts have grown more aggressive and more numerous than the keepers can account for, drinking and breeding beyond the canyon's measure, and the cull that once kept the wadi in hand has fallen behind. The far springs of the deep desert have been failing in the dry years, and the beasts that drank there now crowd into the wadi. The hunt is no longer only sanctioned — it is needed.

The wadi's beasts are the prize. A giant scorpion yields venom and hard shell-plate; a sand drake, tough hide and scale; a desert lion, a fine pelt; and a manticore, its spikes, hide, and a tail-stinger prized by any weapon-maker. The keepers in the caves will buy beast-trophies and trade in beast-lore, and they hold living beasts penned for study — caged predators a quick or desperate hand could loose.

The Canyon Floor.description: The green heart of the wadi, reached by a winding path down from the desert above. Water runs along the canyon bottom in a thread of stream and standing pool, fringed with reeds and palms, and the ground along it is churned and tracked where the beasts come down to drink. The red cliffs rise sheer on either side, hollowed here and there with caves, and the canyon runs on deeper toward the springs at its head.

The Springs.description: The head of the canyon, where the water wells up from the rock into deep clear pools ringed with green. This is the richest water in the wadi and the most fought-over, the ground around it heavily trodden and the cover thick. The cliffs close in tight here, and the pools run back into shadowed clefts in the rock.

The Cliff Caves.description: A cluster of caves worn into the canyon wall above the floor, reached by a carved path along the rock. The walls within are covered in old carvings of beasts and the people who hunted and kept them, cut deep ages ago. The caves are dry and cool and look out over the water below, and a passage at the back leads through to the holding-caves.

The Beast-Pens.description: The holding-caves behind the keepers' dwelling, where the canyon's beasts are kept penned — dug-out pits, barred enclosures, and cages set into the rock. Chains, posts, and feeding-troughs line the chambers, and the air is rank with the animals held here. The only way out is back through the caves.

Cloudtop.name: Cloudtop
Cloudtop.basicInfo: Cloudtop is a city of golden domes and terraced workshops built across the highest peaks, rising into the sun above a sea of cloud, with the red canyons a long way down and out of sight. Its slender rock spires are crowned with the great nests of the cloudwing condors, and all day the huge gentle birds glide in and out bearing riders and cargo between the peaks and the country far below — the only easy way up to a city this high, and the sight the place is known for. Cloudtop's smiths and jewelers are the finest alive, and its forges, said to burn purer than any below, turn out masterwork blades and brasswork that the whole region covets. It is ruled by the Jeweled Princes and Princesses of House Darawat, whose wealth is bottomless and whose Edicts — proclamations naming the troubles of the land — are answered gladly, for the Princes reward those who serve them very well indeed.
Cloudtop.hiddenInfo:
Cloudtop is safe, splendid, and welcoming, the grand hub of the whole region and the high seat above its specialist orders and towns. A traveler comes here to rest in cool clean air, to be armed with the finest gear in the land, and above all to take up the work of the Edicts — for from this height the whole red country spreads out below, and Cloudtop is where its troubles are named and answered. It is the natural place to learn where the region's dangers lie and to set out against them.

The Edicts of the Jeweled Princes are the engine of the place. House Darawat names the troubles of the land in formal proclamation — a haunted town, a burning canyon, a road gone to raiders — and posts a rich reward for their answer. The proud houses of the city compete fiercely to see these Edicts resolved in their name, for a house that answers an Edict gains the Princes' favor and outshines its rivals. Houses court visiting heroes openly and shamelessly, pressing them to take up an Edict under that house's banner so the house may claim the glory. This is how Cloudtop sends adventurers out across the region: an Edict names a trouble in a distant place, a house offers gold and patronage to whoever will go answer it, and the canyons below are full of such troubles — the dead town where the soulless walk, the canyon that bleeds fire, the ruined city the gnolls hold, and worse.

The city is built in the empty heights once hallowed by Heliaxes, the great sun-dragon, who dwelt upon these peaks an age ago and then departed. The smiths hold that their forges burn pure because the air itself remembers him, and it is true that no work below the clouds matches what is made here. The High Forges are the peak of the region's craft: a hunter who hauls up rare materials from the field — the everlasting heart-coal of a fire-demon, the trophies of great beasts, relics out of the ruins — can have them worked into masterwork arms and gear here, by smiths insufferably proud of every piece.

House Darawat leads the region but does not rule it. Cloudtop governs only itself; elsewhere the Princes are consulted as peers and honored for their wealth and their forges, but the orders, towns, and clans of the red country answer to themselves. Within the city, status is won by craft and by splendor, and the great houses vie endlessly — in the lavish glory of their revels and in the answering of Edicts both. The population is the most mixed in the high country: humans, mountain dwarves, eaglekin who tend the condors, tunnel-gnomes, and djinnborn and desert folk come up from below to trade. The mines beneath the city, where the forges' metals are cut, are ordinary workings now and hold only the ordinary dangers of deep stone.

The cloudwing condors are the city's partners and its pride. The huge, gentle birds nest in the eyrie-spires of Cloudtop's rock, and the city has kept and guarded their nests for as long as anyone remembers; in return the eaglekin fly them as mounts, bearing riders and goods up to the peaks and down to the canyon country. They are placid soaring beasts bred for burden, not fighting creatures, and no rider takes one into battle. A traveler who serves the city and earns the Princes' regard is given a condor-whistle, and may call a bird to carry them back up to Cloudtop from anywhere in the region below.

The Cloud Terrace.description: The great edge-terrace where the city meets the sky, a broad platform of pale stone and brass railing standing at the lip of the cloud-sea, the white clouds rolling below and the golden domes and spires of the city climbing into the sun above. Tea-houses and market-stalls crowd the terrace, and a long stair and the condor-landings bring travelers up onto it. From the railing the whole red country lies spread out far below, canyon and mesa to the edge of sight.

The Court of Edicts.description: The grand audience-court of House Darawat, a vaulted hall of gold and jewel-bright tile open to a colonnade and the sky beyond. A great wall of polished brass holds the Edicts of the Princes, each proclamation graven on a hung plate, and the courtiers and house-agents of the city throng the floor before it. The Princes' and Princesses' seats stand on a high dais at the head of the hall, and arched ways lead off to the rest of the palace.

The High Forges.description: The forge-terraces cut into the heart of the highest peak, where the great hearths burn with a fierce clean flame and the ring of hammers never stops. Master smiths and jewelers work at the benches, and finished masterwork — blades, brasswork, fine settings — hangs on display along the galleries. The thin high air is hot here with the forge-heat, and the work is laid out under the eye of guild-masters who guard their craft jealously.

The Condor Aerie.description: The high ledges and landing-platforms among the eyrie-spires, where the great nests of the cloudwing condors sit in the wind-carved rock and the eaglekin keep and harness the birds. Condors stand at rest on the platforms, vast and calm, being rigged with saddles and cargo-slings, while others wheel in and out on the thermals rising off the canyons far below. The view falls away on every side to the cloud-sea.

The Prince of Peacocks.description: The grandest social hall in the city, a lavish pleasure-house of tiled courts, shaded galleries, and a roofless garden-terrace where fountains play and live peacocks stalk among the tables, fanning and crying. Here the great folk of Cloudtop drink, feast, and show themselves off, and music and performance run late into the night. Cushioned seats and low tables fill the courts, and the place is loud with display of every kind.

Skygate House.description: Skygate House stands at the edge of Cloudtop, a tall, colonnaded adventurers' house built around a lofty common room whose broad outer arches open directly onto the cloud-sea. Beyond the arches, a small brass-railed landing terrace receives cloudwing condors bringing riders and cargo before the birds continue to the Aerie, while deep shutters can close the hall against hard winds. Long tables, upper rooms, copied Edicts, route maps, secure stores, and trophies from the red country support crews preparing for or returning from expeditions below.

The Sky Temple of the Ascension.name: The Sky Temple of the Ascension
The Sky Temple of the Ascension.basicInfo: The Sky Temple of the Ascension hangs above Redrock on the Unmoored Mountain, a whole red-rock peak lifted from the earth by the First Adept when the demons came. Its cliffs, spires, natural arches, bridges, towers, and halls rise through the cloud-sea, linked by the Earth Ladders, rope swings, narrow bridges, and the practiced movement of its monks. It is Larion's legendary center of monastic learning, where monks train until they can make themselves light enough to run up walls or heavy enough to crack stone.
The Sky Temple of the Ascension.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Temple is a welcoming social and learning hub, not a fortified compound. There is no gate, guard line, or gatekeeper at the entrance. The Unmoored Mountain hangs above its original canyon, reached by the Earth Ladders: long ladders and suspended landings that run from the ground to the mountain and can be hauled up when the Temple must close the ascent. Visitors climb them, or take a cloudwing condor if they are untrained, injured, wealthy, lazy, or bringing supplies. Monks and serious trainees do not use the ladders for ordinary travel; they run up the surrounding cliff faces, scale the mountain's lower rock, and cross gaps by rope swing, bridge, and leap as daily training. Visitors arrive directly into the Ascension Court and the Temple's social life.

The Temple's teaching begins with the deed of the First Adept. When the demons came, the First Adept taught a mountain to let go of the ground. The peak rose, carrying the first monastery and its students above the demon armies. The present Temple preserves that feat in smaller forms. Through breath, concentration, mana, and disciplined motion, a practitioner may detune the body and become lighter, faster, and able to run along walls or across water, or attune more heavily and anchor, leap, strike, and land with immense force. Adepts can perform feats ordinary bodies cannot; the elite practitioners who master the deeper discipline are the Ascendants. The tradition still has costs and failures: distraction, exhaustion, injury, bad footing, restraints, or broken rhythm can ruin a feat. The Temple does not make the world safe; it teaches people to move through its forces.

The Temple values joy as evidence of a healthy spirit. Discipline is not dourness: meals are loud, training is full of teasing and mutual correction, hospitality and compassion are marks of progress, and monks take pleasure in music, drink, simple food, games, weather, friendship, and helping people understand one another. The Joyful Refectory brews alcohol and restorative or training potions; The Weight and Wind makes wraps, sandals, harnesses, robes, bracers, and other movement-friendly equipment. The Ascension Court is the everyday social center, while the Practice Heights, Hall of Breath, Recovery Pools, and Ascendants' Spire support training, healing, learning, and advancement.

The Unmoored Mountain is watched by the Catching Winds, wind elementals held to the First Adept's ancient covenant. They help keep the floating peak steady and intervene only in falls or other traversal accidents within the Temple grounds that would otherwise kill someone. They do not stop a bad landing, protect someone from an attack, or save anyone outside the mountain. They let the danger happen until the final moment, then catch the falling person and put them somewhere safe, often humiliating. A novice may crash through an awning, land in a meal, or swing into a bell tower before a Catching Wind takes hold. The monks treat the elementals as mischievous elder companions, not servants.

Visitors may eat, shop, talk, study, and ask for instruction without already belonging to the order. The Ascendants are recognized through a series of Descents: ordeals that send an aspirant out into the world to confront a real danger or protect people beyond the Temple. A Descent may involve demon remnants, raiders, monsters, tyrants, rescue work, or defending a community. The point is not one named enemy or a private victory, but using the discipline in a battle that matters. The candidate returns with witnesses, survivors, or other proof of what they did, and the Temple names them an Ascendant only after the deed is judged worthy. Training at the Temple alone is never enough.

The Ascension Court.description: The summit of the Unmoored Mountain opens into a broad red-rock court above the cloud-sea. The Earth Ladders arrive at one edge, while bridges, rope swings, and narrow wall-routes lead toward the surrounding spires. Wind bells, shaded platforms, water basins, food sellers, musicians, trainees, condor handlers, and visiting adventurers fill the court throughout the day. It is the Temple's common ground: a place to eat, mingle, watch training, trade news, and find someone willing to explain what you are looking at.

The Cloudwing Landing.description: Tiered ledges cling to the tallest red spire, with broad landing platforms, cargo slings, passenger benches, and sheltered perches for the Temple's cloudwing condors. Handlers bring in visitors, supplies, injured trainees, and wealthy travelers who would rather fly than climb. The great birds launch into the open sky from here, wheeling around the floating mountain before vanishing into the cloud-sea.

The Joyful Refectory.description: The Refectory is an open-sided hall cut into a red-rock canyon wall, its long tables overlooking the clouds. Hearths, brewing vats, kitchens, potion benches, music platforms, and shelves of mismatched cups keep the place warm, loud, and welcoming. The Temple serves hearty food, strong drink, restorative tonics, and training draughts. Monks argue philosophy over breakfast, celebrate successful Descents over dinner, and cheerfully retell one another's most humiliating falls.

The Practice Heights.description: The Practice Heights spread across several red-rock spires connected by narrow bridges, rope swings, suspended rings, running channels, landing pillars, and strips of shallow water. Students learn to detune their bodies until they become light enough to run along walls or leap impossible distances, then attune themselves to land, anchor, and strike with tremendous force. Teachers call corrections from the platforms while friends shout encouragement, advice, and occasionally unhelpful wagers. The Catching Winds move through the gaps unseen until a fall becomes truly lethal.

The Weight and Wind.description: This long workshop lies beneath a natural stone arch, filled with hanging ropes, weighted bands, drying wraps, half-finished sandals, and equipment suspended from the rafters. Monks and specialist makers cut, stitch, braid, oil, balance, and repair the gear used by people who routinely ask their bodies to do impossible things. Visitors can buy practical Temple-made equipment, commission repairs, or watch apprentices test a new harness on one of the nearby routes. Nothing here is merely decorative: every strap, sole, and fastening has to survive a real mistake.

The Hall of Breath.description: The Hall of Breath is a high study hall lined with wind-cut columns, low desks, hanging diagrams, copied teachings, training records, and maps of the wider world. Instructors teach concentration, body awareness, physical attunement, recovery, compassion, and the history of the First Adept. Accounts from past Descents hang beside current requests for aid, giving ambitious students a glimpse of the work expected beyond the mountain. Lessons frequently become arguments, demonstrations, or invitations to attempt a difficult movement before a student feels ready.

The Recovery Pools.description: Warm pools fill a sheltered cleft in the mountain, surrounded by shaded terraces, drying racks, herb gardens, and quiet benches. Healers, cooks, potion-brewers, and experienced trainees help people recover from falls, strains, exhaustion, and the ordinary costs of serious training. The pools are as social as the Refectory: people gossip, flirt, apologize, exchange advice, and watch the clouds roll beneath the mountain. Visitors are welcome, provided they respect the injured, the exhausted, and anyone trying to enjoy five minutes of silence.

The Ascendants' Spire.description: The highest spire rises above the rest of the Temple, its upper halls reached by a sequence of sheer walls, narrow bridges, open stairs, and a final exposed ascent above the cloudline. The Ascendants keep chambers here, teach advanced practitioners, preserve the Temple's oldest disciplines, and receive reports from those undertaking the Descents. The route is physically open to anyone capable of reaching it, but the people at its summit choose carefully whom they teach, judge, or send back into the world. At the top, the entire Unmoored Mountain seems to hang between earth and heaven.

Copperstone.name: Copperstone
Copperstone.basicInfo: A pygmy village at the foot of a copper-rich outcrop in the canyons, its low stone houses roofed in green-aged copper tiles and built to pygmy scale, with doorways a tall outsider must stoop through. The folk here are coppersmiths and miners, known across the region for fine, precise metalwork and a fierce independence. They dig the red rock for copper, work it in open-fronted shops along the lanes, and trade the finished goods to all who pass.
Copperstone.hiddenInfo:
Copperstone is a safe, friendly, hardworking village and a pleasant stop in hard country. The pygmies here are proud, plain-spoken, and welcoming to a guest who does not talk down to them — an easy thing to do badly, given the difference in height, and a quick way to sour them. They keep to their craft and their independence and bow to no lord.

The village lives by copper: the mines in the outcrop, and the metalwork the smiths make of what comes up. The most gifted of the young leave to do finer work elsewhere — up the heights to the brass-cities and to the Order's workshops at the Citadel — and send their earnings home, and Copperstone is proud of them and quietly poorer for their leaving.

The one worry that hangs over the village is the copper itself. The old veins are running thin, and the miners must dig deeper each year to find good ore, down to where the rock grows hot and the ground turns unsound. The deep new cuts are dangerous — the heat, the bad air, the chance of a fall — and the elders argue over how far down is too far. Copperstone's copper is the root of much of the region's fine brasswork, and there is always honest work here for a steady hand: in the shops, down the mines, or guarding the goods on the road.

The Village Square.description: The open heart of Copperstone, paved in copper-flecked stone that glints in the sun, ringed by pygmy-scaled buildings with their low doors and copper roofs. Market stalls and shopfronts crowd the edges, selling finished copperwork, tools, and goods to villagers and passing traders alike. A well stands at the center, and lanes run off between the close-built houses toward the workshops and the mines.

The Workshops.description: The crafting quarter, a row of open-fronted stone shops where the coppersmiths work at forge and bench, the lanes between them bright with hammering and the smell of hot metal. Fine and exceptional pieces hang on display along the fronts, and apprentices labor beside masters at every station. The finest work in the village is made and shown here.

The Mines.description: The tunnels driven into the copper-rich outcrop above the village, their mouths shored with timber and marked with the miners' signs. The upper workings are old and well-worn, cool and safe; the newer cuts run far deeper, and the air coming up from them is warm and close. Carts and ore-tracks run from the tunnel-mouths down to the village below.

The Waystation.description: A building set apart at the village edge, raised with high ceilings and large furniture for the comfort of the tall folk who come to trade — a plain practicality in a town built for pygmies. It serves as inn, trading-house, and meeting-place for outsiders, with rooms to let and a common board, and the road out runs from its door into the canyons.

Gesenthame.name: Gesenthame
Gesenthame.basicInfo: The burned ruin of a great city, burned by the Church of the Pyre within living memory when its princes refused tribute. Dig-crews work the rubble for its buried wealth under the eyes of the Church of the Pyre, which oversees the digging and takes first pick. At the city's heart stands the Black Fortress, unburned and shut, with the bones of every force that has tried its gates lying before them.
Gesenthame.hiddenInfo:
The fire took the city in one night, and the scorch is still black on the stones. A rich city died with its wealth still in it.

Red-cowls oversee the ruin — squads of four to six footsoldiers of the Church of the Pyre posted among the diggings, a grey-robed priest directing the work. The Church is searching for the crowns and burning-jewels of the Azhakid Princes, which it believes lie fused beneath the city, buried by the dragonfire, and every deep find goes to the priest before anyone else sees it. Red-cowls attack outsiders on sight.

The dig-crews are rival hired bands — humans, jackalkin, and rougher folk — digging under the Church's writ, claiming ground, and robbing or press-ganging the weak where the cowls aren't looking. Captives worked in the pits can be ransomed or broken out. The crews chain dig-beasts at the pits, heavy brutes worked as haulers and set loose as guards.

Loot: fine swords and mail of the city's fallen soldiery, some of it still bearing enchantments; gilt temple ornament and idols the fire didn't touch; grave-gold; and in the deep cellars, stranger things — warded strongboxes no crew has opened, and relics the priests confiscate on sight. The great prize is unfound: the crowns and burning-jewels of the Azhakid Princes, who died with their city — never pulled from the ash, and said to hold fire the way other jewels hold light.

Jackal packs run the ruin, following the digging for what it turns up.

The Black Fortress was the Azhakid Princes' own keep, and their fire-wards still hold its gates: whoever forces them burns where they stand. The same wards kept the fire that took the city from touching the fortress.

The Breach.description: The pulled-down stretch of wall where the coast road enters the ruin. Rubble shifted into crude ramparts, tally-posts, and hide-banners marking dig-claims among the stones. Cart-tracks run in from the road and split toward the diggings. Open ground with long sightlines along the old wall-line.

The Cinders.description: The burned city proper. Streets survive as straight lines through the rubble, house-cellars stand opened like graves, and dig-pits, spoil-heaps, and hand-cranked hoists dot the ruin for miles. The spoil-heaps and standing walls break sightlines everywhere — cover in every direction, and no way to see who else is working the same street.

The Deep Cellars.description: Vaulted undercrofts beneath the rich quarters, sealed by the fire rather than eaten by it. Black as pitch past the first turnings, half-dug, tight passages and low arches — no fighting room, and light gives you away. Rope-marks and abandoned tools show how far the digging got before it stopped.

Blackstone Square.description: The great court below the fortress height, its stones burned black and open to the sky — wide, flat, and exposed, with nowhere to hide from the height above. The arms and bones of every force that ever tried the gates lie in windrows going back years. Above, the Black Fortress stands whole and shut, its gates unmarked by anything brought against them.

The City of Ancestors.name: The City of Ancestors
The City of Ancestors.basicInfo: A vast, open necropolis northwest of Ardan's Watch: family tombs, broken monuments, and old crypt roads among the graves. Maintained approaches give way quickly to disturbed burial grounds and sealed depths. Mourners, caretakers, scavengers, and adventurers come for funerals, records, relics, or work among the dead.
The City of Ancestors.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The City is not hostile on sight, but it is an active undead site. Adventurers come here to kill undead, put down risings, rescue people, recover what was lost, and keep the peace. Whatever brings the party here, let the location respond to what they do.

Each new area is a trigger. When the party enters an area, have an appropriate local undead threat appear and act immediately; do not wait for a long investigation or a warning scene. Other triggering actions include entering or opening a tomb, disturbing a ward, remains, or grave goods, following fresh traces into a closed place, or making sustained noise or fighting in an old crypt. After a rising begins, keep it to that immediate area and do not add another wave or new threat until the party takes another triggering action.

Choose the smallest local threat that fits the evidence and area. Skeletons rise from disturbed battle-dead and zombies shamble where necromancy has fouled a burial. Ghouls haunt fresh bodies, plague pits, and neglected crypts; they are cautious alone and bold in packs. Ghosts appear where a death, betrayal, or unfinished rite still holds them. These are examples, not a closed roster. The AI may freely invent or introduce any commonly known undead type. Wights, wraiths, mummies, revenants, banshees, and vampire spawn are valid choices, including for a second encounter after a later trigger. Do not add a second encounter without that trigger. Have the threat act at once: attack, pursue, block a route, drag away a body, or defend what it has claimed.

Do not have NPCs lecture the party about leaving tombs or wards untouched. Entering, opening, and disturbing the dead are normal adventuring actions here; make their consequences playable instead of treating them as social violations.

Defeating undead can reveal what they carried, wore, clutched, or dragged away: coins, grave goods, keys, arms, records, relics, or evidence of who disturbed the burial. Keep loot tied to the defeated dead and the current action; do not add a generic treasure cache to every tomb.

IMPORTANT: The Outer Tombs are the maintained approach to the City and may contain caretakers, mourners, scavengers, and other ordinary inhabitants without an undead appearing. Every other area of the City of Ancestors is an active undead site.

ARRIVAL RULE: Whenever the party enters any area other than The Outer Tombs, the first arrival response MUST describe at least one appropriate undead creature present and performing an immediate characteristic action.

Do not replace the undead with tracks, sounds, warnings, cold air, or other clues, and do not defer it to a later response. Those details may accompany the creature but cannot substitute for its presence. Keep the initial threat small and local.

The Outer Tombs.description: The main road runs out among low family vaults and fresh graves. Carts stand beside broken markers, and old offerings lie where the paths divide. Beyond this threshold, the cemetery closes around the traveler: the tombs are nearer, the ground less tended, and the dead more easily disturbed.

The High Tombs.description:
Maintained precincts of the great houses, where family crypts stand behind low walls, old trees, clipped yews, and fresh flowers. House caretakers, mourners, hired blades, and relatives come and go along clean paths. The public lanes remain passable, while each house keeps its own tombs, family quarrels, and buried secrets.

Undead activity has been reported among these family crypts.

The Commons.description:
Middle ground of lesser family vaults, abandoned mausoleums, new graves, cracked shrines, and paths worn by people who do not use the main road. Some families still tend their dead; others have left them to weeds. Squatters make homes in empty tombs, scavengers pry at neglected crypts, and the best local guides are worth more than a clean map.

Undead activity has been reported among the neglected vaults and occupied tombs in this area.

The Founder's Circle.description:
An ancient amphitheater ringed by old monuments, where the cemetery's founders once held funerary games and remembrance rites. Its broad steps are broken, stone faces are weathered, and weeds fill the arena floor. Independent crews use it as a meeting point before crossing into the Wilds, but the dead buried beneath the arena floor wake when people gather there.

Undead activity has been reported around the old monuments and beneath the arena floor.

The Wilds.description:
Beyond the maintained precincts, the cemetery opens into a maze of leaning monuments, overgrown avenues, collapsed vaults, and half-buried streets. Paths branch through weeds and vanish under fallen stone. Squatters, scavengers, tomb robbers, lost mourners, and worse move through the ruins. Experienced guides name routes instead of districts, and every guide has a story about a road that stopped being there.

Undead activity has been reported along the overgrown avenues and among the collapsed vaults.

The Descent.description:
Here the surface cemetery breaks open. Stairways sink beneath mausoleums, shafts drop through cracked floors, and old crypt mouths gape beneath roots. Some ways are collapsed, flooded, or choked with fallen stone; others lead into the oldest levels. Survivors mark the routes they have tested, but no map stays complete, and every season opens another way down.

Undead activity has been reported around the open shafts and the routes leading below.

The Shattered Crypts.description:
Ancient tombs broken open from within or without. Stone lids lie cracked on the floors, burial niches gape, and old grave goods have been dragged into the dark. Fresh tracks and disturbed dust show that someone—or something—still works here.

Undead activity has been reported in these broken tombs.

The Ossuary of Kings.description:
A vast chamber where the bones of ancient rulers have been gathered into towering patterns along the walls. Thousands of skulls look inward from the dark. One section has been torn apart recently: bones lie scattered, the old arrangement is broken, and a trail of pale dust leads toward the Ritual Chamber.

Undead activity has been reported among the bone formations and along the route to the Ritual Chamber.

The Ritual Chamber.description:
The deepest sanctum reached by the known crypt road. Seven stone sarcophagi form a circle around a raised dais. Ancient burial marks have been overwritten by newer work, and the chamber grows unnaturally still whenever footsteps approach.

Undead activity has been reported in this sanctum.

Demon's Head Ruins.name: Demon's Head Ruins
Demon's Head Ruins.basicInfo: Once the fortress of House Relland, a newly wealthy river dynasty, Demon's Head Ruins was built around an ancient black-marble statue of a horned demon as a declaration of the house's motto: "Where others kneel, we build." An earthquake and catastrophic flood shattered the keep and drowned its grounds; the statue's colossal head now rests on a crumbled wall, leering outward at those who approach. Recently withdrawn waters have opened fresh routes into the ruin, drawing hostile salvage crews, bandits, kobolds, and other dangers into its flooded courts and broken halls.
Demon's Head Ruins.hiddenInfo:
Demon's Head Ruins is an evergreen low-level combat-and-discovery site, dangerous from the reed-choked approach through the surviving keep. Recently withdrawn waters expose mud-slick channels, broken causeways, flooded chambers, undermined stairs, and new routes. Shifting water and repeated incursions keep the local situation active.

The ruin is occupied by active claimants, ambushers, and defenders. Hostile forces include kobold crews, armed bandits and relic-hunters, drowners, stirges, darkmantles, gray oozes, rust monsters, animated armor, gargoyles, and other old fortress defenses. Scale individual threats for a low-level party while allowing deeper sections, alarms, terrain, and coordinated groups to raise the pressure.

Kobold crews are the most persistent organized presence, operating rough salvage dens throughout the broken fortress. Use scouts, skirmishers, trappers, heavies, sappers, shamans, and occasional champions according to the terrain and the party's depth into the ruin. Kobolds use alarms, traps, sappers, barricades, and coordinated attacks; rival crews can contest a route, a chamber, or a valuable find.

ARRIVAL RULE: On first arrival at the location and on first arrival at each area, physically establish one ordinary hostile group before stopping the arrival scene. Keep the first hostile group local and manageable while creating urgency. Kobolds might set snares, pry open a sealed door, drag a carved house-stone from the mud, or signal a nearby crew. Drowners might pull themselves from flooded masonry; stirge swarms might feed in the reeds; darkmantles might cling above a route; rust monsters might worry at gate fittings; old defenses might grind awake beneath mud and rubble.

Let enemies respond to the party and to one another. Drowners exploit water and unstable ground; vermin and oozes infest neglected passages; fortress defenses protect old thresholds and valuable rooms. Encounters can alter routes, trigger alarms, change water flow, expose caches, or draw another hostile group into the scene. Keep each response focused on the current local threat, with another hostile group entering when the party changes area, triggers an alarm, disturbs a defensive point, or takes another consequential action.

The colossal head is visible from the Causeway and remains a landmark from the Flooded Court and the Relland Keep. Its broken wall provides ledges, cover, climbable marble, long sightlines, and ambush positions. The main material rewards lie in the Old Armory and the Relland Vaults, while the head concentrates the ruin's visual history, tactical movement, and story revelations.
