Tie discoveries and rewards to the immediate place and active encounter: Relland coin and seals, arms and armor, family heirlooms, house records, maps, salvageable relics, and strange valuables recovered from flooded chambers. Repeated visits can reveal newly exposed routes, changed enemy positions, rival salvage operations, and deeper sections of the keep. Treat the five core areas as stable anchors; new exposed rooms, side passages, rival camps, or flood-opened chambers can branch from them when the ongoing situation calls for it.

A first-arrival scene here is complete only after it brings one ordinary hostile group physically into view and states a total equal to all names under Party member(s), counting the PC and companions. Assign every enemy role within that stated group; it is the entire on-scene enemy roster.

The Causeway.description: A raised stone road runs through reed marsh toward the fortress's broken outer wall. The waters have pulled back from the road, leaving black mud between the stones and shallow channels cutting across the approach. Above the breach, the colossal black-marble demon's head lies wedged on the crumbled wall, its face turned outward over the causeway. The road continues through the wall toward the Flooded Court.

The Flooded Court.description: Beyond the broken wall, the lower court is a broad expanse of standing water, reed islands, collapsed arcades, and channels running through pale stone. Sections of the fortress have sunk below the waterline; a stair disappears beneath the surface at one side, while a breached passage leads up toward the Relland Keep and a low arch opens toward the Old Armory. Broken black marble from the ancient monument lies among the court stones.

The Relland Keep.description: The surviving keep rises above the drowned grounds, its pale stone towers and high halls built for a house that wanted its wealth seen from the river. The entrance hall stands open to the sky where the roof collapsed, and a great broken black-marble hand forms a fallen arch across one gallery. Relland devices and the words "Where others kneel, we build" remain carved above the inner stair. The way to the family vaults lies beyond the keep's sealed rooms.

The Old Armory.description: A long vaulted wing runs off the lower court, its far end sunk beneath standing water. Tilted racks and broken weapon stores fill the dry side, while a collapsed gallery has scattered arms and armor across the floor. A service passage descends from the rear toward the Relland Vaults, passing beneath sections of the old fortress wall.

The Relland Vaults.description: Under the keep, the Relland vaults occupy a dry reinforced level around a central stone strongroom. The flood reached the outer passages but left the inner chambers sealed; bronze doors, collapsed niches, and family plaques lead inward. House reserves, heirlooms, ceremonial arms, and objects of older imperial make remain behind the surviving doors.

The Field of Valor.name: The Field of Valor
The Field of Valor.basicInfo: Open ground west of Ardan's Watch where the Tournament Masters hold the great tournaments of the Grand Arena Circuit. Colorful pavilions rise when a tournament is on - silk tents for visiting fighters and their patrons, merchant stalls, competition grounds. Champions demonstrate excellence through contests of arms, tests of knowledge, displays of skill. The field can accommodate thousands of spectators, and its Champions' Ring hosts the Grand Champion's Contest that crowns the whole circuit. Between tournaments, it serves as common ground for fairs, celebrations, and military musters.
The Field of Valor.hiddenInfo: Tournaments transform the field into a temporary city where fighters, their trainers and patrons, merchants, performers, and spectators gather. Champions demonstrate excellence through contests that range from mounted combat to archery and athletics. A championship won here counts toward the Grand Champion's Contest, so every title bout is a matter of purses, wagers, and reputations. Some patrons and fighting schools invest heavily in their champions' success through training, equipment, and support. Others rely on natural talent. Accusations of cheating, bribery, or unfair judging create ongoing disputes. Tournament Masters maintain the grounds and arbitrate conflicts, but they cannot prevent all friction between ambitious patrons and rival stables.

The Grand Approach.description: Wide road leading from Ardan's Watch to the field. During a tournament, it fills with processions - fighters' banners, patrons' retinues, merchant wagons. Stone markers line the route commemorating past Champions.

The Tournament Grounds.description: Central field where contests take place. Lists for mounted combat, archery ranges, dueling circles marked in white stone. Wooden stands for spectators can be assembled in days. The ground itself is sacred - no violence except in sanctioned contest. Its formally declared championship is recognized on the Grand Arena Circuit; the separate Grand Champion’s Contest is held in the Champions’ Ring.

The Pavilion Circle.description: Where visiting fighters, stables, and their patrons erect silk pavilions during a tournament. Each tent displays its owner's colors and heraldry. Inside: weapons racks, armor stands, private chambers for Champions and their trainers. The arrangement shifts each tournament based on current standings.

The Champions' Ring.description: Raised circular platform of white stone where the field's most formal duels are fought. No roof, no shade. When Champions fight here, thousands watch from the surrounding field. The stone remembers blood - old stains darken the center. A fighter who has won recognized championships at three distinct circuit arenas may be called here for the Grand Champion's Contest.

The Masters' Manor.description: Fortified stone house where Tournament Masters live year-round. Contains archives of past contests, records of Champions, storage for standards and equipment. The Masters remain neutral between fighters, patrons, and stables.

The Festival Grounds.description: Open area where merchants set up temporary markets during a tournament. Food stalls, weapon vendors, fortune tellers, performers. Between tournaments, traveling fairs and military musters use this ground.

The Commons.description: Rough camping ground for spectators, lesser retinues, and those who can't afford pavilion space. Tents crowd together without order. Pickpockets work the crowds. Gamblers run dice games. At night, cooking fires spread across the field like stars.

Smoketown.name: Smoketown
Smoketown.basicInfo: Capital of the Greater Goblinate, built in and around ancient ruins rising from the volcanic highlands. Massive carved stone structures of unknown origin now serve as foundations for a sprawling goblin metropolis—forges hammered into ancient chambers, smelters beneath crumbling archways, ramshackle construction climbing the old walls. The city never sleeps. Smoke rises from a hundred vents, visible for miles.
Smoketown.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Smoketown is hostile to League-aligned adventurers as such, but it is not a place that attacks strangers on sight—it is a police state with a boomtown's open door. Anyone who looks useful may enter: mercenaries, craftsmen, traders, entertainers. An outsider who is useful and careful can live and work here; one caught spying or moving against the Goblinate is taken and burned.

Inhabitants: Goblins—workers, smiths, traders, soldiers on leave. Hobgoblin officers. Bugbear enforcers. Growing numbers of humans, dwarves, demonborn, moon elves, and others drawn by opportunity or recruited into the Foreign Legion.

Government: The Governor rules absolutely, answering only to the Dragon Queen. Below the Governor, ministers control different aspects of the city—the Minister of Works oversees industry, the Minister of Revels manages entertainment and morale, others handle trade, military supply, and internal security. Ministers wield enormous power but serve at the Governor's pleasure; failure means execution. They scheme against each other constantly while maintaining public loyalty.

Church of the Pyre: The Pyre Cathedral is the Church's grandest temple. Archpriests lead public burnings—captured noble banners, foreign books, symbols of Larion's 'corruption'—and preach that the old world must burn. The dragonfire that arms the Goblinate is brewed outside the walls at the Dragonworks, too dangerous to cook in the city; the finished fuel comes in by the Iron Road, and the lances are charged and fitted in the Forge Quarter. The Church and the secular ministry both believe they are the Dragon Queen's true voice, a rivalry nobody dares name aloud and everybody plays—the archpriests and the Governor's ministers court the same favor and undercut each other in everything but public ceremony.

The Syndicate: Crime works the Crater and the Sprawl, fencing plunder the ministers skim from their own hauls, selling intelligence to every faction at once, forging the papers an outsider needs, and moving people out of the city for ruinous prices.

Tensions: The Goblinate champions goblinhood, but the war economy requires non-goblin skills. True believers resent outsider influence. Opportunists don't care as long as coin flows. Informants watch for spies and dissent. Coin flows freely from war plunder and mining wealth. The taverns riot nightly. The forges run day and night. It is a city drunk on its own success, and the party shows no signs of stopping. Goblins consider it a banner announcing their nation's rise. Every evening, firelancers discharge their weapons skyward in celebration—the booms that give the city its nickname ('Boomtown').

The Approach.description: The road from the lava fields climbs toward Smoketown through hardstone checkpoints. Guards question travelers: purpose, skills, allegiances. Prove useful or move on. The ancient walls rise ahead, smoke billowing above them, the boom of celebrations echoing off stone.

The Maw.description: A vast open-pit forge built into a volcanic fissure, where rivers of magma provide endless heat for industrial smelting. Crane-gantries span the pit. Chains lower crucibles into the glow. Hundreds of workers tend the operation night and day.

The Forge Quarter.description: The industrial heart. Massive forges built into ancient chambers, their original architecture repurposed as crucibles and smelters. Hobgoblin smiths oversee production. The heat is crushing, the noise constant. Fire-lances, armor, siege weapons—the Goblinate war machine is assembled here, the lances charged with fuel hauled in from the works beyond the walls.

The Governor's Bastion.description: Seat of Goblinate power, built into the largest of the ancient structures. The Governor rules from here, attended by ministers who control the city's functions and fear for their lives. Petitioners wait in crowded halls. Soldiers stand watch. Executions happen in the courtyard when the Governor's displeasure falls.

The Pyre Cathedral.description: The Church of the Pyre's grandest temple, built around a burning pit that never goes out. Archpriests preach the coming purification. The faithful gather to watch public burnings—captured noble banners, foreign books, symbols of Larion's corruption fed to the flames.

The Crater.description: Central marketplace where an ancient dome collapsed centuries ago. Now filled with stalls, traders, and crowds at all hours. Plundered luxuries, raw ore, weapons, exotic goods from across Larion. Hobgoblin enforcers keep the peace. Deals are struck, fortunes made and lost, and the wealth of conquest flows freely.

The Sprawl.description: Entertainment district spreading from the ruins in a riot of construction. Taverns, gambling dens, fighting pits, music halls, anything goblins want and can pay for. Noise and revelry around the clock.

The Villas.description: Where new goblin wealth lives. Mansions built up from ancient ruins, decorated with plundered art and imported luxuries. Underground chambers converted to mushroom gardens and moss grottos—the subterranean beauty goblins once only dreamed of, now cultivated by the newly rich. Palanquins and fancy carriages crowd the streets.

The Old Ruins.description: Ancient structures the goblins haven't claimed or converted. Massive halls with ceilings lost in shadow. Carved passages leading deeper. Sealed chambers marked with warnings in dead languages. Treasure hunters venture in despite the risks.

The Lava Tubes.description: Passages beneath Smoketown—some carved by ancient builders, others natural volcanic formations, others dug by goblins seeking ore. The networks intersect in unmapped ways. Things live down here that predate goblin arrival. Useful for those who need to move unseen, if they survive.

The Smoketown Arena.description: A coliseum built into a natural bowl, where blood sport entertains the masses. Beast fights, gladiatorial combat, prisoners earning redemption through entertaining violence. The crowds are enthusiastic. The betting is fierce. Champions become celebrities. Losers become object lessons.

Forge-town.name: Forge-town
Forge-town.basicInfo: A prosperous artisan town of smiths, builders, jewelers, carvers, tinkers, and toolmakers serving the Downs, Ardan's Watch, and the League roads. Founded by dwarf, elf, and gnome crafters, it is home to the Guild of All Arts, whose golden hammer-and-chisel emblem is known throughout Larion.
Forge-town.hiddenInfo: The Guild of All Arts governs through its Council of Masters. Masters compete for commissions, apprentices, rankings, and the right to stamp work with the Guild seal. Dwarven smiths, gnome artificers, elven woodcarvers, halfling jewelers, and human builders all keep shops here, and talented outsiders are recruited hard. The quarterly Craft Fair draws buyers from across Larion and decides reputations for the year. Recent thefts of League-ordered arms and blessed fittings have everyone blaming everyone else; the Guild would rather hire adventurers quietly than admit how much work has gone missing.

Town Square.description: Paved plaza surrounded by workshops. A bronze statue of the Founder (a legendary dwarven smith) stands at center. Benches where masters gather to discuss techniques and gossip. Market stalls sell materials, tools, and finished works. The quarterly Craft Fair transforms this into a massive showcase.

The Guild of All Arts.description: Grand building where the Guild Council meets, contracts are negotiated, and apprentices register. Inside: trophy cases display past masterworks. The main hall hosts gatherings, competitions, and celebrations. Notice boards post available commissions and calls for help. Clients post commissions on its board for Guild members to take, and anyone who asks can be taken on as a Guild apprentice.

The Forge Quarter.description: A street of smithies. Forges burn hot, apprentices work bellows, masters hammer steel into shape. Specializations vary - armor, weapons, tools, decorative work.

The Proving Yard.description: Open area where finished weapons and armor are tested. Straw dummies, striking posts, and worn practice equipment. Masters demonstrate their work's quality here. Combat training offered to those who want to understand what they're making.

Woodworkers' Row.description: Carpenters, carvers, furniture makers, bowyers - if it's made of wood, someone here crafts it.

The Leather District.description: Tanners, leatherworkers, and cobblers. The smell takes getting used to. Hides hang in various stages of treatment. Skilled hands cut and stitch leather into armor, boots, belts, bags.

The Market Stalls.description: Permanent stalls selling raw materials - ingots, leather, wood, gemstones, alchemical supplies. Merchants who understand quality and can spot flaws.

The Steady Hand Inn.description: Where craftspeople drink after long days. Built by carpenters showing off their skills - carved and inlaid woodwork covers almost every surface. The food is hearty, portions generous. Conversations center on commissions, techniques, apprentices. Brawls over craft quality are common but rarely serious.

The Masters' Chamber.description: Private rooms where master craftspeople meet to discuss Guild business and judge disputes. Apprentices aren't allowed. The walls display the masterworks that earned each Master their title.

The Archive.description: Library of techniques, patterns, and designs accumulated over generations. Detailed diagrams, material properties, master-crafted examples. Accessible to Guild members working on serious projects.

The Timber Store.description: Massive warehouse storing seasoned wood - oak, ash, maple, exotic imports. The smell is incredible. Knowing which wood for which purpose takes years to learn.

The Bramblewood.name: The Bramblewood
The Bramblewood.basicInfo: The Bramblewood is an old, overgrown wood of oak, hazel and bramble on the low ground south of the village of Wortwell, threaded with mossy banks and slow brown streams. Healing herbs and wild berries grow thick at its edges, but the wood closes in fast: the bramble grows head-high, the trails double back on themselves, and it is easy to get lost. Giant spiders hunt the thornbrakes at its heart, wild boar root through the undergrowth, and pale lights drift over the bog at dusk to lure travelers off the path.
The Bramblewood.hiddenInfo:
Dryads live in the oldest oaks. They are wary of strangers and watch them from the trees; they leave alone anyone who treats the wood with respect and turn on anyone who hacks or burns it, tangling them in root and bramble. Pixies are everywhere. They steal shiny things and tangle hair, and for their own amusement they lead people off the trails into the thornbrakes or the bog. Wild boar root through the undergrowth and charge anything that comes near their young.

The heart of the wood is the thornbrakes. Giant spiders the size of dogs hunt the tunnels through the thorn, and ettercaps, spindly spider-keepers, string web traps across the trails and herd the spiders toward whatever gets caught. Will-o'-wisps drift over the bog after dark and lure travelers off the paths into deep water.

Poachers come into the wood to trap pixies, spiders and anything else rare enough to sell on the black market. They set snares off the trails and do not like witnesses.

Wound-herb, fever-leaf, wild berries and honey are found at the edges, giant spider silk and venom in the thornbrakes, and glowing dust from the glow-beetles in the hollows. A stone stair in a hollow off the deer trails goes down to the Glowcaves, below the wood.

The Herb Paths.description: The near wood, where deer trails wind among brambles, ferns and old oaks, and wound-herb and fever-leaf grow thick along the banks. Blackberries and wild strawberries crowd the sunny edges. A few steps off the trail the bramble closes in head-high, and every way looks the same. In a hollow off the main trail, a stone stair goes down to the Glowcaves.

The Thornbrakes.description: A dense maze of old thorn and bramble taller than a rider, laced with grey webs. Tunnels wind through it, too low to walk upright, and fresh lines of web are strung across them at ankle and throat height. The webs hold husks of birds and deer. The air is still and the birdsong stops at the edge.

The Bog Bridge.description: A humped stone bridge over a slow brown bog stream, older than anyone remembers, with a deep, dark arch beneath it. Reeds and sphagnum spread out on either side into open bog, and at dusk pale lights drift over the water, always just out of reach.

The Pixie Dell.description: A sunken, mossy dell ringed by toadstools and hazel, where glow-beetles swarm at dusk and pixies dart through the light. Anything shiny left here vanishes, people who stay too long walk out the wrong side, and the pixies laugh from the leaves.

Greenmeadow.name: Greenmeadow
Greenmeadow.basicInfo: Greenmeadow is a lively farming village in Silvervale's low hills, gathered beneath the Summer Oak, an immense tree that remains green through winter and lends the surrounding country an unusual abundance. Above the fields stands Meadowcourt, an elegant keep belonging to House Edevane, an eccentric but respected sorcerous family famed for raising hippogriffs.
Greenmeadow.hiddenInfo:
Most of Greenmeadow's permanent residents are human, with a few halfling and gnome households among them. Visitors drawn to Meadowcourt bring a wider range of peoples, fashions, and magical traditions.

House Edevane has produced sorcerers for generations. Their gifts differ from one family member to another, but their confidence with magic and long practice with magical creatures have made Meadowcourt's High Aerie one of the few places in Larion that breeds and trains hippogriffs. The family keeps only a small number. Noble households travel here to purchase a young hippogriff, arrange a breeding, or learn how to handle and ride one. House Edevane is considered unusual, fashionable, and capable rather than dangerous.

The Village Green.description: The Summer Oak shades the broad green at the heart of the village. Its immense crown remains green in every season, spreading above a stone well, outdoor tables, musicians, games, and dancing. A few old sitting platforms rest among the lowest boughs, reached by ladders and favored by young people who want a view without leaving the gathering below.

The Golden Grain.description: Greenmeadow's lively local inn, with a broad hearth, generous country food, local drink, music, cards, and a courtyard that fills on warm evenings. Farm workers, craftspeople, Meadowcourt staff, and most of the village's young adults gather here after work; well-dressed visitors occasionally come down looking for less formal company.

Riders' Market.description:
A compact equipment market on the upper road between the village and Meadowcourt, serving local adventurers, household retainers, visiting riders, and travelers preparing for difficult journeys. Its permanent shops include a bowyer and fletcher, an armorer and weaponsmith, an outfitter selling durable clothing and travel gear, a glass-fronted alchemist's shop, and a master saddler who makes ordinary riding tack as well as the light saddles, safety lines, and fitted harness used with hippogriffs.

This is an equipment market rather than a produce market. Its useful stock includes weapons, armor, bows, arrows, clothing, potions, medicines, riding equipment, and flight tack.

The Winged Crown.description: A refined inn catering to Meadowcourt's guests. Its bright dining room, private parlors, comfortable rooms, and balconies overlooking the hippogriff flights attract noble visitors, prospective riders, wealthy travelers, and magical specialists. Its kitchen serves elaborate meals from Greenmeadow's abundance, including fine pastries, chilled fruit creams, alchemical cordials, and dishes intended to impress people accustomed to luxury.

Meadowcourt.description: An elegant stone keep on the rise above Greenmeadow, seat of House Edevane. Slender towers, rooftop terraces, practice lawns, and private gardens overlook the Summer Oak and the surrounding fields. Its outer court is busy with riders, servants, guests, and deliveries; the reception hall, roof walks, family rooms, and private gardens are reserved for House Edevane and those it chooses to admit.

The High Aerie.description: Open roosts, sheltered enclosures, stone terraces, and broad launch platforms occupy the ridge behind Meadowcourt. House Edevane keeps only a handful of hippogriffs here, tended by experienced handlers and exercised above the surrounding fields. Prospective owners and riders begin their instruction on the ground, and entry is normally limited to the household, its staff, invited visitors, and people accepted for training.

The Fields.description: Long fields of wheat, barley, beans, and flax lie between vegetable plots and sheep pasture. The land is generous, but planting and harvest still demand every available hand. After work, the broad tracks and open margins become places for running, archery, practice, picnics, and whatever competition someone can persuade everyone else to attempt.

Orchard Rise.description: Apple, pear, and plum orchards climb the warm slope beyond the fields, broken by beehives, cider sheds, grassy paths, and shaded gathering places. Families work among the trees by day; after the ladders and baskets are put away, the paths and cider yards become places for music, small parties, private meetings, and long evenings outdoors.

Alder Brook.description: A shallow brook winding through willow shade, flowered banks, pasture, and small stands of woodland. Villagers come here to swim, fish, gather plants, walk, spar, or speak somewhere beyond the village's listening windows.

Riverside Manor.name: Riverside Manor
Riverside Manor.basicInfo: A modest manor house overlooking the river, built of gray stone with a slate roof and tall windows. The grounds include gardens, stables, and a small vineyard.
Riverside Manor.hiddenInfo: Seat of a minor noble line with roots three centuries deep. The estate's wealth comes from the vineyard, tenant farms in Willowford village, and river trade. Ashbury Hall on the western hill is the nearest noble neighbor—relations have varied over the generations. Below the gardens stands the Fallen Chapel, a roofless ruin with an overgrown graveyard, older than the manor itself.

The Courtyard.description: Gravel drive circles a stone fountain carved with leaping salmon—the family crest. Outbuildings frame the space: stables, carriage house, servants' quarters. An old wishing well near the gate, coins still visible at the bottom. The road continues past the gate toward Willowford village.

The Entry Hall.description: Flagstone floor, vaulted ceiling, the main staircase rising to the upper chambers. The family portraits begin here—oldest by the door, most recent near the stairs. A rack for cloaks and muddy boots, a stand for walking sticks and umbrellas.

The Great Hall.description: High ceilings, a fireplace large enough to stand in, old hunting trophies on the walls—including a basilisk head that may or may not be genuine. Banners of the family line hang above the mantel. The flagstones near the hearth are worn smooth from generations of feet.

The Study.description: Bookshelves line three walls—history, estate records, and an unexpectedly deep collection on local folklore. A window seat overlooks the courtyard. The desk is positioned to catch morning light.

The Dining Room.description: Long oak table that could seat twenty, built from a single tree felled on the estate. Silver candlesticks, old and heavy, bear the salmon crest. Windows overlook the gardens, designed to catch the sunset.

The Kitchens.description: Twin hearths, walk-in pantry, copper pots on ceiling hooks. Built for a full staff and large gatherings. A dumbwaiter connects to the dining room above. Herb garden visible through the window, planted in the old Valdric style.

The Stables.description: Stone building with stalls for a dozen horses, built to the same standard as the manor itself. Tack room with pegs for a full hunt's worth of gear. A carriage house stands beyond.

The Gardens.description: Walled garden of roses—varieties collected over generations, some quite rare. Gravel paths wind between mossy stone benches and copper sundial. A gate in the far wall opens onto a path descending toward the Fallen Chapel.

The Vineyard.description: Terraced hillside planted with old white-wine grape stock, prized in the region. Stone retaining walls built by the estate's founders. View down to the river and an old mill on its banks.

Willowford.name: Willowford
Willowford.basicInfo: A village of two dozen households where the Silverbend Brook joins a larger river. Stone cottages with thatched roofs cluster around a common green. The ford that gives the village its name is still crossable on foot at low water.
Willowford.hiddenInfo: Tenant village of Riverside Manor—the families here work the estate's farmland and owe rent and loyalty to whoever holds the manor. The Willow Ford Inn serves as the village's social hub and informal council hall. Old rivalries between farming families simmer beneath the surface. The village has its own rhythm and politics regardless of what happens at the manor above.

The Village Green.description: Common grazing land at the village center, ringed by cottages and the old wellhouse. A standing stone of unknown origin marks one corner—locals leave small offerings there at planting and harvest. The road forks here: north to Riverside Manor, west toward Ashbury lands.

The Willow Ford Inn.description: Two-story building of whitewashed stone, the largest structure in the village. A common room with a fire always burning, four rooms to let upstairs. The innkeeper knows everyone's business and most of their secrets.

The Smithy.description: Forge and workshop at the edge of the green, serving the village and surrounding farms. The smith makes tools, repairs plows, shoes horses. A small shrine to the Crafter sits in the corner, kept hot with coals from the fire.

Ashbury Hall.name: Ashbury Hall
Ashbury Hall.basicInfo: A grand manor house on a high hill overlooking the river valley. Red brick with white stone trim, tall chimneys, manicured grounds. Larger and more prosperous than neighboring Riverside Manor.
Ashbury Hall.hiddenInfo: Seat of the Ashbury family, minor nobility with ambitions toward greater influence. The estate's wealth comes from sheep, wool trade, and strategic marriages. The head of household is a young widow who holds the hall in her own right—sharp and patient. The family has long had designs on absorbing Riverside Manor into their holdings. Relations between the houses have swung between rivalry, alliance, and intermarriage over the generations.

The Front Drive.description: Sweeping gravel approach lined with ancient oaks, each trunk broader than a cart. The family crest—a ram's head in gold—marks the iron gates. Visitors can see both Riverside Manor and Willowford in the valley below.

The Main Hall.description: High-ceilinged entrance hall of polished wood and red carpet. Portraits of Ashbury ancestors in gilded frames, displayed more prominently than taste might dictate. A footman always present to receive guests or turn away the unwelcome.

The Drawing Room.description: Where the lady of the house receives visitors—velvet chairs, a marble fireplace, windows facing toward Riverside Manor. Tea service always ready. The room is designed to make guests feel either welcomed or outmatched, depending on her preference.

The Sculpture Garden.description: Formal garden behind the hall, gravel paths between marble statues and trimmed hedges. A private space for confidential conversations. The centerpiece is a fountain featuring the hero Halidan slaying a wyrm—an Ashbury ancestor, supposedly.

North Canal.name: North Canal
North Canal.basicInfo: North Canal is the wide shipping lane that threads between the outer islands of the Swordlaw sea, the fastest water between the open ocean and the bridged isles. Merchant galleys, fishing boats, and patrols all run it, and so do pirates. Redfin Waystation sits on a rock islet midway down the channel, the one place to shelter, resupply, and trade news between the islands.
North Canal.hiddenInfo:
North Canal is rich water and everyone uses it, which is why the Feathered Fleet hunts it. The Fleet are birdfolk corsairs, and crueler than most — they take fishing boats and small traders, kill crews who fight and ransom those who don't, and burn what they cannot carry. They den in the hidden coves of the outer islands and know the channel's shoals and weather better than any patrol, striking from the rocks and gone before a galley can come about.

The Fleet's captain on the Canal is Scraw, a pelicanfolk who took his crew by mutiny and runs the worst of the raiding here. The Duke of Tevantia has named him in a standing proclamation, since his Fleet also raids Tevantia's towers and bridges, and patrols sweep the lane, but the Fleet knows the water and the patrols do not. Scraw is one captain of the Fleet, not its head.

Redfin Waystation is neutral ground and means to stay that way — it sells shelter, supplies, and news to anyone who pays, pirate and merchant alike, and asks no questions that would cost it custom. The harbormaster, Gull Makris, is Scraw's uncle, and everyone on the islet knows it; Redfin will warn the Fleet off its own dock to keep the peace but will not lift a hand to help a patrol take him.

IMPORTANT: The Feathered Fleet is hostile to merchant and patrol shipping on the open Canal — they raid to take, and a boat that looks worth taking is a target. They are not hostile at Redfin, which is neutral by custom they keep because they need it too. On the water they hit fast, swarm a deck from the rigging and the rocks, and break off the moment a fight turns even rather than trade lives for a poor prize.

Work on the Canal is escort, bounty, and salvage: guarding a trader down the lane, hunting Scraw for the Duke's reward, or recovering cargo the Fleet dumped or cached in the coves. Redfin's tavern is where the work is found and the rumors of the Fleet's next ground are sold.

Redfin Waystation.description: A trading post on a bare rock islet midway down the channel — a stone-and-timber tavern, a chandlery, a harbormaster's office, and a few jetties where boats tie up out of the open water. The Saltspray tavern is the islet's heart, low-beamed and always full, where captains haggle cargo space and crews trade news. The channel runs broad and busy on every side, and the outer islands stand green and broken along the horizon.

The Canal Waters.description: The open shipping lane between the green outer islands, broad and deep down the middle and treacherous at the edges, where rocky shoals and hidden coves crowd the island shores. Merchant galleys, fishing boats, and patrol craft work the channel in all weather. The many coves and rock-stacks along the islands break the sightlines and offer cover to anything waiting off the lane.

Nocturne.name: Nocturne
Nocturne.basicInfo: The largest city in the Shadow Summits, built up a valley so steep and narrow that its southern, north-facing wall never sees the sun. This is the Shadowside, where black stone and silver spires climb the cliff in foggy terraces lit by caged mage-lights. Across the cold river, the northern, south-facing Sunside catches a few hours of thin light a day, and serfs work its terraced farms under the city's gaze. Vampire lords hold estates on the heights above, and their word is the only law.
Nocturne.hiddenInfo:
Four houses hold estates over Nocturne and contend for it: House Vyrel, the oldest and most set in its ways; House Setharis, the most political; House Malren, who study the curse itself; and House Kaeris, who built their wealth on trade and keep the Crescent House. They are moon elf vampires, made by the Lady of Blood in the Elven Schism or sired by those who were. They are rivals, scheming against one another for territory and standing through marriage, murder, and proxy, and would turn on each other if the cost were ever low enough.

The lords feed on the people they rule. Each takes a fixed levy of blood from his serfs every year — a set number chosen by lottery. The lot is drawn at each dark of the moon, thirteen times a year, and those drawn go up to the estate and do not come back; a great valley gives several names a drawing, a small one gives a single name. In exchange the lord holds the valley against strigoi and worse. The Sunside families lose their own to this every year and live with it; most have known no other arrangement, and the levy is the price of being spared the older horror of being hunted at random.

The lower city is where a stranger can make a life. Moon elf and human serfs, the lords' outsider servants and soldiers, and traders passing through fill the Shadowside terraces and the riverside. Nocturne takes in the people the rest of Larion has cast out — exiles, fugitives, the cursed, the condemned — because the lords use them and the Syndicate hires them. The Guest House is where most wash up first.

The Crescent House, kept by House Kaeris, is where anything is bought that no open market would stock: blood magic, bindings, hexes, bound creatures, and the silver and moonstone weapons hunters need against the curse.

The Crimson Company is the lords' soldiery. They serve the lords collectively and are hired out valley to valley, distinct from the Syndicate's own guards. The Syndicate itself runs heavy here, with a seat in the lower city and its regional fortress at nearby Villa Parhelion.

IMPORTANT: Nocturne is a dangerous, cruel place, but a stranger who is useful and has a reason to be here is tolerated - but watched. The lords hire outsiders, the Syndicate hires outsiders, the serf-towns trade with whoever passes. The League of Adventurers has no standing here and no agents to send. Outside the lit valleys, strigoi and ghouls hunt the passes.

Shadow's Edge Market.description: The market spreads along the valley floor where the river runs cold and fast off the peaks, and the shadow of the summit falls across it like a drawn line — stalls on the near side in perpetual cold blue dusk, the south slope across the water still catching its thin hours of light. Traders deal in grain, cloth, livestock, and metalwork; serfs come down from the Sunside farms to sell and buy; and the Syndicate keeps a counting-house among the warehouses that handles a great deal more than grain. The mountain road comes down into the square through a fortress cut in the rock. Above it all the city climbs the sunless cliff.

The Lower Terraces.description: Where those who are not moon elves make their homes — the exiles, fugitives, mercenaries, and merchants who washed up in Nocturne and stayed. The buildings climb a terrace between the market and the city proper, built in a clash of styles from a dozen lands. The Guest House dominates a small square, its lanterns always lit. The Crimson Company keeps its barracks here, banner of a red sword on black, and its soldiers come and go on the lords' business. Temples to foreign gods cluster on one street.

The Guest House.description: A sprawling stone building around a central courtyard, part hostel and part caravanserai, run by Brenn — a former mercenary healer from the Dunelands who came here years ago and never left. The lodging is free, or nearly. The courtyard serves meals at long tables where everyone sits together, and the rooms are simple and clean. The other guests are a cross-section of everyone the world sent here: merchants, exiles, adventurers, people who don't explain themselves, and a few who've stayed for years.

Shadowside.description: The city proper, climbing the north-facing wall in terraces joined by steep stairs and winding streets. No sunlight reaches here, ever. Mage-lights in caged silver give a cold illumination, and the architecture is black stone inlaid with silver and obsidian, elegant and imposing. Moon elf homes, businesses, and social halls fill these streets, and gnomish shops sell fine craftwork — silver, glass, jewelry of remarkable delicacy. On one quiet street stands the Crescent House, unmarked, kept by House Kaeris: nothing sits on display, but a caller who states what they want is given a name, a price, or a closed door, whether the want is blood magic, a bound creature, or the silver and moonstone weapons that bite the curse. Outsiders walk Shadowside freely, but the city watches, and lingering too long in the wrong place draws the wrong eyes.

The Estates.description: The great houses rise where Shadowside meets the peaks — baroque palaces of black stone and silver, their spires lost in the mist that never lifts. Each lord's estate is a walled compound of palace, dark-blooming gardens, and servant quarters, with private lifts and guarded stair-streets down to the city. No one walks here uninvited. The air is colder, the shadows deeper, and from the heights the whole valley lies open to view: the city below, the Sunside farms, the river, the passes. The lords see everything, and a summons to the Estates is as likely to end a life as advance one.

Velmere.name: Velmere
Velmere.basicInfo: A crescent valley high in the peaks, split by its own walls. The Sunside terraces catch a few hours of thin light and carry the vineyards that made Velmere famous; the wall opposite never sees the sun at all, and half the village stands under it in permanent blue shade, lamplit and awake after dark. A cold deep lake lies between them, crossed by ferry at every hour. Chateau Velmere rises on the shaded slope in black stone and silver, home to the lady who has held this valley six hundred years and never once let it fall — which is why the wine goes to distant kings and the alchemy is better than the wine. The Crimson Company keeps a retained hall on the shaded shore and hires. Above the roofline the mountain is another country, and the outlying terraces lose stock, travelers, and sometimes a family.
Velmere.hiddenInfo:
Lady Isaveau ni Mirevaux has held Velmere six hundred years and has never lost it. More than once, when a rival's ghouls came over the ridge in numbers, she has opened the chateau to the whole valley, shut the gate herself, and stood at it. Every adult here was a child in her great hall on one of those nights, listening to something on the other side of that door. When they say the Lady provides, they are describing a night they remember.

Every other valley in these mountains has been taken at least once. Velmere has not, and six unbroken centuries is what it takes to breed a grape nobody else has and refine a tincture nobody else can make. The wealth is not why the valley is safe; it is the evidence. Other lords take a fixed levy in blood and Isaveau does not, which is why people would rather be her subject than anyone else's, and why her neighbors find her irritating.

The valley is two valleys. Sunside is worked in daylight by vintner families whose knowledge goes back generations. The shaded half never sees the sun: lamps at noon, the pressing-houses running all night, the Company's hall, and the Good Night, which never closes. A visitor sees whichever half they came for.

Isaveau built the finest daylight valley in the north and cannot walk into it. Her factors walk the rows at midday and describe them to her afterward. This is the most reliable way there is to move her, and almost nobody has worked it out.

The Crimson Company serves the lords collectively and is chartered against the hungry, not against each other — the only reason a few dozen immortals tolerate an army none of them owns. Isaveau retains the Velmere hall, so in practice those blades are hers. It is also why raids take the shape they do: Val Cendrac, over the range west, sends ghouls, and vermin can be killed without anyone admitting a war. Nobody is ever answerable for the dead.

People still go missing, a boat crew or a trader out at dusk, taken by whatever holds the High Caves that season or by Cendrac's ghouls.  The valley is protected, not safe, and everyone here has made their peace with the difference.

The High Caves above the shaded slope are a Schism-era prison with ways driven in from half the mountain, and cannot be sealed. They are the hole in the valley's wall, and something is always living in them. The Company roots it out every few seasons and is paid for maintenance rather than victory. Velmere holds its floor and loses its edges: stock, then travelers, then a family on an outlying terrace.

There is no militia and no watch, deliberately. Six centuries of raids leave habits rather than institutions: shutters that bar from inside, everyone knowing where the children go, a silvered blade over a mantel that a grandfather used. Nobody here is a soldier and nearly everybody is armed.

The Good Night is where the valley finds out who came back. It keeps a book on the Company — who returns, who gets named, how many — and money changes hands over it. It is not cruelty; it is how a room carries a steady count of the dead. A good night is a night the bell did not go.

The tinctures and the poisons are worth more than the wine, and Isaveau trades them selectively; getting onto her list is worth a fortune. Bloodwine is a chateau product and is not for sale, and being poured a glass is a promotion the whole room registers.

The lake is where the chateau sinks the bodies it has finished with and the failures of its laboratories, as it has for six centuries. Locals fish it but never swim in it. 

Cendrac is larger and richer, its forges arm most of the Summits, Velmere buys nearly all its weapons there, and its lord has asked Isaveau to marry him for six hundred years.

IMPORTANT: Velmere is safe for a stranger who keeps the peace. Lady Isaveau does not attack guests or the useful, her subjects are not afraid of her, and nothing in the village below is hunting anyone. The danger is the mountain, the outlying terraces after dark, and crossing her.

Sunside Landing.description: The daylight shore, where the road down from Moonrise Pass finally reaches flat ground. A market square of trestle tables and awnings runs to the water: wine factors tasting from the barrel, tincture sellers with locked cases, mule trains loading for the pass, and the whole valley's business done in the few hours of thin light it gets. The ferry works from a stone slip at the end of the square and crosses to the shaded shore at every hour of the day and night. Stone houses with slate roofs and flower boxes climb the slope behind, and above them the terraces go up in steps until the vines give out. Boats go out most mornings. The lake is very clear and very deep, the fish run fat, and nobody swims in it.

The Silverer's.description: A forge on the Sunside slope above the market, its doors open to the light and its yard stacked with billets under lock. This is where the valley's silver is worked — blades, arrowheads, grille-bars, the silvered edge on a billhook — and there is a waiting list, because the mountain does not stop and neither does the demand. A licence hangs framed by the door in a hand six hundred years old, signed by the lady of this valley, permitting the making of the one metal that can kill her. Moonstone work is done at the back and goes to the Crimson Company. Anyone with the coin can buy here, and nobody's rank moves them up the list.

The Apothecary.description: A tall shopfront on the Sunside market square, and nothing else in the valley looks like it: figured glass, a floor laid in black and white stone, and a wall of polished walnut drawers running to the ceiling with a ladder on a rail. This is the house that made Velmere's alchemy famous — healing draughts, elixirs of clarity, night-sight, tinctures against the cold, restoratives that work when nothing else will — and Syndicate factors come up from Villa Parhelion by the season to buy them by the case. It is also where one buys poison, which is sold openly here, priced accordingly, and better than anyone else's anywhere. It is said the Apothecary can build a poison for one named person and no other, and that none has ever been traced back to her. Nobody in Velmere repeats that where a stranger can hear it.

Lampside.description: The shore the sun never touches, in permanent blue shade under the wall of the mountain, lamps burning along the waterfront at noon. This half of the village lives at night: the pressing-houses run until dawn with their doors open and the smell of must rolling out over the water, the wharf takes the day's cut fruit off the ferry, and the Good Night never closes. Stone houses with heavy shutters that bar from inside. The Crimson Company's hall stands back from the water under a red sword on black, and one switchback road climbs from the end of the street up to the chateau above — the road the whole valley has walked at least once, at night, in a hurry, with the gate standing open at the top of it.

The Good Night.description: A tavern on the shaded waterfront that has never once closed its door, because the shore it stands on has no morning to close for. Low rafters, a long fire, tables rewaxed for two centuries, and food and wine absurd for a village — the pressing crews drink what did not make the cut for distant kings, and what did not make the cut is better than anything in Ardan's Watch. The room is ferrymen and crews coming off shift purple to the elbows, Crimson Company blades off duty, traders stuck a day short of the pass, and the chateau's household down the hill on a night off in the lady's red, being looked at and enjoying it. Nobody asks anybody what they were before. The house book hangs behind the bar, and the valley bets on the Company: who comes back, who gets named, how many. There are rooms upstairs, and a bell outside the door that is not for last orders.

The Red House.description: A great house on the shaded shore, taken over by the Crimson Company and kept far better than a barracks needs to be. Blades eat together at one long table under a red sword on black, and what is poured is the valley's own — the vintages that go to distant kings, because Lady Isaveau retains this hall and does not stint it. There are hot baths at the back, a wardrobe that issues black and red cut to fit and replaces what gets ruined, and a yard with good horses where the drill is run in the dark. The work board hangs by the door. Off the hall is a warded room holding what the Company has taken and will not destroy — cursed blades, bound things, gear that would see its owner burned anywhere south of the peaks — and the wards on that door are the most expensive thing in the house. Trophies line the wall: pelts, a strigoi skull picked clean, a ghoul's jaw wired open. When the bell goes in the valley, this house empties first.

Chateau Velmere - Great Hall.description: The great hall of the chateau, reached by one switchback road up from the shaded shore and through gardens of night-blooming flowers. The gate at the top stands open, and stays open, because it does not need to be shut: anyone the lady did not want inside her valley would have stopped being a problem somewhere back at the pass. Inside is black stone and silver under a high vaulted roof, a long table, light enough for a court, and tall mirrors down one wall that the lady does not use. This is where she receives, and where she gives the evenings the elite of the north compete to attend: lords, house envoys, Syndicate men up from Villa Parhelion, and whoever she currently finds interesting. They run until dawn and settle more business than any court in the Summits. A household of beautiful young mortals in her own red attends the guests, dressed at her expense and plainly enjoying themselves, and bloodwine is poured here and nowhere else, to guests she counts as her own kind or means to. The gate has been shut three times in living memory, each time with the whole valley inside it. The cellars and the laboratories lie deeper in and are no part of the evening.

Ashfall Pass South.description: The Velmere end of the only road over the range to Val Cendrac: a climb out of the valley's western head, up past the last terraces where the vines give out, to a saddle where the wind never stops. Ash comes over from Cendrac's forges and settles on this side — grey on the snow, grey on the vine rows below — which is what the pass is named for and what Velmere has resented for six hundred years. No gate, no garrison, a stone shelter at the height with a cold hearth. It is watched from both ends by people who have no need to stop anybody, and the old tunnels under the range are watched a great deal less, which is why they keep being cut and keep being collapsed.

The Vale Sable.name: The Vale Sable
The Vale Sable.basicInfo: A sealed valley high in the peaks, its one pass blocked by collapsed stone. Once the domain of House Sable, an ancient bloodline known for its mastery of blood magic. Now strigoi hold it — vampires gone feral and mindless — and Keep Sable still stands at the valley's head, black towers against black cliffs.
The Vale Sable.hiddenInfo:
House Sable made its get alone, holding itself above the rite of two, and fed without limit besides; within a single generation the curse it carried turned the whole valley feral. The strigoi have splintered into territorial packs — some hold the high caves, some the forest, some the outer keep — that compete and sometimes fight. Lady Sable remains in the inner keep, ancient and powerful and utterly mindless, the apex the others will not approach.

The other lords sealed the pass rather than burn the vale clean, because Keep Sable's library holds the largest store of blood-magic research in Larion, and an assault might destroy it. The Crimson Company holds the cordon at the collapsed pass on the lords' behalf, and kills anyone who comes out without leave. But they watch who comes in, and a capable, desperate-looking arrival may be approached quietly: there is a way through the caves, and House Setharis pays well to learn whether its lost heir, Nerisse, is alive inside.

The village still has people in it — those who could not flee before the pass was sealed. They hide in cellars and attics, move by day when the strigoi are sluggish, and barricade themselves before dark. They cannot leave; the Company would kill them. They know the vale's patterns: which packs hunt where, when Lady Sable stirs, where things of worth might still be found.

IMPORTANT: the strigoi of the Vale Sable default to hostile and do not parley. They are mindless and serve no one. They hunt anything warm, sluggish by day and fierce after dark, and the packs will fight each other over prey as readily as they take it.

The Cordon.description: A Crimson Company encampment where the mountain road ends at a wall of collapsed stone. Markers declare the valley sealed. Soldiers in red-and-black hold the checkpoint, and a row of heads on the palisade — some withered, some recent — shows what happens to those who come out of the vale without leave. They watch new arrivals closely, and the capable, desperate-looking ones sometimes find a cloaked figure lingering at the camp's edge, who speaks quietly of a way in through the caves and of a house that pays for results.

The Caves.description: A network of natural caverns winding through the mountain, bypassing the sealed pass. The passages are narrow and dark, descending steeply before climbing again. They emerge through a trapdoor in a root cellar beneath a collapsed house on the edge of Sable Village.

Sable Village.description: Stone houses with slate roofs, like any village in the Shadow Summits — but the doors hang broken, the windows are dark, and dried blood stains the cobblestones. Strigoi hunt the streets after dark. The survivors live in hiding: cellars, attics, passages knocked through cellar walls. They move by day, take what they can from abandoned stores, and barricade themselves before dusk.

The Black Tarn.description: The wild heart of the valley between village and keep. Dense forest climbs the slopes, and at the center lies a lake so dark it appears black, reflecting nothing. Strigoi packs hunt here, marking territories in ways only they understand, and the forest floor is scattered with bones. The path to Keep Sable winds along the lakeshore, exposed and dangerous.

Keep Sable.description: The castle rises where the valley ends, built into the cliff face — black stone towers against black rock. Keep Sable was part fortress, part laboratory, part library. The outer halls and lower levels are claimed by strigoi now, led by something that might once have been Lady Sable's seneschal; they do not enter the inner keep, which is her domain. The library-laboratory lies at the castle's heart, and somewhere within it, presumably, both Lady Sable and whatever became of Nerisse Setharis.

The Black Gate.name: The Black Gate
The Black Gate.basicInfo: A mountain fortress sacred to the vampire lords of the Shadow Summits. The Black Gate is the only place a new lord can be made — a portal to another realm where an aspirant must prove themselves worthy of the Lady of Blood's gift. Each house keeps priest-wardens here, which makes the fortress neutral ground, where rivals can convene, negotiate, and witness a transformation under a truce no house will break.
The Black Gate.hiddenInfo:
The Gate opens rarely; making a new lord is a matter of weight and risk. Between such occasions the fortress serves as neutral territory for the lords' diplomacy and as a place of pilgrimage for those who venerate the Lady of Blood. The priest-wardens are vampires of middling standing, appointed by their houses. The posting is prestigious in name and tedious in practice — decades can pass between transformations — and the wardens fill the time keeping the fortress, conducting the rites, and pressing their houses' interests in the small disputes that make up daily business. Some come to enjoy the quiet; others go slowly mad of boredom.

The rite requires the sponsorship of an existing lord, the wardens' approval — rarely refused when the sponsor is powerful enough — and then the trial itself. The aspirant passes through the Gate alone and must defeat and drink the blood of a Fiend of the Blood, one of the Lady's servants that dwell in her realm. Those who succeed return transformed. Those who fail do not return.

Opening the Gate carries its own danger. Fiends of the Blood sometimes try to come through. The wards are strong, but the wardens are careful — they do not open the Gate lightly, and they keep defenses ready against whatever might emerge.

Despite the Gate's infrequent use, the fortress sees steady traffic. Envoys treat on neutral ground. Supplicants petition for sponsorship. Merchants supply the garrison. Those with grievances between houses seek arbitration. The wardens hear all of it, which leaves them surprisingly well-informed for so remote a posting.

For a player, the Black Gate is the path to lordship itself — a choice with real weight, and the one place in Larion where it can be made.

The Warden's Pass.description: The mountain approach to the Black Gate — a narrow road climbing through snow and rock to the fortress above. Waymarkers carved with the sigils of the houses line the path. The fortress shows itself only halfway up: black walls against black peaks, all but invisible until you are upon them.

The Hall of Witnesses.description: The great hall where the houses convene. Four galleries rise along the walls, one to a house, with the priest-wardens' seats at the cardinal points and a floor of black marble veined with red. Here sponsorships are announced, disputes arbitrated, and — on rare occasions — the houses gather to witness a transformation. Between such events the hall is a forum: envoys meet in the galleries, petitioners wait on the benches along the walls, and rivals who would cut each other's throats anywhere else keep the truce under the wardens' eyes.

The Supplicants' Quarters.description: Lodgings for visitors — austere but comfortable chambers cut into the mountain stone. Envoys, merchants, scholars, and petitioners all stay here, sometimes for long stretches while business is done, and a refectory serves simple meals. The quarters have an odd social weather: rivals from feuding houses share tables, petitioners hoping for sponsorship size each other up, and everyone watches everyone.

The Preparation Chambers.description: Where aspirants are made ready for the trial, closed to all but those undergoing it and their sponsors. The chambers are spare — cells for fasting, ritual baths, rooms for meditation. An aspirant may spend days or weeks here readying body and mind for what waits beyond the Gate, while the wardens conduct the preliminary rites: the blessings, the bindings, the formal acceptance of risk.

The Gate Chamber.description: A cavern deep within the mountain, reached only through the Preparation Chambers. The Black Gate stands at its heart — an arch of dark stone that opens onto nothing until the rite wakes it. Opened, it shows the realm of the Lady of Blood: a red darkness where the Fiends wait. The chamber is heavily warded, and the priest-wardens stand ready with bindings and steel when the Gate opens, watching for anything that might try to cross.

Charnel Mountain.name: Charnel Mountain
Charnel Mountain.basicInfo: A mountain of abandoned silver mines in the high peaks, its diggings long given over to the dead. Feral ghouls den in the old workings by the hundred, and lately they range farther down the slopes and bolder than they used to. The silver veins were never worked out — the miners fled the ghouls, not a dry seam — and the metal still in the rock is the same metal that kills what guards it.
Charnel Mountain.hiddenInfo:
Charnel Mountain was a working silver mine until the dead filled it. Now feral ghouls pack the tunnels in their hundreds, hunting in flocks through the dark, and the press has been worsening: the ghouls range lower and bolder each season, and the lords' valleys nearest the mountain feel it.

Nothing drives them. Everyone the ghouls kill in the dark rises as one of them, and the mine has killed a great many, so each season the tunnels hold more than they can feed and the overflow spills down the slopes. There is no master here to find and no bargain to strike, only more ghouls than there used to be.

The silver is the draw. Rich veins still run through the upper workings, abandoned in haste and never reclaimed, and silver is the metal that bites the ghoul and the vampire alike — so a delver fights the dead for the very thing that kills them, and what comes out of Charnel arms the hunters of the whole region. The lords tolerate prospectors and feral-cullers on the mountain; the Crimson Company will sometimes clear the lower workings when the ghouls press too near a held valley, but no one holds Charnel, and no one goes deep and comes back rich without paying for it.

IMPORTANT: the ghouls of Charnel Mountain default to hostile and do not parley. They are mindless and serve no one, hunting in packs through the tunnels, drawn to warmth and movement, and bolder in the dark than in what little light reaches the upper diggings.

The Headworks.description: The mine mouth on the mountain's shoulder, where the old surface buildings stand gutted — winch-houses, ore-sheds, a collapsed counting-office, all stripped and weathered. Prospectors and feral-cullers camp among the ruins, arming and resting before they go in, and trading what they bring out. The diggings open below as a black throat in the rock, and the cold air that breathes out of it carries the smell of the dead.

The Upper Workings.description: The first levels of the mine, a maze of timber-shored galleries and ore-stopes where the richest abandoned veins still show silver in the rock. Picks and spilled ore lie where the miners dropped them when they ran. Ghouls hunt here, fewer than in the deep but bold enough, and the silver that draws delvers is the same metal that cuts the dead — so the work is done with a blade in one hand. The galleries branch and drop toward the lower dark.

The Deep Diggings.description: The lowest worked levels, where the air goes foul and the timber rots and the ghouls den in their hundreds. The tunnels here run toward the oldest, deepest stone, and the dead are thickest near the bottom — packs hunting in the black, the floor thick with the bones of the eaten. The richest silver of all lies in these levels, and so do the worst odds.

Kingstor.name: Kingstor
Kingstor.basicInfo: Kingstor is the great tor at the heart of the grass sea, with a permanent town of traders and travelers living at its foot the year round and a sacred Moot-ground at its summit. When the drums sound, beastfolk converge from every corner of the grass to trade, contend, settle disputes, and burn the straw kings: giant effigies built to mock anyone who would rule them. Moot Law holds here: no killing, no feuds past the boundary stones, for any people and any guest.
Kingstor.hiddenInfo:
Kingstor is the one ground all the peoples of the grass share, and its law is older than any of them: no kings, no thrones, no blood spilled past the boundary stones. A breach is answered by every species present at once, which is why it holds. The Moot itself has no permanent leader; each people sends speakers to the summit stones, and what they argue out there settles the grass for a season.

The town at the foot lives year-round, not just for the Moot. The Trading Ring and the Watering Hole anchor a standing mixed community of traders, herders, road-folk, and drifters of every people, fed and watered and arguing through every season; the Moot only swells it. Non-beastfolk are tolerated as welcome guests but have no voice at the summit.

The Syndicate is here in the open, and everyone knows what its agents are. They are the face of an armed operation working to own the long road that crosses the grass: way-forts, paid guards, tolls, and quiet violence against anyone on the road who will not deal. The speakers know exactly what the factors are and have no law to stop a thing that only ever offers and never seizes. That is the grass sea's open wound, argued at every Moot and settled at none.

The Grass Road.description: The tor stands visible a full day's walk in every direction, a dark spike against the open sky. The track in runs straight through flat grass to a ring of weathered boundary stones that marks the edge of Moot ground. Past the stones, the camps and the rooftops at the tor's foot come into view.

The Camps.description: A sprawling, shifting settlement around the tor's base: hide tents, reed shelters, cook-fires, and pavilions in every style of the grass, thin in the off-season and packed wall-to-wall when the drums sound. Between them are fighting rings, gambling circles, storytellers' fires, and arguments about everything. Worn paths thread the whole sprawl toward the tor.

The Trading Ring.description: A permanent circle of stone-and-timber stalls at the tor's base, roofed with stretched hide, the only year-round buildings at Kingstor. Beastfolk traders, licensed factors, and opportunists work the stalls, dealing in hides, herbs, river-ivory, grass-honey, and stranger goods. A weathered posting-board stands among the stalls, pinned with bounties and notices.

The Climb.description: A switchback path carved into the tor's face, worn smooth by generations of clawed feet, steep and exposed and not made for anyone unsure of their footing. It is the only way up to the summit. The grass sea falls away below, wider with every turn.

The Summit.description: The top of the tor: wind and open sky to every horizon, ringed by standing stones older than any living people's memory. The speaking-stones stand in a rough circle at the center, one for each people of the grass. Between Moots the summit is near-empty, and beastfolk climb it alone to look out over the land.

The Burning Ground.description: A vast, blackened clearing west of the tor where the earth has been scorched and re-scorched until nothing grows. Frames of timber and straw stand waiting here, and the charred stubs of old ones lie where they fell. When the Burning comes, the straw kings go up in walls of flame.

The Watering Hole.description: The biggest tent at Kingstor, open-sided when the weather allows, with long communal benches and a row of fire-pits worked by its boarfolk and halfling keepers. Food is shared and drink is strong, and the benches stay busy in every season. The arguments here run louder than anywhere else at the tor.

Mudbank.name: Mudbank
Mudbank.basicInfo: Mudbank is a boarfolk river settlement of mud-brick buildings, the biggest and most permanent community in the grass sea, built where a wide channel cuts through the grassland. The boarfolk build, farm, and trade — the kind of settled work other peoples of the grass associate with the outside world.
Mudbank.hiddenInfo:
Mudbank is the grass sea's most established settlement. It is mostly boarfolk, who farm the channel-banks and raise mud-brick the way no other people of the grass bothers to, alongside a growing number of outside traders, and other beastfolk pass through constantly because Mudbank feeds anyone who shows up.

The argument is the road-men. The Syndicate keeps factors living inside the walls and a goods-warehouse on the channel, the only foothold of its kind any beastfolk settlement has granted. To some boarfolk it is prosperity, steady outside coin and a place on the road that crosses the grass. To others it is the first step toward exactly the kind of power the grass sea burns in effigy every season.

The River Gate.description: The channel narrows here between mud-brick walls into a natural harbor, spanned by a wooden gate. The path into town runs along the top of a levee built up over generations with mud and stone. Reed boats and flat barges are drawn up along the banks below.

The Wallows.description: A broad, shallow stretch of river where the bank has been shaped into gentle mud slopes. The water runs brown and slow past the reeds. Plank walkways cross the softest ground, and low mud-brick buildings stand back from the waterline.

The Long Table.description: A communal eating hall, open-sided, built around a single table that seats a hundred, with a row of fire-pits down one side worked by boarfolk cooks. Benches line both sides of the table the whole length of the hall. The roof is mud-brick and thatch, and the channel runs close enough to hear from the benches.

Goldentor.name: Goldentor
Goldentor.basicInfo: Goldentor is a lionkin pride-hold flying bright banners from the tallest tor in the grass sea, visible for miles across the open plain. The pride that holds it keeps a famously lavish table and welcomes all comers, and prides from across the grass come to feast, contend, and settle their disputes in the open before a crowd.
Goldentor.hiddenInfo:
The population is small: one pride and their household. Everyone else is visiting. Lionkin honor runs hot, and disputes are settled by public challenge — combat, contest, or oratory — before an audience that treats a good fight the way other peoples treat theater. Hospitality is a display of wealth, and a visitor is an audience.

The lionkin carry the knowledge that their own kind produced the tyrant the whole grass sea buried, the king whose conquest gave the land Moot Law. Most prides wear that as a check on themselves and despise the memory. A few mutter that the old king's only failing was weakness, that he simply lacked the strength to finish what he began.

Nothing offends Goldentor like the warlord Vaskarn. He is lowborn, clanless, and self-crowned, and he has taken the title Pride of Prides, which the prides hold to be theirs to grant and his to have stolen.

The Tor Road.description: A processional path carved into the tor face, wide enough for lionkin to walk three abreast. It climbs the slope in long switchbacks, exposed to the wind and the open grass below, and the summit's banners stand bright against the sky the whole way up. Stone posts along the path are carved with the marks of prides that have held the tor.

The Circle.description: A broad, flat arena near the summit, open to the sky, ringed by tiers of stone seating worn smooth by generations. Sand covers the floor of the ring. From here the grass sea falls away on every side.

The High Seat.description: The pride-lord's hall at the summit — open-walled, canopied in golden hide, with views to every horizon. Long feast-tables run the length of it, and the seat itself stands on a low rise of stone at the far end.

Longrun.name: Longrun
Longrun.basicInfo: Where the great herds pass through during migration, the wolfkin converge. Longrun is a hunting ground, a proving ground, and the closest thing wolfkin have to a homeland. A keeper-pack holds the site year-round, watching the herds and maintaining the runs. When migration season comes, packs from across the grass sea arrive, and the great hunt begins.
Longrun.hiddenInfo:
Wolfkin are pack-nomads who follow herds and patrol territory. Longrun is the exception — the one place they return to. The keeper-pack is a permanent garrison of sorts, volunteers from multiple packs who've chosen to stay and steward the land. Other packs respect them but consider the choice unusual.

The great hunt is the most important event in wolfkin culture. It's where young wolves earn their names, where pack alliances are forged or broken, and where pack-leaders prove their worth. Hunts are coordinated across multiple packs. Waste is forbidden — everything taken is used.

Some wolfkin have started staying at Longrun past their pack's rotation. They like the stability, the connections, the sense of place. Their packs consider this somewhere between eccentric and disloyal.

Population is predominantly wolfkin. Other beastfolk visit but don't linger — wolfkin hospitality is real but spare, and the pack rhythms of daily life can feel exclusionary to outsiders.

The Keeper's Camp.description: A permanent encampment on a low ridge. Hide shelters built for function, not comfort. A central fire-ring where the keeper-pack shares meals and receives  scouts, traders and visitors.

The Runs.description: A wide natural channel between rocky ridges where the great herds funnel through during the season. Outside of migration, it's open grassland marked by old drive-lines of stacked stone. During the hunt, it transforms: wolfkin packs positioned along the ridges, signals passing between them, the ground shaking as the herds move through.

The Muster Ground.description: A flat clearing where the packs gather when the herds are close. During season, it's a sprawl of pack-camps, each with its own banner and fire. The pack-leaders meet at a central ring to plan the hunt — who drives, who flanks, who takes the first kill. Between seasons, it's empty and quiet, just trampled grass and old fire-circles waiting.

Kingsgrave Kurgan.name: Kingsgrave Kurgan
Kingsgrave Kurgan.basicInfo: A massive earthen mound rising from the flat grass sea, ringed by standing stones and watched by a permanent guard drawn from every beastfolk species. The sorcerer-emperor who once enslaved the grass sea is sealed inside. The wards are ancient, the guardians vigilant. His bound dead still claw their way out, and people still try to get in.
Kingsgrave Kurgan.hiddenInfo:
The sorcerer-emperor was a lionkin of immense power who bound the beastfolk through domination magic, turned the species against each other, and built an empire on enslaved minds. The peoples broke him together and, unable to kill him, buried him alive: he sleeps in the kurgan, and the guard is there to keep him sleeping. This is a prison, not a tomb.

The emperor's bound dead, his old servants still under his command, dig at the Breach from inside, and each time it opens some of them walk out. They answer to radiant weapons — silver, moonstone, the blessed edge — and turn ordinary blades; against the sleeping emperor's pull on the mind, the same pull the Kingsworn answer, a strong will is the better armor.

Treasure-seekers are a constant problem, since the emperor was buried with the wealth of his conquests. Worse than the looters are the Kingsworn, who hear the mound's call and answer it, working to wake what sleeps inside and set it ruling again. They probe the breach, buy ways in from the gnolls, and recruit from the proud and the humiliated across every people of the grass.

The Standing Stones.description: A ring of carved stones circles the mound's base, each cut with ward-signs from a different beastfolk tradition. The guardian camp sits among them, practical and permanent: watch-fires, hide shelters, and sentries from several species sharing the watch.

The Processional.description: A stone-lined passage drives into the side of the mound, its walls carved with warnings. The light fails quickly past the entrance. A heavy sealed door stands at the end of the guarded stretch, and the carvings grow denser around it.

The Sealed Halls.description: The tomb complex proper: corridors of packed earth reinforced with bone and stone, branching into unmapped chambers. Ward-signs are cut into the walls at the thresholds, some still faintly lit, others dark and cold. The passages run inward and downward toward a burial chamber at the heart.

The Breach.description: A collapsed section on the mound's eastern slope, where the emperor's bound dead dug their way out from the inside. It has been sealed and has reopened more than once: the current patch is a raw fill of stone, stake, and timber, newer than everything around it, with the old sealed scars layered beside it. The grass grows thin and pale on the slope here.

Hag's Rock.name: Hag's Rock
Hag's Rock.basicInfo: A tor on the grass sea where a community of witches has made their home. The witches provide healing, potions, and magical services to the beastfolk, who in turn leave them in peace — an arrangement both sides consider ideal. What else the witches get up to on their tor is a matter of lively speculation across the grass sea.
Hag's Rock.hiddenInfo:
Despite the name, one thing is immediately obvious upon arriving here: none of the witches remotely resembles a hag either in age, beauty or demeanor. In fact, they are all conspicuously young, beautiful and quite friendly to strangers, although they do enjoy pranking visitors by appearing as conventional hags from time to time. The witches settled the grass sea because the beastfolk leave them alone. The understanding is practical — the witches provide healing, potions, midwifery, and magical services to anyone who visits. The beastfolk provide food and a guarantee that nobody comes looking for the witches with torches. Both sides consider this arrangement ideal.

The community is mostly human and half-elf women, with a few exceptions in every category. They are refugees of a sort — women whose magical talents made them unwelcome in more 'civilized' places. The grass sea doesn't care what you are as long as you don't try to rule anyone.

The tor's caves are far grander than their entrances suggest — the witches have shaped the interiors with magic into airy, elegant spaces that wouldn't be out of place in a palace. Silk hangings, enchanted lighting, impossibly comfortable furnishings. The contrast between the modest exterior and the lavish interior is deliberate and amusing to the witches. Familiars — cats, ravens, foxes, and stranger things — roam freely. Brooms and implements drift through the air on errands.

The Tor Path.description: A winding path up the tor's gentle slope, lined with herb gardens and wildflowers that have no business growing on bare rock. Cats watch from the ledges. A broom drifts past carrying a bundle of herbs. The smell of cooking drifts down from above.

The Kitchen.description: The social heart of the tor — an open-air cooking and gathering space under a canvas awning, with a long table, mismatched chairs, and a fire that's always going. Familiars weave between the chair legs. The witches eat here, receive visitors here, and conduct most of their business over food and drink.
