The Apothecary.description: A cave carved into the tor's upper face, shelved floor to ceiling with jars, bottles, dried herbs, and things in suspension that are best not examined closely. The witches' workshop and storefront. Potions, salves, remedies, and more exotic preparations are available for trade. The prices are fair. The advice that comes with them is free and unsolicited.

The Caves.description: The witches' private quarters, carved into the tor and shaped by magic into something that has no right to exist inside a rock. Vaulted ceilings, silk hangings, enchanted lights that follow you from room to room. Brooms and bottles float through corridors on errands. Every cave is different — one witch's chambers are a candlelit library, another's a moonlit garden that can't possibly be underground. Visitors are welcome by invitation. The invitation usually comes with wine.

New Anthara.name: New Anthara
New Anthara.basicInfo: New Anthara is a great free city of canals and quays built against the Whitemount, the pale stone ridge where the River Saranadi meets the sea. It is the richest port in the south and the gateway to the jungle interior, a loud, thriving melting-pot of a dozen peoples, demonborn most of all. The city is famous up and down the coast for its tame infernal beasts, which work the docks and the streets and answer to demonborn handlers. No crown rules New Anthara; it is a prosperous, lawless, opportunity-rich place where powerful families and crews make their own way.
New Anthara.hiddenInfo:
New Anthara was founded by the Dravanya, the Masterless — demonborn who freed themselves of the demon princes of Ur and built this city so they would never be ruled again. Their creed is the city's soul: Ur will not have them back, and it will not have this land. They stand against anyone who would raise Ur's relics whole and turn them loose, the Children of Ur above all.

The Dravanya are the masters of fighting Ur with Ur's own power. Where the Children let the infernal master them, the Dravanya master it: they train and keep the demon-beasts — hellhounds for keepers and guards, imps for messengers and errands, heavier beasts to haul the cargo — and they teach a student to wield a cursed blade or an infernal art and stay himself rather than be eaten by it. They will cleanse a corrupted thing or train a bearer to carry it free. This is the work of Dravanya Hold, and a newcomer earns a place among them by standing against Ur in the field.

The river brings Ur-things down out of the ruins, and the Dravanya want every one of them brought to the Hold to be mastered and turned to good use. The danger is what slips past them: relics smuggled through Old Anthara across the river, sold to the Syndicate to move abroad, or worse, to the Children of Ur, who want the corruption left whole and working. Both trades run side by side and everyone knows it.

No one governs the city day to day. It runs like a frontier: the great families and trade-crews hold their own ground and make their own justice, the Dravanya hold the city to its creed without ruling its streets, and a newcomer who keeps out of trouble finds a land of opportunity. The peoples of the river all pass through — Vanarin and gajanari come down to trade and to feud where they meet, frogkin pilots and traders work the canals, serpentkin bring medicine and poison down from the mesa, and humans, halflings, and outsiders of every kind crowd the quays.

The Dock Market.description: Where the Saranadi meets the sea: ocean ships and jungle boats crowd the quays, and traders sell straight off their decks and from stone stalls along the water — jungle fruit, spice, timber, reagents, live creatures, river fish, and relics out of the deep jungle laid out beside charm-sellers and reagent-stalls. Tame infernal beasts work the docks among the crowd. A demonborn beast-handler will sell a trained imp or hound.

The Burned Garden.description: Once a noble estate that reached for power over the free city, stormed and burned and now the finest public garden in New Anthara — terraced green, water channels, and open pavilions where the city comes to eat, drink, argue, and celebrate. Cook-fires and wine-sellers crowd the paths, musicians play under the pavilions, and a corner is given over to a fighting-ring where the crews settle scores and stake coin on bouts. Word and work pass freely across the tables here.

Dravanya Hold.description: The fortified seat of the Dravanya, terraced into the pale stone of the Whitemount above the city, its walls carved in relief with the city's founders breaking their chains. Hellhounds pad the terraces and the gates. Within, open colonnaded halls and warded vaults shelter the work of mastering the infernal: cursed arms held safe, demon-beasts kept and trained, and the teaching of those who would wield such power and stay free.

Old Anthara.description: Across the river from the city proper, the ruins of an older demonborn settlement strangled by jungle, now a poor and lawless quarter built into the broken stone. The streets are crowded and rough nearer the water and give way to overgrown ruin and wild jungle the further back they run. This is where the fences, the smugglers, and the trades the city won't name keep their business.

Revanasi Village.name: Revanasi Village
Revanasi Village.basicInfo: A farming village on the lower slopes of the Whitemount, ringed by rice terraces and jungle orchards. Revanasi takes three rice harvests a year and ships rice, fruit, and spice down to New Anthara. The village gathers under a great spreading tree at its heart, and its hedge-witches are known up and down the river for their jungle remedies and charms.
Revanasi Village.hiddenInfo:
Revanasi is a warm, settled farming village and a good place to put down roots. The families here have worked these terraces for generations and take in newcomers who are willing to work. Demonborn and half-orc families hold most of the land and work it by hand; catkin caravan-families have settled in among them, and frogkin keep the irrigation channels running. Governance is by open meeting under the great tree, where the whole village has a voice.

The jungle is the village's one constant adversary. Left untended for a season, a terrace or grove is swallowed back into green, so there is always more clearing and holding work than there are hands. This is the standing work a newcomer can pick up: holding the edge, guarding the harvest.

Revanasi's hedge-witches are the village's pride and its draw. They read the jungle and brew from it, making fever-cures, snakebite and leech draughts, wardings against the wild, and charms for a safe harvest, with a little coaxing of weather and growth. A newcomer with the gift can be taught the craft by helping and tending, the way it has always been passed down.

The terraces, the drying-barns, and the orchard groves lie around the village and can be visited or worked when a story calls for them.

The Greattree.description: The village heart: a huge spreading tree over a packed-earth common, the terraced green hillside rising behind it. Benches, cookfires, and a low speaking-stone sit beneath the branches, where the village holds its open meetings. Paths run off between the houses toward the market and the riverbank.

The Market.description: A small open market of woven awnings and plank stalls. Farm tools, seed, and woven goods are sold alongside a hedge-witch's stall of dried jungle herbs, brewed remedies, and charms — fever-bark, snakebite cure, leech-draughts, and harvest-wards. Cookfires at the edge sell rice and river fish.

The Sleeping Croc.description: The village common-house, a long timber hall on stilts over the riverbank, named for the old crocodile that suns itself on the mud below and that the village has long since decided to leave be. Rice wine, the local catch, and a long shared table within; a deck out over the water where the croc can be watched at a safe distance.

Kalanth Landing.name: Kalanth Landing
Kalanth Landing.basicInfo: Kalanth Landing is the riverside estate of House Kalanth, the wealthiest family on the lower Saranadi, built where the river bends around their own private landing. Part plantation, part trading house, part pleasure-retreat, it spreads across terraced gardens and spice groves around a great open hall built for entertaining.
Kalanth Landing.hiddenInfo:
House Kalanth is the demonborn merchant-house that grew richest on the lower river, and everyone on the Saranadi knows that the spice and timber are only half of it. The other half is the river's dirty work. The house runs grave-bronze and old-grove amber out of the jungle's demonborn ruins for buyers who want the find to stay quiet, and on the darker side it moves the things dug out of the demonborn dead: Ur-ichor, the black blood that grants demonic strength to whoever drinks it and burns the humanity out of them; wakeful idols that lend power to the one who rouses them and claim a piece of him in return; and cursed demonborn arms and armor that make the bearer stronger and slowly less himself. The family never handles any of it directly and has never once been caught with a thing it shouldn't have. It is too rich, too well-defended, and too useful to too many people for the great families or the Dravanya to move against, and House Kalanth knows it.

Kalanth is always hiring the right sort — people who can move a shipment quietly, recover something from the Swallowed Cities. A newcomer is received graciously, sized up, and given small work; those who prove useful and discreet rise into the family's trust and its real business. The pay is good, the living is fine, and the work is steadily more lucrative and more dangerous the higher you go.

The household keeps gardens, spice groves, and a guarded strongroom of coin and leverage around the hall.

The River Bend.description: The estate's private landing on the river bend: a broad stone dock with warehouses behind it and the Kalanth banner flying above. Trade-barges load spice and timber at one end; the family's own boats are moored apart at the other. Goods come and go here without passing the city's downriver inspections.

The Great Hall.description: A great open-air hall of pale stone and dark timber facing the water, built for entertaining, with long tables, deep couches, and a view down the river. Guest quarters lie off to one side, conspicuously comfortable; the family's own rooms sit above, private and guarded. The terraced gardens step down toward the water beyond.

Sangamadi.name: Sangamadi
Sangamadi.basicInfo: Sangamadi is a frogkin village built where two great tributaries meet the Saranadi, half on the banks and half on the water — stilt-houses, floating platforms, and boats moored so long they have become buildings. Every vessel going upriver stops here, because past the confluence the river narrows and turns dangerous, and only a Sangamadi pilot knows the way through.
Sangamadi.hiddenInfo:
Sangamadi runs the upper river. The frogkin pilot families hold a near-monopoly on the dangerous water above the confluence, and they are cheerfully, completely aware that the whole river depends on them and they depend on no one. They are warm hosts and hard bargainers, unhurried, and serenely certain that Sangamadi is the most important place on the Saranadi — which, since nothing reaches the upper river without them, is difficult to argue. The rival pilot families compete fiercely for the richest upriver contracts, and that rivalry is the village's favorite long-running sport.

Information reaches Sangamadi before it reaches New Anthara. Every crew that stops to hire or resupply trades news at the floating common, and the frogkin remember all of it. A newcomer who is good company and not in a hurry is made welcome at the table; trust and a pilot's friendship are earned slowly and worth a great deal upriver.

The grief under the warmth is the Hookmarsh. Ghessek's warband prizes Sangamadi's pilots above any other catch, because a taken pilot brings a ransom and a stranded boat both. Most families here have lost someone to the marsh or paid to get them back, and a pilot gone missing on an upriver run is the village's standing sorrow and its standing call for help.

The Docks.description: The natural anchorage where the two tributaries meet the Saranadi. Boats of every size crowd the moorings, frogkin houses stand on stilts above the waterline, and the pilots' boards advertise routes and rates for the upper river. This is where vessels put in to hire and resupply.

The Float.description: The village's social heart: interconnected floating platforms anchored in the calmest water, set with cook-fires, low tables, and woven mats, with guest platforms for visitors out at the edge. In the evening the lanterns come out and the whole village gathers on the water. There is always room made at a table for one more.

The Fish Market.description: A broad covered platform where the morning catch is sold, smoked, salted, and cooked. Smoked river-fish packed for New Anthara is a major trade here, and the cook-stalls along the edge compete fiercely over who fries the best of it.

The Still Pool.description: A warm, clear pool fed by a thermal spring and shaded by ancient trees, set apart from the working water. It is sacred to the frogkin, a place of quiet, reflection, and ceremony. Visitors may sit at its edge but do not enter the water uninvited.

Mounagiri.name: Mounagiri
Mounagiri.basicInfo: Mounagiri is a settlement of the Mounari, a chameleon-kin people, built into the sheer walls of a river gorge. Houses cling to the cliff at every angle, vine bridges span the gap, and the river runs far below. The Mounari are the finest climbers and infiltrators in the south, and the gorge is home and school both, where they raise their young to the discipline and teach it to the few outsiders they judge worthy.
Mounagiri.hiddenInfo:
The Mounari are sworn against the Ur-trade — the demonic things the Children of Ur dig out of the ruins: the black Ur-ichor, the wakeful idols, the cursed arms that corrupt whoever takes them up. The Mounari hunt that trade with the one craft suited to it, moving unseen through jungle and ruin to steal the corruption back and destroy it before it can spread. They go after the cult's diggers, the shipments on the water, and the houses that fence the goods. It is a quiet war, against a cult and against rich, dangerous fences who would gladly see Mounagiri burned for it.

The Mounari teach climbing, stillness, and moving unseen, and to outsiders only the lesser version of it — the chameleon-craft that lets a non-Mounari blur against stone comes only after long training. A newcomer is taken in, tested, and taught by degrees; those who prove worthy and hold to the cause are trusted with the real work, the strikes against the trade itself.

The masters set the trials, and the trials are the war: reach a place no one can reach, retrieve a thing unseen, follow a shipment, get into a Children dig and out again with what they raised. The proving grounds are the region itself — the Swallowed Cities, the upriver jungle, the heights of the river citadels, the Hookmarsh.

The Mounari live their whole lives on the cliff and are quietly delighted by an outsider's fear of the drop. A guest clinging to the rock while they lounge at the lip of a lethal fall is, to them, a fine and reliable entertainment, and they will not be hurried into sympathy about it.

The order's worst enemy is its own. A Mounari who breaks the discipline and sells the craft — to a fence, to the cult, to anyone who pays — is the one threat the masters cannot simply hide from, because a fallen one knows every way they move.

The Gorge Rim.description: The lip of the gorge, where the jungle gives way to open air and the whole vertical village shows below: houses fixed to the cliff faces, vine bridges crossing the gap, and the river a thin line at the bottom. A single switchback trail starts down from here, narrow and steep, the only walked way in.

The Cliff Village.description: Houses clinging to the gorge walls at every angle — on horizontal ledges, against vertical faces, tucked beneath overhangs — joined by vine bridges and carved steps. The Mounari move across the faces in three dimensions, shifting color against the rock. Quarters for outsider students sit at the village edge.

The Big Ledge.description: The village common, which the Mounari call the Big Ledge: a natural shelf of rock partway down the gorge wall, cook-fires and shared mats laid across it, open at its edge to a sheer drop to the river far below. There is no rail and no wall. To the Mounari it is broad and comfortable ground, and they take their ease at the very lip of it.

The Training Ground.description: The school's working heart, set across a sheer face at the gorge's narrowest point. The rock is carved with holds and trial-routes climbing from simple to nearly impossible, and worn ledges below serve as ground for drilling stillness and breath. The drop from the routes is sheer to the river.

Shilaghar.name: Shilaghar
Shilaghar.basicInfo: Shilaghar is the temple-mesa of the serpentkin, a flat-topped height of carved stone rising warm and sun-baked above the canopy over the Saranadi. The serpentkin who hold it are the finest alchemists in the south, masters of medicine, venom, and the craft that lies between, and their cures, antidotes, and poisons travel far up and down the river.
Shilaghar.hiddenInfo:
Shilaghar is the south's great school of alchemy, and the place an alchemist comes to be made a master. The serpentkin teach the whole of the craft to a student with the gift — brewing, medicine, venom, antidote, and balance — taken in, taught by degrees over long warm seasons, and set free only once they have learned to hold life and death in the same two hands.

To the serpentkin the craft is one thing, not two: the knowledge that brews a cure brews a death, and they neither hide it nor make a drama of it. They are warm, unhurried, and dryly funny, gracious hosts with nothing left to prove, and they find the feuding hotheads of the lower river a little exhausting. A guest is welcomed onto the warm stone and fed and made comfortable; the serpentkin are slow to take offense and impossible to fluster, having long since stopped being frightened of anything.

Their neutrality is real and self-interested. Holding themselves keepers of the balance between life and death, they stay clear of the river's quarrels, which is why every rival power trusts them and no one moves against the mesa.

Some serpentkin turned to the Children of Ur, the cult that digs the demonic things out of the ruins, and went to serve them — the worst breaking of the balance there is. The temple disowns these kin utterly and works against them, and the masters set their proven students and capable outsiders to hunt the cult's work and bring back the corrupted things to be destroyed.

The Dispensary.description: The mesa's broad market terrace, where the serpentkin sell their work from stone stalls and shopfronts: medicines, antidotes, and remedies on one side, venomwood blades and darts on another, and the poisons sold plainly alongside the cures for them. Buyers come up from the river to trade here, and the canopy spreads out below the warm terrace edge.

The Workshops.description: Sun-warmed stone halls where the alchemy is taught and done: stills, presses, and worktables of cut green glass, racks of dried reagents, and warded cabinets for the dangerous stock. Masters work at the long benches and set their students to the slow labor of the craft, healing and venom both.

The Venom Gardens.description: Terraced gardens stepping down the mesa's flank, planted with venomwood and the herbs, vines, and fungi the serpentkin draw their craft from. Tenders move among the rows in gloves and veils, and the rarest and most dangerous growths are kept behind low walls at the garden's heart.

The Coil.description: The warm heart of the mesa: a great open hall at the summit built around a sun-warmed basking-floor, ringed with low couches, quiet pools, and the slow smoke of cook-fires. The serpentkin take their long meals and slow talk here, draped at their ease, and a guest is given a place on the warm stone. The whole river-country spreads out below through the open colonnade.

Citadel Uchaghar.name: Citadel Uchaghar
Citadel Uchaghar.basicInfo: Citadel Uchaghar is the seat of the Vanarin, a monkeyfolk people, built into and onto a great stone island where the Saranadi narrows between high jungle banks. The Vanarin have held this rock for as long as anyone can remember and have never lost it.
Citadel Uchaghar.hiddenInfo:
Uchaghar is the seat of the Vanarin and the home of the proudest people on the Saranadi. A High King rules from the summit hall; succession comes by acclaim, challenge, and elaborate contest. The Vanarin are fast, fearless warriors who fight in three dimensions, dropping from the canopy and the rope-slides onto anything that threatens the river-narrows, and they hold that the rock has never fallen because they are the ones holding it.

The Vanarin are one of the two great martial powers of Ntar Vanna, and they take the open fight to the Children of Ur — ranging upriver and into the demonborn ruins to meet the cult's diggers with steel and burn out what they raise. This is the work that wins regard at the High Court, and a newcomer who fights the cult well can earn a name among them.

The feud with the gajanari of Durg Sthira is old and bottomless, and at root it is about which of them is the river's true shield. The Vanarin think the gajanari hide behind walls and armor and craft, fighting pretty and slow; they are certain that valor, speed, and the unconquered rock make the Vanarin the first people of the Saranadi. Neither side will ever concede it, and both are proud enough to keep score forever.

The Vanarin welcome boldness and despise caution. A guest who is brave, generous, and good in a fight is taken up gladly; one who is timid or stingy is mocked openly and without malice.

The Stone Market.description: The broad platform at the island's base where the current slackens and boats put in. Permanent shops and stalls are carved into the rock — jungle fruit, canopy herbs, river fish, woven and carved goods — and the great stone island rises overhead from here, terraces and galleries climbing to the summit far above.

The Long Drop.description: A tavern and inn set in a natural cave halfway up the rock, with a stone terrace hung with hammocks out over a sheer fall to the river far below. Fruit wines and fermented jungle drinks are served at all hours. The warriors take their ease and their boasting here, lounging at the very edge.

The High Court.description: The island's summit: a great hall of stone and timber where the High King holds court, receives visitors, and presides over feasts. Banners and the trophies of old fights hang from the rafters, and the throne is carved from the rock of the island itself. The view reaches out over the canopy on both banks.

The Rope Launch.description: A platform near the summit where thick braided ropes stretch down and away to the canopy on both banks. The ropes slope outward from the rock, so the Vanarin can launch into the trees at speed but no one can climb them inward. Warriors drill formation launches here, and scouts set out from it into the deep jungle.

Durg Sthira.name: Durg Sthira
Durg Sthira.basicInfo: Durg Sthira is a great fortress and town raised by the gajanari, an elephantfolk people, on a bend of the Saranadi. It is the finest built architecture in Ntar Vanna — pale grey walls, towers, and buttresses that seem grown rather than built, set on a bluff of shaped stone above the river. Below the citadel, the town is known across the south for its smiths, artificers, and enchanters, and buyers come from far away for gajanari-forged work.
Durg Sthira.hiddenInfo:
Durg Sthira is the craft seat of Ntar Vanna and the home of its finest makers. The ruling matriarch governs with the family matriarchs, who remember every agreement, precedent, and debt exactly as it was made — gajanari memory is perfect, and among them memory is law. The town forges the best arms, armor, jewelry, and enchanted work in the south, and the gajanari practice arcane memory: a spell witnessed once is reconstructed through perfect recall. Their war-forgers go to battle in masterwork armor of their own making.

The gajanari are one of the two great martial powers of Ntar Vanna, and they meet the Children of Ur with weight where the Vanarin meet them with speed. Their war-forgers are the heavy line that goes into the demonborn ruins and holds, and their forges arm the whole fight against the cult. A maker or a fighter who proves themselves against the cult earns standing here.

The feud with the Vanarin monkeyfolk of Uchaghar is old and bottomless, and at root it is about which of them is the river's true shield. The gajanari hold that the Vanarin are reckless acrobats who fight pretty and die young, all valor and no staying power, while real defense is the wall that holds and the armor that turns the blow.

The Forge Quarter.description: The town's working heart, reached from the stone quays at the river bend: streets of smithies, armories, jewelers, and artificers' workshops climbing toward the citadel. Finished arms, armor, and enchanted goods are sold from the shopfronts, and buyers come from across Larion to commission work.

The Thunderfoot.description: The town's largest tavern, built around a courtyard with a stone stage for gajanari musicians and their deep drums, reed pipes, and bass voices. Slow-roasted meat, river fish in banana leaf, and spiced rice are served at long tables. A posting wall along one side carries dangerous work beyond the forge-families' ordinary obligations — stolen masterwork, armed river trouble, cult signs, ruin expeditions, and great beasts requiring more than a town watch. Petitioners mark what they will pay, and gajanari veterans add blunt corrections when a danger has been understated.

The Proving Yard.description: A broad stone courtyard where finished work is tested and the war-forgers train, sparring in full armor of their own making. Targets, test-frames, and weapon-stands line the walls. Disputes between rival forge-families are sometimes settled here, in the open.

The Matriarch's Court.description: An open courtyard at the citadel's heart with a fountain at its center, where the ruling matriarch holds council and the family matriarchs attend on carved stone seats set in a half-circle. The inner walls are cut in a single continuous relief, the gajanari history rendered in stone the length of the court.

The Grey College.description: The gajanari school of magic, set in the cool halls of the citadel: arcane memory, enchantment, warding, and artifice taught from master to student. Workrooms and warded vaults open off the teaching halls, and students come from across Larion to learn what only the gajanari teach.

The League Chapterhouse.description: A pale-stone hall opening onto the Forge Quarter, with wide doors and shaded tables overlooking the river. Gajanari war-forgers, jungle hunters, and visiting adventurers compare weapons and expedition plans beneath mounted tusks and fragments of armor recovered from the Swallowed Cities. River charts and work notices cover one wall.

Caranthoria.name: Caranthoria
Caranthoria.basicInfo: The capital of the Empire of Light, a city of colonnades, forums, and canals, built on land reclaimed from the lagoon beside the drowned capital of the old Empyrean Empire. Above it floats the Eye of God, an enormous sky citadel of gold-bright brass. It is the seat of the empire and the busiest port on this coast, and people of every kind come here to trade, to take the empire's coin, and to make a life under its law.
Caranthoria.hiddenInfo:
Caranthoria is a bright, orderly city, the capital of the Empire of Light. The empire takes citizens of every people, and the streets show it: humans, lizardfolk and frogkin off the water, turtlefolk masons and engineers, ratkin in the tunnels below, and outsiders from every region come for the work. The day-to-day is run by the empire's prefects and kept by the legion; the Empress reigns from the Eye and rarely comes down.

The Eye of God is the citadel floating above the city — the throne of the empire. She raised it from the lagoon when she came home and refounded the empire, and the work of finishing it never stops overhead. No one goes up to the Eye without the Empress's invitation.

The legion is the city's great institution and always hiring. To swear in is to take three things together: citizenship, the sun-brand at the neck, and the Unity — the mind-bond that lets a century fight as one, shields locking without an order spoken, no soldier ever alone in the line. The Harrowers keep a hall in the Legion Quarter: a small sworn order who hunt the demon-tainted.

The empire's war runs west into the fens, against the lizardfolk dragon-kingdom of the Reedmoot Fens; the Forum's bounties post swamp-creature culls and outlaw-hunts for that frontier and for the deserter-ruins east of the city.

The Syndicate works out of the Warrens, smuggling past the legion and fencing salvage the empire would confiscate. It moves nullmetal — a dull grey alloy that deadens the mind-arts and the Unity, which the empire pays bounties to keep off the market.

The Forum of Light.description: A grand public square paved in reclaimed marble, ringed by colonnades and open to the sky, with the Eye hanging bright overhead. A dais stands at one end for proclamations and public audience; a great noticeboard near it posts the empire's edicts, work-levies, and standing bounties on the swamp-creatures and outlaws that trouble the lagoon. Causeways and canal-streets run off the square into the city.

The Canal Market.description: A network of canals lined with merchant stalls, workshops, and floating barges, where the goods and the peoples of the lagoon mix most freely. Fishmongers sell the morning catch off the boats, stone-carvers and craftsfolk work under awnings, and traders cry herbs, hides, and salvage from barges that tie up and cast off through the day.

The Legion Quarter.description: Barracks, training yards, and armories, kept immaculate. At the center stands a chapel of the Light, its gilded dome bright against the sky, and before it the open yard where recruits are sworn. The recruiting hall stands at the quarter's edge, doors open to the square, with the muster-rolls posted outside; apart from it, behind its own wall, stands the hall of the Harrowers.

The Solarian Arena.description: A stone amphitheater of reclaimed marble, its tiers open to the sky and the Eye above. Below, the sand floor is raked between bouts; gated passages and holding-cells run beneath the seating, and a victor's gate opens onto the road back toward the Legion Quarter. Its declared championship is recognized on the Grand Arena Circuit; matches are judged under formal rules and stopped at surrender, incapacity, or the announced condition.

The Warrens.description: A district the planners never drew: ramshackle structures broken up between the legitimate buildings where the drainage-tunnels surface, ladders and props running down into the dark below the city. The ways twist, the levels stack without order, and passages run on underground out of sight.

All Roads End Tavern.description: A tavern of reclaimed stone and timber where the main causeway meets the canal and the road runs out at the water's edge. Heavy tables, a long bar, and a rooftop terrace over the lagoon.

The Imperial Ascent.description: The guarded lower station of the Eye of God, built around one of the citadel's immense brass tethers near the Imperial Palace. An enclosed imperial lift travels up the tether to the citadel, but its doors open only for scheduled work crews, sealed summonses, recognized envoys, and guests whose names appear on the invitation rolls. Petitioners wait beneath a sun-bright portico while legion guards and court clerks inspect credentials. There is no bridge, stair, or public road through the air.

The Eye of God.name: The Eye of God
The Eye of God.basicInfo: The Eye of God floats above Caranthoria, a vast sky-citadel of gold-bright brass raised from the drowned old capital by Empress Aurianax III. Ancient domes, towers, and solar ornaments stand beside new scaffolds and unfinished plates, and a great eye-like lens opens in its underside. The Eye is the throne of the Empire of Light; visitors ascend from the city by invitation, while the work of rebuilding it continues overhead.
The Eye of God.hiddenInfo:
The Eye of God is not a neighboring site on the ground. Its position beside Caranthoria on the map represents the ascent from the city into the citadel above it. The Imperial Palace below conducts the empire's daily government; the Eye is Aurianax's residence, court, and throne.

Aurianax raised the wreck from the lagoon when she came home. Much of the old citadel is sound, but whole sections remain drowned, broken, or sealed behind ancient defenses. Imperial dredgers recover its fallen fabric from the old city, and engineers, artificers, and labor crews fit those pieces back into the structure. Reconstruction never stops, although the inhabited court is kept bright, orderly, and ceremonially complete.

Entry is controlled. The principal ascent runs from a guarded imperial station in Caranthoria to the Ascension Hall. Invitations are issued for embassies, imperial summonses, judgments, triumphs, and exceptional service; an invitation grants access only to the named guest and the permitted parts of the Eye. Winged approach, climbing the tethers, or entering with the work crews is possible but treated as an attack on the imperial throne.

The great lens is a weapon of the old Empyrean Empire, built to gather and focus sunlight upon the land below. It is not yet fully restored. The Lensworks and the older mechanisms behind it are among the most restricted places in the empire, and only Aurianax and a small circle of sworn engineers know how near the work is to completion.

The Ascension Hall.description: The formal entrance to the Eye, a many-tiered hall of gold-bright brass where the imperial lift from Caranthoria arrives beneath armed galleries. Winged couriers land on open balconies above it. Guests surrender weapons or declare them, invitations are checked against sealed rolls, and escorts wait beside doors marked for the court, the household, and the work crews.

The Court of Light.description: Aurianax's audience hall, built around a long open nave beneath a radiant brass dome. The imperial throne stands on a shallow dais before tall apertures overlooking Caranthoria and the lagoon, so the city lies visibly below every audience. Envoys, commanders, petitioners, and honored servants of the empire are received here under the banners of the refounding.

The Hall of Concord.description: A guarded suite of council chambers, map rooms, archives, and offices serving the imperial court. Prefects come up from the palace, legion commanders report from the front, and sealed dispatches arrive from across the empire. Doors from the public chambers lead toward the restricted works deeper in the citadel.

The Lensworks.description: The restricted heart of the rebuilding project: concentric galleries surrounding a colossal lens assembly of glass, crystal, mirrors, and articulated brass. Scaffolds cross the open shaft, salvaged pieces wait under guard, and shutters in the citadel's underside expose Caranthoria and the lagoon far below. Entry is limited to sworn engineers, guarded work crews, and those admitted by the Empress herself.

Gorren Crossing.name: Gorren Crossing
Gorren Crossing.basicInfo: A sprawling frontier town at the ford of the River Gorren, where the orc steppe meets the settled south. No clan claims it. Every clan trades here. The old stone center was built by merchants generations ago; the rest grew up around it in timber and hide and optimism. Gorren Crossing runs on iron, horses, cattle, and the fact that everyone needs a place to do business on neutral ground. Duels in the street are legal. Theft gets you hanged. Everything in between is negotiable.
Gorren Crossing.hiddenInfo:
Gorren Crossing exists in a political gap. No orc clan claims sovereignty, but Clan Drokash considers the town within their sphere of influence—a position Clan Vorren increasingly contests. The town's continued independence depends on being useful to everyone and owned by no one.

Vorren's Hold, the stone fortress of the settled iron-builders, lies upriver in the iron hills; Camp Drokash, the great tent-city of the roving horse-lords, moves with the season out on the open steppe. Both sell their goods through Gorren—Vorren iron and Drokash horses—and both keep factors and kin in the town. The clans welcome any outsider who will fight for the Wold, and the work that draws adventurers to the steppe—hunting the beasts that prey on the herds, riding against the Oathbreakers in the south, holding the borders against raiders—is first heard of here, in the town's taverns and from the clans' agents.

Governance is layered and informal. The Watch keeps rough order—they'll break up a riot and hang a thief, but an honest fight between willing parties isn't their concern. They're funded by the mercantile houses of the Stone Quarter, which means they serve mercantile interests first. The Crossing Court, a tribunal funded by the same houses, judges disputes for those rich enough to bring them and hires bounty-hunters to enforce what it decides.

Beyond the Stone Quarter, real authority belongs to the ward bosses—local figures with no legal standing who collect protection fees and settle disputes. In Downwind Ward, the boss rules through intimidation and consistency. In Sunset Ward, the boss rules through popularity and loyalty. The two don't get along.

Mercantile houses hire mercenaries to protect their interests, which creates its own problems—armed enforcers loyal only to money. And in the gaps between the houses, the ward bosses, and the Watch, the Syndicate works the town's underside: smuggling goods past the customs shacks, fencing what the wards skim and what raiders sell, lending at the knife's edge, and buying the quiet cooperation of whoever can be bought.

The population is mixed: humans, halflings, orcs who've settled permanently (viewed with anything from tolerance to contempt by clan riders), Whitehold dwarves running trading posts, beastfolk up from the grass sea, and every kind of frontier drifter. Orc clan riders pass through constantly, and rivalries between Vorren and Drokash riders spill into taverns and streets regularly—brawls and contests of pride, not killing, for the clans hold their feud short of blood and settle the rest at the Gods-Anvil.

Despite the disorder, enormous wealth moves through Gorren Crossing—iron from the Mogra mines, horses and livestock from the steppe, trade goods up from Westmarch and the settled south and across from the dwarf-holds of the Whiteholds. It's rough, rich, and alive.

The River Market.description: The heart of Gorren Crossing: a packed strip along the south bank of the ford, where the flat-bottomed ferries land and the road becomes the town. Stalls, trestle tables, and blankets spread on mud run the length of the bank—iron tools, weapons, leather, fur, dwarf-wrought goods, southern luxuries, charms and remedies of dubious merit. Ferrymen shout for fares at the landing, customs men work the warehouse row, drovers and traders and orc riders shoulder through the crowd, and the noise carries clear across the river. No livestock—that's the Stockyards. Everything else is here, and so is everyone.

The Stone Quarter.description: The old town. A single paved road climbs from the river through two blocks of proper stone buildings—the only ones in Gorren Crossing. Mercantile house offices with iron-barred windows. The Crossing Court and the Watch House are located here.

The Stockyards.description: Pens, corrals, and auction blocks spread across trampled ground south of the market. Cattle, horses, mules, and the occasional exotic beast. Drovers and clan riders do business with dwarf buyers and southern agents.

Downwind Ward.description: East of the market, downhill, where the wind carries everything nobody wants to smell. Tanneries, dye-works, rendering yards, alchemical processing. The buildings are stained dark by years of output and the streets run strange colors after rain.

Sunset Ward.description: The western sprawl. Warehouses, cheap lodging houses, tent camps at the fringe. Where caravan goods get stored, where the people who haul them sleep, and where anyone who needs to disappear can find a room with no questions.

The Crowned Ox.description: The finest establishment in Gorren Crossing, which its owner will remind you of. A stone-built tavern and inn on the Quarter's main road with actual glass in the windows, a wine list, and chairs that match. Mercantile agents, visiting dignitaries, and anyone who wants to feel civilized for an evening. The owner enforces a dress code that amounts to no visible bloodstains. Good food, clean rooms, and the best place in town to overhear a scheme worth a fortune.

The Pit.description: A fighting pit with various taverns and eateries at its rim. A huge sunken ring, timber-walled, with tiered seating around the rim and drinking establishments built into the structure on every side. Honor disputes, grudge matches, exhibition bouts, and bare-knuckle entertainment run from sundown until the declared finish, surrender, or the crowd loses interest. Orc riders, human brawlers, anyone with something to prove. Sanctioned circuit bouts have declared terms, seconds, and surrender; private grudge matches may be harsher. Its declared championship is recognized on the Grand Arena Circuit.

The Hearthstone.description: A halfling-run inn on the waterfront near the ferry landing. Whitewashed walls, a copper-roofed porch over the river, window boxes with herbs. Inside: checked tablecloths, a hearth the size of a cart, and food that has no business being this good in a town like this. The proprietor keeps standards that would shame establishments in cities ten times the size. Clean rooms, fine ale, and a rule against fighting indoors that is somehow universally respected.

The Baths.description: A long, low building behind the Stone Quarter, fed by the river and heated by boiler-furnaces that run day and night. Stone pools, steam rooms, a cold plunge. The one place in Gorren Crossing where clan riders, merchants, ward rats, and mercenaries share space as equals.

The House of Many Banners.description: The House of Many Banners is a broad timber-and-stone adventurers' hall near the River Market, with a long common room and a hard-packed yard behind it for training and mustering. Its rafters carry the banners of companies, riding bands, caravan guards, clan warriors, and foreign fellowships that have performed worthy service for the Wolds and its people. Route maps, work postings, secure stores, upper chambers, and a great company table support crews preparing to leave or returning from the road.

Gods-Anvil.name: Gods-Anvil
Gods-Anvil.basicInfo: A flat-topped mesa rising from the open steppe, visible for miles in every direction. Orc creation myth holds that the gods forged the first orcs on its summit. No clan claims Gods-Anvil. All clans hold it sacred. When an Anvil Moot is called, the clans ride in from every corner of the Wold to camp at the mesa's base and settle their affairs on the summit above. Between Moots, a handful of keepers tend the site and the trails. No permanent settlement. No fortification. To build on Gods-Anvil would be sacrilege.
Gods-Anvil.hiddenInfo:
Gods-Anvil is the political and spiritual heart of the Wold, and it is safe ground. The first law here is the truce: no blood may be shed on or around the mesa, by anyone, for any cause. Breaking that truce is the gravest shame an orc can earn, and the offender's whole clan bears it. Even the bitterest rivals keep this law. The Oathbreakers—orcs cast out of the clans for breaking their oaths—are not welcome here, for the truce is the very bond they broke.

An Anvil Moot can be called by any chief with a grievance that touches more than one clan, and the great Moots of spring and autumn draw every clan in the region. On the summit, chiefs sit and speak in a ring of ancient standing stones; any orc may climb up and be heard, though interrupting a chief carries consequences. Non-orcs may attend only as the guest of a chief, which is a high honor—and Gods-Anvil is where an outsider who has fought for the Wold can be granted real standing among the clans, sworn and witnessed on sacred ground.

The rivalry between Clan Vorren and Clan Drokash runs through every Moot: Drokash expects to speak last and loudest as old tradition allows, and Vorren increasingly refuses to defer. In the camps below, riders of the two clans clash in contests that are friendly only on the surface. But here the feud stays in words and trials and wagers—never in blood, because blood on this ground is unthinkable. This is the pressure-valve that keeps two proud clans from open war.

The keepers are a small order of all clans who tend the mesa, guard the trails, and oversee the trials and oaths. They answer to no chief and are respected by all.

The Base Camps.description: Open ground around the mesa's foot, worn flat by generations of use. Each clan has its traditional camping ground, marked by firepits and picket-lines that never fully disappear between Moots. During an Anvil Moot, this becomes a temporary city—thousands of orcs, their herds, their banners. Contest rings for wrestling, riding, and archery. Cook-fires and song circles and arguments that stop just short of violence. Between Moots, a few keepers maintain the trails and tend the site.

The Summit.description: The flat top of the mesa, reached by a single trail carved into the rock face. A ring of standing stones marks the Moot Circle where chiefs sit and speak. At the center stands the Anvil—a great slab of dark stone, flat-topped and roughly rectangular, split down the middle by a crack that legend says was struck by a god's hammer. Oaths sworn on the Anvil are the most binding words in orc culture. On clear days you can see the steppe in every direction to the horizon.

Lord Rhadan's Court.name: Lord Rhadan's Court
Lord Rhadan's Court.basicInfo: The one fixed place in the Shadelands — a vast ruined palace that Lord Rhadan holds against the grey in service to the Black Tower. At its heart, a round courtyard catches the Beacon: a single shaft of cold light falling from the black clouds, the only safe ground in the realm and the only way back to the living world. The Pale Hound guards the court against the dead, and Rhadan holds the rest. Those who cross the Pit arrive here, and set out from here when their work takes them deeper into the grey.
Lord Rhadan's Court.hiddenInfo:
Lord Rhadan's Court is the Black Tower's foothold in the land of the dead — an embassy, a waystation, and the only stable point in a realm with no fixed geography.

The Beacon is the way in and the way home: a crosser from the Pit of Shadow lands in the courtyard, and to return stands in the light and wills themselves back. If the Beacon ever failed, anyone in the Shadelands would be stranded. The Pale Hound — a great hound of cold pale fire, bound to the light — devours any shade that crosses into the courtyard uninvited, and so keeps the transit point clear. It lets the living pass, and watches them every step.

Rhadan is not a king of the dead and does not rule the Shadelands. He was a king in life, in an age so old its name is lost even here, and one of the sworn fellowship of the hero who threw down the Fourth Empire; his charge was the border of the dead, and he has held it ever since. His hall is not a dreamed world like the rotting palaces around it — it is a watchtower he holds by will against the grey, and the one place in the Reaches that is not going to ruin. He is bound to this post and cannot leave it; were he to fall, the Court and the Beacon would fall with him. He knows the realm as no living thing can — which dreamed worlds have soured, which shades have turned dangerous, where a disturbance among the dead is bleeding up into the living world — and those who come to end such things start with him.

The dreamed worlds of individual shades are not reached by walking. A crosser learns from Rhadan, or from the Tower, which shade is the root of their trouble, and crosses toward it from here — the realm folding them toward the place that shade dreams. Each such dreamed world is its own delve, stable only while its shade holds together.

The Courtyard of the Beacon.description: A round court at the heart of the ruined palace, and the only safe ground in the Shadelands. A single shaft of cold light falls from the black clouds overhead into the center of the court — the Beacon, the way in and the way home. A hunter crossing from the Pit of Shadow arrives here; to return, stand in the light and will it. Broken colonnades ring the court, and beyond them the palace climbs into ruin and nothing. Shades do not enter here. The Pale Hound sees to that — a hound of cold pale fire the size of a warhorse, bound to the light, that devours any dead thing crossing the threshold uninvited. It lets the living pass. Its white eyes never stop scanning for interlopers.

Lord Rhadan's Hall.description: Past the courtyard, in the ruined heart of the palace, Lord Rhadan holds his court. A long hall of cracked marble and toppled columns, raised from a memory so old its kingdom has no name. A single throne stands at the end, and the grey king upon it. He keeps this place in the Tower's service and does not leave it. A hunter come to end a haunting at its root starts here: Rhadan knows which shade has soured, where grief has turned to rising, which dreamed world holds the thing they hunt. He directs them, and from here they cross toward it.

The Imperial Baths.name: The Imperial Baths
The Imperial Baths.basicInfo: A vast pleasure district of the old Fourth Empire, buried beneath Silvervale by the Flood and reopened beneath great sinkholes. Green daylight falls through the shafts onto moss-soft marble, wild pale gardens, steaming bath-halls, and a ruined arena. The warm water and shelter make the Baths the most fought-over place in Grell Hollows: kobold hosts, goblin crews, and other underfolk all claim pieces of the old resort.
The Imperial Baths.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Imperial Baths are not a safe settlement, but they are not a static kill room or automatically hostile on arrival. This is an active contested ruin: Grell kobold hosts, goblin salvage crews, splinter raiders, cave creatures, and delvers all use parts of it. Let the site respond to what the party does.

When the party first enters an area for the first time, always stage one immediate local challenge in that area. The threat must act now: attack, pursue, seize salvage, cut off a route, drive the party away from the warm water, or trigger a piece of old machinery. Choose the smallest threat that fits. At The Broken Gate use kobold scouts, skirmishers, or trappers; in The Garden Halls use kobold scouts, shrieker fungus, violet fungus, or a creature in the growth; in The Bath of Princes use kobold heavies or raiders defending the pools, or a danger caused by steam, water, or bad air; in The Ur Arena use a kobold champion or heavy, a chained or escaped beast, or a half-working arena mechanism. Do not wait for a long investigation or warning scene before the first challenge.

After that first challenge, do not add another encounter merely because the party won. A later encounter requires a new triggering action: entering another area; opening a sealed door or beast-pen; following fresh tracks into a closed space; disturbing, stripping, or carrying off imperial fittings or salvage; making sustained noise, bright light, fire, or combat; resting conspicuously in the baths or gardens; or pursuing a fleeing group. Each trigger produces at most one immediate local encounter. Keep it in the area where the trigger occurred, and do not stack waves without another trigger.

Use escalation only when the party's actions justify it. A quiet intrusion may draw scouts, a warning, a retreat, or a bargain. Repeated noise, theft, injury, or attacks can bring a larger raiding party, a kobold heavy or champion, a rival host seeking the same claim, or a deeper creature displaced from the growth or pools. The Baths are contested, so different groups may react differently; do not turn every threat into one unified faction. If the party negotiates, hides, retreats, or leaves a threat unresolved, honor that choice and let later consequences follow from what was actually disturbed.

Do not have local NPCs lecture the party about avoiding the ruins. Entering, opening, salvaging, and taking risks are normal adventuring actions here; make the consequences playable. Loot should be tied to the defeated threat, abandoned camp, disturbed fitting, or current action, not a generic treasure cache. The warm baths can provide shelter only while the party can hold the approaches.

The Broken Gate.description: Where you come in, through a collapsed stretch of the quarter's outer wall. Marble underfoot, moss-furred, and ahead the quarter opens out under shafts of green sinkhole-light. Old statues line what was a grand avenue, most toppled, a few still standing. Tracks in the moss — goblin, kobold, and things with claws — all heading in.

The Garden Halls.description: Pleasure-gardens gone vast and pale in the dark, cave-growth and luminous fungus swallowing the colonnades, fed by the warm springs. Statues and fountains stand drowned in fern and creeper. Beautiful and overgrown, good cover, easy to get lost in. Things den in the deep green.

The Bath of Princes.description: Great bath-halls, the pools full again and steaming, fed by springs that never stopped running. Cracked marble, silver fittings gone black, the warm water the reason anything lives down here. Whoever holds the baths holds the only warmth in the Hollows.

The Ur Arena.description: The heart of the quarter. Tiered stone seating climbs up into the dark, the sand still in the pit, the gates and beast-pens beneath it half-working still.

The Scrabble.name: The Scrabble
The Scrabble.basicInfo: A wide, broken cavern in Grell Hollows where the Delvers' Lift from Ardan's Watch lands on a bolted ledge beside a cold pool fed by a stream that falls from the surface. The walls are old cut stone, the buried streets and halls of the dead city choked with rubble and worn into a warren of small chambers. The Scrabble is the League's only regular foothold and main staging place for work in the Hollows: crews form up here, salvage is caged and tagged, maps are chalked on boards, and a League field representative keeps local jobs moving. Kobold raiders attack the landing from the old street-warrens, trying to cut the lift, steal cargo, or drag injured delvers into the dark.
The Scrabble.hiddenInfo:
The Scrabble is the League's lift-bottom foothold in Grell Hollows, not a safe town. It exists because the Delvers' Lift can bring crews, rope, lamps, stretcher cases, packframes, and guarded salvage straight down from the Basement of Ardan's Watch. Brelka Tharn, the League field representative here, keeps the landing working under pressure: she knows which crews are below, which tunnels are hot, which claims are honest, and which jobs are fit for Copper, Bronze, or stronger adventurers.

Use this location to award Grell Hollows quests while the party is physically in the Grell Hollows region. Appropriate work includes scouting fresh passages, rescuing missing crews, clearing kobold pressure from the landing, escorting salvage, checking monster signs, mapping routes toward the Shrine or the Imperial Baths, and settling immediate field problems before they become disasters. Brelka can report completion, pay hazard bonuses, and send news of larger deeds up to Tobiah Finch and the League Hall.

Kobolds probe The Scrabble often. They shoot from old doorways, rush the barricades when the lift is loaded, cut lamps, spoil rope, and use flooded side passages to appear where no one expected them. The landing has patched barricades, alarm bells, a casualty cot, supply lockers, and salvage cages, but the dark around it belongs to whoever can hold it. The stream-shaft up to the surface remains a secondary natural route up and down; it is slower, wetter, and more dangerous than the lift.

Darkwater Cavern.description: The lift-bottom landing of Grell Hollows: a wide cavern of broken imperial stone where the Delvers' Lift stops on a bolted ledge above a cold pool. Lantern gantries, patched barricades, a signal bell, salvage cages, a casualty cot, and a chalk route-map crowd the ledge while the old streets of the dead city fan into rubble-dark beyond. A stream from the surface falls down a shaft along one wall, marking the slower natural climb back toward daylight, and the pool drains through a flooded passage deeper into the Underworld. Kobold raiders strike from the street-warrens often enough that every crew here keeps a weapon within reach.

The Imperial Shrine to Avarice.name: The Imperial Shrine to Avarice
The Imperial Shrine to Avarice.basicInfo: A remote deephold in a drowned Fourth Empire temple, built around a vast cavern flooded at its heart. On an island stands a stripped marble idol of Avarice, the goddess of greed the Fourth Empire worshipped, one gemstone eye still sparkling across the black water. Pale hungry things hunt below the surface, so underfolk hold the shore and old halls but leave the island alone.
The Imperial Shrine to Avarice.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Imperial Shrine to Avarice is a dangerous deephold, not a static kill room. Rival underfolk use the shore halls, but no one controls the island or the black water. Let the shrine respond to the party's movement, noise, greed, and attempts to cross.

When the Meet with Baska quest is accepted and grell_baska_met is not yet true, the authored Baska-at-the-Shrine event fires as the party arrives at the shrine. Baska is at The Shrine Mouth; two specialized kobolds attack immediately, then the muster and war-shrieker sequence unfolds. Do not add a separate passive scout or replace this event with generic exploration.

When the party first enters an area for the first time, always stage one immediate local challenge in that area. The threat must act now: attack, pursue, block the route, cut off a retreat, drag something into the water, or force the party to choose ground. At The Shrine Mouth use kobold scouts, trappers, or raiders emerging from the old avenue; in The Shore Halls use a small kobold or goblin hold, darkmantle, shrieker fungus, or other local creature; at The Black Water have a gulper or other pale water predator attack from the edge, or have a shore party use the water against the characters; in The Deepway use a kobold patrol, darkmantle, grick, grimlock, or another deeper threat. Do not wait for a long investigation or warning scene before the first challenge, and do not require the party to cross to the island.

After that first challenge, do not add another encounter merely because the party won. A later encounter requires a new triggering action: entering another area; approaching, touching, lighting, throwing something into, or attempting to cross the Black Water; opening a shrine chamber or disturbing carved stone, offerings, fittings, or the idol's soulstone eye; searching or stripping a den; making sustained noise, bright light, blood, or combat; following the Deepway beyond the shore; or resting conspicuously beside the water. Each trigger produces at most one immediate local encounter. Keep it in the area where the trigger occurred, and do not stack waves without another trigger.

Escalate only when the party's actions justify it. A quiet intrusion may draw a lookout, a warning, a withdrawal, or a bargain. Repeated disturbance, blood in the water, attempted crossing, or taking valuable relics can bring more coordinated shore defenders, a larger aquatic attack, or a deeper creature forced toward the lamps. The shore and water are separate pressures: do not make every threat one unified faction. If the party negotiates, hides, retreats, or leaves the island alone, honor that choice and let later consequences follow from what was actually disturbed.

Do not have local NPCs lecture the party about leaving the shrine untouched. Delving, crossing, opening, and taking risks are normal adventuring actions here; make the consequences playable. Loot should be tied to the defeated creature, abandoned shore hold, disturbed shrine fitting, or current action, not a generic treasure cache. The idol's gem eye is a soulstone and the richest prize in the shrine. There is only one, and taking it means crossing the Black Water.

The Shrine Mouth.description: The old avenue ends at a broken portico above the flooded temple cavern. Marble steps descend between toppled columns, the stone worn smooth by generations of feet and claws. The black water glimmers beyond, and the only light comes from sinkholes far overhead and lamps set along the shore.

The Shore Halls.description: The temple's near-side halls have become a maze of dens, salvage piles, sleeping ledges, and half-collapsed chambers. Carved walls emerge from the rubble, their old reliefs hacked at or covered with kobold claims. Doorways open toward the black water, the Deepway, and the Shrine Mouth.

The Black Water.description: Dark water fills the heart of the cavern, ringing a central island where the bare marble goddess stands with one gem-eye still sparkling across the gap. Broken piers jut from the shore, but no boat remains tied for long. Something moves below the surface, and the water is deep enough to hide it.

The Deepway.description: Beyond the shore halls, a flooded imperial street slopes into the deeper dark. Water runs through the paving stones, old doorways open into submerged chambers, and the route leads toward the Imperial Baths and other buried districts. The lamps from the Shrine do not reach very far here.

The Flooded Forum.name: The Flooded Forum
The Flooded Forum.basicInfo: A drowned civic district of the old Fourth Empire, where a broad avenue descends into a sunken forum beneath a line of broken sinkholes. Public buildings, carved steps, toppled statues, and water-dark administrative halls surround a stone floor marked by the old Floodline. Kobolds, delvers, and salvage crews come here for records, imperial fittings, and whatever still moves beneath the flooded streets.
The Flooded Forum.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Flooded Forum is not a safe ruin, but it is not a static kill room. It is an active salvage and archaeology site where kobold claimants, delvers, oozes, bad air, and unstable buildings compete for the same drowned civic quarter. Let the Forum respond to what the party does.

When the party first enters an area for the first time, always stage one immediate local challenge in that area. The threat must act now: attack, pursue, cut off a route, spoil the party's light, trigger a collapse, or defend records and salvage. At The Drowned Avenue use kobold scouts, skirmishers, or trappers, or a threat emerging from the standing water; at The Civic Steps use a kobold salvage party, sapper, darkmantle, or shrieker fungus; in The Records Hall use kobold trappers or sappers, a gray ooze or gelatinous cube, or a collapsing shelf-line; at The Floodline use kobold sappers, a waterlogged hazard, an ooze, or a creature disturbed near a sealed civic vault. Do not wait for a long investigation or warning scene before the first challenge.

After that first challenge, do not add another encounter merely because the party won. A later encounter requires a new triggering action: entering another area; opening a sealed office, vault, or flooded door; disturbing or carrying off tablets, records, seals, reliefs, or imperial fittings; crossing deep water or changing its level; following fresh tracks into a closed space; making sustained noise, bright light, fire, or combat; resting conspicuously in a dry hall; or pursuing a fleeing salvage crew. Each trigger produces at most one immediate local encounter. Keep it in the area where the trigger occurred, and do not stack waves without another trigger.

Escalate only when the party's actions justify it. A quiet intrusion may draw a lookout, warning, retreat, or bargain. Repeated salvage, noise, injury, or attacks can bring a more organized kobold recovery team, a sapper-led collapse, a larger ooze, or a creature displaced from the flooded rooms. The Forum's pressures are mixed; do not turn every threat into one unified faction. Kobolds may misread the inscriptions and overwrite them with Grell claims, but do not make an NPC lecture the party about the history. Let records, objects, and consequences reveal it through play.

Loot should be tied to the defeated threat, abandoned salvage pile, opened civic room, or current action, not a generic treasure cache. The Forum can yield evidence about the Fourth Empire and the Flood, but discovery should require risk, interpretation, or a deliberate choice to carry something out.

The Drowned Avenue.description: A broad imperial avenue slopes down through standing water toward the sunken civic quarter. Broken statues and lamp-posts line the paving, while sinkhole shafts throw pale daylight onto the first flooded steps. Fresh tracks cross the mud between old doorways.

The Civic Steps.description: Tiered stone steps descend into the forum floor, their lower courses underwater. The buildings around the square carry a dark Floodline, and old reliefs have been chipped, smeared, or covered by kobold claims. Echoes travel far across the open space.

The Records Hall.description: A long administrative hall with collapsed shelves, clay tablets, bronze seals, and swollen wooden doors. Some rooms are dry enough to search; others open onto black water or air too foul to breathe for long. Someone has recently dragged salvage toward the deeper passages.

The Floodline.description: The lowest surviving section of the Forum, where the Flood's old waterline cuts across walls and columns far above the present floor. Submerged offices and sealed civic vaults lie below, reached through broken stairwells and narrow flooded passages.

The Imperial Arsenal.name: The Imperial Arsenal
The Imperial Arsenal.basicInfo: A buried military complex of the old Fourth Empire, hidden behind massive gatehouses and a maze of stone courtyards. Racks of rusted weapons, toppled soldier-statues, sealed storehouses, and a command hall lie beyond the gates. The halls still bear the order of an army that vanished, though recent movement has disturbed the dust.
The Imperial Arsenal.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Imperial Arsenal is the provisional command center of the unified kobold host. It is an active military ruin, not a safe settlement and not a static kill room. The old complex, the new host, and the hostile stone-boring beetles drawn by Big Buzzer all respond to intrusion. Let the Arsenal's defenses reflect what the party touches, breaks, steals, or announces.

When the party first enters an area for the first time, always stage one immediate local challenge in that area. The threat must act now: attack, pursue, raise an alarm, cut off a route, activate a signal, or force the party out of a defensible position. At The Arsenal Gate use kobold scouts, skirmishers, or trappers; in The Muster Yard use kobold heavies, raiders, or a champion drilling a small force; in The War Stores use kobold sappers, a rust monster, or a dangerous failure among the old arms; in The Boring Hall use a hostile stone-boring beetle attacking on sight, a Buzzer disturbance, or kobold sappers; in The Command Hall use a kobold champion, heavy, or organized guard defending the court. Do not wait for a long investigation or warning scene before the first challenge.

After that first challenge, do not add another encounter merely because the party won. A later encounter requires a new triggering action: entering another area; taking or damaging imperial weapons, armor, standards, maps, or command fittings; crossing a marked defensive line; disturbing Big Buzzer or a fresh bore; breaking a sealed signal fitting; making sustained noise, bright light, fire, or combat; resting inside the complex; issuing a public challenge; or pursuing a fleeing kobold. Each trigger produces at most one immediate local encounter. Keep it in the area where the trigger occurred, and do not stack waves without another trigger.

Escalate only when the party's actions justify it. A quiet intrusion may draw a sentry, a warning, a retreat, a bargain, or a rival host seeking leverage. Repeated attacks, theft, injury, or interference with the Boring Hall can bring coordinated skirmishers, heavies, sappers, a champion, a collapse, or a larger organized force. Do not treat every kobold as equally loyal to the warlord: fear, equipment, rivalry, and grandiose belief all matter. A stone-boring beetle can create a new danger, but it is a hostile animal attracted and irritated by Big Buzzer, not a machine the kobolds control.

After the unified host is broken, let the Arsenal return to contested, factional Grell play unless a later event establishes another occupant. Loot should be tied to the defeated defenders, opened stores, broken command, or current action, not a generic treasure cache. Do not have local NPCs lecture the party about leaving the military ruin alone; make the consequences playable.

The Arsenal Gate.description: A massive gatehouse of fitted imperial stone, its doors tall enough for a human army and scarred by generations of forced entry. Toppled soldier-statues flank the approach, while crude kobold perches and watch-slits have been built into the old walls. The halls beyond carry the smell of oil, rust, and disturbed dust.

The Muster Yard.description: A broad stone courtyard where old formations once gathered. Ranks of oversized armor, shields, and weapons stand propped against the walls, mixed with patched kobold standards and rope-secured salvage. The yard is large enough for drilling, mustering, and a loud argument between rival hosts.

The War Stores.description: Long storehouses packed with imperial arms, empty racks, bent shields, and piles of metal sorted according to whoever last claimed the room. Rust blooms across neglected weapons while kobold sappers strip useful parts from anything they cannot carry. Some sealed chests still bear the marks of the old army.

The Boring Hall.description: A deep Fourth Empire hall where surveyors and stonecutters bored passages into the buried city. Dozens of old tunnel mouths converge here, their rims pale with stone dust and their floors worn by traffic from below. At the center, on a squat bronze-and-stone plinth, rests Big Buzzer: a directional ground-vibration artifact the kobolds recovered from the Arsenal and carry to chosen surface sites. Its pulses attract and irritate stone-boring beetles but do not command them. Kobold sappers use hand tools, rope, braces, and scavenged timber to exploit the beetles' fresh tunnels; the floor trembles whenever the Buzzer is active.

The Command Hall.description: A high hall with a raised imperial dais, walls built for maps and standards, and a throne-sized chair dragged from some larger court. New banners and salvaged armor crowd the old military reliefs. The room can be a war council, a court, or a battlefield depending on who has reached it first.

The Upper Halls.name: The Upper Halls
The Upper Halls.basicInfo: The top level of the Darek Deep, where the great shaft from Deepgate drops into a hall of huge stone figures of dareks lining the walls. A broad road of polished black stone runs the length of the floor with iron constructs standing on it in a line, all toppled and shattered, a procession that halted and never resumed. Delvers have fortified the ground beneath the shaft, but the hall stretches into darkness in every direction.
The Upper Halls.hiddenInfo:
The Great Hall is the military heart of the dead city. The dareks built their constructs in the forges below, marched them through this hall along the black road, and deployed them along the three ways out. The iron figures on the road are the last march — halted when whatever ended the dareks ended them, shattered, rusted and silent.

Delvers have fortified the shaft-foot into a base camp: lanterns, rope stores, cached supplies, a fire. This is the one safe ground in the Deep, held by numbers and habit. Kobolds and goblins from the Underworld creep into the hall's edges; morlocks come up from the warrens; a construct intrudes now and then. The camp holds, but the dark around it does not belong to the surfacers.

The three roads out follow the black road's branches. Toward the forges where the constructs were made — machines, black iron, the old works. Toward the warrens where morlocks now live in darek barracks gnawed into dens. Up the high stair toward the seat of rule, the grandest and most dangerous part of the city.

The Great Hall.description: Where the shaft from Deepgate comes down. The cages land in a hall so large the far walls are lost in the dark. Stone figures of the dareks stand along the walls, twice the height of a man, stern and watching. A broad road of black stone runs the length of the floor, and on it iron constructs lie toppled. Delvers have roped off the ground beneath the shaft and built a base camp of lanterns and fire. Beyond the light, the hall belongs to the dead city.

The Black Forge.name: The Black Forge
The Black Forge.basicInfo: The forge-halls of the Darek Deep, down the Forge-Road from the Upper Halls, where the dareks made their iron soldiers. Great cold forges and dead machines fill halls that go deeper than a lamp will show. The salvage here is the richest in the Deep — black iron, darek alloy, soulstones, and mechanisms worth a fortune topside.
The Black Forge.hiddenInfo:
The Black Forge is the construct-works of the dead city, and it is actively defended. The constructs here are not dormant sentries that wake when you stumble on them. They are garrison troops holding their facility, and they fight like it: ambushes from side passages, traps rigged from old mechanisms, chutes that drop intruders into lower halls, forge-vents that blast heat, corridors that seal behind you. They use the terrain because they built it and they know every door and mechanism in it.

Black iron is common here — raw stock, finished parts, weapons. Soulstones can be pried from downed constructs: the souls in them can be freed (an act of mercy, since the Princes of Ur bound them there) or the live stones can be taken for the fortune they fetch from wizards and the desperate. The deeper you push, the better the salvage and the smarter the defense.

Greloq's Company runs expeditions here regularly and knows the upper halls well. Independent parties who venture in may find Greloq's crew already working a corridor — or find their exit route suddenly occupied.

The Forge-Gate.description: Where the Forge-Road from the Upper Halls ends at a heavy passage built to be held. The walls narrow, the ceiling drops, and the marks of old fighting are everywhere — gouged stone, broken iron, the wreckage of crews and constructs both. Beyond this chokepoint the halls open into the forges.

The Forge Floor.description: The main working halls, where great dark furnaces stand cold and lines of dead machines run off into shadow. Stripped-down, half-built constructs stand in rows between the forges.

The Crucible.description: A side-hall off the Forge-Gate where soulstones were set into finished constructs. Stone cradles line the walls.

The Deep Forge.description: The lowest halls, where the oldest forges stand and the best iron was worked.

The Morlock Warrens.name: The Morlock Warrens
The Morlock Warrens.basicInfo: The lower halls of the Darek Deep where the morlocks live, past the Warren-Mouth from the Upper Halls. Once these were darek halls. Now they are fouled and packed with the nests and refuse of a living people. The morlocks are pale, cunning, and many, and they know these halls better than any delver alive. Not everything in the warrens is ruin. Somewhere deep in the back, past the nests and the hoard, the morlocks keep a place they will not enter themselves.
The Morlock Warrens.hiddenInfo:
The Warrens are the morlock holdfast of the dead city, reached past the Warren-Mouth from the Upper Halls.

The morlocks are the dareks — or what became of them. The people who built this city did not all die. Some remained and sank into the dark across uncounted ages, forgetting what they were, dwindling into the pale cunning things that now squat in halls their own forebears raised. They do not know this. They have forgotten everything but habit.

Morlocks are hostile to surfacers. They do not trade, do not parley, and do not tolerate intrusion. They attack from ambush, in numbers, using traps and knowledge of every passage. They are not mindless — they are cunning, coordinated, and fight to kill. A party entering the warrens is in enemy territory against a force that knows every inch of it and wants them dead. Do not have morlocks attempt to communicate, negotiate, or show curiosity toward the party. They are defending their home from invaders and that is all.

The secret of the Darek Deep is in the Kept Hall, the sanctum at the back of the warrens that even morlocks will not enter. There a single morlock unlike the others works alone among clean darek stone and functioning tools, mending broken constructs with procedures passed down through generations as ritual. The constructs it mends get back up and walk out into the halls. This is why the Deep's guardians have not broken down after an age of neglect.

The Foul Halls.description: The border of morlock country, past the Warren-Mouth. Old darek stone gone black with filth, stacked with bones and nesting material. Morlock sentries watch from the dark. Beyond this point the halls belong to them.

The Nests.description: The crowded heart of the warrens, where the morlocks den and breed in halls packed close and stinking. They are thickest here and fight hardest for it. The noise is constant — shrieking, scraping, the knock of stone tools. This is their home ground.

The Hoard-Deep.description: The deepest part of the warrens, where the morlocks keep what they have stolen from the dead city over the ages. Darek treasure, black iron, salvage, and stranger things lie heaped in the dark, guarded by the strongest of them. Past the hoard, a single passage runs further back into a part of the warrens the morlocks themselves avoid.

The Kept Hall.description: A darek workshop at the back of the warrens, behind the hoard, through a passage the morlocks will not follow. The stone here is clean. The tools on the racks are whole and ordered. A workbench holds a construct laid open, its parts arranged with care. Everything in this room has been maintained while the rest of the city fell to ruin. Something has been working here for a very long time.
