The Temple of Dominion.name: The Temple of Dominion
The Temple of Dominion.basicInfo: The temple-seat of the Darek Deep, where the dareks ruled and worshipped. This is where the soulstones were made, and the treasures here are the richest and strangest in the Deep. Grand halls of carved stone climb toward a great sanctum, and over all of it presides a vast idol of the demon the dareks served. It is the deepest the constructs run, and the strongest of them keep these halls.
The Temple of Dominion.hiddenInfo:
The Temple of Dominion is the holy and cruel heart of the dead city, climbed by the High Stair from the Upper Halls. It holds the deepest lore, the richest singular treasures, and the worst danger in the Deep.

Here the dareks served an Ur demon of dominion — mastery, the owning of others, the binding of the living into endless service. This is the idea behind the whole Deep: every soulstone is a person made property, every construct a slave that cannot die or rest. The demon princes of Ur made the soulstones in this temple, binding souls into gems by a great rite, and turning the darek arts to their cruelest end.

The binding-engine still stands in the deepest chamber, but it is destroyed — shattered into pieces and fused and warped, wrecked by some hand of a heroic age and left broken past any working. What it did is still plain, because a huge relief carved in elderstone covers the wall: the rite shown whole, a soul drawn from a bound victim into a waiting stone, darek priests attending, the demon of dominion above them all. And the way to the engine runs through the cells where the victims were held — rows of stone pens, long empty, the bones of the used-up still in them.

The Processional.description: The top of the High Stair, where it opens into the temple. A grand ceremonial way runs inward, lined with tall darek figures carved in stone, worn but still imposing. The grandeur of the dead city is plainest here. The way leads on to the great hall.

The Hall of the Idol.description: The great hall of the temple, where the dareks ruled and worshipped. A vast idol of the demon of dominion stands over a high seat, carved in dark stone, looming over the whole chamber. The richest singular treasures of the Deep lie here. Strong constructs keep this hall, and more stand between it and the chambers beyond.

The Cells.description: Rows of stone pens below the great hall, where the victims were held before the rite. They are long empty now, but the bones of the used-up still lie in them. The way to the deepest chamber runs through here.

The Binding-Hall.description: The deepest chamber of the temple, where the soulstones were made. The binding-engine stands at its center, shattered — broken into pieces and fused and warped, wrecked by some great force long ago. On the wall behind it, a huge relief carved in elderstone shows the binding rite: a soul drawn from a bound victim into a waiting stone, darek priests attending, the demon of dominion above.

Drusavia.name: Drusavia
Drusavia.basicInfo: Drusavia is the capital of the Duchy of Drusavia: a gracious city of pale stone, steep roofs, arched bridges, and high gothic towers, rich on the wine, timber, and silver of its dales. Two heights crown it. On one stands the Temple of Galard, bright and gothic, raised to the god of courage after the Liberation. Opposite it rises the Black Tower, seat of the Shadow Inquisition, the duchy's hunters of the restless dead. The duke rules from the square between them.
Drusavia.hiddenInfo:
Drusavia is human-led, prosperous, and proud of itself: an old city that broke its vampire lords two hundred years ago and has lived well since. The ducal house governs city and land with a fair hand and a light one; the duke blesses both the Temple and the Inquisition and commands neither, and keeping it that way is the ducal family's oldest skill. A small but wealthy moon elf community lives among the city's upper circles. Its old families keep townhouses near the Grand Galleries and Ducal Square, fund magical workshops and salons, compete for noble patronage, and maintain private traditions of spellcraft, dueling, and courtship. They are not a separate government, but their money and magic open doors that remain closed to most of the city. Dwarves hold many of the finest workshops in the Grand Galleries, working blessed arms, silver, moonstone, jewelry, instruments, and other beautiful commissions for the Temple, the Tower, nobles, and ambitious young buyers. The city keeps the country's customs at city scale: old stone, high manners, strong drink, public ceremony, and a lively appetite for fashion, music, games, and gossip.

The city runs on the dales' trade — Rovena's wine and cordials, Kolbeck's grimwood and carving, grain, silver, fine clothing, jewelry, food, and high-end craft. Work for capable strangers is everywhere: merchant houses hiring escorts for the dale roads, families wanting someone found or brought home, nobles looking for discreet agents, and the Temple and the Tower recruiting in their own fashion. The Syndicate runs quiet business through the city's fences, but most of Drusavia's daily life is bright, social, and prosperous enough to make people forget how close the old danger remains.

Ducal Square.description: The civic heart: the ducal palace and offices, watch posts, petitioners at the steps, carriage traffic over polished stone, and public ceremonies that draw nobles, adventurers, and curious onlookers. From the square, the Temple of Galard shows bright on its height to one side and the Black Tower dark on its height to the other. The duke's herald, Velanthe, receives visitors in the palace's audience chamber. Wren Lane opens off the square toward Grey Gables, a pale-stone townhouse with three steep slate gables.

The Grand Arcade.description: A huge covered market beneath high stone vaults and galleried balconies. Stalls and shops sell food, clothing, instruments, jewelry, travel gear, books, games, and goods from every dale, while performers, recruiters, gamblers, and young people looking for trouble fill the broad central walks. It is the easiest place in Drusavia to find a crew, a patron, a bargain, or a rumor.

The Red Moon Inn.description: The Red Moon Inn is a lively, elegant tavern in the Grand Arcade, welcoming adventurers, young nobles, travelers, merchants, performers, and moon elves beneath the same roof. Moon elves say that a red moon brings fortunate encounters, and the inn has made that belief its ethos: strangers share tables, conversations are welcomed, and unexpected connections are treated as good luck. Guests come for food, music, games, and the chance to find companions, patrons, useful specialists, or trouble. Its polished style never makes it exclusive, giving it a reputation as Drusavia's best place to meet someone worth knowing. By custom, the young nobility come here to slum under the red moon, and no one asks their names.

The Grand Galleries.description: An elegant quarter of arched workshops, showrooms, balconies, and private salons where master makers display beautiful work. Dwarven smiths, jewelers, armorers, tailors, instrument makers, and moon elf spellwrights compete for noble commissions and the reputations that follow them. Moon elf houses host private demonstrations, duels, and courtship gatherings behind polished doors. Duelists, Templars, Inquisitors, and ambitious adventurers come here for distinctive arms, armor, jewelry, magical work, and equipment that says who they are.

The League Chapterhouse.description: A pale-stone hall off Ducal Square, with tall arched windows and a hearth framed in carved grimwood. Young adventurers and visiting veterans gather over dark wine beneath trophies brought back from the haunted dales. Notices hang beside a map marked with estates, villages, and ruined castles.

The Moonstone Hall.description: A grand hall off Ducal Square, its pillars and floor inlaid with moonstone that glows softly when music plays. By day it holds receptions, concerts, recitals of spellcraft and the old families' gossip; by night it doubles as the duchy's finest ballroom, where the season's matches are made and the moon elf families hang spell-lights in the air like stars.

The Velvet Room.description: A candlelit private club of the old families above the Grand Arcade, all dark velvet, deep chairs and polished wood. Its members play cards and dice for ruinous stakes, fence and test their spellcraft on the floor of its long room, and conduct the duchy's quieter scandals. A guest needs a member's word to enter.

Black Tower.name: Black Tower
Black Tower.basicInfo: The Black Tower is the headquarters of the Shadow Inquisition, Drusavia's ghost-hunters and occult investigators. It rises opposite the Temple of Galard, dark and narrow where the temple is bright and open. New members start as Initiates and work one supervised case. Then they may go down into the Pit beneath the tower and bond with a Shade, a spirit of the dead that becomes their partner, to become full Inquisitors.
Black Tower.hiddenInfo:
The Black Tower is not a League chapterhouse and not a ducal office. It is an independent specialist institution blessed by Drusavia because no one else can do its work. The duke blesses the Inquisition but does not command it; the Temple distrusts its methods and depends on the results.

The Shadow Inquisition is a heroic and prestigious institution in Drusavia. Its Inquisitors are known for striking personal style, distinctive weapons, decisive action, sharp exchanges, and the confidence to face supernatural threats directly. They take pride in protecting the living and in doing difficult work with skill and courage. Drusavians may find the Tower's work unsettling, but they respect its results and rarely obstruct an Inquisitor acting under its authority.

Every accepted member begins as an Initiate and receives the Mark of Rhadan, an oath-mark that identifies them to the Tower and anchors authorized contact with the Shadelands. The Mark is not Inquisitor rank and does not grant a Shade. An Initiate works one qualifying field case under a mentor. If the case is decisively resolved, the Initiate may return to the Pit for the authorized Rite of Bonding. Only by knowingly accepting that permanent bond and emerging with a Shade are they recognized as a full Inquisitor.

Inquisitors investigate hauntings at their root, hunt necromancers and the Gravebound, the cult that raises the dead from defiled graves, and cross into the Shadelands when a case cannot be resolved from the living side. After three recognized Inquisitor cases they may be raised to Adept, trusted to lead deep descents and other operatives. After four further recognized Adept cases they may be raised to Master and share authority over the order's deepest work, assignments, methods, and defense of the Pit.

The order binds Shades through consent and warded rite. A bonded Shade is a supernatural partner and shield, not automatically a servant with a fixed personality. Its manner of communication and relationship with its Inquisitor emerge through play. The bond grants Shade-Sight and forms the basis of the Inquisitor's later Shade techniques.

Lowlamp Lane.description: The narrow lane at the Tower's base, full of low blue lamps, quiet doors, nervous petitioners, and shops that serve people who deal with hauntings.

Harran's Place.description: A warm, discreet tavern for Inquisitors, informants, and people who need courage before asking the Black Tower for help. The regulars like it because it remembers the living are still alive.

Silver & Salt Outfitters.description: A cramped outfitter selling silver wire, salt, moonstone settings, black candles, funerary chalk, and practical tools for work around the restless dead.

The Hall of Shadow.description: The Black Tower's working hall: case boards, oath records, Initiates learning the work, Shade-Bonded Inquisitors returning with evidence, and Jett watching over it all with dry patience. Cases are recognized here, and Adepts and Masters are raised here before the order.

The Pit of Shadow.description: A black shaft in the Black Tower's deep chamber, ringed by wards, oath-marks, and cold elderstone. The Pit is the controlled crossing into Tarnished Reaches and the site of the Rite of Bonding. Qualified Initiates enter under sanction to accept or refuse a Shade; full Inquisitors come for authorized descents and work that cannot be solved from the living side. An exceptional summons may gather Initiates in the chamber, but the Mark alone does not permit them to cross.

The Temple of Galard.name: The Temple of Galard
The Temple of Galard.basicInfo: The Temple of Galard crowns the bright height of Drusavia: a great gothic temple of pale stone and shield-hung halls, raised after the Liberation to the god of courage, whose shield stands between the living and the dark. It is the seat of the Templars Adamant, Drusavia's elite holy warriors, who wear beautiful blessed armor and wield radiant arms against the restless dead. Beneath the temple lie the honored crypts of Castian — the champion who broke the vampire lords — and the liberation-dead.
The Temple of Galard.hiddenInfo:
Galard is worshipped here as the Shieldbearer: courage as the wall between the living and the dead. The Templars Adamant are not negotiators, mediums, or keepers of shades. They do not bind the dead for questioning, bargain with them, or use them against other enemies. They blind and burn shades with radiant force, destroy the bodies and objects that anchor the dead, and close every breach they can reach. Their long purpose is to seal the Pit of Shadow and shut the Shadelands away from the living world.

The Temple also keeps Galard's Proving-Year custom, which predates the schism with the Knights Vigilant. Any willing person may take up a plain iron Road-Shield, travel beyond the temple, and return here or to another recognized Galard site with accounts, witnesses, or proof of substantial deeds of courage. Three distinct recognized deeds complete the demanded proof. The aspirant then may seek the Shieldbearer oath here, seek the Swordbearer oath above Aldwall, visit both orders, postpone the choice, or swear neither; the Road-Shield grants no order membership before that choice.

A person who freely swears the Shieldbearer oath enters as a Templar Initiate and receives the White-Silver Shield Clasp. One supervised first shield-work earns reception as a full Templar Adamant trusted with independent work. Three recognized works as a Templar Adamant earn promotion to Templar Captain, with authority to direct warders, sealing rites, and willing Templars in the field. Four further great works as Captain may earn acclamation as Templar Champion, trusted with the order's largest defenses, purges, and strategic campaigns. First Sword and the leadership of the Temple are appointed offices, not ordinary ranks beyond Champion.

The Temple's board of works offers concrete danger: protect warders while they seal a breach, escort a priest through a haunted village, recover a blessed relic from a grave-site where the dead are following it, purge an undead stronghold, or defend a living person whose presence is keeping a haunting open. The Templars hire capable outsiders for work that requires more hands than their order has, but they expect obedience once the rite begins.

The duchy supports the Temple publicly but fears its demand to close the Pit. The Shadow Inquisition insists that the dead will continue to return and that sealing the crossing would leave Drusavia unable to enter the Shadelands and answer the threat at its source. The Templars Adamant consider this argument a confession of dependence on the enemy. The duke does not want the two orders to come to open blows.

Beneath the temple lie the crypts of Castian and the liberation-dead: the fallen of the war against the vampire lords, buried with full honor under radiant wards, tended daily and visited by pilgrims from across Larion. These dead rest. The crypts are the Temple's proof that the dead can be kept out, and the Templars guard their peace with absolute force.

The Temple Steps.description: Wide stairs climbing the bright height through votive lamps and shield banners, the city spread below and the temple doors above. Pilgrims, guards, and petitioners come and go all day.

The Hall of Shields.description: The great hall: memorial shields on every pillar, training circles worn into the stone floor, an altar of pale stone under high windows, and side-chapels where the Templars Adamant bless steel and armor for the work against the dead. Beautiful armored warriors cross the hall beneath the banners, and a board of works stands by the doors.

The Crypts of Castian.description: Honored crypts beneath the temple floor: ranked tombs of the liberation-dead under radiant wards, lamps kept burning, and at the heart the great tomb of Castian, shield-carved, with fresh offerings at its foot. The Templars Adamant keep the crypts sealed against every shade and destroy anything that tries to cross the wards.

House Saravel.name: House Saravel
House Saravel.basicInfo: House Saravel is the most glittering estate in the wealthy dales of Drusavia: a great house of pale stone and famous gardens, seat of the duchy's oldest noble family.
House Saravel.hiddenInfo:
The Saravels are old blood. Before the Liberation, the Saravels, like the great houses of Drusavia, served the vampire lords — and when the Liberation came, Saravel turned on its masters, opened its gates, and fought. Every other great house of that age burned. Saravel was spared, and has been the first family of the dales ever since. House Saravel today is Lord Saravel, his lady, a crowd of siblings, cousins, and heirs, and the finest household staff in the dales. The family are pale, long-lived, and charming; they hunt, duel, gamble, and marry well, and the estate runs a nearly continuous season of balls, hunts, card evenings, and salons. Half the gentry of Drusavia owes the house money, favors, or a marriage, and invitations to Saravel are currency across the duchy. The family collects interesting people — champions, artists, hunters with names, clever strangers — and a capable guest who amuses them is fed, flattered, introduced to everyone worth knowing, and remembered. The family's private quarters, the oldest part of the house, admit no one but family — not guests, not staff, no exceptions.

A house this old, rich, and watched has troubles it cannot air: debts of honor, relations gone to bad company, letters that must come home. The Saravels handle such things privately, and quietly hire discreet, capable outsiders to handle them — the kind of work that pays extremely well and is never spoken of again. A guest who proves both able and closemouthed will sooner or later be taken aside.

Saravel Grounds.description: The approach to the great house: clipped hedges, pale gravel drives, fountains, and famous gardens kept perfect to the last leaf. Liveried staff meet visitors at the gates, and carriages come and go through the season.

Saravel Great Hall.description: The heart of the house's entertaining: a long hall of pale stone and candlelight, portraits of two hundred years of Saravels, a musicians' gallery above and the famous table below. Doors open onto card rooms, the library, and the ballroom.

The Daravaine Reaches.name: The Daravaine Reaches
The Daravaine Reaches.basicInfo: The Daravaine Reaches are lightly forested hills in the east of Drusavia, strewn with the burned estates of the houses purged after the Liberation. The ruins have never been emptied: grave-goods, hidden plate, and sealed strongrooms still turn up in the cellars, and crews still come to dig for them. The hills are lawless. Petty warlords the dales call the Hill Lords hold ruins and crags here, crack the old crypts, and rob whoever the roads deliver.
The Daravaine Reaches.hiddenInfo:
The purges burned the estates of the old houses and emptied them of the living, but not of everything else. The cellars and crypts of the Reaches still hold the wealth of broken houses — plate, coin, grave-goods, sealed strongrooms the purges never found — and the restless dead of the purged families that rise when their vaults are opened. Barghests, the black grave-hounds, range the burned estates and hunt the hills at dusk.

IMPORTANT: The Hill Lords are half a dozen rival bands, not one force, and they move — a crag held this season stands empty the next, and a band may be out raiding, digging, or feuding with a rival when travelers pass. Where they are met, they are hostile: they rob whoever they can take and kill whoever resists. Two exceptions, flat: anyone worth coin is ransomed rather than killed, and anyone hard enough to walk into a camp with something to sell can trade — the Hill Lords buy and sell grave-goods, relics, and worse without questions, and their camps are the dirtiest market in the duchy. Syndicate buyers come to that market, and so do cultists of the Gravebound, a necromancer cult buying grave-goods to raise the dead with; the Hill Lords sell to both without caring which is which.

The digging is the hills' economy and its danger both. A cracked crypt yields loot or wakes its dead, and the Hill Lords crack them anyway because the odds usually favor them. Independent crews come up from the dales to dig the ruins the bands haven't claimed, and the bands take their hauls on the roads home when they can.

The Old Estate Roads.description: Broken hill roads winding between overgrown fields, blackened gateposts, and toppled boundary markers. Ruined estates show on the heights in every direction, and cart tracks — some old, some fresh — turn off toward the diggings.

The Burned Estates.description: The purged houses themselves: fire-hollowed manors and halls on the hilltops, walls standing roofless, cellar mouths dark under the ruins. Some doorways are choked with rubble, some pried open, and dig-spoil and broken vault-stones lie outside more than one.

The Hill Lords' Crags.description: Rocky heights above the estates, crowned with broken watchtowers and fortified ruins. Rough palisades patch the old walls, fire-rings and refuse mark the camps, and here and there a banner no lawful house recognizes hangs from a tower — some camps living, some cold and abandoned.

Mirgreth Mire.name: Mirgreth Mire
Mirgreth Mire.basicInfo: Mirgreth Mire is poor, wet farmland in southeastern Drusavia: reed beds, black ditches, eel-traps, and hamlets on pilings, joined by raised causeways across the fen. The fenfolk keep old customs with the fen's dead — offerings left at ancient tribute stones, doors marked, the causeways not walked after dark — and they keep them for good reason.
Mirgreth Mire.hiddenInfo:
Mirgreth is poor, wet farmland the duchy has never much protected, and the fenfolk long ago made their own peace with what shares the fen. The wet ground holds old dead — drowned dead from before the duchy, and the unaccounted dead the purges pushed into the water — and the fenfolk keep them quiet with courtesies: offerings of bread, milk, and small silver left at the tribute stones, doors marked, the causeways not walked after dark. Nobody explains the customs and nobody argues with them. The Temple calls it superstition; the Shadow Inquisition has never once told the fenfolk to stop.

The fenfolk are human, closemouthed with strangers, and unimpressed by the duchy — help has never come from Drusavia and none is expected. They are not unfriendly, only practical: a stranger who lends a hand, keeps the customs, and doesn't ask stupid questions will find a dry bed and a hot meal. One who mocks the stones will find every door shut.

IMPORTANT: The fen's dead rise at night from the black water — drowned dead, heavy and silent, that drag the living into the ditches and meres. Will-o'-wisps drift over the deep fen, luring travelers off the causeways into drowning ground. Both keep to the wet and the dark: the causeways are safe by day, and a marked door with a kept threshold is not entered. Where the courtesies are kept, the dead mostly let the living be; where offerings have stopped or been defiled, they hunt.

The old peace is fraying. Offerings that held for generations are lately refused — stones found overturned, gifts untouched, dead walking where they never walked — and the fenfolk don't know why. Cultists of the Gravebound are working the deep fen: defiling tribute stones to break the old courtesies, raising the drowned dead where they can, and coming to frightened households as friends, saying the old ways are failing and offering stronger ones. Some households have started listening.

The Reed Causeways.description: Raised paths running between wet fields and black drainage cuts, the reed beds standing higher than a rider. Marker posts stand at the branchings, and open meres show dark through the reeds beyond.

Mirgreth Stead.description: A hamlet of low houses on pilings above the wet, peat smoke over the roofs, marked lintels on every door, nets and eel-traps drying on racks. A plank commons runs between the houses, with a shared well and a bell-post.

The Tribute Stones.description: Ancient leaning stones out in the fen, moss-grown and older than the duchy, offerings fresh and old at their feet — bread, ribbons, small silver in the mud. Here and there a stone lies overturned, its gifts scattered.

Fort Blackwing.name: Fort Blackwing
Fort Blackwing.basicInfo: Fort Blackwing is a burned fortress-estate in the hills of eastern Drusavia, seat of the worst of the necromancer-houses broken in the Liberation. The fires that destroyed the house were also its lords' prison: they were sealed in the cellars below. The fort is considered to be cursed and has never been reoccupied, and travelers give it a wide berth.
Fort Blackwing.hiddenInfo:
House Blackwing was the deepest of the old houses in the traffic with the dead, and its lords had gone far enough that death would not keep them: killed in the storming of the fortress, they began to return. Destroying them for good was beyond the Liberation's armies. So the priests entombed the lords in the house's own cellars and burned the fortress over them as a seal — consecrated fire, the whole house made a ward. It has held for generations. Yet the lords of Blackwing are below still, and every year the seal is older.

IMPORTANT: Cultists of the Gravebound come to dig at the sealed ways, working rites with bound dead as labor and guard; they attack intruders on sight, their bound dead leading. The Shadow Inquisition breaks their workings whenever it finds them, so the cult can never dig in for long, and the fort stands empty and silent more often than not. Inquisitors met here are wary of armed strangers but not hostile, and have work for capable hands. Ward-marks, smashed diggings, and the wreckage of both sides' work lie through the ruin from years of this.

The riches of a great house remain in the black halls — plate, arms, and the instruments and treasures of the old traffic — untouched, because no robber in Drusavia will enter Blackwing.

The Charred Gates.description: The burned gatehouse and the bare ground before it: an open approach under the blackened walls of the fortress, the stones scorched.

The Black Courts.description: The fortress shell: courts and halls burned to black stone, roofless. Ward-chalk of different ages marks the doorways, and the floors show old diggings, some smashed, some re-sealed.

The Hollowhill Catacombs.name: The Hollowhill Catacombs
The Hollowhill Catacombs.basicInfo: The Hollowhill Catacombs are an ancient burial site cut into a wooded hill in the countryside. They were built to seal away the tainted dead defeated in the Liberation. To work the seal, rich grave-goods were laid to rest with them: silver, jewels, blessed arms, the wealth of the Lost Houses. Over the ages, as more and more dead were bound away here, the Catacombs grew upward and outward, until it became too easy for grave-robbers to dig their way in. Now the hillside is riddled with entrances, some collapsed, many open. Yet everyone in Drusavia knows the rule: take from the dead of Hollowhill, and the dead come to take it back.
The Hollowhill Catacombs.hiddenInfo:
The Catacombs were built downward first: after the Liberation, the victors sealed the vampire lords and necromancer-nobles of the Lost Houses at the hill's root, under the heaviest wards and the richest grave-goods, and each generation since dug new galleries above, cheaper and shallower, until the newest work broke through to cellars, badger-sets, and quarry-cuts all over the hill. No one has been buried here for a generation. The Shadow Inquisition hunts tamperers and puts down the risen, but cannot clear or destroy the site: unsealing or collapsing the vaults in numbers risks waking the hill entire.

IMPORTANT: The dead of Hollowhill lie quiet in their vaults, anchored by their grave-goods. Take from a vault and its owner rises within hours and hunts the taker. Because robbers work the hill constantly, risen dead are a common sight in the galleries, hunting whoever holds their goods and venting their rage on any they cross paths with. The risen do not speak, do not bargain, and do not stop. They are put down by destroying them outright. The oldest dead of the Old Work are the exception: nothing short of returning what was taken, or radiant destruction by capable hunters, ends them.

Plunder runs richer and danger worse with depth: modest silver and weak dead in the Shallows; funerary silver, marked jewels, coin-hoards, and blessed arms among the stronger dead of the Long Galleries; and in the Old Work, armory-grade grave-goods — blessed radiant arms, moonstone, regalia — sealed with the lords of the Lost Houses themselves.

Syndicate bravos work the Catacombs by night in small crews, prying vaults, sacking goods fast, and attacking anyone they run into. Deeper in, cultists of the Gravebound wake the purged dead deliberately, binding them as servitors. The cultists attack any they encounter on sight, their undead minions leading.

The Hollow Hillside.description: A great wooded hill honeycombed with tunnel mouths — some collapsed, some half-hidden by ivy and bramble, some worn open by regular use.

The Shallows.description: Rough-cut galleries just below the surface, where daylight falls through collapsed roofs and dug break-ins. New vault-stones stand in fresh mortar beside pried-open doors and rubble. Passages descend at every turn, and the newest wards, chalked and silvered, mark the interments of the last few years.

The Long Galleries.description: Vaulted corridors running beyond lamplight in every direction, tier over tier of sealed doors — some plain, some under defaced heraldry, some standing broken with dark rooms behind. The stonework changes style from gallery to gallery, generations of different hands. Side passages branch, double back, and dead-end without pattern.

The Old Work.description: Grand halls of flawless masonry at the hill's root, colder and drier than the levels above. Shrouded statues line a processional avenue toward great sealed vaults, each standing alone, each ringed by ward-lines cut deep into the floor. The doors here are unbroken.

Kolbeck.name: Kolbeck
Kolbeck.basicInfo: Kolbeck is a rich timber town at the edge of the Harrowwood, famous across Drusavia for grimwood: the blackened oak of the wood's great trees, which the risen dead cannot abide. Its carvers work grimwood into arrows, bows, staves, weapons, and charms, and their craft is on the town itself — bright painted townhouses bearing generations of carved figures, the housewains, that watch over every door and gable.
Kolbeck.hiddenInfo:
Kolbeck lives on the Harrowwood: timber, charcoal, and above all grimwood, cut only from the great Watch-Oaks that grow over the wood's staked plots. Ordinary timber is felled year-round; a Watch-Oak is felled rarely, under blessing, with an Inquisitor or a priest of Galard in attendance and hired steel guarding the party. The master-carvers are the town's aristocracy — proud, prosperous, loudly opinionated about each other's work, and feuding for years over whose housewain holds the best corner of the square. They sell finished goods to anyone, but harrow-stakes and blessed pieces only to Inquisitors, Temple folk, and hunters the guild has come to trust.

The townsfolk are woodsmen and carvers, well-off, hospitable, and matter-of-fact about the wood's dangers the way miners are about damp: there are rules, the rules work, and they are proud of their record. Felling crews hire guards for any work near staked ground, and every crew carries a stake-map. When a stake-line is found pulled or the dead are seen walking, it is reported at the White Rooster first, and the town sends word to the Shadow Inquisition in the city.

Oldwain Square.description: The market square, ringed by tall painted townhouses whose carved facades hold generations of housewain statues — hunters mid-draw, dancers, oxen, laughing woodsmen in blackened oak. Carved poles at the square's center carry the oldest wains in Kolbeck. Around the edges, the carvers' shop-fronts sell grimwood arrows and bolts by the sheaf, bows, staves, hafted weapons and bucklers, and carried charms for the road.

The White Rooster.description: The town's tavern, under a grimwood rooster carved mid-crow above the door — regulars touch its foot going in. A long common room with a great hearth, crew tables, and a slate of who is hiring and who is overdue.

The Mustering Ground.description: A broad yard at the wood-road end of town where parties bound for the Harrowwood form up: felling crews assembling at dawn, timber wagons loading for the capital, stacked gear, and a muster-board of posted contracts. The wood-road runs out between the last carved houses into the trees.

The Harrowwood.name: The Harrowwood
The Harrowwood.basicInfo: The Harrowwood is the great hill-forest around Kolbeck, worked for timber and charcoal along its edges and older and darker at its heart. Parts of the wood are cursed ground: burial plots where the dead rise if the earth is disturbed, each one staked and marked and left uncut. The oldest oaks in Drusavia — the Watch-Oaks — grow over those plots, and their grimwood is worth a fortune.
The Harrowwood.hiddenInfo:
The cursed plots are scattered through the wood, worst and largest in the deep stands. Each is ringed by a stake-line of grimwood harrow-stakes; the risen dead of a plot are put down by driving a stake through them into the earth of their own grave, and a harrowed plot sleeps until someone disturbs it — pulls the stakes, turns the earth, or buries something in it by the old rite. Nobody knows why the ground does this. The woodsfolk hold it was a battlefield before the duchy; the Temple-minded say a purged house's curse soaked the land; drunks say the purges themselves angered so many dead at once that the earth learned the habit.

IMPORTANT: Whatever is buried in a woken plot by a living hand rises within three nights, bound to the one who buried it. The risen are wrong — obedient, tireless, silent, and not the person they were. Unbound risen from a disturbed plot attack the living on sight. All risen dead flee sunlight and walk only by night or in deep shade; from cockcrow to dusk the wood is safe to work, and crews caught out at nightfall near a woken plot are in serious trouble.

By day the outer wood is busy: felling crews on the drag-roads, charcoal-burners at their mounds, hunters, and hired guards watching the stake-lines. The deep stands are another matter — the Watch-Oaks stand there, colossal and uncut, over the largest plots, and the best timber in the duchy grows exactly where nobody dares fell it.

Cultists of the Gravebound come into the deep stands by night to pull stakes and bury their dead, raising bound servitors. They work in small parties, post lookouts, and attack witnesses rather than leave them. Pulled stakes, fresh-turned earth, and grave-dirt tracks on the drag-roads are the signs they leave. When a waking is found, Kolbeck sends for the Shadow Inquisition, and the harrowing rite — priests or Inquisitors re-staking the plot grave by grave through one night, while everything still risen converges on the ritual — is how a waking ends.

The Working Wood.description: Broad drag-roads and open cuts through hill-forest: stacked timber, charcoal mounds, sawpits, and stake-lines of blackened grimwood posts marking the plots the roads bend around. Wagon tracks run back toward Kolbeck.

The Deep Stands.description: Old-growth forest under a closed canopy, dim at noon. The Watch-Oaks rise here, vast blackened trunks generations older than anything in the outer wood, standing over the largest stake-lines. Between them: overgrown plot-markers, weathered stakes, and here and there raw turned earth.

Rovena.name: Rovena
Rovena.basicInfo: Rovena is a rich brewing town in the vineyard dales of Drusavia, famous for its dark hill-wine and for brews that are proof against ghosts — for these beautiful dales are haunted, and the dead of a bad old time still rise at night among their tombs. Rovena is prosperous, handsome, and loud despite it: at sunset the hearth-bell rings from the Shrine of Galard, everyone gets behind a lit hearth, and the town goes on with its evening.
Rovena.hiddenInfo:
The burning of Rovena in the Liberation left the dales full of restless ghosts — the dead of those days, never honored, haunting the tombs, battle-graves, and burned places. The people of Rovena know all this and don't care to dwell on it. The ghosts are dangerous, they are a fact of life, and talk of them is practical or not at all: which one, where, who was taken, what it will take. The history behind them bores and tires the locals in equal measure.

IMPORTANT: The ghosts rise only at night and cannot abide sunlight. They cannot cross a threshold with a living hearth burning behind it — homes and halls with lit hearths are safe. Outside after dark, they attack the living on sight: beautiful, terrible figures in the dress of the old burning, mad with rage and grief, beyond speech or bargain. Their touch is chillfear, the killing cold terror; some victims die where they stand, and others are carried off to hidden tombs in the dales, imprisoned, and slowly drained. The taken can still be rescued while they last. Radiant weapons and balefire destroy the ghosts.

The town itself is young, loud, and alive: vintner and distiller families rich on the trade, harvest festivals, full halls every night, and an unspoken rule that nobody walks alone after the bell. The distillers sell hearth-cordial, which steadies the heart against chillfear, and balefire brandy, drunk by the shot or thrown by the flask to bloom in white flame. When ghosts take someone or a haunting turns bad, the town calls the Shadow Inquisition by the crow-perch at the shrine — and hunters who happen to be closer find eager customers.

Demijohn Square.description: The market square, crowded with stalls of bright glass demijohns in wicker: hill-wine, cordials, and balefire brandy, with carts rolling in from the estate breweries and vineyards on the slopes. Stone houses with deep cellars ring the square, and the terraced dales rise beyond the rooftops.

The Dead be Damned Tavern.description: Rovena's great wine-hall, built around the biggest hearth in the dales, candles on every table and barrels racked to the ceiling. Long tables, music, and room for every crew, wedding, and harvest gang in the valley.

The Shrine of Galard.description: A stone shrine with a tall belfry that rings the hearth-bell at sunset, heard across the whole valley. Its priests uphold Galard's old Proving-Year custom independently of either estranged order: they may give an aspirant the plain iron Road-Shield and recognize worthy deeds upon it. The shrine's stone is scarred where defacements have been chiseled and scrubbed away, more than once. In the yard stands an old iron crow-perch.

Castle Ondrave.name: Castle Ondrave
Castle Ondrave.basicInfo: Castle Ondrave is a great half-ruined estate in the haunted dales near Rovena. Most of it burned and was never rebuilt: a vast overgrown park, dead wings open to the sky, and the tombs of the household in the woods. One wing still lives. House Ondrave holds it yet — old blood, poor and proud, keeping a hearth that is said never to have gone out.
Castle Ondrave.hiddenInfo:
House Ondrave held its ground in the Liberation. The house fought, the house burned, and most of the house died. The family keeps the sound wing and keeps faith: the names remembered, rites kept at the tombs by daylight, and the great hearth of Ondrave Hall fed every night without fail — for while it burns, the hall is proof against the dead, and the family will not abandon its home. The Ondraves are poor, formal, and proud past their purse, and every generation sends its best to serve: there is an Ondrave sworn at the Black Tower and another in the Temple of Galard's halls. The old lord holds the estate with a small household and receives guests with threadbare grandeur.

IMPORTANT: The ghosts of the burned household rise at night in the park and at the tombs — figures of the old burning, mad with rage and grief, attacking the living on sight. Their touch is chillfear, which kills where it strikes or leaves victims to be carried off and drained in hidden tombs, where they can still be rescued. The ghosts cannot abide sunlight and cannot enter Ondrave Hall while its hearth burns. Radiant weapons and balefire destroy them. By day the grounds are safe to walk.

The Ondrave Woods.description: The estate's park gone to forest: the carriage drive lost under moss and root, burned shells of stables and folly-towers in the green, and garden statuary drowned in briar. Rows of household graves show through the trees on the old lawns.

Ondrave Hall.description: The one living wing of the great house: tall windows lit at dusk, worn splendor within, and a great hearth at the heart of the hall whose fire is banked but never dead.

The Old Tombs.description: The family crypt and the graves of the household, deep in the woods: a stone vault-front in the hillside, leaning headstones in ranks, and fresh offerings — flowers, bread, small candles burned to stubs — left by daylight hands.

Astarieth's Court.name: Astarieth's Court
Astarieth's Court.basicInfo: The western half of the drowned capital of the old Empyrean Empire, its towers, domes, and colonnades standing to their shoulders in the fen. This is Astarieth the Risen's own ground, and even her lizardfolk kingdom does not enter.
Astarieth's Court.hiddenInfo:
Astarieth keeps the city empty. Her kingdom holds it forbidden: no camps, no court, no pilgrims.

A handful of dragon-champions ward the deep districts — lizardfolk remade by her gift into drake-scaled warriors in gilded hoard-plate. A champion who spots intruders roars a challenge and comes on openly; a challenge anywhere in the deep districts brings the others.

IMPORTANT: the champions attack all intruders without parley. Astarieth sleeps within the Gilded Cathedral and wakes only when intruders enter it, bursting up from the flooded nave in black water. There is no sneaking past her in her own lair.

Champions fight with greatswords and poison-spit, charge through water, and die before her door.

Loot in the Sunken Palaces: imperial silver bars, gilded arms, jeweled temple-plate, and high-shelf strongboxes the water never reached. Loot in the Cathedral: coin-chests, crowns, regalia, gilded armor, jeweled vessels, reliquaries, and fine weapons heaped in the crowned statue's palms and lap.

The Broken Quarter.description: The eastern edge of the drowned city, where the water runs shallowest: wadeable avenues, walkable upper storeys, and whole blocks collapsed into rubble-islands.

The Avenue of Triumphs.description: The great processional artery running west through the city's heart — a drowned boulevard lined with triumphal arches and toppled colossal statues. The water is waist-deep, the sightlines run far, and there is nowhere to hide.

The Sunken Palaces.description: The deep districts: imperial halls, temple domes, and pillared courts in still black chest-deep water. Broken vault doors gape below; high walkways, window-ledges, and fallen beams offer dry routes for climbers.

The Gilded Cathedral.description: A white-stone cathedral with its dome split open and its flooded nave sheathed in gold leaf. In the apse, a crowned statue stands above the altar, palms and lap heaped with the hoard. The statue's dais is the only dry ground.

Vaudania.name: Vaudania
Vaudania.basicInfo: Vaudania is an old huntsman village deep in the western wood of Carendon, set where the worked land gives out and the wild wood begins. It is a proud, comfortable place that lives by the hunt — game and fur and the dangerous beasts — but it bars its doors after dark, for the wood beyond is werewolf country.
Vaudania.hiddenInfo:
Vaudania is a proud village of huntsfolk who have lived their whole lives at the edge of a wood that wants them dead, and have decided to be cheerful about it. They hunt the wood for game and fur, feud with the wolves that hunt them back, breed hounds against them, and make the best field-remedies in Carendon because a hunter who can't patch himself dies out here. They are warm to a fellow hunter and short with a soft outsider, full of boasts about the great boar and gallows-jokes about the cousin the wolves took back. The population is ordinary human wood-country folk; the wolves are out in the trees, not in the village.
Werewolves live in the deep wood. The curse is old and passes by bite, simply a fact of this stretch of the western wood. They take stock and travelers on the bad roads, and now and then a villager who went out too far or too late and did not come home. Whether the missing were eaten or became wolves themselves is the kind of thing nobody knows and Vaudania does not dwell on.
IMPORTANT: unless a story is already underway here, the village's default is ordinary life — the hunt, the kennels, the trade, drinking and boasting — with the danger out in the wood, not in the streets. Do not stage Vaudania as though a fresh killing or an active hunt is always happening.
The wolves answer to the Grey Mother, the first werewolf, a grey she-wolf the size of a horse who dens deep in the Wolvesholt Range. The villagers do not discuss her openly.

The Village.description: The village proper, arrived at where the last fields give way to the trees. A working huntsman's town: hound-runs loud with the breeder's pack, hides and trophies hung to cure, a bowyer at his bench turning out bows and arrows, and the apothecary's shopfront where the woodcraft salves and draughts are sold. The dark wood stands close past the last houses, and everyone keeps an eye on it. A hunter outfits here — a hound, good arrows, the oils and worts that keep you alive in the trees.

The Hound and Horn.description: The village tavern and its social heart, named by the huntsfolk and a point of some pride. The hunters hold court here of an evening — boasting over their kills, arguing whose hound is finest, trading the gossip of the wood — and it is where a newcomer finds work, a warm welcome if they've the look of a hunter, and people worth knowing.

Wolvesholt Range.name: Wolvesholt Range
Wolvesholt Range.basicInfo: The Wolvesholt is a long range of wooded hills in the west of Carendon, the deep heart of the duchy's wolf-country. Game is rich here and so is fur, but the wood is werewolf-haunted, and the beasts take stock, travelers, and the unwary off the bad roads.
Wolvesholt Range.hiddenInfo:
The Wolvesholt is the hunting ground at the heart of Carendon's curse — a steep, heavily wooded range west of the worked land, where dire wolves run the draws and werewolves den in the deep folds. The curse is old and passes by bite: the werewolves make wolves of those they wound and do not kill, and have for as long as anyone remembers. Hunters come here for the richest game and fur in the duchy and for the bounty on the beasts, and the careful ones treat every run as a hunt that could turn the other way.

The werewolves are cursed beasts — hungry, dangerous, and pitiable, no more evil than a starving wolf is evil. Some were villagers once; the cull is mercy as much as bounty, and the wood never empties: put one pack down and the curse makes more.

The standing local craft is ordinary: hunters, trackers, and the hounds bred against the wolves, working out of huts at the wood's edge rather than any garrison.

Deep in the high folds of the range dens the Grey Mother, the first werewolf of the Wolvesholt: a woman so long in wolf shape that she no longer takes any other, now a grey she-wolf the size of a horse. Every werewolf in the range carries her bite, or the bite of one she made.

IMPORTANT: the wolves and werewolves of the Wolvesholt default to hostile toward people caught in the wood, and hunt by preference at dusk and after dark and on the bad roads. By day, in the worked edges and near the hunters' huts, ordinary life holds — tracking, trapping, curing hides — and the danger is out in the trees.

The Woodsman's Hut.description: A hunter's hut at the foot of the range, where the cart-track ends and the trees begin — smoke from the chimney, hides curing on the rails, a run of lean hounds, and the wood standing close and dark past the last clearing. Whoever keeps it knows these hills better than anyone: what's been moving, where the packs are denning this season, which roads have gone bad. A hunter without a guide of their own can find one here, for coin or good company, and outfit for the trees.

The Wolvesholt Deep Wood.description: The range proper, climbing away from the worked land into close, steep, trackless forest. Game trails and kill-sign, draws where the dire wolves run, and the deep folds where the werewolves den and come down from at dusk. A hunter cuts sign, runs the beast down or sets where it will come, and gets out before dark.

Wolvesholt Heights.name: Wolvesholt Heights
Wolvesholt Heights.basicInfo: The Wolvesholt Heights are the high country above the Wolvesholt Range, crowned by the ruin of a great hunting estate abandoned long ago. No one lives here now but the Ferals — werewolves who took the curse willingly, and hold the heights as their own.
Wolvesholt Heights.hiddenInfo:
The Heights are the black heart of Carendon's wolf-country: the high reaches above the Wolvesholt Range, where a lordly hunting estate once stood and now lies in ruin, taken over by the Ferals. The Ferals chose to become what they are — they are men and women who went up to the heights to be made wolves, trading their humanity for the strength, the freedom, and the pleasure of the predator. They are cunning, organized, and proud.

The estate was a great house built for the hunt, a lord's seat for running game across the high country with hound and horn. The Ferals keep it as their den and their mockery: hunters who became the hunt, lairing in the bones of a place built to master the wild. They take the bitten and the willing, the desperate and the cruel, and turn them — so the pack refills no matter how often it is thinned. Their alpha holds the deep lodge and decides who is made and who is meat.

The Order of the Silver Sword and the duke of Carendon both send hunters up to the Heights to cull the Ferals, by writ and never by garrison. It is the worst work the Order takes in the duchy and the surest place to die. The Ferals revere the Grey Mother of the deep range and speak her name in their rites, though she is a beast and pays their rites no mind.

CRITICAL: the Ferals of the Heights default to hostile and do not parley. They are willing predators who hunt and kill by choice, and they treat any intruder as prey or as a recruit to be broken. There is no safe arrival here and no ordinary life.

The Overgrown Approach.description: The old carriage-road up to the estate, swallowed by the high wood — broken gateposts, a collapsed gatehouse, and the great hall rising ruined ahead through the trees. Hunters' marks and older bones lie among the roots.

The Ruined Hall.description: The shell of the great hunting hall, roof fallen and walls open to the sky, hung still with the rotted trophies and rusted weapons of the lord who built it. The marks of the pack's kills and their making are everywhere. From here the ways run down into the deep lodge below and out to the kennels.

The Deep Lodge.description: The lower levels of the estate, dug back into the hillside — the old cellars, the cold-rooms, the lord's deep chambers.

The Old Kennels.description: The estate's hound-yards, where a lord once kept the finest pack in Carendon for the chase.

Carendon.name: Carendon
Carendon.basicInfo: Carendon is the walled capital of the duchy that shares its name, a gracious and prosperous river-town set in the wooded hills at the heart of the realm. It is the seat of the duke and his court, an old city of stone bridges and fine houses grown wealthy on the trade of the wood, and behind its walls it has lived gracefully and safely for centuries while the wild presses close beyond them.
Carendon.hiddenInfo:
Carendon is the bright, comfortable heart of a wealthy wood-country duchy: a walled river-city of merchants, courtiers, and the duke's household, where the realm's coin is made and spent and the good life is on open display. The population is mixed and human-led, with the forest peoples of the duchy — elves, half-elves, half-orcs, beastfolk traders, and the dwarf smiths who arm the hunters — passing through its markets and quarters. The city is safe and gracious by long habit; its dangers are political and social, not monstrous, and the monstrous is kept where it belongs, out in the wood.

The duke rules from the Palace on Ducal Hill with a watch and a standing army for ordinary defense, but monsters are not the duchy's work. They belong to the Order of the Silver Sword, the brotherhood of hunters seated at Castle Harstone to the northeast, sworn to no duke and beholden to none.

The great houses keep their seats on Ducal Hill, the noble quarter above the town — among them House Harstone, the old family that gave its ancestral castle to the Order and still holds a voice at court. The houses do not deal with strangers; they deal with people who have made themselves worth dealing with.

The honest trade in monster-parts, silver and steel weapons, and hunters' gear is worked on Silver Row. The dishonest version — poached kills, restricted materials, the things the duke would control — happens outside the eastern wall at Houndsditch, the squat the gracious city prefers not to look at.

The River Market.description: The wide market on the Vaudenne, where a hunter arriving in the capital first sets foot — the busy, prosperous trade-floor of a wealthy town, loud with custom along the water. The stalls and shopfronts here include a weaponsmith with good steel and silver-edged blades, a bowyer turning out bows and well-fletched arrows, an armorer, and an apothecary stocked with the salves, antidotes, and draughts the trade runs on. Barges work the quays behind it all, carrying the duchy's timber and fur downriver.

The White Hart.description: The capital's finest old tavern and the social heart of the town, a warm and handsome house named for the duke's beast and proud of it. Hunters, travelers, and townsfolk drink and gather here of an evening — boasting of kills, trading the news and rumor of the duchy, and arguing the price of a good hound. By custom, the nobility of Ducal Hill drink here on hunt nights, and any rank may share a table. Guests who ask how to get involved with the great households can be directed to Dalia at the Palace on Ducal Hill. Tybalt may make an introduction, without requiring anyone to swear loyalty.

Silver Row.description: The street of the hunters' trade. The silversmiths work here, setting the radiant metal into blade and bolt and arrowhead for the things ordinary steel won't kill; the tanners and renderers buy what hunters drag back from the wood — hide and horn, claw and stranger trophies — and the alchemists turn the rest into spell and crafting ingredients and remedies. What can't be sold honestly here moves at Houndsditch instead.

The Wildward House.description: The Wildward House stands in Carendon's northwestern quarter, close to the roads leading into the western forests and the northern hills. The broad stone-and-timber adventurers' hall is built around a long common room, with upper chambers, secure stores, route maps, trophy beams, and an enclosed yard for training and mustering. An old League emblem remains worked into the stone above an inner doorway. Hunters, travelers, patrons, and crews gather at its tables before leaving the city or after returning.

Ducal Hill.name: Ducal Hill
Ducal Hill.basicInfo: Ducal Hill is the noble quarter of Carendon, the gracious height above the river-town where the duke's Palace stands and the great houses of the duchy keep their seats. It is a quiet, wealthy district of fine townhouses, walled gardens, and liveried servants, set apart from the trade and bustle below.
Ducal Hill.hiddenInfo:
Ducal Hill is where the duchy is governed and where its old families live when they are not on their country estates: the Palace at its crest, the great houses ranged below it, and the Coronet Club where they take their leisure. The watch here is attentive and the servants well-trained, and both can tell at a glance who belongs and who does not. No one is turned away at the gate — Ducal Hill is not hostile to outsiders — but a stranger receives courtesy and nothing more until they have given the quarter a reason to receive them.

The houses deal with people who have made themselves worth dealing with. The surest way into their regard is to solve the kind of problem a great house cannot solve for itself and would rather not make public: the beast in the woods of a country manor, the rival to be quietly embarrassed, the heir who rode out and did not come home, the matter that wants a discreet and capable outsider rather than the duke's soldiers. A hunter with a name and a kill behind them is exactly such an outsider, and a service well done is worth more on Ducal Hill than any letter of introduction.

House Harstone keeps its townhouse here, the old family that gave Castle Harstone to the Order of the Silver Sword an age ago and has lived on its name and its court connections since. They are proud, reduced, and well-informed, and they hold opinions about the brotherhood squatting in their ancestral seat. The duchy's own relationship with the Order runs through this quarter: the duke needs the Silverblades and cannot command them, consults their master like a peer, and keeps a court that includes both those who would see the Order brought to heel and those who know better than to try.

The Quarter.description: The streets of Ducal Hill, climbing from the gate toward the Palace — fine old townhouses behind low walls and iron gates, carriages and sedan-chairs, servants on errands who mark a stranger's face and weigh it. House Harstone's townhouse stands among the great seats here, its arms weathered above the door. A lime-tree lane descends to Linden House, a townhouse kept for grants of court service.

The Palace.description: The duke's seat at the height of Ducal Hill, a handsome old pile of halls and audience-rooms and the offices of the duchy. Petitioners and courtiers wait on the duke's business and the duchy's; commissions are given here to those the duke trusts or finds useful, and the politics of the realm are conducted in its corridors as much as its chambers. Reaching the duke's ear is a matter of standing, and standing is not freely given. The Duke of Carendon's herald, Dalia, receives visitors in the Palace's long gallery. Dalia hears requests in the long gallery. Ask her about matters before the court to hear two social matters and an adventure, or present a completed matter for recognition. No title is needed to ask. The Guest Wing provides hospitality to invited guests and the court's recognized knights.

The Coronet Club.description: The exclusive club of Ducal Hill, where the gentry and the well-connected take their leisure — dark wood, deep chairs, good wine, and fine attire, behind a door that opens to members and their guests. Reputations are made and unmade in its rooms, introductions are arranged, and a great deal of the duchy's real business is settled over cards and conversation. An outsider enters on a member's arm or not at all.

The Greenwood Lodge.description: A great timbered lodge at the edge of Ducal Hill where Carendon's nobility gathers between hunts, firelit and comfortable, with a few prized trophies above the hearths, long tables, deep chairs and a gallery for musicians. The houses come here to feast, play at cards and dice, wager on hounds and hawks, shoot at the butts in the yard, and trade the news of the wood. Strangers with a good story are welcome.

The Guest Wing.description: The Palace's guest wing has private bedrooms, a shared breakfast room and a little terrace above the gardens. Invited noble guests and recognized knights of Carendon's service may stay with their companions; others need a host's invitation. A frank young household officer keeps introductions easy and disputes about noisy visitors brief. Guests meet over breakfast, trade news, practice music and make plans for the day.

Houndsditch.name: Houndsditch
Houndsditch.basicInfo: Houndsditch is the old carcass-quarter outside Carendon's eastern wall, where the renderers, tanners, and knackers handle the messy end of the hunting trade that the gracious city won't have within its gates. It is a poor, hard-working district built along the offal-ditch that gives it its name, loud with the half-wild dogs that scavenge it.
Houndsditch.hiddenInfo:
Houndsditch is the unlovely back-end of the duchy's monster-economy: the place the carcasses go. Carendon will not have hide-yards and rendering-pots and gut-wagons inside its walls, so by old custom the whole filthy, necessary trade collected outside the east gate, along the drainage-ditch, and the people who work it have lived there for generations. It does work the duchy needs — and it is exactly why the Syndicate is here.

The black trade hides in the honest one. In a quarter where monster-carcasses come and go all day and a hundred hands handle hide and horn and bone, no one can tell an honest kill from a poached one — a pelt is a pelt once it is off the beast, and the wood is wide and no one watches who takes what in it. The Syndicate launders its goods through that flow: poached kills, the duke's deer and other ducal game of the duchy's forests, the parts and powders the duke keeps out of common hands, all moving out alongside the honest trade to buyers who don't ask. The watch knows the Syndicate works Houndsditch the way it knows crime sits in any poor and crowded place, but the trade is legal, the crime is real but unpinnable to any one carcass, and most in the city would rather take its cut and look away.

The population is the city's poorer and rougher sort — the renderers and tanners and their families, the desperate who take the work no one else will, and threaded among them the Syndicate's own: fences, fixers, and bravos. There are a fair number of failed and struck-off hunters here too, men and women who know the wood and the work and found the Syndicate pays better than the bounty. Houndsditch is dangerous in the ordinary way of a hard, lawless quarter — thieves, bravos, and old scores, not beasts. A visitor with coin, a name, or honest-enough business is dealt with civilly; a soft mark is robbed.

The Syndicate's operation in Houndsditch runs out of the Black Boar, and it answers to a single figure — the boss who holds the quarter's trade and takes a cut of every poached carcass that passes through it. A newcomer does not meet him. The fixer at the Black Boar hands out the work, the fence buys the goods, and a hunter who proves useful and discreet rises by degrees — tolerated, then trusted, then brought through to the back where the real business and the real money are.

The Ditch.description: The quarter proper, sprawled along the old drainage-ditch beneath Carendon's eastern wall — the hide-yards and rendering-sheds, the knackers' blocks and tanning-pits, carcasses coming in off the wood and hide and bone going out by cart. Scavenging dogs work the gutters and hard-faced tradesfolk work the blocks, and a buyer who knows who to ask can sell a carcass here that Silver Row would have questions about, or buy a pelt with no story attached.

The Black Boar.description: The one good room in Houndsditch and the haunt of its hard men — a low-beamed tavern of dark wood and banked fires, strong drink, dice and cards, and a long bar kept by a man who misses nothing. The renderers drink here and so do the Syndicate's people. The fixer keeps a table, work changes hands quietly over the cups, and a door at the back leads to rooms a visitor does not enter until they are asked.

Castle Harstone.name: Castle Harstone
Castle Harstone.basicInfo: Castle Harstone is a great old castle in the wooded hills northeast of Carendon, grand and proud and half-fallen to ruin, given an age ago to the Order of the Silver Sword and held by them since. It is the seat of the brotherhood of monster-hunters called the Silverblades.
Castle Harstone.hiddenInfo:
Castle Harstone is the home of the Order of the Silver Sword, the duchy's brotherhood of monster-hunters. It is a great house gone half to moss and ivy — a lordly old seat the Order has neither the coin nor the care to keep whole, its grand wings shut up and crumbling, the parts they use warm and lived-in and hung with the trophies of a hundred kills. The brotherhood is mixed and welcoming to the worthy of any people: human, elf, half-elf, half-orc, beastfolk trackers, weapon-users of every kind, spellcasters, and the dwarf armorers who set the silver. They are hunters sworn to no duke, beholden to none, taking contracts from anyone with a monster they cannot answer themselves.

The Order runs by memory, witness, and reputation. Hunters take work from the Muster board or from senior hunters, then ride out and do it. When they return, they tell the story in the Great Hall, show what they brought back, and answer questions from hunters who know the ground. There are no clerks, filing rooms, or forms in the Order. A hunter's standing comes from the people they bring home, the monsters they overcome, the proof they return with, and the trust of the brotherhood.

A newcomer accepted by the Order begins as an Initiate: a candidate under a Veteran Silverblade, not yet a full Silverblade. An Initiate carries no Order horn and receives no Order silver. They must complete one supervised trial hunt, making the decisions while the Veteran observes and bears witness. When the quarry has been decisively resolved, the Initiate returns to Castle Harstone, the hunt is recounted before the Great Hall, and the Veteran gives witness. If the Order judges them worthy and they swear the oath, they are sworn as a Silverblade, receive an Order horn from the Hornwall, and choose Order silver suited to their calling.

The ranks are Initiate, Silverblade, Veteran Silverblade, and Master of the Hunt. A Silverblade is a full sworn member who takes contracts in their own name. After four recognized Silverblade hunts, they may be judged for Veteran rank and trusted to lead hunts, supervise Initiates, and direct junior hunters. After five further recognized Veteran hunts, they may be judged for elevation to Master of the Hunt, one of the senior authorities who commission great hunts, assign hunters, and judge admissions and promotions.

The name Silverblade is traditional, not a restriction to swords or even to martial hunters. Full members carry radiant silver in the form their work requires: silvered spears, axes, bows, arrows, knives, hammers, or other weapons; silver-faced shields; and silver-bound magical focuses or implements through which a caster works aspected magic against unnatural quarry. The silver comes from Argenval and is worked by the Order's armorers and the smiths of Silver Row.

The Grandmaster of the Hunt holds the Grandmaster's Tower and gives the commissions too grave or strange for the common board. House Harstone, the old family that gave this castle away an age ago, keeps only a townhouse in the capital now and a voice at court. A younger daughter of the house turned the family's huntsmen into a brotherhood sworn to no duke, and when she inherited, she gave them the castle; the family has regretted the gift ever since.

The Great Hall.description: The heart of Castle Harstone, arrived at through the broken-grand courtyard — a vast old feasting-hall the Order has made its common room, warm with banked fires and loud with hunters at the long tables. The trophies of famous kills hang the length of the walls, skull and hide and stranger things, and the lean, scarred, dangerous folk beneath them are the brotherhood at its ease, drinking and arguing and trading the lore of the hunt. The grander wings of the castle stand shut and crumbling beyond the lived-in rooms. Along one wall hangs the Hornwall: the silver-chased horns of hunters who did not come home, each waiting to be given to a new Silverblade.

The Muster.description: The Order's muster room, where hunters gather to take work and prepare to ride. Contracts are posted here — bounties on the beasts of the wood, calls for help from villages and country manors, the standing cull-work in the Wolvesholt — and the quartermaster keeps the stores: silvered weapons and ammunition, silver-bound focuses and implements, silver-faced shields, oils, remedies, and the practical gear of a hunt.

The Trials Yard.description: The drill-yard within the old walls, where the Order makes hunters. Initiates train here under older hands in their own weapons or magic, the use of silver, beast-lore, tracking, fieldcraft, and the practical work of surviving unnatural quarry. Veterans train here too, and a candidate's measure is taken on this ground before a supervised trial hunt.

The Grandmaster's Tower.description: The old keep-tower the Grandmaster of the Hunt holds, above the common life of the hall. The grave commissions are given here — the contracts too strange or too dangerous for the open board, and the brotherhood's own business — and the Grandmaster's regard is the thing a rising hunter works toward. A newcomer does not enter here uninvited; a hunter with a name and kills behind them is sent for.

Argenval.name: Argenval
Argenval.basicInfo: Argenval is Carendon's silver-mining town in a high mountain valley. Miners, traders, hunters, families, dwarf delvers, and young makers fill its streets. The town supplies the silver used by Carendon's monster-hunters and keeps its own watch beneath the troll-haunted Crags.
Argenval.hiddenInfo:
Argenval is the source of Carendon's radiant silver and a close-knit, mixed working town of miners, smelters, smiths, haulers, shopkeepers, inn families, caravan hands, local hunters, visiting Silverblades, and dwarf delvers who have made the deep trade their own. Children race ore-cart ribbons down the safe slopes, families share courtyard ovens, and the town's favorite drink is blackberry-and-ginger miner's tea cut with strong spirits. Its favorite music is hammer rhythm, fiddle, and whatever a tired crew can sing badly after midnight.

The Deep Cup hosts the weekly Shift-Off: miners' crews challenge one another at stone-skipping, arm-wrestling, knife-dart, and improvised songs, while matchmakers, recruiters, traders, and information brokers work the room. The Lantern Steps below the miners' guild become a market and dance floor on feast nights, hung with blue-white lamps made from thin silver glass. The biggest celebration is the First Vein festival, when the first rich ore of the season is paraded through town, children receive sugared nuts, makers unveil stylish new tools and jewelry, and every crew claims its foreman is the reason Argenval prospers.

Local pride is warm but not gentle. Old mining families resent ducal officials and outsiders who take the silver's value downhill while calling Argenval backward; younger workers want fame, better pay, romances, and a chance to form crews of their own. Gossip travels through the Cup and the bathhouse: who is courting whom, whose mine claim is disputed, whether a missing lamp or tool was stolen by a trow, and whether the duke will send someone to ban the town's next custom.

IMPORTANT: Argenval proper is safe and ordinary by day and lively by night. The danger is up in the Crags and down in the Mine; the watch, walls, and terrain keep the trows and trolls out of the streets. The town still fears a cave-in, a bad shift, a lost child near the mine entrance, and the day the Crags stop staying above them.

The old troll tribute is now forbidden by the duke. Some families are furious that the duke outlawed the bargain without clearing the Crags; others are ashamed that their grandparents paid monsters at all; a few quietly believe an offering would save lives. Silver kills the unnatural beasts of the wood, while the Crags' trolls and trows are resistant to it, making Argenval's proudest export useless against its oldest enemy.

The mine remains the town's wealth and wound. The richest seams meet the trow-warren, so hunters can earn recurring cull contracts, miners can become heroes or disappear, smugglers can move high-grade silver through friendly crews, and makers can sell clever lamps, climbing gear, charms, weapons, jewelry, or fashionable protective workwear. Natural scenes include a crew recruitment duel, a festival theft, a missing shift-worker, a disputed mine claim, a court-versus-town argument, or a rescue in the mine.

Memorable locals include a glamorous young silver-smith who wants to design the next hunter's blade, a beloved Deep Cup singer who hears every secret, a mine-rescue captain building an independent crew, a ducal courier trying to look brave, and a sharp-tongued child who knows every safe shortcut.

The Town.description: The mountain road opens into Argenval's high valley, with slate roofs, ore-carts, family gardens, covered stalls, and a central fountain. Miners come off shift, traders call from the market, and children play in the square. The miners' guild and buildings around the mine entrance are visible from town.

The Deep Cup.description: A low tavern built around a black iron stove and a small stage. Shift crews eat pepper stew and honey bread here, hunters compare scars, traders bargain over ginger liquor, and the keeper's family serves gossip with every bowl. On Shift-Off nights the room fills with songs, dares, courtship, crew recruiting, and arguments between rival crews.

The Lantern Steps.description: A broad run of stone steps below the miners' guild, overlooking the valley road. Makers display silver-threaded gloves, tool-belts, charms, jewelry, climbing hooks, and hunter gear here; families gather on the ledges while musicians play. On feast nights it becomes a dance floor. On ordinary nights, visitors find guides, crews, deals, and gossip here.

The Silver Mine.name: The Silver Mine
The Silver Mine.basicInfo: The Silver Mine supports Argenval, its tunnels cut deep into the mountain at the head of the valley. Miners dig silver from the upper tunnels; the deepest veins reach caves where trows break through, making the richest silver the most dangerous to extract.
The Silver Mine.hiddenInfo:
The Silver Mine is the source of Carendon's silver and the place where trows from the mountain caves threaten Argenval’s miners. The upper and middle tunnels are busy mining passages, full of miners cutting the radiant ore the duchy's hunters depend on. The deepest tunnels, where the richest veins run, have been dug far enough to meet the natural caves that riddle the mountain — and through the broken seams the trows come: the small, vicious, swarming cave-kin of the trolls, lesser things of the same ugly house, that den and breed in the dark without number. Clearing them is endless work, because the warren up in the crags always fills what is emptied below, and it is the standing hunting-contract of the region — the everyday cull a working hunter takes again and again.

The trows are dangerous in the way of a pack of malicious, half-clever animals: cowardly alone, deadly in the swarm, fond of ambush in the dark and of dragging a lone miner off into the cracks where no rescue follows. They break into the deep seams through fissures too tight for a person to follow, so the mine cannot be cleared at the source from below; the warren proper is reached only by the crag-trails above the town, not through the mining tunnels.

The trows here are resistant to silver — the town's own metal does not bite them as it bites the beasts of the wood, because the warren has bred in silver-veined rock for so many generations that the metal has lost its bite on them.

IMPORTANT: the trows of the deep seams default to hostile and hunt by ambush in the dark.

The Mine Mouth.description: The entrance to the Silver Mine at the top of the valley. Sheds house the machinery that raises and lowers loads, ore-carts stand on rails, and miners come off shift beside the main shaft descending into the mountain.

The Workings.description: Lamplit tunnels supported by wooden beams, with ore-carts on rails and the sound of miners cutting silver from the rock. This is the safe end of the mine: busy and ordinary. Deeper tunnels lead toward the richest veins, where lamps grow fewer and miners do not go without hunters ahead of them.

The Deep Seams.description: The deepest tunnels, where the richest silver runs through the rock and the wooden supports end at natural caves. Trows squeeze through narrow cracks from the warren within the mountain. These openings are too tight for people to follow; the route into the warren is through the crags above.

The Argenval Crags.name: The Argenval Crags
The Argenval Crags.basicInfo: The Argenval Crags are the high broken cliffs above the silver-town, troll country since before Argenval was built. A maze of impassable rock and caves without number, it is where the trolls den and the trows breed.
The Argenval Crags.hiddenInfo:
The Crags are a maze of cliffs and caves above Argenval, home to the trows that invade its mine and the trolls that prey on its people. The trows breed in the caves below the trolls’ high dens. People reach the warren by the cliff paths; the cracks linking it to the mine are too narrow to follow.

The trows are the swarming cave-kin of the trolls, lesser things of the same house: cowardly alone, deadly in numbers, denning in the foul branching caves past counting. Above them, far fewer and far worse, are the trolls proper — and the old troll of the warren, the great ancient one the town's tributes were always meant for, lairing in the deep den with the hoard of generations: the livestock-bone and ore and grave-gear of every toll paid and every hunter who climbed this far and did not climb back down.
