For generations Argenval lived by leaving the trolls their toll, and the old tribute-shrine stands in the caves where the trails meet the warren — the place the town left its livestock and ore and, at the worst of it, more, before the duke forbade it.

The trolls and trows here are resistant to silver, because the warren has bred in silver-veined rock for so many generations that the metal has lost its bite on them.

CRITICAL: the trows and trolls of the Crags default to hostile and hunt by ambush. There is no safe ground here and no ordinary life — this is the warren's own country, climbing from bad to worse the higher it goes. The old troll does not parley as a reasoning creature would, but it is greedy and it remembers the toll.

The Crag-Trails.description: The climbing trails up into the broken cliffs above Argenval, where the worked land ends and the warren's country begins — steep bare rock, cave-mouths in the cliff-faces, and the bones and leavings of the warren scattered on the approaches. The way climbs on into the warren proper.

The Trow-Warren.description: The cave-maze of the warren, climbing back and up into the mountain — a foul, close tangle of trow-dens, bone-littered and stinking of the swarm, branching past counting. The ways run on to the old tribute-shrine and, higher still, to the trolls' country and the deep den.

The Old Shrine.description: The tribute-place, set where the trails meet the deep warren — a rough shrine of stacked stone and worn offering-niches, smoothed by generations of Argenval's tolls left here for the trolls above. Bones and rusted gear and the leavings of old tribute lie about it.

The Troll's Den.description: The deep lair of the old troll of the warren, high in the impassable crags where the caves run back into the dark — the great ancient one the town's tributes were always meant for, lairing among the hoard of generations: livestock-bone and stolen ore, and the gear and bones of every hunter who climbed this far and did not climb back down.

Drowner's Deep.name: Drowner's Deep
Drowner's Deep.basicInfo: Drowner's Deep is the great marsh in the low west of Carendon, where the river spreads into a maze of black water, reed, and sunken wood. It is named for the hostile aquatic species that lives in it. The fenfolk who cut peat and snare eels at its edges do not go far into the water, and the bad paths through it swallow travelers and livestock alike.
Drowner's Deep.hiddenInfo:
Drowner's Deep is Carendon's drowned country — a wide, slow marsh of black channels, reed-islands, and the rotted stumps of a wood the water took, where the duchy's western river loses itself. It is a different hunting-ground from the forest and the crags, and a different bestiary. The drowners are the lords of it: pale, clammy, drowned-looking things, man-shaped and worse, that lurk under the water and drag down whatever crosses the bad fords — they hunt in numbers and they are always here, breeding in the deep meres. With them in the water are the things a marsh holds: leeches and serpents grown large, a fen-hag in the deepest reeds for the worst of it, and the will-o'-wisps that lead the unwary off the path and into the meres where the drowners wait.

The fenfolk live at the dry edges — peat-cutters, eel-snarers, reed-folk — hard and insular and unsurprised by death, and they will guide a hunter who pays and warn one who doesn't. The marsh is worth the danger: it yields what a marsh yields, the reagents and rare growths of the deep fen, the things drowned travelers carried down, and the parts of the drowners themselves that the alchemists of Silver Row will buy. A hunter takes contracts here to clear a ford, recover a body or a cargo the marsh took, or put down whatever has been pulling people under that season.

IMPORTANT: the drowners and the other beasts of the deep marsh default to hostile and hunt by ambush from the water. The dry margins where the fenfolk work hold ordinary life; the danger is in the channels and the meres, and worsens the deeper into the water a hunter goes.

The Fen-Edge.description: The dry margin of the marsh, arrived at where the lowland road runs out into the reeds — peat-stacks and eel-traps, the fenfolk's stilt-huts on the firm ground, flat-bottomed boats drawn up, and the black water and reed-maze running away beyond. The fenfolk work here and watch the water.

The Black Water.description: The marsh proper — a maze of slow black channels, reed-islands, and drowned stumps, the bad fords and the deep meres where the drowners lurk. Wisp-lights drift over the water at dusk, and the way is easy to lose.

Harpy's Peak Ruins.name: Harpy's Peak Ruins
Harpy's Peak Ruins.basicInfo: Harpy's Peak is a ruined old fort on a crag above one of Carendon's forest roads, abandoned long ago and given over to the harpies that nest in its broken towers. They roost in the ruin and stoop on the road below, and travelers who must pass it go quickly and watch the sky.
Harpy's Peak Ruins.hiddenInfo:
Harpy's Peak Ruins is a fallen frontier fort on a rocky height over an old forest road — a crumbling keep of broken walls and roofless towers, abandoned in some long-forgotten trouble and never reclaimed, because the harpies took it. They nest in the high broken towers in a foul squabbling flock, line their roosts with the leavings of their kills, and stoop on whatever travels the road below — livestock, lone travelers, the careless. They are always here; thin the flock and it breeds back into the towers within a few seasons, so passing the Peak is a standing danger and clearing it a standing contract.

Harpies are vicious, cunning, and greedy for bright things, and their roosts are middens of generations of plunder — the coin and trinkets and gear of everyone they have dragged up to the towers, fouled and scattered among the nests. That hoard is the reason a hunter climbs the Peak beyond the bounty: the harpies themselves are worth nothing, but what they have stolen is worth the climb, if the flock can be put down. The old fort below the roosts holds its own leavings too — whatever the garrison left when it fell, picked over but not empty.

IMPORTANT: the harpies of the Peak default to hostile and attack from the air in numbers. There is no safe ground in the ruin while the flock roosts — they stoop and harry and drive intruders toward the drops.

The Broken Gate.description: The ruined gatehouse and shattered courtyard of the old fort, arrived at up the crag-path — fallen walls, a roofless hall, and the broken towers rising above. Old bones and the leavings of kills lie among the rubble. The ways run up into the towers.

The Roosts.description: The broken towers where the flock nests, open to the sky and fouled with generations of harpy plunder — the nests heaped with the coin, trinkets, and gear of everyone the harpies have carried up here, scattered among bone and filth. The flock attacks anything that climbs to them.

Reaver Road.name: Reaver Road
Reaver Road.basicInfo: Reaver Road is a long stretch of forest road in Carendon — the old maps give it another name, but no one uses it, because the road is reaver country. Outlaws hold the deep wood along it and prey on the timber-wagons, fur-trains, and travelers that must pass through. The duke's soldiers ride it and drive the bandits back, and the bandits crop up again, and so it has gone for years.
Reaver Road.hiddenInfo:
Reaver Road is the bad stretch of Carendon's road-network: a long run of the forest highway, deep in the wood between settlements, where outlaws have preyed on traffic for as long as anyone bothers to remember. The duchy's wealth travels these roads — timber and fur and the silver out of Argenval — and where rich cargo runs through deep cover, reavers gather. They hold camps back in the trees off the road, hit the wagon-trains and the lone traveler, and melt into the wood when soldiers come. The duke sends patrols and breaks the bands and hangs what they catch, and within a season new men have taken the camps, because the wood is wide, the cover is good, and there is always coin on the road and always the desperate to take it. The road is never clean and never quite lost.

The reavers are ordinary human trouble: outlaws, deserters, broken men, and the hard sort who find robbery pays better than honest work — some merely desperate, some genuinely cruel, and a quest can pitch a given band either way. They run from a leader who holds the road that season, take prisoners for ransom when the prisoner is worth it, and fence their take where they can. A hunter or a sword-for-hire takes work here from the duke's coin, from a merchant who has lost a train, or from a family whose traveler did not arrive: clear a camp, escort a cargo through, or bring back someone the road took.

IMPORTANT: the reavers of the road default to hostile toward travelers who cannot fight back, and prefer ambush from the cover of the wood. A strong, armed party they may shadow and let pass, or try to parley, or rush if the prize is worth it; a soft mark they take.

The Road.description: The forest highway through reaver country — a long wooded stretch of the duchy's road, deep cover crowding both sides, with the wrecks of looted wagons rotting in the ditches and the cover thick enough to hide a band a few yards off the verge.

The Reaver Camp.description: A reaver camp back in the trees off the road, wherever the band that holds the road this season has made it — a rough huddle of lean-tos and a fire, the loot of the latest takes, lookouts on the trails in, and the leader who runs it. The camps move and change hands as the duke's patrols break them and new men take the road, but there is always one.

Branton.name: Branton
Branton.basicInfo: A stone-walled hill-village in the northern foothills of Westmarch, a half-day's ride from Marrenford and the closest settlement to the orc lands. Sheep and goats on the thin hill-pastures, a smith, a hedge-healer, and a militia that drills on its own walls. Branton keeps a beacon on its watchtower that signals Marrenford when the border is threatened.
Branton.hiddenInfo:
The reeve runs Branton — elected, tough, and short on patience for outsiders who haven't proved useful. Pays honestly for border work.

Human-led, with a handful of half-orcs among the younger generation. The half-orcs are tolerated and watched — the village has buried family to orc reavers, and the distinction between the enemy's kin and the peace's children is one they make with their heads, not always their hearts.

Orc reavers stage from the Scarps, the broken crag-country an hour northwest. Ogres den in the same crags and sometimes run with the raider bands. The militia are better hill-fighters than the Westmarch Riders — they drill on the walls, know the terrain by feel, and have fought more actions than most professional soldiers.

Branton Yard.description: The open yard inside Branton's gate, packed dirt worn smooth. A smith's forge stands against the wall — working steel, not fine: heavy spearheads, crossbow bolts, frontier armor, and repair work. A hedge-healer's stall nearby sells poultices, herbal remedies, and hill-country antidotes. The reeve posts militia work on a board nailed to the hall's outer wall: patrol shifts, reaver-trail tracking, and bounties on orc raider bands spotted in the Scarps.

Branton Hall.description: The village's one hall — court, tavern, and feast-room in the same stone chamber. The reeve holds business at a table by the door in the morning. In the evening the militia drink after watch and shepherds come down from the hills. A veteran militia sergeant teaches ambush tactics, crag-country movement, and the hard arithmetic of defending a walled position with too few people.

The Beacon Wall.description: Branton's walls and watchtower, with the border beacon at the top. The walls are rough local stone, rebuilt so many times the older courses are a different color from the new. Militia stand watch in shifts and drill between — crossbow from the parapet, spear at the gate, and how to hold a wall with fewer than you need. They will train a willing volunteer. The view north from the tower shows the Scarps and the open hills beyond. On clear nights, Marrenford's lights are visible to the south.

The Scarps.name: The Scarps
The Scarps.basicInfo: Broken crag-country in the northern foothills above Branton, where limestone ridges shatter into ravines, scree slopes, and shallow caves. The Scarps are orc reaver territory — raider bands stage here before striking south into Westmarch. The Westmarch Riders and Branton's militia patrol the approaches but do not hold the ground.
The Scarps.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Scarps are hostile territory. Orc reavers use the crags as staging ground before raids on Branton, the hill-pastures and the valley settlements. They are not a permanent garrison — bands move through, camp for days or weeks, and leave. Every visit to the Scarps is different.

Orc reavers operate in small bands. They are experienced ambushers who know the terrain. They post lookouts on the high points, use ravines to channel pursuers into kill-zones, and withdraw deeper into the crags rather than fight losing battles in the open. They are raiders, not berserkers — they want to survive to spend the plunder. A cornered band fights hard; a band that can retreat will.

Ogres den in the deeper caves of the high crags, alone or in pairs. The reavers tolerate them as useful muscle and sometimes bribe them with meat and stolen ale to join a raid or guard a camp approach. An ogre den stinks before you see it.

Encounter variety for the narrator to draw from: a raider band returning from a raid, loaded with plunder. A scouting party watching Branton from the ridgeline, counting the militia. A cold camp, abandoned — they have already moved south, and the ashes tell you how recently. A wounded reaver left behind by his band, who will trade what he knows for his life or a clean death. An ogre asleep in its den with a reaver camp just below, using the ogre as an unwitting sentry. Two rival reaver bands in the same stretch of crags, avoiding each other badly — the player walks into the middle of it.

Loot: orc-forged weapons — heavy cleavers, brutal hand-axes, iron-shod spears, all rough-made but hard-hitting. War-gear stripped from the reavers' kills — Westmarch-made swords, shields with house-marks, a Rider's helmet. Coin and valuables from caravans. The crags themselves turn up old war-king era equipment — centuries-old steel and bronze weathering out of the scree where frontier battles were fought in the old wars. Occasionally something that does not belong in a reaver camp: a restored war-king era blade with blood-channels scored into the steel, or a ritual cutting-knife with fresh blood on the edge. These are Bloodsworn gear, traded for or stolen from the blood-cult crusaders who hold their rites at Wolfgar Keep.

Wolfgar Keep is visible from the highest points of the high crags on clear days, a dark ruin on a crag to the east. Reavers sometimes mention it as a place they avoid on the nights the Bloodsworn gather there.

The Lower Scarps.description: Broken foothills where the pastureland gives way to limestone ridges and scree. The trails narrow between ravines and the ground is loose underfoot. Reaver tracks, cold fire-pits, and stripped bones mark campsites used and abandoned. The approaches to Branton and the hill-pastures are visible below.

The High Crags.description: Deep crag-country: shattered ridgelines, overhangs, and cave mouths in the limestone. Orc reaver bands camp in the sheltered ravines and use the caves for stores and shelter. Ogres den in the deeper caves, their leavings piled at the mouths. The ground is bad for horses and good for ambush. On clear days Wolfgar Keep is visible to the east, dark against the skyline.

Wolfgar Keep.name: Wolfgar Keep
Wolfgar Keep.basicInfo: A ruined frontier fortress on a high crag in the contested hills north of the Greatwall. Wolfgar Keep was the war-kings' northernmost outpost, abandoned when the borders pulled back after the peace. Orc reavers shelter in the ruins between raids. The keep is visible from the Scarps and from the Greatwall's watchtowers.
Wolfgar Keep.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Wolfgar Keep may be hostile. Orc reavers and Bloodsworn crusaders, a human blood-cult out of Westmarch who cross into the Everwood to burn groves and hunt renegade elves, sometimes shelter in the yard and lower tower between raids, and treat intruders as enemies. The keep is not permanently garrisoned — bands come and go. A player may arrive to find it occupied, empty, or mid-arrival.

The keep was built by Wolfgar, a war-king of Westmarch, at the farthest reach of the old frontier. His name is carved over the gate in letters taller than a man's hand. The stonework is old, heavy, and built to be held by few — a square tower, a walled yard, and an undercroft dug into the crag. When the peace was made and the borders pulled back, it was abandoned.

Orc reavers sometimes use the yard and lower tower as shelter. Fire-blackened walls, stripped fittings, camp-trash, stolen goods stashed under canvas.

Bloodsworn crusaders sometimes also use Wolfgar Keep as a gathering-place for their rites. They come in small groups on nights they choose, rarely more than a dozen, and scatter before dawn. Between gatherings the keep holds no trace of them above ground. The undercroft may yield signs of their blood magic activity, including blades with blood-channels and dark stains on the stone.

Loot: orc-forged weapons and stolen Westmarch gear from the reaver camps in the yard. In the upper tower, old war-king era arms and armor. In the undercroft, the Bloodsworn leave their ritual tools between gatherings.

The Yard and Gate.description: The outer wall half-collapsed on the eastern side, the gate still standing with Wolfgar's name carved deep into the lintel. Inside, a trampled yard with the remains of orc reaver camps — fire-pits ringed with blackened stone, stolen goods under canvas, a horse-pen knocked together from salvaged timber. The outbuildings along the wall are roofless and used for storage. The keep's square tower rises from the northern end of the yard.

The Tower.description: A square stone tower, three stories, the top floor open to the sky where the roof collapsed. The ground floor shows signs of being used as a shelter — the marks of cook-fires, and the soot of many seasons on the walls. The upper floors are partially collapsed. The stair down to the undercroft is at the back of the ground floor.

The Undercroft.description: Stone cellar under the tower, the oldest part of the keep, dug into the crag itself. A stone slab at the center holds the remains of a recent fire.

Waldgate.name: Waldgate
Waldgate.basicInfo: A timber-built village on the western border of Westmarch where the farmland meets the Everwood, a few hours' ride west of Marrenford. Waldgate's woodcutters work the forest margin — old-growth Everwood timber, the best in the region. The buildings are master-joinery in heavy beams, carved lintels, craft passed down through generations. A timber-yard trades in lumber and Everwood bows. The ford across the river into Sanctuary Vale is a short walk from the village.
Waldgate.hiddenInfo:
Human-led, with half-elves common among the younger families — the ford brings marriages as well as trade. Wood elf rangers cross occasionally from Sanctuary Vale. The woodcutters are forest-competent and proud of it; they go armed into the margin every working day.

Elf renegades raid from the Deadfall Gulleys, a stretch of stream-cut ravines under heavy Everwood canopy a half-day into the forest, where old-growth deadfalls across the gullies make a natural maze. The renegades know the paths; outsiders climb over trunks and walk into arrows. They hit the village, the ford, and cutting crews to provoke conflict between the high elves and the March.

Owlbears nest on the forest margin where the cutting crews work — territorial and aggressive, the most common physical danger of the trade. Giant spiders web the deeper ravines toward the Deadfall Gulleys.

Dryads from the deep Everwood kill woodcutters and travelers who go too far under the canopy, and take young girls to raise as dryads of their own. The village has lost people for as long as anyone remembers. Everyone knows a name.

A Westmarch Ranger is posted at the ford and watches what crosses. Syndicate bravos move contraband through the river-crossing — goods out of Sanctuary's Underhalls — and the Ranger knows it and cannot stop all of it.

Waldgate Green.description: The commons inside Waldgate's palisade, ringed by carved-wood buildings. A master fletcher sells Everwood longbows and composites and teaches bowmanship — the best archery training in Westmarch. An enchantress works Everwood timber into staves, wands, and foci for spellcasters. A kennelmaster breeds and trains forest hounds for tracking under deep canopy — working animals a hunter can buy or bond. A board outside the reeve's house posts cutting-crew escort, deep-forest scouting, and bounties on elf renegade bands spotted near the village.

The Two Banks.description: Named for the view across the river toward Sanctuary Vale. Waldgate's inn, built around a common room with a long hearth. Woodcutters, half-elf traders, the occasional wood elf, and travelers crossing at the ford. Sanctuary Vale goods on the tables — forest herbs, dyes, elven leatherwork. The Westmarch Ranger posted at the ford drinks here and knows everyone who crosses.

Deadfall Gulleys.name: Deadfall Gulleys
Deadfall Gulleys.basicInfo: A stretch of stream-cut ravines under heavy Everwood canopy, a half-day west of Waldgate. Enormous deadfalls — old-growth trees toppled by age and storm — lie across the gulleys like walls, with dense regrowth threading through the gaps. Elf renegades use the Gulleys as a staging ground for raids on Waldgate, the ford, and Westmarch cutting crews.
Deadfall Gulleys.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Deadfall Gulleys are hostile. Elf renegades operate from camps hidden in the ravine maze and treat outsiders as enemies. They are guerrilla fighters, not a garrison — camps shift, trails change, and the maze is different every visit.

The renegades are elves who want Westmarch pushed back from the Everwood. They raid to provoke — hitting woodcutters, burning timber-yards, ambushing at the ford — so that Westmarch retaliates against the high elves, and the high elves withdraw the peace. They are skilled archers and forest-fighters who know every gully, root-bridge, and sight-line in the maze.

They fight at range and withdraw. They pin intruders in the gulleys with arrows from the deadfall tops, then fall back deeper where the ravines narrow and the footing worsens. They do not hold ground — they bleed pursuers and vanish. Chasing them deeper is what they want. A band that cannot withdraw will fight hard with short blades at close quarters in the ravine bottoms.

Giant spiders web the deeper gulleys where the canopy blocks all light. The renegades navigate around the webs or use them as barriers — a pursuing party that breaks through a renegade ambush may stumble directly into silk. The spiders are not allies of the renegades; they are terrain the renegades have learned to use.

Encounter variety for the narrator to draw from: a renegade scouting party watching the forest margin near Waldgate, marking cutting-crew routes. A recently used camp with cold fires and elven boot-prints leading deeper in. An ambush triggered by triplines of spider silk strung across a game trail. A woodcutter's crew pinned down behind a deadfall, taking arrows from above, needing rescue. A renegade wounded by a spider, willing to talk rather than die in the web. Two renegades arguing in Elvish over whether the next raid should hit the ford or a cutting crew — the player overhears a plan. A deadfall bridge across a deep gully, rigged to collapse under weight.

Loot: elven-made bows and arrows — lighter and better-crafted than anything in Waldgate's shop. Short fighting blades of elven steel. Cloaks and leathers worked for deep-forest movement. Renegade camp supplies, some of which bear marks from Sanctuary Vale — the renegades have supporters across the river who provision them. Spider silk in quantity, valuable to any enchantress or fletcher who knows how to work it. Occasionally a message-scroll in Elvish, carried between renegade bands, naming targets, dates, or contacts in Sanctuary Vale.

The Outer Gulleys.description: Where the forest floor breaks into shallow stream-cuts under thickening canopy. The deadfalls begin here — trunks broader than a cart blocking the ravines, root-plates standing vertical, regrowth filling every gap. Game trails thread through but the footing is treacherous.

The Deep Ravines.description: The heart of the maze. The gulleys narrow and deepen, the canopy closes overhead, and giant spider webs span the gaps between deadfalls. Renegade camps sit in hollows beneath root-plates and overhangs — cold fires, elven gear, sight-lines cleared in every direction. The air is still and dark.

Morcroft Hall.name: Morcroft Hall
Morcroft Hall.basicInfo: A stone manor-castle and small village in the southeastern farmlands of Westmarch, seat of House Morcroft. The Morcrofts are an old military family with the finest warhorses and heaviest cavalry in the region. Their household warriors drill in the yard daily and ride the southern roads in good order. House Morcroft has served the Corwins loyally for generations, though the two families agree on very little.
Morcroft Hall.hiddenInfo:
House Morcroft holds that the Corwins are sentimental stewards spending the region's wealth on an unfinished wall and grand feasts while the border bleeds. Their own estate is ready for a war nobody has declared.

Lord and Lady Morcroft receive visitors with formal hospitality and offer work — patrol escort, hunting, horse-breaking, and courier rides. Pay is good and often comes in gear rather than coin: a Morcroft-forged blade, a trained warhorse, riding armor from the estate's own smiths. The household warriors are a belonging ladder — ride with them, prove yourself, and earn a place at the duke's table and arms from the family's stocks.

The Morcrofts believe the peace with the orcs and elves is a temporary reprieve the Corwins are wasting. They advocate for finishing the Greatwall, garrisoning Wolfgar Keep, and pushing the border north to the old war-king lines. This position is popular among the southeastern gentry.

Some Morcroft household warriors ride with the Bloodsworn, the human blood-cult that burns the Everwood's groves, and the family quietly shelters them; in public the Morcrofts deny it and point to their unblemished military record.

The Training Yard.description: Warhorses in the paddocks, men-at-arms drilling with real steel, and a master smith forging cavalry arms and heavy armor. The stables breed the finest horses in Westmarch — big, sure-footed, trained for battle. The smith sells quality weapons, riding armor, lances, and warbows. A horse-master teaches horsemanship and mounted combat. The household warriors accept volunteers for patrol-rides.

Morcroft Hall.description: The great hall where the family holds court and dines with their warriors. Long tables, weapon-racks on the walls, old campaign banners from the war-kings' era. The lord or lady receives petitioners and guests here and offers work to those who impress.

Ancestral Hall.name: Ancestral Hall
Ancestral Hall.basicInfo: A long, low stone hall on the far shore of the Marrenmere, visible from Marrenford across the water. Ancestral Hall holds the arms and armor of Westmarch's war-dead, tended by a keeper of noble family. Warriors come to swear oaths before the dead, ask to carry a hero's weapon into battle, or have a blade blessed.
Ancestral Hall.hiddenInfo:
The hall is older than Castle Westvigil — some of the stonework is war-king era. The door faces the lake; you arrive by boat or by the shore-path and enter facing the northern hills where the war-kings fought. A stone hearth at the center is kept burning as a duty. The fire represents the living memory of the dead.

The walls carry real weapons of the honored dead — each set with a name-plate and a carved stone marker. The tradition is that a warrior may ask to hold a dead hero's weapon before battle. The keeper grants or refuses based on whether the asking is worthy. The weapons are old, named, and good — some are war-king era steel, Superior or Masterwork grade, with history attached.

Weapons held in the hearthfire and spoken over by the keeper carry a blessing against the undead for a time.

A stone dais at the far end of the hall is where vows are sworn to the fallen. A warrior who swears before the dead and keeps the oath earns standing in Westmarch.

The keeper is traditionally of a noble family, often a Morcroft. The role draws those with genuine devotion to the war-dead — and opinions about whether the peace honors their sacrifice.

Ancestral Hall.description: A long stone chamber lit by the hearthfire at its center. The walls carry the arms and armor of Westmarch's honored dead — swords, shields, spears, helmets, each hung with a name-plate and a stone marker beneath. Some of the weapons are centuries old. The keeper tends the fire and knows every name on the wall. He blesses weapons in the hearthfire for those riding against the dead, lends the heroes' arms to those he judges worthy, and swears oaths at the stone dais at the far end of the hall. He posts work on a board by the door: arms-recovery, body-escort, and grave-tending in the border country.

The Outer Ring.name: The Outer Ring
The Outer Ring.basicInfo: A ring of half-built structures and broken wall outside Sanctuary's walls, where the city once tried to grow outward and the wood took it back. What is left is a wide band of abandoned buildings, with the Everwood grown up through it, roots splitting floors, trees standing in roofless halls, creepers swallowing the stone a little more each year. No watch comes here and no wards hold here. People still go out into it, and some live in it, because past the wards a body can do what the city will not permit.
The Outer Ring.hiddenInfo:
No watch, no authority, no wards. The Syndicate is the heaviest presence but holds nothing whole - it is too large and too broken for that, and the edges are too dangerous to want. Independent fences, squatters, deserters, and people hiding from law or grudge keep their own corners. Everyone deals with the Syndicate or around them.

The Ring is where Sanctuary's stolen goods are fenced, where smugglers run cargo past the city's gates and tolls through the broken wall, and where a buyer finds what the watch would seize inside - poisons, restricted reagents, weapons taken off the sanctioned market. Deals are struck at the Unfinished House; harder business is done in back rooms and never spoken of.

Danger worsens outward, and so does the wood. The occupied core sells drink, deals, and beds to anyone with coin. The unfinished frames stand empty and half-overgrown, giant spiders webbing the upper floors. At the broken wall the Everwood comes straight in over the rubble, root and branch through every ruin and no wards to hold any of it - an owlbear holds the worst of the gaps. Name the danger as it is reached: cutpurses and enforcers in the core, spiders in the frames, the wood and what dens in it at the gaps.

The Dead Ring.description: The half-built streets of the failed circuit. The lived-in stretch nearest the wall is where the Ring does its business: a rough market of barrows and blanket-stalls selling what the city would seize, fences weighing goods in doorways, smugglers loading mule-trains for the gaps, and hard-eyed locals on every corner marking who comes and goes. Past the occupied blocks the streets run out into empty shells and deeper overgrowth.

The Unfinished House.description: The Outer Ring's one real establishment: a finished mansion of the failed district, meant for some family that never came, now tavern, doss-house, and dealing-floor at once. The great hall below is where the Ring drinks and bargains, every table its own quiet negotiation; the upper rooms are let by the night. It is the closest thing the Ring has to neutral ground, and to safe, which is not very. The Syndicate keeps a table here that is always theirs.

Yslaine's Demesne.name: Yslaine's Demesne
Yslaine's Demesne.basicInfo: A stretch of deep old forest west of Sanctuary, held by the dryad-queen Yslaine and her dryads, who let no outsider in. People do go missing near its edges - girls most of all - and the wood-wise will tell you to keep well clear of it. Those who have gone in past the treeline and come back out say the same thing: the forest itself turns you around, the paths fold back on each other, and you end up walking out the way you came, if you are lucky enough to come out at all.
Yslaine's Demesne.hiddenInfo:
The demesne is Yslaine's, and it cannot be entered by force or by stealth. The wood turns the intruder back: paths fold and loop to the edge he came from, thorn and deadfall wall the way deeper, and the deep wood is never reached by anyone simply walking into it. As he wanders, the dryads strike from cover - arrows out of the green, roots snaring the feet, magic that turns his own senses against him - until he leaves or dies. No one storms this place and no one talks his way in. The one exception is a young girl left at the edge: the dryads take her in and make her a dryad. A grown woman is killed at the threshold like any other intruder.

IMPORTANT: The demesne is hostile to every outsider and does not parley. The dryads attack from concealment; they do not show themselves to talk, negotiate, or warn, and they mean to drive off or kill. Treat the demesne as impassable - a place a visitor is turned back from, not one he passes through, clears, or reaches the heart of. Whatever draws someone here, the wood's answer is the same.

The Edgewood.description: Where the ordinary Everwood ends and the old wood begins. The trees here are vast - trunks wide as towers, crowns so high and dense the ground lies in green half-light. The undergrowth thickens into walls of thorn and bramble between the trunks, and deadfall lies heaped where great limbs have come down and never been cleared. Little grows low to the ground but moss and pale fungus, and there is no birdsong, no track, no sign of any path worn by foot or hoof. A fallen limb from these fey-grown trees can be witchwood.

The Eastwood.name: The Eastwood
The Eastwood.basicInfo: A broad eastern stretch of the Everwood, where the deep forest thins toward the open country of Westmarch - a wide frontier of old timber broken by clearings, brush-choked ridges, and stream-cut hollows, going on for miles.
The Eastwood.hiddenInfo:
The Eastwood is the front of a fight the high elves will not dirty their hands with. Human Bloodsworn crusaders cross from their bases in Westmarch to hunt the elf renegades who hide in this wood, and they do not much care what they burn to flush them out - groves, holdings, whatever stands between them and their quarry. The high elf Wardens avoid open war with the crusaders and leave these outsiders to Sanctuary and the Wildkeepers, who hold the Eastwood as best they can.

The crusaders are an active, moving presence, not a fixed force. They range the wood in war-parties, throw up camps and abandon them, and burn as they go, so the Eastwood is never the same wood twice: a fresh burn-scar, a war-band on the move, a camp pitched in a clearing for a few days and gone. They are not found in one fixed place - dealing with them means hunting for them, patrolling the wood, cutting their trail, scouting a camp, lying in wait.

The elf renegades the crusaders hunt are real, and shelter deeper in the Everwood; they raid Westmarch to provoke war, and every grove the Bloodsworn burn is proof to them that the outsiders must be driven out.

IMPORTANT: Human Bloodsworn crusaders default to hostile and attack others they find in the wood. They are blood-cult zealots who hold their crusade righteous, and they take any armed stranger for an enemy or an obstacle. The wood holds ordinary dangers besides - it is deep, broken country, and dire wolves run the hollows in packs while giant spiders web the old timber where the canopy grows thick. A careless traveler can come to grief here without any help from the crusaders.

The Open Wood.description: The lighter reaches of the Eastwood, open enough to ride through - stands of old timber spaced over fern and leaf-mould, clearings where the canopy breaks, and low ridgelines rising between stream-cut hollows. The wood closes in and darkens toward its depths. In places the ground is churned by the passage of men on the move.

The Wildkeeper Camp.description: A Wildkeeper forward camp pitched on a defensible rise - a ring of lean-tos and a longhouse of green logs behind a low palisade, with a watch-platform up in the crown of an old oak. This is where those who hunt the crusaders rest, treat their wounds, and trade word of where the Bloodsworn struck last and which way the war-bands moved. Wildkeepers hold it, but they are not the only ones who shelter here - rangers, hunters, and others with cause to fight the crusaders come and go.

The Deep Wood.description: The depths of the Eastwood, where the timber stands close and old and the going turns hard - brush-choked ground, deadfall, ridges and hollows that swallow sound and sightline. Giant spiders web the old timber where the canopy grows thickest.

The Riddlewood.name: The Riddlewood
The Riddlewood.basicInfo: A stretch of hilly Everwood riddled with caves and hollows, the slopes broken by limestone outcrops and the dark mouths of old sinkholes and worn-out dens. Renegade elves hold it, and a rough host of outsider bandits and cutthroats shelters among them - raiding the forest roads, robbing travelers, and falling back into the caves where no one comes to dig them out.
The Riddlewood.hiddenInfo:
The Riddlewood is a robbers' haven, and it is one because the high elf Wardens hold back from it. The renegade elves who hold the wood have taken in every brigand, deserter, and cutthroat who will fight for a roof and a share, and to come in after them the Wardens would have to kill those outsiders by the score - which they will not do. So the wood is left to Sanctuary and whoever Sanctuary will send, and the renegades and their hired scum range out of it as they please.

The renegade elves are the core and the cause: they want the outsiders driven from the Everwood for good, and they raid Westmarch, the human region to the east, to push the high elves and the humans toward the war they want. But most of the host is not ideological at all - they are bandits, in it for plunder, drawn by a safe base no authority will raid. The two suit each other. The renegades get numbers and a shield of outsider bodies; the robbers get protection, a launching point, and caves to vanish into. The host grows as word spreads that the Riddlewood pays and the law does not come.

They stage their raids from camps in the wood and warrens in the caves, strike the forest roads and the lonelier holdings, and carry the take back into the hills. Breaking them means going in after them - clearing the camps, hunting them through the caves, cutting the raids before they ride.

IMPORTANT: The renegade elves and their bandit host default to hostile. They are raiders and killers who take any stranger in the wood for a mark, a threat, or a recruit worth pressing, and they fight to rob, drive off, or kill. The cave country is dangerous in its own right - sinkholes, dark warrens, and the things that den in deep cave-dark away from the light.

The Broken Slopes.description: Hilly forest where the ground rucks up into limestone ridges and outcrops, the trees thinning over bare grey stone. Cave-mouths and sinkholes pock the slopes, some no wider than a badger's hole, some big enough to walk into and lose the daylight. Game-trails and harder-worn paths wind between the rocks.

The Warrens.description: A cave-system in the heart of the slopes, worked over by long use into something between a den and a strongroom - mouths worn smooth, soot black on the rock above old fire-scars, hide-scraps and rope and refuse trodden into the floor. The passages open into chambers off the dark, the larger ones bearing the marks of being lived in and fought over. Deeper galleries run back beyond where the smoke-stain reaches, into rock left alone.

The Deep Hollows.description: Where the caves run down past any den into true dark - cold passages, drip-water, and galleries going down.

The Sundwen Mire.name: The Sundwen Mire
The Sundwen Mire.basicInfo: A drowned stretch of the Everwood in the region's low country - black water, reed-islands, and trees standing to their knees in the murk. The Sisterhood of the Hunt hold it: a band of women warriors most reckon plain bandits, who rob and kill travelers in the mire - men worst of all - take in women who run to them, and believe they serve the dryad-queen Yslaine by carrying girls to the edge of her wood.
The Sundwen Mire.hiddenInfo:
The Sisterhood of the Hunt believe they serve the cause of the dryad-queen Yslaine. Yet her dryads have never accepted that service - they refuse to speak with the Sisters and attack them when approached, the same as any other outsider. So the Sisters further the queen's cause as they can from the mire, hunting those who despoil the wood.

The Sisters have seen that a girl left at the edge of Yslaine's demesne is taken in and made a dryad, and they hold it the surest service they can render the queen. So they take girls, willing or seized from the wood's edge and the roads, and carry them to the threshold. The new dryads attack the Sisters on sight like all the rest; it has not stopped them.

Women go missing into the Sundwen two ways: some girls are seized for the offering, and some women run to the Sisters and are not given back.

IMPORTANT: The Sisterhood default to hostile toward men and toward any outsider they judge a despoiler of the wood, and toward most travelers as marks to rob or kill. They strike from the water and reeds with bow and spear and mean to kill or drive off. The mire itself is bad ground: deep water, sucking mud, and the things that live in a drowned wood.

The Black Water.description: The open mire, where the Everwood stands drowned - trees rooted in slow black water, reed-banks and islands of higher ground between them, and channels winding off in every direction under a low canopy. The footing is water, mud, and the odd causeway of fallen timber and trodden reed. Old sign marks the through-ways: a swamped cart sunk to its bed, a campsite picked clean.

The Sisters' Hold.description: The Sisterhood's seat, raised out of the water on stilts and on the larger islands - longhouses of reed-thatch and bound timber, drying-racks and drawn-up boats, walkways of planking strung between the trees above the murk. Smoke stands over it, and the spoils of the mire are kept here: penned and stored goods, and what the Sisters take off the people they catch in the Sundwen.

The Cold Iron Caverns.name: The Cold Iron Caverns
The Cold Iron Caverns.basicInfo: A cave-riddled hillside in the Everwood beyond Sanctuary's walls, the one place cold iron is found. The grey ore lies in veins threaded through the deep stone where the roots of the Everwood reach down into it, and those after it go in armed and in company, because the caverns are full of things that kill.
The Cold Iron Caverns.hiddenInfo:
Cold iron is forest iron from veins the Everwood's roots have grown down through, found nowhere but here. It must be mined and worked cold, never touched by forge-fire, or the wild burns out of it and it is only iron. Worked cold, its edge bites the fey and the magical as plain steel cannot. The diggers haul the rough ore back to Sanctuary, where the Underhalls smiths hammer it cold into blades and heads.

The ore is not lying about to be gathered. Finding it means searching the worked faces and the root-veins deeper in, and the caverns do not give that time freely - the monsters come while a digger looks. A spell of searching, through a fight or two, turns up a modest amount of ore and no more; no one walks out of the Cold Iron Caverns with a hoard. That is why cold iron is dear, and why the diggers go armed and pay for blades.

IMPORTANT: The caverns are infested and hostile. Pressing into them and moving deeper draws what lives in the dark. The threats are ankhegs that tunnel through the root-and-earth and burst up through a gallery floor; stirges that come off the cave roof; darkmantles that drop from the root-choked ceiling; and gricks that lie still as dead root in the wall-crevices until something passes.

The Entrance Cave.description: The wide cave-mouth where the diggers gather before going in - daylight reaching back over a floor of trodden stone, a few fires, gear and tools stowed against the walls, and the diggers and their hired guards resting, dividing the day's ore, or working up the nerve for another spell in the dark. Armed men watch the deeper passages. Two ways lead on: down into the worked galleries where the cold iron is cut, and off along a dark tunnel that runs toward Sanctuary's Underhalls.

The Workings.description: The cut galleries where the cold iron is dug - stone laced through with the pale roots of the Everwood reaching down from above. Pick-marks and abandoned tools mark the worked faces, and the passages run deeper into unworked dark where the roots grow thicker and the water drips. The ground is broken in places where something has come up through it.

The Underhalls Tunnel.description: A long passage running underground from the caverns toward Sanctuary's Underhalls, old and rough-walled, the roots thinning as it leaves the wood behind and the stone closing in. It is the way the dwarves come and go between the city and the diggings. Nothing tends it and nothing keeps it lit, and what dens in the caverns ranges through it.

Terlothis.name: Terlothis
Terlothis.basicInfo: A ruined elven fortress deep in the Everwood, broken and abandoned since the Kindred War and left well alone ever since. Its walls still stand among the trees that have grown up through them, but the dead hold it now. The wood-wise know it by name and give it a wide berth.
Terlothis.hiddenInfo:
Terlothis was a high-elven war-fortress, and it fell in the Kindred War an age ago. The garrison died here, and the dead never left: the ruin is held by restless elven dead who fall on anything living that comes within the walls. They cannot be cleared for good - cut them down and they rise again where they fell, the same as they have for an age - which is why the fortress still stands unclaimed and why even the high elves leave it be. It is more trouble than any treasure in it is worth.

The sealed door beneath the keep closes an old war-tunnel down into the Rootdark. The garrison shut it from above in the last days of the war and died holding the line in front of it, and under the Sundering it must stay shut: opening it would open a road into the dark elves' realm, and both kindreds would call that war. The dead are thickest and worst the deeper one goes. Let the place tell its own story: the sealed door, the dead fallen at their posts as if still holding a line, the elven war-carvings worn under moss.

IMPORTANT: The dead of Terlothis default to hostile and attack the living on sight within the walls. They do not parley, do not speak, and do not relent - they strike to kill.

The Broken Keep.description: The shell of the old fortress, its curtain walls breached and its towers fallen, the Everwood grown up through the courtyards and great halls until root and branch hold the stone together as much as mortar does. Fallen elven dead lie where they dropped an age ago, armor and bone gone green under the moss, some still at the arrow-slits and gatehouse as if the assault never ended. A way leads down beneath the keep, into the dark below.

The Underkeep.description: The vaults and lower halls beneath the fortress, unlit and unfallen where the keep above is open to the sky. The elven dead lie thickest here, and the deeper passages run toward a great sealed door of elven work, barred and warded from the outside and never since opened. Old carvings cover the walls about it, worn but not gone.

Maanvalta.name: Maanvalta
Maanvalta.basicInfo: Maanvalta, the great cavern-city of the dark elves and the capital of their realm beneath the Elfwood. It stands at the center of a tunnel-network that runs under the whole forest and far beyond, built into the stalactites and stalagmites around World-root and the underground lake at its foot, all of it lit by the amber-to-violet glow of the Root-sky. Under the terms of the Sundering the dark elves keep off the surface, but they do not turn surfacers away from the deep — and many make the journey, because dark-elf illusion, craft, and the goods of the deep earth are found nowhere else.
Maanvalta.hiddenInfo:
The dark elves were driven below after the Kindred War, the Sundering holds them there, and they have spent an age making their exile glorious. Forbidden from the surface of Elfwood except at Ilunethel, they built tunnel-roads that reach under half of Larion and emerge beyond the high elves' realm, carrying dark-elf trade, agents, and influence into the wider world. They are the finest illusionists in Larion and its most accomplished thieves and assassins, and they prize wit, craft, and style the way other peoples prize virtue — being dull is worse than being wrong.

Competing noble houses run the city's trade and its intrigues, and they court surfacers constantly as agents, partners, and useful fools. A clever visitor can make a fortune here; a careless one finds an early grave. The dark elves are charming, decadent, and hospitable, but charm and the knife are the same hand here, and a guest is rarely sure which he is being offered.

Maanvalta is the hub of the soulstone trade. Its tunnel-network gives it perfect reach into the surface regions where soulstones are banned, and the houses move them at enormous profit along the deep roads no surface power can watch.

The Unseen, the cross-house brotherhood of spies and assassins seated at the Needle, answer the high elves of Vigil Gorge blow for blow: where the Legion of the Vigil raids the dark elves' tunnels in secret, the Unseen retaliate below the line, and the slow war neither capital will admit to is fought hardest in the dark between them.

The Ledgeways.description: A series of carved stone ledges high along the cavern's upper wall, where tunnels open from every direction and paths wind down toward the lake far below. From these ledges the whole city reveals itself at once: the huge World-root piercing the cavern ceiling and descending into the underground lake at its heart, the Root-sky glowing amber to violet overhead, and the stalactites and stalagmites — crowded with carved structures and strung together by bridges — climbing from the dark water. Dark-elf wardens watch the stairhead and mark every surfacer who comes down.

The Lakeshore.description: The waterfront that rings the great underground lake called the World-spring, where the business of the city happens. Markets spread along the shore — dark-elf craftwork in carved stone and deep-wood, glowing fungi, deep-earth spices, and the pale metals and gems of the under-earth. Boats load and unload at stone quays. Dark elves and surfacers throng the shore, trading, arguing, and eating at the stalls.

The Still Isle.description: An island in the underground lake reached by boat. On it rises a monastery of dark stone where a dark-elf monastic order known as the Still Ones study shadow magic, illusion, and the arts of concealment.

The Needle.description: A thin stalactite high above the lake, reached by a single bridge. Home to the Unseen, the cross-house brotherhood of spies and assassins who guard the dark elves' interests above and below. Their apothecaries are famous for poisons that leave no trace.

The Kettle.description: A deep hollow in the cavern floor where hot springs bubble up from below, filling the air with mineral steam. Serpentfolk, deep gnomes, and other underground peoples have settled here, a neighborhood that runs by its own customs. The steam makes it hard to see far, which suits the residents fine.

The Hang-Over Inn.description: An inn and tavern in a hollow stalactite over the Lakeshore, opened up with arched windows that look out across the underground lake. The best tavern in the city, or at least the one where surfacers are most likely to end up. House agents drink here alongside merchants, off-duty soldiers, and ordinary dark elves.

World-root.description: The great root-column at the city's heart, wide as a castle. The dark-elf court meets in chambers grown within the living wood. Temples occupy the deepest hollows where the roots meet the water. Bridges and stairways spiral up through the tangle, crowded with petitioners, courtiers, and priests.

The Stoneways.description: Where most dark elves live. Stalactites and stalagmites carved into dense warrens of apartments, workshops, and local markets, connected by stone bridges at every level. Some columns are wealthy house compounds behind carved gates. Others are packed neighborhoods where laundry hangs from bridge-rails and arguments carry across the gaps.

The Stonetome.description: A great hollow stalactite carved into a walkable history of the dark-elf people. Visitors enter at the top, where dioramas cut from living stone begin with the one elven kingdom whole. The path spirals down through the Kindred War, the high elves' Betrayal, and the Sundering that sealed the dark elves below. At the bottom comes the Exodus, the dark elves descending into the earth, and then the passage opens onto the Lakeshore and the glittering city they built to prove the surface wrong.

The Dims.description: Where the stalactites and stalagmites grow so dense the root-light barely reaches. A maze of narrow bridges, tight passages, and carved-out chambers stacked on top of each other. Dark elves who've lost house patronage end up here, and so do the trades the city prefers not to acknowledge — fences, forgers, brokers of dark magic.

The Farwall.description: The cavern's far reaches, where dark-elf soldiers garrison the tunnels leading deeper underground. They keep the gates on the deep tunnel-roads and stop every traveler who comes up them.

Ilunethel.name: Ilunethel
Ilunethel.basicInfo: Ilunethel is a rough, thriving trade-town in the overgrown ruins of a fallen elven city destroyed in the Kindred War, built around the only open way between the surface and the dark-elf realm below. By the terms of the Sundering, it is the one place the dark elves are allowed to walk the surface, and the one place on this whole stretch of the Elfwood where the high elves' law does not reach. The deep's goods are sold in the open, coin buys passage down the stair, and a bold outsider can make a fortune here running the dark elves' business above ground — if the work, or the town, doesn't get them killed first.
Ilunethel.hiddenInfo:
The dark elves were driven below after the Kindred War, and Ilunethel is the single place the high elves suffer them above ground. A dark elf caught on the surface within Elfwood, beyond the town's bounds, is killed. The High Wardens watch the edges and will not set foot within, though they are known to spy on the goings-on here through non-elven agents. Still, everyone in Ilunethel knows the Wardens cannot touch them here as long as they do nothing obviously illegal, and the town has the swagger of it.

It is run by its merchant houses, dark-elf and surface both, who answer to no one and settle their differences themselves, sometimes through open violence. The open trade is real enough — deep-earth spell ingredients, dark elf spells, carved stone and deepwood, dark elf weapons and armor, the metals and gems of the under-earth. The dark elves' other craft is sold more discreetly: false faces, illusion magic, and disguise-work a spy or a thief would kill for.

The dark elves cannot leave the city, so the houses hire surfacers to do their work above ground, and they are always hiring. Most of that hiring happens over a drink at the Queen of Ales, where house factors and Syndicate fixers work the tables. The jobs run the whole range and the pay runs with them. At the honest end: take this crate to Canopy, collect a debt, carry a message. At the far end the work turns to theft, smuggling, and worse — move a person out of the trees who does not want to go, see that someone stops being a problem.

The Syndicate holds the other half of the trade. Where the houses are the clients, the Syndicate moves the stolen, the smuggled, and the taken across the surface the dark elves cannot cross, fences what comes up the stair, and runs the routes that link Ilunethel to its buyers across Larion.

The Root Arch at the town's heart is the open stair down to Maanvalta, the dark-elf city below. Lawful trade moves in the open and pays its way, so only the soulstone trade (gems with a soul trapped inside, banned across Larion's surface) and the darkest goods have to move hidden in the honest flow. Nethel, the old city's picked-clean ruins, is an overgrown sprawl of roofless marble halls where the poor and the unwelcome squat, where the Syndicate brokers the work nobody wants brokered in daylight.

The Undermarket.description: The great lit terrace at the town's heart, the rebuilt tiers of the old elven city climbing above it. Stalls and stone-fronted shops crowd the terrace, the goods of the deep laid out in the open: spell ingredients and dark vintages, carved stone and deepwood, worked weapons and armor, the pale metals and gems of the under-earth. It is loud, crowded, and mixed - dark elves and outsiders of every kind, haggling in the open and watching each other over the tables.

The Queen of Ales.description: A tavern in the one wing of the old palace still standing - the queen's quarters, by the worn carvings, though the rest is rubble and green overgrowth on every side. The great chamber has been made over into a drinking hall: a long bar built along one wall, tables and benches crowded across the old stone floor, a fire in a hearth meant for grander things.

The Root Arch.description: At the town's heart the roots of a great tree have been shaped into a vast arch over an open stair going down into the dark. It has no door and no guard, and its lamps are kept always burning. Laden porters, dark elves, and the bold come and go on the steps between the surface and the city below.

Nethel.description: Past the reclaimed tiers, the old city lies overgrown and picked clean - broken marble halls open to the sky, columns toppled and grown through with the forest, washing strung between them and cookfires burning in rooms with no roofs. The narrow ways run crooked between the ruins.

Carrion Spire.name: Carrion Spire
Carrion Spire.basicInfo: A broken elven tower standing high above the canopy, half-fallen and open to the sky. Harpies nest in its heights, and the roost is famous for what they have stripped from the dead over the years: worked elven blades, silver ornaments, and old enchanted arms gone green with age, richer pickings than any common nest holds.
Carrion Spire.hiddenInfo:
The harpies of the Carrion Spire are hostile and do not bargain.

They hunt by lure and ambush. They mimic the high-elven singing that once filled these ruins to draw climbers up the open stairs, then drop from above in a screaming mob, raking and trying to knock prey off the ledges into the long fall. They fight as a flock, never singly, and press hardest when they have height and numbers. Hurt them badly or kill two or three and the rest break off, wheel out of reach, and wait for a better moment rather than dying for the nest.

The loot sits at the top, in the roost-midden: generations of stripped kills, and because some of those kills were elves with good gear, the better pickings - worked elven arms, silver, the odd enchanted blade - lie mixed in among the bones and the cheap leavings.

The Broken Stair.description: An open elven stair spiralling the outside of the ruined spire, the treads cracked and gapped, the canopy falling away far below. The stone is old and worked, the wind constant, and there is no rail where the rail has fallen. The way up is exposed the whole climb.

The Roost.description: The spire's broken crown, open to the wind, its ledges and fallen chambers crusted with old nests. Bones and stripped gear litter the floors. Among the common leavings lie older, finer things.

Windreach.name: Windreach
Windreach.basicInfo: A high crag breaking through the canopy at the forest's edge with griffons and hippogriffs nesting in its cliffs. The eyries are strung with what the beasts drag home - gear and ornaments off fallen travelers and riders, and now and then something fine a griffon took a liking to - and a broken griffon is among the best mounts in Larion. The bold climb for the plunder, or for the prize of a mount, if they can take one and live.
Windreach.hiddenInfo:
The griffons and hippogriffs of Windreach are hostile and defend their nests savagely.

They open by stooping from above, hard and fast, and try to drive climbers off the ledges before closing to beak and claw. Griffons are the fiercer and fight to hold the nest; hippogriffs are a shade less aggressive and more likely to break off if badly hurt. A beast guarding eggs or young will not retreat at all, and the rest of the crag answers a screaming nest-mate.

The plunder is in the eyries - griffon nests higher and richer, hippogriff lower and leaner - strung among bones and feathers, with the better gear in the high griffon nests. Eggs and eyasses are there too, for the reckless.

The Lower Ledges.description: Wide cliff ledges reached by a hard scramble, crusted with old nests, the canopy a green floor far below and the wind hard and cold. The nests here hold bones, feathers, and stripped leavings. Above, the higher crag rises sheer.

The Griffon Crag.description: The high cliffs at the crag's top, the wind fierce enough to stagger a climber. The eyries here are bigger, built up over years and strung with bones, feathers, and the brighter things dragged home. Eggs lie in the deeper nests.

The Stone Warren.name: The Stone Warren
The Stone Warren.basicInfo: An old badger-warren and tumble of rocks at the wood's edge, dotted with statues - birds, foxes, a goat, and here and there a person, all turned to stone mid-step. Cockatrices nest in the burrows. The petrified still hold what they carried when they froze, good steel and gear under the grey, and the cockatrices themselves are worth taking: the gland behind the beak, ground right, makes the salve that turns stone back to flesh, and alchemists pay well for it.
The Stone Warren.hiddenInfo:
The cockatrices of the warren are hostile and rush anything that comes near the burrows.

They are not clever and not large, but they come in ones and twos from the holes and go straight for exposed skin - their bite turns flesh slowly to stone, and one solid bite can cripple a fight. They scatter when struck and dart back in, more nuisance than terror singly, dangerous in numbers and in a cramped space where they can swarm. Kill a few and the rest grow wary but do not flee their nests.

The loot is on the petrified dead - a stone hand closed on a stone sword that is real steel under the grey, a frozen pack, a ring - prised loose from victims nobody came back for; the older statues deeper in the burrows hold the better leavings. Cockatrice glands and feathers are worth taking off the kills.

The Statue Field.description: Open ground before the burrows, scattered with petrified victims frozen mid-stride. A stone traveler stands with a stone sword half-drawn; the steel inside is still good. Low holes pock the rocks and roots beyond. The statues stand thicker the closer the ground runs to the holes.

The Burrows.description: The dug-out warren itself, a cramped maze of rock and root, low and tight. More statues stand here, packed close among the holes - the unlucky who went in after something. The older petrified, deeper in, hold the finer leavings.

The Churn.name: The Churn
The Churn.basicInfo: A stretch of the iron hills where land-sharks den in numbers, and the ground shows it: turned over, heaved into ridges and sinkholes, the grass growing back in patches over raw earth. They take cattle off the hill pastures and horses off the picket-line, and a careless rider on open turf with them. Both clans pay well to thin them, and the hides are worth the ride: a land-shark's back-plates turn a blade like good steel.
The Churn.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Churn is hostile. The land-sharks here are wild predators that hunt anything that moves across their ground, and they are always hungry. They do not pause, do not threaten, and cannot be reasoned with. A hunter comes here to kill them or to be killed.

The broken country is the work of generations of land-sharks denning and breeding in the soft iron-veined earth. There are always several, and there are always more coming — the clans cull them and the ground fills again.

A land-shark hunts by what it feels through the ground. It lies buried with only the ridge of its back breaking the surface, senses the footfalls of anything heavy enough to be food, and bursts up beneath it — through turf, through a picket-line, through a standing rider. On open ground a man on foot cannot outrun the strike. The orcs who hunt them do it from horseback, in pairs, keeping moving and keeping to the bare stone shelves where the beast cannot dig, baiting it up and taking it as it surfaces. A land-shark that misses its lunge is slow to turn and slower to dig back down; that is the window.

The back-plates and ridge-hide are the prize, sold to the armorers of both clans and worth a season's coin for a clean kill.

Combat profile: ambush predator, armored, fast off the line. Opens from below with no warning — a single explosive lunge that can swallow a man or break a horse. Bites and thrashes, throwing riders and scattering a hunting party. Heavily plated along the back and flanks; the soft places are the underside and the joints of the jaw, reachable only when it rears up out of the ground. Wounded, it does not flee — it digs, vanishing into the earth to surface again somewhere else moments later. Hunts alone but several may rise if a party blunders across more than one den.

The Broken Ground.description: The edge of the Churn, where the hill pasture gives way to turned earth. Ridges of raw soil run in long lines where land-sharks have moved beneath the surface; the grass grows in islands between them. Old bones surface here — cattle, horses, the occasional picked-clean rider — and the bare stone shelves stand up out of the dirt where the digging cannot reach. Hunters stage on the stone and watch the ground for the tell-tale ridge of a back breaking the surface.

The Dens.description: Deeper in, the ground is all sinkhole and tunnel-mouth, collapsed in places where the warrens beneath have caved. This is where the land-sharks lie up between hunts, buried in the soft iron-veined earth with only their backs breaking the surface. The biggest of them den here, and the ground is thickest with bone. Bare stone is scarce and the footing is treacherous; a hunter who comes this far has nowhere safe to stand.

Roc Bluffs.name: Roc Bluffs
Roc Bluffs.basicInfo: Wind-scoured tors rising sheer from the open grass, white with bird-lime and crowned with the great stick-nests of rocs. The birds are enormous — wide enough across the wing to throw a shadow like a passing cloud — and they hunt the steppe for anything they can carry: cattle, horses off the picket-line, a rider and his mount together, now and then a whole wagon. What they carry up, they keep. Generations of nests sit on those crags stuffed with the leavings of everything a roc ever took, and a climber bold enough to reach one can come down rich. Most who try come down in pieces, or not at all. Both clans prize the flight-feathers, and the maddest riders dream of carrying down an egg.
Roc Bluffs.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Roc Bluffs is hostile. The rocs are animals and defend their nests without hesitation — a roc that sees a climber on its crag will stoop on him, and there is no warning and no parley. They are most dangerous near the nests and most absent at midday, when they range far out over the grass to hunt.

Rocs have always nested on these tors and always will; the clans cannot drive them off and have stopped trying. There are several nests and the birds come and go with the seasons.

A roc carries its kill back to the crag to feed, and over generations the eyries have filled with everything its prey was carrying when it died: coin and jewelry, arms and armor stripped from the bones of taken riders, saddle-tack and harness, a snatched merchant's strongbox, trade-goods, and now and then the enchanted blade of a knight who went up screaming in a roc's grip.

The birds themselves are worth nearly as much. The great flight-feathers are sought by the fletchers of both clans, who fletch their finest war-arrows with them — arrows that fly farther and truer than any other in the region, and command a high price. The talons and the hooked beak are worked into spearheads, knives, and tools; the down lines winter gear and padded armor.

And in the nests, sometimes, an egg — pale and vast and worth a fortune whole, the one prize that draws the truly reckless. A roc egg sells for a king's ransom, and a roc raised from the shell can, the boldest claim, be broken to the saddle and flown. Most who reach for an egg find the parents come back early.

Combat profile: aerial apex hunter. Opens with a diving stoop out of the sun, talons first, fast enough to pluck a rider from the saddle or knock a climber off the rock. Climbs, wheels, and stoops again rather than landing to fight; on the ground it is less sure but its beak and talons still kill in a stroke, and a buffet of its wings scatters a party and fouls bowshots. Defends the nest to the death and will not be driven from it. Two may stoop together if a nest holds a mated pair.

The Windward Tors.description: The foot of the crags, where the wind comes off the grass hard enough to lean on and the white-limed rock rises sheer overhead. Looking up, the great nests are dark masses against the sky on the highest pinnacles; looking down, the ground is littered with what the rocs have dropped on the way up — cracked bones, a buckled shield, the splintered boards of a wagon, the occasional coin trodden into the dirt.

The Eyries.description: The nest-shelves near the summits, reached by a brutal climb up wind-blasted rock. The nests are huge tangled platforms of branch and bone and carried-off wreckage, fouled with lime and thick with the leavings of generations of kills. This high there is nothing to hide behind and nowhere to run.

Saber-Grass.name: Saber-Grass
Saber-Grass.basicInfo: A swathe of the deep steppe where the grass grows higher than a mounted rider, a green sea that swallows sound and sight together. Saber-tooths hunt here, and the tall grass is theirs: a rider sees nothing until the grass moves, and by then the cat is already in the air. They are huge, patient, and unafraid of horses. The clans hunt them for the great fangs and the striped pelts, and a saber-tooth taken clean is a deed worth telling.
Saber-Grass.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Saber-Grass is hostile. The saber-tooths are animals and hunt anything that enters their range — they stalk unseen through the high grass and strike from ambush, and they do not threaten or parley before they do. They are boldest where the grass is tallest and thickest.

Saber-tooths have always ranged this stretch of steppe, drawn by the herds that graze the deep grass, and the tall cover is what makes them so deadly: it hides a beast the size of a horse until the moment it leaps. There are always several working the grass, and the clans cull them without ever clearing them.

The great curved fangs are the prize, carved into knife-hilts and spear-points and the honor-trophies a hunter wears to show what he has taken, and bought by both clans for good coin and better standing. The striped pelts are worked into cloaks, bedrolls, and the war-harness of chiefs, who prize a saber-tooth hide above any other; a whole unmarked pelt fetches a small fortune. The claws are set into gauntlets and charms, the heavy bones worked into tools.

Combat profile: ambush predator, huge and silent. Stalks unseen through grass that hides it completely, then breaks cover in a single long leap onto the back of horse or rider. Bears its kill to the ground and works the throat; if the first leap misses, it circles back into the grass and stalks again rather than fighting in the open. Fast over short distances, tireless at the stalk, and unafraid of numbers — several may be working the same stretch of grass, and a party that kills one may find it was never the only one watching.

The Grass Edge.description: The edge of the deep grass, where the steppe rises from horse-high to higher than a rider's head and the wind moves it in long slow waves. Trodden runs wind away into the green where heavy bodies have pushed through — herd-paths and hunting-paths both, impossible to tell apart. Bones lie in the flattened hollows where kills were made and eaten, half-grown over. Sightlines end at arm's length.

The Killing Grounds.description: Deeper in, where the grass is tallest and the runs converge on the trampled hollows the saber-tooths use to lie up and feed. The ground here is littered with the bones of horses and oxen and the occasional rider, and the grass stands like walls on every side. There is no high ground, no clear line, and no way to see what is moving until it is close.

The Northern Foothills.name: The Northern Foothills
The Northern Foothills.basicInfo: The Wold's northern edge, where the grass climbs into cold stony hills beneath the white peaks beyond. The air bites here even in summer, the high ground stays rimed and slick, and the country belongs to the things that come down out of the mountains. Yetis raid the foothills in packs, and the clans ride north to throw them back as they always have.
The Northern Foothills.hiddenInfo:
Yetis are hostile and do not negotiate. They come down out of the white peaks in packs to raid: great white-furred brutes, fast over snow and stone. They hunt by ambush off the high slopes and run down what flees, and they drag their kills and their plunder back to fouled dens in the rocks. A yeti den is worth finding: the brutes carry off everything that glitters, and generations of raiding pile up in the back of a lair — coin, arms and armor off dead herders and raiders, the goods of broken steadings, and the bones beneath it all.

Frost drakes den in the high rocks, and the heights are theirs. No true dragons — cold-blooded crag-lurkers the size of a warhorse that creep the boulder-fields and snow-choked gullies, ambush what comes near, and kill with a breath of killing frost and a serpent's rush. They are hostile and do not parley. They come and go as they please, and do not keep a single fixed lair. A drake hoards as its kind do, dragging kill and carried-off plunder into a hidden den.

The yetis carry thick white pelts the clans prize against the cold, and long claws and heavy fangs worked into charms and tools. The drake is the greater prize: its hide and scales turn cold aside and are sought by the clans' armorers, its frost-gland a rare thing the shamans and alchemists pay dearly for, its fangs worked into spears.

Combat profile, yeti: fast, strong, pack-hunting brute. Opens from ambush off the high ground, several rushing together to drag down a single target with claw and fang. Fast over snow and broken rock, tireless on the chase, and bold in numbers; a pack that loses badly will break and flee uphill rather than die to the last.

Combat profile, frost drake: ambush predator of the rocks. Lies still among the boulders and breaks cover in a rush, opening with a cone of freezing breath to stagger its prey before it closes with fang and claw. Fast in the first rush, less so in a long fight; if its ambush fails it withdraws into the rocks and stalks again. Defends its den and its heights to the death.

The Rimed Slopes.description: The lower foothills, where the grass thins and breaks against cold grey stone and the wind comes down off the peaks hard and constant. The ground rises in long bare shoulders, frost-slick even in the warm months, with loose scree underfoot that slides and clatters. Sightlines are open and long across the slopes, with little cover but the occasional standing boulder or fold of ground.

The Boulder-Fields.description: Higher ground strewn with great ice-split stones, some the size of huts, fallen from the peaks over ages. The boulders stand close enough to break any line of sight and large enough to hide something huge between them. Ice fills the gaps and sheets the leeward faces; the footing is broken, uneven, and treacherous, and a straight path through is impossible.

The High Gullies.description: Steep snow-choked ravines cut into the upper foothills, climbing toward the white peaks beyond. The gully walls rise sheer and close, packed with old snow and hung with ice, and the floors are loose stone under drift. The cuts branch and narrow as they climb, command is from the high lips above, and the snow muffles sound and hides what lies beneath it.

The Western Border Woods.name: The Western Border Woods
The Western Border Woods.basicInfo: Where the open Wold runs up against the eastern edge of the great Everwood, the grass gives way to old trees and tangled understory. Elf raiders out of the deep wood have long camped in this vast region to strike at the steppe — burning out herders, cutting down travelers, vanishing back under the canopy before riders can answer.
The Western Border Woods.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The elf renegades who are often found in this location attack anyone they find — orc, outsider, traveler, it makes no difference. They will not parley, because they are here to kill and to make trouble, and anyone who sees them is a witness they cannot allow. They strike first, from cover, and ask nothing.

These renegades are the radical edge of the high elves of the forest: the faction that holds the wild peoples have no place at the forest's borders and that peace between elf and orc is a betrayal. The renegades raid the Wold not for plunder but to provoke: every burned steading and murdered traveler is meant to push the orcs and the elves toward the war the renegades want. They take orc goods and travelers' coin when it is to hand, but ruin is the purpose, not profit.

They fight as raiders, not soldiers. Small bands move through the woods and cannot be pinned to one place — they range the whole location, striking and slipping away. They favor the bow and the ambush above all: arrows from cover, then a rush with curved blades. They know the ground and use it, breaking line of sight and circling to strike from behind.
