Cornered, they fight to the death rather than be taken, because a captured renegade compromises the rest.

The woods carry their own dangers besides. Dire wolves run the deep timber in packs, and they do not distinguish raider from hunter. An owlbear dens somewhere in the heavy growth and kills anything that crosses its range.

What the renegades carry is worth the taking: elven war-bows and the long curved blades of the forest, and elven mail, light and strong. Their arrows are elf-fletched and fly true. Among a band's leaders there is sometimes elven work with old enchantments on it — a blade that bites cold, a bow that never misfires, a cloak that turns the eye.

Combat profile, elf renegade: light, fast, deadly at range. Opens with arrows from cover before the target knows they are there. Closes only with advantage — a rush of curved blades, several at once on a single foe — and breaks off the moment the advantage is lost, fading into the trees to loop around and strike again. Never holds ground it does not have to. Fights as a band, never alone if it can help it, and covers a withdrawal with massed bowfire. Will die before surrendering.

The Wood's Edge.description: The march between grass and forest, where scattered old trees stand in the long grass and thicken as the land rises westward. Sightlines are long here at the steppe's edge and shorten with every pace into the trees. The ground is broken by deadfall and bramble, with open lanes of grass running between stands of timber — fast going in the open, slow and blind in the thickets.

The Deep Timber.description: Heavy old forest where the canopy closes overhead and the light goes green and dim. The trunks stand close, cover is everywhere. The understory is thick enough to hide a crouching figure within arm's reach. Game-trails and older paths wind through it, the only fast ways through a wood that otherwise swallows movement.

The Hollow Ground.description: A stretch of broken forest floor where the land folds into gullies and dry stream-cuts under the trees, choked with deadfall and root-tangle. The cuts run deep enough to hide a moving party below the lip of the ground, and the high banks command everything below them. Footing is bad and loud — dry sticks and loose stone — and the gullies branch and rejoin so that a straight line through is impossible.

The Southern Badlands.name: The Southern Badlands
The Southern Badlands.basicInfo: Broken, dry country at the Wold's southern edge, where the grass fails into cracked earth, dust-gullies, and bare stone ridges. The Oathbreakers hold this waste — orc raiders cast out of the clans, who ride from here to burn and plunder south across the border and prey on anything that crosses the badlands. The clans name them kin no longer.
The Southern Badlands.hiddenInfo:
The Oathbreakers are hostile and will not parley. They are orcs who broke the clan-oath — the loyalty sworn at the Gods-Anvil that binds rider to clan and clan to the Wold. They hold that the clans have gone soft: that tolerating Gorren Crossing, taking in outsiders, and keeping the truce between Vorren and Drokash is weakness, and that the Wold's strength should be spent burning Westmarch and the Everwood to the ground. The clans disown them utterly, for to an orc there is no fouler thing than an oathbreaker.

They ride to Blood-Altar Mountain to take the Wrath-Speakers' rites, and come back worse.

They are raiders, not soldiers, and have no single chief — bands gather under whoever is strongest that season and scatter when beaten. They cannot be pinned to one camp; they range the whole waste, striking from the gullies and the broken ground and riding down what flees. Worgs run with them — wolves the size of horses, cunning and cruel and able to speak, that scout, flank, and hunt alongside the riders and are no dumb beasts to be herded but allies in the killing. Carrion-birds trail the bands across the badlands, and where they circle, the Oathbreakers have lately been.

What the Oathbreakers carry is reaved plunder — coin, arms and armor, and the goods stripped from burned steadings and broken caravans on both sides of the border — along with their own war-gear, hard-used and well-kept. The worgs wear collars and harness taken from their kills, sometimes with worked metal and coin braided into them as trophies.

Combat profile, Oathbreaker raider: mounted, fast, and vicious. Strikes from ambush out of the broken ground, looses arrows from horseback, then closes with axe and blade in a screaming rush meant to break nerve as much as line. Fights alongside worgs that flank and drag down the isolated. Gives no quarter and expects none; a band that loses badly scatters into the gullies to regroup rather than die in place.

Combat profile, worg: cunning pack-hunter. Runs with the raiders or hunts in its own pack, flanking to drive prey onto the riders' blades. Fast, tireless, and clever enough to lay an ambush; speaks to coordinate the hunt. Bold in numbers and cowardly alone, breaking off when the odds turn.

The Dust Gullies.description: A maze of dry, steep-sided ravines cut into the badland floor, deep enough to hide riders below the level of the plain. The gullies branch and rejoin without pattern, the walls are crumbling earth and loose stone, and the floors are soft sand that muffles hooves. A party in the gullies cannot see far and cannot be seen, and command belongs to whoever holds the high lip above.

The Cracked Flats.description: Open hardpan between the gullies, the earth split into a dry crazed pattern and scattered with bleached bone and wind-worn stone. The flats run wide and level, with nothing to break a sightline and nothing to hide behind — fast riding for anyone crossing, and no cover at all when something comes out of the gullies.

The Ridges.description: Bare stone spines rising above the waste, their flanks broken into ledges and notches and their tops commanding the flats and gullies below. The rock is split and weathered, with caves and overhangs worn into the higher faces. From the ridgelines the whole badland lies open to view; the climbs to reach them are loose and exposed.

Blood-Altar Mountain.name: Blood-Altar Mountain
Blood-Altar Mountain.basicInfo: A flat-topped mountain of red stone rising from the Wolds, its bare summit streaked dark down the cliffs so that from below it looks like an altar with blood running off it. Forest cloaks the slopes; the red plateau stands bare above. The Wrath-Speakers come here to work their rites, and sacrifices they carry up the mountain do not come down again.
Blood-Altar Mountain.hiddenInfo:
The Wrath-Speakers are hostile and do not parley. They are orc shamans who took the spirit-fury that the warrior-lodges master and gave it instead to demons — the Wraths, and the Lady of Wrath they serve, a demon of battle-rage who feeds on the sacrifices made to her — in exchange for power. They do not hold the mountain in force; they come to it for their rites and are gone between them, denning in the wooded slopes when present, leaving only the altar and its dead when not. The Oathbreakers ride here to be blessed before their raids.

The rite is sacrifice. The Wrath-Speakers take captives — raid-prisoners, travelers, enemies bound and dragged up the slopes — and kill them on the altar to feed the Lady of Wrath, who answers with her blessing: a battle-frenzy that makes the blessed faster, stronger, and unfeeling of wounds until the fury burns out. Captives are held bound in the slope-camps and on the plateau awaiting the knife.

When the Wrath-Speakers work, they call the Lady's servants through: Wraths — demons of rage that burn with a fury of their own and throw themselves at anything living — and lesser imp-like things, petty demons summoned in numbers to swarm and harry. These fade when the summoner is killed or the rite broken.

What is taken here is worth the climb: the goods of the sacrificed piled by the altar, the Wrath-Speakers' own ritual work — fetishes, bone-charms, and blades blooded for the rite that carry the Lady's fury in them — and offerings of coin and worked metal heaped at the altar's foot. The demon-things leave behind matter the alchemists and shamans prize.

Combat profile, Wrath-Speaker: shaman and frenzy-caller. Fights from the back, working the blessing onto its allies to send them into killing rage, and calls Wraths and petty demons through to fight in its place. Drives the frenzied forward and itself stays clear; cornered, it takes the fury into its own body and comes on heedless of wounds, fighting to the death. Killing the Speaker ends its summons and breaks its blessing.

Combat profile, Wrath: demon of rage. Comes on without caution or self-preservation, fast and furious, throwing itself at the nearest living thing and striking until destroyed. Does not flee, does not relent.

Combat profile, petty demon: imp-like swarmer. Summoned in numbers to harry, claw, and distract; weak alone, dangerous in a mob. Winks out when its summoner dies.

The Wooded Slopes.description: Steep forest climbing the mountain's flanks, the trees red-barked and close, the ground rising in switchbacks and rocky shelves toward the bare summit above. Cover is thick and broken, with hollows and overhangs worked into the slope where the rock breaks through. The canopy hides the plateau overhead and breaks any sightline to more than a stone's throw.

The Altar Plateau.description: The mountain's flat red summit, bare stone open to the sky and the wind, ringed at its edges by the last of the trees. At its center stands the altar — a great split slab of dark-stained red rock, channels cut into its surface running to its base. The plateau is open ground with no cover but the standing stones and the altar itself, and the whole Wold lies visible below the cliffs on every side.

Vorren's Hold.name: Vorren's Hold
Vorren's Hold.basicInfo: The great ancestral stone seat of Clan Vorren, raised on a high tor above the iron hills it works, ringed in dark stone walls, its forges burning day and night and its smoke visible across the Wold. The hold is open to traders and to anyone who comes in peace.
Vorren's Hold.hiddenInfo:
Vorren's Hold is safe and welcoming to those who come honestly; the Watch keeps order within the walls and the clan prizes guests, traders, and any outsider who will fight for the Wold. Lead with orcs in any scene here, but the hold is mixed: settled clan-orcs throughout, but non-clan orcs visiting should be quite common as well.

Clan Vorren is ruled by its chief and a council of elders, and rule passes by blood and seniority. Vorren hold that the Wold is kept by the wall and the line: by standing fast, building strong, and arming the clans with good iron. They reckon Drokash reckless and Drokash reckons them slow, and the two have warred in the past, but Vorren considers orc infighting a waste of arms needed to defend the Wold against outside threats. Vorren, like Drokash, disowns the renegade orc Oathbreakers utterly.

The hold's wealth and identity are iron. The Mogra mines in the hills below feed the forges, and Vorren smiths are the finest armorers and weaponsmiths in the Wold. Kobolds have broken into the deep workings of the mines and hold the lost galleries, and the clan pays well to see them culled. South of the hold, in the broken badlands, the Oathbreakers raid and burn, and Vorren riders ride against them; the clan has standing work for any who would hunt kin turned reaver. The land-sharks of the Churn take Vorren cattle off the hill pastures, and the clan's armorers pay good coin for the hides.

Vorren is a place to belong: to swear to the clan, take the settled warrior's path of shieldwall and heavy iron, learn the forge-crafts, and rise in the clan's esteem from guest to sworn to honored.

The Gate Court.description: The hold's entry, a broad walled courtyard inside the great iron-bound gates, cut into the living rock of the tor. Wagons of ore come up from the mines and wagons of finished iron roll out for the south; traders' stalls cluster along the walls, and the clan's banners hang from the ramparts above. The forge-smoke hangs over everything, and the ring of hammers carries down from the smithies. From the wall-walk the whole iron-hill country lies open below.

The Great Hall.description: The clan's stone feast-hall, vast and beam-roofed, its walls hung with the arms and trophies of generations and the lineage-banners of the Vorren chiefs. Long tables run its length, a fire-pit burns at its heart, and the chief's seat stands at the far end before the council benches of the elders. This is where the clan gathers, where oaths are sworn and feasts held, where work is given and disputes are judged.

The Forge Quarter.description: The working heart of the hold, a long district of smithies, foundries, and armories built against the inner wall where the heat can vent. Forge-fires roar in rank, ore from the Mogra mines is smelted and worked, and the clan's smiths — orc and dwarf side by side — hammer out the blades, axes, and heavy armor Vorren is known for. Finished work hangs racked for trade and for the clan's own warriors; the best pieces, the masterwork arms of named smiths, are kept apart and sold dear.

The Mogra Mines.name: The Mogra Mines
The Mogra Mines.basicInfo: The iron mines that feed Vorren's Hold, cut deep into the hills below the fortress. The upper workings are busy day and night — Vorren miners hauling ore up to the forges above. But the deepest galleries have been lost. Kobolds broke into the lower workings from somewhere below and have held them since, and the miners no longer go down past the flooded levels.
The Mogra Mines.hiddenInfo:
The upper mine is safe and worked, watched by Vorren mine-guards; the danger is below, in the lost galleries. The kobolds there are hostile and attack intruders in numbers, though they are weak in any single fight and break when badly beaten — only to mass again. They broke through from the deeps and have spread into the lower workings, and the clan culls them without ever clearing them for good.

The kobolds fight as their kind do: not in open battle but by trap, ambush, and weight of numbers. The galleries they hold are seeded with deadfalls, pits, snares, and rigged collapses; they swarm out of side-passages and crawlways too small for a warrior in armor, loose bolts and stones from the dark, and fall back when met head-on to draw pursuers onto their traps. They see in the dark and know every tunnel; an intruder who brings no light fights blind, and one who brings light is seen first.

Combat profile, kobold: trap-setter and swarmer. Avoids a fair fight; opens with traps and missiles from cover, swarms an isolated or wounded target, and flees the moment a fight turns against it. Dangerous in numbers and on its own ground, where every passage is rigged and every shadow holds another. Cowardly alone; relentless in a mob.

The Upper Workings.description: The active mine: broad timber-shored tunnels and galleries lit by hung lamps. Vorren miners work the faces here, and guards stand at the heads of the shafts that lead down. The main shaft descends past worked levels toward the flooded galleries below, where the lamps end and the timber gives way to older, rougher stone.

The Lost Galleries.description: The deep workings, below the flooded levels, where the cut stone gives way to a warren of older tunnels and natural crawlways branching off into the dark. The passages are close and lightless, riddled with side-crawls and drops, and the floor is treacherous with rigged ground and old collapse.

Camp Drokash.name: Camp Drokash
Camp Drokash.basicInfo: The great moving seat of Clan Drokash, a tent-city pitched on the open steppe wherever the grass and the season call it. There are no walls here, only horse-lines running to the horizon, hide tents in their thousands, and the chieftain's great pavilion at the heart of it all. Drokash are the roving clan, horse-lords and riders, rich in herds and proud of the open ground no wall can hold. The camp welcomes traders, horse-buyers, and anyone who comes in peace.
Camp Drokash.hiddenInfo:
Camp Drokash is safe and welcoming to those who come honestly; the riders keep their own order and the clan prizes guests, traders, and any outsider who will fight for the Wold. Lead with orcs in any scene here, but the camp is mixed: roving clan-orcs throughout, traders and herders of every kind, and drifters who follow a tent-city for the work and the coin.

Clan Drokash is ruled by a war-chief who won the place by deeds and holds it the same way, with a war-council of the clan's proven riders at the chief's side. Rank here is taken, not inherited — a rider rises by what they do, and a chief who weakens can be challenged. Drokash hold that the Wold is kept by the charge and the open ground: by riding hard and striking first. They reckon Vorren slow and penned, and the two clans have warred in the past, but they agree that orcs must band together to defend their lands from hostile outsiders. Both clans disown the Oathbreakers utterly.

The camp's wealth and pride are its herds — the finest horses in the Wold, bred and broken here and sold south through Gorren Crossing. The clan has standing work for riders. Rocs out of the Bluffs stoop on the horse-lines and carry off beasts and herders alike, and the boldest riders dream of climbing for an egg and breaking a roc to the saddle; the clan pays for the raptors thinned and prizes the flight-feathers. The saber-tooths of the deep grass take the herds and the hunters both, and to bring one down whole is a deed that makes a name. And when the yetis come down from the Northern Foothills onto the grazing, Drokash musters to throw them back, as the clan always has.

Drokash is a place to belong: to ride with the clan, take the horse-warrior's path of lance and saddle, win a name in the contests and the hunt, and rise by deeds from guest to rider to a voice on the war-council.

The Muster-Ground.description: The open heart of the camp where the riders gather, a broad trampled common ringed by the hide tents and the horse-lines. Mounts stand picketed in their hundreds, riders come and go at the gallop, and traders' wagons cluster at the margins where the camp meets the open grass. Banners on tall lances mark the clan's companies, and the whole steppe rolls away unbroken on every side.

The Chieftain's Pavilion.description: The great tent at the camp's center, vast and many-poled, its hide walls hung with the trophies and war-banners of the Drokash chiefs and floored with the spoils of a hundred raids and hunts. Here the war-chief holds court among the council of proven riders, feasts are thrown and oaths sworn, work is given and disputes judged, and a stranger comes to be weighed and heard. The fire-pit at its heart never goes cold while the clan is camped.

The Contest Ground.description: A wide stretch of cleared steppe set aside for the trials that win a rider standing: mounted races, the tilt and the lance, wrestling, archery from the saddle, and the breaking of wild horses. Riders test themselves and each other here from dawn, the crowd thick at the rails, wagers passing hand to hand. A name is made on this ground, and the deeds that decide rank in the clan are done in the open for all to see.

The Underfloes.name: The Underfloes
The Underfloes.basicInfo: A wide plain of fractured sea-ice and frozen flats in the north, where rimewyrms tunnel beneath the surface and burst up through it. The flats are open and look empty, which is the danger. Hunters come for rimewyrm hide and fangs, and for what the wyrms churn up from the deep ice — old wrecks and lost caravans the freeze swallowed, and now and then a vein of frostjade.
The Underfloes.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Rimewyrms are always hostile and hunt by ambush. A rimewyrm runs beneath the ice and follows vibration — footfalls, sled-runners, a struck blow — then erupts under its prey, strikes, and submerges to circle for another pass. They do not hold ground or guard a den so much as patrol a hunting-stretch, and a heavy, noisy crossing draws them faster than a light one. The young are smaller and burrow in the shallows near the broken ice.

The flats are a graveyard of the freeze. When the wyrms tunnel, they break open what the ice closed over long ago: foundered ships of the Northrealm, caravans that never reached shelter, the goods and gear of people the cold caught in the open. This wreckage is common in the broken ground and is the steady draw. Frostjade is the rare one — raw veins of the cold-bound stone, exposed only where a wyrm has cut deep, worth the risk to anyone who can carry it out.

The richest churned ground lies in the Underbreaks, where the ice is most shattered and the wyrms den deepest.

The Floes.description: A vast flat of sea-ice and frozen ground, level and open to the horizon, with no cover and nothing to break the wind. The surface is sound in places and thin in others, scored with old fracture-lines and ridges of heaved ice. Footing is the only warning of what runs below.

The Underbreaks.description: A stretch where the ice has shattered into tilted slabs, pressure-ridges, and open breaks down into blue dark. Slabs lean against each other to form hollows and crawlspaces, and broken shapes are visible frozen in the walls of the deeper gaps — timber, iron, the edges of things the ice took. Sound carries strangely between the slabs.

The Herdways.name: The Herdways
The Herdways.basicInfo: The open tundra-track in the north where the great herds move on their seasonal circuit — dire elk and winter mammoth in their hundreds, crossing the white in slow rivers of horn and tusk. Hunters and trappers work the migration for hide, meat, mammoth ivory, and the pelt of the dire snow-lynx, which fetches a luxury price in the south. The herds are not the danger. What hunts them is.
The Herdways.hiddenInfo:
The great herds are not aggressive, but they are enormous and easily spooked, and a stampede of winter mammoth flattens whatever stands in front of it. Dire elk lower their horns and drive when cornered; mammoth defend their young without hesitation. The harvest is rich and mostly a matter of patience, weather, and not being underfoot.

IMPORTANT: The dire snow-lynx defaults hostile to a lone or wounded target and hunts by ambush. White against white, it is nearly invisible until it moves — it shadows the herd from cover and ridgelines, drops onto the straggler, the young, or the lame, and is gone before the herd turns. It does not pace prey in the open the way wolves do; it waits above a line of travel and takes the one at the edge. Two or three may work the same stretch without coordinating, which means a kill drawn into the open invites the next.

The ivory and the pelts are the wealth here, carried south as luxury goods. The lynx den in the broken ground of the Snowveil, where the cover they hunt from is thickest.

The Migration.description: A broad sweep of open tundra and wind-scoured snow, level and exposed, where the herd-track runs from horizon to horizon. The ground is churned and trampled along the route, packed hard by the passage of thousands. There is no cover on the flat itself — only the herds, and the distance.

The Snowveil.description: Broken country flanking the migration track — low ridges, drifted hollows, stands of wind-stunted scrub, and folds of ground that break the sightline. Snow lies deep and soft in the hollows. The high ground overlooks the herd-track below, and the cover runs unbroken along the edge of it.

Northport.name: Northport
Northport.basicInfo: The dead capital of the Northrealm, on the northwest coast where a glacier has come down over the old harbor city. In the warm age this was a great seaport, and its fleet is still here — ships at their moorings with the sea frozen solid around the hulls and the ice grown up the masts.
Northport.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Northport is held by the draugr of the old Northrealm — the armed dead of the city that died here. They do not roam, hunt, or parley. Each holds the ground it was laid in: a doorway, a deck, a barrow, a hall. A draugr lets the living pass until they touch what it guards, then it rises in silence and does not stop. A careful party can move through much of the city; a greedy one wakes it.

The dead were a seafaring people, and they fall into ranks the way they lived — house-warriors in the streets and harbor, captains aboard their iced-in ships, and the old crowned dead deepest, in the hall above the frozen anchorage. The cold has kept everything: the city is not picked over, because almost no one who goes deep comes back to spend what they found.

The wealth of a kingdom lies where its dead lie. The arms and grave-gold of the Northrealm are thickest aboard the moored ships and in the high hall, and the regalia of the old crown — the dead-king's circlet and blade — rests with the king himself, on a throne above the harbor where the whole drowned-and-frozen fleet can be seen below.

The Frozen Harbor.description: The old anchorage, where the sea lies frozen hard around a fleet of moored ships. Hulls stand locked in the ice at their berths, masts and rigging sheathed in frost, gangplanks frozen to the stone quays. The waterfront buildings rise behind, half-swallowed where the glacier has pushed through, open where it has not. Ice underfoot and the ships for cover.

The Ice-Locked City.description: The streets above the waterline — stone and timber halls of a northern port, roofed in ice, some sound and some crushed where the glacier came down. Lanes run between the buildings, choked with drift and fallen masonry, narrowing where the ice has closed them to one body's width. Doorways stand dark and open. The way climbs toward the high ground at the back of the city.
paths: The Hall of the Drowned Fleet

The Hall of the Drowned Fleet.description: The great hall on the height at the back of the city, above the frozen anchorage. A long stone chamber, vaulted and rimed, its far end open to a terrace that overlooks the whole iced-in harbor and the fleet locked below. A throne stands at the chamber's head, sized for a man, set so its occupant faces out over the ships. One way in, by the climb from the city.

Stillwater.name: Stillwater
Stillwater.basicInfo: A dead snowlander town on the ice, a day from Warmwater, that the cold took. Its hot spring kept it open and alive the way Warmwater's still does — until the spring went dead one winter and the town froze solid, people and all. They called it Brightwater when the water was warm. They call it Stillwater now.
Stillwater.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Stillwater is bitterly, unnaturally cold — colder than the open ice around it, because the Long Night choked its spring dead and worked their rites there to feed the cold. The cold itself is the chief danger to the unprepared. Ice mephits gather thick in the dead streets, drawn to where the cold runs deepest, and rime-wights drift among the buildings — the town's own people, some of them, walking the streets they died in. The wights do not hunt; they wander, and turn on what disturbs them.

There are no bodies in the houses. The lamps were lit and the tables were laid when the town froze; then its dead rose as rime-wights and walked out of their homes. Some still wander these streets, and the rest have joined the processions on the open ice.

The Frozen Streets.description: The lanes of a snowlander town, carved-timber houses rimed white and roofed in ice, lamps frozen in their brackets at the doors and windows. Snow has drifted against the walls and filled the open spaces. Doors stand shut, frozen in their frames; some windows are clear enough to see the laid tables and cold hearths within. The streets run inward toward the town's heart.

The Dead Spring.description: The hollow at the center of the town, where the hot spring once rose and kept the cold off. The pool is a plug of black ice now, the stonework around it sheathed in frost, the bathhouse and gathering-hall that ringed it standing dark and iced. The cold is hardest here.

The Temple of the Hearth.name: The Temple of the Hearth
The Temple of the Hearth.basicInfo: The greatest shrine of the old Northrealm, raised over a sacred hot spring where the Lady of the Hearth was worshipped — the warmth rising from the earth that kept the Widow's cold at bay. Now the spring has been choked shut and the shrine frozen over,  its fires dead.
The Temple of the Hearth.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Temple of the Hearth is held by the Long Night and its cultists default hostile to any intruder. They are zealots of Hrimnara, the Widow of Winter, and they kill to keep their holy ground and to feed the cold.

The Long Night holds that the warm age was a lie and the cold is the world's true and final state — and they mean to help the Widow finish it. They choke the springs that keep the towns alive, leave the living and the dead to the cold as offerings, and revere the walking dead of the white as the Widow's own. Killing this temple's spring was their first and greatest work: the murder of the Hearth in her own house. Stillwater was a smaller one. Every failing spring in Aurora is their hand.

The cult's rites are worked at the dead spring at the temple's heart, and what they have gathered there — relics taken from the towns they have killed, and the ritual goods of their worship — lies with it.

The Frozen Steps.description: The approach to the temple — a broad stair of rimed stone climbing to a pillared front, the whole face sheathed in ice and hung with frozen runoff where warm water once spilled down it. The doors stand open and dark. Carved figures of the Lady flank the way, faces worn and frost-cracked. Open ground, no cover but the pillars.

The Inner Shrine.description: The temple's main hall, a high pillared chamber roofed in ice, the old hearth-altars cold and choked with frost down its length. Where fires once burned there is only black stone and rime. The hall runs back toward the spring at the temple's heart, and side-chapels open off it into dark.

The Dead Spring.description: The sacred spring at the temple's heart, the reason the shrine was raised — a wide pool in a domed sanctum, now a plug of black ice, the stonework around it white with frost. The cold is hardest here, harder than the open ice outside. The deepest sanctum lies beyond, behind the spring.

Aurora Icefields.name: Aurora Icefields
Aurora Icefields.basicInfo: The vast open white at the heart of the north — trackless icefields and wind-scoured snow running flat to the horizon under the auroral sky, with nothing on them but distance, weather, and what the ice has kept. Travelers cross only when they must, and many who cross do not arrive. The aurora stands overhead at night, and the snowlanders say that is the Widow walking.
Aurora Icefields.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The open ice is dangerous chiefly for its weather. Blizzards rise fast and without warning, and the wind off the high ice can flay exposed skin, knock a traveler down, and bury a stopped party where it stands. A storm caught in the open kills more surely than any beast, and the white offers no shelter and no landmark to steer by.

What moves on the ice is the Widow's. By night, rime-wights — the frozen dead of those the white has taken — cross the fields in slow processions, and the snowlanders' law is plain: stand aside and let them pass. The wights do not hunt and do not heed the living unless the living get in their way, and then they turn and do not stop. Ice drakes hunt the high ground at the edges of the fields, and rimewolves range the open in packs, pacing travelers for miles before they close.

The ice is a graveyard of the freeze, and buried shapes show through the blue ice on clear days: foundered ships and lost caravans of the Northrealm, common across the fields, and far rarer, the white stone of things older than any kingdom. The dead and the cold have kept what they swallowed, for anyone willing to dig it out of the ice.

The Frozen Colossus is the greatest of the coldstone guardians made by the people who built the white city in the Crevasse. It has stood asleep on the ice since its makers died, and like their other constructs it can still wake.

The Open White.description: A flat of wind-packed snow and bare blue ice running to the horizon in every direction, featureless and exposed, with no rise or rock to break the wind or mark a path. Shapes show frozen in the ice underfoot in places — timber, iron, the edges of things the freeze took. The sky is wide and the aurora burns across it after dark. The old beast bone frozen in the blue ice is rimebone. A remorhaz hunts beneath the sled-tracks here, melting its pits under anyone who stays long in one place.

The Frozen Colossus.description: A titan of a figure standing alone on the icefield, a vast humanlike shape of grey-white stone, its features worn smooth, far larger than anything built in Larion today. The ice for a long way around its feet is studded with frozen shapes: gear, sledges, and the dead of those who came to it and did not leave. Frost sprites and ice mephits swarm thick here, where the cold runs deepest in all the fields.

The Firwood.name: The Firwood
The Firwood.basicInfo: The great snow-mantled fir forest along Aurora's southern rim. It is the gentlest country in the north — sheltered under the trees, worked by snowlander loggers and charcoal-burners. Old Northrealm holdfasts and hunting-halls stand scattered and ruined through the deep wood, raised when this was a living kingdom, and the gear and goods of the old realm still lie in them, where the snow-trolls den.
The Firwood.hiddenInfo:
The snowlanders who work the Firwood are hardy, plainspoken, and used to strangers coming up the road. The logging steads and charcoal-camps are safe and will trade, shelter, and point a traveler onward.

The danger is in the deep wood, and it is the snow-trolls. They are great cold-hardened trolls, and they have taken the ruined Northrealm halls scattered through the forest for their dens — drawn to the old stone shelters, denning among whatever the dead kingdom left in them. IMPORTANT: snow-trolls in their dens default hostile and attack anything that comes near, and they heal from any wound that is not burned or seared shut; they go sluggish and slow in the deepest cold and rouse to fury in a thaw or near fire. A troll-held ruin must be taken from the troll.

The Northrealm built well, and what its people left when the cold drove them out still lies in the ruins the trolls now hold: old arms and armor of fine northern make, worked gear, and the buried goods of a vanished kingdom. The richest of it lies deepest in the wood, in the largest of the old holdfasts, where the biggest trolls den.

The Logging Steads.description: A cluster of snowlander work-camps — carved-timber longhouses, stacked cordwood, charcoal-mounds smoking under their turf, and sledge-tracks running off among the trees. The wood here is thinned by the axe and open to the sky in patches. People work and trade here, and the road runs on north and deeper in.

The Deep Firs.description: The old growth, where the firs stand close and tall and the canopy holds the snow off the forest floor in a dim green hush. Game-trails and overgrown tracks wind between the trunks. Among the trees, ruined stone — fallen walls, broken halls, the mossed-and-rimed footings of old Northrealm holdfasts — stands half-swallowed by the wood, dark openings leading down into them.

The Old Holdfast.description: The largest of the ruined Northrealm halls, deep in the wood — a great stone shell of a building, roof long fallen, walls standing to the height of two men and hung with ice and creeper. The interior opens into cold stone chambers and a way down into vaulted cellars below.

Warmwater Township.name: Warmwater Township
Warmwater Township.basicInfo: The chief town of the snowlanders and the last warm light of the north. It sits on the shore of Warmwater Lake, where hot springs keep the near water open and steaming all year in a country locked in ice. Carved-timber houses with lamps in every window climb from the steaming shore to the Ice Gardens, where great sculptures of ice glow from within and the Pearl Houses' glass-roofed manors stand around them. The exiled court of the Northrealm, the Winter Crown, holds court here, and the old castle of Whitewatch on the height above holds the Long Watch, the knights who keep the signal-fires burning across the ice.
Warmwater Township.hiddenInfo:
The snowlanders are a proud, warm, glamorous people: the last of the old Northrealm, the kingdom the cold killed, and they keep its light burning on purpose. They dress bright against the white — cobalt, crimson, and cream wool, silver clasps, carved serpents and wolves — and they are generous to anyone who comes in off the ice. "Come Hrimnara or hot water," they say of anything they have set their minds to.

The town has three layers. Along the lakeshore is the warm daily life: the springs, the market, the fishing, the bathhouse, the kennels, the Hearthhouse. Around the Ice Gardens is the wealthy district: the manors and Glasshouses of the Pearl Houses, the families who own the hearthpearl vents, and the Winter Court of the exiled ducal house. Above, up the climb, is the old Northrealm castle of Whitewatch, seat of the Long Watch and the League of Adventurers' foothold in the north.

The springs are why the town lives. They are volcanic, but the snowlanders hold them to be the gift of the Lady of the Hearth. The Hearth faith is kept as custom: a fire always burning, a lamp in every window, the words "your hearth, my life" said before food or drink passes the lips indoors, and carved housewardens watching outward from every gable. Hearth-spirits are the town's treasures, and icelings, small spirits of living ice, live in the sculptures of the Ice Gardens.

The court is where the intrigue lives. The Winter Crown wants to march north and retake Northport; the Pearl Houses fund the court and quietly oppose the war that would cost them everything; and every house wants to marry into the old royal line, whose twin heirs refuse to choose anyone. On aurora nights the whole town throws the Aurora Ball in the Ice Gardens. The town is bright, glamorous, and full of wonder, and the cold around it is beautiful and dangerous.

The Market.description: The town's bright trading-square on the warm shore, the heart of its daily life. The near water of the lake steams and glitters at its edge while the far reaches stand frozen white, and carved-timber halls painted cobalt, crimson, and cream crowd around it under steep snowy roofs hung with lanterns. Stalls glow with hearthpearls in velvet trays, iron-and-glass hearth-lanterns, furs dyed in jewel colors, silver clasps and carved housewardens, hothouse oranges from the Glasshouses, and the rare wonders that come in off the ice: drake scale, serpent-pearl, and stranger things. Snowlander merchants, dwarves up from the northern holds, and bright-coated travelers from the south haggle and gossip over hot spiced cider, and a walled road climbs from the square to the old castle on the height above.

The Steaming Pools.description: The hot springs themselves, where the warm water rises from the earth into a series of stone-rimmed pools along the shore, steam standing thick over them in the cold air. This is the town's gathering-place and its bathhouse both — folk soak, talk, and settle the day's business in the warm water, the one place in the north a body can be truly warm out of doors. A shrine-niche to the Lady of the Hearth stands at the largest pool, kept always alight. By custom, everyone bathes together, duke and fisher alike, and rank is left with the clothes.

The Kennels.description: The sled-yards at the town's edge, where the snowlanders keep their teams of rimewolves, the great white wolves of the north, half-wild, proud, and bred for speed. Painted racing sleds hang under carved eaves, lead wolves wear bright harness-bells, and the frozen lake beyond is flagged for the race course. The rescue teams that ride out to bring home anyone lost on the ice keep their quarters and their hearth-lanterns here.

The Hearthhouse.description: The great common hall of the town, a long carved-timber building hung with bright woven banners, with a fire-pit running down its center that has never been allowed to go out and is home to the town's oldest hearth-spirit. The snowlanders gather here to eat, drink, sing, and shelter through the dark season, and a traveler can find a hot meal, a bed by the fire, and the talk of the whole town. The door faces the lake, away from the white.

The Watch-Hall.description: The great hall of Whitewatch, the old Northrealm castle on the height, reached by the walled climb up from town. Its ancient grey stone is carved with serpents and warmed by roaring hearthfires, and snowlander banners in cobalt, crimson, and cream hang over the old Northrealm carving. The folk-moot meets here to settle the town's affairs, and the League of Adventurers keeps its northern contract-board along one wall.

The Lamp-Tower.description: The highest tower of Whitewatch, the seat of the Long Watch, reached by the walled climb up from the town. A great lamp of brass and crystal blazes at its top, home to a hearth-spirit of the Watch, one of a chain of signal-fires set across the icefields, and from here the watch reads the others — and the dark gaps where a fire has gone out. A wide map of the region is kept here, marking the steads, the springs, and the white between them, and the watch keeps careful count of what the map shows: the steads whose springs are failing one by one, and Stillwater chief among the lost — the town's own sister settlement, a day across the ice, its spring choked dead and its people frozen where they stood. The watch holds the Long Night to blame, the cult that serves the Widow and means to feed the cold until it covers the world, and reads the failing fires for the cult's hand. The view runs out over the whole frozen north, and the wind is constant.

The Ice Gardens.description: The heart of the wealthy district: a terraced garden of great carved ice on the slope above the warm shore, where sculptures of serpents, wolves, kings, and dancers stand taller than houses and glow from within at night. Channels of spring water steam between the terraces, and the Pearl Houses' manors of pale stone and carved timber stand around the garden under steaming glass roofs. The town walks, courts, and shows off here, and on aurora nights it holds the Aurora Ball. Icelings live inside the sculptures, and some carvings shift when no one is looking. Among them stands a slender spire of ice, the studio-tower of the town's frost-mage artist.

The Winter Court.description: The hall of House Ormsvald, the Northrealm's ruling house in exile, on the upper terrace of the Ice Gardens. A high timber hall hung with cobalt and silver banners, its beams carved as serpent-prows from the old royal fleet, its hearth fed day and night. At its end stands a throne of pale stone for a kingdom that lies under ice, with a great map of the old Northrealm behind it and Northport marked in silver. Suitors, Pearl House lords, and petitioners come here to be seen. The Winter Court's herald, Embla, announces everyone who comes before the throne.

The Glasshouses.description: The hothouses of the Pearl Houses, long halls of glass and iron on the slope behind the Ice Gardens, fed by channels from the hot springs. Inside it is summer: orange and fig trees, vines, melons, and greens growing in warm, wet air while snow lies on the glass above, the only fresh fruit for a hundred leagues. Below them the hottest vents steam in stone basins where the hearthpearls grow, and the Pearl Houses entertain their guests among the orange trees.

The Shore Cottages.description: A row of snug carved-timber cottages along the warm shore between the Market and the Steaming Pools, each with a spring-fed bath behind it, a lamp in the window, and a stone hearth inside. They are let to newcomers and adventurers who mean to stay a while, and some of their hearths hold a sleeping hearth-spirit that has not been woken in years. A low stone bridge nearby leads across the steaming water to Svanholm, the Winter Crown’s island residence held for a grant of court service.

The Frost Fair.description: A standing fair on the frozen lake below the Ice Gardens: a little town of striped pavilions and carved ice halls, its paths lit by lamps and braziers. Inside the pavilions it is warm with hearthpearls, music, spiced wine and furs; outside, the cleared ice is busy with skaters, races and the odd duel. Stalls sell hot food, trinkets and furs, sculptors show their work in halls of glittering ice, and the Pearl Houses keep their own pavilions in their colors. Nobles, fishers and Long Watch knights all come to the Fair.

The Orange Court.description: A sheltered guest wing adjoining the Winter Court: two stories of pale stone and carved timber enclose a spring-heated garden beneath a steep snowy glass roof. Orange trees grow in tiled beds beside breakfast tables and a screened warm bathing pool. An upper gallery holds comfortable chairs beside the warm chimney and private guest chambers. Invited visitors, recognized knights and their companions share meals, receive friends and linger in the warm garden.

Villa Parhelion.name: Villa Parhelion
Villa Parhelion.basicInfo: Villa Parhelion is a vast, windowless, fortress-like structure of black stone on the high pass between the Shadow Summits and the dwarven holds to the south, and the seat of the Syndicate in the north. Most who would trade with the vampire lords, or buy what is outlawed elsewhere, come through Parhelion to do it.
Villa Parhelion.hiddenInfo:
Parhelion was built by a vampire lord who could not bear the sun and would not live without the day. Its vast indoor halls are wonders of magic and mechanisms that seem like sunlit, outdoor spaces. Every bird, beast, and even insect in these worlds is a clockwork mechanism, every tree and blade of grass made of inert but real-seeming materials; all water and air circulating within is moved by hidden pumps and fans.

Parhelion's builder was slain by other vampires with the aid of the Syndicate after he grew too ambitious, and now the Syndicate uses it as its base of operations.

The Syndicate and vampire lords don't trust each other, but need each other: most trade with the vampire lords flows through Parhelion, since normal merchants won't deal with vampires. The goods sold here cannot easily be found elsewhere in Larion: the tools of blood-sorcerers, the workings of blood-magic, the spells and instruments of necromancy and psionic arts prohibited elsewhere.

The High Men who run the Syndicate gather here: the richest and most feared crime-lords alive, rivals who rule through tribute, debt, and murder. But Parhelion is safe, neutral ground, on pain of being declared an enemy to the entire Syndicate.

The Grey Guards are the Syndicate's own soldiers and the garrison of Parhelion. They keep the truce within the walls and turn their hands to nothing else: hard, competent, dead serious, courteous to those who merit it and cold to those who do not.

Parhelion Gate.description: The pass road climbs to a gate in a wall of black stone, squat and immense. A sun in bas-relief is carved into the black stone above the gate. The Syndicate's Grey Guards hold the yard and the doors.

Garden Hall.description: A vast hall containing a wide formal garden in daylight — gravel walks between clipped hedges, flowering beds, a fountain playing at the center, a false sky overhead. It serves as Parhelion's receiving hall. Guests wait on benches to be seen; servants and Grey Guards move among them and send each where their business lies, to the Market or down into the working halls, and turn none loose to wander. There are rough sorts here as well as fine, and most wait a little nervously.

Market Hall.description: A vast hall containing a walled garden of cottages under a gentle false sun, flower-bordered paths running between them, each cottage a quiet shopfront for a different dark trade — the tools of blood-sorcery in one, the instruments of necromancy in another, hexes and curses, the proscribed arts of the mind. A guest is received, judged, and shown within by a servant or a guard, and what is for sale is brought out behind a closed door to those thought worthy of seeing it. The custom here is unhurried and exclusive, the courtesy of a house that asks no questions of buyers who can afford its wares.

The Back Rooms.description: Service rooms that have no pretense of being out of doors. Hidden doors in the outdoor halls lead to bare stone corridors where the great pumps and fans and engines that drive Parhelion's counterfeit skies run day and night. Here the Grey Guards barrack and take their briefings, and bravos and hired hands wait between jobs. Those who work for the Syndicate may rise from hired hand to trusted to a name the High Men know by doing the deeds that need to be done.

The Dungeon Cells.description: Bare black stone, cell after cell behind iron, with Grey Guards walking the passages. The Syndicate keeps prisoners here for ransom and for leverage.

Idyll Hall.description: A vast hall containing a wide summer meadow at the height of day, tall grass and wildflowers running to a soft bright haze on every side, a still lake at its heart with rowboats drawn up at a little jetty. Fine lodges stand along the shore, and a great hall at the meadow's edge is where the made men of the Syndicate take their ease among comforts looted from a dozen kingdoms. The stair to the high tower climbs from here.

Celestial Hall.description: At the top of the tower, a vast hall made to seem the very heavens, a chamber of cloud and brilliant gold-white light where one stands as if lifted into a sunlit sky. A great orrery turns slowly at its center, the sun and wandering stars wheeling on golden arms, and a shaft of radiant light falls through it to strike a sphere of polished brass that blazes like a second sun. Beneath the orrery stands a long table where the High Men of the Syndicate meet in a council they call the High Table.

The Firewild.name: The Firewild
The Firewild.basicInfo: The unclaimed volcanic badlands east of Smoketown and the works—cinder-flats, sulfur vents, and fields of black lava-glass that even the Goblinate leaves alone. Fire-drakes den in the vents and hunt the open ground; their scales and the raw emberglass underfoot are worth a fortune to anyone who survives the taking.
The Firewild.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Firewild is wilderness, not a settlement—the creatures here default hostile to anything warm-blooded that enters their ground, and they do not parley. There are no inhabitants to bargain with.

The land itself is a threat. Sulfur vents, unstable lava-glass, and sudden ground-heat kill the unready as surely as any beast.

Fire-drakes are lesser kin of true dragons, vent-denning, territorial, and aggressive. They open from the air or burst from a vent-mouth, breathe fire, and fight to hold their ground. Their scale, claws, and eggs are the prize. Salamanders bask on the lava-glass and lash with fire when crowded. Magma oozes pool in the cooled tubes, slow and engulfing, dissolving what they catch.

Giant fire beetles scuttle the cinder-flats in numbers, their glands prized for the cold-light they shed; and the odd basilisk suns itself among the glass, deadly at a glance, given a wide berth even by the drakes.

Loot here is fire-aspected material. Drake scale is thick overlapping plate shed in moltings or stripped from a kill; worked into armor it turns flame and the breath of fire-things. Salamander-hide is supple and heat-proof, prized for fireproof garments and glove-leather. A fire beetle's glands hold a cold blue light that shines for days once cut free, a lantern that needs no flame and gives off no heat. Basilisk parts—the eye, the gizzard-stones—are the base for a salve that wards against petrification, the only common guard against the creature's own gaze. Raw emberglass is the great prize: a volcanic glass that holds fire in its heart, cut from seams in the lava-glass and the vent-walls. A blade or arrowhead of emberglass deals fire damage in place of its ordinary edge, and bites hardest into plants, fungi, trolls, venomous beasts, and things of frost.

The Cinder Flats.description: An open expanse of black ash and grit broken by sulfur vents that hiss and gout. The ground is warm underfoot and treacherous where crusted ash hides soft heat below. Bones of large beasts lie scattered and half-buried. Sightlines run long across the flats, broken only by drifting vent-smoke.

The Glass Fields.description: A plain of black volcanic glass, fused smooth and sharp-edged, glinting where the light catches it. Slabs of it can be quarried with effort and care. The petrified shapes of past wanderers stand here and there among the panes, frozen mid-stride.

The Vent-Dens.description: A broken country of fissures and old lava tubes where the heat pools thickest. Deep vent-mouths open in the rock, and cooled tubes hold slow-moving pools of molten residue that glow in the dark. Scattered scale and old moltings litter the approaches to the larger openings.

The Slag Warrens.name: The Slag Warrens
The Slag Warrens.basicInfo: An old goblin mine-works dug into the volcanic rock and then abandoned, its tunnels left half-collapsed when whatever broke in from below drove the diggers out. The goblins fled in a hurry and left their hauls behind—ore, tools, and locked caches still sitting in the dark. Something large dens in the deep galleries now, and the gobbos have not gone back.
The Slag Warrens.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Slag Warrens are abandoned and hostile—the thing that drove the goblins out still holds the deep galleries and attacks anything that comes within reach. It does not parley. Lesser vermin breeding in the warmth are equally hostile. There are no inhabitants to bargain with.

The works are unstable. Propped tunnels, flooded lower levels of cooled slag, and bad air in the deep cuts make the place a danger before anything attacks. Old goblin trap-lines, some still set, guard the better caches.

The deep galleries are denned by an ankheg grown huge in the heat—a burrowing thing with a chitin shell, great serrated jaws, and a spray of acid it spits to soften prey and stone alike. It moves through the rock itself, bursting up through floor and wall without warning, and drags what it catches back underground. It does not hunt the surface; the Warrens are its ground, and it defends them.

Giant fire beetles and worse vermin have bred in the abandoned cuts, swarming the upper tunnels in numbers.

Loot here is what the goblins left and what the burrower's nature provides. The abandoned caches hold raw ore, smithing tools, and coin locked away in the rush to flee—ordinary goods in quantity, the wages of a mine emptied overnight. An ankheg's shell-plates are thick acid-proof chitin, worked into armor that turns acid and the bite of acid-spitting things. Its acid gland, cut intact, yields a corrosive prized for eating through stone, locks, and hardened metal. The fire beetles here carry cold-light glands: a gland cut free shines blue for days, a flameless and heatless lantern.

The Mine-Mouth.description: The entrance works: a timber-framed entrance driven into the rock, with ore-carts abandoned on rusted rails and a winch-house gone to rot. The framing sags, and rubble half-blocks the way down. Daylight reaches only the first stretch before the tunnels go dark.

The Upper Cuts.description: A warren of narrow mining tunnels branching and doubling back, propped with failing timber and cut at odd angles to follow old seams. Side-chambers hold stacked crates and locked strongboxes left behind. The air grows close and warm the deeper the cuts run, and several passages end in fresh collapse.

The Lower Galleries.description: The lowest workings, where the diggers cut into natural caverns and stopped. The floor is broken and tunnel-bored in places, riddled with holes too large for any goblin tool, and pools of cooled black slag fill the low ground. The heat is heavy here and the dark complete. Bored shafts lead off into the surrounding rock.

Loot Landing.name: Loot Landing
Loot Landing.basicInfo: The Goblinate's war-harbor on the eastern shore, where raider fleets put in heavy with plunder and the docks turn into a marketplace the moment a prize-ship ties up. Cranes haul spoils onto the wharves, auctioneers bawl over the crowds, and crews flush with shares spend them on the worst the harbor offers. Cargo, captives, and raw materials all come ashore here.
Loot Landing.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Loot Landing is Goblinate military ground, run by the harbor-master's goblins and the marines who crew the fleet. It is not openly hostile to outsiders the way a monster lair is—a useful stranger with cargo to sell or coin to spend is tolerated and watched, the same as Smoketown. But it is a war-harbor under guard: spies are taken, and anyone caught freeing captives or moving against the fleet is killed or thrown in the pens.

The harbor runs on plunder. Prize-ships arrive and their hauls are auctioned dockside—luxuries, arms, ore, captured steel, anything the fleet has taken. Coin and treasure flow up to the Goblinate; raw materials, sulfur, timber, and ore flow on to the works. The marines are dangerous, drunk as often as not, and quick to violence, but they answer to the harbor-master and the harbor-master answers to the Governor.

The prisoner pens hold what the raiders take alive: pressed rowers for the galleys, captives held for ransom, and the unlucky bound for sale or the pyre.

The Syndicate works the harbor's underside, fencing goods the marines skim from their own hauls and selling passage and forged papers to those who can pay.

The Wharves.description: A long stone waterfront of berths and jetties, crane-gantries leaning over the water to haul cargo from the holds. Ships of the raider fleet ride at anchor and tie up at the quays, low and lean and built for speed. Ramps and gangplanks run down to the dock, and stacked crates and barrels crowd the open ground between cranes.

The Auction Yard.description: A broad cobbled square set back from the water, ringed with auction-blocks and trestle-stalls. Raised platforms stand where goods are shown and cried. Strongrooms and counting-houses line the landward edge, their doors iron-bound and guarded. The square is built to hold crowds.

The Cranehouse Rows.description: The harbor's working district behind the auction square: warehouses, ship-chandlers, rope-walks, and the drinking-dens and gambling-halls where crews spend their shares. Narrow lanes run between the storehouses, easy to lose a tail in. The buildings are timber and salvaged ship-timber, packed close.

The Pens.description: A walled compound of holding-cages and barred sheds at the harbor's edge, set apart from the trade. Heavy gates and a guarded yard control the way in. Stocks and chaining-posts stand in the open ground. The compound backs onto the water, where galleys take on rowers.

The Dragonworks.name: The Dragonworks
The Dragonworks.basicInfo: The Church of the Pyre's great alchemical works, set apart from Smoketown out on the lava-fields where a live fissure feeds the vats. This is where dragonfire is brewed in bulk—the alchemical fuel that charges every Goblinate weapon. Blast-walls of heaped earth ring the yards, the air shimmers with heat and fumes, and the whole place is built to keep its fire from spreading to anything the Goblinate cares about.
The Dragonworks.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Dragonworks is a Church of the Pyre stronghold under heavy guard, and its perimeter shoots first. Pyre wardens and Goblinate marines hold the gates and the walls; the alchemist-priests within suffer no unauthorized step inside the yards. Anyone who reaches the works without leave is treated as a saboteur and killed. The creatures of the surrounding fields are hostile wilderness.

The works exist because dragonfire is too dangerous to brew inside the city—even the goblins will not sleep beside it. Drawing on the heat of the fissure, the alchemist-priests cook raw reagents down into the finished fuel in great vats, decant it into sealed vessels, and send it up the Iron Road to the Firelance Foundry and the mountain. The labor is done in sealed vestments against the fumes, and accidents take workers regularly.

The place is built around the danger it makes. The yards are split by earthen blast-berms so a blast in one cannot reach the next. The vat-house holds the cooking. The decanting-floor fills and seals the vessels. The stores hold finished fuel and raw reagents apart from each other, since together they are catastrophe. A fire loosed in the stores or the vat-house would gut the works and cripple the Goblinate's weapon-supply for a season—the place is one spark from destroying itself, which is its great weakness and the reason the perimeter is so absolute.

The alchemist-priests are zealots who hold that the fire they brew is the holy instrument of the world's burning. They do the work as a sacrament.

Loot here is the finished product and the means of making it. Sealed vessels of dragonfire are the prize: an alchemical fuel that ignites on contact and clings, burning fierce and hard to quench, ready to charge a weapon or set a fire nothing will put out. The alchemist-priests' stores hold rare reagents—the costly stock that goes into the brewing, valuable to any alchemist. Pyre vestments are heat-proof and fume-proof sealed garments, proof against fire and choking air both.

The Gatehouse.description: The single guarded entrance through the earthen ramparts that ring the works: a fortified gate with a checkpoint, watch-platforms, and a killing-ground of open cinder before it. The blast-walls rise beyond, heaped earth and slag taller than a man, with smoke and shimmering heat showing above them.

The Vat-Yards.description: The heart of the works: a compound of great iron vats and brick furnaces divided into bays by earthen blast-berms, so each stands apart from the next. Pipes and flues run between them, and a fissure glows red at the yard's center, feeding heat to the vats above it. Catwalks cross overhead. The ground is stained and scorched.

The Decanting Floor.description: A long shed of workbenches and filling-rigs where the finished fuel is drawn off into sealed vessels and crated for transport. Racks of empty and filled vessels line the walls behind blast-shielding. Loading-bays open onto a yard where wagons are made ready. Everything here is built low and heavy against accident.

The Stores.description: Two separate magazines set well apart behind their own berms: one for crated reagents, one for finished fuel, kept distant from each other by design. Heavy doors, thick walls, and warning-marks guard both. The ground between them is open and watched from the walls.

The Firelance Foundry.name: The Firelance Foundry
The Firelance Foundry.basicInfo: The works where the Goblinate's fire-weapons are built and tested, set on a scorched hillside within reach of Smoketown. Firelances and heavier engines are assembled here, charged with dragonfire, and proof-fired into the bare slope until they are trusted to work. The crack and roar of test-firing carries for miles, and the hillside above the foundry is burned black and littered with the wreckage of weapons that failed.
The Firelance Foundry.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Firelance Foundry is Goblinate military ground under guard. Hobgoblin master-smiths and goblin crews run the works; marines hold the gates and the proving-slope. Outsiders without leave are taken for spies, and the prototype-stores are the most closely watched ground in the foundry. The surrounding country is hostile wilderness.

The foundry assembles what the Dragonworks fuels. Tubes, hafts, and fittings are forged and fitted; the finished weapons are charged with sealed dragonfire and carried out to the slope to be proof-fired before they go up the Iron Road. The master-smiths guard their methods jealously, and the newest designs—heavier lances, multi-shot engines, weapons not yet in the field—are kept under lock in the prototype-stores.

The proving happens on the bare hillside above the works, fired into the empty slope. When a minister or an archpriest visits, the test is sometimes made on bound prisoners instead of the slope, a demonstration dressed as a trial.

The foundry's true value is its designs. The working weapons can be stolen or copied; the prototypes are worth more than the finished lances, since they are what the Goblinate will field next and what its enemies most need to understand.

Loot here is weapons and the knowledge of them. A firelance is the Goblinate's signature arm: a hafted metal tube, charged with dragonfire, that throws a gout of clinging flame at what it is aimed at—deadly, short-ranged, and dangerous to a careless wielder. The prototype weapons are stranger and stronger: heavier lances that throw farther, engines that fire more than once, designs not yet loosed on Larion. The smiths' design-plates and pattern-books are worth as much as the weapons, the means to build or counter what the foundry makes.

The Foundry Gate.description: The guarded entrance to the works, a fortified gate in a stockade wall with watch-platforms above and a yard of scorched ground before it. Smoke rises from the forge-stacks beyond the wall, and the burned hillside looms over everything, dark and scarred.

The Assembly Hall.description: A long forge-hall of furnaces, drop-hammers, and fitting-benches where weapon-tubes are worked and assembled. Racks of hafts, fittings, and finished lances line the walls. A charging-bay set behind heavy shielding stands apart, where the dragonfire is loaded. Wide doors open onto the proving-slope.

The Proving Slope.description: The bare, blackened hillside above the foundry, fired into until nothing grows on it. Firing-stands and earth-banked positions face the slope from below. The ground is cratered, slagged, and strewn with the burst and twisted wreckage of weapons that failed their test. Chaining-posts stand among the firing-stands.

The Prototype Stores.description: A locked and shielded magazine set apart from the assembly hall, walled in heavy stone and barred at the door. Racks and crates within hold the foundry's newest and most guarded work behind blast-shielding. A single watched approach leads to it.

Dun Teine Watch.name: Dun Teine Watch
Dun Teine Watch.basicInfo: A dwarven fortress in the high snows of the southern peninsula, holding the one approach down into the volcanic country below. Its walls are thirty feet of fitted stone and it has never been taken—the Goblinate has reckoned the cost and left it alone. The watch keeps a long vigil over the smoking land and the road that climbs from it.
Dun Teine Watch.hiddenInfo:
Inhabitants: dwarves of an old mountain line, the garrison and the families who keep the Watch—smiths, wardens, watch-keepers, and the few traders hardy enough to climb here. Outsiders fleeing the Goblinate, deserters off the works, and adventurers with business below are taken in if they are not a danger. Population is dwarf-led and mixed at the hearth.

The Watch holds because taking it would cost the Goblinate more than ignoring it does, and because the dwarves keep the one defensible approach down to the volcanic country. They are not strong enough to march on Smoketown and know it; their work is to hold the gate, keep the count, and shelter those who come up off the peninsula alive.

The Watch keeps the old lore of the mountain below. Its archives and its eldest hold what the Goblinate has forgotten: the deep history of Fire Mountain, the wards the old dwarven vigil raised over the fire-breach, the name and binding of Suleyvan the Sealer, and the thing of blue flame that stands the breach. They keep a tally of what goes up the Iron Road and into the Fissure—the relics, the reagents, the prisoners of particular kinds—and they read in that tally the shape of what the Pyre is preparing.

The Watch is the natural seat for work on the peninsula. Its people know the ground below: the war-machine and its arteries, the harbor at Loot Landing, the works that brew and build the Goblinate's fire, the mountain and its garrison. They take in those who would move against any of it, and they pay for what hurts the Goblinate or thins the road. Honest goods are sold here at hard prices—frost-gear above all, the rimebone and frostjade and frost-blessed steel that the wilds and the fire-things below make necessary, carried up at ruinous cost.

The Gate-Tunnel.description: The only way in: a stone tunnel driven through the curtain wall, gated and portcullised at both ends, with murder-holes above and guard-niches to either side. Snow drifts against the outer gate. The tunnel opens inward onto the fortress yard, and the cold of the pass gives way to the warmth of stone and fire within.

The Watch-Yard.description: The fortress's central court, ringed by the inner keep, the forge, and the barrack-halls built against the curtain wall. Stairs climb to the wall-walk and the watch-tower above. Snow is kept swept from the flagstones, braziers burn at the corners, and the smoking land below is visible through the embrasures of the high wall.

The Long Hearth.description: The great common hall of the Watch, a long stone room dug into the keep with a fire-trench running its length and benches and trestle-tables down both sides. Casks line one wall and a kitchen smokes at the far end. It is warm, low-ceilinged and close, hung with the banners and trophies of an old garrison.

The Forge-Hall.description: The Watch's smithy, built around a deep forge that burns day and night against the cold. Anvils, quenching-troughs, and racks of tools and finished steel fill the hall. Stores of ore and stranger stock—pale frost-metals among them—are kept in side-vaults.

The Watch-Tower.description: The highest point of the fortress, a stone tower above the wall-walk with a railed top open to the wind. From here the whole smoking peninsula spreads below: the road climbing from the lowlands, the haze over Smoketown, and the dark cone of Fire Mountain at the far cape. A signal-brazier and a great horn stand ready at the parapet. Within, beneath the lookout, a vaulted room holds the Watch's scrolls and tomes about Fire Mountain.

The Watch-Tower-Lookout.description: The railed crown of the tower, open to the sky and the cutting wind, where a watcher stands at all hours. The view runs the length of the peninsula in clear weather. The signal-brazier and the warning-horn are here.

The Rumblehorn Run.name: The Rumblehorn Run
The Rumblehorn Run.basicInfo: A long upland glen contested by Stonewall and Stormhammer, threaded by old droveways and dotted with cairns. A half-wild herd of rumblehorns runs here — huge, shaggy, foul-tempered highland cattle that both clans claim by founding-right and neither will cede. No one holds the glen. Both clans send crews in to cut beasts from the herd, brand them, and drive them home, and the crews cross each other doing it. Wargs den in the high crags and hunt the herd's stragglers.
The Rumblehorn Run.hiddenInfo:
The glen is contested ground. Stonewall says their forebears first penned the rumblehorn line; Stormhammer says possession settles it and rides in to take beasts whenever they please. Both send rustling crews each season to brand prize beasts with their clan's mark and drive them home, and to cut loose any beast the rival branded first. The rules are unwritten and both sides pretend not to know them: no killing over a beast, no burning a rival's cairn, everything else fair. An outsider crew can hire on to either clan, run both, or cut beasts for themselves and sell to whoever pays.

The rumblehorns are the first danger. They are not malicious, but a bull weighs as much as a loaded cart and a spooked one will flatten a crew without noticing. They move where they like and gore anything that crowds them wrong. Cutting one prize beast clear of the herd and getting it home is the whole game and most of the risk.

IMPORTANT: the wargs of the high crags are hostile and hunt the glen by their own appetite. They den in the broken rock, run in packs, and work the herd's edges — cutting off the straggler, the wounded, the lone. They open by circling and harrying from cover, drive prey toward the rocks where the rest of the pack waits, and break off only when badly outmatched, returning after dark. A crew busy wrestling a bull is exactly the straggler they want.

The old cairns are droving-burials, generations of herders and clan-dead laid under stone along the paths. Most are quiet. A few of the larger barrows hold barrow-wights: drovers of old laid in their grave-arms to guard their kin, who rise and fight anyone who breaks into the barrow.

A branded rumblehorn is a prize beast worth a season's coin, and a champion bull is clan-wealth on the hoof. Both clans pay bounties for beasts brought to their own mark, and pay better for beasts cut loose from the rival's. Warg pelts and fangs are hunt-trophies and crafting stock. The barrows hold old arms, bronze ornaments, and grave-silver, and the deepest hold grander grave-goods under a guard.

The Droveway.description: A worn cattle-track climbs between low shoulders of heather and grey stone, then crests and opens onto the glen below. The ground falls away into a long green hollow ringed by crags, droveways crossing it like old scars, cairns standing here and there along the paths. Far across, the rock breaks into a tumble of scree and shadowed clefts under the high ridge. A standing waystone at the crest is carved on two faces — a Stonewall mark cut deep on one, a Stormhammer mark cut deeper over it, and both re-cut again above.

The Glen Floor.description: The hollow's grassy bottom, wide and open, cropped short by grazing and churned to mud along the droveways. Small cairns of piled stone stand at the path-forks, some no higher than a knee, weathered smooth. The grass hides dips and runnels deep enough to turn an ankle or screen a crouching shape. Broad trampled lanes mark where the big beasts move. Toward the ridge the ground rises and the stones grow thicker; toward the lower end a stream cuts a muddy ford.

The Warg Crags.description: The glen's upper end breaks into a steep tumble of grey scree and split rock, riddled with clefts and low caves. Bones lie scattered among the stones — cracked, gnawed, dragged. From the high shelves the whole glen lies open to view, the herd's lanes and the droveways small below. The footing is loose and treacherous, and a slip starts a slide. Cold air moves down out of the dark openings in the rock.

The Old Cairns.description: A stretch of the upper droveway where the burial-marks cluster — dozens of stone cairns, and among them a handful of true barrows: long low mounds turfed over, entrance-stones half-sunk in the earth. Some mounds have settled and split, showing black gaps into the dark beneath. Carved kerbstones ring the larger barrows, worn but still legible: bulls, knotwork, the marks of droving-families long gone. The grass grows rank and undisturbed here, and even the herd keeps off this ground.

Tuskhollow.name: Tuskhollow
Tuskhollow.basicInfo: A giantborn stead in a high cattle-vale above the dwarf country, where the Tuskhollow folk raise enormous shaggy bulls and settle every dispute by feats of strength. They claim descent from the first giants who shaped the mountains, and they hold a stretch of Stonewall grazing-ground and a Stormhammer drove-road as theirs by that birthright. The dwarves say otherwise. The boundary gets argued every season, sometimes with fists. The vale's high crags hold predators that come down for the calves.
Tuskhollow.hiddenInfo:
The Tuskhollow giantborn are impossible neighbors. In peace they are open-handed, loud, and generous; they feast hugely and laugh louder. But they take honor with absolute seriousness, settle everything — debts, disputes, insults, who was right about a bull's bloodline — by wrestling and feats of strength, and they remember a slight for generations. Insult one and you face a challenge that ends in broken bones; back down from a fair challenge and you are nothing to them ever after. They are half again a human's height and strong past any dwarf, and they know it.

The trouble with the dwarves is a boundary. The Tuskhollow claim a high meadow Stonewall has grazed for ages and a drove-road Stormhammer uses to move beasts, both theirs, they say, since the first giants walked. They drive off dwarf herds, block the road, and answer complaints with a grin and an offer to settle it in the ring. Neither clan can shift them by force without a war nobody wants, and neither will concede the ground.

The Tuskhollow hire out the work their own hands are too big or too few for: a prize bull gone down a crevice too narrow for them, calves taken by crag predators, a beast strayed onto ground they would rather not be seen crossing. They pay well and they pay in their own coin — giantborn-forged gear, fine cattle, and favor, which from a people this strong is worth more than silver. They honor a debt as long as they remember a slight, which is to say forever.

IMPORTANT: the predators of the high crags are hostile and hunt by their own hunger, not on anyone's command. Hill-cats — great tawny mountain hunters the size of ponies — den in the rocks above the vale and come down for stragglers and calves. They open from cover with a rushing charge, drag down the isolated, and break off when met with a real fight, slinking back to try again later. The Tuskhollow treat losing a calf as an insult to answer rather than a danger to flee, which is how a fence-mending job becomes a hunt.

Giantborn-forged gear is oversized, plain, and brutally well-made — work-tools and arms built to a giantborn's hand and reach. Tuskhollow prize cattle are clan-grade beasts worth real coin at market. Hill-cat pelts are luxury hunting-trophies and their fangs and claws are crafting stock.

The High Track.description: A steep path switchbacks up out of the dwarf valleys into thinner, colder air, the grass turning to high meadow. Ahead the vale opens: a broad green bowl under bare peaks, longhouses sized for folk half again a human's height, stone-walled bull-pens stretching toward a stream, and a great standing stone at the boundary carved with a horned, broad-shouldered figure.

The Vale Common.description: The heart of the stead — an open common of cropped turf ringed by oversized longhouses, their doors built for giantborn with smaller doors cut alongside for ordinary visitors. A wrestling-ring of standing stones marks the center, the grass inside worn to bare earth. Graduated lifting-stones line one edge, the largest a boulder taller than a dwarf. The chief's longhouse stands at the head of the common; the largest hall, doors flung wide in daylight, serves food and drink at tables a dwarf must climb onto. The bull-pens lie just beyond, and the high fences mark where the meadow runs up toward the crags.
