The Bull-Pens.description: Massive dry-stone enclosures holding the stead's prize bulls apart from the main herds — animals shaggy, horned, and ill-tempered, each pen built to a scale that dwarfs a human. Beyond the pens the vale opens into grazing land, the main herds scattered across the slopes. A deep, narrow crevice splits the ground past the furthest fence, the rock dropping away into shadow too tight for a broad-shouldered body to follow.

The High Meadow.description: The disputed high ground — a wide upland meadow of good grass, dwarf grazing by long custom and giantborn ground by claim. A drove-road crosses it, rutted by generations of cattle. Boundary-stones stand along the edges, and someone has been at them: a dwarf clan-mark cut on one face, a horned giant figure carved over it, the dwarf mark re-cut deeper above that. Above the meadow the slope steepens into grey scree and split rock, riddled with dens and shadowed clefts, the whole vale laid out below it from the heights.

The Crookback.name: The Crookback
The Crookback.basicInfo: A wind-bent tor on the high trade road, its summit a crooked finger of rock, the gullies beneath it a warren of camps. Clan Bighorn holds it — a clan of goatfolk who style themselves the Cloven People, ruled by a thane, flying a war-banner, and utterly convinced they are a highland clan the equal of any dwarven house. They keep the road as their clan's own, demand tribute from all who cross, and take by horn and blade from anyone who refuses.
The Crookback.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Clan Bighorn are bandits and default to hostile. The 'tribute' they demand is robbery dressed as a clan's lawful due — there is no safe passage truly bought, only what a frightened traveler can hand over to buy a few more steps. They favor the shakedown over the kill because a robbed traveler can be robbed again, so a fat purse and a respectful manner may buy a way through; a thin purse, a sneer at their clanhood, or a party worth stripping brings the charge instead. They are goatfolk — horned, hoofed, and shaggy — and they fight with a headlong butting rush down the gullies and good salvaged steel.

The Cloven People believe in themselves with their whole hearts. They have watched the dwarves keep clans and holds and thanes and honor for ages and decided they will have all of it and do it better, having been born with the horns for it. They have a thane, a war-banner of their own design, a roll of grudges, and a fierce touchy pride in the dignity of the clan — and they are deadly serious about every scrap of it. Insult Clan Bighorn's standing and you have done worse in their eyes than refuse the tribute. What the dwarves find an outrage and a mockery, the Cloven find simple truth: they are a clan, the road is their clan's ground, and the dwarves are merely sore about the competition.

The thane is a massive grey-pelted goatfolk with horns scarred from a lifetime of settling matters skull-first, who rules the clan from the hall atop the tor and takes any slight to its honor as a thing to answer in person. He wants a seat at the Folkmoot and a clan's respect across the highlands, and the dwarves will see the Crookback burned before they grant a goat-clan either.

Clan Bighorn lives by what the road brings and by trades no honest crew will touch — fencing stolen goods, running rustled cattle through the gullies, holding the occasional captive for ransom. Both Stonewall and Stormhammer want the thane's head, and neither has spared the warriors to climb the tor and take it.

The thane's hoard holds the pick of years of robbery — coin, plate, trade-cargo, fenced goods. Cattle penned in the gullies carry the high glens' brands and drive back for clan-bounty. The thane is wanted by both dwarven clans, and his head pays from either hand. Bighorn arms and armor are a patchwork of good salvaged gear, often dwarven-made, worn now by the Cloven who took it.

The Narrows.description: The trade road bends into the tor's shadow and the walls close in — a gully barely two carts wide, the rock rising sheer on both sides, the crooked summit looming over the rim. Boulders and the dragged-out wrecks of old wagons choke the verges, stripped to the axles. Ledges and clefts notch the walls above, well-placed for watching the road or raining stones down on it. The way ahead twists out of sight; the way back is just as narrow.

The Gullies.description: A maze of steep-sided ravines beneath the tor, crammed with Clan Bighorn's warren — lean-to camps and shacks of salvaged timber wedged into the clefts, rope-bridges slung between the rims, cookfire smoke hanging in the still air. Stolen goods sit stacked under tarps in the dry hollows, and a clan-banner of stitched hides and painted horns hangs from a high pole. A wider cleft holds dry-stone pens churned to mud, thick with the smell of penned cattle. The paths branch and double back, the walls cutting every sightline short and climbing too sheer to scale. A switchback trail climbs toward the summit.

The Crook.description: The tor's crooked summit, a bent spire of wind-scoured rock with a broad shelf beneath the finger where Clan Bighorn has raised its hall — a long structure of fitted salvage and hide, grander than the camps below, the great clan-banner snapping above it. Trophies of the clan's making line the approach: dwarven shields with the marks defaced and re-painted in Bighorn's colors. The whole sweep of the road lies open from here, gullies and narrows small below, the high country rolling away on every side.

Varric's Span.name: Varric's Span
Varric's Span.basicInfo: A stretch of the great trade road where it crosses a deep gorge on a series of high dwarven bridges, ancient stonework spanning a drop that swallows the river-roar below. Trolls have taken the bridges — denning in the piers and the dark beneath the arches, hunting the road by night. It is the fastest way through the high country and the most dangerous, and it is the ground where a clan muster once broke in blood, a place every dwarf in Highheath knows by name.
Varric's Span.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: the trolls of the span default to hostile and hunt anything that crosses after dark. They den in the gorge piers and under the arches, hauling prey down off the road and into the dark to feed. They are slow to rouse but relentless once roused, and their wounds knit shut as you watch — cuts close, bone resets, a felled troll rises again unless the hurt is burned. Fire stops them; nothing else stops them for long. By day they hole up in the cold dark beneath the spans, and a fast crew can cross unmet; by night the bridges belong to them.

The Day at Varric's Span is the region's one true grudge, and it is not joked about. A generation back, Stonewall and Stormhammer mustered together against a troll-horde that had closed the road. Stonewall formed the wall and held it; Stormhammer charged ahead of the line and died on the bridge, cut off and overwhelmed while the wall stood fast and did not break to reach them. Stormhammer says the wall stood by and watched their kin butchered. Stonewall says the charge broke discipline and doomed itself. Every dwarf in Highheath knows someone who was there.

The troll-dead and the war-dead lie tangled in the gorge below, where bodies fell from the bridges and were never recovered — the drop is sheer and the trolls den at the bottom.

Troll-hide and troll parts are hunt-trophies and crafting stock, prized by those who know that what regenerates is worth the taking. The arms and armor of the fallen muster still lie on the spans and in the gorge where dwarves died — a broken Stormhammer warmaul, Stonewall shields rusting where the wall held the line, clan-marked blades — old work, finely made, and heavy with meaning to anyone who carries it home. The gorge floor holds what fell and was never climbed down for.

The Approach.description: The trade road climbs to the lip of a vast gorge, where the first of the high bridges leaps out across the drop. The stonework is old dwarven make — fitted blocks, carved piers, arches thrown across a chasm so deep the river is only a white thread and a distant roar far below. Wind funnels up the gorge and over the road. Cairns stand along the verge before the first span, weathered grey, some carved with clan-marks. The bridge runs out ahead into open air, the next pier rising from the dark below.

The Spans.description: The crossing proper — a chain of high arched bridges leaping pier to pier across the gorge, the road running narrow along their backs with low parapets and long drops to either side. The piers plunge into shadow below, their bases lost in the dark where the river runs. Rusted gear lies scattered along the stonework and caught in the parapet-joints — blades, shield-rims, a helm wedged in a crack. Dark openings gape in the pier-tops and under the arch-springs, leading down into the bridgework. The wind never stops.

The Underspan.description: Below the bridge-decks, a world of cold stone and shadow — the great piers descending into the gorge, ledges and galleries cut into the rock between them, the arches springing overhead and the drop falling away beneath. Bones lie heaped in the sheltered hollows, cracked and gnawed, tangled here and there with rusted iron and rotted leather. The river roars somewhere below in the dark. The deepest ledges run down toward the gorge floor, where the light does not reach.

Storm Crag.name: Storm Crag
Storm Crag.basicInfo: A high peak wrapped in a storm that never breaks — a black thunderhead clamped over the summit year-round, lightning walking the crags, thunder rolling down the passes below. The Laughing Jarl holds it: a rogue storm giant who answers to no one and made the mountain his seat, his tribute-beasts ranging the slopes and his plunder heaped in the hall at the top.
Storm Crag.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Storm Crag is the Laughing Jarl's ground and everything on it is hostile. The beasts he has gathered — warg packs, hill-trolls, and worse — range the slopes as his hunters and tribute-takers, and they attack anything climbing toward the summit. The Jarl himself does not parley; he toys. He is a mountain of a giant, vast even by giant measure, and he finds the whole world funny, most of all the small things that come to kill him. He will talk, taunt, bargain in bad faith, and laugh the while — and the laughing is a trap, because he is never more dangerous than when he is amused.

The Jarl took the storm-peak for sport and appetite and made it his own. He gathers beasts and broken things to him as a warlord gathers a warband, breaks bridges and crushes caravans for the joy of it, ransoms what he takes, and sets the dwarf clans at each other with cruel jokes that cost lives. Half the songs sung in Dun Solas are about him, and it is said he enjoys hearing them. The stone giants of the high valleys, who keep an old pact with the highland dwarves, disown him utterly and would pay richly to see him fall.

In a fight the Jarl throws stone and calls the storm down — lightning answers his hand, and a struck blow can fling a dwarf off the mountain. He fights like the contest is beneath him, careless and grinning, until the hurt is real, and a giant who stops laughing is a giant fighting for his life. He keeps his beasts between himself and danger and laughs when they die for him.

The Jarl's hoard is generations of ransom and plunder heaped in the summit hall — coin, plate, fine arms and armor, the wealth of a hundred crushed caravans. His tribute-beasts yield warg pelts and fangs, hide, and trophy parts to those who can take them. The captives he holds for ransom are worth more returned alive than anything else on the mountain.

The Thunder Road.description: The pass climbs toward the storm-peak, the air growing heavy and charged, thunder rolling down to meet the climber. The trail switchbacks up bare grey rock toward a black wall of cloud clamped over the summit above, lightning flickering inside it. Scorch-marks blacken the stone where strikes have fallen. Wind drives down the slope hard enough to stagger.

The Crag Slopes.description: The mountain's broken shoulders, a wilderness of scree, boulder-fields, and shadowed clefts climbing into the storm. Dens and lairs notch the rock — bone-littered hollows, beast-trampled ground. The cloud closes lower here, rain and lightning lashing the heights, visibility cut to grey murk between the strikes. Switchback trails and goat-paths climb toward the summit, and the footing is loose and steep and treacherous in the wet. Where lightning strikes the same rock again and again, the stone has fused into streaks of thunderglass.

The Storm-Hall.description: The summit, inside the storm — a vast open shelf of black stone beneath the heart of the thunderhead, lightning falling close. A great hall stands here, giant-built from raised slabs and the bones and timbers of what the Jarl has broken, its roof open to the raging sky. Plunder is heaped within and spilling out across the shelf — coin, arms, the splintered wealth of crushed caravans. The whole of Highheath lies spread out far below through the gaps in the cloud, tiny and distant. The shelf around the hall is scarred with thunderglass from a thousand strikes.

The Folkmoot.name: The Folkmoot
The Folkmoot.basicInfo: A contest-ground at the crossing of the high roads, built around the Stone of Bonds — an ancient black monolith that binds any oath sworn before it. This is where the clans settle what they cannot let lie: not with axes, but by out-doing each other.
The Folkmoot.hiddenInfo:
The Folkmoot is how Highheath settles a grudge without going to war. A debt, a boundary, an insult three generations stale — you do not raid over it and you do not sue, you bring it to the Moot and settle it in front of the whole highlands. An oath sworn at the Stone of Bonds binds; a contest fought and lost in fair sight is over, and the Stone makes it stick. This is the only reason Stonewall and Stormhammer have not burned each other down: the Moot lets a dwarf lose without losing face.

The contests are deadly serious and gloriously stupid in equal measure, and no one here sees any contradiction in that. The drinking matches are real tests of a dwarf's standing and not entered lightly. The stone-lifts run up to a boulder only a handful of giantborn have ever raised. And the Aurochs Stand is exactly what it sounds like: a dwarf plants their feet, a penned rumblehorn is loosed, and brow meets horn, and the one who holds the line wins. The wall of names runs back generations, and some of the names are crossed out.

The Moot-keeper is a barrel-shaped old dwarf with a voice that carries across the whole ground and a record at the Stand no one living has matched. She runs the contests, witnesses the oaths, and bellows insults at champions twice her size to get a rise out of the crowd. Her neutrality is iron, because she has beaten everyone and owes nothing to anyone, and she is the only soul both clans trust to call a match fair. She is loud, rude, gleeful, and entirely incorruptible.

An outsider can earn standing here with no clan's leave — enter the contests, take the Stand, swear a Moot-oath that means something. A thane will sponsor a promising stranger against a rival's champion, and the side-bets on a good match run heavy. A visitor can settle their own business under a binding oath, or win another's grudge for them in the ring.

IMPORTANT: the Stone of Bonds is real and an oath sworn before it binds in earnest — the narrator should treat a Moot-oath as a genuine, weighty commitment, not empty ceremony. A crew called the Stake-men work the contests on the quiet, fixing matches, shaving the odds, and leaning on fighters to throw a bout. They are the Syndicate's hand at the Moot and they keep it well hidden, because rigging the Stone's own ground is the one thing that would turn the whole highlands against them.

A Moot-oath is a binding commitment witnessed by the Stone and the crowd both. Standing won at the Moot is a real reputation in dwarf country that opens doors a stranger's coin cannot. Thanes pay well to see a rival's champion humbled, and the side-betting makes a good fighter coin.

The Crossing.description: Where the high roads meet, marked by a carved waypost worn smooth by hands. Low stone buildings with bright-painted doors line both roads, and the Stone of Bonds rises dark from the center of it all — a black monolith twice a dwarf's height, its surface carved over every inch with the marks of oaths sworn across the ages. Stalls and traders crowd the road-edges. From here the ground falls away toward a natural hollow ringed with stone seats, and a roar of voices rises from it.

The Contest Ground.description: A natural hillside amphitheater, stone seats rising in worn tiers around a beaten-earth floor. A wrestling-ring of standing stones marks one end, the grass long since stomped to bare dirt. Graduated lifting-stones line the floor's edge, the heaviest a boulder taller than the dwarves who fail to shift it. A stout-fenced pen stands at the far end where a great shaggy rumblehorn waits, and before it a worn patch of ground where the Stand is taken. A board fixed to the amphitheater wall is crowded with carved names, a good many struck through.

The Steaming Pools.description: Open-air hot springs at the ground's edge, stone-lined pools steaming in the cold air, ringed by benches and low tables. This is where the contests cool off and the real talk happens — challenges thrown, bets laid, oaths agreed before they go to the Stone.

The Skarn.name: The Skarn
The Skarn.basicInfo: A high glacier-pass through the white peaks, where a frozen river of ice grinds down between black cliffs and a field of ice-scoured boulders. It is a hard shortcut between the holds, days faster than the low roads and far more dangerous. Yetis den in the ice-caves along the walls and hunt the pass.
The Skarn.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: the yetis of the Skarn default to hostile and hunt the pass as their own ground. They are huge, white-furred, and near invisible against the snow until they are on you, and they take prey by ambush — rushing out of cover, a cliffside, or a snowbank, to seize and drag the catch back toward the ice-caves. They are strong enough to break a dwarf in two and patient enough to stalk a party for a long way before they strike. In a real fight they will haul off a single victim and let the rest flee rather than face a braced and ready crew, then return for the stragglers once the party is strung out and tired.

The pass is the fast way between holds and the white country beyond, which is why crews keep risking it despite what dens there. Storms close it without warning, whiteouts cut sight to an arm's length, and the ice underfoot hides crevasses deep enough to swallow a wagon.

The ice-caves where the yetis den hold what they have dragged off the pass over the years — the gear and goods of travelers who did not make it, frozen into the cave-ice and the packed snow. Yeti pelts are thick winter-hide, prized for cold-country gear, and their great claws and fangs are crafting stock.

The Pass Mouth.description: The trail climbs to where the glacier spills down between two black cliff-walls, the ice cracked and blue-shadowed underfoot. The way narrows into the pass ahead, the boulder-field beyond half-buried in old snow. Dark openings notch the cliffs to either side, high and low. Wind drives loose snow down the throat of the pass in stinging gusts, and the light off the ice is hard and white.

The Boulder Field.description: The pass widens into a long field of ice-scoured boulders, some the size of houses, scattered across the glacier's back and packed around with drifted snow. Sightlines break every few strides — a crew can see clearly one moment and be walled in by stone and snow the next. The glacier groans and shifts underfoot, and cracks open here and there into blue depths. The cliffs rise sheer on both sides, pocked with cave-mouths, and the high white peaks crowd close overhead.

The Ice-Caves.description: Cave-mouths in the cliff base, opening into a warren of ice-walled hollows and snow-packed tunnels that run back into the rock. Bones lie scattered and broken in the entrances, dwarf and beast both, frozen into the floor. Gear and frozen bundles are half-sunk in the cave-ice — a pack here, a haft of steel there, the shapes of things older and deeper in. The cold is hard and still away from the wind, and the deeper hollows fall into blue dark.

Wyrmtarn.name: Wyrmtarn
Wyrmtarn.basicInfo: A frozen mountain tarn high in the white peaks, its surface a sheet of cracked grey ice ringed by snowbound scree. Rimewyrms tunnel through the ice and the frozen ground beneath it — long pale serpents that burst up through the surface to take prey, then vanish back into the dark below. The ice is littered with the wreckage of those they caught: shattered carts, scattered bone, dark holes punched up through the sheet.
Wyrmtarn.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: the rimewyrms of the tarn default to hostile and hunt the ice as their hunting ground. They move unseen beneath the frozen surface and the packed earth around the tarn, tracking the tread of anything heavy crossing above by the vibration of it, then erupting up through the ice to seize prey in a single rush before submerging again. They are long, pale, and cold-blooded, blind but for the shaking of the ground, and a crew that stops moving or moves lightly can pass where a heavy, blundering party draws a strike. A wounded wyrm dives and waits rather than pressing a losing fight, and surfaces again when the prey has let its guard down.

The tarn freezes thick enough to walk and thin enough in places to drop a careless step into black water beneath. The wyrms' tunnels honeycomb the ice and the frozen banks, and the surface can give way over a fresh one.

The old bone of dead wyrms, frozen deep in the tarn's ice, is rimebone, and the living wyrms' hide and fangs are crafting stock for those who can take them. The ice of the tarn holds what the wyrms dragged down and lost — gear and goods of past catches, frozen into the sheet and sunk in the shallows where a strike went through.

The Frozen Shore.description: The trail comes down to the rim of the tarn, a flat sheet of cracked grey ice ringed by drifted scree. Dark holes punch up through the surface here and there, rimmed with shattered ice and refrozen at the edges. Wreckage juts from the sheet — a cartwheel, splintered timber, the curve of a ribcage frozen mid-sink. The far shore is a pale blur across the open ice, and the peaks stand white and close around the bowl.

The Ice Sheet.description: The frozen surface of the tarn, wide and open and offering nowhere to hide. The ice is grey and cracked, clear in patches over black water and snow-dusted over others, and it shifts and booms underfoot with the weight of a crossing. Holes gape across the sheet where things have come up through it, some old and refrozen, some raw. The ice thins toward the tarn's center, and dark shapes move slow beneath it where the light filters down.

The Sink-Holes.description: The tarn's far edge, where the wyrms' tunnels break the surface in a cluster of jagged holes and the ice is broken into tilted plates. Meltwater pools dark between the slabs, and the frozen banks are bored through with burrow-mouths running down into the earth. Gear and frozen bundles lie caught in the shallows below the broken ice, visible through the murk. The banks rise into snow-choked scree, and the dark openings exhale cold from below.

Twicehold.name: Twicehold
Twicehold.basicInfo: An old dwarven holdfast on a high crag, broken open and squatted by ogres who call themselves the Twicelings. They reason that if halflings are the small folk, they are the large folk — twice the size and so, plainly, twice as great — and they hold the ruined hold as the seat of the finest folk in the mountains. They have knocked it about to fit their bulk, piled it with what they have taken, and they demand toll from the roads below in the firm belief that this is their due.
Twicehold.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: the Twicelings default to hostile and take what they want from anyone smaller and weaker, which is nearly everyone. They are huge, slab-muscled, and slow-witted, and they fight by wading in and swinging — clubs, torn stonework, whatever is to hand — trusting their size and thick hide to carry them through. A traveler who flatters them, hands over tribute, or amuses them may be let pass or even welcomed as an honored small guest; a traveler who insults the Twicelings' obvious greatness, or simply looks like easy pickings, gets grabbed. They are not clever, but they are not always wrong about who to grab.

The Twicelings believe in their own magnificence completely and without strain. They took the hold because it was the grandest thing they had ever seen and grand things belong to great folk; they wear dwarven armor beaten out flat to fit, sit on dwarven thrones built for far smaller bodies, and have given themselves enormous titles they cannot quite keep straight. They are genuinely hospitable to anyone who treats them as the lords they know themselves to be, and genuinely baffled and hurt when the dwarves come to throw them out of a home they are so obviously improving. The dwarves want the hold back and want the indignity of ogres in it ended, and have not yet mustered the strength to do either.

The Twicelings hoard everything bright or interesting they take off the roads, with no idea what most of it is worth — they will trade a masterwork blade for a shiny bauble and feel they got the better of you. Their hall is heaped with plunder: coin, plate, arms and armor, fine goods carried up from the valleys. Dwarven gear taken from the hold and from travelers lies among it, much of it ruined by ogre handling, some of it still good.

Voice note: when Twicelings boast, charge, celebrate, or work themselves up, give them blunt doubled slogans and chants in this register: 'KILL TWICE! EAT TWICE! TWICELINGS!' They should sound huge, delighted with themselves, and proudly stupid rather than clever.

The Broken Gate.description: The holdfast's gate stands torn half off its hinges, the stone archway above cracked and the dwarven carvings on it scarred and chipped. The road up to it is littered with the wreckage of carts and the leavings of crude meals. Past the gate a courtyard opens, its fine flagstones heaved up and broken under heavy tread, dwarven statues toppled and a few stood back up wrong. Crude lean-tos of timber and hide huddle against the old stone walls.

The Ruined Court.description: The holdfast's main yard, once handsome, now a Twiceling camp. Dwarven masonry stands cracked and soot-blackened, doorways knocked wider to admit ogre bulk, and oversized firepits scar the flagstones. Piles of taken goods sit heaped against the walls under no order at all — timber, sacks, bright wreckage. Broken dwarven furniture has been dragged out and crudely re-purposed into seats and tables built up to ogre scale. A wide stair, its steps cracked under heavy use, climbs toward the great hall above.

The Great Hall.description: The holdfast's feast-hall, its high carved ceiling now hung with crude trophies and stripped banners. The dwarven lord's seat still stands on the dais, far too small for the bulk that has tried to claim it, with a larger crude throne of stacked stone and timber built up beside it. Plunder lies heaped along the walls and spilled across the floor — coin, plate, arms, the bright leavings of the roads. The dwarven hearth at the hall's end has been widened with smashed masonry into a great rough firepit.

The Coldrun.name: The Coldrun
The Coldrun.basicInfo: A grim stretch of mountain road below Deepgate, where the way runs through narrow cuts and broken ground between the holds and the delving-town. Bandits work this road, preying on delvers carrying hauls up out of the dark and on any traveler who looks worth the trouble. Crews go missing here, gear turns up for sale that belonged to the vanished, and few who travel it alone come through unrobbed.
The Coldrun.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: the bandits of the Coldrun default to hostile and exist to rob those who pass, above all delvers laden with what they hauled up from the Deep. They do not delve themselves — they let others go down, bleed for the loot, and stagger back up, then take it on the road. They prefer a robbed traveler to a dead one when the taking is easy, so a crew that yields its haul and looks too hard to fight may be let go lighter, while a rich haul or a weak party gets jumped outright. They ambush from the cuts and the high ground, fight with numbers and dirty work, and scatter the moment the one who leads them goes down.

The gang answers to a thing they call the Foreman — a great iron construct they dragged up out of the rubble and patched back into motion, meaning to make it a guard. It is not a guard. It is a darek construct, and the soul trapped in the soulstone in its chest woke enough to take the gang in hand, and it has run them ever since, and run them well. The Foreman plans the ambushes, sets the watches, splits the takings, and holds a pack of squabbling cutthroats sharper and harder than they could ever manage on their own. They half-worship and half-fear it, and do not entirely grasp that the thing they think they own is the thing that owns them. It is huge, iron, and patient, and it fights like something that has done so for an age and forgotten how to lose.

The gang's holes and camps along the run are heaped with stolen hauls — coin, plate, arms and armor, salvage, raw stone and ore taken off the delvers they robbed. The Foreman is built of old iron and bears a soulstone in its chest, cracked and dimmed but still a thing of rare worth to those who know what it is.

The Cut.description: The road narrows into a steep-walled cut through the cold grey rock, boulders and rockfall choking the verges, the way twisting so a traveler cannot see far ahead or behind. Ledges and clefts notch the walls above, set well for watching the road or dropping onto it. Stripped pack-gear and the wrecks of carts lie shoved into the rocks, picked clean. Wind funnels through the gap in a steady cold rush.

The Broken Ground.description: Past the cut the land opens into a waste of tumbled stone and scrubby snow-pocked hollows, the road threading between knolls and rockpiles that break the sightlines at every turn. Cold campfire-scars and trampled ground mark where the gang has held up. Paths branch away into the rocks toward hidden camps. A ruined stone works squats off to one side — some old mountain holdfast or pump-house, long fallen, its black doorways gaping.

The Fallen Works.description: The ruin of an old stone works set into the broken ground, its roof long gone and its walls cracked and soot-stained. Dead machinery rusts in the gloom inside — frozen gears, broken pipework, a silted pit in the floor. The gang's main camp sprawls among the wreckage: bedrolls, cookfires, and stolen goods stacked wherever there is room. A cleared space at the heart of it is swept and ordered against all the surrounding mess, ringed with the best-kept gear, a heavy seat of stacked iron facing the door.

Hodremur.name: Hodremur
Hodremur.basicInfo: A high snowbound vale in the northern reach of the white peaks, where a war-band of nanukin, the white bearfolk of the far north, has made its winter-camp. They came down out of the far north and took to raiding — striking the holds, the roads, and the camps of the lower mountains, carrying off plunder and beasts and people, and falling back into the high snow where the dwarves are loath to follow.
Hodremur.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: the bearfolk of Hodremur default to hostile and raid the lower mountains for plunder and thralls. They are huge, white-furred, and built for the cold and the kill, and they fight as raiders — fast and savage, hitting hard and pulling back into the snow before a defense can form, or standing and fighting with terrible strength when cornered. They take captives to work the camp and beasts to feed it, and they are not minded to parley with the soft folk of the low holds, though a worthy enemy or a bold guest who proves their strength may earn a hearing where a weak one would only be killed.

These are renegades, not the whole of their kind. The nanukin of the far north, whose garrison holds Fort Redclaw in Aurora, are a proud people who keep their own law and their own honor, and most would name this band oath-broken and shameful. Their chief lost a feud at home and was exiled with those who followed him; they have set their old law aside and live now by the raid, taking from the weak what they will not work for. Their chief rules by strength and holds the band together by the spoils, and a richer raid is always wanted to keep the war-band fed and loyal.

The camp is heaped with raid-plunder — coin, arms and armor, furs and stores, fine goods carried up from the holds and roads. Captives are held here to be ransomed or worked, worth more returned alive to those who would pay for them. Beasts taken on the raids are penned among the tents.

The Snow Road.description: A hard climb up into the high vale, the trail buried deep in snow and marked only by the passage of heavy feet and dragged sledges. The peaks crowd close and white on every side, and the wind drives loose snow in stinging sheets. Ahead the vale opens between the heights, and the smoke of fires rises against the cliffs. Trampled tracks and the ruts of laden sledges run up toward the camp.

The Winter-Camp.description: The war-band's camp, sprawled across the floor of the snowbound vale — great hide tents banked against the drifts, fires burning in pits dug into the snow, racks of drying meat and stacked plunder between them. Pens of lashed timber hold taken beasts at the camp's edge. The largest tent stands at the vale's head, broad and skin-walled and hung with trophies. The cliffs rise sheer and white around the whole of it, and a single buried trail climbs toward the high ground beyond.

The High Ground.description: A windswept shelf above the camp, where the cliffs break into snow-choked rock and the whole vale lies open below. Lookout-cairns and the cold ash of watch-fires mark the heights. Drifts lie deep between the stones, and the way climbs on into the trackless white of the high peaks beyond, where the band falls back when the hunt turns against them. The wind never lets up here, and the cold is the killing kind.

Clanhold Stonewall.name: Clanhold Stonewall
Clanhold Stonewall.basicInfo: A great ring-fortress of grey mountain stone, seat of Clan Stonewall, built as walls within walls within walls. The Stonewall dwarves are shielddwarves — they fight in a locked shieldwall that does not break, and they hold that a held line beats a wild swing every time. They forge the finest armor and shields in Highheath, drill the wall like it is the only thing worth doing, and boast that no enemy has ever broken into their hold.
Clanhold Stonewall.hiddenInfo:
Clan Stonewall are the shielddwarves, and their whole creed is three words: the line holds. They fight locked shield to shield, every dwarf covering the next, moving as one wall, and they believe — loudly, constantly, and with great satisfaction — that discipline beats fury and a wall that does not break beats a charge that does. The wall is half religion and half the best sport in the mountains, drilled in the yards with the cheerful ferocity of folk who are very good at a thing and know it, and their feast-halls are as loud as anyone's once the shields come off.

The clan's craft is protection. Stonewall armorers forge the finest plate and shields in Highheath — heavy, beautiful, and proof against nearly anything — and a Stonewall shield is a thing a warrior keeps for life and hands down after. Their hold has never been broken into, and they will tell you so within the first breath of meeting you, and again shortly after.

The great rivalry is with Clan Stormhammer, and most of it is sport — four hundred years of rustled rams, sabotaged feasts, kill-counts kept on every joint hunt, and a grudge-roll of insults neither clan will let die. Stonewall thinks Stormhammer are reckless louts who mistake breaking things for skill, and says so at every chance, and is delighted when they take the bait. But one grudge is not sport. At Varric's Span, a generation back, a joint muster against a troll-horde broke: Stonewall formed the wall and held it, and Stormhammer charged ahead of the line and died on the bridge, cut off and overwhelmed. Stormhammer says the wall stood fast and watched their kin butchered. Stonewall holds that the charge broke discipline and doomed itself, and that a wall that breaks to save fools saves no one — and they do not joke about that day, because they lost kin watching it happen.

The thane holds the hold and the wall-creed, a broad old shielddwarf who has never lost a drill-match he cared to win and will cheerfully bury you in opinions about why the wall is superior to the hammer.

The Muster Yard.description: The hold's great drill-yard and gathering-ground, ringed by the innermost wall, where the shieldwall is practiced with more noise and good humor than a battlefield ever sees — ranks locking and wheeling, shields crashing, a sergeant bellowing cheerful abuse at anyone out of step. Spectators line the wall-walks to watch and wager on the day's matches. The clan's armory-hall stands across the yard, its racks bright with shields and plate, and the doors of the Brimfull Boss stand wide at the yard's edge.

The Brimfull Boss.description: The clan's tavern, loud and warm and packed with off-duty warriors arguing the day's drill, named for the house custom: a dwarf who is toasted must drink from the hollow boss of an upturned shield, which holds a fine pool of ale and sloshes the lot over the inner rim and down the drinker's beard the moment it tilts. A battered drill-shield hangs behind the bar for exactly this purpose, and a soaked beard is the mark of an evening going well. Long tables fill the common room, the ale is strong, and a stranger who buys a round is half a friend by the second.

The Armory-Hall.description: The clan's great forge and armory, where Stonewall's famous plate and shields are made — anvils ranged down the hall, smiths working steel into heavy, beautiful armor, finished pieces gleaming on the racks. Shields of every weight hang the walls, from drill-shields scarred to splinters to masterwork pieces fit for a thane. Apprentices haul steel and run errands between the stations, and the masters who work here are glad to show off, glad to sell, and gladder still to tell you why Stonewall steel turns a blow no other will.

The Ringwalls.description: The hold's layered defenses, walls within walls climbing the mountainside, gate behind gate behind gate, with killing-grounds and stepped battlements between each ring. From the high walls the whole approach lies open, every road to the hold watched and walled, and dwarves on the wall-walks keep an easy eye on the country below. The stonework is old, fitted, and proud, carved here and there with the marks of musters that held the line. The innermost gate stands open in daylight onto the yard within.

Burlwick.name: Burlwick
Burlwick.basicInfo: Burlwick is a busy canal village of painted timber houses and workshops where gnome and human families make and sell foci: wands, staves, rods, orbs and rings. Gnome-sized and human-sized doors stand side by side along the lanes, and nearly every one opens onto a shop. Mages come from all over Larion to buy here, and Tarnholme students come for a first focus and come back for a better one. The famous old workshops charge whatever their names will bear, the market stalls sell rods cut by the dozen, and every shop in between has an opinion about the others. Its witchwood comes from Hollin Coppice, the grove beside the village.
Burlwick.hiddenInfo:
Burlwick's people are makers and sellers of every kind. The old workshops, most of them gnome families, have fitted mages for generations and trade on their names; their work is superb and their prices are worse. The middling shops turn out sound, plain foci for honest money. The market stalls sell cheap rods of every quality, from bargains to kindling. A few quiet masters work only by appointment and turn away more buyers than they serve, and a couple of smiling dealers sell foci that look far better than they cast. Haggling is expected everywhere except the old workshops, where it is an insult.

A good fitter watches a buyer cast and can tell from one spell what is wrong with their old focus; a bad one tells them whatever will sell. The gnome workshops carve and fit by hand, the human workshops are quicker and cheaper, and the two have argued about which is better for as long as anyone remembers.

Witchwood comes from Hollin Coppice and is seasoned in the workshops' own lofts, and glass blanks for orbs come by canal boat from Wortwell.

Not every focus sold here is as good as its maker swears, rival workshops accuse each other of stealing designs, and fake Burlwick foci turn up in other towns.

The Canal Quay.description: Clear water enters the village here through a stone arch, running bright between mossy quay-walls. Flat-bottomed boats tie up along the steps to unload glass from Wortwell and timber from the yard. Painted houses with gnome-sized and human-sized doors lean over the channel on both banks, and a little humpbacked bridge crosses to the lanes beyond.

The Foci Market.description: A cobbled square under patched awnings, its stalls laid with foci on velvet and straw, from polished showpieces to bundles of rods sold by the dozen. Stallholders shout their prices over each other, buyers try foci on the spot, and sparks and the odd misfire fly across the square; at least one awning is always freshly scorched. The market's warning is painted over the square in letters a yard high: TRY IT BEFORE YOU BUY IT, AND STAND WELL BACK.

The Clearwater.description: A timber tavern built out over the canal on stilted piers, its windows of thick leaded glass glowing amber after dark. Inside, low beams, a wide hearth, and long scrubbed tables; a balcony at the back hangs over the water.

Workshop Row.description: A narrow lane along the upper canal, lined on both sides with workshops of every size, their doors propped open to the street. Shavings drift on the water, and the air is loud with carving, filing and the crack of test spells. Painted signs boast of famous customers, true and otherwise. The cheap rod-cutters crowd the market end; the old gnome houses stand at the far end, quiet, with no prices posted.

The Misfire.description: A big, rambling tavern on the edge of the market, one long timber hall where mages buy, sell and swap secondhand foci over drinks. Old wands, rods and staves hang from the rafters in bundles with prices chalked on their tags, traded in by mages who outgrew them, broke them or swore at them. Everyone tries before they buy, right there at the tables, so sparks fizz over the ale, a chair floats now and then, somebody's hair is always briefly blue, and the whole hall cheers every misfire. The beams are scorched black, and nobody minds.

The Wild Magic Badlands.name: The Wild Magic Badlands
The Wild Magic Badlands.basicInfo: The Wild Magic Badlands are a country of wind-carved red stone, caves and dry gulleys in the southeast of the Jade Tarn, and the one place on the Tarn where magic storms happen. A magic storm is a slow, low cloud trailing colored light. It crosses the badlands at a walking pace and passes in about an hour. While it passes, any spell cast beneath it comes out wrong: bigger, the wrong kind, or off its aim. Where its lightning strikes, it leaves thunderglass. Blink hounds, vanishing cats, winged stags, basilisks, drakelings and manticores hunt here, and rogue mages camp in the high stone.
The Wild Magic Badlands.hiddenInfo:
Magic storms are the badlands' weather, the way squalls are a coast's. A storm passes in four stages: it is seen far off on the Stoneflats; metal hums and ears pop; it passes over, with odd-colored lightning, rain that falls warm or glittering, and small magic happening unbidden; then it moves on, leaving scorched rings, puddles that glow until dawn, and thunderglass. Shelter, a ward or running are all fair answers. The farms at the Redbreak see one a few times a season.

The beasts each carry a gift in their bodies. Blink hounds hunt in packs and blink from place to place; their sinew, worked into a charm, carries the blink. Vanishing cats fade from sight but for their eyes, and their pelt hides its wearer. Winged stags graze the high ledges, and their feathers lift a working into the air. Basilisks lie in the gulleys; a basilisk's gaze-gland cures being turned to stone, and is poison raw. Drakelings nest in the Spires, manticores are the deadliest hunters here, and will-o'-wisps drift after the storms and lure the lost.

The rogue mages are expelled students, dropouts and hedge-mages who catch beasts to sell to the Syndicate and gather thunderglass. The Heart-Eaters keep a camp in the caves of the Spires. They go out masked in bone after a storm, when stunned beasts are easy to run down, and eat the hearts of what they kill. They kill gatherers who come too near the Spires and offer the desperate ones a place.

Gatherers come out after every storm for the thunderglass, and pay for wards on their camps and for someone to calm or kill a storm-maddened beast.

The Redbreak.description: The edge of the badlands, where the green farmland of the Tarn runs out against a wall of broken red stone. The ground rises in shelves of cracked rock, dry washes cut down between them, and the grass thins to nothing within a few paces of the line. Beyond, the land opens into wind-carved country, and on most days a magic storm can be seen somewhere over it, trailing colored light.

The Stoneflats.description: A wide reach of bare red rock and rolling broken ground, weathered into ridges, knobs and shallow basins as far as the eye carries. There is little cover and a long line of sight, so a magic storm can be seen from a great way off, crawling slowly across the open. Thunderglass glints in scorched rings where lightning has struck again and again, and blink-hound tracks start and stop in the dust.

The Gulleys.description: A maze of dry channels cut deep into the stone, narrow and winding, their walls rising so close overhead that the sky is only a bright, crooked seam. When a storm passes over, green and violet light washes along the rock. Stone-grey lizards, birds and a rabbit stand frozen in the side channels where a basilisk has hunted. The channels branch and rejoin without pattern.

The Spires.description: The high country of the badlands, where the red stone is carved into tall pinnacles, arches and sheer-sided towers. Ledges and caves pock the heights, drakelings scream from their nests, and smoke rises from camps in the caves, where bone masks hang drying on the ledges. The climbing is hard and exposed. From the tops the whole country lies open below, with storms crawling across the flats.

Battle Mages' Isle.name: Battle Mages' Isle
Battle Mages' Isle.basicInfo: Battle Mages' Isle is the home of the College of Battle Mages: a long, rocky island of separate rises joined by stepping-stones and swaying plank spans over the green shallows. Its buildings are squat round towers and long halls of dark red granite, with thick walls, iron-studded doors and crimson banners. Students drill, duel and learn to ride flying sky-skates here, and crossing the island is half the training: one shove of force or a gust off the water, and a careless student goes into the Tarn. Visitors come to watch the duels and the riders.
Battle Mages' Isle.hiddenInfo:
Battle Mages live and train here with their masters under the Head of Battle Mages. They are loud, physical and hard to rattle, and they talk about magic the way fighters talk about footwork and timing. Their saying is "stand in front": when something goes wrong, a Battle Mage goes toward it and puts a ward between the trouble and everyone else.

Knocking each other into the Tarn on the crossings is the island's favorite game, and visitors from other Colleges are fair game. Nobody minds a dunking; a Battle Mage who wards on instinct and comes up laughing is the kind the island admires. The hall keeps a rack of towels by the door.

Duels on the island are fought to Three-Touch: three clean hits win, quick wards count, nobody gets maimed, and the argument over who really won lasts all evening.

Sky-skates are broad flying rays, saddled like horses and bred at the Moorings. They are curious, greedy for eels and fond of riders who scratch under their fins. Beginners ride in harness, and good riders stand loose.

Battle Mages pull down magic storms. When a storm drifts out of the Wild Magic Badlands toward the Tarn, the muster bell rings, riders fly out on sky-skates, turn the storm with wards, and drag its lightning down onto Shock-Rock. The muster also rides out to escaped summons and to trouble at the shore farms.

A portal arch on the island connects it to the Main Island and the other College isles, and members of the Academy step through it to cross between islands in a single stride. No boats run between the islands; skiffs only cross between the Main Island and the mainland at Tarnport, the port town on the shore.

The Leaping-Stones.description: The way across the island: stepping-stones, swaying plank-spans, and tall leaping-stones strung between rises above cold green water. Students cut across at speed, dodge each other, and sometimes help a friend into the Tarn for educational reasons. An iron-bound portal arch hung with crimson pennants stands on a round granite court at the near end, opening to the other islands for members of the Academy.

Battle Mages' Hall.description: The Battle Mages' hall and lodgings: a long, low hall of red granite with a squat round bell tower at one end. Inside are scrubbed tables, bunk-galleries, weapon-racks, shield-stands and riding tack, and crimson banners won in old duels hang under the rafters. Wet boots steam by the hearth. The muster bell in the tower can be heard across the islands.

The Dueling Rings.description: Raised stone circles along the southern rise, ward-hazed and worn smooth at the center, with benches beside the largest ring. A posting-board at the row end is thick with chalked names, challenges, and Three-Touch standings.

The Moorings.description: The Academy's skate-cote at the island's edge, where the sky-skates are bred and kept. Timber perches, padded roost-ledges, saddle-rigs and bridles stand under a long lean-to roof. A fenced stretch of warm shallows holds the young skates, and the open water is kept clear so the grown ones can rise and settle. Students crowd the rail at dusk to watch the riders come in.

Shock-Rock.description: A bare rocky islet off the isle's edge, used for hard training and for pulling down magic storms. Its flats are scorched, frost-cracked and cratered by generations of ward-breaking spells. Tall iron lightning-poles stand among the scars, fused black at their tips, and thunderglass glitters in the cracks.

Artificers' Isle.name: Artificers' Isle
Artificers' Isle.basicInfo: Artificers' Isle is the home of the College of Artificers, the Academy's enchanters and makers. It is a steep heap of red-brick workshops with green copper roofs and tall chimneys, stacked up the slope and joined by iron stairs, gantries and plank bridges that get rebuilt every term. Glass-roofed forge galleries glow at night. Constructs clatter through the lanes on errands, and every day students race to build something that works from a random handful of parts. Students from every College come here when they need something made, mended or improved: a charm or a lamp, a lock or a ward-stone, an enchanted tool, a cracked focus, or a construct of their own that will not do as it is told.
Artificers' Isle.hiddenInfo:
Artificers live and work here with their masters under the Head of Artificers. They make things that hold magic: charms, lamps, lifts, portal arches, enchanted tools, and constructs that move on their own. They talk about their craft like smiths, in terms of feel, fit and the work of their hands. Their saying is "make it work with what you have."

Each morning the masters post a challenge above the Piece Pit, and the Claw, a great iron grab on a gantry, deals each student a random hand of parts from the heap: movers, grippers, eyes, cores and oddments. The contests are races, not fights. A construct wins by reaching the goal, carrying the prize or crossing the course. It may take a rival's part only by attaching it to itself on the spot, and clever sabotage gets a cheer. Yesterday's constructs go back into the Pit by dawn, and a student who turns an impossible hand into a win is talked about for years.

The island is full of the College's leftover work. Walking trays carry tea up the stairs, brass messenger birds fly notes between workshops, and old constructs nobody took apart sweep the lanes and stack crates.

A portal arch on the island connects it to the Main Island and the other College isles, and members of the Academy step through it to cross between islands in a single stride. No boats run between the islands; skiffs only cross between the Main Island and the mainland at Tarnport, the port town on the shore.

The Workshop Climb.description: A crooked climb of open-fronted workshops, forge-galleries, and tinker-lofts stacked up the slope, joined by stairs and plank-bridges that may not lead where they led last week. Tools and parts spill into the lanes, and half-built constructs wait in every bay. At the foot of the climb, a fluted brass-and-copper portal arch opens to the other islands from a brick court cluttered with crates of parts.

The Piece Pit.description: The island's heart: a round shaft filled with a slow-churning heap of brass limbs, lenses, grasping arms, wheels, springs, and glowing cores. Builders work around the rim beneath the Claw's gantry, beside the slate board showing the day's challenge and standings.

The Gallery.description: The Artificers' commons, a tiered hall of balconies built over the Pit, with long tables, deep chairs, and rails overlooking the work below. Walking trays, word-pour taps, brass messenger birds, and unreliable student gadgets serve the room.

Summoners' Isle.name: Summoners' Isle
Summoners' Isle.basicInfo: Summoners' Isle is the home of the College of Summoners, who call creatures and spirits, raise beasts and learn to take a beast's shape. It is a steep, green island of round fieldstone halls with turf roofs grown thick with grass and wildflowers, terraced up the slope among walled enclosures of hot stone, frost, wind and wet, each built to hold the kind of creature called there. Animals and called creatures are everywhere, and the island is never quiet. Students from every College come to watch the daily trials in a sunken stone maze.
Summoners' Isle.hiddenInfo:
Summoners live here with their masters under the Head of Summoners, along with a changing crowd of called creatures and the beasts the College raises. They call, bind, bargain with and send back elementals, imps, sprites and small fey. They talk about it like animal trainers, in terms of temperament, patience and trust. Their saying is "ask before you bind, and send back what you call."

Shapeshifting students lope, flap and waddle around the island in their practice shapes, and their friends keep their clothes folded on the walls until they come back. Changing back before nightfall is the island's one hard habit, and everyone goes looking for anyone who is late.

Called creatures serve all over the island. Drink-sprites race cups down the tables in the hall above the Run, cook-imps work the kitchens and fish for praise, and fire spirits keep the hearths and lamps, flaring with the singing and brightening over a good story.

Each morning the masters post a creature and a task above the Run, and the pairing is usually unfair: fire across water, a burrower up a crag, a proud creature told to fetch. A student must call something suitable and get it through the trial before dusk by coaxing, bargaining or tricking it, never by forcing a fight. The masters step in fast when a circle slips.

Called creatures have wants, limits and tricks of their own, and now and then one slips its binding and gets loose on the island.

A portal arch on the island connects it to the Main Island and the other College isles, and members of the Academy step through it to cross between islands in a single stride. No boats run between the islands; skiffs only cross between the Main Island and the mainland at Tarnport, the port town on the shore.

The Habitats.description: Walled little climates crowd the slope, divided by narrow warded lanes: hot stone, frost-rimed pool, wind-crag, wet burrow, bright meadow, and stranger pens. Each ground has circles, stalls, tether-rings, and gates built to hold what is called there. Where the lanes meet the water, the portal arch stands inside double iron circles graven with binding marks, hung with green pennants.

The Run.description: The island's heart: a sunken maze of stone walls, water-channels, bridges, blind turns, and dead ends, open to the sky and watched from galleries above. A slate board at the rail shows the day's creature-class, task, and standings.

Summoners' Hall.description: The Summoners' hall of food and drink, set above the Run with windows over the maze. Full cups skim down the tables to whoever calls for one, dishes come through the kitchen hatch faster than any cook could manage, the hearth-fire flares with the singing, and the lamps brighten over a good story.

Healers' Isle.name: Healers' Isle
Healers' Isle.basicInfo: Healers' Isle is the home of the College of Healers, the Academy's healers and curse-breakers. It is a low, gentle island of cream-plastered houses with sky-blue tiled roofs and shady arcades, set among gardens and terraces of warm, steaming pools that step down to the water under willows. Students from every College come here to be patched up, soak off bruises and spell-burns, eat and gossip. Patients from across Larion come hoping the Healers can mend what no one nearer home could.
Healers' Isle.hiddenInfo:
Healers live here with their masters under the Head of Healers, and the isle always has patients: students from the other isles, farmers and carters from around the Tarn, and travelers from farther off. Healers talk about their work like good nurses and herbalists, plainly and practically, and care more about rest and food than about spells. Their saying is "everyone gets a bed": anyone who comes hurt is taken in, friend or stranger, rival or enemy.

Battle Mages come in bruised from the rings, Summoners singed from their circles, and Artificers with their hands briefly stuck as claws. The pools and the Long Table are the Academy's favorite place to gossip, make up after a quarrel, start a romance or argue waist-deep in warm water. Healers' familiars, mostly cats and small owls, sleep on the patients' beds, and teapots pour for whoever sits down.

There is always someone at the pool's edge with a story: a hunter whose wound opens again each dawn, a child who will not wake, a carter caught out in a magic storm, a farmer whose hand will not stop glowing. Most are mended in a day.

A portal arch on the island connects it to the Main Island and the other College isles, and members of the Academy step through it to cross between islands in a single stride. No boats run between the islands; skiffs only cross between the Main Island and the mainland at Tarnport, the port town on the shore.

The Warm Pools.description: Terraced healing pools stepping down toward the Tarn, warm and faintly steaming, with broad stone rims, shallow steps, and shade-trees leaning over the water. Students crowd the edges at all hours, soaking bruises, comparing disasters, and pretending not to listen to each other. At the top of the terraces, an arch of cream stone wound with living vine opens to the other islands as a portal arch for members of the Academy.

The Gardens.description: Lush herb-beds, flowering walks, grassy banks, and shaded corners around the pools. Healers gather ingredients here, patients take slow walks, and students vanish into the greenery when they want a private word.

The Long Table.description: A warm open hall facing the gardens, its tables always laid with restorative food, tea, broth, fruit, and whatever someone has just baked too much of. The hearth never goes cold, and half the Academy drifts through when hungry, shaken, or pretending to be neither.

The Resting-Lawns.description: Open-air recovery lawns above the pools, set with beds and low couches under weather-wards that hold off rain and chill. Hedges and hanging sky-blue cloth give privacy. A sleepy hush hangs over the place: visitors drop their voices without being asked, and the wind chimes in the hedges ring only in a whisper.

The Quiet Ward.description: A gated garden at the island's far edge for the dangerous cases: curses that spread, minds that need shielding, wounds with magic still moving inside them. Low warded rooms stand among the hedges, and the gate is watched.

The Main Island.name: The Main Island
The Main Island.basicInfo: The Main Island is the largest island in the Jade Tarn and the common ground shared by all four Colleges of Tarnholme Academy. Skiffs carry passengers between the mainland and the island from dawn to dark, and portals connect it to each College isle. Its buildings are tall and narrow, built of pale limestone with steep slate roofs, and joined by covered walkways and stone stairs that climb the island's hill. Students from every College cross over to eat together, study, see their masters and pick up the odd jobs townsfolk pin up for students. First-Years who haven't yet joined a College live here, and so do visitors on Academy business.
The Main Island.hiddenInfo:
Portal arches at the Five Arches connect the Main Island to each of the four College isles, and members of the Academy step through them to cross between islands in a single stride. Skiffs only run between the Main Island and the mainland at Tarnport, the port town on the shore. The Five Arches also hold the permanent portal to the Watchtower in Ardan's Watch.

Students from all four Colleges mix here every day in their College scarves, with First-Years among them, their Tarnholme stars still plain silver. Trunks and satchels trot after their owners along the covered walkways, brooms sweep the stairs on their own, and familiars ride on shoulders, doze in window seats and beg at the dining tables. Students talk shop like athletes: whose wards are quick, whose fire finally caught, who has the knack for portals. Every College courts promising First-Years here with pastries, loud stories and invitations to come and watch a duel or a trial.

The masters keep their offices in the Masters' Wing, doors open between classes. They are friendly and busy. A student with a question gets tea and an answer, or is walked down the corridor to someone who knows. When students break something, or each other's pride, a master sits them down and talks it through.

The Five Arches.description: A broad limestone quay at the foot of the island's hill, with water-steps where the skiffs tie up. Five portal arches stand in a row along it: the tall old arch to the Watchtower in Ardan's Watch, and four smaller ones, each hung with a College's colors, opening to the College isles for members of the Academy. Students pour through at all hours with armfuls of books, and a brass bell over the water-steps calls out the name of each skiff's passengers as it docks, usually wrong. The porter's lodge keeps the skiff times and a cupboard of lost property that rattles when its owners walk past.

The Grounds.description: Lawns and gravel walks climb the island's hill between tall, narrow limestone buildings, joined by covered walkways and steep stone stairs. Hedges clipped into the shapes of old Heads of the Academy change their poses when nobody is looking. Students sprawl on the grass trying spells out on each other, folded paper birds flap notes from building to building, and somebody is always chasing an escaped pet toad across the lawn. Notice-boards by the stairs are thick with club meetings, lost pets and dares.

The Great Hall.description: The dining hall: a long, high-roofed limestone hall with tall windows, where each College's tables run under runners in its colors and the First-Years sit in the middle. Glass lanterns hang from the rafters on long chains, each holding a small swirl of captured sunlight, and water jugs top up any cup set down empty. The masters eat at the high table and are interrupted constantly. One wall holds the Practica board, thick with postings.

The Masters' Wing.description: A tall wing of offices near the top of the hill, one master to a room, each door painted with its owner's name and usually standing open. Inside are crowded desks, teapots, half-finished experiments and a chair for visitors. The heads of the four Colleges have offices here. Students drop in between classes to ask a question, borrow a book or get help with a spell that won't come right. Some of the closed doors have brass knockers charmed to answer, telling a visitor whether the master is in, out or busy, and a few of them are a good deal ruder about it than their owners.

The Newcomers' Hall.description: The First-Years' lodgings: a tall limestone house of bunk-galleries and small rooms above a common room with a wide hearth, where students who have no College yet live alongside visitors on Academy business. It is crowded and loud at every hour. Doors bang, students barge into each other's rooms, pranks run up and down the galleries, and familiars get underfoot everywhere. The common room is where First-Years trade news, make friends fast and plan their nights out in Tarnport, the port town on the shore, and nobody gets much sleep.

The Library.description: The Academy's library: a tall hall of galleries, ladders and reading tables under a painted ceiling. Its books shelve themselves, flapping back to their places when a reader sets them down, and whenever something new is learned a new book grows on the shelves, so the Library is never quite the same size twice. Study partners claim the window tables.

The Muster Court.description: A broad paved court on the hilltop, ringed by tiered stands of pale stone and hung with banners in all four College colors. The stands hold the whole Academy at once. Students cut across it between lessons and sit in the stands to be seen.

Tarnport.name: Tarnport
Tarnport.basicInfo: Tarnport is the port of the Jade Tarn: red-brick warehouses, tarred timber wharves and tall slate-roofed houses on the lake shore where the river leaves the lake and runs east to the Tarn Sea, the bay beyond. Seagoing ships come up the river and tie up beside the lake. The magical goods of the region ship out from here, and everything the Academy needs comes in. Sailors, dockhands, merchants and craftsfolk from every coast crowd its streets, and after dark the town fills with street food, theater crowds and gamblers. The skiffs of Tarnholme Academy, the school of magic on the lake's islands, cross from here to the Main Island, and students come over on free evenings to eat, drink and get away from school.
Tarnport.hiddenInfo:
Tarnport is run by its Harbor Council, the heads of the town's merchant houses, who meet in a hall on the waterfront and appoint a harbor master to run the water: the berths, the tolls, the river pilots and the harbor watch. The town values trade, coin fairly counted, a contract kept and a good night out, and anyone who pays a berth fee is welcome.

Most Tarnporters are not mages. They are mostly humans and halflings: shipwrights, dockhands, sailors, carters, shopkeepers, clerks and their families. Dwarves work in the shipyard beside the human shipwrights. Catkin and foxkin crew the ships. Merfolk pilots swim ahead of every ship on the river and guide it through the shoals, and ratkin dock gangs hold the loading work on the quays. Travelers off the foreign ships, dark elves, orcs, giantborn, demonborn and dragonkin among them, walk the waterfront in their own fashions. Magic is something Tarnport hires: a ward on a hull, a charm against rot in the hold, a lifting spell on a heavy day.

Students are welcome custom and a standing nuisance. They pack the taverns and show off, and some rent rooms and live in town. Dockhands and craftsfolk resent students who hire out spells for less than an honest day's wage, and sailors and students settle their quarrels in the ring at the Ballast. A fight there is for coin: each fighter puts up a purse, the whole room bets on the bout, and a bout ends at a knockdown or a yield. Magic is welcome in student bouts, and those draw the heaviest betting. The Academy buys nearly everything it needs through Tarnport, and the merchant houses haggle hard with its buyers. Every house courts the Academy's custom, and the promising students who might one day ward its ships.

Everyone in Tarnport knows the Syndicate runs the town's crime, and nobody pretends otherwise. Its boss keeps the back room at the Ballast. Its people smuggle stolen Academy goods, charms and wild-caught beasts down the river on night barges, hidden in honest cargo, to ships waiting in the Tarn Sea. The Syndicate owns the pawnshops and moneylenders of the Sumps, takes the bets on the Ballast's fights and takes a cut from the ratkin dock gangs. Its men wear an open black hand tattooed on the neck or forearm. The harbor watch keeps them out of the market, and does not go into the Sumps after dark.

Cutpurses work the night market crowds, crews brawl on the waterfront, and cargo goes missing from the quays.

The Academy's skiffs leave the lake end of the Long Pier for the Main Island of Tarnholme Academy all day and late into the night. Carts come in every day from Burlwick and Wortwell with foci, potions and glass for the ships.

The Long Pier.description: A broad stone pier running far out into the jade-green lake from the foot of the town, wide enough for carts and lined with cargo cranes. Seagoing ships lie along it two deep, tall-masted traders from the southern coasts beside river barges, while dockhands swing cargo up from the holds and merfolk pilots wait in the water for the next ship bound down the river. The Academy's skiffs tie up at their own stone steps, and students come ashore with familiars on their shoulders. Stalls crowd the pier, selling to crews before they sail: an apothecary's barrow of healing draughts and remedies, a trader in materials off the ships from far coasts, a seller of spell components and warding charms, and an outfitter's stall of oilskins, cloaks and boots.

The Pennant Market.description: A great cobbled square above the waterfront, named for the pennants of the merchant houses strung on lines across it. Each house pays a fortune for its pennants, long silk banners woven and painted with its own bold design, and new ones go up every season to outdo the rest, so the sky over the square is a canopy of color. By day it is the port's open-air trading floor, where the Tarn's wool, cider and grain go out, silk, spices and stranger goods off the ships come in, and whole cargoes are auctioned from the backs of carts. At dusk the traders pack up and the night market takes the square: braziers and cook-fires, long benches, and street food from a dozen coasts. Fire-eaters, a knife-thrower and a strongman work the crowd, students juggle spells for coins, and after-dark stalls sell masks, fortunes and love charms.

The Playhouse.description: A tall, red-painted theater on the market square, its front hung with painted boards announcing the company's plays. Inside, a horseshoe of galleries rises around a deep stage under a great chandelier, from cheap standing room in the pit to curtained boxes for the rich. The company plays most nights.

Backstage.description: The actors' tavern, behind the Playhouse, entered from an alley off the student quarter through a famous red door that every student in Tarnport knows. Inside, it is dressed like the wings of a stage: old painted scenery for walls, velvet curtains, racks of costumes, masks hung everywhere, and a low round stage in the middle with the tables crowded close around it. A chandelier salvaged from an old production hangs over the room, and a gallery runs above. Through the walls, on a show night, the audience can be heard laughing on the other side, and a narrow door behind the bar opens straight onto the wings: actors barge through it between scenes, still in costume, gulp a drink and rush back.

The Ballast.description: The roughest tavern in Tarnport, on the ground floor of a rotting warehouse on the waterfront: small barred windows, black beams, knife-scarred tables, and a ring of rope and sawdust in the middle of the floor where fights are held for coin, with the whole room betting. The drinkers are the worst the port has: smugglers and deserters, crews off ships nobody asks about, ratkin gang bosses, cutthroats for hire and card sharps. A student who walks in is the evening's entertainment. A curtained door at the back leads to the room where the Syndicate's men sit, and nobody goes through it uninvited.

Skiff Hill.description: A steep tangle of streets and stairs crowded with tall old houses let out room by room to students, with familiars sunning themselves on the sills. Cheap cookshops sell noodles, pies and fried dough at every hour, a secondhand bookseller's stall spills old spellbooks into the street, and a tailor sells and mends robes and clothes.

The Dovecote.description: A rambling lodging house of many floors, rented room by room to students who would rather live in town than on the islands. The students run it themselves: they share one big kitchen, argue the house rules on a slate by the door, and keep a flat roof where owls and familiars roost.

The Ropewalk.description: A long, straight, tree-lined street of tall brick townhouses, built along the old ropewalk where the town once spun its rope: painted front doors, brass knockers, window boxes, walled gardens at the back, and attic windows looking across the roofs to the lake and the Academy's towers. Shipwrights' families, retired captains, merchants' clerks, young couples and a few well-off students live here, a baker at the corner sells bread still warm before dawn, and neighbors talk across the garden walls. Houses here are often for sale or to let.

Chandler Street.description: A busy, respectable street of shops where crews outfit for voyages and travelers for the road, each shop under its painted trade sign. An apothecary sells healing draughts, mana philters and remedies over a counter of green glass jars. A dwarven weaponsmith and an armorer share a forge yard, where a blade or a breastplate can be fitted or mended in an afternoon. An outfitter sells cloaks, boots and oilskins, and works hides and cloth from far coasts into field gear. A reagent seller keeps a wall of little drawers full of thunderglass, witchwood, venom glands and powdered emberglass. A bookbinder sells blank spellbooks, vellum and inks, and binds or mends any book left with her.

Cinder Yard.description: A soot-black yard ringed by sheds around a disused foundry chimney, where makers do work the Academy frowns on. A forge here turns out hexed blades that bite deeper than honest steel and take something back from the hand that holds them. An enchanter's shed re-cuts the cores of broken constructs to drive new ones, which do not always remember who their master is now. A carver makes foci of bone and of wood cured in her own blood, copies keys and seals from a wax impression without asking whose they are, and sells charms that work, with side effects she mentions only if asked.

The Sumps.description: Low ground behind the warehouses, where the river floods every spring: a warren of damp lanes, plank walkways over standing water and old timber houses propped on stilts. Pawnshops keep barred windows full of other people's rings, swords and instruments. Gambling dens run dice, cards and crab races all night behind shuttered fronts. A moneylender's door has no sign and never lacks a queue, and men with open black hands tattooed on their necks call on the shops to collect. Ratkin dock gangs hold the corners. By day it is poor, crowded and busy, with cheap rooms and washing strung between the houses. After dark the harbor watch does not come in, and a stranger is sized up at every corner.

Wortwell.name: Wortwell
Wortwell.basicInfo: Wortwell is the potion village of the Jade Tarn, a cheerful huddle of brick brewing houses and thatched cottages in the south country, with the Bramblewood at its back. It brews the potions, draughts and salves the Academy uses, and it blows the Tarn's alchemy glass, from phials to stills. A spring-spirit lives in the village well and drowns whatever fouls it, so Wortwell has the purest potion water on the Tarn.
Wortwell.hiddenInfo:
The Wortwell folk are human and halfling families who have kept the same stillrooms for generations. They are careful, generous, house-proud and stubborn about their craft. A little small beer is still brewed, mostly for the Tun and Tale.

The spring-spirit is plain village fact. It keeps the well clean, and it pulls under anyone who washes boots in it, dumps a spoiled batch or poisons it. The village leaves it a cup of the first brew of each season.

The oldest brewhouses are dug into the slope, and their back doors open into the Glowcaves. Wortwell buys the molds, caps and ferments its potions depend on from the myconids there, and owes them more than trade: once, in a hard winter, they sheltered the village's children in the caves for a month.

Wortwell's gatherers go into the Bramblewood for herbs, honey, spider silk and venom.

Pixies raid the Herb Garden, and the two big potion houses squabble over turns at the Glasshouse's furnace.

The Green.description: The village common: a broad green ringed by brewhouses, drying sheds and cottages, with the old well at its center under a mossy stone canopy. A worn track runs in from the Tarn road. Carts stand about loaded with crates of phials and sacks of herbs, and a cup is always left on the well's rim.

The Brewhouses.description: Stillrooms dug into the slope behind the green, cool and dim, where copper stills tick, racks of phials cool, and the air smells of herbs and spirits. The oldest run deep into the hill. At the back of them, heavy doors open into the Glowcaves, where the myconids come to trade.

The Glasshouse.description: The glassblowers' furnace hall, a long brick building with three roaring furnaces. Phials, flasks, alembics and stills are blown here and cooled on long racks, along with the glass blanks Burlwick turns into orbs. The heat is fierce and the work is fast, and a chalked rota by the door shows which potion house has the furnaces today, with angry corrections.

The Herb Garden.description: Walled herb beds behind the brewhouses, laid out in labeled rows of wound-herb, fever-leaf, knitbone and stranger plants under glass.
