Students learn to gather here before they are trusted in the Bramblewood. Nets over the beds and a scarecrow hung with bells are meant to keep the pixies out, and mostly don't.

The Tun and Tale.description: The village alehouse, a low, warm timber house facing the green, where the potion-makers drink of an evening. The taps run small beer and cider, and a potion counter beside them serves anyone who needs a draught instead. The talk is all of herbs and weather and whose batch came out best this season.

Suleyvan's Folly.name: Suleyvan's Folly
Suleyvan's Folly.basicInfo: A vast palace-city half-buried in the sand of a low canyon, beautiful even in ruin — toppled statues, drifted courtyards, columned halls half-swallowed by sand. This was the house of Suleyvan the Sealer, the old master-binder who kept the dangerous spirits of an age sealed in vessels beneath his own roof. The locks held while he lived, but a catastrophe befell the palace after his death, and it has lain abandoned ever since. Even after all these years, many of the old vessels are still here — lamps, rings, jars, bottles by the hundred — and a bold hand can still carry out a fortune.
Suleyvan's Folly.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Suleyvan's Folly is full of bound spirits, sealed in the vessels and still here. The seals are old and failing. Open a vessel, break one, or disturb one too far gone, and the spirit inside comes out — and a freed spirit attacks: a loosed djinn, ifrit, or shaitan that has spent an age in the dark fights the one who freed it. The Folly is dangerous to walk; vessels are everywhere, and a binding can fail on its own.

Freed spirits fight to type. A djinn is wind and force: it hurls a foe across the hall, throws loose stone and brass, and stays in the air out of reach. An ifrit is fire: it burns, throws flame, and sets the room alight, and it kills without speaking. A shaitan is guile: it lies, wears a borrowed face, turns a person's own fears and words against them, and fights dirty.

Some few spirits will deal instead of kill, and these are worth seeking on purpose: an ifrit will swear a single binding favor to whoever frees it and is held to its word; a marid, the rarest sealed here, knows true answers and will trade one for its freedom; a djinn pressed in the dazed moment can be bound into service rather than fought. A shaitan offers bargains too, and a shaitan's bargain is always a trap. Free a spirit blind and it fights; corner the right kind and force the right terms, and it serves.

The loot is the vessels and what the spirits leave. A sealed vessel — a lamp, ring, jar, or bottle with a spirit still bound inside — is the prize: carried out intact it sells for a fortune to the right buyer, or it can be broken to loose what is in it. A slain ifrit leaves emberglass and fire-cinder, fire-hot materials for a forge or a flame-weapon; a slain djinn leaves thunderglass, a wind-charged crystal; a shaitan leaves nothing but the brass it was bound in. Suleyvan's own sealing-gear lies throughout the halls — empty warded bottles, sealing-rings, and binding-chains that a trained hand can use to catch and hold a spirit instead of fighting it. Brass relics, old coin, and jeweled settings from a master's house lie scattered everywhere, thickest and best-sealed in the vault wing and the sanctum.

The Drowned Gate.description: The entrance to the palace-city, a colossal brass gateway toppled and half-swallowed by a dune that pours through the gap and out across the threshold. Beyond it the ruin opens wide — broken towers, sand-filled courts, and columned roofs sunk to their middles in drift, running back toward the canyon wall. Sealing-marks cover the standing stone of the gate.
paths: The Hall of a Thousand Seals

The Hall of a Thousand Seals.description: A great columned audience-hall, its roof open to the sky where beams have fallen, sand banked high against the bases of the pillars. A brass throne stands on a stepped dais at the far end. Alcoves line the walls.

The Dune Courts.description: A run of open courtyards between the palace wings, each sunk into a bowl of sand, with the dry stone channels and empty basins of old water-gardens crossing between them. Toppled statuary and the tops of buried walls break the dunes. Doorways open off the courts into the deeper halls.
paths: The Hall of a Thousand Seals

The Vault Wing.description: A wing of treasury-rooms and store-chambers running deep under the palace, the air close and hot, the floors crowded with sealed vessels and shelved with the brass and goods of a master's house. Sand has forced through cracks into the outer rooms; the inner ones stand dry and dark behind heavy doors carved over with locks.
paths: The Hall of a Thousand Seals

Suleyvan's Sanctum.description: The deepest and hottest chamber of the Folly, the master's own workroom. Work-tables, racks, and sealed vessels stand where they were left.

The Bonecrags.name: The Bonecrags
The Bonecrags.basicInfo: A run of high red cliffs above the canyons, white-streaked and littered at their feet with broken bone. Dire vultures nest on the ledges — huge, patient, ugly birds that circle the badlands for anything traveling alone, carry it up in their talons, and dash it on the rocks below to crack it open. They are drawn to anything that shines, and an age of it has packed their cliff-nests with the bright leavings of the dead: coin, buckles, rings, blades, and gold stripped from everyone they ever took.
The Bonecrags.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: the Bonecrags are hostile. The dire vultures are animals and there is no parley with them. Out over the open ground they hunt by snatch-and-drop: a vulture stoops on a target, seizes it in its talons, hauls it up, and lets it fall to the rocks to break it open. They pick the lone, the weak, and the already-wounded first, and leave a strong, close-packed group mostly alone — the danger out here is to stragglers and the hurt. At the nests it is different: the birds defend their hoard and their young without limit, stooping again and again, fouling a climber's footing and bowshots with their wings, and fighting to the death on the ledges.

The nests are the prize. Each is a midden of shattered bone and the bright metal the vultures magpie out of everything they kill — loose coin, gold and silver ornaments, buckles and rings, and the odd whole blade or piece of armor stripped off the dead and worth carrying out. A slain dire vulture yields a hooked beak and talons that make a fine piercing weapon, and broad stiff flight-feathers. The richest nests sit highest, on the worst ledges.

The Bone Ground.description: The open rock at the base of the cliffs, pale with bird-lime and strewn with broken bone where the vultures drop what they catch. The ground is exposed on every side, with no cover and a clear view up the red rock face to the ledges and the dark clutter of nests far above.

The Lower Ledges.description: The first reachable shelves of the cliff, narrow and wind-scoured, the rock fouled white and crusted with old nest-litter. Bone and bright scraps lie wedged in the cracks. The face steepens sharply above, the larger nests visible higher up on ledges that thin to nothing.

The High Nests.description: The top of the cliffs, where the biggest stick-and-bone nests sit on the highest and narrowest ledges, open to the sky and the long drop. The footing is bad and the wind is strong. From here the whole run of canyons spreads out below.

The Flamebleed.name: The Flamebleed
The Flamebleed.basicInfo: A canyon where fire bleeds up out of the ground. The red rock is split open and burning from within, flame welling from the cracks, and up through the same cracks crawl fire-demons — small, fierce, and many — out of the dark below. A fire-demon is made of living flame, and a slain one can be cut for its burning heart, the prize of any weapon-smith who wants to forge a blade that never goes cold. The canyon has killed treasure-hunters and plunderers for an age, and what they carried is still down there in the ash, for anyone who can take it off the demons that took it first.
The Flamebleed.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: the Flamebleed is hostile and nothing in it will parley. Fire-demons climb up out of the burning seams — quick and fierce, throwing fire from range and rushing in to burn what they reach, bursting back to ash when killed. Fire-imps come in swarms, each weak but many together, and scatter when their nerve breaks. Burned beasts den among the seams too — badland jackals and lean drakes warped by long years in the heat, ember-veined and cracked, that shrug off fire and fight like cornered animals.

The open fire is its own danger. Seams gout without warning, the glassed ground breaks over pockets of heat, and a fall into a burning crack kills on its own.

A slain fire-demon's heart is a coal of living flame that never cools, prized by a weapon-smith or enchanter for a fire-weapon. The burned beasts yield ember-veined hide and scale that turn fire. Old coin, blades, and gear lie in the ash where the dead were stripped, thickest along the deeper seams.

There is a greater prize than a dead demon: a live one. The Desert Rose hunters do not kill what they catch — they seal the demon whole into a warded vessel, and a bottled fire-demon is worth a fortune to them and to others who deal in such things. With a warded bottle and a sealing-ring, in the dazed breath after a demon surfaces from a seam, one can be caught and corked alive instead of killed. Some buyers want it locked safely away. Some want it for worse.

The Mouth of the Bleed.description: The open end of the canyon, where the red rock first cracks and the ground begins to smoke. Thin seams of fire thread the walls, faint here and brighter ahead, and the stone is scorched black in patches. The air shimmers down the length of the gorge, and the way runs deeper between steepening, burning walls.

The Glassways.description: The middle of the canyon, where the walls and floor are burned to black glass, smooth and sharp and glinting with the firelight welling up through them. Wide seams of open flame split the ground, and the rock between them is cracked and uncertain. The gorge narrows and darkens ahead, the glow growing stronger. Here and there the black glass is voidglass, reflecting stars that are not overhead.

The Quick.description: The deepest reach of the canyon, where the seams run together into broad pools and falls of open fire and the heat is fiercest. The black-glass walls glow from within, lit red-gold by the flame beneath them. A narrow, broken path threads between the burning, the rock fractured and bleeding fire on every side. Voidglass runs through the glowing walls.

Redgate Caravanserai.name: Redgate Caravanserai
Redgate Caravanserai.basicInfo: A ruined waystation on the canyon road, a square fort of red mudbrick built long ago to shelter caravans for the night — walls, a gate, a courtyard, and stabling, half-fallen now and scoured with sand. Its place on the road makes it a prize for raiders: gnoll bands hold it again and again, denning behind its old walls to fall on the wagons that still must pass this way. A band in the caravanserai means plunder heaped in the courtyard, beasts chained in the stalls, and captives taken off the road penned in the cellars below.
Redgate Caravanserai.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: when a gnoll band holds Redgate it is hostile, and the raiders attack any stranger on sight — there is no toll and no parley here; this is a raider den, not a place that deals. The gnolls fight as a pack: they swarm a target together, the strongest forward and the rest harrying the flanks, and they break and run for the walls or the cellars when their leader falls or their numbers are badly cut. They keep beasts on chains — hyenas and worse — loosed to run down anyone who flees, and a few raiders hold the gate-towers with bows.

Captives taken off the road are held alive in the cellars for sale, and freeing them is the reason most come to Redgate. The courtyard and the raiders' quarters hold the take of raided caravans — coin, trade-goods, weapons, and gear stripped from dead guards, the better pieces kept by whoever leads the band. The chained beasts can be loosed against their own keepers by a quick hand.

The Broken Gate.description: The road runs straight up to the caravanserai's only entrance, a high mudbrick gateway with one leaf of its great doors fallen and the other hanging. Flanking towers of crumbling brick rise on either side, with a clear line down the road in both directions and up at the walls. Sand has drifted against the base of the walls and through the gap.

The Courtyard.description: The open square within the walls, ringed by the collapsed arcades and stalls where caravans once unloaded. A well stands at the center, and broken wagons and the litter of long use clutter the ground. Low doorways open off the yard into the stabling and the ruined lodging-rooms, and a stair at the back corner drops into the dark below.

The Stables.description: A long open-fronted range along one wall where the caravans once kept their animals, the stalls now fouled and broken down. Chains and iron posts line the walls. The roof has fallen in along part of its length, letting in bars of light, and a gap in the back wall opens to the canyon outside.

The Cellars.description: The vaulted brick undercroft beneath the lodging-rooms, dug to keep stores cool and since partitioned with bars and rough gates into pens. The air is close and the only light comes down the stair from the courtyard. Cramped passages run between the cells, deeper under the fort than the floor above would suggest.

The Ruins of Naran-Kadish.name: The Ruins of Naran-Kadish
The Ruins of Naran-Kadish.basicInfo: The broken city of the Flame Princes, sprawled across a wide red canyon floor — a once-great place of domed palaces and pillared courts, burned and fallen an age ago and half-swallowed by sand. Gnoll clans hold it now, each prince ruling a quarter of the ruin from a palace he has crowned himself in, draped in stolen finery and waited on hand and foot. The greatest of them styles himself the Sultan. Strangers can come and go and even trade here, for a price and a careful tongue, but the peace is thin: the gnolls are tyrants under their silks, and a guest who gives offense can become a prisoner.
The Ruins of Naran-Kadish.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Naran-Kadish is dangerous but not hostile on sight. The gnoll princes suffer outsiders who come to trade, pay their tolls, and show respect, and a visitor can walk the ruin, deal, and ask questions if he minds his manners. This holds only so long as he is useful and deferent. Give offense, cheat a prince, free a captive, or be caught somewhere forbidden, and the welcome ends at once — the gnolls turn on a guest in a breath, and the captured are killed or chained and sold. The princes are vain, greedy, and quick to take insult, and they scheme against one another constantly; a clever outsider can play one quarter against another.

Naran-Kadish burned by its own hand. When the demons came, the Flame Princes, the djinnborn nobles who ruled here, burned their own city in a great working to drive them out. It worked, and the demons were thrown back, but the fire never fully died — it still smolders far below, and the ground stays warm and the demons still leak up from the deepest ruins. The gnolls neither know nor care what their city sits upon.

The princes set captives and the desperate to digging the ruins for buried treasure, and they sell what comes up to anyone who pays. Most is old gold, glass, and djinnborn relics. But the diggers also turn up shards of the old sealing-work and stranger things touched by what burned here, and a quiet sort of buyer comes for exactly those — robed strangers who pay well, ask for the marked pieces by description, and are let in where ordinary traders are not. They are a small cult of demon-callers who want to learn how the old sealing-work was made so they can break the seal under the city and let the demons up. The princes think them harmless cranks with deep purses.

The palaces hold a sultan's plundered wealth — gold, jewels, fine arms, and the relics dug from the ruin. Captives are held throughout for labor and sale. A prince's favor, his treasury, or his hoard of dug relics are all there for an outsider bold or cunning enough to take them.

The Shattered Gate.description: The old ceremonial entrance to the city, a colossal broken arch of red stone leaning over the canyon road, carved with the worn figures of winged, crowned beings. Crude banners and gnoll trophies hang from it now. Beyond, the ruined avenues open out, and sentries watch the approach from perches in the broken stonework. The wide street runs in toward the heart of the ruin.

The Market Ruins.description: A great fallen plaza where the gnolls trade, the toppled colonnades and dry fountains strung with awnings and stalls. Goods of every kind change hands here in the open, watched over by armed gnolls. Lanes thread off between the broken buildings, and a guarded way leads down toward the digging-grounds at the city's lowest edge.

The Palace Quarters.description: The grand ruined palaces where the gnoll princes hold court, each a domed and pillared hall crowned with stolen splendor and guarded by its prince's own crew. Sand-choked gardens and dry pools lie between them, and the quarters of rival princes stand walled off from one another in wary distance. The Sultan's palace, the largest, rises at the center.

The Diggings.description: The lowest part of the ruin, where the city sank deepest into the canyon floor and the rock is broken open into pits and tunnels. The ground here is hot to the touch and threaded with smoke rising from far below. Diggers work the rubble under guard, and the oldest, most buried halls run down into the dark beyond where the digging has reached.

Saffra.name: Saffra
Saffra.basicInfo: A djinnborn town built into a walled box canyon, sheer red cliffs on three sides and one way in at the mouth. Inside, the canyon floor and its terraced walls are crowded with forges, market-lanes, and caravan-yards. The djinnborn here are the finest fire-smiths in the badlands, working brass and metal into blades that hold flame, and they deal openly in the relics that come up out of the ruined city nearby.
Saffra.hiddenInfo:
Saffra is a safe, friendly town and a welcome stop in hard country — the warm social ground of the canyons and the last easy place before the deep badlands. It is djinnborn through and through: fire-eyed folk, proud and theatrical, generous to a guest who treats them well and sharp with one who does not. Outsiders of every kind pass through to trade, hire, and outfit, and are made welcome.

The djinnborn of Saffra are the descendants of the nobles who once ruled the ruined city nearby, before it burned. They hold this canyon because the country is theirs by old right, and they have no love at all for the gnoll princes squatting in their ancestors' halls. They are far too few to drive the gnolls out and know it, so the grudge stays a grudge: they trade with the gnolls when they must, despise them always, and would gladly see them gone if someone else did the work.

The forges are Saffra's wonder and the root of its craft. They burn with a strange blue-white flame, hotter and cleaner than any ordinary fire, fed by small fire-spirits the djinnborn bind into the coals — little living flames a careful eye can see moving in the heat, kept and worked, not tormented. With them the smiths forge blades and gear that hold fire, and they will work the raw fire-materials a hand brings in — a fire-demon's everlasting heart-coal and the like — into finished weapons for the right price.

The djinnborn know old djinnborn work better than anyone alive, and the relic-dealers of the bazaar buy, sell, and appraise what comes up out of the ruins honestly, telling true relics from gnoll-fenced junk. The caravan-yards outfit and launch the trade across the badlands: mounts, water, supply, guides who know the roads, and guards for hire.

The Bazaar.description: The crowded market filling the floor of the canyon, a sprawl of stalls and awnings strung between the standing rock and the terraced buildings climbing the walls. Goods of every kind are laid out here — metalwork, relics, fire-cured spice and incense, food and cloth — and lanes wind off between the buildings and up the terraces. The red cliffs rise close on three sides, and the way out to the canyon mouth lies at one end.

The Forges.description: The smithies worked into the lower terraces of the canyon wall, their open fronts glowing with an odd blue-white light that does not look like ordinary fire. The flame in the hearths burns strange and bright, and the air above the terrace shimmers with heat. Finished metalwork and brass hang on display along the fronts, and stepped lanes connect the forges one to the next.

The Caravan Yards.description: The open staging-ground near the canyon mouth, fenced into pens and loading-yards where the caravans form up. Desert mounts are kept here, water-troughs and store-sheds line the walls, and gear and supply lie stacked under awnings. From here the single way out runs through the canyon mouth and onto the open road.

Fountain Court Inn.description: A large open courtyard ringed with shaded porticoes, roofed only by the sky and the canyon walls above. Shade trees grow from the stone floor and a fountain plays at the center, and low cushioned seats are set on rugs across the ground. It is cool and green here in the red heat of the canyon, a place to sit, drink, and talk.

Citadel of the Pact.name: Citadel of the Pact
Citadel of the Pact.basicInfo: A fortress-monastery of rose-pink stone, raised on a high crag of the same rock above the red canyons. The stone is desert-rose, which the dark cannot well up through, and the crag is the largest outcrop of it in the land — so the citadel is the one safe ground in a country that bleeds demons, and the demon-hunters of the Desert Rose have made it their home. Brass domes and arches rise warm and rosy over courts and workshops, and at its sealed heart the Order keeps the Gate of Gaol, through which the demons they catch are cast out of the world for good.
Citadel of the Pact.hiddenInfo:
The Citadel of the Pact is a safe, welcoming place and the home of the demon-hunter in the Redrock. The Order of the Desert Rose holds it — a sworn order, open to any who would learn the work, that takes recruits, trains them, and sends them out under writ against the demon-haunted places of the land. A newcomer who proves willing is taken in and taught; one who proves able rises to ride out as a sworn hunter of the Rose. The Order welcomes outsiders, sells its lore and its craft, and asks only that its work and its Gate be respected.

The Order's way is neither to kill demons nor to keep them. A demon cannot truly be killed — cut down, it gathers itself again in time — and a demon kept is a demon that will one day get loose. So the Rose bind what they hunt, sealing it whole into a warded vessel, and carry it back here to be cast through the Gate of Gaol and gone for good. This is what it means to keep the Pact: not to slay the dark, but to put it back where it cannot return from. The Order will take in a bound demon a hunter brings and see it banished, and a sealed vessel is worth a great deal to them.

The Gate of Gaol is a great arch the Order made and keeps, standing in a locked and guarded vault at the citadel's heart. It opens on an abyss — a prison from which nothing comes back — and anything at all that passes through the arch is banished the same as any demon, living or dead, willing or not. For that reason it is sealed away and opened only for the rite, never left for anyone to wander into.

The demon-hunt is dangerous work and the Order is always short of hands. It sends its hunters across the whole region: into the dead town where the soulless walk, down into the burning canyon where fire-demons crawl up from below, and against any place where the dark breaks through. The Order also watches the ruined city the gnolls hold with dread, for the old fire still smolders far below it and demons leak up from its deepest ruins. The workshops here make and sell the tools of the work — warded vessels to catch a demon in, sealing-rings, and brass gear — and the masters will teach the binding-craft to those who earn it.

The Rose Court.description: The great open court at the citadel's entrance, floored and walled in warm rose-pink stone, ringed with brass-domed colonnades that throw bands of shade across the ground. A fountain plays at the center, and from the stone of the court itself grow clusters of pale rose-crystal, the desert-rose that gives the place its name and its warding. The court is wide and welcoming, with arched ways leading deeper into the fortress and a long view back over the red canyons far below the crag.

The Chapter Hall.description: The Order's great hall, a high rose-stone chamber under a brass dome, hung with the banners and tokens of the Desert Rose and lined with long tables. Here the Order gathers, takes in its own, and gives out its writs. Doorways open from it to the inner fortress, and a guarded passage leads down toward the sealed heart of the citadel.

The Workshops.description: A long brass-roofed hall of workbenches, forges, and crafting-stations where the Order makes the tools of its trade. Warded brass vessels in every size stand on the racks, alongside sealing-rings, chains, and half-finished gear, and the walls are hung with the patterns and diagrams of the binding-craft. Apprentices work the benches beside the masters here.

The Training Yard.description: An open rose-stone yard within the walls, set about with marked circles, posts, and warded pens. The ground is scuffed and scorched in places from hard use. Racks of practice-gear and warded vessels stand along one side, and the yard looks out past the parapet to the drop below the crag.

The Vault of Gaol.description: A sealed chamber deep in the rose-stone at the citadel's heart, behind locked and guarded brass doors. Within stands the Gate of Gaol: a great ornamental arch of brass and rose-stone, beautiful and intricate, framing a darkness that is not the wall behind it but somewhere else entirely. The chamber is bare otherwise, kept empty and shut, the only way in through the hall above.

Tomb Crags.name: Tomb Crags
Tomb Crags.basicInfo: Rock crags rise from a sand-sea in the open desert, the only high ground for miles. The sand between them is sand-wyrm country: the great worms feel movement through it and come up under anything that crosses. A Sun-King army was broken here in the old age, and the dead still lie on the crags where they fled the worms. Their sun-gold blades and regalia rest among the bones on the high rock. Most reachable crags have been picked over; some have not. Raiders camp on the rises to dig for the gold that is left and to rob whoever else comes for it.
Tomb Crags.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The raiders here default to hostile. They are a crew of Khenret's Company working the crags, and they treat every other person in the sand as competition to rob or kill. They may parley if badly outnumbered or offered a cut worth more than a corpse. The sand-wyrms are not hostile in the social sense; they are animals that hunt vibration, and they take anything that moves across open sand.

The crags are the safe ground and the sand is the killing-floor. The wyrms cannot reach onto the high rock, so everything that works here clings to the crags and crosses the sand only when it must. The crew holds the largest central crag as a camp and ranges out to the others. A fight that spills off the rock and onto the sand ends when the ground opens.

Sun-gold lies thickest on the crags farthest out, where the army climbed highest and the dead have not been stripped. The near crags are picked clean. Reaching the far rock means crossing more open sand, which is the trade the place makes: the richer the crag, the longer the run to it.

Loot is found on the bodies and in the old dig-sites among the bones. Sun-gold blade: radiant, bites undead, demons, and shadow-things hardest. Sun-gold regalia: radiant war-ornament of a Sun-King soldier. Wyrm tooth: a cast tooth pulled from the sand, large enough to be worked into a blade-core.

The Sand-Sea.description: An open plain of dunes with the crags standing out of it in the distance, dark rock against pale sand. The footing is loose and shifting, every step sinking and dragging, with no cover and no high ground until the rock. Old tracks and the bleached timber of broken wagons surface here and there where the dunes have shifted, then vanish under the next drift.

The Near Crags.description: Low rock rises breaking out of the sand, close enough to the plain's edge to reach without a long crossing. The stone is sun-cracked and scattered with bones and rusted iron, and the ground between the bones is dug over and turned, pocked with old holes where the dead were stripped. From the height the dune-sea spreads on all sides, the far crags standing thin and small against the horizon.

The Far Crags.description: Tall rock standing alone far out in the sand-sea, reached only across open dune. The crags here rise steep and high, and the bones lie thick on the upper ledges where men climbed as far as the stone went. Sun-gold catches the light among them, blades and ornament still on the dead, the rock here unturned and undug.

Sweetwater Pool.name: Sweetwater Pool
Sweetwater Pool.basicInfo: A wide spring-fed oasis deep in the sand, ringed with date palms and flowering green, its water clear and cool and sweet. It is the most beautiful place for many days' travel and the most welcoming sight a parched traveler could ask for. Lamia hold it: cunning man-eaters with a woman's face and a serpent's body, who have made the oasis their hunting ground. Caravans know the name and the warning that rides with it, and still the  lamia devour their share of victims who wander in out of the desert.
Sweetwater Pool.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The lamia attack intruders. They are cunning and patient and can speak, and a clever or determined visitor might draw one into talk or a bargain, but the pack defaults to the hunt and treats anyone who comes to the water as prey. They do not announce themselves; a lamia will pass for a woman at a distance and close the gap before striking.

A family of lamia holds the oasis: man-eaters with a woman's upper body and a great serpent's coil below, fast over open ground and faster through the reeds and palms. They hunt by drawing prey in close, and the oasis is the draw, so they let it stay beautiful and let the desert deliver the thirsty. They keep to the water and the green and do not range far into the sand.

The pack keeps prey alive in the rocks behind the spring, chained, until they are wanted. The goods of everyone the oasis has killed lie among the rocks and around the pools where packs rested: coin, weapons, caravan-stock, and the fine things travelers carried. Loot is found in the rocks and at the water's edge. Most of it is ordinary plunder; the rare good piece turns up where a wealthy traveler fell.

The Waters.description: A broad, clear spring at the heart of the oasis, cool and still, fed from below and rimmed with smooth stone and soft grass. Date palms and flowering green ring the water and throw deep shade over it. Beyond the green, the open sand runs flat to the horizon in every direction; this is the only water and the only shade for days.

The Palm Grove.description: A dense ring of date palms, tall reeds, and flowering brush around the spring, thick enough to lose sight of the open water from within it. Narrow tracks wind between the trunks, and the ground is soft and green underfoot. The grove gives shade and cover, and a clear line of sight nowhere; a few steps in, the palms close around.

The Rocks.description: A low stony hollow behind the spring, screened from the water by the green. Old iron chains are bolted into the rock and lie slack across the stone, and a deep cleft sinks into the ground at the back, dark and dry. Travelers' goods lie scattered among the stones, and worn tracks lead in from the grove.

The Mirror-Waste.name: The Mirror-Waste
The Mirror-Waste.basicInfo: A crater of black glass miles wide, where two flying citadels of the old Empyrean Empire clashed and fell, fusing the desert to glass in the impact. The ground is jagged and mirror-bright, spires and sheets of it throwing back the sun and every reflection until a traveler cannot tell a real shape from its image or judge any distance. Great broken pieces of the fallen citadels lie half-sunk in the glass, some whole enough to enter. The citadels' guardians fell with them and still walk the wreck: mirror-bright metal soldiers, near-invisible against the glass until they move. Treasure-hunters come for the empyrean brass and sun-bright metal embedded in the crater, and the glass and its guardians take a share of them.
The Mirror-Waste.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The citadel guardians attack anyone who enters the wreck. They are constructs with no minds to reason with and no reason to spare anyone; they default to destroying intruders and do not stop, parley, or tire. The glass itself is a standing hazard apart from them: its edges cut, its glare blinds at midday, and its reflections hide what is coming.

The guardians are the sky-citadels' war-automata, mirror-bright metal polished to throw back the glass around them, so they stand unseen among the spires until they move. They hold to the citadel-wreck they fell with and patrol the embedded pieces, thickest around the largest fallen hull. A few fire-things still haunt the crater's hottest stretches, loosed when the djinn-engine that powered the citadels, a fire-spirit bound in brass, burst and made the glass: salamanders and lesser fire-spirits that never left the heat.

The loot is the Empyrean Empire's make, embedded in the wreck and carried in the broken hulls. Citadel-shard: a piece of empyrean make worked into brass and sun-bright metal. Guardian-core: the power-stone drawn from a fallen automaton. The constructs are unmade by shock, and their brass eaten by acid; the fire-things take frost.

The Glass Flats.description: The open floor of the crater, broad sheets of black glass flowed smooth and frozen, mirror-bright and blinding under the midday sun. The flats run level for a long way before the ground breaks into spires ahead, and the dark shapes of fallen citadel-wreck stand half-sunk in the glass on the far side. There is no shade and no cover, and the heat off the glass is worst where the surface runs newest and clearest near the crater's heart.

The Spires.description: A field of shattered glass risen in jagged spires and leaning sheets, close-packed and taller than a man, throwing back the light and every reflection from a hundred angles. There is no true line of sight here; the same shape repeats across a dozen surfaces, and distance cannot be judged among the mirrors. Narrow lanes of broken glass wind between the spires toward the wreck beyond. Now and then a shard among the spires holds stars in its depths: voidglass.

The Fallen Hull.description: A great broken section of a sky-citadel half-buried in the glass, large enough to walk into, its canted brass corridors and shattered chambers tilted where it struck. Sun-bright metal and empyrean make stud the walls and lie loose in the broken rooms, much of it fused into the glass that flooded in. The passages run deep into the hull, dim and angled, with glare from the crater outside cutting through every break in the metal.

Widow's Way.name: Widow's Way
Widow's Way.basicInfo: The only road through this stretch of open desert, a hard track of sand and broken stone that caravans must take because there is no other way across. Bandits and gnoll packs hunt it, and the burned wrecks of the caravans that did not make it lie strung along its length, their cargo and strongboxes spilled and half-buried in the sand. Travelers call it Widow's Way and cross it anyway, because crossing it is the only way through. The wrecks are picked at by every raider on the road and never quite emptied.
Widow's Way.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The bandits and the gnoll packs on this road default to hostile and treat travelers as prey and plunder. The bandits may parley if outmatched or paid; the gnolls hunt and do not. Both fall on anyone crossing the road, and on each other when there is no easier kill.

Two kinds of raider work Widow's Way. Human bandit crews hold the higher ground and the chokes, robbing what crosses and killing what resists. Gnoll packs range the open road and run with giant hyenas, hunting in numbers and dragging off the living along with the dead. The two sides raid the same caravans and fight over the spoils as often as they share the road.

The loot is what the failed crossings left behind, scattered through the wrecks and buried where wagons fell: trade-cargo, coin, strongboxes, and the goods travelers carried. The wrecks are stripped over and over and never bare, because more caravans keep trying the road. Most of it is ordinary plunder; the rare good piece turns up in a strongbox no raider got open.

The Open Track.description: A long stretch of road running straight across flat open desert, sand drifted over broken paving, with no cover to either side for as far as the eye reaches. Burned wagons and scattered cargo lie along the verges and out in the sand where they were dragged, half-buried and bleached. The ground is hard enough to march and exposed enough that anything on the road is seen from a long way off.

The Narrows.description: Where the road threads between low rock outcrops and a cut bank, the open desert pinching to a single hard track with high ground close on both sides. Wrecked wagons stand thick here, jammed and overturned where crossings were caught in the choke, their cargo spilled across the road and into the rocks. The high ground overlooks the whole length of the pass.

The Hollow.description: A sheltered hollow off the road, walled on three sides by rock and screened from the track by a spur of stone. The ground is trodden flat and ringed with old fire-pits and the rotted timber of broken-up wagons, and looted cargo lies stacked and half-sorted against the rock walls. One narrow mouth lets onto the road; tracks run from it down to the track and away into the open sand.

Tomb of the Drowned King.name: Tomb of the Drowned King
Tomb of the Drowned King.basicInfo: A pyramid-tomb of the Sun Kings that sank into a buried spring and flooded, its lower halls drowned under cold dark water. Raiders work it half-submerged, wading and swimming through the sunken passages for the grave-goods that lie in the silt and the sun-gold gone green on the dead. The deepest chambers, where the king was laid, are wholly underwater.
Tomb of the Drowned King.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The dead here default to hostile and attack anything that enters the flooded halls. They do not parley, tire, or stop. The water is a standing hazard apart from them, dragging at armor and gear and offering no firm footing in the deep chambers.

The tomb was a Sun-King's, drowned when the ground gave under it, and its honor-guard drowned with it. Water-logged dead crowd the sunken halls, grasping up from below and from the silt, slow on land and quick in the water. Mummified crocodiles, embalmed as the king's tomb-guardians, hunt the flooded passages and strike from beneath the surface. Eels and serpents nest in the drowned rooms. The deepest threats keep to the burial chamber at the bottom, where the water is blackest.

The loot lies in the silt and on the drowned dead, richest in the lowest flooded chambers. Sun-gold blade: radiant, bites undead, demons, and shadow-things hardest, gone green under the water. Sun-gold regalia: radiant war-ornament of a Sun-King, sunk in the silt. Drowned dead and mummified flesh take fire poorly while wet; the dry upper passages are another matter.

The Tilted Entrance.description: The pyramid's mouth, canted where the ground sank beneath it, half its steps run down into standing water. The upper passages are dry and close, sloping steadily downward until the floor disappears under a black waterline. Old rope and the rotted boats of earlier raiders lie at the water's edge, and the air below is cold and still.

The Flooded Halls.description: Drowned corridors and chambers half-full of cold dark water, the carved walls running down below the surface into the dark. The water is waist-deep to overhead by turns, with no firm footing and no clear sight beneath it. Sunken grave-goods and the litter of the drowned settle in the silt, and broken galleries open off in every direction.

The Sunken Vault.description: The burial chamber at the bottom of the tomb, wholly underwater, a great drowned hall of carved stone vanishing into black water. The king's sarcophagus and the richest of the grave-goods lie below the surface in the silt and the dark. The Crown of the Drowned King may remain among them unless it has already been removed. The water here is coldest and deepest, and no light reaches the floor.

Tomb of the Sun's Eye.name: Tomb of the Sun's Eye
Tomb of the Sun's Eye.basicInfo: A pyramid-tomb of the Sun Kings, crowned with a great aperture open to the sky that the raiders call the Eye. Within, the halls are bright and full of mirrors and lensed brass, and the burial chambers run deep with the king's sun-gold and the bright-craft of his tomb. Metal guardians hunt the passages, and the light itself is turned against intruders. Raiders cannot wait for darkness to slip in; the tomb stays lit day and night. Few who try the Eye come back.
Tomb of the Sun's Eye.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The guardians attack anyone who enters the tomb. They are constructs with no minds to reason with; they default to destroying intruders and do not stop, parley, or tire. The light is a standing hazard apart from them: the focused beams burn what stands in their path and the glare blinds.

The tomb was built to judge intruders with light. Mirror-bright flying constructs, brass drones shaped as scarabs and hawks, rest in the lower tomb and boil up into the lit halls when anyone enters, darting through the beams and turning the focused light to sear. They are fast and small and hard to strike, and they come in numbers. They hold thickest in the depths around the king's chamber.

The halls themselves are the weapon. The Eye at the peak takes sunlight by day, and a vast crystal at the tomb's heart holds the light and pours it back through the halls by night, so the tomb is never dark and intruders cannot wait out the light. Mirrors and lenses fed by the Eye and the crystal throw beams of focused light across the chambers, the same craft the empyreans set in their sky-weapons. The mirrors can be turned by a careful hand to bend a beam aside, onto a guardian, or onto a sealed way. Standing in a beam burns; the glare off the mirrors blinds at the wrong angle.

The loot is the king's sun-gold and the bright-craft of the tomb, richest in the deepest chambers. Sun-gold blade: radiant, bites undead, demons, and shadow-things hardest. Empyrean focusing-glass: a lens of the sun-craft, worked into a weapon or a tool. Lenses, mirrors, and sky-glass fittings throughout. The constructs are unmade by shock, and their brass eaten by acid.

The Aperture.description: The pyramid's high entrance hall, lit from above through the great open Eye at the peak, a shaft of sky-light falling straight down the center. The walls are set with polished mirrors and lensed brass that catch the light and throw it inward, and the chamber stays bright whether the sky beyond is day or dark. Passages lead down and inward, each one lit, none of them dark.

The Mirror Halls.description: A maze of chambers and corridors strung with angled mirrors and lenses, beams of focused light crossing the rooms at fixed lines and pooling bright on the carved walls. The mirrors stand on pivots and rings, some hanging, some set in the floor, and the light bends wherever they turn. There is glare in every direction and shadow almost nowhere; the lit lanes weave deeper into the tomb.

The Crystal Vault.description: The burial chamber at the heart of the tomb, where a vast cut crystal stands above the king's sarcophagus, blazing with light gathered from the Eye and pouring it across the whole hall. The chamber is the brightest in the tomb, lit white and gold from the crystal day and night, and the richest of the grave-goods and sun-gold lie ringed around the dais in the glare.

Tomb of the Embalmers.name: Tomb of the Embalmers
Tomb of the Embalmers.basicInfo: A pyramid-tomb of the Sun Kings where the dead were made: the great embalming-works that wrapped a king's whole household to lie with him. Its halls are lined with rows of the bound dead, wrapping-vats, and jars by the thousand, and the dead here do not lie still. They come in numbers, more than any raider can cut down, drawn up out of the lower halls by anything that enters. The embalming-gold and the household's grave-goods lie deep among them, and the tomb is named for the bound host that fills it.
Tomb of the Embalmers.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The dead here default to hostile and attack anything that enters. They do not parley, tire, or stop, and they come in numbers; the danger is being overwhelmed, not overpowered by any single thing. There is no master to find and no head to cut off, only the host.

The tomb embalmed and wrapped a Sun-King's entire household to be buried with him, and the work was never finished when the empire fell. The halls are full of the bound dead: lesser mummies in their hundreds, wrapped and half-wrapped, standing in rows and stacked in niches, that rouse and shamble toward intruders and keep coming. Scarab swarms nest in the corpses and the wrapping-jars and pour out in clouds that strip flesh. Among the host are the embalmer-dead, the wrapped priests who did the work, tougher and quicker than the rest. The host is thickest in the lower halls and presses up from them.

The loot is the embalming-gold and the household's grave-goods, scattered through the workrooms and the burial niches and richest in the lower halls. Sun-gold ornament: radiant, bites undead, demons, and shadow-things hardest, worked into the wrappings of a household lord. Embalmer's tools and canopic gold lie among the vats. The bound dead are dry and take fire badly; flame runs through the wrappings and the host.

The Outer Workrooms.description: The tomb's upper halls, wide stone workrooms strung with the gear of embalming: stone slabs and drained vats, racks of tools, and shelves of sealed jars stacked floor to ceiling. Wrapped shapes lie on the slabs and lean in the wall-niches, still and bound. Passages run inward and down, and the rooms grow more crowded with the dead the deeper they go.

The Wrapping-Halls.description: Long galleries lined floor to ceiling with the bound dead, wrapped and half-wrapped, standing in rows and packed into niches down the length of the walls. Broken jars and split wrappings litter the floor, and the air is thick with dust. The galleries run on into the dark, the rows unbroken, sloping down toward the lower tomb.

The Lower Halls.description: The deep burial halls at the bottom of the tomb, where the household was laid and the wrapping-work was densest. The dead are stacked thickest here, niche on niche and row on row, and the king's household goods lie heaped among them in gold and bound cloth. The halls open wide and low, and the rows run back further than the eye can follow into the dark.

Tomb of the Risen Host.name: Tomb of the Risen Host
Tomb of the Risen Host.basicInfo: A pyramid-tomb of the Sun Kings where a king was buried with his army, ranks of his soldiers laid down in formation to rise and guard him. The wrapped dead still stand in their ranks through the halls, armored and ordered, and they do not lie quiet. At the heart lie the king and his winged honor-guard, and the richest war-gear in the necropolis lies with them.
Tomb of the Risen Host.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The dead here default to hostile and attack anyone who enters. They do not parley or tire. They fight as soldiers, in ranks and with discipline, and the danger is the order and weight of them rather than sheer numbers; a careful crew can draw the ranks out, fight through a hall, and work toward the center, but the host holds its ground and does not break.

The tomb was a Sun-King's war-barrow, his soldiers entombed in formation to rise as his guard. Mummified soldiers fill the halls in ordered ranks, wrapped and armored, fighting with shield and spear and holding their lines as they were drilled to. Deeper in stand the heavy dead, the king's chosen, and at the center his honor-guard: mummified empyreans, winged and outsized, the strongest and slowest to fall in the tomb. The ranks are thickest around the king's bier and lighter toward the entrance.

The loot is the army's war-gear, richest at the center where the king and his guard lie. Sun-gold blade: radiant, bites undead, demons, and shadow-things hardest. Sun-gold war-regalia: the armored ornament of a Sun-King's soldier or his winged guard. The dead are dry and take fire badly, and the armored ranks are broken open by heavy impact.

The War-Gate.description: The tomb's entrance hall, a broad martial approach lined with carved soldiers and the standards of the old empire cut into the stone. Wrapped figures stand in still ranks along the walls, armored and ordered, spears grounded. The hall runs straight and wide inward, opening toward the ranked halls beyond.

The Hall of Ranks.description: A great pillared hall where the dead host stands in formation, rank behind rank of wrapped and armored soldiers filling the floor in ordered lines. The pillars break the hall into lanes, and old weapons and fallen standards lie among the ranks. The formation runs deeper and heavier toward the chambers at the back.

The King's Array.description: The burial chamber at the tomb's heart, where the king's bier stands ringed by the heaviest of his dead. Great winged figures stand guard close around the bier, taller than the ranks behind them and richly armored, and the finest war-gear and sun-gold of the tomb lie heaped about the dais. The chamber is high and pillared, the array drawn up tight around the king.

Tomb of the Beast-King.name: Tomb of the Beast-King
Tomb of the Beast-King.basicInfo: A pyramid-tomb of the Sun Kings where a king was buried with his menagerie, his hunting-beasts and sacred animals embalmed to rise and guard him. The wrapped beasts still prowl the halls: great cats, hawks, crocodiles, and serpents, and worse things in the depths. They strike from the dark and the high places, fast and varied, and no two halls are guarded the same way. The king's sun-gold and the gold of his beasts lie deep in the tomb, behind everything that hunts there.
Tomb of the Beast-King.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The beasts here default to hostile and attack anything that enters. They do not parley or tire, and they hunt as the animals they were, by ambush, by speed, and from above and below; the danger is being caught off guard by varied attacks rather than worn down by numbers.

The tomb was a Sun-King's, and his hunting-beasts and sacred animals were embalmed and laid in to rise with him. Mummified great cats stalk the halls and spring from cover. Wrapped hawks and vultures roost in the high dark and stoop on intruders. Embalmed crocodiles lie in the old water-channels and the deeper pools. Bound serpents nest in the niches and the rubble. In the depths stand the heavy beasts, larger things the king kept and hunted, the slowest to fall. The beasts range the whole tomb, thickest around the king's chamber.

The loot is the king's sun-gold and the gold-worked harness and ornament of his beasts, richest in the deepest halls. Sun-gold blade: radiant, bites undead, demons, and shadow-things hardest. Sun-gold beast-harness: the gilded collar or trapping of an embalmed beast, worked in radiant metal. The beasts are dry and take fire badly.

The Hunt-Gate.description: The tomb's entrance hall, its walls carved with the king at the hunt, lions and hawks and great serpents cut into the stone in long friezes. Wrapped animal shapes lie still in the wall-niches and along the floor, bound and gilded. The hall runs inward past pillars and old dry channels cut into the floor, opening toward the halls beyond.

The Beast-Halls.description: A run of high pillared chambers broken by dry water-channels, pits, and ledges, the kind of ground the king's beasts were kept and shown in. Cover stands everywhere: pillars, fallen stone, the dark mouths of the channels, and ledges high in the walls above the light. Wrapped beasts lie among the rubble and in the niches, and the halls run on deeper into the dark.

The King's Den.description: The burial chamber at the heart of the tomb, a great vaulted hall set like a beast's lair, with pits and channels and high stone ledges ringing the king's bier. The largest of the embalmed beasts were laid here close around their king, and the richest of the sun-gold and the gilded beast-harness lie heaped about the dais. The hall is dim and broken-ground, with cover and high places on every side.

Tombs of the Sun Kings.name: Tombs of the Sun Kings
Tombs of the Sun Kings.basicInfo: A necropolis of the old desert empire, where great pyramids stand arrayed across the badland flats, raised over the dead god-kings called the Sun Kings. The pyramids are heaped with the kings' sun-gold and grave-treasure and guarded by traps, wards, and the dead, and the desert around them is the staging-ground of the tomb-raiding trade: crews camp on the flats, outfit, and go in for fortune.
Tombs of the Sun Kings.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The pyramids themselves default to deadly, each guarded by its own dead and wards, and the raider company that holds the First Pyramid attacks rivals on its ground.

The Sun Kings were the god-kings of the old empire, entombed here with their wealth, their households, their armies, and their beasts, each under its own pyramid. The dead do not rest, and the deeper a tomb is worked the worse its guardians. Seven pyramids stand on the flats, each a separate grave with its own dead and its own way of killing: the First and the Third, and the tombs of the Drowned King, the Sun's Eye, the Embalmers, the Risen Host, and the Beast-King.

The First Pyramid is held by Khenret's Company, a raider crew under the jackalkin Khenret, who took the smallest and most-worked tomb as a base and runs digs from it. They rob what crosses their ground and fight other crews for the richest tombs. The Third Pyramid was broken open and is being dug by the New Sun, the cult that means to wake the Sun Kings; since they broke it open, the dead in the other pyramids wake sooner to footsteps and walk farther up their passages, and tombs the crews once worked safely are safe no longer.

The loot is the kings' sun-gold and the grave-treasure of the tombs, richest in the deepest and least-worked graves. Sun-gold blade: radiant, bites undead, demons, and shadow-things hardest. Sun-gold regalia and grave-gold throughout. The near and most-worked tombs are picked over; the wealth is in the ones still guarded.

The Plaza of Kings.description: The vast flat at the necropolis's heart, where the seven pyramids stand arrayed across the sand in a fixed pattern, their faces sheer and their peaks catching the light. A great cracked altar of stone stands at the center of the arrangement, and the ground between the pyramids is open and trodden, scattered with the camps, tracks, and leavings of the crews who stage here. The pyramids rise on every side, and the open desert runs out beyond them.

The First Pyramid.description: The smallest of the seven pyramids, its entrance open and its upper passages cleared and shored, the traps long since sprung or disabled. The upper chambers have been made over into a camp: cleared rooms, stores, and defended ways, with the old burial-passages running down into the dark below where the lower levels stand sealed. Jackal skulls are set over the entrance.

The Third Pyramid.description: A pyramid broken open down its northern face, the collapse laying bare passages and chambers that were sealed for ages. Fresh digging runs through the breach and into the rooms beyond, props and tools and cult-marks left along the way, and the carved doors at the end of the deep hall stand ajar. The passages run down past disturbed sarcophagi into the lower dark.

Halfway Rock.name: Halfway Rock
Halfway Rock.basicInfo: Halfway Rock is a lone tor with a cold spring, standing where the long road that crosses the grass meets its own midpoint. The catkin caravan-families who hold it water any traveler, host any traveler, and share the news of three lands over tea.
Halfway Rock.hiddenInfo:
Halfway Rock belongs to the catkin caravan-families, and they run it the way they run the whole road: by hosting, not by charging. Water, fodder, a safe night, and a place at the lantern-fire go to anyone who asks and plenty who don't. The families are gracious, unhurried, endlessly nosy, and quietly certain the grass would grind to a halt without them.

The Syndicate has offered to buy the families out, to post its own guards for safety, to set a fair toll and split it, and the families have purred through every offer and granted none. A road given away cannot be owned, and the road-men know it.

The catkin hear everything. Every line that crosses the grass passes word here, so the families know who is moving, who is hunting whom, and what waits down which track, often before the people involved do. They share it gladly with travelers they have taken a liking to, and they take their time deciding. A stranger earns their way up by proving useful and decent on the road: walk as a hand, drive a wagon, ride as a line-rider, and one day be trusted with the word itself.

The Wagon-Ring.description: The flat ground at the tor's foot, where wagons stand parked nose-to-tail in wide rings, wheels chocked and shafts down. The long road runs in from the grass on one side and out into the grass on the other, straight and pale and visible for miles each way. Lantern-lines on poles cross overhead between the rings, and the spring's overflow runs out in a stone channel toward the fodder-troughs.

The Lantern-Hall.description: A long hall of grey timber and stretched hide built against the rock, its open sides hung with the same lanterns that light the wagon-rings. Inside are low tables, piled cushions and hides, and a row of iron kettles over a banked fire-trench. The walls are pinned with road-tokens, route-scratches, and the small painted boards caravan-families leave to mark a safe passage.

The Spring.description: A worn path climbs the tor's side to the spring itself, a cold pool welling up in a basin of pale rock near the summit. From the top the grass runs flat to every horizon, and the road shows as a thin line dividing it, one way toward the far ports and the other toward the desert road. Old caravan-marks are cut into the rock around the basin, layered over each other for generations.

The Highgrass.name: The Highgrass
The Highgrass.basicInfo: Where the grass grows tallest it stands higher than a rider, and the largest beasts in the grass sea live inside it: aurochs in ground-shaking herds, and behemoths the size of barns. Grass that high hides everything until it is already on you.
The Highgrass.hiddenInfo:
The danger in the Highgrass is that there is no seeing in it. Grass this tall swallows a behemoth whole; a rider learns what stands in front of him when it is an arm's length away and not before.

Aurochs move through in great herds, placid until startled, and a startled herd becomes a wall of horn and hoof that flattens everything in its lane. Behemoths are barn-sized and nearly unkillable, slow to anger and unstoppable once roused; a wounded behemoth rolls straight through grass, herd, and hunter alike. The true killers are the grass-tigers, striped to vanish in the stalks, which stalk the lone and the wounded and strike from cover, so the one that takes a traveler is the one he never saw.

A behemoth's hide is thick as a door and turns most blades; cured into plates it makes armor only a lance will pierce. Its horns run longer than a man and are harder than iron. A grass-tiger's pelt is vast and striped and prized whole, and its fangs are as long as knives. Aurochs horn and hide are humbler trophies, but the herds are many.

The Margins.description: The grass at the edge stands waist- to shoulder-high, low enough to see over from horseback, and behind it the open grass sea runs flat and pale to the horizon. Ahead, the grass climbs into a green wall taller than a rider, with no gap and no end to it either way. Narrow tracks press into the wall where heavy bodies have shouldered through.

The Trample.description: A wide swath beaten flat through the tall grass, the stalks crushed and the black earth churned and printed with tracks the size of platters. It runs straight a long way before the grass closes over it again, and along its length it is the one place inside the Highgrass where the eye carries any distance. Bleached bone lies half-trodden into the mud where the grass crowds the edges.

The Wallows.description: Broad pits of churned mud and standing water where the ground dips, rimmed by grass flattened in wide circles. Horns, ribs, and the great curved bones of fallen beasts lie bleaching around the water and sunk in the mud.

Drover's Rock.name: Drover's Rock
Drover's Rock.basicInfo: Drover's Rock was once a watering-stop on the south road, until the warlord Vaskarn took it for his seat. His band holds it now, takes what crosses the grass nearby, and calls it tribute. Travelers who cannot pay or fight go around.
Drover's Rock.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Vaskarn's band, the Vaskarni, hold Drover's Rock and default to predation. A lone or weak traveler is robbed, taken, or killed; a strong or useful one may be sized up, taxed, or invited to join rather than fought. They are not a mindless lair, since Vaskarn is recruiting and a hard fighter is worth more to him standing than dead, but refusing him, crossing him, or mocking him to his face turns the whole Rock hostile at once.

Vaskarn is a lionkin warlord who styles himself the Pride of Prides and holds court here as if Drover's Rock were a true pride-hold and he a great pride-lord. He claims no crown, only what any pride-lord claims, he says: one pride set above all the others, and then above all the peoples of the grass. He gathers to himself the clanless, the exiled, and the repudiated of every species, who find in the Vaskarni the pride that cast them out. The tribes refuse him his title and call him the Straw King, fit only for the Burning Ground; he has killed for the name, and it has not stopped spreading.

The Vaskarni carry better steel than a road-band should, sold to them quietly by the gnolls of the Carcass, who profit from the grass staying dangerous, and the tribute squeezed from the road piles up at Vaskarn's seat: coin, gear, and those good bought weapons.

The Roadgate.description: The south road runs straight up to the foot of the rock, where a wall of stacked stone, wagon-wrecks, and sharpened stakes has been thrown across it, with a single gap wide enough for one cart. The old wagon-ground around the foot is a war-camp now, hide tents and picket-lines churned to mud and ringed with the burnt-out frames of wagons that did not pay. Trophies and skulls are lashed to poles along the wall-top, facing the road.

The Lion's Seat.description: The top of the rock holds the old waystation's hall, a long stone building hung now with banners, hide trophies, and the painted boards of caravan-families taken off the road. A high seat of horn and hide stands at the far end, raised on a dais of stacked paving-stones. Around it the rock falls away on all sides to the grass, with the road and the war-camp laid out far below.

The Carcass.name: The Carcass
The Carcass.basicInfo: The Carcass is the skeleton of a creature so vast and ancient nobody agrees what it once was, lying half-sunk in the grass with its ribs arching overhead like a hall. Gnoll packs have moved into the bones and made them a warren of dens, stalls, and rope-bridges. Whatever you cannot buy honestly anywhere else in the grass sea, you can probably buy here.
The Carcass.hiddenInfo:
The Carcass runs on bluster, extortion, and a black market. Pack alphas hold stretches of the skeleton and carry ridiculous earned titles — the Lord of the Long Grass, the Thrice-Blooded King — and a failed alpha faces a challenger before sundown.

The gnolls trade in things no one else will touch, take mercenary work no one else will take, and keep the worst banditry concentrated in one place where everyone can see it. The only rule of the market is pay up front.

The Carcass is the region's broker and rumor-mill. The gnolls sell maps and ways into the old burial-mound, word of where Vaskarn's band is striking and what it is worth, and good steel to anyone with coin — including, it is widely understood, to Vaskarn himself. They will sell the same secret twice and to both sides, and consider that good business.

The bones are harder than stone and faintly warm to the touch.

The Jaw.description: The way in, through the creature's mouth: the lower jawbone forms the threshold, the upper jaw arches overhead, and teeth the size of standing stones flank the gap. Hide awnings and the first stalls crowd the opening, and rope-lines climb from here up into the skull above.

The Ribcage.description: The great hollow of the chest, where ribs arch overhead like the vaults of a hall, strung between with hide tarps for shade. Dens and platforms are built up against the inner curve of the bones at several heights, linked by ladders and swaying rope-walks. A long open floor runs down the center between the ribs.

The Gut.description: The ground between and beneath the bones, roofed over by the ribs and platforms above so the light comes down grey and broken. The market lives here: stalls and dens packed into the permanent shade, deals struck in low voices. Narrow lanes wind between stacked goods, bone, and hide.

The Tail.description: The long line of the spine runs out from the ribcage into the grass, vertebrae the size of huts strung one after another. Dens are carved and built into the gaps between the bones, the largest at the base of the tail where an alpha keeps a seat. The far end trails off into open grass.

Bryngard.name: Bryngard
Bryngard.basicInfo: Bryngard is a kingdom drowned in the fen, its streets and halls standing under black water. Its dead are still fighting the battle they died in, on and on with no end to it, and the arms and grave-gold of a whole army lie down there among them.
Bryngard.hiddenInfo:
The scattered remnants of two dead armies still fight Bryngard's last battle, neither knowing it died: Bryngard's own defenders, who hold the keep and the drowned streets, and the besieging host that broke in through the Breach. The rank and file are revenants; the captains and knights are wraiths, faster and far worse, who rally the footsoldiers.

IMPORTANT: the dead ignore the living at first, absorbed in their war. Someone who keeps to the edges and touches nothing can pass through them. They turn on the living when given a reason: stepping between the two forces, taking up arms or a banner of theirs, striking one of them, or making enough noise or light to break their attention.

The two sides of the battle can be set against each other or slipped past while they are locked together. Raising a fallen standard draws the dead who follow it.

Loot is the war-gear of two drowned armies, scattered thickest where the fighting was worst and richest in the keep and wherever a captain fell: blades, shields, mail, banners, grave-gold, and war-pay. Among it are old blades that cut the restless dead as easily as living flesh, and fallen standards the dead still rally to, following whoever raises one.

The Dam.description: A long earthen dam runs across the head of the basin, torn open through the middle. Streets and squares under a shallow black flood, with rooftops, a leaning tower, and the bulk of a keep standing clear of it. Broken stone and reed make the slope down toward the streets.

The Drowned Streets.description: The streets of Bryngard run as shallow flood between buildings standing in the water to the height of a door. The water lies no more than thigh-deep along the lanes, dropping away into the odd cellar-mouth or sunk well, so most of the city can be crossed on foot. Side-streets run off in every direction into a sunk market, a row of drowned houses, and a well-yard gone to a pool, any of which can be worked through toward the keep or the broken wall.

The Keep.description: The keep stands above the flood. A wide stair climbs out of the great hall into galleries and chambers overhead. An armory opens off the hall, its racks and chests still holding old mail and arms. Higher up, a strongroom door stands shut at the end of a gallery, and narrow stairs run on toward the roof and the leaning tower.

The Breach.description: A length of the city wall has been smashed inward here, leaving a bank of broken stone half-buried in the shallows. Siege-ladders and a shattered ram lie where they fell against it, and the ground inside the gap is churned and littered with splintered shields. Shallow water covers the rubble, with deeper pits where the assault tore the ground open. Beyond the breach the open fen shows through the gap.

Avelmere.name: Avelmere
Avelmere.basicInfo: Avelmere is a wealthy city that died twice: first of a plague that swept through it, then under the flood that closed over what the plague had left. Its riches lie beneath the flat black water still, and its plague-dead wait in it for anyone who wades in after them.
Avelmere.hiddenInfo:
Avelmere's dead are the diseased dead: ravenous, mindless ghouls and the rotted dead that drowned with the city. They lie submerged in the flat water and wait in the dark wet rooms. They swarm, rising out of the flood without warning, dragging the living under, coming on in numbers, and they are thickest toward the great hall at the heart.

IMPORTANT: Avelmere's dead are hostile and attack any living thing among them. They do not parley or relent, and they hunt by swarming, lying still and submerged until the living draw near, then surging up to drag them down and bury them in numbers.

The dead are clumsy on dry footing and deadliest in open water, where weight of numbers tells and they pull the living under.

Loot: at the heart, with the king, his crown of gold and stones and his sword, a blessed old blade that bites the dead and the cursed far harder than steel. Behind the dais, a strongroom holding a rich kingdom's hoard of plate, coin, and jewels. Lesser grave-gold and the goods of a drowned town lie through the streets, the temple, and the chambers off the hall.

The Causeway.description: A raised stone road runs out from the dry edge into the flooded city, dropping lower until the water closes over it. From it Avelmere lies still and grey under flat water, its streets gone to dark channels and its squares to dead pools. A great hall stands clear of the flood at the city's heart, gold gone dull on its roof and its high windows above the water.

The Reed Streets.description: The streets stand flooded and still between buildings sunk to their upper floors, the water dark and flat and grown at its edges with reeds. Lines of sight close fast between walls and half-drowned roofs, so a stretch of open water gives way to a narrow passage and then to another sunk court. Roofs and the tops of walls stand clear above the flood, dry footing over the deeper channels, and shutters, furniture, and the goods of a town drift caught in the reeds.

The Temple.description: The temple stands at the head of a drowned square, its doors open to the water and its floor flooded between rows of pillars. Cots and biers stand crowded the length of the nave where they were set, most under the flat water now, a few on a step of raised floor still clear of it. Side-chapels open off the aisles, a stair runs down into a flooded crypt below, and another climbs into a bell-tower that stands well above the flood.

The Throne-Hall.description: The great hall stands above the flood at the heart of the city, water lying flat across its floor and a long aisle running toward a raised dais and a stone throne set clear of it. Gold fittings and the wealth of a rich court show dull along the walls, hangings rotted to threads, and the high tables of a hall still standing in their places. Doors behind the dais open on private chambers and a strongroom, and a gallery runs above the aisle around the hall.

Carrowgate.name: Carrowgate
Carrowgate.basicInfo: Carrowgate is a raiders' stronghold out in the bog, a ruined fort held by the worst men on the moor. They rob the dry country and the graves alike, and sell what they take to anyone with the coin and the stomach for it.
Carrowgate.hiddenInfo:
The reavers of Carrowgate are marshfolk out of the low fen, a warband that holds the old fort and preys on the moor: raiding the villages, breaking open barrows for grave-gold, and taking captives to ransom. They fear nothing on the moor but the Knights Vigilant and the dead.

IMPORTANT: the reavers are predatory but not mad. They size up a newcomer before they move: anyone who looks hard, useful, or worth a deal is heard out, and they will trade, fence, sell, or hire; anyone who looks weak, lost, or soft and rich is robbed, ransomed, or killed. They respect strength and coin and nothing else. Cheat them, threaten the camp, or move on their plunder or their captives, and the whole warband turns at once.

Their plunder is the wealth of the moor's dead and its raided living, kept in a vault under the fort: grave-gold, coin, raided goods, and the barrow-silver and blessed arms that bite the dead. They fence it to the Syndicate and to any buyer with coin. Captives are penned in the cells below and held for ransom. The chief keeps the best of everything.

The Landing.description: A muddy landing on a bog island, boats drawn up in the reeds and a track leading up into the camp. The ruined fort stands above it, and brown bog water spreads flat on every side.

The Camp.description: A sprawl of huts and tents and shelters built from wrecked boats, crowded between the landing and the fort. Cookfires and a long drinking-shed stand at its middle, with stacks of plunder under awnings nearby. Tracks run up to the fort and down to the boats.

The Gatehouse.description: The fort's old gatehouse, a shell of broken stone walls and towers the reavers hold as their stronghold. A vault in its base holds the best of the plunder, and captives are penned in cells below. Stairs climb the towers to lookouts over the bog.

The Barrowlands.name: The Barrowlands
The Barrowlands.basicInfo: The Barrowlands are open heath covered in the burial mounds of an older age, where the war-dead were laid with their silver and their gold. The wights that guard those graves rise on anyone who breaks one open, and grave-robbers work the mounds all the same.
The Barrowlands.hiddenInfo:
The mounds are the graves of an age of war long before the drowned crowns, and a barrow-wight lies in each, bound to its hoard. The Syndicate works the field openly, digging the mounds for barrow-silver; its diggers are armed and will fight or deal as it suits them.

IMPORTANT: a barrow-wight lies still until its mound is entered or its grave-goods are touched, then rises and fights without quarter to defend its hoard. The wights are bound to their barrows and do not follow far beyond them, but the older and richer the grave, the worse the thing that holds it.

The graves hold grave-gold, old arms, and barrow-silver, the bright metal that bites the dead and the cursed harder than steel. The Great Barrow holds the most, and the worst guardian; the Syndicate's dig holds whatever it has pulled up and not yet carried off.

The Heath.description: Open heath rolling to the horizon, set all over with grass-grown burial mounds and the odd ring of standing stones. Some lie sealed, others stand broken open where they have been dug into. A worked excavation scars one stretch of the field, and a track leads off toward the largest mound of all.

The Dig.description: A worked excavation in the open heath: spoil-heaps, work-tents, and timber props shoring the dug passages, with crates of pulled-up finds stacked under an awning. Open mouths lead down into the barrow being worked.

The Great Barrow.description: The largest mound on the heath, a long grass hill faced with old stone and sealed by a low doorway. Inside, a stone passage runs down to the burial chamber at its heart, with side-cells branching off along the way.

Brackenhill Village.name: Brackenhill Village
Brackenhill Village.basicInfo: Brackenhill is a working village out on the dales, peat-cutters and eel-fishers and herders who pay a tithe to the Deathless, the death-knights of the dales, for protection. The reavers and the dead that plague the rest of the moor mostly leave it be, and to a traveler crossing Whitemoor it is a rare safe place to stop.
Brackenhill Village.hiddenInfo:
The tithe is paid in living people. Once a year the village draws lots at the moot, and the chosen are given over when the death-knights' riders come, to serve in the Deathless halls and, once dead, to rise as their soldiers; in return the Deathless keep the reavers and the dead off the dale. It is no secret, and the village does not pretend otherwise. The bargain has held longer than the old folk can remember, and Brackenhill is safer for it than any walled town on the moor.

Brackenhill is moorfolk and marshfolk: humans and halflings cutting peat and herding sheep on the dales, frogkin netting eels in the fen-bottoms below. They keep the old moor-customs and the moot, the moor-wives keep cures and charms, and they have no wall and no guard, having never needed either.

The bargain makes the village's life. An elder keeps it and draws the lots; some households have given up their own and others have not; there are always a few whose turn is feared to be coming, and now and then one who runs rather than be given over. Not everyone holds the cost worth paying, and they do not all agree on what else there is to do. The death-knights' riders are the only outsiders the village both fears and depends on.

For a traveler the village is a rare safe rest on the deep moor, and it trades peat, wool, eels, and the moor-wives' cures, and sells guidance across the fen to those who can pay. The folk speak plainly of what they pay and why, but they have no love for an outsider who would meddle with it, having a great deal more to lose by it than he does.

The Green.description: An open green at the heart of the village, a market-cross and well at its middle and the long moot-hall standing along one side. Stone-and-turf houses ring the green, and lanes run out into the dales and down toward the fen.
