The Moot-Hall.description: The village's long hall, a great hearth at one end and tables and benches down its length, with ale on tap and a board where work and notices are posted. An old lot-stone sits on a stand near the hearth.

The Steads.description: Peat-cuttings, eel-races, and sheep-pasture spread across the dales and down into the fen-bottoms, set with byres, drying-sheds, and outlying steads. Stone walls and cut banks divide the ground, and tracks wind off toward the open moor.

The Temple of the Sword Vigilant.name: The Temple of the Sword Vigilant
The Temple of the Sword Vigilant.basicInfo: The Temple of the Sword Vigilant is the fortress-seat of the Knights Vigilant on the cliff above Aldwall, a sworn order of Galard the Swordbearer. Its knights ride Whitemoor openly against restless dead, return to recount recognized rides in the Feast-Hall, and rise from New-Sworn to Moor-Knight, Banner-Knight, and Champion Vigilant.
The Temple of the Sword Vigilant.hiddenInfo:
The Knights Vigilant fight the moor's dead in the open and by force: war-dead of the drowned crowns, barrow-wights, dead riders, drowned things, and the death-knights of the Deathless, the dale gentry who turned to necromancy. They are not occult investigators like the Black Tower. They identify what must be put down, ride directly to threatened people and places, and use radiant arms, courage, and fellowship to end it.

The Feast-Hall also recognizes Galard's Proving-Year custom, which predates the order's estrangement from the Templars Adamant. Any willing person may take up a plain iron Road-Shield without swearing the Swordbearer oath, then have three distinct deeds of courage recognized here or at another Galard site. Completing the proof permits but never requires an oath. Until the aspirant freely swears, they are not New-Sworn, receive no moonstone oath-brooch, and hold no authority in the Knights Vigilant.

Galard the Swordbearer loves the bold and loyal: the knight who rides hardest at the worst of the dead and the knight who never leaves another to them. The Vigilant are proud, competitive, and tightly bound. Glory is social, but advancement rests on recognized rides established before the Feast-Hall through a true account, witnesses, trophies, rescued people, or consequences the order can verify. A knight need not boast personally; others may tell the deed.

A newly sworn member receives a moonstone oath-brooch and begins as New-Sworn. One supervised first ride earns recognition as Moor-Knight and the right to answer independent calls. Three recognized Moor-Knight rides earn a personal banner and elevation to Banner-Knight, trusted to lead other knights and larger rides. Four recognized great rides as Banner-Knight may earn acclamation as Champion Vigilant, with authority to command the order's greatest responses and judge the deeds of others.

The Temple is where the moor's blessed arms are made. Dwarf silversmiths and moonstone-cutters work its forges, setting silver, moonstone, and sun-gold into weapons, shields, armor, and holy focuses that bite the dead and defend the living. Promotion rewards should suit the knight's actual build rather than assuming every Vigilant uses a sword.

The Vigilant welcome any bold and honest comer, but they are a proud armed order. Cross them, steal from their stores, or shield necromancers and dead-traffickers, and the whole brotherhood answers in force.

The Forecourt.description: A walled forecourt on the cliff-top behind the Temple's gates, the fortress-monastery rising beyond it in grey stone and tall windows. From the wall the whole of Aldwall lies spread below, and the moor past it, with a long stair cut down the cliff-face to the town.

The Feast-Hall.description: A long feast-hall down the middle of the fortress, ranged with trestle tables and a great hearth, ale-casks along one wall. Banners hang from the rafters and trophies of famous undead kills crowd the stone. Galard's altar stands at the head, where oaths are sworn, fallen knights named, completed rides recounted, promotions acclaimed, and personal banners first raised. A board beside it carries standing hunts against the dead.

The Training Yard.description: A broad open yard behind the fortress, level ground for drill and the mounted charge, set with practice-posts and racks of arms.

The Forges.description: The order's forges: furnaces, anvils, and benches for fine metalwork, with silver, moonstone, and sun-gold set out to be worked into steel. Racks of finished blessed arms line the walls, and barrels of ore and ingots stand below them.

Aldwall.name: Aldwall
Aldwall.basicInfo: Aldwall is the Shining City, the last surviving walled town of Fethloren, the fallen realm of Whitemoor. Pale dwarf-cut ramparts form a star-fort above the heath, enclosing steep slate roofs, busy squares, and the duke’s hall beneath the cliff-fortress of the Knights Vigilant. Deep interlocking runes cover the ancient stone. At dusk the carvings kindle and the stone itself shines pearl-white: gate towers, house arches, halls, and ramparts light the streets and cast a pale reflection across the dark fen. Music and warm windows fill the city within the shining walls.
Aldwall.hiddenInfo:
Aldwall shelters inside fort-craft the dwarves raised in Fethloren's great age and cannot reproduce now. By night its runed stone shines with a pale, steady light that the dead cannot bear: they will not cross it, and the moor's restless things circle the walls at a distance until dawn. The knack of cutting such stone is lost. The town lives within the walls, bright and proud and loud; the Knights Vigilant hold the cliff above and ride out against the moor's dead; the duke holds his hall below. The duke carries the older honor and the order the harder power, and both keep their pride about it.

Knights come swaggering down the cliff-stair to drink and trade boasts over whose kill was greater. The people of the Shining City make a point of living well inside the light: festival lanterns, music on the walls, and knights who come home from the dead-lands to dance as hard as they fight. Dwarf carvers corner strangers to argue what the wall-runes mean and swear blind they once knew. The watch knows every face in town, and the moor-guides name their fee in drink before coin.

Under the carved walls the market trades the goods of a hard country: armorers and the Temple's overflow of blessed arms, silver and moonstone work, moor-cures and draughts from the marsh-wives, horses and moor-ponies, salted provisions, and guides who will take a stranger across the fen for the right price. A fence works the back lanes for those who know to ask.

The moor's troubles are common talk in the market and the tavern, and they point outward. The drowned cities of Bryngard and Avelmere lie out in the fen, full of the dead and their grave-gold. Reavers raid from a bog stronghold called Carrowgate. The barrow-fields are worked by grave-robbers and guarded by wights. Below the talk runs the real fear: the Deathless, old gentry of Fethloren's dales who turned to necromancy and now ride as death-knights, take the living from villages like Brackenhill to serve in their halls and, once dead, to rise again as their soldiers. And the Syndicate moves stolen radiant goods through the town, having bought a gate-captain, a quartermaster, and a chaplain's silence.

Aldwall is human-led and old-chivalric, with dwarves at the forges and the carvings, halflings and frogkin in from the heath and fen, and the odd beastfolk or giantborn up from the grass sea. It is a refuge and a place to belong: the Vigilant take recruits, the market gives work, and the Stonesaga is where strangers become regulars.

The Shining City’s light belongs to the surviving ancient stone. At dusk its deep carvings brighten first, then the surrounding masonry takes on a soft pearl-white radiance. Within the streets and halls this is comfortable, steady light; outside the ramparts the illuminated stone marks the boundary the moor’s dead cannot cross. Timber, slate, cloth, and newly laid ordinary stone retain their natural colors. The old craft remains lost, and moving a carved fragment does not establish a new warded refuge.

The city’s protection supports an active evening life: late market trading, shared suppers, dancing, visits along the wall-walks, and welcomes for returning patrols. The duke’s hall offers commissions and public recognition; the Knights’ Hall offers company and practice, while formal Vigilant recruitment and ride recognition belong at the Temple of the Sword Vigilant. Oona’s Stonesaga offers beds, meals, guide introductions, expedition news, and a familiar table on return. Its maps are ordinary travellers’ maps maintained from reports and fieldwork; its stonework shares the city’s light but supplies no changing map or prophetic scene.

The Runestone Market.description: A broad paved square lies beneath Aldwall’s luminous inner ramparts, with the cliff-fortress above the roofs and the landward gate nearby. Deep geometric carvings light the pale stone along one side; storm-blue awnings shelter armorers, silver and moonstone sellers, runecarvers, and merchants of moor-cures and travelling gear. Shops remain busy after dusk under the steady stone-light. Moor-guides meet customers beside the gate, with the horse-market and pony-lines beyond the main stalls. Returning riders bring news, craftspeople display useful commissions, and households hire help for work beyond the walls.

The Stonesaga.description: Oona Bellwater’s lively tavern occupies a broad chamber of Aldwall’s old fort-stone. Pearl-lit carved arches rise between dark timber beams, a great hearth warms the long shared tables, and a polished oak bar serves ale, moor-spirits, and hot suppers. Benches and a few quiet booths line the sides; tables can be pushed back for music and dancing. Guides spread ordinary maps and route notes over a side table, comparing safe crossings and news from returning riders. Rooms upstairs give travellers somewhere to return to. Knights, craftspeople, moor-folk, and newcomers drink together; on boasting nights, a good story earns more attention than a title.

The Duke's Hall.description: A long, gracious chamber of pale dwarf-cut stone stands below the cliff, its carved piers and arches shining softly after dusk. Storm-blue cloth, silver storm-stars, and the old banners of Fethloren’s three crowns hang above side benches. Tall windows overlook the town and moor; the duke’s high seat stands on a low dais at the far end, with doors to household rooms and a guard-room nearby. Emrys receives visitors, presents petitions and returning crews, and arranges introductions while household guests exchange news along the benches. Public recognition and ducal commissions bring townspeople and visiting adventurers into the hall.

The Walls.description: Wide wall-walks connect Aldwall’s sharply angled bastions, gatehouse, and cliff-stairs. Deep runes cut into the pale parapets shine at dusk, illuminating the paving and the faces of those walking beside them. Inside the walls are warm windows, music, and the market roofs; outside stretch dark heath, silver fen channels, and distant barrows. Watch patrols share the broad walks with residents taking the evening air and families waiting for returning riders. At night the restless dead remain far beyond the shining stone. Stairs lead down to the market and up toward the knights’ town hall and cliff-fortress.

The Knights' Hall.description: The Knights Vigilant’s town hall stands below their cliff-fortress: a broad room of pearl-lit stone piers, heavy timber rafters, storm-blue banners, and a large hearth. Long tables hold shared suppers while an open practice floor and side racks of training weapons serve sparring and wrestling. Off-duty knights mix with the duke’s household, craftspeople, guides, and visiting adventurers. Experienced riders offer practice and talk through the dangers of the moor; music, dice, and vigorous arguments carry on around them. The hall welcomes company at table as readily as talent on the practice floor. Formal recruitment and recognition of Vigilant rides remain at the order’s Feast-Hall in the Temple of the Sword Vigilant.

The Kitchen Garden.description:
Climbing flowers shelter a small garden beside Crownstone House’s kitchen wing. A wooden table and mismatched chairs stand among beds of herbs, with benches against the warm stone wall. Residents take breakfast here, neighbors stop for a drink, and supper guests linger outside while food is prepared.

The ancient tower rises above the garden, its pale blocks dwarfing the later kitchen roof. After dusk, the crownstone casts a soft pearl-white light over the table and flowers.

The Round Room.description: Crownstone House’s broad circular main room has been made into a comfortable place to live. Ancient stone walls curve around timber floorboards, thick rugs, upholstered chairs, and a generous hearth. A wide table serves for meals, games, and spreading out a map; bookshelves and fitted cupboards occupy the spaces between deep window recesses, where cushioned seats overlook Aldwall’s roofs. At dusk, old carvings around the arches give a soft pearl-white light, warmed by the fire and shaded where heavy curtains are drawn. The oversized doorway and immense stone blocks show how much older the room is than its furnishings. A winding stair follows the wall to two private bedrooms and a washroom above.

The Stone Shallows.name: The Stone Shallows
The Stone Shallows.basicInfo: The Stone Shallows are the sunken heart of the drowned capital, the old empyrean city that sank into the lagoon ages ago, lying half-drowned beside Caranthoria, which the empire built on the dry ground to the east. The streets are mostly walkable — the pavement holds at the height of the upper storeys, while the lower city lies under water and the buildings stand sunk to their windows on either side. Broken colonnades, flooded squares, and the stumps of old statues mark out the old districts. The empire works it for salvage and pays well: old imperial gold, regalia, and cut stone come out of it by the cartload, and its legion hires outsiders for the flooded structures its own soldiers won't enter. The water is open to the fens, and what comes in from the swamp dens in the drowned buildings, so the salvage crews go armed, and rarely work the flooded buildings alone.
The Stone Shallows.hiddenInfo:
The salvage crews are drawn from every people the lagoon holds: humans, lizardfolk, frogkin, ratkin, turtlefolk, and outsiders who came for the work. The legion runs the operation from winch-stations along the Boundary Wall and holds the dry edge, but leaves the flooded streets to the crews and their flat-boats.

IMPORTANT: giant eels den in the flooded lower city and the sunken side-streets and default hostile to anything in the water. They lie still in submerged doorways and below the surface of the squares, strike without warning, and drag prey under; they do not follow onto dry stone. The open water is theirs.

Lizardfolk war-parties of the dragon-kingdom come up from the fens to raid the salvage, take hauls, kill crews, and cut the winch-lines, sometimes driving a mire drake ahead of them, and they do not parley with crews working for the empire. Rival scavenger crews are the nearer danger — armed, set on a building they have claimed, and ready to settle a disputed haul with steel where the legion cannot see.

The old city's wealth went down with it. Cut stone, bronze fittings, and drowned household goods lie scattered through the upper storeys and side-streets, but the prize is under the Forum of the Sun, where the imperial treasure-vaults stand flooded with their doors still on them — old coin, regalia, and worked goods behind them. The deeper a building has sunk, the more is left in it and the harder it is to reach.

Dryfoot.description: The strip of dry ground where the city's pavement gives out at the foot of the Boundary Wall. Winch-frames and crane-arms stand along the water's edge over the first of the sunken streets, with recovered stone and timber stacked between them and lean-to shelters built up against the wall. Plank causeways and tethered flat-boats run out from here into the ruin, where the pavement drops below the water and the drowned buildings begin.

The Colonnade Walk.description: The old city's great avenue, and the one road through the ruin that still stands above the water. A raised stone causeway runs its length between two rows of standing columns, the pavement cracked and tilted where it has settled. Sunken shopfronts and house-doors sit at the waterline on either side, and flooded side-streets open off the avenue between the buildings, running back into open water.

The Forum of the Sun.description: The old imperial heart, a wide flooded square with the broken Sun-Temple standing at its head. The square lies wadeable, the water waist-high over cracked marble, and the toppled statues of old emperors stand out of it. The temple's outer hall holds dry above its columns; at the back, a stair runs down into the flooded sanctum.

Eelfen Village.name: Eelfen Village
Eelfen Village.basicInfo: A village of stilt-houses and eel-traps where the lagoon's salt water runs into the marsh, west of Caranthoria. The eelers have worked these flats for generations, the catch is good, and the village is older than the new city by an age.
Eelfen Village.hiddenInfo:
The village is mixed — humans, frogkin, and lizardfolk eelers who have worked these flats together for generations and want nothing to do with the swamp kingdom in the deep fens.

The lizardfolk who come for the tithe are the dragon-kingdom's tithe-takers, out of the Reedmoot Fens to the west. Most years the tithe is eels, salt, and goods. Some years they ask for people, and the ones chosen walk west into the reeds and do not come back. The village pays because it is old enough to remember the villages that refused.

The Solarian prefect comes for the imperial tax and takes a cut to keep his reports quiet, so the tithe goes out into the reeds as it always has.

The eelers are proud, blunt, and unimpressed by both their masters. They have fed themselves off these flats since before the empire had a name and expect to be here after it falls, and they treat the tax-collector and the swamp's tithe-takers as two kinds of weather to be endured. A stranger who can pull an oar or mend a trap is fed and housed; one who comes asking after the tithe gets blunt answers and a long look.

The Stilt-Town.description: The village raised on pilings over the tidal mud: plank walkways and rope bridges strung between the stilt-houses, boats tied up in the water beneath, and ladders running down to the flats at low tide. Reed-beds close in to the west where the dry pilings give out and the marsh begins.

The Trap-Flats.description: The tidal flats where salt water meets marsh, staked end to end with eel-traps, weirs, and drying-racks. Channels wind between the reed-beds for the flat-boats; at low water the mud stands open and walkable, at high water it is all current.

The Tide-Hall.description: The village's gathering-hall, the largest platform in the stilt-town, open down one side to the water and built so the high tide runs under the floorboards. Long tables, a great hearth, and barrels of the village's own eel-liquor; the eelers eat, drink, settle their business, and take in travelers off the water here. The carved house-posts holding up the roof are older than Caranthoria, and the eelers will tell you so.

The Reedfront.name: The Reedfront
The Reedfront.basicInfo: The western fens, where the empire's war runs into the swamp. The empire pushes its border west through the marsh and the lizardfolk of the deep fens fight it every yard, raiding the work, ambushing the columns, and falling back into water the legion cannot hold. The free-marsh folk who live here want neither the empire's law nor the swamp kingdom's, and the fighting runs back and forth across their ground.
The Reedfront.hiddenInfo:
This is the contested border between the Empire of Light and the dragon-led lizardfolk kingdom of the Reedmoot fens, the region to the west, and the front moves with the season. The Solarian legion drives causeways and embankments west to drain and hold the marsh; the lizardfolk tear the work down and bleed the columns that build it. Neither side holds the Reedfront for long.

The dragon-kingdom's lizardfolk war-parties come east out of the deep fens to raid. IMPORTANT: they default hostile to Solarians and to anyone working for the empire, fight from cover and water, and do not parley with the legion's people. They sometimes drive a mire drake ahead of them — a poison-breathed marsh reptile that wallows in the channels and comes up under boats and wading men. Toward the deep-fen tracks west, the war-parties are thicker, surer of the footing, and more willing to give battle.

The free-marsh folk — humans, frogkin, and lizardfolk fenfolk who have lived here longer than either power — want neither the Empire nor the dragon. They fish, net eels, and move through the reeds by ways the legion cannot find, and they will guide, warn, hide, or sell to those who treat them fairly. Some have lost kin to the tithe; some have lost kin to the legion's press-gangs. They are the ground both sides fight across and the people most worth knowing here.

The situations the front throws up are constant: a Solarian work-column stalled and waiting to be relieved or finished off, a war-party massing in the holts before a raid, a drake loose in the channels, a marsh family burned out and run off their island, salvage and dead left in the water after a fight, and prisoners taken by one side or the other being moved deeper in.

The Channels.description: Broad reed-fen cut through with winding water-channels: standing reed-beds, stretches of black water and sucking mud, and low islands of firmer ground between them. Sightlines end at the next wall of reeds, and the footing changes with the tide.

The Sunken Holts.description: Where the fen thickens: dense reed-islands and drowned thickets standing in the water, the channels narrowing between them. Old drowned ground — the tops of field-walls and the stumps of dead trees break the surface, and the firm tracks wind blind between the holts.

The Mire-Paths.description: The deep-fen tracks west, where the marsh closes over and the footing is hidden: causeways sunk just under the water, reed-tunnels, and channels that branch and double back.

East Edge Ruins.name: East Edge Ruins
East Edge Ruins.basicInfo: Ruins on the dry eastern edge of the lagoon — the dry eastern quarters of the drowned capital, which stood here long before the empire raised Caranthoria. Solarian deserters often hole up here in numbers, living off the road and the salvage — robbing travelers, raiding the work-crews, and selling what they take.
East Edge Ruins.hiddenInfo:
Every sworn legionnaire is branded at the neck. Inside the empire it is an honor; outside it is a verdict, and a sun-branded neck is known in every inn in Larion. A deserter cannot lose himself in an ordinary town, so the deserters gather here, in the one place a scarred neck draws no second look, and there are far more of them than the legion likes to admit. They are humans, lizardfolk, frogkin, and every other people the legion takes, run from the line for every reason men run.

IMPORTANT: the deserters default hostile to anyone who comes into the ruins. They are criminals by trade now, they assume a stranger is either the legion come for them or prey come to be robbed, and they will rob or kill on that assumption. The one thing that buys a hearing instead of a knife is being plainly no friend of the empire and carrying something they want — coin, a fence, news, or a job worth more than what is in your pockets. Even then it is a wary hearing among armed and frightened men, not a welcome.

There is no fixed camp to storm. When a legion cohort comes in force the deserters melt back into the Hollow Quarter and the vaults under it, leaving the approaches trapped behind them, and trickle back when the soldiers give up. When they are dug in, the Throat is manned and overlooked; when they are scattered, it is only the traps and tripwires left behind. A band this size has leaders — the hardest and longest-surviving men hold the rest together — and they run the trade in stolen goods, ransom prisoners worth ransoming, and sell what the legion would confiscate to buyers who come quietly by the eastern road.

The cellars of the Hollow Quarter are not held by the deserters alone. Giant eels have come in from the lagoon through the flooded cellars and den in the dark water under the broken foundations, and the deserters keep to the dry vaults.

The Broken Streets.description: The edge of the old district where it meets the dry shore: collapsed tenements and roofless halls along streets choked with fallen stone, the lagoon on one side and the gutted city running inland on the other. Sightlines break at every rubble-pile and standing wall.

The Throat.description: The one sound way deeper into the district, where the fallen blocks pinch the route down to a single overlooked passage between standing walls and high broken floors. Murder-holes and firing-points look down on it from above, and the narrows are strung and rigged where the way bends.

The Hollow Quarter.description: Where the district collapsed worst, blocks fallen into their own cellars and the streets dropping away into rubble-choked vaults below. The footing is bad and the ways twist underground between the broken foundations, on and on into the dark.

The Greatwild.name: The Greatwild
The Greatwild.basicInfo: The Greatwild is the upriver interior of Ntar Vanna, where the Saranadi is broad and slow and no village stands. The jungle here is the oldest and largest in the region, and so are the beasts: crocodilians longer than a barge, tusked herds that flatten the brush they cross, big cats that hunt from the canopy. Hunters come up from the river towns for ivory, hide, horn, and the strange materials the deep jungle grows.
The Greatwild.hiddenInfo:
The Greatwild has no settlements, no rulers, and no law. It is open hunting country: river crews come up from the towns to take big game and the materials and go back down to sell.

The beasts are the region's everyday danger here, all scaled large. Dire crocodiles lie still as logs in the shallows and explode on anything at the waterline. Goliath boars move in tusked herds and trample in a mass, dangerous in number more than singly. Canopy tigers stalk a crew from the branches and drop on the one at the back. River drakes, wingless water-serpents, crest and strike at boats and are the apex of the open water. Thunder-tusks, elephantine giants, reshape the ground by walking and are not aggressive unless pressed, and lethal when pressed. On the far banks the old jungle grows things past all natural size: bloat-spiders, giant spiders swollen past any natural size, den deep, so meeting one means a crew went too far.

IMPORTANT: river bandits called driftmen work the Greatwild and are hostile. They are not one band but scattered outlaw crews who gave up hunting beasts and hunt hunters instead — letting other crews take the game and the risk, then taking the haul. They run fast skiffs, camp on any bank, and move when the hunting moves. They hold no ground and fly no flag, which is why no one has cleared them out.

Loot here is what the beasts yield. Thunder-tusk ivory: a single tusk is a fortune, carving-grade, sold by weight. Goliath boar hide: tans into heavy armor-leather that turns a blade. Canopy tiger pelt: a luxury skin, and the long fangs make weapons. Dire crocodile hide: plate-hard scute for shields and armor-facing. River drake bone: light and strong, prized by bowyers and shipwrights. Bloat-spider venom-sacs: raw poison stock for alchemy.

Venomwood grows in the oldest jungle along the river.

The Open River.description: The upper Saranadi runs broad and slow, braided around long sandbars and gravel banks. The channel-markers have ended and the forest stands back from the water in high green walls. Boats can put in almost anywhere along the shallows.

The Floodforest.description: Forest standing in still black water, the trunks rising on buttress roots like walls. Sightlines are short, the channels narrow and winding, and hanging vine closes overhead. A boat can thread the waterways; on foot the roots and water make for slow, broken footing.

The Trample.description: Open low ground churned flat — cropped grass, snapped saplings, and wide mud wallows. Sightlines run long here after the forest, and the bare earth shows the tracks of heavy things. The ground is soft and the going is firm only on the higher ridges.

The Swallowed Cities.name: The Swallowed Cities
The Swallowed Cities.basicInfo: The Swallowed Cities are the ruins of the demonborn cities raised here an age ago, burned long ago and overgrown ever since. Roots have split the plazas and tipped the towers, and the walls still carry carvings of a king no one living has seen. Relic crews work the ruins for grave-goods, and the trade that fills New Anthara's markets starts here.
The Swallowed Cities.hiddenInfo:
The Swallowed Cities are vast demonborn ruins strangled by jungle, and the grave-goods trade begins here. Relic crews dig the ruins for demonborn arms, regalia, and carved stone, then carry the haul down to New Anthara's assay houses. Nothing here is governed; crews work the ruins by force of arms and against each other.

The jungle has grown the wildlife oversized. Giant constrictors coil in the trees and toppled stone and ambush what passes. Goliath scarabs work the ruins in carrion-swarms, dangerous in number. Dire apes hold the high ruins as territory and own the fallen tower. Stranglevine grows thick enough to seize and hold a person where the roots have broken the ground. A giant crocodile dens in the flooded shrine beneath the great temple — the largest thing in the ruins, and the hardest to reach.

IMPORTANT: rival relic crews and a cult both work the ruins and default hostile. Rival crews fight when the haul is worth it and a target looks beatable. The cult are the Children of Ur, diggers who want the demon power sealed in these ruins raised whole; they are after sealed relics, not grave-bronze. They turn on anyone who finds their diggings.

Beneath the throne-dais, a hold of Ur Spawn, demons in the flesh, occupies chambers cut below the Royal Court. A band of four to six ranges above it: Flameskin Imps in the court, a Snatch-Tail Fiend in the Strangled Ways, and a Flamewhip Overseer Fiend driving them back toward the dais when they stray. An Archfiend, the greater demon that rules the hold, keeps its deepest chamber.

The Spawn guard the way down, seize intruders, and make Children of Ur diggers carry relics and prisoners into the hold. The cult calls this service; the archfiend calls it ownership.

Loot is demonborn grave-goods and what the beasts yield. Demonborn grave-bronze: ritual arms and regalia, arcane-touched, valuable and sometimes still holding a working. Old-grove amber: a sap-stone grown thick in the old groves, an alchemical reagent and a wardstone. Constrictor hide and scarab shell: armor materials. Ur-ichor: black blood sealed in the demonborn dead, drunk for demonic strength at the cost of the drinker's humanity. Wakeful idols: carved demonborn figures holding a sleeping Ur-thing, rousable for power that claims a piece of the one who wakes it. Cursed demonborn arms and armor: Ur-touched gear that makes the bearer stronger and slowly less himself.

The Royal Court.description: A vast roofless palace-plaza pried open by a single colossal tree growing up through its center, roots heaving the flagstones. A raised throne-dais stands at the far end, and the longest carved walls in the ruins run the length of the court. Toppled statues of horned, tailed demonborn figures lie among the roots, some still upright along the dais. The footing is broken stone and root.

The Sunken Temple.description: A stepped pyramid-temple half-collapsed into standing black water. The lower shrine is flooded and dark; the upper terraces are climbable, rising in broken tiers above the waterline. Drowned passages run back under the stone where the light gives out.

The Toppled Spire.description: A great tower fallen across the ruins, its length now a long bridge of broken floors and snapped stairs climbing from the ground to the high air. The upper chambers sit out of easy reach above the canopy, opened to the sky where the tower cracked. The vantage from the top reaches across the whole ruin-field.

The Strangled Ways.description: The streets and lesser plazas between the great structures, pried apart by roots and choked with stranglevine. Walls lean at angles and toppled statues of demonborn figures lie in the green, the cut stone showing through wherever the growth thins. The going is slow and the sightlines short.

The Hookmarsh.name: The Hookmarsh
The Hookmarsh.basicInfo: Hookmarsh is a backwater of reed-channels and mud islands where a tributary feeds into the Saranadi. A lizardfolk warband holds it under a warlord named Ghessek, and they make their living off the river: they block the main channel and force passing boats to detour through the marsh, then take them in the reedways and ransom back the people aboard. The channels are staked and snared, and Ghessek's men watch the water from blinds in the reeds. An old stone fort on the marsh's one dry island is where the warband keeps its captives and its plunder.
The Hookmarsh.hiddenInfo:
Hookmarsh runs on ransom. Ghessek's warband blocks the Saranadi with sunk timber and chain, so boats must turn off into the marsh, where the channels are staked, snared, and watched from reed blinds. Boats that detour are taken in the reedways and their people held for ransom.

Ghessek honors ransoms that are paid. This is known on the river, and it is why the trade works: pay, and your people come back. A captive can also buy their own freedom by handing over everything they carry.

The still water hides giant leeches that fasten on in the shallows. Giant centipedes nest in the reed-mats and the rotten timber of the fort.

IMPORTANT: the warband defaults hostile to anyone in the marsh. The single exception is ransom business: money on the table or a captive to redeem buys a conversation. They do not parley over anything else.

Loot is the warband's plunder, held in the fort: coin, ransom-chests, and cargo stripped from taken boats. Captives worth redeeming are held in the dry cells. Leech glands yield a blood-thinning draught; centipede venom is alchemical poison stock.

The Stakes.description: The tributary mouth, where the Saranadi's current dies into brown still water and boats are forced off the blocked main channel. Rows of sharpened stakes break the surface, and the way narrows into walls of reed higher than a standing man. The water is shallow and the mud below it deep.

The Reedways.description: A maze of narrow channels and low mud islands winding back into the marsh. Reed blinds and stilt-platforms stand over the water, snare-lines are strung across the gaps, and pens of stake and rope sit on the firmer ground. Sightlines are short and the channels easy to lose.

The Reed Fort.description: An old stone fort on the marsh's one solid island, its walls patched and raised with lashed timber and bundled reed. A fortified landing sits below at the waterline; dry cells and storerooms fill the upper floors, above the reach of the marsh.

Falselight Reefs.name: Falselight Reefs
Falselight Reefs.basicInfo: Falselight Reefs are a low island walled in black rock and broken water, the worst wrecking-ground in the Swordlaw sea. Wreckers live here. On bad nights they move the shore-fires to false places, and ships steering by them come apart on the reef; on any night, the rocks and the storms do the work for free. The wreckers strip what washes up and kill what walks out of the surf, and they have grown rich on it. Every sailor knows to give Falselight a wide berth, and every sailor blown there anyway learns why.
Falselight Reefs.hiddenInfo:
The wreckers are a clan of perhaps forty hard coast-folk who live by the reef and nothing else. They show false fires on storm-nights to draw ships onto the rocks, then put out in skiffs to gaff survivors and strip the wrecks before the tide takes them. They are humans and a few frogkin, raised to it from birth, and they do not see themselves as monsters — the sea sends them ships, and they take what the sea sends. Outsiders are either prey or a problem, never guests.

The reason the false light never fails sits at the island's far point, in the old lighthouse the clan calls the Lure. An honest tower once, until the wreckers and the thing that came to live in it struck their bargain. A coven of three sea-hags holds the tower now. The hags raise the false light, foul the water, and sing the fog down off the headland; the wreckers strip the wrecks and leave the hags the drowned. Both sides feed. The clan knows exactly what lives in the Lure and would no sooner climb to the lamp-room than walk into the sea, and they will warn an outsider off it not out of mercy but because a meddler who stirs the coven ruins the catch for everyone.

IMPORTANT: This is a hostile location. The wreckers attack outsiders who come ashore — not in endless waves, but hard and in numbers, with gaffs, fish-spears, and cutlasses, fighting on ground they know in water they don't fear. They will parley only with someone who plainly has the upper hand or something they want more than a fresh wreck, and even then they bargain like people who eat what washes up. The sea-hags in the Lure are hostile without exception and beyond reason; they do not negotiate, they lure and they drown. A grown sea-hag is far past a single fighter — three together are a site-boss.

The wreckers fight as a pack and a home crew: they let a stranger come in off the shingle, then close from the rocks and the huts on three sides, drive him toward the water, and gaff him in the surf where his footing fails and theirs holds. Wounded or outmatched, they break for the Holt and the skiffs rather than die for pride, and a clan-head who falls is mourned by nobody scrambling for his share. The hags fight from the tower: glamour and false voices to split a party and walk men off the gallery, fouled water and grasping weed at the tower's foot, claw and drowning-grip up close. Losing, a hag flees into the deep water under the Lure and is gone.

Loot is the harvest of a hundred lost ships. The Holt's salvage-shed holds stripped cargo — bolts of ruined silk, casks, ship-fittings, a captain's strongbox no one's forced yet, charts worth more than the gold — and the wreckers wear and carry the good steel and oddments off the dead. The Lure's lamp-room and the rock beneath it hold what the hags keep: drowned-men's rings and teeth, a sea-hag's brine-charm that turns a calm sea foul, and the great lamp itself, an Empyrean bridge-lantern the wreckers hauled up from a sunken span, which throws a light that carries for miles and can be made to lie.

The Cove.description: The one break in the island's black reef-wall, a steep shingle cove of grey stone and tide-wrack. The bones of broken ships lie everywhere the water reaches — split hulls, snapped masts, rigging fouled in the rocks — and more of it grinds in the surf with every swell. Black headlands climb on both sides, and a narrow path of cut steps and driftwood ladders works up the southern point toward the huts above. The far point of the island, where a stone tower stands over the worst of the reef, is visible across the water.

The Wrackers' Holt.description: A clutch of low stone huts roofed and walled with ship-timber, dug into the lee of the southern headland above the cove. Drying-racks, skiffs hauled up on rollers, and stacks of salvaged spars stand between the houses. The largest building is a long salvage-shed, its doors barred, packed with stripped cargo. Paths run down to the cove behind and out along the shore toward the tower at the island's far point.

The Lure.description: An old stone lighthouse at the island's seaward point, standing on a spur of rock the reef has all but cut off from the rest of Falselight — reachable by a tidal causeway of slick black stone that the sea covers at the high water. The tower leans, weed-grown to the gallery, its door long gone.

Garrock's Island.name: Garrock's Island
Garrock's Island.basicInfo: Garrock's Island is a lush green peak alone in the Swordlaw sea, where the pirate captain Garrock is said to have buried a fortune before he died. The island is cursed now, and the dead walk it. None of that has ever stopped the crews who land in every season to try their luck.
Garrock's Island.hiddenInfo:
Garrock was a pirate captain who took a fortune and meant to keep it. He put his crew to cutting a hole in the mountain to hide it, then killed every man who dug, so that none could lead another back to it. He died before he could return, and the gold is still in the rock where he left it.

The island is cursed, and the curse feeds on greed. Anyone who dies here with greed in their heart rises and walks — which is why the murdered crew were the first of the dead, and why every grasping crew that has landed since and not left has swelled their number. The dead are thickest at the diggings, where the most men have died clawing at the rock, and thinnest at the shore.

The danger from the living is rival treasure-crews — there is usually one or another somewhere on the slope, digging, lost, or already turning on each other, and they meet a newcomer as competition: warily, ready to deal, rob, or fight depending on who looks stronger and who got there first. Past their cold camps and hauled-up boats, the island is overgrown and trackless, and giant reptiles den in the green: constrictors thick as a mast in the gulleys, monitor lizards big as ponies, and snapping things in the standing water.

IMPORTANT: The dead of Garrock's Island come in kinds, by where men died: drowned dead in the surf and the wet lower ground, waterlogged and slow, rising out of the tide-line and the bog; gallowsmen in the Greenwall, the mutineers and thieves Garrock hanged, dropping from the branches with the rope still on; bonecrews in the diggings, the old picked-clean pirate dead, fast and many, fighting with rusted cutlass and boarding-axe in the way they fought living; gravechewers among them, the greedy dead who never stopped digging, clawing at the rock and at the living, drawn to gold above all.

Loot is what a hundred buried and drowned crews carried: coin and plate in the wet ground and the workings, good steel and pistols on the bonecrews, rings and grave-gold on the gravechewers, and the charts and oddments in the cold camps of crews that did not leave. Garrock's own hoard sits somewhere in the deepest workings — gold, gems, and the famous pieces a great captain dies owning. The giant reptiles give hides, monitor venom, and constrictor skin worth carrying out.

The Beach.description: A single reef-fringed strand of pale sand below the island's green slope, the one easy landing on a coast otherwise walled in rock and surf. The mountain rises straight up from the treeline behind it, and high on its flank the bare scarred rock of the diggings shows through the green, dark with openings. Rotting boats lie hauled up past the tide-line, a fire-pit long gone cold sits in the dune-grass.

The Greenwall.description: The overgrown slope between the shore and the peak, dense drowned jungle over old ground. Cut trails run up it half-swallowed by growth, branching and doubling and dead-ending in gulleys, standing pools, and curtains of vine. Stretches of bog and slow green water lie in the low places, and the canopy closes overhead until the light goes dim and the way is easy to lose.

The Diggings.description: The mountain's height, a slope of broken rock where generations of crews have hacked the old cave-mouths open and torn the ground apart chasing the hoard. Dark workings run back into the peak — cut tunnels, half-collapsed shafts, and chambers Garrock's crew carved and the diggers since have widened — opening one into another in no order anyone planned. Abandoned tools, and shored timber lie everywhere the digging reached. The deepest cuts run far enough into the rock that daylight does not follow.

Freehaven.name: Freehaven
Freehaven.basicInfo: Freehaven is the pirate capital of the Swordlaw sea, a city built across a scatter of rocky islets joined by bridges and skiffs, off the bridge-network and reachable only by sail. No crown rules it and no flag flies over it — it is the freest port in the world, run by the crews who harbor here and held together by one law, the Swordlaw: settle your quarrel with steel, and the winner's word stands. Pirates come to fence their hauls, refit their ships, find a crew or a captain, and spend their plunder loud. Anyone can make a new life here, and a careless one can end it just as fast.
Freehaven.hiddenInfo:
Freehaven has no governor, no watch, and no court; the crews hold their own ground and their own ships, and the captains everyone has heard of are the nearest thing to power. Duels and other challenges are frequent; a challenge given and accepted binds both parties to abide the outcome, and the winner's word stands after.

Reputation matters greatly here. Nobody asks where a newcomer came from or what he was before — Freehaven is where a man starts over — but everybody watches what he does here, and he rises or falls by it. A stranger who carries himself well, keeps business flowing, and does not flinch is left to his business and soon known; one who reads as easy money is tested, and the sea is close on every side.

Crews are found and built in the taverns, above all at the Above Board, where captains hold court and recruit and the day's work is spoken: a berth on a raid, a fence who needs a thing recovered, a treasure-rumor for sale, a run no honest crew will make.

The population is every people the salt sea throws together: humans and halflings throughout, parrotfolk carrying messages dock to dock, dwarf and giantborn shipwrights at the yards, and dark orcs, half-sea-elves, demonborn, and birdfolk crewing alongside everyone else.

Goods and loot move through the Careenage: the cargo and fittings stripped from captured ships, weapons and gear off the dead, charts, and the odd plundered relic, all sold cheap and fast by dealers who do not ask where it came from. A crew flush off a prize will spend the whole share here in a week and sail out for more.

Ligeia's Landing.description: The broad arrival square where ships put in, a stone terrace between the cliff and the sea at the heart of the haven. A grotto cut into the cliff holds a weathered statue of a siren queen, and the rest of the islets climb away around the harbor, bridged and laddered together, masts thick in the anchorage. Criers, hawkers, and recruiters work the crowd coming off the boats, and challenges called here draw a ring fast. Ways lead off to the taverns, the drinking-island, and the working wharves.

The Above Board.description: The haven's great tavern, built from a gilded war-galleon hauled up and grounded at the waterline, decks and holds opened out into a warren of bars, gambling tables, and bunk-corners. A long plank runs out over the water from the seaward rail, where Swordlaw matters are settled and the sea decides who climbs back up. The upper deck is captains' ground; the common decks below roar at all hours. A footbridge crosses to the drinking-island alongside.

Rumrun Isle.description: A whole islet given over to drink, a packed warren of taverns, grog-houses, and gambling-dens stacked wall to wall up the slope, lantern-lit and loud day and night. Narrow ways run between them, spilling with music, smoke, and crews between voyages. There is little here that is not a place to drink, wager, or carouse. Bridges connect it to the great tavern and back to the landing.

The Careenage.description: The working waterfront of the haven, where captured ships are hauled out on the shallows to be careened, stripped, broken, or rebuilt. Carpenters, riggers, and chandlers work the strand, and the dealers' shops behind them buy plundered cargo and sell everything off it — fittings, weapons, gear, charts, and goods of every provenance. Cranes, slipways, and beached hulls in every state line the water.

The Sea-Troll Skerries.name: The Sea-Troll Skerries
The Sea-Troll Skerries.basicInfo: A scatter of bare rock islets in open water, ringed with broken ships. Every captain in the bay tries to avoid the skerries, but the winds and currents here run vessels straight onto the rocks — and when they do, the sea-trolls are waiting. The trolls wreck what the sea brings them and carry the crews back to their dens alive.
The Sea-Troll Skerries.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The sea-trolls are hostile by default and do not parley. They attack anything that moves on or near the skerries.

The trolls attack from the water first, tipping boats and pulling swimmers under, then dragging them ashore. On land they are slower, hulking, and stupid, but very strong. They keep captives alive in their dens for days or weeks against future hunger, which is why rescue crews put out from the hub whenever a ship goes missing near the skerries — there is usually still someone to save.

Loot: the dens hold wreck cargo piled by the trolls — chests, casks, weapons, coin, and the belongings of the eaten. Troll grease, rendered from a dead troll, is the base of alchemical burn-salves and sells well to any alchemist. Sea-troll hide, once fire-scarred, no longer regrows and can be worked into tough armor.

The Outer Rocks.description: Bare islets rising from open water, wreck timbers jammed on every reef. Across the channels, the den-caves show as dark mouths at the waterline.

The Channels.description: Tight water between the islets, hull-breaking rocks just under the surface. The only way to the dens is across.

The Larder Caves.description: Waterline caves heaped with wreck-plunder and gnawed bones. Deeper alcoves hold whatever the trolls have carried back and not yet eaten.

The Serpent Runs.name: The Serpent Runs
The Serpent Runs.basicInfo: Open water where strong currents meet, so thick with fish that the surface boils — and the sea serpents follow the fish. Serpents run these waters in numbers found nowhere else, and hunting them is how the bay's crews earn their shares. Hunting boats work the runs in every season. So does everything that eats.
The Serpent Runs.hiddenInfo:
Three kinds of serpent are most common in these waters, each hunted differently. Reef serpents are man-length pack-hunters that swarm over the shallow banks — they coil and constrict swimmers and tip small boats by weight of numbers. Silverback serpents are the staple catch: boat-length, silver-crested, and fast, they breach clear of the water and crash down on hulls to break them. Bull serpents are old silverbacks grown huge, scarred with the broken harpoons of every crew that failed — a bull kill makes a hunter's name for life. Serpents are cunning, aggressive when hungry or struck, but they can be baited, driven, tired out, and outsmarted, and a fed serpent ignores a quiet boat.

Hunting crews are on the water in all weather: harpooners standing in the bows, boats running lines to a struck serpent, a mauled crew bailing and limping for home. Crews hail each other on sight, and a boat in trouble gets help — that is a courtesy of the bay, and everyone keeps it.

Loot: serpent scale sells by the sack as light armor stock. Serpent oil, rendered from the fat, is lamp-oil and an alchemy base. A reef serpent's venom gland sells whole to alchemists. A bull's harpoon-scarred hide is armor-grade and worth a share on its own. Serpents taken alive and unmarked fetch triple from the live-trade — and live capture is three times the danger.

The Boiling Bay.description: Open water where the currents meet and the fish run so thick the surface churns. Hunting boats scatter across the swell; serpents breach in the distance.

The Shallow Banks.description: Drowned sandbars under a few feet of clear water, dark with fish. The broken boats of careless anchorages lie on the bars.

The Deep Current.description: The big water: deep blue, hard current, long swells. The largest wakes and the widest breaches are out here.

The Tanglewater Estuary.name: The Tanglewater Estuary
The Tanglewater Estuary.basicInfo: A great river meets the bay here in a mangrove maze miles wide — stilt-rooted trees standing in the tide, threaded with channels that shift with every flood. The brackish water breeds prey found nowhere else in the bay, and hunting crews pole flat skiffs into the tangle after hides, glands, and ink that alchemists and armorers pay dearly for. The deeper you go, the richer the hunting — and the more that hunts you back.
The Tanglewater Estuary.hiddenInfo:
The estuary's prey, each hunted its own way. Snapdragons are crocodile-sized drakes that lie in the channels like drifting logs, spit a gob of caustic spit, then lunge — the acid gland and drake scale of each sell high. Great morays, thick as a man, den in the stilt-root hollows and strike from their holes; hunters bait the den-mouths. Eelskin is supple armor-grade leather, and the jaw-glands go to alchemists whole. Bog krakens are barrel-bodied lurkers that anchor themselves among the roots of the deep pools and take waders and skiffs from below — the estuary's biggest prize and worst way to die. Kraken ink and arm-hide fetch a season's shares.

IMPORTANT: Grindylows stalk the deep channels in packs and are hostile by default — they do not parley. Goblin-sized, weed-haired, long-fingered water-lurkers, they let hunting crews do the dangerous work, then swarm a loaded skiff at dusk to rob the catch, cut throats, and drag the dead under. The richer a skiff rides in the water, the more eyes follow it from the weeds. They fear fire on the water and break off from a burning brand, but they come back.

Hunting crews work the margins and channels by day and are gone by dark. A skiff poling out heavy is at its most dangerous hour on the way home.

The Mudflats.description: Low-tide banks at the estuary mouth, the mangrove wall rising beyond. Skiffs work the margins; channels open into the tangle in every direction.

The Channels.description: Poling water threading between stilt-root cages, sightlines ten trees deep. Log-shapes drift in the current. Den-mouths show as dark hollows in the root-tangles.

The Black Pools.description: Deep still water in the heart of the maze, shaded to twilight under the canopy. The surface does not move, and the bottom cannot be seen.

Flensers' Cove.name: Flensers' Cove
Flensers' Cove.basicInfo: A high-walled cove screened behind tall rock pillars, invisible from open water. Flensing ramps, boiling-pots, and bone-racks stand on the shingle beach inside. This is the butchering ground of the Flensers, the outlaw hunting crew — the one place in the bay they are known to return to.
Flensers' Cove.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Flensers do not welcome outsiders and attack most on sight. They fight dirty — hooks, nets, thrown harpoons, a man's own boat set alight under him. If outmanned they retreat to their ships and put to sea, burning their stores and caches rather than leaving them.

The Flensers are not always in the cove. When they are: ships careened on the beach, pots boiling, lookouts on the rock pillars, a dozen or more armed flensers working fast. When they are not: cold pots, fresh butchering sign, cached bone and oil under guard of a few left-behind hands, and sometimes a chained prisoner in the caves — merfolk herders seized when they caught the crew in the act, kept for leverage or sale.

The works show what the crew is: calf bones in the racks, merfolk herd-brands on rendered stock. 

Loot: cached leviathan bone and calf-bone, casks of rendered oil, the crew's plunder in the caches, and the Flensers' own gear — good harpoons, good hides.

The Outer Water.description: Open sea off a wall of tall rock pillars. The cove's mouth shows as a single dark passage between the pillars; the cliffs give no other way in. Small boats can hold off here beyond bowshot.

The Watch Rocks.description: The passage between the rock pillars, deep-water and narrow. Lookout perches are cut into the high pillars, reachable by rope and ladder.

The Rendering Beach.description: A shingle beach under high rock walls. Flensing ramps run from the waterline, boiling-pots stand in fire-pits, and bone-racks line the cliff base. Room to careen two ships.

The Caches.description: Cut caves at the back of the cove, dry above the tide-line, fitted with doors and iron rings. Stacked casks sit in the outer caves; the deeper ones are barred.

Shipfall Isle.name: Shipfall Isle
Shipfall Isle.basicInfo: An island crowned by the Stormspire, a bare peak that draws lightning and wears a slow-turning storm most days. Storm sorcerers live on it and call storms out of clear sky, and the currents run inward, driving ships onto the wreck-choked banks that ring the shore. Centuries of hulls lie piled on the shoals, and the sorcerers come down to strip what the sea drives in.
Shipfall Isle.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Stormcallers are hostile by default and attack anyone who comes near their caves or the Stormspire. They are storm sorcerers — wild, savage, and sophisticated in nothing but their craft. In a fight they call lightning down on the banks, drive walls of wind that flip boats, and crack thunder that knocks men flat. They are descendants of the wrecked who learned what the isle offered, and they feed the storms with living sacrifices: blood given to the sky brings the weather up, and the weather brings ships.

The Stormcallers live in cave-mouths in the hillside below the Spire and come down to strip what the sea drives in. Sacrifices are taken alive from grounded ships and held in the caves until the next storm is fed. Generations of looted cargo — coin, cargo, arms, everything the wrecks carried — is piled in the deeper caves.

A storm drake nests on the Stormspire and hunts when the sky darkens. The Stormcallers feed it sacrifices too — they give blood to the sky and the drake alike, and cannot always tell which one answers. Lightning eels swarm the charged water around the wreck-banks in any weather, and touching the sea near a surfaced shoal of them bites like a whip.

Loot: the Stormcallers' hoard in the caves; storm drake scale and charge-glands; lightning eel glands; thunderglass, fused where lightning has struck the banks, prized by enchanters; and the cargo of every age of wreck on the shoals — the richest unworked salvage in the bay, for anyone fast enough to work it between storms.

The Outer Banks.description: Wreck-strewn shoals ringing the isle, passable by small boat in fair weather. Ahead, the island rises to the Stormspire and its turning crown of cloud.

The Wreck-Field.description: Hulls of every age driven together on the banks — modern wrecks heaped on old ones, old ones on ancient. Cargo spills from broken holds; fused glass streaks the timbers where lightning has struck.

The Hillside.description: Steep scrub-slope climbing from the shore toward the peak. Cave-mouths open in the rock at every height, some hung with wreck-timber doors, and worn paths run between them.

The Stormspire.description: The bare peak, blackened and glassy where lightning has struck it a thousand times. A stone ledge below the summit is stained dark, and the storm turns slow overhead.

Drakerider Isle.name: Drakerider Isle
Drakerider Isle.basicInfo: A small island with a dormant volcanic peak, home of the bay's sea-drakes and the families who ride them. The isle's black-sand beaches are warm from the rock beneath, and the drake herds haul out on them to bask and breed as they have for generations. Saddled sea-drakes carry riders across open water faster than any sail, and people come from across the bay to earn one — the drakes cannot simply be bought.
Drakerider Isle.hiddenInfo:
Sea-drakes are flippered, long-bodied, and fish-eating — placid toward people, which is why a village of families lives on a beach full of them. They swim at the surface and plane when they sprint, and a rider grips the finned crest. The danger in them is mass, not malice: a drake that does not want the saddle throws its rider, rolls, and drags them through the surf. Wild-born pods run the isle's home shallows, claimed by family line and known by name; each season's young are driven into the tide-pens and gentled.

A drake bonds to the person who breaks it — this is nature, not custom. A drake broken by someone else obeys grudgingly and swims home given the chance. So the isle sells the breaking, not the beast: anyone who wants a drake works the season in the pens, is there for the gentling, and lets the drake take to their hands. The breaker-families judge who is worth teaching, and they are not quick about it.

Rustling and drake-poaching are the isle's unforgivable crimes. A stolen drake is a sullen drake, but there are buyers who do not care, and foals taken before bonding can be broken elsewhere. The families keep watch on their herds and pay well for word of poachers.

The Drake Crown is the isle's great annual race — riders and their drakes around the whole island through open water and surf. Winning it makes a rider's name in every port in the bay.

Trade: drake-tack and saddlery found nowhere else, the breaking-season itself, and stud and brood arrangements between the family lines.

Warmsands Beach.description: Black sand, warm underfoot from the rock below. Drake herds haul out along the whole strand, foals among them in the shallows, and riders run the surf beyond the breakers.

The Tide-Pens.description: Roped pens standing in the working shallows, a breaking-yard on the sand above them. The season's young drakes circle the pens; tack-sheds and gentling-gear line the yard.

Bridle Row.description: The village's one street, running up from the beach: saddlers' and tack-makers' workshops, the breeder-families' porch-fronted houses, and the season-board listing the year's foals and their lines.

The Home Beach Inn.description: An open-air inn on the sand: driftwood posts, a wide palm-thatch roof, no walls on the seaward side. Long tables look straight down the strand at the basking herds, and drakes doze in the shallows in front of it.

Pearl Cave Island.name: Pearl Cave Island
Pearl Cave Island.basicInfo: A rocky island rising to a sea-cave tall as a cliff — the den of the Mother of Serpents, the vast pearl-white serpent every hunter in the bay measures themselves against. She does not stay here, but she comes: the cave holds the great ships she has broken and carried back across the generations, and its shores glitter with pieces of her shed scales.
Pearl Cave Island.hiddenInfo:
The Mother of Serpents is as big as a fleet — her back breaching reads as an island, her eye stands taller than a man, and she has bitten warships in half. She is crested and mother-of-pearl, her hide scarred with generations of broken harpoons. She is not hostile by default: she is sovereign. She ignores small things on her island unless her collection is robbed in her presence or she is struck — and then she is absolute. She has surfaced beside crews, looked at them, and left them alive. When she returns to the cave, the water tells it first — the pool stirs, then breathes, then rises. She surfaces from the shaft without warning, anywhere in the cave's water.

She keeps what she breaks. The finest vessels she has ever destroyed lie laid up in the cave's dark water, carried there by her. Among them is the bow half of the Serpentsbane, the greatest ship ever built in the bay, bitten in two on the great hunt that founded the city's fortunes. Its lost relics — founders' arms, the figurehead — are worth fortunes to the great houses.

The island's scavengers do the everyday killing. Wreck eels, thick as a leg and vicious, den through every hulk in the cave — looting the collection means reaching past their holes. Scuttle crabs, dog-sized and armored, swarm the rocks and strand in numbers and come to blood. Reef serpents haunt the island's shallows thicker than anywhere else in the bay.

Loot: scale fragments litter the shores. Intact shed scales are rare, found mostly inside the cave, and prising one loose is slow, loud work.

The Scale Strand.description: A shore glittering with shards and worn slabs of mother-of-pearl among the shingle. Reef serpents trace the shallows, and the island climbs from the beach toward the cave-mouth above.

The Carcass Rocks.description: Tide-flats and rock fields where the sea leaves what she leaves — ribcages bigger than boats, hull timbers, wave-worn bones. Scuttle crabs work the leavings in swarms.

The Wreck Hall.description: A cavern vast enough to hold ships, and it does: great vessels laid up in the dark water, the Serpentsbane's sheared bow among them. At the center of the pool, a shaft drops away into blue-black depth.

Coriva.name: Coriva
Coriva.basicInfo: The great hunting port of the southern coasts, built where the shipping lanes cross the richest monster waters in the world. Coriva's crews hunt the sea serpents and leviathans that plague the lanes, and the city has grown rich on the harvest. Its harbor is crowded with hunting ships, and its two ruling houses — Tessaro and Cavarin — fly their colors from half the masts in port.
Coriva.hiddenInfo:
House Tessaro hunt the bay's monsters and hold that this is what keeps its people alive. They wear silvered scale-armor, carry silver-barbed harpoons, sail ships hung with banners, and parade to the docks before every great hunt. A Tessaro crew never abandons anyone: they will die to the last soul before letting a monster take a fisherman, and a mast flying their colors means help is coming.

House Cavarin capture monsters alive and put them to work: their broken beasts tow the fastest vessels in the bay, haul what no crane lifts, and guard their harbors, and their handlers bond hunting-beasts the way others break horses.

Both houses scout the Water Arena for recruits, and a promising fighter can expect agents from each at their table by nightfall, talking the other house down.

The Serpentsbane's stern stands in drydock on the plaza — the greatest ship ever built in Coriva, bitten in half by the Mother of Serpents on the great hunt that founded the city's fortunes. Oaths are sworn on her timbers.

Coriva's streets: humans, halflings, and giantborn hunters; merfolk trading at the waterline; frogkin everywhere. Hunters are celebrities and act like it — entourages, feuds, terrible poems about themselves. Crews recruit loudly on the plaza and lie about their prospects.

The Coriva League Chapterhouse posts the bay's work: hunts, escorts, rescues, salvage charters, and bounties.

Serpentsbane Square.description: The harbor plaza: quays where hunting ships land their catches, market stalls under awnings, and criers, recruiters, and crowds at all hours. The sheared stern of the Serpentsbane stands in drydock above it all, her open end facing the sea.

The Coriva League Chapterhouse.description: A stone League hall off the square, its boards facing the door: hunts, escorts, rescues, salvage charters, monster bounties, and outlaw bounties. Long tables fill with bay crews, serpent hunters, divers, and young adventurers looking for a first sea-road. The chaptermaster's table stands beneath trophy-sign, where hunts are heard and standing recognized.

The Harpoon House.description: The great tavern of the hunting trade, a sea-serpent's jawbone arching over the door and its beams hung with the bones of famous kills. Crews recruit from the long benches, and captains filling a roster buy rounds for the whole room. The year's champion hunters hold their own tables. A slate by the bar lists ships forming up, their quarry or destination, the dangerous berth still open, the offered pay or share, and when they sail.

Scale Street.description: The craft street of the monster trade: scale-smiths hammering serpent hide into armor, bone-wrights turning leviathan bone on great lathes, renderers' shops selling oils, venoms, salves, and inks. Racks of finished work stand outside every door.

The Water Arena.description: A seawater arena built into the harbor's edge, tiered stone seating around a netted pool. Fighters face captured sea creatures before roaring crowds; the betting stalls never close. Handlers, nets, and gate crews keep ordinary bouts within their announced terms, and new fighters face dangerous but manageable stock. Its declared championship is recognized on the Grand Arena Circuit.

Tessaro Hall.description: A banner-hung hall of pale stone above the harbor, the house's hunting banners floor to ceiling, oldest first. In the muster-yard, sworn crews drill with harpoon and line, and candidates are tested before the recruiting officer's table. The armory issues silver-barbed harpoons and silvered scale-armor to those who have earned them. When the muster-bell rings, a hunt is forming.

The Cavarin Yards.description: The beast-wrights' waterfront is a menagerie of the sea: pens and flooded paddocks along the quays holding serpents, tow-beasts, and stranger catches, each at some stage of its training. Handlers work the animals from walkways over the water — gentling the new, harnessing the ready, feeding the unconvinced. The pen-masters buy live catches at the weigh-cage, and the sponsorship desk at the gate takes on anyone with the nerve for the work.

Fleetwrack Isle.name: Fleetwrack Isle
Fleetwrack Isle.basicInfo: A low sand isle off the fen coast where the Golden Fleet of the Empire of Light burned at anchor — set ablaze by the dragon that rules the Fens. Dozens of scorched hulls still stand beached on the bars and heeled in the shallows. It is said the fleet's gold and fire-stores were never recovered: the wrecks are infested with drakes and worse, and the salvage crews that put in mostly don't come back.
Fleetwrack Isle.hiddenInfo:
Merrow — hulking aquatic ogres — den in the flooded lower decks of the outer wrecks. They drag victims into the dark water and drown them, and they hoard what the fleet carried: coin, arms, and plunder heaped in the deepest holds. They can be baited with treasure thrown into the water and will break off a fight to guard a threatened hoard.

A rookery of mire drakes — swamp-dwelling lesser dragons, poison-breathed — holds the flagship at the anchorage's heart. They came for the dead when the fleet burned and never left. They nest on her upper decks, sun on the rails, and defend the hulk in numbers when a nest is disturbed.

Giant crabs scuttle through any flooded hold and ambush from dark water.

IMPORTANT: everything living on the isle is hostile by default. The merrow are cruel and greedy but can be baited or bought off with treasure; the drakes are animals and cannot be reasoned with — they break off only when badly wounded or drawn away from their nests. The crabs fight until hurt, then bolt for the water.

The outer wrecks hold silver coin stamped with the sun, legionnaires' short swords and spears, sun-blazoned shields, and casks of lamp-oil and wine in their silted holds. The flagship holds the fleet's pay-chests of gold and silver sun-coin, and in the officers' cabins gilded breastplates, blessed radiant blades, sun-gold rings and medallions, and the admiral's sunburst standard. A sealed magazine deep in her stern holds the fleet's fire-stores — clay vessels of alchemical fire that burn even on water, the surest weapon against the drakes that guard them. Drake hide turns poison and drake venom glands sell well. The merrow hoards hold what the merrow prized: gilded arms, sun-gold jewelry, and coin heaped in the flooded holds.

The Strand.description: The bare isle itself: dune grass, driftwood, and the burned fleet standing in the shallows on every side, masts leaning, hulls charred to the waterline. Cold fire-pits and drag-furrows mark old salvage camps. Sun-bleached bones and cracked crab shells litter the tideline, and broken, abandoned gear lies half-buried in the sand.

The Burned Line.description: The outer wrecks — smaller hulls broken on the bars, boardable by wading. Charred decks, dead men where they fell, splintered spars and rigging fouled across the holds, silt drifted deep in the cabins. The lower decks are flooded and dark.

The Flagship.description: The great hulk at the anchorage's heart, upright on a bar with her decks above water. Claw-scored rails, gnawed timber, and heaped wreckage-nests crowd her upper decks. Below, burned companionways descend past silt-choked cabins into the dark of her stern.

The Stiltwood.name: The Stiltwood
The Stiltwood.basicInfo: A drowned mangrove forest on the fen coast, where the trees stand on stilted roots taller than a man and the ground is water, mud, and root-tangle for miles. It is heronfolk country — tall wading birdfolk who live high in the mangroves and want no visitors. Trespassers are shot from the canopy by archers they never see, and the fen-strip folk give the place a wide berth.
The Stiltwood.hiddenInfo:
The heronfolk are tall, lean birdfolk with long legs, grey-white plumage, and spear-straight bearing. They live in roost-villages high in the mangrove crowns, fish the channels, and hunt with longbows from the canopy. They are not raiders — they never leave the Stiltwood to attack anyone — but they kill trespassers who push into their country, and they are very good at it.

IMPORTANT: heronfolk default to hostile toward anyone who enters the Tangle, but their hostility follows a strict custom. The first arrow is a warning shot, placed close and deliberate. An intruder who stops, lays down arms, and turns back is allowed to leave. One who keeps coming is shot to kill, from cover, from above, by archers who reposition after every volley and never close to melee while they hold the high ground.

The boundary stakes at the Root Margin are a trading place. Goods left at the stakes — steel arrowheads, salt, good rope, cloth — are taken overnight and paid for in kind: smoked fish, feather-fletched arrows, pearls, and salvage the heronfolk pull from the drowned wood. Fair traders are remembered by face. A proven friend — one who has traded fairly, kept the custom, or done the roosts a service — is invited up: a climbing-rope lowered from the canopy, a place at the cook-fires, and heronfolk guides who know every channel in the Fens. The heronfolk trade in what they know as much as what they make; nothing moves in the wetland that the roost-sentries have not seen.

Heronfolk fight from height and distance. Opening volley from three directions at once, then silence and repositioning. Wounded intruders are left to retreat; dead ones are stripped and their gear hung on the boundary stakes as warning. If the roosts themselves are attacked, every adult fights, and the staked water below the platforms does the rest.

Loot: heronfolk longbows are prized — man-tall bows of laminated mangrove that outrange anything made on the strip. Their feather-fletched arrows fly true, and roost-pearls pulled from the drowned beds sell well anywhere.

The Root Margin.description: The outer edge of the mangroves, where the open fen meets the first stilt-roots and the going is still passable by punt or wading. Feathered stakes stand in a ragged line through the shallows, hung with bones, shell, and weathered gear. Beyond them the trees thicken and the light goes green.

The Tangle.description: The maze itself. Root-arch over root-arch, channels that fork and dead-end, mud that swallows boots to the knee. No sightline runs longer than a spear-throw, and the canopy is closed overhead. Old arrow-shafts stand in the snags, and small platforms and rope-ways show high in the trees, always empty when looked at.

The Roosts.description: A village of woven platforms, walkways, and roundhouses built high in the crowns of the biggest mangroves, joined by rope-bridges and reached only by climbing-ropes lowered from above. Cook-smoke drifts through the canopy, and drying-racks of fish and hides hang between the houses. The water below the platforms is staked.

The Drowned Road.name: The Drowned Road
The Drowned Road.basicInfo: An old imperial road running west into the deep Fens — broken, half-sunk, and still the only firm footing through miles of bog, mire, and quicksand. Its stone bed stands a stride above the water in places and vanishes beneath it in others. Everyone who moves through the Fens moves on the Drowned Road, and not everyone on it wants to be seen.
The Drowned Road.hiddenInfo:
The road belongs to the dragon-kingdom of the Fens — the lizardfolk realm that closed the wetland to outsiders a generation ago — but the kingdom does not garrison it. Lizardfolk war-parties travel it moving east and west, some with mire drakes on the leash, and they attack outsiders on sight. Between their passages the road carries quieter traffic: smugglers moving goods west, salvagers and egg-hunters slipping toward the drowned ruins, and captives being marched west under guard to be given to the dragon's brood.

IMPORTANT: lizardfolk war-parties on the road are hostile by default and do not parley. They take the strong captive and kill the rest; captives are bound and marched west. They do not pursue far off the road — the bog is their ally, and they let it do the killing. Anyone hiding off the roadbed in the mire risks quicksand, snakes, and giant leeches instead.

War-parties, captive columns, and smuggler crews are traffic, not fixtures — the road is empty as often as not, and what a traveler meets on it is a matter of timing and luck. A captive column is guarded but slow; its guards will not abandon their charges to chase anyone.

Giant crocodiles hold the sunken stretches where the road dips underwater, and constrictor snakes hunt the reed-choked verges. In the far west, where the road runs between drowned imperial ruins, mire drakes den in the broken stonework.

Loot: travelers who died on the road lie where the bog took them, with their packs, coin, and steel. The drowned ruins along the western stretch hold old imperial stonework, gilded fragments, and sealed cellars the water never reached.

The High Causeway.description: The eastern stretch, where the road runs best: a raised stone bed a stride above the water, wide enough for a cart, its paving heaved and cracked but sound. Reed beds stretch flat to the horizon on both sides. Old wheel-ruts, cold campfires, and bootprints in the mud at the road's edge mark recent passage.

The Sunken Miles.description: The middle stretch, where the road fails. The stone bed dips beneath dark water for spans at a time, forcing travelers to wade the flooded roadbed or detour through mire and quicksand on rotten plank-ways laid by those who came before. Drag-marks scar the mud banks, and the reeds stand torn where something large has passed.

The Ruined Miles.description: The western stretch, where the road runs between the remains of drowned imperial buildings — columns leaning out of the water, roofless walls, sunken courtyards green with weed.
