The paving here is scattered and the way weaves between the ruins. Broken stonework rises on every side, and the water between the walls is still and deep.

Dragon-Brood Mounds.name: Dragon-Brood Mounds
Dragon-Brood Mounds.basicInfo: A field of great earthen mounds rising out of the deep fen — the holy ground of the dragon-kingdom of the lizardfolk, where their brood of drakes is hatched and raised. It was here that a priestess entered the oldest mound and came out a dragon, and the kingdom has held the place sacred and forbidden ever since. Outsiders taken in the Fens are brought to the mounds, and they do not come back.
Dragon-Brood Mounds.hiddenInfo:
The mounds are the practical seat of the priest-kings — the lizardfolk high priests who rule the Fens in the dragon's name. They keep no city and hold no court; they live among the mounds, tend the brood, lead the rites, and send the war-parties out. Warriors, drake-handlers, and hatchling-tenders live and work across the mound field in numbers.

The brood is the kingdom's pride: clutches of mire drakes — swamp-dwelling lesser dragons, poison-breathed — hatched in the warm earth of the mounds and raised as war-beasts. Captives taken in the Fens are held in pens near the mounds and given to the drakes at the rites, some at each new moon and more at the great feasts. Captives are kept alive and fed until then — a rescue that comes in time comes home with everyone.

IMPORTANT: everyone and everything at the mounds is hostile to outsiders on sight, without parley and without exception. This is the kingdom's holiest ground, and an outsider walking on it is the worst desecration its people know. They do not take prisoners here — prisoners are already here. They fight to the death in its defense, and horns raise the whole mound field within minutes of an alarm.

The priest-kings fight with venom-magic and drake-packs at their call. Warriors fight in coordinated bands with spear, shield, and blowgun, and drake-handlers loose their beasts first. The pens are watched but lightly guarded — the kingdom does not imagine anyone would dare — and the mound field between them is broad, dark at night, and loud with drake-calls that cover careful movement.

The First Mound at the field's heart is the oldest and greatest, ringed with offering-posts, its entrance flanked by drake skulls. Within it the priest-kings keep the kingdom's holiest treasures: offerings of gold and arms taken from the sacrificed, laid up in its inner chamber for the dragon.

Loot: the offering-chamber of the First Mound holds gold, weapons, and armor taken from the kingdom's victims over a generation. Drake eggs are worth a fortune to the right buyer. The priest-kings carry regalia of gold and drake-fang, and their venom-tipped weapons sell high.

The Reed Flats.description: The open fen around the mound field — flat reed-marsh crossed by narrow paths of trodden earth, with the great mounds rising ahead like green hills out of the water. Offering-posts stand along the paths, hung with drake fangs and painted bones. The reeds are tall enough to hide a crouching man.

The Mound Field.description: The mounds themselves: dozens of great earthen hills, grass-grown and steaming faintly in the cool air, threaded with paths, hide shelters, drying racks, and fire-pits. Openings in the mound sides breathe warm air from the hatching chambers within. Claw-marks and shed scales litter the ground between them.

The Pens.description: A cluster of stake-walled pens on the mound field's edge, floored with mud and roofed with lashed reeds. Rope bindings, feeding troughs, and worn paths ring the stockade. A single gate of heavy timber faces the mounds.

The First Mound.description: The greatest mound, at the heart of the field — old enough that trees grow on its flanks. Its single entrance is flanked by two drake skulls the size of horses and framed with gold-leafed posts. A broad rite-ground of packed, fire-blackened earth spreads before it, ringed by standing offering-posts.

Port Lucre.name: Port Lucre
Port Lucre.basicInfo: A ramshackle port on the fen's north coast — docks, warehouses, taverns, and shanties piled inside a timber stockade, the only place on the closed fen coast where a ship can land and a stranger can walk around. It is a smugglers' town, run by no one and owned by the Syndicate, where anything can be bought, sold, or hired and nobody asks where it came from. Rough, loud, and lawless — but the walls hold, and trade is trade.
Port Lucre.hiddenInfo:
Port Lucre exists by an open arrangement: the Syndicate — the criminal brotherhood whose port this is — lands steel, tools, and forge-goods, ships out salvage and plunder, and keeps its own stockade against the fen. The lizardfolk dragon-kingdom that rules the Fens tolerates the port by its dragon's word and never comes inside the walls. The trade goes on; nobody pretends it's anything but what it is.

There is no law in Port Lucre, only the Syndicate's one rule: nothing touches the take. Syndicate bravos — armed, tattooed, unhurried — guard the warehouses, the docks, and the Roost, and they do not police anything else. Brawls, card-cheats, alley robbery, and shanghaiing the dead-drunk are entertainment; a fight that damages cargo or a hand raised against Syndicate business ends with the offender face-down in the harbor by morning. Strangers are welcome exactly as long as they are paying or useful.

The town is every flag and species the sea washes in: human smugglers, halfling fences, frogkin dockhands, giantborn stevedores, moon elf deserters, and crews that don't name their home port. Everything is for sale in the Glut: salvaged imperial arms and sun-gold, fire-stores at gouge prices, weapons, kit, passage out, fen-guides, and information priced by the question. The Roost hires: salvage crews for the burned fleet's wrecks, guards for smuggling runs west, and hard people for jobs nobody explains twice. The Syndicate's ladder here has one rung — prove useful and get paid, or become cargo — but a name that proves useful more than once starts getting the better jobs and the quiet nod at the door.

Port Lucre robs the careless as cheerfully as it serves the paying. Purses are cut on the Landing, drinks are drugged in the shanty-taverns, and a rich-looking stranger who flashes gold walks out of the Glut with an escort he didn't hire. The wise deal sharp, drink light, and sleep behind a bolted door.

The Landing.description: The crowded harborfront: three long timber docks, ships working cargo at all hours, and a waterfront strip of taverns, flophouses, and shanties leaning against each other. Cranes swing bales and crates over the heads of crews, hawkers, gamblers, and drunks. Gulls fight over the fish-gut barrels, and the stockade's spiked timber wall closes off the landward end.

The Glut.description: The market — a roofed sprawl of stalls, auction blocks, and locked strongbox-booths packed between the warehouses, named by its own traders and proud of it. Salvage lots go under the hammer, fences weigh goods on doctored scales, outfitters rack weapons and fen-gear, and chalkboards post charters, bounties, and passage for sale. Everything has a price and half the prices are lies.

The Roost.description: The Syndicate's house: a fortified stone warehouse at the town's heart, iron-shuttered, with a tavern floor at ground level and business above. Bravos flank the doors, the good liquor is behind the bar, and a balcony overlooks the floor where charters are signed and pay is counted. The vault below is the best-guarded room on the fen coast.

Reedmoot.name: Reedmoot
Reedmoot.basicInfo: A palisaded village on the eastern edge of the Fens that refuses to submit to the lizardfolk clans and their dragon ruler. It stands behind a timber wall, governed by an honest moot and beholden to nobody.
Reedmoot.hiddenInfo:
Reedmoot is fenfolk humans, frogkin, and halfling eel-netter families in roughly equal measure — young, loud, and stubborn. They fish, net eels, cut reed, and salvage. Lizardfolk war-parties probe the strip and people are taken, carried west to be sacrificed to the kingdom's brood; the moot mounts rescues, and rescue parties never want for volunteers.

The moot governs through speakers, not chiefs. Belonging runs in visible rungs: strangers eat at the guest-planks; taking wall-watch gets a name chalked on the roster and a greeting by name after; the militia oath is sworn with a hand on the raid-bell; the moot's full trust means a named peg in the Moot Hall and a voice at moot. Villagers treat each rung as real and defer accordingly.

The fire-stores — clay vessels of salvaged alchemical fire, locked in the stone store-house — are doled out by the moot for the wall's defense and never sold. Offering to buy them causes offense.

Behavior: halfling netting families feud over water-rights and race eels on feast days; everyone mocks the dragon out loud because everyone fears her. Frogkin watermen hire out as fen-guides. Work on offer: wall-watch, salvage crews, guide-work, reed-cutter escort, and rescues. When the raid-bell rings, everyone armed goes to the wall, and a stranger who goes with them is family after.

IMPORTANT: Reedmoot is safe ground and welcoming to outsiders. The wall and militia exist for what comes out of the fen, not for guests.

The Common.description: The village heart: a broad trodden green inside the wall, ringed by stilt-houses, drying racks, and reed-thatched workshops, with the great common table running down its middle under a rain-roof — guest-planks at its foot, feast-boards at its head. Market stalls, cook-fires, and the village's noise fill it from dawn. The raid-bell hangs from a high timber frame where every corner of the village can see it.

The Netting Stairs.description: The waterside: tiered timber stairs and docks stepping down from the village into the fen channels, hung with eel-traps, nets, and punts tied three deep. Smoke-houses line the top stair, and the water below is staked into family netting-grounds marked with painted posts.

The Moot Hall.description: A long reed-thatched hall on the green's north side, its walls hung with pegs — each peg named and worn smooth — and its floor ringed with benches around a speaker's stone. Beside it stands a squat stone store-house with an iron-bound door and the moot's three locks.

The Wall.description: The palisade: a fighting-wall of driven timber ringing the village landward side, with a walk behind the spikes, ladder-towers at the corners, and the gate flanked by a chalked watch-roster board white with names. Beyond the wall, cleared ground runs to the reed-line, and smoke-signal pyres stand ready on raised platforms up and down the strip.

The Slagrun.name: The Slagrun
The Slagrun.basicInfo: A canyon of fused black glass cut through the coastal hills by the crash-landing of the Celestial Citadel of Alar, which came down burning, plowed the miles of the cut, and came to rest in the mountain it broke at the canyon's head. The floor is slag, sand, and wreckage shed along the whole length of the fall. Fires burn in the glass with nothing to feed them, and fire-creatures loosed by the crash den among them — the deeper the cut, the worse both get. The Church of the Pyre forbids the wreck to looters, but no one can guard a cut this long — Red-cowl patrols sweep it, and desert folk loot it anyway.
The Slagrun.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Red-cowl patrols sweep the cut at unpredictable hours — six to ten footsoldiers of the Church of the Pyre in red cowls, spears and crossbows, one veteran leading. They attack looters on sight, no hail, no questions. They can be fought, hidden from, or outrun; when a patrol finds nothing, it moves on.

Enemies of the cut itself: fire mephits in the slag banks of the lower cut, spiteful and drawn to anything that gleams; salamanders denning among the standing fires of the narrows; fire elementals loose in the cracked glass near the Fallshead — bound things that outlived their bindings when the citadel broke. The standing fires are flame spilled from the citadel's broken engines along its fall; they burn without fuel and cannot be put out. Everything worsens toward the Fallshead.

Loot: citadel brass, the elemental core of each broken construct, sealed binding-vessels, Sun Kings' ornament, raw voidglass. Thin at the Scatter, rich at the Fallshead, where whole hull sections lie unopened.

The Scatter.description: The wide mouth of the cut, where the glass walls stand low and the floor runs broad and open — long sightlines, little cover, footing of drifted sand over slick glass. Debris lies strewn thin: broken fittings, glass-crusted masonry, brass gone green-black.

The Standing Fires.description: The mid-cut, where the canyon narrows to a walled corridor and the heat climbs. Fires burn in clusters straight out of the black glass, and the air above them bends and shivers, breaking sightlines past a stone's throw. Hull-pieces stand half-buried in the floor, big enough to shelter behind or climb into, their torn openings dark. Burrows open in the slag banks between them.

The Fallshead.description: The head of the cut, beneath the broken mountain and the citadel resting in it. Hull sections the size of towers lie canted in the glass, making a maze of scorched stone and brass — short sightlines, deep shadows, interiors that go back farther than light reaches. The floor splits into cracks that breathe heat and glow faint red at night, and the fires burn biggest and steadiest here.

The Miragelands.name: The Miragelands
The Miragelands.basicInfo: Deep desert running inland from the coast, vast and trackless, where heat-shimmer thickens until the horizon cannot be trusted and mirages look real enough to walk toward for hours. The Desert Tribes live hidden in this vastness, and the Church cannot control it — Red-cowl columns ride into the sand after them and do not always come back. The Tribes are said to gather at secret places deep in the desert, known only to their own and to the few they choose to guide there.
The Miragelands.hiddenInfo:
Red-cowl hunting parties range the outer desert — a dozen riders of the Church of the Pyre in red cowls, lances and crossbows, a veteran leading, hunting any Tribesfolk they can catch. They attack Tribesfolk and known fugitives on sight.

Riders of the Desert Tribes range the whole country and are hostile on sight to Red-cowls. A traveler who is plainly none of these is shadowed, sometimes approached, and sometimes guided in to Meshara — at the Tribes' judgment, not the traveler's asking.

The Tribes are the survivors and descendants of Gesenthame and of everyone the Church has burned out since. They raid the Church's tribute caravans, and they hide and smuggle fugitives out of the region. An outsider's standing is earned in steps: a stranger is fed at the guest-fire and traded with; one who deals fairly or does the Tribes a service is known; the trusted are offered guiding; and of the very few counted as the Tribes' own.

What the Tribes want from outsiders: messages carried to the resistance inside Serendipity, arms and salvage the Church forbids, and information about tribute caravans so they can raid them.

The Glare.description: The outer dunes, where heat-shimmer doubles the horizon and distant shapes ripple and lie — sight is long but nothing seen far off can be trusted. Wheel-ruts and track-lines run in from the coast road and grow aimless deeper in. Caravan wrecks lie scattered along them, cargo still lashed to dead animals, and the dune-crests give high ground to watch the tracks from.

The Deep Sands.description: The interior: high dunes in long ranks, hard gravel flats between them, and no landmarks that keep their place. The dune-valleys hide anything in them until the crest is topped — riders appear and vanish at a ridgeline's distance. Old wells, some dry and some kept, mark the only sure points, and the sand around the kept ones is always fresh with hoofprints.

Meshara.description: The Tribes' camp around a deep stone well, tents in loose rings, horse-lines along the swale, everything made to be packed and gone within an hour. Guests are received at a broad fire set apart from the tents.

Manywrecks.name: Manywrecks
Manywrecks.basicInfo: Manywrecks is a maze of low shoals where a hard current drives ships onto stone crags, and has done for centuries. The hulks lie piled on the reefs in their hundreds, masts standing out of the water like a dead forest. Their holds were never emptied — everyone knows the wrecks are full, and everyone knows why they stay full. The drowned of the deep kingdoms hold that what the sea takes, the sea keeps, and they come up for anyone who touches it. Ships steer wide of Manywrecks; the ones that don't join it.
Manywrecks.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: Manywrecks is hostile ground. The drowned — once surface folk, remade for the water — enforce the kingdoms' law here: what the sea takes, the sea keeps. A vessel passing wide is ignored. Anyone who anchors, boards a wreck, or takes from one is answered. They surface in parties of four to eight, quiet, from the water side — cutting lines and holing boats before showing themselves — and they prefer taking the living down alive to killing them.

Low tide opens wading paths between the outer hulks and bares the teeth; high tide closes the paths, floods the lower decks, and gives the field to the drowned. Fresh wrecks happen with every storm, and survivors sometimes fort up in a sterncastle for days, fighting at the rails at high water and resting at low, until the kingdoms' patience or their water runs out. Reaching them first is the one errand that brings anyone here on purpose.

Giant reef crabs den in the flooded holds, and great morays hunt the dark water between hulls.

The wrecks hold what they sank with: sealed cargo chests, navy paychests, ships' bells and bronze cannon, officers' plate and swords, charted rutters, enchanted compasses, and wine and spice untouched in sealed holds.

Dream coral, a pale reef coral that stirs old memories in whoever holds it, grows over the oldest hulks in the Old Field. Cutting it counts as taking from the wrecks, and the drowned answer it the same way.

The Dry Bar.description: A long sandbar standing above the high-tide line, bare except for driftwood and old timbers half-buried in the sand. Open ground, firm footing, and clear sight in every direction over the shoal water. The nearest hulks lie a short wade off its western end at low tide.

The Old Field.description: The outer wrecks, oldest and most broken, heeled over on the shallowest teeth. At low water, sand paths and exposed reef run hulk to hulk; at high water the paths drown and the hulls stand isolated. Decks are rotten and tilted, holds are flooded to the waist, and broken spars bridge some of the gaps. The standing water between the hulks is dark and deeper than it looks.

The Masts.description: The heart of the field, where the current rafts the newer wrecks against each other in a tangle of hulls. Ships lie boardable deck to deck, and the standing masts and rigging offer high lines of sight and crossings that never touch the water. Sterncastles and sealed holds sit intact above the waterline. Between the rafted hulls, gaps of open water drop away black.

The Copperclad.name: The Copperclad
The Copperclad.basicInfo: The Copperclad is an ancient Empyrean warship, run aground on a stone shoal an age ago and never sunk. The League of Adventurers mans her now, and outsiders are welcome to shelter aboard: dry decks, hot food, and a bunk for anyone who comes up the side in peace. The drowned of the deep kingdoms have tried to take her several times, and failed every time.
The Copperclad.hiddenInfo:
IMPORTANT: The Copperclad is safe ground and welcoming to outsiders.

The League came out here because of Orichala: a dragon is said to lair in the drowned city, and the drowned here answer to it. The Copperclad is the League's one foothold in these waters, and they hold it by force of arms. The drowned have assaulted her several times — coming up through the flooded lower decks and over the sides at night — and been thrown back every time, so far. The lowest decks are flooded, dark, and sealed off, and the garrison watches the seals.

What people get up to aboard: rescue runs to fresh wrecks at Manywrecks — a looking-glass on the sterncastle stays trained on it — standing to arms when the drowned raid, escorting ships through Seadeep water, and expeditions toward Orichala, which is the work the veterans respect and the work that gets people killed. Veterans talk anyone they can out of Manywrecks and outfit the ones they can't.

Aboard her: the League garrison, sailors of every people, crews sheltering from weather or worse, and the captains of the ships moored under her protection.

The Weather Deck.description: The Copperclad's open upper deck, reached by a broad gangway up her seaward side, tilted a few degrees to port. Traders' stalls stand along the high rail, and cookfire smoke drifts from the hatches. In her lee, the shoal bends around a pocket of calm water where ships lie moored under the garrison's watch. From the deck, the dead masts of Manywrecks stand on the horizon, and on very clear days, far south, the towers of Orichala.

The Wardroom.description: The stern castle, built for officers three times too grand for the present age — high brass ceilings, tall windows over the shoals, and a chart table the size of a longboat scattered with rutters and soundings. The looking-glass is mounted at the south windows, trained on Manywrecks. One wall carries the contract board: rescue postings, escort work, and standing bounties.

The Berth Deck.description: The long covered deck below, ports open for light and air. A galley amidships with fires always lit, a bar built across the bow under a mounted sea-serpent skull, an outfitter's cage racked with arms and gear, and bunks in rows down both sides. Carved wooden panels and flags off wrecked ships dress the brass walls. The drink of the house is whatever the last ship in carried.

The High Caves.name: The High Caves
The High Caves.basicInfo: A prison complex cut into the mountain above Velmere, built long ago and disused for longer than anyone has kept records. Nobody can seal it. The moon elves who built it drove ways in from half the mountain so their keepers could move, and those ways are still open. So whatever wants a defensible hold within a night's walk of a rich valley takes it — strigoi, worse things down from the peaks, and sometimes people. Velmere loses stock, then travelers, then a family on an outlying terrace, and the Crimson Company goes up and roots out whatever is living in there. It has been rooted out many times.
The High Caves.hiddenInfo:
WHY THIS PLACE NEVER STAYS EMPTY: it is a purpose-built stronghold, hidden, defensible, and an hour above a wealthy valley that cannot defend its outlying terraces. Clearing it does not solve it — clearing it creates a good empty lair next to Velmere, and something always takes the vacancy. The Company knows this. The work is maintenance, not victory, and it is paid as maintenance.

THE BUILDERS: moon elves, during or just after the Schism, when the Lady of Blood's gift was new and going wrong constantly and the first lords needed somewhere to put their failures. The architecture is institutional and competent: cell corridors, keeper stations, silvered grilles, chain-and-counterweight gates, murder-slots, and drops cut deliberately across the floors. Much of it still works. It was abandoned, not destroyed, and nobody now living knows the whole of it.

WHO IS IN THERE varies by visit and is established on arrival. Use exactly the occupiers the arrival brief names, and do not mix tenants:
- STRIGOI: mindless, no parley, sluggish by day and fierce after dark, wall-crawlers, denning in the cells the place was built to hold them in.
- A FERALS PACK: werewolves and beast-shifters who took the curse willingly. Organized, they post watches, they hold ground, and they talk — which nothing else up here does. Silver and moonstone bite them.
- RAIDERS: people. Outlaws, deserters, a Company crew that went bad. They parley, ransom, bluff, and betray, and they may be holding somebody from the valley.
- GHOULS: down from Charnel Mountain, in numbers, with no tactics, dug into the lower cells.

WHAT IS WORTH TAKING, in two kinds. First, the keepers' own arsenal, cached and mostly untouched because most tenants cannot use it: exact catalogue names Moonstone Dagger of Radiant, Silver Binding Chain, Silver-Tipped Bolts of Radiance, Vampire Hunter's Crossbow, Iron Shortsword, Leather Jerkin. Second, and this is what makes the site worth returning to, whatever the current tenant has dragged in: coin, stock, road-plunder, trophies, a strongbox, the effects of people who did not come home. That refills every time the tenant changes.

ARRIVAL RULE: name who holds the place this visit and how dug in they are before anything else, then make contact immediate and physical at or just inside the outworks.

IMPORTANT: the Unmapped is the reason this site cannot be closed. The plan runs out down there, the builders cut into natural cave, and there are ways in from the mountain that nobody has ever found. Never let the party permanently seal, collapse, or end the site. They can clear it, and clearing it is worth doing and worth paying for.

The Outworks.description: The built face of the complex, cut square into the shaded wall a hard climb above the vineyard terraces: a gate arch wide enough for a cart, guardrooms either side of it, and slots in the stone above that were made for shooting down through. The gates themselves are long gone. On the shelf outside, the Crimson Company keeps a cull-camp — fire ring, spear rack, a bench, and a post with a tally cut into it that has run out of room twice. Daylight reaches through the arch and a good way down the first corridor, and nothing that lives here comes past that line while it lasts.

The Cells.description: The ordered body of the complex, and the part somebody drew a plan of once. Corridors of cells with silvered grilles gone dull and grey, keeper stations at the junctions with their slate boards still bolted up, chain-and-counterweight gates that can still be worked by anyone who reads how, and drops cut across the floors in places that make sense only if you were herding something. Whatever holds the complex dens along these corridors and stores what it takes in the cells.

The Unmapped.description: Where the plan runs out. The builders cut into natural cave and kept going, and the levels below that are collapsed, flooded, or simply unrecorded. Cold air moves through here from somewhere, steadily, which means the mountain is open to it in places nobody has ever found. This is where whatever leads the current tenants sleeps, and it is why the front gate was never the problem.

Val Cendrac.name: Val Cendrac
Val Cendrac.basicInfo: A wide valley beyond the range west of Velmere, and the largest fief in the western Summits. Cendrac's forges have burned day and night for longer than anyone has counted, and what falls on the town is as often ash as snow — grey on the roofs, grey on the statues, grey underfoot by morning. The town beneath is beautiful even so: elegant stone townhouses in tiers up the valley side, wide walks lined with the statues of its ancient Peers, and a bathhouse the size of a temple, heated off the furnaces and free to anyone who walks in. Silver and moonstone out of Cendrac's workshops arm most of the Shadow Summits, the Crimson Company included. Lord Bertran ni Verrone holds the valley from Keep Verrone above the town, and one road joins it to Velmere: Ashfall Pass.
Val Cendrac.hiddenInfo:
Lord Bertran ni Verrone has held Val Cendrac a long time and has asked Lady Isaveau ni Mirevaux of Velmere to marry him, at intervals, for something close to six hundred years. She has never accepted and has never quite closed the door either, and the correspondence is famous among the Peers in the way a long joke is famous.

What he says he wants is water. Cendrac is furnaces on dry black rock, and forges at this scale drink more than the valley can give; Velmere holds the largest body of water in the Summits, cold and deep and fed off the peaks. He also says, and it is harder to answer, that a lord with no heir is a valley that will one day be masterless — and a masterless valley on his border becomes another Vale Sable, and his problem forever. He does not say that he also wants Velmere itself, the one valley in the Summits that has never fallen, and everybody knows.

Cendrac keeps the levy and keeps it strictly. The chosen go up to Keep Verrone and do not come back, thirteen times a year, and the fief counts it the highest honour it can give: the family is compensated generously and permanently, and households put themselves forward. This is not resented here. It is competed for. The valley is large, rich and proud, and considers Velmere's refusal to take a levy at all to be sentimentality that its neighbours will eventually pay for.

Ghouls out of Cendrac come over the ridge onto Velmere's outlying terraces. Nobody says so. Ghouls are vermin, vermin can be killed by the Crimson Company without anyone admitting a war, and both houses get what they want out of the arrangement. Every few years it worsens, and it worsens after a refusal. The connection has never once been stated aloud by anyone who matters.

Ashfall Pass is watched from both ends and garrisoned at neither, because neither lord needs a gate. The tunnels are the real traffic: old workings and cut ways through the range, used by smugglers, by Cendrac's people, and by whatever wants to cross unseen. Isaveau collapses them as she finds them. She has been finding them for six centuries and has never found them all.

The two valleys cannot afford to finish this. Cendrac's silver and moonstone are the only things that reliably kill what comes down out of the peaks, and Velmere buys nearly all of its weapons here; Velmere's water is the only water at that volume, and its tinctures and poisons are traded nowhere else in Larion. Each holds something the other cannot manufacture, which is why six hundred years of this has never once become a war.

Bertran has married, more than once, and has get: a real house of made vampires, properly sired by the rite of two, several of them centuries old and holding offices in the valley. He is aware that Isaveau has none, and mentions it only by being seen with his.

IMPORTANT: Val Cendrac is safe for a visitor who keeps the peace. It is a wealthy, orderly, well-policed fief, its people are neither cowed nor secretive, and they will discuss the levy with a stranger quite happily. Nothing in the town is hunting anyone.

The Statuary.description: The town's long central walk and the place everyone crosses to get anywhere else, laid in pale stone that never looks pale for long. Statues of Cendrac's Peers stand down both sides in two unbroken ranks, carved in the fashion of whichever century put them up, each with the years of their holding cut at the foot. Elegant townhouses rise in tiers behind them with iron balconies and shuttered ground floors. Ash comes down out of the sky most days, mixed with snow or instead of it, and there are people whose whole trade is sweeping it, working the walk from end to end and starting again.

The Long Evening.description: The house where Cendrac receives anyone worth receiving: a tall stone building off the Statuary with a lit portico, a doorman who knows faces, and rooms that run back further than the frontage suggests. Inside is panelling, low light, deep chairs and very good glass. Envoys of the houses stay here, Syndicate factors take rooms by the season, and people waiting on an audience at the Keep wait here, sometimes for weeks. The kitchen is superb. The lord's own get come down of an evening and are given the best table without anyone asking. Business is done at the tables in plain sight, quietly, and the staff have been trained for generations not to hear it.

The Peers' Gift.description: A bathhouse the size of a temple, built over the vents that carry the forges' waste heat, and free to anyone who walks through the door — miner, factor, envoy, or beggar, with no attendant at the entrance to ask which. Vaulted halls in grey and green stone, pools graded from scalding to snowmelt, steam standing in the roof, and mosaics of the valley's Peers set into the floors where bathers walk over them without a thought. It is the warmest place in the Shadow Summits and the loudest room in Cendrac: half the valley's business, gossip, courtship and quarrelling happens here, undressed and unarmed. An inscription over the entrance names which Peer gave it and in what year, and nothing else.

Keep Verrone.description: Lord Bertran's seat, standing on the shoulder of the valley above the town and lit along its whole face at night so the town can see it. Black stone, no rougher than it needs to be, with tall glazed windows and a long stair up from the Statuary that is swept before dawn every day of the year. Inside is warm — the same vents that feed the bathhouse run under these floors — and hung with six centuries of acquisitions arranged by somebody with taste and time. His get hold offices here and are visible about the place, several of them older than most of the visitors who come to see their sire. The correspondence room is kept as a room in its own right, and the letters in it go back further than the town does.

Ashfall Pass North.description: The Cendrac end of the only road over the range to Velmere: a long grey climb out of the valley between black walls, switchbacking up past the last of the terraces to a saddle where the wind never stops. Ash blows through it constantly and settles on the eastern side, which is how the pass got the name and why Velmere resents it. There is no gate and no garrison, only a stone shelter at the height with a cold hearth in it, and the certain knowledge that the crossing is watched from both ends by people who have no need to stop anybody. Cart traffic goes over in convoy. Everything else goes over alone and quickly.

The Glowcaves.name: The Glowcaves
The Glowcaves.basicInfo: The Glowcaves lie under the Bramblewood: deep, quiet cave halls lit blue and green by the glowing fungus of the myconid farms, with beds of molds and mushrooms stretching away into the dark. A peaceful colony of myconids lives and farms here, and trades with the potion village of Wortwell, whose brewhouses open into the caves.
The Glowcaves.hiddenInfo:
The myconids were under the wood before Wortwell was built. The village's founders dug their brewhouses into the slope and broke into the caves, and the first trade was ferments for potions. Once, in a hard winter, the myconids hid Wortwell's children and old people in the caves for a month, and the village has not forgotten.

Myconids are slow to decide and decide together in the Meeting Hall, so a visitor who wants an answer on anything that matters may have to come back for it. They understand any spoken language and answer into the listener's mind. They do not lie, and surface hurry baffles them.

Fire is their terror. A lamp is tolerated in the Trading Room and nowhere else, and a student who throws fire in the caves has caused a diplomatic incident. They cannot bear strong daylight either, so they never go up into the wood.

Giant centipedes as long as a man come up from the deep tunnels to eat the lower beds, and in spring they swarm the grow-halls. Blight sometimes kills a grow-hall, and Syndicate diggers come down to poach the best caps.

The Cellar Stair.description: The way down from the Bramblewood: a broad stone stair that Wortwell's founders cut, winding down from a hollow in the wood into the cool dark. Past the first turn the walls begin to glow with blue fungus, and the air grows damp, still and faintly sweet.

The Grow-Halls.description: Long cave halls of terraced beds, where the myconids farm molds, caps and glowing fungus in ranks under a ceiling lit blue and green. Myconids move slowly among the beds, tending them, turning leaf mould and carrying baskets. The far halls run deeper than any visitor has walked.

The Meeting Hall.description: A round, high cavern of pale fungus pillars, where the colony gathers to decide. The myconids stand together in silence for hours at a time. A visitor feels the edge of their talk as a soft, wordless pressure, like a crowd murmuring just out of hearing.

The Trading Room.description: A dry, square cave behind the oldest of Wortwell's brewhouses, where heavy doors open from the village side. It is the only room in the Glowcaves lit by lamps. Wortwell folk and myconids meet here across a long stone table, trading crates of caps and ferments for leaf mould, glass and iron tools.

Dimbly Hatchery.name: Dimbly Hatchery
Dimbly Hatchery.basicInfo: Dimbly Hatchery is a meadow village on the north shore of the Jade Tarn: a long lane of low whitewashed houses with turf roofs, barns and paddocks running down to the water. It is named for the Dimblys, a big, sprawling family of creature-keepers who hatch and raise familiars of every kind, from owls, ravens and cats to rarer magical creatures. Students come here to find a familiar, and the Dimblys let them into the runs to meet the young creatures and win one over.
Dimbly Hatchery.hiddenInfo:
The Dimblys are a big human family, and most of the village is Dimblys: cousins, aunts, uncles and children, all in the trade and all with opinions about everyone's animals. The other households, human and halfling, work alongside them as keepers, carters and hands. Their saying is "a familiar is a companion, not a tool," and they won't hand a creature to anyone who treats it like one. The family charges for a creature's keep and training up to the day it goes home with its student, never for the creature itself. They come to check on a familiar if they hear it is unhappy, and anyone they catch mistreating one is not served again.

Every creature is hatched and raised here, from egg to grown. Besides the common familiars, the Dimblys are known for rarer ones: pseudodragons, dragons the size of a cat; volucats, which are winged cats; blink cats, which vanish and reappear a few steps away; fire salamanders, small lizards that live in flame; and drakelings, little fire-breathing dragons. Whatever a student hopes for, the family can usually find or hatch something close. A creature that never takes to a student stays on as village stock or is set free.

A student wins a familiar over by spending time with it: feeding it, playing with it and earning its trust, with a keeper nearby to give advice. Each kind wants something different. Drakelings respect boldness, volucats love to be chased and never caught, pseudodragons want good manners and a little flattery, blink cats test patience, and owls and ravens like to be talked to as equals. A student who works a day alongside the keepers often finds that a creature has taken to them along the way, and the Dimblys will gladly hatch and raise an egg that a student brings in. The family goes up into Kittle Crags, the wild crags beyond the village, to find sleeping eggs, which the creatures leave hidden there, and bring them home to hatch.

Egg smugglers prey on the clutches to sell on the black market, and stray familiars, abandoned by their owners or never settled, run half-wild around the village, raiding larders and picking fights with the stock.

Dimbly Lane.description: The village street: a long lane of low whitewashed houses with turf roofs and wide doors, every porch full of baskets, perches and sleeping animals. Children chase escaped hatchlings between the gardens, cousins shout across the lane, and the north-shore meadows roll down to the water behind the houses.

The Hatching House.description: A long, warm stone barn where eggs of every size lie in trays of warm sand and straw, turned by hand and watched day and night. Fire salamanders curl in the hearths along both walls to keep the heat even. A chalkboard by the door lists every clutch and the day it should hatch.

The Lofts.description: A tall timber barn of perches, ledges and roosting shelves rising to the rafters, where young pseudodragons and drakelings learn to fly. The air smells of smoke and straw, and scorch marks blacken the beams. At feeding time, keepers in leather gauntlets climb the ladders.

The Cattery.description: A rambling cottage and garden given over to volucats and blink cats. There are cushions on every ledge, rope walks across the ceiling, and a high net over the garden to keep the winged ones in. Blink cats vanish from one windowsill and appear on another, and nothing small is ever where it was put.

The Runs.description: A walled stretch of meadow with low trees, warm stones and climbing frames, where young creatures of every kind run free. Students come here to meet them, feed them, play with them and win one over, and a keeper is always close by to give advice.

The Pens.description: Paddocks and stone pens along the meadows, holding grown stock and the goats and fowl that feed them, ringed with fences and watch-posts. The keepers walk the fences morning and evening.

The Brooding Hen.description: The village tavern: a low, warm room with a big hearth, where the Dimblys drink, argue over bloodlines, and tell visitors at length about their animals. Familiars sleep on the settles and the stew is good. By tradition, a student who wins over a familiar buys a round for the whole house.

Cold Kell Mountain.name: Cold Kell Mountain
Cold Kell Mountain.basicInfo: Cold Kell Mountain stands alone at the edge of the Jade Tarn country, a steep, broken mountain of cliffs, ravines and dark pine forest climbing to a bare grey summit where snow lies into spring. High on its flank is the Cold Kell, a spring that was once a shrine where the sick came to drink and be healed, until its water turned black and cold as winter. The mountain is the stronghold of the Heart-Eaters, rogue mages who gave up their human shape to run as werewolves, and has been for a generation. Its trails lose themselves, fog rises out of a clear sky, and few who have gone up after the pack have come back.
Cold Kell Mountain.hiddenInfo:
The Heart-Eaters on the mountain are the beast wing of the rogue mages: mages, most of them once Tarnholme students, who took a wolf's shape through the Ferals' blood rite and stopped coming back. They practice life sacrifice. Their rite is the Hunt, in which they run down a creature or a person and eat its heart for its strength.

They are hard to find and harder to corner. They never keep to one place or one habit for long, and they move through the mountain's cliffs, ravines and deadfall as easily as a road, where anyone else has to climb. Their wards turn trails back on themselves, call fog down over a slope, and hide a camp in plain sight. The creatures of the mountain answer to them: cursed wolves, huge and black with eyes like embers, who run with the pack; ravens who watch the trails and carry word; and the dead of the Hunt, who rise again and run with the pack that killed them.

The Cold Kell was a healing shrine kept by pilgrims until the Heart-Eaters desecrated it with a life sacrifice. Its water turned black and cold, the shrine was abandoned, and the curse that lies on the mountain spreads out from it. The mountain's beasts grow wrong the nearer they live to it.

A werewolf pelt, worn as a cloak, turns aside magic that would change the wearer's shape.

The Lower Pines.description: Dense old pines on the mountain's lower slopes, their trunks straight and grey and their floor a soft brown carpet of needles that swallows every footstep. Little light gets through, and no birds sing. Trails fork, fade and come back to where they started.

The Ravines.description: Deep clefts and sheer cliffs cut into the mountain's flank, choked with fallen trunks and loose boulders, where the only way forward is to climb. Water drips somewhere below in the dark. Claw marks score the rock at the tops of drops no person could jump.

The Cold Kell.description: The ruined shrine of the spring: a roofless stone well-house above a flight of worn pilgrims' steps, with old offerings rotted to nothing on the ledges. The spring's pool is black, still and freezing even in summer, and nothing grows within a stone's throw of it. The air here is silent and very cold.

The High Slopes.description: Snow, scree and wind-bent pines below the bare grey summit, open to the sky and the wind. From the high ledges the whole Jade Tarn lies spread small and green far below, and wolf tracks cross the snow patches in every direction.

The Feasting Hollow.description: A deep hollow under the roots of the oldest pine on the mountain, reached by a hidden way down from the Ravines. A long table cut from a fallen trunk runs its length, set with bowls of bone and horn, and antlered skulls stand on stakes around a great black fire pit. Heaps of picked bones lie against the root walls. A high seat is carved into the largest root at the head of the table, and the air smells of smoke and old blood.

Hollin Coppice.name: Hollin Coppice
Hollin Coppice.basicInfo: Hollin Coppice is the witchwood grove beside the village of Burlwick, where the village cuts the timber for its foci. Its witchwood trees grow in wide rings, each cut back to the stump and sprouting straight, springy rods, tended by the same families for generations. Holly and hazel fill the gaps between the rings. The grove is beautiful and well kept, but it is no place for the careless: its oldest trees are awake.
Hollin Coppice.hiddenInfo:
The oldest witchwood trees are treants, slow and grumbling, who walk a few steps in a year. They let Burlwick's cutters take rods only from trees that have been asked properly and given something back, and they crush anyone who cuts without asking or brings fire near the groves. Sprites nest in the cut stumps; they trade gossip for honey, lead the polite to the best rods and the rude into nettles. Twig blights, small brittle creatures of dead bramble and witchwood, rise from rotten or wrongly cut trees and swarm whatever is warm. Owlbears hunt the deeper groves at night, which is why the cutters work in pairs and go home by dusk.

Witchwood rods and staves come from the rings, and sprite-honey from the stumps. Seasoned heartwood from a fallen treant is rare and worth a fortune to a focus-maker.

The Cutting Rings.description: Wide rings of cut-back witchwood stumps, each sprouting a crown of straight, pale rods, with holly and hazel grown up between them. Cutters' marks and little offerings of honey and ribbon sit on the stumps. A cart track runs out to Burlwick's workshops.

The Old Groves.description: Deeper in, the witchwood has never been cut. The trees are huge and gnarled, their roots heaped like sleeping animals, and some of them stand in places they did not stand last season. The air is green and still, and it creaks.

The Windfall.description: A tangle of fallen and rotting witchwood where a storm brought down a stand of old trees years ago. Brittle dead branches lie everywhere, grey fungus climbs the trunks, and the brambles grow thick and pale. The dead wood rattles when nothing is moving.

Kittle Crags.name: Kittle Crags
Kittle Crags.basicInfo: Kittle Crags is a stretch of wild, broken country on the north shore beyond Dimbly Hatchery: grey crags, warm springs steaming among the rocks, and twisted woods of oak and pine growing out of the cracks. It is where the creatures that become familiars live in the wild, the pseudodragons, volucats, blink cats, fire salamanders and drakelings, and where they leave their sleeping eggs. The Dimblys and others who know the signs go up into the crags to find those eggs and bring them home to hatch, but the crags are dangerous ground.
Kittle Crags.hiddenInfo:
The familiar kinds lay two sorts of egg. Most hatch in the nest and are raised there. A few in every clutch are sleeping eggs: the parent tucks each one into a warm, hidden place, a crack in the rock, a hollow under a root, the edge of a hot spring, and leaves it. A sleeping egg can lie dormant for years and only wakes in the warmth of a mage's hands, so in the wild most are never found and never hatch. Finding one saves it.

Those who know the signs read the crags for them: scorch marks on the rock where drakelings roost, shed scales, tufts of volucat fur caught on the thorns, and a stone that stays faintly warm after sundown. A sleeping egg is warm to the touch and heavier than it looks.

The wild familiar kinds themselves are curious and harmless, and often follow visitors around. The danger comes from what else lives here. Cockatrices nest in the scrub, and their glance stiffens a limb to stone for a while. Giant hornets build in the hollow oaks and swarm anyone who knocks a branch. Stirges roost in the rock cracks and come out after dusk to feed. The rock itself is loose, the springs scald, and fog comes down off the crags fast.

The Broken Woods.description: Twisted oak and pine growing out of cracked grey rock, with thorn and bracken between, where the meadows of the north shore give way to the crags. Paths here are made by animals, not people, and wind upward through the trees. Hollow oaks hum where hornets nest, and small winged shapes watch from the branches.

The Warm Springs.description: A hollow among the rocks where hot springs steam in pools of green and rust-red stone, the air warm and wet even in winter. Fire salamanders bask on the hot rocks at the water's edge, and the stone around the pools is cracked and warm to the touch. Some pools are pleasant to dip a hand in; others scald.

The Ledges.description: Narrow shelves of rock climbing the crag face, scorched black in places where drakelings roost and littered with shed scales. Pseudodragons sun themselves along the edges and drift off as visitors come near. The rock is loose underfoot, and the cracks between the ledges are deep and warm.

The High Crags.description: Bare grey summits above the trees, open to the wind, with the whole Jade Tarn spread out far below. The rock is split by deep, dark cracks, and fog rolls in off the heights without warning, hiding the way down.

Linden House.name: Linden House
Linden House.basicInfo: A handsome cream-stone townhouse below the Palace, with green shutters and lime trees leaning over its garden wall. Inside are comfortable rooms for the owner and their companions, a drawing room made for music and supper, and a kitchen that always seems to have someone visiting. Court is within walking distance, and the enclosed garden offers quiet evenings away from its bustle.
Linden House.hiddenInfo:
Linden House is a furnished ducal townhouse granted for court service. Its household allowance covers ordinary staffing and upkeep. Private bedrooms accommodate residents, guests and companions; shared grants provide separate private rooms and common reception spaces.

Merrit Vale runs the household and arranges dinners, parties and introductions. Sella Reed brings musicians and visiting woodland relatives, connecting the house to gatherings and expeditions beyond the city. They are old friends who enjoy each other’s company and disagree about guests. Merrit favors impressive company; Sella champions people whose talents deserve an audience. Fifi knows Sella through club musicians.

Callers gather in the Drawing Room, musicians rehearse before supper, and the Lime Garden hosts lessons and games. The Kitchen Court brings workers and visiting friends together over food and gossip. Merrit handles routine affairs while residents travel; Sella’s lessons and the household’s friendships continue throughout the year.

The Drawing Room.description: Tall windows light green chairs, polished wooden tables, and a small musicians’ dais. There is room to clear the floor for dancing or pull the chairs close around a card game. Callers visit through the day; musicians rehearse before supper. A staircase leads to private bedrooms, including rooms the owner can keep for returning companions.

The Lime Garden.description: Lime trees shade a long breakfast table and a little wooden pavilion. Music lessons take place here when the weather is kind, and the open lawn serves for games, sparring, or lying in the sun. A side gate admits friends without sending them through the formal rooms. Conversations carry less easily here than they do across the supper table.

The Kitchen Court.description: The kitchen opens onto a sunny paved court, with a broad hearth, baskets from the market, and a table shared by household workers and visiting friends. Someone is usually preparing a meal, arguing about a recipe, or bringing news from another house. The household’s host often comes to inspect dinner and stays to gossip.

Rookwood Hall.name: Rookwood Hall
Rookwood Hall.basicInfo: A broad timbered hunting house among oak woods west of Reaver Road, with a stone hearth, comfortable private rooms, kennels, a riding yard, and an old apple orchard. Returning expeditions gather by the hearth for food, rest and stories of what they encountered.
Rookwood Hall.hiddenInfo:
Rookwood Hall is a furnished hunting residence held by the duke for grants of court service. Its household and the neighboring woodland families have longstanding ties. Estate income covers ordinary staffing and upkeep; private rooms accommodate residents and guests, with separate accommodation for co-owners.

Tamsin Rook leads hunts and trains riders and hounds. Jory Pell knows the working woods and neighboring families, and follows leads to lost treasure and dangerous discoveries. They are friends and fierce archery rivals. Tamsin welcomes new riders and hunters; Jory values the access and livelihoods of the people who use the woods daily. Ciara receives his reports, and Tamsin has hunted beside Lucan.

Woodland rides end with supper and songs. Returning guests find help with their horses, food by the hearth and company eager for their stories. The Kennels and Yard bring trainers, beginners and visiting hunters together; neighbors gather beneath the Orchard Green’s apple trees for tracking lessons, cider-making and meals.

The Long Hall.description: A long supper table and deep chairs gather around a broad stone hearth beneath oak beams. A gallery leads to private bedrooms for the owner and companions. Songs, cards, and hunting stories fill the evenings, with occasional arguments about whose shot actually brought the beast down. There is room for new friends at the table and for the owner’s trophies alongside the residents’ belongings.

The Kennels and Yard.description: Stables, roomy hound runs, archery targets, and a broad practice yard stand beside the hall. Riders and hounds train here. Companions can learn to ride, train an animal, spar, or challenge a visitor. Beginners practice alongside experienced visitors.

The Orchard Green.description: Old apple trees shade picnic tables and a cider press beside paths into the working woods. Neighbors trade news and gather for tracking lessons here. Autumn brings cider-making, music, and fiercely competitive pies. Village families share the tables with visitors and friends.

Fernvale.name: Fernvale
Fernvale.basicInfo: Fernvale is a sheltered river valley northwest of Carendon, with a comfortable stone manor above orchards, meadow farms, and a busy willow-shaded landing. A small village gathers around the green below the house. The Count’s seat has private apartments, rooms for companions and guests, and a garden terrace overlooking the water. Its people have kept the valley prosperous through changes of owner.
Fernvale.hiddenInfo:
Fernvale is a settled river valley whose farms and orchards support the manor’s household and ordinary upkeep. The manor is a ducal grant for court service, with private apartments for its owners and rooms for companions and guests. Village households keep their own homes, work and customs; shared decisions about the valley are discussed among its owners and affected neighbors.

Aven Holt runs the manor, arranges celebrations and visiting company, and helps residents host guests from the village and other courts. Runa Marr practices witchcraft from her cottage beside the River Landing, where villagers seek remedies and private advice and travelers bring unusual magical problems. They organize the summer river feast together, bringing music, dancing and company to the Village Green.

The Manor Hall receives household guests and visiting delegations over supper. The landing brings fishers, growers, guides and travelers together; river outings, boat races and meals along the bank connect the manor with village life. Artisans demonstrate their work at celebrations, and visitors from Carendon mingle with local families. Aven handles routine arrangements while the manor’s residents travel.

The Manor Hall.description: A sunny stone hall overlooks the river, with a generous supper table and broad window seats. The household receives visiting delegations, village guests and friends over shared meals. Private apartments and guest rooms lie upstairs; residents gather downstairs for ordinary meals and conversation.

The Village Green.description: A bakehouse, teaching room, and covered space for dancing face an orchard-edged green. Market stalls, picnics, and lawn games bring neighbors together. Musicians rehearse, friends reserve seats, and people remember how their visitors danced last time. The summer river feast fills the green with music, dancing and guests from neighboring households.

The River Landing.description: Willows shade moored boats and an open boatwright’s workshop where unfinished craft rest on trestles. A witch’s cottage stands beside the landing; villagers come for remedies and private advice, while travelers bring news and unusual finds. Friends gather outside for supper or arrange river outings with local guides. Fishers, orchard growers, and visitors from Carendon trade news along the bank.

Gullwatch House.name: Gullwatch House
Gullwatch House.basicInfo: Gullwatch House is a white-stone seaside manor a short journey from Tevantia, with blue shutters, terraced lemon gardens, and a long supper terrace above a sheltered fishing cove. A small landing welcomes boats from the city. The house offers private rooms, space for companions and guests, and an established household among the families who fish and build boats below.
Gullwatch House.hiddenInfo:
Gullwatch is a furnished ducal estate awarded through Tevantia’s court. Its household, treasure-hunters and fishing families already live and work here. Estate income supports ordinary upkeep and hospitality. Shared grants provide each owner private accommodation while preserving the homes of existing residents.

Armel Bellac runs the household and gathers fascinating guests for celebrations and expedition suppers. Wenna Roux follows coastal tales to pirate caches, drowned shrines and magical heirlooms. They grew up together and share a lively circle of sailors, neighbors and visiting adventurers. Armel organizes the company; Wenna brings stories and prospects for voyages.

The House and Terrace host meals, cards and returning travelers. The Lemon Gardens draw neighbors for swimming, fencing and picnics. In Gullwatch Cove, Wenna gathers company for beach suppers and discusses expeditions; the boatyard handles local repairs and voyage preparations. Fishing households supply the manor and maintain its boats, while the estate maintains the landing and road to market.

The House and Terrace.description: A white-stone manor with blue shutters and terracotta roofs stands above the cove. Its comfortable hall opens onto a shaded supper terrace where household members and visitors eat, play cards, and trade news. Private rooms upstairs give the owner and invited companions somewhere to sleep, keep possessions, and receive friends. Guests often stay longer than planned; returning residents find familiar company eager to hear about their travels.

The Lemon Gardens.description: Lemon trees grow on walled terraces below the house. A sheltered lawn offers space for fencing practice, picnics, and celebrations, while benches overlook the boats. Stone steps descend to a sheltered bathing inlet. Household members and neighbors come here to swim, share fruit, and spend time together; friends can arrange an afternoon without making it a formal occasion.

Gullwatch Cove.description: Fishing boats gather at a small landing beneath the manor. Net sheds, an open boatyard, and working households line the sheltered water. Sailors, travelers and neighbors gather for beach suppers, exchanging tales of coastal treasures and plans for expeditions. The boatyard handles local repairs and voyage preparations. Fishing families supply the house and maintain its boats; the estate maintains the landing and road to market. Visitors arriving by sea are spotted from the quay long before they reach the house.

Highbridge House.name: Highbridge House
Highbridge House.basicInfo: Highbridge House is a handsome cream-stone townhouse built across a broad ancient bridge within Tevantia, with plum shutters and terracotta roofs. Its two wings enclose a sheltered courtyard above a public shop arcade. Windows overlook the sea on both sides. The palaces and theater are within walking distance, and private apartments give the owner and invited companions a home amid the city’s social life.
Highbridge House.hiddenInfo:
Highbridge House is a furnished townhouse held by the duke for grants of court service. Its private apartments and shared reception rooms stand above an arcade of independent shops. The bridge passage remains public. The household allowance covers ordinary upkeep; shared grants provide separate private rooms.

Sidonie Falret hosts private theatrical performances, brings actors and patrons together, and arranges lively suppers around a production. Her younger brother Loic is the illusionist and tailor in the Bridge Arcade, making clothes and disguises and preparing magical entertainments. Their circles overlap in the house and the neighborhood, and their affection survives disagreements about guests and performances.

The salon hosts music, theater, cards and conversation. Residents breakfast and practice fencing in the Courtyard, while shopkeepers share supper under the arcade after closing. The household handles routine affairs during its owners’ travels; returning friends find familiar company, invitations and news of recent performances.

The House and Salon.description: A comfortable salon fills the main floor of a cream-stone townhouse above Tevantia’s bridges. Tall windows look out over the sea; plum curtains, card tables, a small keyed string instrument, and chairs drawn into conversational groups make room for music and company. Furniture can be moved aside for dancing. Private apartments and rooms for invited companions lie upstairs. The household welcomes returning residents with news and invitations, and friends can gather here after the theater without arranging a formal reception.

The Courtyard.description: The house’s two wings shelter a garden courtyard above the public arcade. A small fountain, climbing greenery, and breakfast tables surround an open paved space used for fencing practice. Neighbors lean out of nearby windows to offer unsolicited advice. A stone balustrade overlooks the sea and distant towers. Household members meet here for breakfast, practice, or an unhurried conversation away from the salon.

The Bridge Arcade.description: A baker, an illusionist’s tailoring shop, and a small wine shop occupy the stone arcade beneath the house. A broad public walkway continues along the ancient bridge beside them, open to sea views between the arches. After closing, neighbors pull chairs together and share supper outside their shops. Visitors can buy bread, commission clothes or disguises from the tailor, arrange magical entertainments, choose wine, or join ordinary conversation.

Windcrest Hall.name: Windcrest Hall
Windcrest Hall.basicInfo: Windcrest Hall is a country seat on the high coastal downs near Tevantia, surrounded by vineyards, grazing horses, and old windmills. Honey-colored stone, green shutters, and a long terracotta roof overlook the sea. Its household welcomes riding parties, hunters, and visiting companions to a crowded supper table, with private apartments and guest rooms above.
Windcrest Hall.hiddenInfo:
Windcrest is a furnished ducal estate awarded through Tevantia’s court. Its household, stable workers, vineyard families and millers maintain the property and its livelihoods. Estate income supports ordinary staffing and hospitality. Private apartments accommodate owners and guests; shared grants preserve separate rooms and existing households.

Josette Varlan leads rides and hunts, investigates extraordinary quarry and joins expeditions with her bow. Remond Savrel runs the vineyards and cellar, collects rare wines and delights in introducing unusual people. They organize outings together, combining her appetite for adventure with his love of a long outdoor supper.

The Hall brings the household and visitors together for meals. In the Riding Yard, Josette and the riders prepare for outings, teach and exchange stories. Remond welcomes company for tastings, walks among the vines and harvest celebrations. Those who stay home share news over supper when the travelers return.

The Hall.description: A broad stone hearth warms Windcrest’s comfortable hall. Long supper tables and deep window seats gather the household, companions, and visiting friends after rides and hunts. Green shutters open onto the coastal downs; stairs lead to private apartments and guest rooms. Returning adventurers find a place at the table and people eager to hear where they have been. Meals, games, and plans for tomorrow’s outing keep the hall lively without requiring a formal occasion.

The Riding Yard.description: Timber stable wings enclose a spacious yard beside the hall. Horses wait by open stalls, tack hangs inside, and a fenced practice ground holds training weapons and a straw dummy. The huntmaster and household riders prepare for outings across the downs and welcome company at a suitable pace. Visitors can arrange a ride, practice weapons, help with the horses, or watch and talk.

The Vineyard Slopes.description: Paths wind between terraced vines, low stone walls, grazing fields, and old windmills on the high coastal downs. Sheltered grassy places offer room for picnics, while the ridges look out over the islands. Workers and household residents share news along the paths. Friends walk here, bring supper outdoors, or pause beneath the olive trees after a ride. The hall’s green shutters and terracotta roof remain visible uphill. The cellar’s keeper welcomes company for a walk, a tasting, or an outdoor supper.

Castle Sun and Moon.name: Castle Sun and Moon
Castle Sun and Moon.basicInfo: Castle Sun and Moon is a luxurious fortified oasis estate in a sheltered sandstone valley outside Oasis, receiving distinguished travelers, patrons, explorers, and guests invited by its owner. Pale stone towers, shaded courts, and generous apartments rise on terraces above date groves and a clear spring-fed pool. Low hills and connecting walls enclose the green valley. Its sole ground approach passes through an ancient gatehouse, where a golden sun and silver crescent face one another above great bronze doors.
Castle Sun and Moon.hiddenInfo:
The sun and crescent were already carved into the gatehouse stone when the abandoned stronghold was reclaimed and rebuilt. Some accounts identify them as the emblems of rival powers reconciled here; others interpret them as a promise of shelter by day and night. The metalwork now covering the carvings was added during the restoration.

A separate legend names Samhar, a pupil of Suleyvan the Sealer, as the binder of the spring's marid. During a destructive war, Samhar established a refuge here where enemies could meet under protection. He bound the marid to defend anyone attacked within the enclosure. The refuge grew into a residence, fell into ruin, and was eventually restored; the binding endured throughout.

A reservoir and irrigation channels distribute spring water through figs, pomegranates, herbs, and vegetable plots beneath the palms. The household produces dates, date syrup, dried fruit, and garden produce. About thirty people live and work here, including gardeners and their families, household servants, stable hands, and a small guard. Six generous guest apartments accommodate a handful of visiting parties. Kitchens, stores, stables, and staff quarters occupy a service court beside the residence.

Zareen manages the estate for its owner and cultivates its company. Rafi receives visitors and protects the household. The owner determines invitations, patronage, and allegiances. Introductions can bring a patron's resources together with an explorer's discovery or a sorcerer's expertise. Invitations can recognize achievement, useful knowledge, friendship, or an interesting proposal.

Nahravan manifests when violence breaks out within the enclosed valley, attacking aggressors and protecting those they threaten. It can appear even inside closed rooms, without nearby water. It vanishes when the fighting ends, never leaves the valley, and cannot be called forth through summons or conversation.

Small sand cats live among the warm rocks and date stores. Broad-eared and sandy-coated, they hunt rodents and sleep in shaded corners. This local magical variety can sink into loose sand and emerge a few paces away, leaving a small hollow behind. Some tolerate familiar people nearby; they remain independent animals.

The Great Court.description: A broad limestone courtyard forms the social heart of the castle. Deep arcades shelter low tables, cushioned seats, and carved doors opening into the guest apartments. Wide arches lead into a high supper hall, whose long tables can be arranged for an intimate gathering or a lavish feast. A narrow watercourse crosses the court toward the gardens, and an upper gallery joins the private rooms above. Rich textiles, flowering pots, and objects brought back from distant journeys give the court the character of an inhabited home.

The Spring Gardens.description: A deep spring pool lies beneath a sandstone outcrop, its irregular banks crowded with reeds, date palms, and low fruit trees. Clear water passes between rocks into narrow irrigation channels serving the cultivated grove. Worn steps reach the water at one sheltered spot. A shaded pavilion and scattered stone benches offer places to sit together, while footpaths wander between roots, garden plots, and warm boulders where sand cats rest. The castle rises above the grove, and enclosing desert hills remain visible beyond the palms.

The High Pavilion.description: A broad pavilion occupies an upper terrace of the castle, shaded by a heavy timber roof carried on carved stone pillars. Plum cushions, woven rugs, low tables, and loose curtains furnish the sheltered space. A thick crenellated parapet overlooks the irregular palm crowns and rocky spring below; a square castle tower stands close beside it. Potted herbs and a climbing vine soften the masonry. The owner receives friends here for meals and private conversation.

Hidden Garden House.name: Hidden Garden House
Hidden Garden House.basicInfo: A small white villa stands on a low rise among the palm groves just outside Oasis. Beyond its garden walls, cultivated ground gives way to desert; from its roof terrace, the city’s domes rise above the trees. Shaded galleries shelter comfortable guest rooms. At the end of its fountain court stands a great cedar door covered in a mosaic of a lush garden: fruit trees, flowering vines and blue pools picked out in glazed tile. Visitors know the house for this beautiful picture of a garden hidden behind high walls.
Hidden Garden House.hiddenInfo:
The mosaic depicts the house’s actual hidden garden, an ancient cultivated oasis within a small enchanted realm. The cedar door in the courtyard is its only entrance. It opens onto the garden for the rightful owner and people they have invited. Standing invitations can admit household residents; knowing the secret or operating the door does not admit anyone else.

From inside the garden, the same threshold appears as an opening back into the villa’s courtyard. Anyone inside can return through it, even while the owner is away. Time passes normally on both sides.

The garden has its own sunlight, gentle rain, and warm evenings. An immense flowering tree, date palms, and fruit trees surround a clear spring-pool. Old mosaic steps, a rose-covered bridge, and a stone lion fountain survive among the growth. The sandstone and dunes beyond its groves lie within the enchantment; they offer no overland route back to Oasis.

The villa contains the household’s bedrooms, guest rooms, kitchen, and stores. The garden has shaded places to rest and entertain, but no residential buildings. Samir lives in the villa. Household staff tend the house and garden while its owner travels.

The Mosaic Court.description: A low fountain splashes into a tiled basin beside shaded benches and a supper table. Blue-glazed bowls, flowering pots, and striped cushions brighten the pale walls. At the far end stands a great cedar door bearing a mosaic of a walled paradise: laden fruit trees, tangled flowers, and streams joining deep blue pools. Its glazed pieces catch the light beneath a plain stone arch.

The Sitting Room.description: A cool room of pale plaster, woven rugs, and blue cushions. Low tables hold coffee cups, cards, and objects brought home from travels; a broad table provides space to spread out maps or examine a discovery together. Latticed windows admit the sound of the courtyard fountain.

The Hidden Oasis.description: An immense clear spring-pool lies beneath a twisting tree heavy with pale flowers. Date palms and fruit trees crowd its banks, with sunlit sandstone and golden dunes beyond the groves. Turquoise mosaic steps descend into the water. A stone lion pours a stream from its mouth, and a little bridge disappears beneath climbing roses. Rugs, cushions, and low supper tables occupy the shade of the great roots.

Svanholm.name: Svanholm
Svanholm.basicInfo: Svanholm stands on a small island just off Warmwater Township, joined to the shore by a low stone bridge. Hot springs keep the surrounding water open and steaming, and white swans shelter here through the winter. A tall manor of crimson timber and pale stone rises above its terraces, with steep snowy roofs, carved gables and broad windows facing the town. From the island, Warmwater climbs in a sweep of lamplit houses, glowing ice sculptures and glass-roofed manors toward the Winter Court and Whitewatch. On aurora nights, colored light fills the sky above them.
Svanholm.hiddenInfo:
Svanholm is an island residence held by the Winter Crown for grants of court service. It has private chambers for its owners, rooms for companions and guests, a great hearth hall, a spring-fed bathhouse and a sheltered landing. Shared grants provide separate private apartments; invitations and use of the common rooms are arranged among the households.

Malena Svale runs the household. Mikkel Strand rents a chamber and arranges treasure sales and expeditions, receiving clients with the household’s permission. Malena and Mikkel are childhood friends who renewed their friendship after her return from the south. Their swimming, meals and evenings with friends are part of the house’s ordinary life.

A feast lights the hall’s broad windows and can be seen from the shore. Friends come over the bridge, share a bath, take a boat onto the sheltered open water, or watch the town and aurora from the terrace. The wider lake remains frozen and dangerous beyond the spring-warmed water. Swans shelter naturally around the island. The household’s ordinary expenses are supported by its grant.

Malena receives guests in the Hearth Hall and brings company onto the Swan Terrace after crowded evenings indoors. Mikkel receives collectors and explorers by arrangement; he sometimes meets a returning explorer on the terrace or shows a recent find to interested company.

The Hearth Hall.description: The manor’s high timber hall, with a broad stone hearth, carved roof beams and crimson and cream woven hangings. A long dining table occupies one side; cushioned benches and deep chairs gather around the fire. Tall windows face Warmwater across the steaming water, and glazed doors open onto a sheltered terrace. A musicians’ gallery runs above the hall, leading to private chambers for the owner, companions and guests. The tables can be laid for a feast or drawn close for a quiet supper.

The Bathhouse.description:
A low stone wing beside the lake holds a spring-fed bathing pool beneath a vaulted ceiling. Tall windows overlook Warmwater, while wooden screens divide quieter bathing spaces. Residents and guests linger in the warm water after outings, trade news, and arrange to meet friends here.

An adjoining resting room has couches, dry robes, and a small hearth. Tea is served here, and conversations often continue long after everyone has dressed. Outside, a sheltered terrace stays warm underfoot, with snow along its stone parapet.

The Swan Terrace.description:
A broad terrace stretches between the manor and the island’s sheltered landing. Deep eaves shelter cushioned benches and small tables, where residents and visitors gather for late breakfasts, cards, and conversation. Hot drinks and meals are brought outside when the weather permits.

Steps descend to a small pleasure boat and spring-warmed water where swans shelter through winter. A low stone bridge connects the island to shore. Across the water, Warmwater’s houses rise toward the Winter Court.

Firhaven Lodge.name: Firhaven Lodge
Firhaven Lodge.basicInfo: Firhaven Lodge stands on a rocky shoulder above a lake in the wooded foothills near the Firwood. Its steep roofs carry deep snow, and its great fir beams rise from a foundation of pale stone. Forest steads occupy sheltered clearings below, linked by snowy paths and little bridges over steaming streams. Hot springs emerge among the boulders beneath the lodge and feed a sheltered cove; the rest of the lake lies frozen between wooded ridges. Smoke rises through the firs, and beyond them the northern mountains stand white against the sky.
Firhaven Lodge.hiddenInfo:
Firhaven Lodge is an established holding of the Winter Crown, separate from Tirsa Hellemark’s hopes for a new settlement. Its court grant supports the household’s ordinary expenses. Private apartments accommodate titled owners and their companions, with guest rooms and common household spaces. Shared grants provide separate apartments; use of the common rooms and estate grounds is arranged among the households.

Bjorn Halden runs the estate and carves wooden figures in his free time. His elder sister Dagny Halden, a Long Watch knight, keeps a chamber off the Great Hall’s gallery between patrols. They share affection, suppers and swims, though Bjorn now has responsibility for the household.

The surrounding steads, snowy shore and springs bring neighbors and lodge guests together for celebrations, skating, hunting and bathing.
