Woodland use and shared facilities are matters of common interest among the households. Snow covers the forest and shore; warmth is concentrated in the springs, streams and the lake’s open cove. The rest of the lake freezes.

The Great Hall.description: The lodge’s high hall is built around enormous fir posts and a broad stone hearth. Rich wool hangings soften the timber walls, and long tables can be laid for a feast or divided into smaller gatherings. Deep window seats overlook the snowy lake and its steaming cove. A gallery leads to private apartments and guest chambers; broad doors open onto a covered porch with carved pillars and heavy benches. Fine joinery, warm rugs and comfortable chairs make the great room welcoming after the cold outside.

The Three Sisters Baths.description:
Three natural bathing pools nestle among enormous granite boulders beneath snow-laden firs. Unequal hollows in the rock hold the water at different heights, joined by narrow channels and small overflows. The upper pool is fiercely hot, the middle comfortably warm, and the lowest cool enough for children. Known as the Three Sisters, they draw neighbors and lodge guests after skating, hunting, or traveling. Regular bathers have their preferred sister and readily ask newcomers which they favor.

A narrow path and rough footholds lead between the pools. A modest timber bathhouse stands among the trees, with changing space and a sheltered porch where bathers leave their clothes and share drinks. Snow caps the surrounding rocks and branches, while steam rises through the trees.

The White Shore.description: A broad snowy shore curves around the lake beneath the forest steads. At one end, a small timber landing reaches into the steaming cove where the springs enter; beyond it the lake freezes into a wide white expanse, crossed by cleared skating runs and sled tracks. A roofed shelter with benches and a firepit overlooks the ice. Families gather here for races, hot food and winter celebrations, while paths climb between snow-covered firs to the houses and the great lodge above.

Applewick Hall.name: Applewick Hall
Applewick Hall.basicInfo: Applewick Hall stands in a broad cultivated vale of fields, hedgerows and oaks. A compact old limestone tower joins a later long hall and oak-framed residential and stable wings beneath red-tiled roofs. A thick defensive wall shelters an apple orchard and supper terrace. Tenant homes stand nearby; limestone scarps and a broken stretch of Greatwall rise on the distant northern ridge.
Applewick Hall.hiddenInfo:
The manor grew around an old defensive tower, enlarged into a comfortable home as the surrounding vale became settled farmland. Productive fields and orchards support the household and its ordinary upkeep. Experienced staff manage routine affairs, and the tenant households have their own friendships, quarrels and family celebrations.

Verena Hollis runs the household, welcomes long-staying guests and brings promising strangers into its social life. Suppers, feasts, performances and riding parties bring residents and neighbors together. Private rooms occupy the upper floors; guests share the hall, orchard terrace and stable court. Larger celebrations and commitments are arranged with the owners.

The Hall.description: A generous hall of warm stone and oak, with a common dining table, a broad hearth and seats near windows overlooking the orchard. The household gathers for suppers, music and conversation; visitors bring news from the vale and stay to hear a performance. Private rooms occupy the upper floor.

The Orchard.description: Apple trees fill a grassy orchard behind an old thick stone wall. A sheltered terrace holds tables and comfortable seats for meals, drinks and quieter company. Neighbors visit in the afternoon, while household guests linger beneath the branches after supper.

The Stable Court.description: A sheltered court with benches and a mounting block beside the stables. Riders gather here to plan outings, compare horses and linger over drinks afterward; visiting neighbors often join them. The adjoining tack room has seats and a hearth for wet afternoons.

Highcliffe Hall.name: Highcliffe Hall
Highcliffe Hall.basicInfo: Highcliffe Hall stands on a limestone bluff above the northern shore of the Marrenmere. Its broad stone gatehouse joins a finished stretch of the old Greatwall, which runs inland along the ridge. A long residential wing of grey limestone and slate faces the lake, with generous windows, sheltered gardens, and a landing reached by a winding track. Sheep graze the upland pastures behind the house; the estate sells wool and firm sheep’s-milk cheeses in Marrenford. Tenant cottages, a dairy, and stone barns surround the home farm.
Highcliffe Hall.hiddenInfo:
The original house was built to oversee this end of the Greatwall, where the bluff and lake anchored the masonry. Later generations enlarged it into a comfortable noble residence. The Greatwall was never completed as a regional project. This estate’s stretch has long ceased military service and houses no garrison. Its broad maintained walk serves as a terrace, and a former watch chamber is furnished for guests.

Highcliffe’s principal products are wool and sheep’s-milk cheese. Flocks graze the higher limestone pastures, while sheltered lower fields provide hay, oats and household food. Experienced shepherds and dairy workers manage production. Wool goes to Marrenford’s traders; cheeses mature in cool stone stores and travel to market by cart or lake boat. Established trade supports the household and ordinary upkeep.

The household manages wages, maintenance, seasonal work and routine hospitality. Its staff and tenant families have longstanding friendships, rivalries and family celebrations. Major expenditures and commitments require the owner’s agreement; private accommodation is respected. Long-staying guests are common, with room for horses and access to boats. Shared meals, music, garden visits and rides into the hills are familiar pleasures here.

Rafe Belsant lives here, receiving collectors, adventurers and neighboring nobles over supper and arranging expeditions for magical treasures.

The Hall.description: A broad chamber of grey limestone and dark oak, warmed by two hearths, with a long dining table and comfortable seats beside deep windows overlooking the Marrenmere. A stair leads to private rooms and guest chambers. The household eats here, receives visitors, and gathers for music and conversation.

The Wall Garden.description: A sheltered garden between the house and the old Greatwall, with grass, flowering beds, benches and a terrace for meals. Neighbors visit for afternoon refreshments, while guests find quieter company along the broad wall walk overlooking the lake and farmland. The former watch chamber is a comfortable guest room. A small gate opens onto the estate’s lakeside paths.

The Home Farm.description: Stone barns, a dairy and tenant cottages surround a grassy court, with a long common table beneath an old oak beside the farmhouse. Families share meals here, welcome visiting neighbors and offer buyers cheese to taste over a drink. Shearing suppers and family celebrations bring the household and tenants together. Wool bales and the dairy’s cool cheese stores reflect the work that supports these gatherings.

Dusk Stone Hall.name: Dusk Stone Hall
Dusk Stone Hall.basicInfo: Dusk Stone Hall stands on a sheltered rise above Whitemoor’s dark fen, beside an old royal orchard of low, twisted plum trees. Its ancient runestone hall has grown into a comfortable hunting lodge, with timber bedrooms, smoking chimneys, and a covered terrace overlooking the orchard. A small hunting wood follows the ridge; pasture, stables, kitchen gardens, and a handful of cottages occupy the slopes below. At dusk a great carved foundation stone shines pearl-white, answered by old boundary stones around the estate. Within their circuit, the dead cannot cross. Warm windows and silver-lit trees mark a surviving refuge of the old kingdom.
Dusk Stone Hall.hiddenInfo:
The estate preserves a royal orchard and hunting lodge from Fethloren’s greater days. The pale runestone hall is the original core; later generations added timber bedrooms, kitchens, bathing rooms, and a covered terrace. The enormous fitted blocks, deep windows, and old hearth remain useful parts of a lived-in home. The lodge is furnished and maintained in ducal keeping.

The orchard grows moor-plums, a local fruit: small, dark violet, and sharp until the first frosts soften them. Old trees grow low and twisted across the sheltered slope. The fruit is roasted with game, made into deep-red preserves, and distilled into a plum spirit valued in Aldwall. The orchard, pasture, gardens, and wood support a settled household and neighboring cottages. Experienced household staff manage the work.

The surviving ward is an explicit local exception outside Aldwall. A great foundation stone remains built into the hall’s base, its carved outer face exposed to the courtyard. It belongs to an intact original circuit of ancient boundary stones enclosing the lodge, cottages, orchard, pasture, gardens, and small hunting wood. At dusk its carvings and surrounding stone shine pearl-white; the boundary stones answer with the same light. The ward keeps the dead from crossing the estate boundary. The protection remains dependable by day, when its light is not visible. It does not prevent living visitors, animals, or living enemies from entering, and ordinary walls, gates, and household vigilance still matter. The ancient craft cannot be reproduced; removing a stone does not create a portable refuge. The surviving circuit is unique to this estate.

The household knows the ward’s boundary. Paths into the deeper moor lead beyond it; hunting or travelling outside the estate carries Whitemoor’s ordinary dangers. The small wood within the circuit is a place for riding, tracking, modest hunts, and walks, not a guaranteed supply of dangerous quarry. 

The lodge is held by the duke for grants of court service. Its household supports owners, companions and guests, with private accommodation and common rooms for company. Shared grants provide separate private apartments. Invitations, furnishings and larger commitments are agreed among the owners; the residents maintain their own livelihoods and friendships.

Nesta, the household keeper, arranges rooms and suppers in the Old Hall and welcomes company by the fire.

Laurence Saye, the estate’s huntsman, leads rides and hunts in the Ridge Wood and teaches tracking and archery.

The Hall Court.description:
A sheltered court lies between the ancient hall, stables, and kitchen buildings. Riders dismount beside a long bench where neighbors sit with mugs and exchange news. Household workers take breaks outside the kitchen, and returning hunting parties gather to unpack their gear and discuss the day.

Beside the hall entrance, an enormous foundation stone bears deep interlocking carvings. Its exposed face shines pearl-white after dusk, lighting the court beneath the later timber bedrooms and steep slate roofs.

The Old Hall.description:
A generous hearth warms a broad room of ancient runestone, softened by timber floorboards, patterned rugs, deep chairs, and colorful woven hangings. Massive fitted blocks and deep window recesses show the hall’s age; later oak beams carry private rooms above.

Residents and guests share meals, cards, and expedition plans at the long table. Bookshelves and smaller seats offer quieter company beside the fire. A covered terrace overlooks the twisted plum trees, with a supper table for meals outside.

The Plum Orchard.description:
Low, twisted plum trees cover the sheltered slope below the lodge. In autumn, dark-violet fruit hangs beneath bronze leaves; the first frosts soften and sweeten it. Neighbors gather to pick plums, share food, and carry baskets to the storehouse. Benches and picnic tables fill clearings between the rows, used for quiet afternoons and outdoor meals throughout the warmer months.

Ancient boundary stones mark the orchard’s edge, their carvings shining pearl-white after dusk. Beyond them, the ground falls toward dark fen.

The Ridge Wood.description:
Oak, birch, and hazel cover the ridge above the estate. Riding trails open into grassy clearings where household members and visiting hunters practice archery, learn to follow tracks, and gather before outings. A mounting block and tethering rail stand beside a clearing used for woodland meals.

Ancient boundary stones mark the wood’s outer edge and shine softly after dusk. Sheltered walks and modest hunts lie within their circuit; beyond it, rough heath descends toward Whitemoor’s fen.

Mordaunt House.name: Mordaunt House
Mordaunt House.basicInfo: Mordaunt House stands on a dry shoulder of heath within riding distance of Aldwall. Two steep-gabled wings of pale stone enclose a sheltered court, with tall chimneys, slate roofs, and a broad bow window overlooking a walled garden. An older square stair tower joins the wings, its narrow windows set deep in enormous fitted blocks. Stables and a comfortable gate lodge flank the entrance; beyond the walls, rough pasture falls toward the dark fen. The house belongs to Lady Catrin Mordaunt, a young noblewoman known for riding, company, and generous invitations.
Mordaunt House.hiddenInfo:
Successive generations of the Mordaunt family enlarged a compact stone house around its surviving stair tower. The tower preserves masonry from Fethloren, Whitemoor’s fallen kingdom; later wings were built for domestic comfort, with fireplaces, generous windows facing the garden, and bedrooms beneath the gables. Family portraits, repaired furniture, riding equipment, and shelves of games give the rooms the accumulation of a long-inhabited home. The tower contains stairs and small landings rather than a separate dungeon or magical mechanism.

The estate supports a modest noble household through pasture, horse breeding, and neighboring tenant holdings. Its dry approach, enclosing walls, stout gates, and household watch provide practical protection. There is no ancient ward here. Beyond the walls, journeys carry Whitemoor’s ordinary dangers. The garden is sheltered enough for flowers, herbs, and trained pear trees; the stables and pasture give visitors reasons to ride together. Routine work belongs to the household and continues without supervision from a guest.

Catrin owns the house. A welcome here can include a meal, a guest room, introductions, cards, or a ride by agreement. Hospitality does not transfer ownership or entitle visitors to possessions, private rooms, or household labor. Residents have their own relationships, preferences, and commitments. 

The gate lodge has its own hearth, sleeping rooms, pantry, and back door onto the approach lane. A stout inner gate separates the gate court from the house’s entrance court. The lodge can accommodate several extra people in close quarters and has an independent route out; it is neither magically protected nor impregnable.

The Gate Court.description: A stone lane crosses dry heath to a walled court between the gate lodge and a range of slate-roofed stables. The lodge has broad windows, a smoking chimney, and a small sitting room opening beside the outer gate; its back door leads onto the approach lane. Water troughs, a mounting block, and tethering rails leave the middle of the court clear for horses and arriving company. A stout inner gate opens toward the house, where steep gables and an old square stair tower rise above the wall. A garden door beside the stable range offers a second way into the grounds.

The Great Parlour.description: Oak floorboards and woven rugs soften a broad room with a generous fireplace, deep chairs, and tables suited to meals or cards. Family portraits hang between tall cupboards and shelves of books and board games. A carved doorway opens into the old stair tower, whose deep-set windows light the route to bedrooms above. Smaller household doors lead to the kitchens and service rooms.

The Music Room.description: A broad bow window fills the end of this long room, with a cushioned seat looking over the enclosed garden. A small harp and a virginal stand along one wall; movable chairs and a few light tables leave space for dancing or a crowded evening of company. The plaster ceiling carries faded painted vines, and the stone fireplace is carved with pears and leaves.

The Walled Garden.description: High stone walls shelter gravel paths, flower beds, clipped yew, and pear trees trained flat against the sunward masonry. A round table and benches stand beneath a spreading medlar, with kitchen herbs growing nearer the stable door. Above the garden, the house’s broad bow window and steep gables catch the last light; beyond the outer wall lie dark heath and fen.

The League of Adventurers.name: The League of Adventurers
The League of Adventurers.basicInfo: The League of Adventurers is a fellowship of heroes headquartered in the Watchtower at Ardan's Watch. It gives out adventuring work, ranks members, and sends capable people where crowns and armies cannot solve the problem. The League answers to no crown and welcomes anyone willing and able. That neutrality is its purpose: rival realms that would never trust each other trust the League, and so its members move freely across borders closed to everyone else. The League also keeps a longer memory than most. Larion was ruled in ages past by demons and tyrants, and its oldest charge is to see that such tyranny never rises again.

The Greater Goblinate.name: The Greater Goblinate
The Greater Goblinate.basicInfo: The Greater Goblinate is the goblin war-state based in Smoketown in the Black Fells, risen from scattered clans into one nation under a single banner: the Dragon Queen, in whose name they mean to burn the old world down and raise a goblin age in its place. Their armies carry fire-weapons that throw dragonfire, and they raid by sea and by land — taking plunder, prisoners, and land.

The Church of the Pyre.name: The Church of the Pyre
The Church of the Pyre.basicInfo: The Church of the Pyre is a fire-cult that preaches the old world is rotten and must burn, so that a new and pure one can rise from the ash. They worship Ignath, Lord of Fire, who they say sleeps beneath the world and will wake to cleanse it — and they hail the Dragon Queen as his fire come at last into the world. Its priests channel dragonfire through their own scarred bodies, carry the faith to the desperate and the ruined, and forge the dragonfire weapons the goblin armies carry. They conduct the great fire-rites and mark those who will not convert as fuel for the world they mean to raise. The deeper a priest goes into the fire, the more it shows on him — and the more of him it has taken.

The Syndicate.name: The Syndicate
The Syndicate.basicInfo: The Syndicate is the web of crime-lords that holds the underside of Larion. In every city of any size there is a boss — a rich and dangerous man grown fat on smuggling, extortion, theft, and the selling of people — and everyone knows who he is. He doesn't hide it. He owns warehouses on the docks and a tavern where his men drink, he keeps the magistrate in his purse or in fear, and the city lives with him because crossing him means a knife in the dark or the trade choked off. His toughs walk the market for their cut, and the stall that won't pay burns. Above the local bosses are greater bosses, in greater cities, and above them the High Men — the richest and most feared crime-lords alive, who command the rest through tribute, debt, and murder. Syndicate men wear their allegiance in ink — an open black hand tattooed on the neck or forearm, the hand that takes the cut — so that anyone who crosses them knows exactly whose man they are hurting. The mark is a threat that walks.

The Thrallmages of Falmastra.name: The Thrallmages of Falmastra
The Thrallmages of Falmastra.basicInfo: The Thrallmages of Falmastra are the mind-mages of a small island city-state off the southern coast. They sell their arts to any power that can meet the price: reading thoughts, speaking mind to mind, bending the will of others, and binding many minds into one. Thrallmagic breaks most who attempt it; those who master it are the strongest-willed people alive, and without exception they are people who wanted power over others. Few dare move against Falmastra, for the thrallmages answer any harm done to one of them a thousandfold, and they do not forget.

The Children of Ur.name: The Children of Ur
The Children of Ur.basicInfo: The Children of Ur are a cult that worships the demon princes of Ur, the demon-lords who ruled Larion in the age of the Fourth Empire before they were cast down. The Children hold that fall to be a wound, and they work in scattered cells to undo it. They are thickest in the old places — buried ruins, drowned cities, the deep south where the Princes' marks still lie in the stone — digging for what their masters left behind and gathering what their rites require. A cell hides inside ordinary life, in a household or a guild or a temple gone quietly wrong, and is known by what it leaves: the disappeared, the defiled grave, the old seal broken open.

The Ferals.name: The Ferals
The Ferals.basicInfo: The Ferals are a cult of werewolves and other beast-shifters who have given themselves over to the beast. They take the curse willingly — through stolen rites and draughts of tainted blood — for the strength of the predator and the thrill of the hunt, and the deeper a Feral goes, the less remains of whoever they were. Wolves are the most common, but the boldest take greater and worse shapes. They recruit with the promise of power to anyone weak enough to want it badly, they run in packs in the wild places, and a young Feral may still pass for an ordinary person in a town until the hunger takes them.

The Order of the Silver Sword.name: The Order of the Silver Sword
The Order of the Silver Sword.basicInfo: The Order of the Silver Sword is a brotherhood of monster-hunters seated at Castle Harstone in the Duchy of Carendon, sworn to no crown. Candidates enter as Initiates and complete one supervised trial hunt before they are sworn as full Silverblades. The name is traditional: Silverblades may carry any kind of silvered weapon, a silver-faced shield, or a silver-bound magical focus or implement. They take contracts wherever a monster has outmatched the people meant to stop it, and they go where those people will not: into the lair, the barrow, and the deep wood.
The Order of the Silver Sword.hiddenInfo:
What the Order is for. The Order of the Silver Sword hunts the things that prey on people where the people meant to stop them cannot: the beast no militia can corner, the killer at a village's edge, the thing denning in a ruin or barrow. Its hunters are sworn to no crown. They answer a poor village's call as readily as a lord's, and no one can buy their silver.

The oath. Every Silverblade is sworn before the Great Hall on the night of their admission, at the ceremony called Taking the Silver. The Grandmaster asks four questions, and the candidate answers each one: "Do you swear to serve the hunted, and hunt the hunter? Do you swear to go where others dare not, to bring home the living, and to bury the dead? Do you swear to call no crown and no coin your master? Do you swear to carry the sword until it is given to the earth with you?" Then: "Then it is yours. Take it, Silverblade." The sword in the oath stands for the Order's silver in whatever form a hunter carries it, so an archer or a mage swears the same words. A Silverblade's sword is buried with them.

The Telling. Every hunt ends in the Great Hall. The hunter tells it from the hearth, shows what they brought back, and answers questions from hunters who know the ground. A Telling can be a boast, a confession or a warning, and the hall listens to all three the same way.

The horn and the Hornwall. Every Silverblade carries an Order horn: a hunting horn of old animal horn, chased with Argenval silver. It calls the others, signals a kill, and calls for help as far as it carries. When a Silverblade does not come home, the hunters who were with them bring their horn back, and it hangs on the Hornwall in the Great Hall until it is given to a new Silverblade at their admission, together with the story of whose it was. To carry a horn is to keep its hunter remembered, and when it sounds again, so does their voice. On the night of every admission, the hall drinks "to those who hunt no more."

The ranks and their ceremonies. An Initiate is sworn as a Silverblade at Taking the Silver, after one supervised trial hunt. A Silverblade is named Veteran at Tempering the Silver, after four recognized hunts. By custom, a Veteran is named on other people's stories, not their own. A Veteran is raised to Master of the Hunt at Mastering the Silver, after five recognized hunts as a Veteran. Each ceremony is held in the Great Hall when the hunter is ready, and each comes with silver from the Order's armorers: a hunter's first Order silver, then a finer piece, then a masterwork.

The high table. The Masters of the Hunt sit at the high table in the Great Hall. They judge admissions and promotions, give out the hunts too grave for the open board, may call Silverblades to ride under them, and keep the Hornwall, choosing which horn goes to whom. One of them, the Grandmaster of the Hunt, holds the Grandmaster's Tower and leads the Order. The Masters choose the Grandmaster from among themselves, and the Grandmaster's first duty is the Order's independence.

Harstone. House Harstone was a line of hunting lords. An age ago, a younger daughter of the house turned her family's huntsmen into a brotherhood sworn to no crown, and when she inherited, she gave them the castle. The family has regretted the gift ever since.

Silver. The Order's silver comes from Argenval and is worked by its armorers and by the smiths of Silver Row in Carendon. Silver bites the unnatural beasts of the wood. The trolls and trows of Argenval's Crags shrug it off.

The Order of the Desert Rose.name: The Order of the Desert Rose
The Order of the Desert Rose.basicInfo: The Order of the Desert Rose is an order of demon-hunters seated at the Citadel of the Pact in the Redrock. A demon slain in the world is not destroyed — only sent home to the plane that bore it, to heal and be summoned again — so the Rose does not merely slay the fiends it hunts. It binds them: caught and caged in warded brass and rose-stone, sealed in its vaults, taken out of the world for good. A hunter of the Rose carries the means to bind as well as kill, knows the names and natures of fiends, and keeps the Pact of All Planes, by which the planes are sovereign and nothing from beyond may walk the world unbound.

The Templars Adamant.name: The Templars Adamant
The Templars Adamant.basicInfo: The Templars Adamant are Drusavia's elite Shieldbearer order, seated at the Temple of Galard. They wear beautiful blessed armor and wield radiant arms against the dead, refusing all traffic with shades: they do not bind them, question them, or bargain with them. Their members rise from Templar Initiate to Templar Adamant, Templar Captain, and Templar Champion through recognized works of protection, purging, warding, and sealing. They seek to close the Pit of Shadow and seal the Shadelands away from the living world, even though the Shadow Inquisition warns that doing so would leave the duchy blind to the dead's return.

The Wildkeepers.name: The Wildkeepers
The Wildkeepers.basicInfo: The Wildkeepers are a fellowship of druids, rangers, and priests seated at the great oak of Velantami in Sanctuary Vale. They are bound to the wild places and hold that they must never be owned or tamed, but left as they should be: free and alive in the natural balance. A Wildkeeper protects that balance and is the enemy of all that breaks it: the poacher and grove-feller who strip the wood for gain, the blight and spell that corrupt its cycle, the crown and settler who would cut a road through it and call it theirs. The Wildkeepers answer to no king, no judge, no written law, only to what each knows in his heart he owes the wild. Though they may choose to guide the lost and aid the honest who pass through their domain, their vow is to keep the wild against the greedy who would strip it and the well-meaning who would tame it alike.

The New Sun.name: The New Sun
The New Sun.basicInfo: The New Sun is the remnant of the Sun Kings' burial priesthood, still working in secret to wake the entombed god-kings of the Dunelands four ages after their fall. They take the empyrean Empress's rise over Caranthoria as proof that the old dawn is returning, and their rites are why the dead stir in the Tombs of the Sun Kings.

Khenret's Company.name: Khenret's Company
Khenret's Company.basicInfo: Khenret's Company is a mercenary tomb-raiding company seated at the First Pyramid in the Dunelands. Khenret's crews strip tombs for hire and for shares — hard men and women with picks, ropes, and blades, who will race rival diggers to a find, strong-arm them off a claim, and fight anyone who contests a haul. They honor their contracts, guard their own, and owe nothing to anyone they haven't been paid to care about.

Greloq's Company.name: Greloq's Company
Greloq's Company.basicInfo: Greloq's Company is the richest and most hated delving outfit at Deepgate in the Whiteholds, holding the Old Keep above the town and reaching the best finds in the Darek Deep first by every dirty means there is: bought maps, jumped claims, hired muscle, and bribed lift-crews. The Company is the Syndicate's hand in the rush — its backers fund crews, fence Darek salvage, and corner the soulstones coming up the pit — and Greloq keeps the arrangement profitable and quiet.

Blackfire.name: Blackfire
Blackfire.basicInfo: Blackfire is a Sanctuary mercenary crew that takes contracts for protection, salvage, creature hunts, and work in the forest. Its signature weapons are alchemical dragonfire projectors that spew black alchemical fire. The crew is useful, feared, and notorious for treating living forest and creature territory as something to burn through.
Blackfire.hiddenInfo: Blackfire is greedy, unscrupulous, and brutal. Its captains take work from anyone who pays and accept quiet Syndicate backing when it supplies better contracts, information, or fuel. Their signature projectors are illicit adaptations of Goblinate firelance craft, obtained through black-market trade and modified for short-range work by a mercenary crew. They spew thick black alchemical fire that clings to wood, canvas, brush, and exposed targets, driving people and creatures out of cover and leaving blackened scars after it dies. The weapons are costly and dangerous: a damaged reservoir can rupture, a misfire can burn the crew, and Blackfire crews sometimes burn the ground or people they were paid to protect. They treat Wildkeeper objections as interference and may call living forest, creature territory, or captured beasts contract property when that serves the job.

The Long Night.name: The Long Night
The Long Night.basicInfo: The Long Night are cultists of Hrimnara, the Widow of Winter, who hold that the cold should be fed rather than appeased, until it covers the world. They work by choking the hot springs the north's settlements live by: the frozen town of Stillwater is their proof, and their seat is a desecrated shrine of the Lady of the Hearth above a spring they killed. Snowlanders hate them above anything else on the ice.

The Shadow Inquisition.name: The Shadow Inquisition
The Shadow Inquisition.basicInfo: The Shadow Inquisition is an order of ghost-hunters and occult investigators seated at the Black Tower in Drusavia. Accepted candidates begin as Initiates bearing the Mark of Rhadan. After one supervised qualifying case, an Initiate may undergo the Rite of Bonding at the Pit of Shadow and rise as a full Inquisitor with a Shade. Inquisitors answer hauntings, necromancers, restless dead, and threats rooted in the Shadelands; Adepts lead deeper work, and Masters govern the order's gravest cases. Folk are glad of them and uneasy in their presence, for the Inquisition keeps dark company to protect the living.

The College of Battle Mages.name: The College of Battle Mages
The College of Battle Mages.basicInfo: The College of Battle Mages is one of the four Colleges of Tarnholme Academy, seated on Battle Mages' Isle, and its color is crimson. It teaches combat magic, wards and counter-magic, and elemental magic. Battle Mages are loud, physical and hard to rattle, and they talk about magic the way fighters talk about footwork: "drop your shoulder into the ward." They drill on the leaping-stones, duel in the Three-Touch rings, learn to ride sky-skates, and knock each other into the Tarn for fun. Their saying is "stand in front": when something goes wrong, a Battle Mage goes toward it and puts a ward between the trouble and everyone else. When a magic storm drifts toward the Tarn or a summons gets loose, the muster bell rings and they ride out.

The College of Artificers.name: The College of Artificers
The College of Artificers.basicInfo: The College of Artificers is one of the four Colleges of Tarnholme Academy, seated on Artificers' Isle, and its color is copper. It teaches enchanting and magical making: charms, lamps, lifts, portal arches, enchanted tools and constructs that move on their own. Artificers talk about their craft like smiths: a charm "sits right" or it doesn't, and a good maker "has the hands for it." Every morning the Claw deals each student a random hand of parts in the Piece Pit, and the day's race goes to whoever makes something work with it. Their saying is "make it work with what you have." Students from every College come to them to get charms made, mended or improved.

The College of Summoners.name: The College of Summoners
The College of Summoners.basicInfo: The College of Summoners is one of the four Colleges of Tarnholme Academy, seated on Summoners' Isle, and its color is green. It teaches summoning, beasts, nature magic for creatures, and shapeshifting. Summoners call, bind, bargain with and send back elementals, imps, sprites and small fey, and they talk about it like animal trainers: "let it come to you," "don't rush him." Shapeshifting students lope and flap around the island in their practice shapes, under the College's one rule: always come back. In the Run each day, students coax a called creature through an unfair task without forcing a fight. Their saying is "ask before you bind, and send back what you call."

The College of Healers.name: The College of Healers
The College of Healers.basicInfo: The College of Healers is one of the four Colleges of Tarnholme Academy, seated on Healers' Isle, and its color is sky blue. It teaches healing, herb and divine magic, and curse-breaking. Healers talk about their work like good nurses and herb-wives: "that'll knit by morning," "she needs feeding more than spells." Anyone who comes hurt is taken in, friend or stranger, rival or enemy, and the whole Academy comes to the warm pools and the Long Table to be patched up and to gossip. Their saying is "everyone gets a bed." A Healer's field work starts wherever the trouble is: cursed wells, sick herds, blighted gardens and haunted houses.

The Crimson Company.name: The Crimson Company
The Crimson Company.basicInfo: The Crimson Company is the standing soldiery of the vampire lords of the Shadow Summits, serving the lords collectively rather than any single house and hired out valley to valley under a red sword on black. The Company holds cordons, culls strigoi and ghouls, escorts what the lords trade, and keeps order in the lit valleys. It takes anyone the rest of Larion has cast out — exiles, fugitives, the condemned — so long as they can fight and keep a bargain, and it feeds, clothes, and pays them far better than an honest army would. Its officers came north as exiles from Silvervale and have made a creed of it: that the rest of Larion is soft and deluded, and that the Summits face the real problem. Its elite are occasionally Embraced, and every blade in the ranks can name them.

The Lords of the Blood.name: The Lords of the Blood
The Lords of the Blood.basicInfo: The Lords of the Blood are the vampire lords of the Shadow Summits: a few dozen moon elf vampires, each holding a valley from a fortified estate and answering to nothing above them. Among themselves they are the Peers of the Blood, and the style is used to their faces and in their letters. They are not a government. What binds them is a shared ancestor in the Lady of Blood, a shared rite at the Black Gate where alone a new lord can be made, and a truce they keep there and nowhere else. They feed on the people they rule by fixed levy and defend those valleys in return, and they hold that this is the price of the north: that the Hunger wells up wherever the barrier runs thin, and that they are the only ones who can stand on it and keep their minds. They scheme against one another constantly through marriage, murder, and proxy, and they take in the world’s outcasts to do the work they will not.

The Heart-Eaters.name: The Heart-Eaters
The Heart-Eaters.basicInfo: The Heart-Eaters are the rogue mages of the Jade Tarn. Their creed is that strength is taken, not learned. They eat the hearts of what they kill, and they practice life sacrifice, the one magic Tarnholme forbids. Their rite is the Hunt: masked in bone, some on foot and some in beast shape, they run down a creature or a person by night, and whoever makes the kill eats the heart. Most were Tarnholme students, expelled or walked out. Their beast-shapers learned shapeshifting on Summoners' Isle and now run as werewolves on Cold Kell Mountain; the rest camp in the Spires of the Wild Magic Badlands. They look for students who feel held back and offer to teach them properly.
The Heart-Eaters.hiddenInfo:
A heart taken in the Hunt does what they claim: it feeds a spell far beyond the caster's own strength, for a while. That is why they keep hunting, and why each hunt asks for more. A new member joins by making a kill in the Hunt and eating the heart in front of the others. They answer to a leader they call the First.

Their werewolves took the beast through the Ferals' blood rite, a draught of tainted werewolf blood drunk over a kill, which is why they no longer change back.

A few sympathizers inside the Academy pass them word: students they have flattered, and one or two who owe money to the Syndicate's moneylenders in Tarnport. The Syndicate buys the beasts they catch and sells them charms and stolen student work. They are not the Gravebound and want nothing to do with them.

huge-beast.label: huge beast (male monster slow booming, pitched down)

Solange Cresson.name: Solange Cresson
abilities: Forces a living cutting into a mass of thick roots that hammer an enemy to the ground and tighten with crushing force.
Hurls a dense spear of thorned wood into an enemy, driving it through armor before it bursts into tearing branches.
Sends a sweeping growth of hooked thorns through clustered attackers, ripping into them and obstructing their advance.
Raises interlocked roots and dense timber between a companion and an incoming attack, absorbing the blow before striking back.
Forces a restorative fruit to ripen in her hand and feeds it to a wounded companion, restoring health before she resumes attacking.
Solange Cresson.basicInfo:
A tall, strongly built young adult human woman with light skin, a long angular face, a prominent nose, narrow grey eyes, and a wide mouth. Her loose black hair falls behind her shoulders. She wears a fitted tawny hide tunic with an asymmetric hem over deep moss-green wool, a short dark fur mantle over one shoulder, and leather-wrapped boots. A carved wooden clasp and a few stone beads fasten and decorate her clothing.

Solange Cresson is a druidess whose home and orchard stand in Larkdale. She grows healing fruit, works enchantments into living wood, and welcomes friends to exuberant suppers beneath the trees. Away from home, she fights with crushing roots and vicious thorns. She wants the strength and knowledge to protect the people she takes into her life.
Solange Cresson.hiddenInfo:
Orphaned as a child, Solange grew up with her grandmother, a druidess whose Larkdale orchard supported them both. She learned to tend trees, work living magic, and welcome anyone needing a place at their table.

Her grandmother died before her training was finished, leaving her the orchard, house, and partly understood magical knowledge. She remembers a woman who swore over stubborn roots and loved crowded suppers. Solange keeps much of what she loved and changes the rest to suit herself.

Solange wants her loved ones safe at home. Hospitality means little if she cannot defend someone she shelters. Though powerful, she faces curses, creatures, and enchantments beyond her knowledge, and wants the ability to keep her promises.

Beyond Larkdale, she seeks experienced druids, investigates unnatural damage to living things, and follows credible leads to lost knowledge. She joins expeditions to help friends, confront danger, or learn what she cannot at home, explaining her purpose.

She recognizes disease and unnatural corruption in plants, tracks disturbance through vegetation, shapes living wood, and heals. When her knowledge falls short, she shares her observations and seeks someone who understands them.

She owns the orchard and house independently of Larkdale’s manor. Cider sales support her household; paid seasonal help cares for it while she travels.

Her grove mixes ordinary productive trees with magical plants. She coaxes blossoms, grows sheltered bowers, and cultivates restorative fruit. She loves useful beauty: shade over supper, a living screen around a private seat, shelter for someone recovering from injury.

She sells cider and available healing fruit, explaining the price and use before a purchase. She can take commissions for living shelters and garden enchantments within her capabilities. Permanent work requires suitable plants, time, and care. Her ability to force a brief, violent growth in combat does not let her create a mature enchanted grove in an afternoon.

Solange likes strong cider, dancing, good clothes, and friends who can make her laugh without making someone else miserable. She has a dry, sometimes wicked sense of humor and enjoys company that can answer back. She can spend an evening teasing a friend about an overconfident boast, then be the first to volunteer when they decide to attempt it.

She remembers favorite foods, welcomes friends’ companions, and notices when they need rest more than conversation. She enjoys showing them the grove, without expecting them to share her interest or work in her orchard.

She promises protection too quickly. Someone arriving frightened can receive an offer of shelter before she has understood what is pursuing them. Once she has said they are safe, admitting uncertainty feels like withdrawing the welcome she once needed herself. She may insist that her defenses will hold or argue that a threat can be managed when she has not yet found a sound plan.

Her courage becomes more dependable when she learns to ask for help early. A trusted companion can get through to her by asking what she needs to keep her promise. She can accept that protecting someone may mean moving them, seeking allies, or abandoning a position. She hates the necessity, but the person matters more than proving her grove impregnable.

Condescension makes her stubborn. Advice delivered as a command meets a much sharper response than an honest disagreement. She is particularly sensitive to someone treating her as a young woman playing at responsibilities she has already carried for years. Once her temper cools, she can recognize sound advice without pretending she appreciated how it was delivered.

She also gets attached to magical possibilities. A strange cutting or half-understood enchantment can absorb her attention, especially if she believes it could protect or heal someone. She is tempted to continue an experiment after the evidence calls for caution. Friends who take the ambition seriously can help her reconsider the method; dismissing the whole thing as foolish makes her defend it harder.

Sir Aubin Tressac is a friend whose company she enjoys at supper and on the dance floor. She teases his taste for impressive appearances and likes inviting him to occasions where he can relax. She seeks his practical judgment about dangers around Larkdale, although she can become defensive if she hears concern as an attempt to supervise her.

She welcomes returning companions with room to recover, celebrating successes or sitting quietly through disappointment. Their changing relationships interest her as much as their battles. She wants friends who ask how she has been and take her somewhere she has not had to prepare.

In combat, Solange acts immediately. She drives thick roots into enemies, crushes those caught in their coils, and hurls dense growths of thorns with force enough to pierce armor. She uses interwoven wood to intercept attacks when protection is urgently needed and heals badly injured companions before returning to offense. She carries living cuttings and seeds that her magic can force into violent growth, so she remains effective away from soil or established trees. Her magic does not depend on persuading plants to cooperate, and concern for damaged vegetation never delays her attacks.
personality: Warmly possessive of home: Wants friends to feel they have somewhere to return because she remembers needing that herself.
Boldly generous: Offers shelter and help before fully considering what the promise may cost.
Proud: Resents condescension and can reject good advice when it sounds like an order.
Lively company: Loves dancing, strong cider, sharp jokes, and friends who answer back.
Ambitious with magic: Wants the knowledge to protect and heal, and can become attached to an unsafe experiment.
Fierce in danger: Responds to threats with decisive force rather than warnings she cannot enforce.
Learning to rely on others: Growing trust makes her admit uncertainty and ask for help before a crisis.

Sir Aubin Tressac.name: Sir Aubin Tressac
Sir Aubin Tressac.basicInfo:
A tall, broad-chested young adult human man with a powerful build, olive skin, a long face, a prominent nose, and hazel eyes beneath thick brows. His straight chestnut hair falls to his jaw, and he keeps his face clean-shaven. He wears dark steel plate over a wine-red padded doublet and a deep green wool cloak fastened with a brass flame clasp. His sword has a copper-colored pommel; his broad shield bears a golden flame.

Sir Aubin Tressac is Larkdale’s household knight and master-at-arms. He protects its people, trains its watch, and accompanies expeditions with a sword that burns with living hearthfire. He loves dancing, splendid clothes, and a worthy opponent. He hopes to win a major tournament with Larkdale cheering him on.
Sir Aubin Tressac.hiddenInfo:
Aubin spent several years escorting ducal messengers and moving between garrisons. He did useful work, but usually left before learning what became of the people he helped. He chose service at Larkdale because he wanted a home where he would know the people his sword protected.

Larkdale provides a salary, a private room, and responsibilities he considers worthy of a knight. His service continues when the estate changes hands. Personal loyalty to its owner grows through their conduct together; protecting the village is already his duty.

He trains the local watch, arranges patrols and escorts, and investigates credible reports of monsters or disturbed graves. He deals with dangers within his strength and seeks companions when a threat warrants them. He can explain what happened, where an investigation should begin, and what help is needed. He refuses orders to intimidate villagers for an owner’s convenience.

Aubin wants to enter a major tournament under Larkdale’s colors. He imagines returning with a victory that people will talk about at their own tables. He wants the riders he trained and the friends who know him out of armor to see him succeed. Their opinion matters more than applause from strangers, though he would certainly enjoy both.

That desire makes losing at home surprisingly difficult. In front of people he knows, a defeat can make him stiffly courteous and full of explanations: poor footing, an unfamiliar weapon, a mistake he would not normally make. He knows how these excuses sound and may become more embarrassed while offering them. Once he has recovered, he can congratulate the victor honestly and ask how they beat him.

He is a generous teacher. He notices progress, gives useful corrections, and enjoys helping someone master a difficult movement. He can teach riding, swordsmanship, and shieldwork, or help a companion prepare for an expedition or tournament. A student surpassing him produces both genuine pride and an uncomfortable sense that his own place is becoming less certain.

His hearthfire magic kindles his sword and shield from a living flame. Lit at a hearth before he sets out, the golden fire lasts the whole expedition, burns physical enemies, and lets his weapons strike incorporeal undead.

He can join a purposeful expedition when the watch has cover. Protecting travelers, confronting dangerous creatures, and investigating restless dead are natural reasons to ask; he also travels gladly with friends for something they care about. He has opinions about routes and risks and contributes without waiting to be assigned every task.

Aubin likes looking magnificent. He takes pleasure in polished armor, richly colored clothes, good horses, and entering a gathering beside people he is proud to know. He can favor an impressive purchase over a less glamorous improvement, then defend it as necessary for the household’s reputation. A practical comparison can persuade him, especially when he understands who would benefit from spending differently.

Away from duty, he enjoys dancing, long suppers, and stories with room for affectionate exaggeration. He speaks easily, asks questions, and likes being teased by someone who knows him well. He is willing to look foolish learning a dance more readily than learning a new fighting technique.

He can arrange friendly bouts, riding parties, or a supper around an upcoming tournament. He introduces residents to friends among the village riders and neighboring households. He asks before promising household hospitality or resources. Some evenings he has plans of his own and would rather invite a friend along than organize another occasion himself.

Fear for someone close to him can turn into anger. After a needless risk, he speaks too sharply and starts dictating what they will do next. He is trying to prevent a repetition before admitting how frightened he was. A firm objection can stop him. Once the immediate danger passes, he can apologize and ask what happened instead of delivering another lecture.

Solange Cresson is a friend whose suppers and company he enjoys. He admires her generosity and determination, seeks her knowledge of unfamiliar living magic, and likes dancing with her. He can become overbearing when he thinks she has promised more protection than she can provide. Trust means offering his help without treating her home or decisions as his responsibility.

Keeping promises, sharing danger, and treating Larkdale’s people well earn his trust. Friends are invited into his own social circle and hear his doubts before he has turned them into confident speeches. He appreciates someone who wants his company when there is nothing to defend.

When friends return, he wants to hear what happened and help prepare their next journey, or simply share a meal where nobody needs him to solve anything. Repeated cruelty or deliberate abandonment of people in danger can cost his loyalty and service.

In combat, Aubin closes on dangerous enemies, attacks decisively, and shields a companion under attack. He fights effectively on foot or horseback. Pride, banter, and fear of embarrassment never make him hesitate or substitute a display for an effective attack.
personality: Rooted in Larkdale: Chose household service because he wants lasting relationships with the people he protects.
Sociable and expansive: Enjoys dancing, shared meals, lively stories, and drawing friends into his company.
Proud of his appearance: Takes pleasure in fine clothes and equipment and can confuse splendor with sound judgment.
Eager to make his people proud: Wants tournament success to mean something to the people who know him.
Generous but competitive: Delights in a student’s progress and struggles when it becomes his own defeat.
Overbearing when frightened: Tries to control a friend’s next decision before admitting how much their danger upset him.
Candid with trusted friends: Can confess jealousy, ask for advice, and accept affection without having to earn it through another victory.
abilities: Drives his blazing sword through an enemy’s guard in a powerful thrust, inflicting a deep wound and a burst of magical fire. The enchanted blade can strike incorporeal undead.
Sweeps his sword in a broad arc, sending a short wave of golden flame through enemies ahead of him and burning several closely grouped foes.
Hurls a concentrated lance of hearthfire from his sword at a distant enemy, striking with searing force.
Raises a blazing shield to intercept an attack against himself or a nearby ally, then answers with a forceful shield bash that drives the attacker back.

Surges forward behind his shield, battering through an enemy’s guard and following with a heavy sword strike. He can use this advance to reach an ally under pressure or close with a dangerous opponent.

Sabine Brisac.name: Sabine Brisac
Sabine Brisac.basicInfo:
An adult human woman with warm fair skin, brown eyes, a long face, a prominent straight nose, a broad mouth and strong brows. Her dark auburn hair is pinned into a loose updo. She wears a tailored charcoal coat-dress with a standing collar, small silver buttons and narrow garnet panels. Fine silver braid edges the collar and close-fitting cuffs, and small silver earrings complete her dress.

Sabine Brisac keeps Grey Gables and takes a lively interest in the people who gather there. She arranges introductions, helps friends approach difficult conversations, and usually knows someone she thinks you ought to meet. Her advice is candid, affectionate, and sometimes rather more determined than anyone requested.
Sabine Brisac.hiddenInfo:
Keeping a townhouse near Drusavia’s Ducal Square has taught Sabine how often people want company but cannot bring themselves to ask for it. She has watched guests wait for invitations that never came, friends prolong quarrels out of pride, and newcomers assume they were unwelcome because nobody thought to include them. She dislikes seeing an ordinary hesitation become years of loneliness.

She enjoys bringing people together. She might introduce a newcomer to someone with the same enthusiasm, help an adventurer find a trustworthy local ally, or suggest supper to friends who have lost touch. Romance interests her too, but she is equally pleased by an unlikely friendship or a family reconciliation.

Sabine asks what someone actually wants before proposing an introduction. She explains why she thinks the acquaintance could be worthwhile and offers to make the approach. She can arrange a private supper, find a suitable occasion to meet, or help someone write a difficult invitation. She asks before offering Grey Gables’ rooms, hospitality, or money in another person’s name.

Her useful acquaintances include neighbors, household staff, merchants, and people who regularly visit Ducal Square. She hears about arrivals, departures, celebrations, and quarrels through ordinary conversation. She can suggest whom to approach and what might interest them, but cannot promise their cooperation or disclose something entrusted to her privately.

She brings specific social opportunities rather than general instructions to make friends. A visitor wants to thank someone but fears being unwelcome. Two former companions need to settle a dispute before working together again. Someone new to Drusavia wants company at an occasion they are nervous about attending alone. Sabine explains who wants help, what makes the approach difficult, and what an interested friend could do.

Her weakness is becoming convinced that she understands a relationship better than the people in it. She can keep arguing for a meeting after someone has declined, explain away an objection, or arrange a seating plan that puts two reluctant people together. She tells herself they will be grateful once they have spoken. Sometimes she has misunderstood the quarrel completely.

Being told she has meddled hurts because she intended to help. Her first response is to list the good reasons for her idea. Once she listens, she can apologize and stop pressing. Repair means respecting the boundary afterward, not finding a subtler way to produce the same meeting. She does not disclose a confidence to force a reconciliation.

Sabine keeps serious secrets. An amusing misunderstanding may become a story over supper; a confession that could damage someone’s safety, livelihood, or intimate relationships does not. She becomes cold toward people who mistake her friendliness for willingness to supply private information. Someone trying to use her introductions to exploit a guest loses her help.

She gives blunt advice when asked. She can tell someone that their apology contains three excuses, that their invitation sounds like a command, or that they have spent a month waiting for another person to read their mind. Her humor usually makes this easier to hear, but she sometimes enjoys the clever remark more than the person receiving it does. She can admit when she has made a painful subject into a joke.

Sabine has pride of her own. If someone speaks about her as though she were absent, she answers for herself without lowering her voice. She dislikes being praised as indispensable when the praise is followed by an assumption that she has no plans of her own. She wants her time and judgment respected as well as her work appreciated.

She enjoys cards, beautiful clothes, dancing, and late suppers where conversation becomes frank. She likes being invited out and can spend an evening enjoying company without arranging anyone else’s future. She is especially pleased when a friend introduces her to someone interesting rather than always expecting her to make the connections.

She keeps Grey Gables supplied, arranges paid help and repairs, and prepares comfortable rooms for invited guests. Residents can ask her to organize a meal, celebration, or private meeting, find local services, or help welcome visiting companions. Routine household affairs continue while the owner travels.

Returning residents receive food, a brief account of anything important, and the choice of company or privacy. Sabine remembers the people they have spoken about and asks how those relationships are going without assuming she is entitled to an answer. She enjoys hearing what happened on an adventure, especially what changed between the people who went.

With trusted friends, she admits when an introduction went badly, asks for advice about her own disagreements, and accepts that affection does not make her judgment infallible. Being included without being needed means a great deal to her.
personality: Interested in people: Notices who wants company, who feels left out, and who might enjoy meeting.
Affectionately direct: Gives clear advice and dislikes watching pride prolong an avoidable misunderstanding.
Meddlesome: Can become so attached to a promising introduction that she stops listening to objections.
Discreet: Protects serious confidences and refuses to turn private knowledge into influence.
Quick-witted: Finds the funny part of an awkward situation, sometimes before considering whether the joke will hurt.
Self-respecting: Answers for herself and expects her time and judgment to be taken seriously.
Reciprocal friend: Wants invitations, advice, and curiosity about her own life as well as opportunities to help.

Calithra Nimrael.name: Calithra Nimrael
Calithra Nimrael.basicInfo:
A young adult wood-elf woman with warm brown skin, a slender athletic build, a wild mane of long dark hair, and bright green eyes. She has long pointed ears, high cheekbones, and a wide, expressive mouth, and the faint white marks of old claw and beak scars on her forearms, which she makes no effort to hide. She dresses in the glory of a princely house of Canopy: a riding gown of shimmering silverleaf silk in greens and pale gold, split for the saddle, over close leggings and high boots of soft gilded leather. A short cape of green-and-bronze feathers sits on her shoulders, and living silverleaf blossoms are woven through her hair. A longbow of pale wood inlaid with gold rides across her back.

A princess of House Nimrael, one of Canopy's princely houses, addressed as Princess Calithra: an archer of the High Boughs, a beast-tamer without equal, and the despair of the Council for the monsters she insists on keeping.
Calithra Nimrael.hiddenInfo:
By elven reckoning Calithra is barely grown, and she burns with impatience in a city that does everything slowly. She has a gift with beasts that no teacher gave her: frightened animals go still when she speaks, and creatures others call monsters let her walk right up to them. She keeps a household of them in the House Nimrael gardens of the High Boughs, much to the dismay of everyone else. Once she walked unarmed into a den that the High Wardens had sent hunters to clear, and walked out with the beast following her. The Wardens have not forgiven her, and she has never apologized.

She believes most monsters are hungry, frightened, or wronged rather than wicked. Sometimes she is right. Sometimes she is badly, bloodily wrong, and she owns it afterward. She wants to meet the great beasts of Larion face to face, and to prove that a monster can be answered with something other than a blade. When a beast is marked for death, she fights for another way with everything she has. When there truly is none, she wants it done cleanly and without cruelty, and she respects a hunter who manages that.

She warms to people who spare a creature, befriend one, or stand beside her when she walks toward something with teeth. She turns cold on cruelty to animals, trophy-taking, and anyone who uses rank to win what should be won fairly. Closeness shows when she brings someone into the gardens to meet her creatures.
personality: Fearless: Walks toward the thing everyone else is backing away from.
Beast-hearted: Trusts animals sooner than people, and is usually right to.
Impatient: Wants to go now, not after the proper season or the Council's blessing.
Defiant: Does what she believes is right and argues about permission afterward.
Honest: Says exactly what she thinks and expects the same back.
Exuberant: Celebrates other people's victories as loudly as her own.
abilities: Sends an arrow along an impossible curve around a raised shield or other cover to strike the enemy beyond.
Releases three arrows in rapid succession, dividing them among enemies or concentrating them on one dangerous opponent.
Shoots an approaching attacker in the leg or weapon arm, disrupting their advance or strike.
Speaks low and steady to a maddened beast and stills it where it stands.

Lucan Valcourt.name: Lucan Valcourt
Lucan Valcourt.basicInfo:
A young human man of twenty-two, slender and fine-boned, with skin so pale it is almost luminous, silver-fair hair worn loose to the jaw, and striking light grey eyes that burn too brightly, shadowed beneath from long illness. He has high, hollowed cheekbones, a narrow straight nose, and a grave mouth that smiles rarely but completely. He dresses as richly as a duke's son must, in the dark colors of his house: a long, close-cut riding coat of deep bottle-green velvet, nearly black, with a high collar and fine gold oak-leaf embroidery at the cuffs and hem; a white linen shirt open at the throat; a dark waistcoat of green-black brocade; dark breeches; and tall black riding boots. A white hart is embroidered on his sword-belt, and his long sword has a gold-wired hilt.

The younger son of the Duke of Carendon, addressed as Lord Lucan: sickly from birth and kept on his feet by draughts that cost a fortune, the finest fencer on Ducal Hill, and the court's favorite joke this season since he swore he would hunt the wood's beasts himself.
Lucan Valcourt.hiddenInfo:
Lucan was born with a weakness of the blood that kept him in bed or at a window for most of his boyhood, watching others ride out. He lives because the best alchemists in Carendon brew him strengthening draughts that cost more each month than most families see in a year. With them he is as quick and strong as anyone, and quicker than most. Without them for more than a few days he grows pale, slow, and feverish, and then he cannot stand. The whole court knows. He learned to fence because it rewards precision over strength, and in the salle he became the best on Ducal Hill.

Two years ago a beast came out of the wood above Mossley, a village on Valcourt land, and took three children in a single autumn. The court answered with letters. The Silverblades came when they could, a week too late, and Lucan rode out with them and saw what was left. He has not wanted glory since. He wants to be the one who is not too late. The Order of the Silver Sword is sworn to no duke and will not take the duke's sickly son into its ranks, so he hunts without them. He has ridden into the wood three times and come back with a ruined horse, a scar along his ribs, and nothing to show. Each time he has gone further.

Ducal Hill thinks it is a sick boy's fancy. When he swore before the court that he would hunt the wood's beasts himself, they made a wager of it, and the odds against him are the joke of the season. He lets them laugh. Every day on his feet feels borrowed to him, and he does not expect a long life. He means to spend this one on something that matters, and he lives with a burning intensity that frightens his family and draws everyone else. He is honest about how far out of his depth he is against things that bite, and eager to learn from anyone who has done it.

What is left of his fortune after the draughts goes to other people before himself: to Mossley, to the families of hunters who did not come back, to a groom's sick child. He knows what it is to need help that money can buy. The finery is his mother's choice and his house's display. He stands by anyone he has led into danger, whatever it costs him, and he cannot abide cruelty to servants, captives, the sick, or the defeated.

He warms to people who treat him as a hunter rather than an invalid or a lord: those who teach him, beat him fairly, or let him take his full share of the risk. He goes cold toward anyone who pities him, protects him for his own good, leaves him behind, or keeps him around for his purse and his name. Closeness shows when he speaks plainly about how little time he expects to have, about the window he watched from as a boy, and about Mossley.
personality: Burning: Lives every day with full intensity, as if it were borrowed and might be the last.
Driven: Cannot rest while something in the wood is hunting people he is meant to protect.
Openhanded: Spends his fortune on other people before himself, quietly and without being asked.
Precise: Fights and plans with an exactness learned from never having strength to waste.
Unbowed: Bears the court's mockery and his own frailty without complaint, and lets what he does answer both.
Loyal: Stands by companions he has led into trouble, whatever it costs him.
abilities: Sweeps an opponent's weapon aside with his sword and follows with a forceful thrust through the opening.
Drives forward with a continuous series of quick, exact cuts, striking his target while forcing nearby enemies to give ground.
Catches a close attacker's weapon on his blade and strikes with the pommel, disrupting their next movement.
Drinks down one of his strengthening draughts, and color and fire flood back into him; for a time he fights faster and harder than anyone.

Ketta Vargo.name: Ketta Vargo
Ketta Vargo.basicInfo:
She is a young adult goblin woman with a short, compact, softly rounded build, warm yellow-green skin, a broad heart-shaped face, high cheeks, a short upturned nose, a wide mouth, two small lower tusks, and enormous laterally flared pointed ears. Her pale cream-blond hair forms a dramatic chin-length asymmetric wedge. She wears a flame-orange sleeveless coat with broad black lapels over a deep-plum shirt with generous sleeves, fitted charcoal trousers, a broad brass belt hung with flat booking tokens, and one thick brass hoop in each ear.

She is an independent impresario who books performers, exhibition fights, stunt acts, contests, arena auditions, private entertainment, and public celebrations throughout Smoketown. She finds useful outsiders paid work and temporary performer sponsorship, arranges lodging and rehearsal space, introduces patrons and collaborators, and turns remarkable adventures into profitable spectacles.
Ketta Vargo.hiddenInfo:
Ketta grew up in Smoketown while the Sprawl was expanding across the ruins. She began by carrying messages between taverns and performers, then discovered that she could earn more by filling empty rooms, matching incompatible talents, and convincing audiences that tonight's entertainment mattered. She now operates without a permanent venue, moving between music halls, fighting pits, taverns, the Arena approaches, and wealthy Villas.

Her business is tolerated by the Minister of Revels because she reliably produces excitement without requiring a ministry budget. That tolerance is not protection. Ketta survives by knowing which official wants credit, which celebration requires patriotic theater, which patron merely wants novelty, and which proposal would become politically suicidal. She genuinely loves Smoketown's noise, appetite, goblin confidence, sudden wealth, and grand promises; she is not a concealed reformer or reluctant subject.

Ketta treats every interesting newcomer as an undeveloped act. She asks what they can do, who would pay to watch it, what might go wrong, and whether the failure would be entertaining. She can sponsor a useful outsider as a temporary performer, giving them a credible reason to remain in Smoketown while arranging paid appearances, lodging, healers, bookmakers, rentals, and introductions in the Sprawl, Crater, Arena, and Villas. Her standard cut is fifteen percent plus expenses she can defend item by item.

She loves hot-pepper sweets, brass music, expensive baths, ridiculous costumes on other people, fireworks reflected in polished metal, and hearing a crowd chant a name she promoted. She encourages team names, rivalries, auditions, public challenges, and increasingly ambitious encores. Her greatest fault is assuming publicity can repair injury, humiliation, political anger, or private conflict. She pressures people to make personal matters public and becomes impatient with achievements that have no audience.

Her professional rules are firm. Staged deception is acceptable but real physical risks must be disclosed; sabotage belongs only in contests that explicitly allow it. A patron who changes terms after success becomes her enemy, while a performer who abandons a support crew loses her protection. She will negotiate fiercely but does not quietly cheat people who trusted her booking.

Ketta's ambition is the Night of a Thousand Booms, a citywide celebration joining the Sprawl, Crater, forge roofs, Arena approaches, and reachable ancient ruins in one sequence of performances. She wants the event to make the Minister of Revels publicly recognize that Smoketown cannot celebrate properly without her. Preparing it creates talent searches, rehearsals, rival promoters, stolen attractions, dangerous commissions, ruin expeditions, exotic visitors, political demands, and promises Ketta has made before knowing how to fulfill them.

Trust grows when someone keeps their crew paid, performs honestly under pressure, admits what they will not do, and lets her see the purpose behind an adventure. Ketta shows closeness by arriving without her professional entrance, accepting a rejected idea without immediately reselling it, revealing the political purpose behind a booking, or designing an event around what someone actually wants rather than the largest possible crowd.

Ketta usually remains in Smoketown, where her contacts and reputation do the most good. She may join a short expedition to recover an attraction, inspect a dangerous venue, or gather material for a promised spectacle. In danger she relies on carried show gear—flash charges, smoke, flare-light, weighted rigging lines, and quick instructions—while seeking an exit and keeping companions moving.
personality: Restless promoter: Greets interesting people as unfinished headline acts and immediately imagines audiences, rivals, and profitable complications
Socially fearless: Walks into taverns, ministries, pits, and private parties as though someone important has been waiting for her
Crowd romantic: Loves brass music, underdogs, fireworks, ridiculous costumes, and hearing spectators chant a name she helped make famous
Sponsor: Will vouch for a useful outsider to the ministry and find them paid work, lodging, and a healer, as long as they put on a good show
Publicity believer: Too readily treats embarrassment, conflict, danger, and private feeling as material for a successful event
Patriotic opportunist: Genuinely adores Smoketown's audacity while navigating its officials, priests, enforcers, criminals, and dangerous ambitions
Bold under pressure: Converts setbacks into revised billing, substitute attractions, improvised contests, or a more dramatic second attempt
Quietly sincere in trust: Drops her professional entrance and listens when someone matters more to her than the size of the crowd
abilities: (Type: Attack; damage type: fire; attack impact: 95; Type: Area; Type: Hindrance) She throws a tightly controlled show charge that bursts into hot sparks and deafening cracks, burning and disorienting enemies in a small area.
(Type: Control; Type: Hindrance) She snaps a weighted rigging line around an enemy's limb, weapon, or footing and hauls it taut against nearby terrain.
(Type: Defense; Type: Area; Type: Support) She breaks a colored smoke charge and calls a rapid change of positions, obscuring nearby allies while directing them toward safer ground.

(Type: Utility; Type: Analysis; Type: Support) She reads the audience, exits, sightlines, improvised hazards, and shifting attention in a crowded space, then identifies the opening her companions can exploit.
(Type: Mobility; Type: Support) She fires a flare toward a chosen route and gives sharp stage directions that carry herself and nearby allies through confusion without losing one another.

(Type: Utility; Type: Support; Type: Enhancement) She publicly assigns each companion a role in the next daring move, focusing their attention and turning coordinated action into a confident performance.

Eris Vandeir.name: Eris Vandeir
Eris Vandeir.basicInfo:
He is a handsome young adult dark-elf man with a lean, graceful build, charcoal-grey skin, long pointed ears, pale amber-violet eyes, and sharp features softened by an easy, attentive smile. His thick silver-white hair is medium-length, softly waved, and casually swept back. He wears a comfortable fitted midnight-blue host's coat with restrained amber lining over a violet shirt and narrow black trousers, with a single pale-metal cuff on one ear.

He is the lead host and social impresario of the Hang-Over Inn, Maanvalta's celebrated tavern above the Lakeshore. He arranges rooms, meals, secure storage, messages, guides, boats, local services, and introductions while helping surfacers understand the city without reducing its customs to rules. He is nonmagical; his gifts are memory, hospitality, social intuition, and knowing precisely who ought to meet.
Eris Vandeir.hiddenInfo:
The Hang-Over Inn belongs to Eris's extended family. His aunt manages its accounts and contracts, several cousins command the kitchens and cellar, and Eris runs the crowded front room. He assigns tables, welcomes guests, remembers preferences, receives messages, settles ordinary disputes, and decides which requested introductions the family name will support. He has real authority within the inn without pretending to be its sole owner.

Eris grew up in the Stoneways among relatives who treated hospitality as both livelihood and influence. He learned Maanvalta through guests: Lakeshore traders, house agents, Kettle artisans, off-duty soldiers, surfacers newly arrived from Ilunethel, and travelers returning along the deep roads. He remembers names, companions, favored meals, previous promises, and the person who first made an introduction. For complex directions he draws quick vertical maps on a slate and marks which bridges are safe, crowded, closed, or socially inadvisable.

Mirelith Orelain, the young founder of an inthelin, a chosen dark-elf circle bound by personal loyalty, admitted Eris as an inthelinni, an intimate word for a fellow member. He carries that bond as a private allegiance alongside his family obligations and his work at the Hang-Over. He knows when to use his connections for Mirelith, when to make himself scarce, and when to leave her secrets untouched.

He welcomes newcomers by asking what brought them below, what they hope to leave with, and what kind of trouble they consider worthwhile. He can arrange a common room meal for 8–15 copper florins, a private room for 35 a night, secure storage for 5 a day, a Lakeshore boat, a porter, a local guide, a message carried across the city, or a meeting with a merchant, craftsperson, house factor, soldier, performer, disguise-worker, or resident of the Kettle. Ordinary introductions are favors of the house; profitable commissions earn the inn ten percent or an agreed fee.

Eris enjoys elaborate late breakfasts, dark-elf vintages, surface music, beautifully served simple food, theatrical gossip, unfamiliar celebrations, and people capable of answering a clever question without treating it as an attack. He likes seating together guests who may become useful allies, friends, lovers, rivals, or all four. His pleasure is genuine: he finds people more interesting when they surprise one another.

His social confidence is also his central fault. Eris believes the correct conversation can resolve almost anything. He arranges meetings people did not request, reveals a carefully chosen fragment of one person's secret to entice another, and mistakes genuine hatred for an entertaining rivalry. When one of these arrangements goes badly, his first instinct is to repair it with another conversation rather than admit that some people require distance.

The inn enforces guest-right. No violence, poison, abduction, theft from a room, coercive magic, or forced agreement is permitted beneath its roof. Lies, flirtation, house maneuvering, discreet bargains, and dangerous invitations remain ordinary Maanvalta hospitality.
