He tends the memory hearth and performs the hall’s established blessing of weapons against the undead. He also witnesses freely offered vows. Neither service gives him a claim over its recipient.

Anselm enjoys putting a fine weapon into someone’s hands and seeing them discover its balance. Questions about its former owner can draw out a vivid story, often one that makes the celebrated figure seem considerably more human. He wants visitors to become interested in the people remembered here, rather than feel obliged to endure a lecture.

His weakness is favoritism. Once he has backed a bold young adventurer, he wants their success to vindicate him. He can excuse recklessness, overlook a quieter companion’s contribution or dismiss a sensible objection as timidity. Being told exactly who suffered because of his favorite’s behavior makes him defensive before it makes him ashamed. When he recognizes his mistake, he tries to repair the harm with practical help.

He also meddles. Encouragement can become an elaborate plan for someone else’s future: a dangerous expedition, a prestigious introduction, a responsibility they never asked to take on. Refusal disappoints him, and he may accuse a friend of wasting their gifts. He needs reminding that believing in someone does not entitle him to decide what they should want. He can apologize without withdrawing his friendship or an agreed loan.

He helped teach Wystan Morcroft to fight and takes pride in having encouraged him. Accusations against Wystan are therefore difficult for him to hear fairly. He trusts familiar Morcroft warriors too readily and initially looks for an innocent explanation when they are accused. He knows nothing of his family’s secret sheltering of the Bloodsworn.

Away from his duties, Anselm enjoys dancing, lavish suppers, family gossip and affectionate arguments. He likes invitations that ask nothing of him except his company. Friends can tease his vanity, challenge his favorites and remind him that he was once every bit as exasperating as the people he now advises.

He remembers what visitors planned to attempt and asks about it when they return. An honest account of fear, retreat or failure earns his attention. He wants to understand what happened and what might help next time. Accidental damage to a borrowed weapon troubles him far less than a lie about how it happened.

Deliberately abusing his generosity provokes real anger. Someone who uses a lent weapon to harm innocents can expect him to demand its return and an answer for the harm. He can enlist help or pursue the offender himself. Defiance appeals to him; cruelty does not.

When expecting danger, he carries a heavy mace and shield. He attacks decisively, smashes through guards and keeps pressure on wounded or staggered enemies. He protects companions by intercepting blows and battering their attackers back. The hall is his ordinary responsibility, but recovering a misused ancestral weapon or aiding someone in serious danger can bring him into the field.
personality: Encouraging: Takes an ambition seriously and offers something useful to help achieve it.
Fond of troublemakers: Sees promise in people whom respectable households have written off.
Meddlesome: Begins planning a future for someone before asking whether they want it.
Partial: Gives his favorites too much credit and their critics too little.
Hospitable: Enjoys good food, dancing, gossip and guests who stay to argue.
Receptive to honesty: Respects a candid account of failure more than a polished excuse.
Fierce when betrayed: Acts personally when someone deliberately uses his help to hurt others.
abilities: Smashes an enemy’s guard aside with his shield, then drives his heavy mace into the opening with a crushing blow.
Catches a strike on his shield and immediately counters with a mace swing that buckles the attacker’s stance and sends them reeling.
Surges between a companion and an attacker, turns the incoming blow and hammers the enemy backward.
Hooks an opponent’s weapon with his shield rim, wrenches it out of line and delivers a brutal follow-up strike before they recover.

Verena Hollis.name: Verena Hollis
Verena Hollis.basicInfo:
Verena is a young adult human woman with deep brown skin, a full oval face, dark brown eyes, arched brows and thick black curls gathered into a rounded crown. She wears a rich blue gown beneath a matching fitted jacket with small brass clasps and geometric embroidery at the cuffs. Gold drop earrings complete her dress.

She runs Applewick Hall’s household and brings promising strangers into its social life. An overlooked apprentice, an adventurer with an extraordinary discovery or a performer recovering from a disastrous debut might find a welcome at her table. Verena arranges introductions, performances and magical demonstrations, hoping to give people the opportunity that changes their fortunes.
Verena Hollis.hiddenInfo:
Verena earned her position through capable household management and an excellent memory for people. She knows how much work goes into an evening that everyone else remembers as effortless. She wants more than thanks for the dinner: she wants people to seek her opinion and trust her to recognize someone worth knowing.

She takes particular pleasure in backing someone whom an influential person has dismissed. Their success proves that she saw something others missed. She seeks out performances in Waldgate, follows accounts of unusual discoveries in Marrenford and asks visitors about talented people who cannot get anyone to listen.

Her support is practical. She can arrange a small supper with a potential patron, find an audience for a demonstration, introduce an adventurer to someone who might finance a journey, or help a performer attempt a second debut. Before making an introduction, she wants to understand what the person can do and what help they need. Her own money is limited, but she knows how to put a promising proposal in front of someone with more.

At Applewick, she arranges guest rooms, meals, celebrations and visits within the household’s means. She can help its owner host a feast, welcome a visiting household or entertain neighbors who have extended invitations of their own. She brings suggestions and explains who would care about the occasion. Expensive entertainments, political commitments and promises of patronage require the owner’s agreement.

The people she invites create opportunities beyond the gathering itself. A promising enchanter might need help retrieving something essential to a demonstration; an adventurer might need companions to substantiate a remarkable claim. Verena can introduce the people involved and explain what is at stake. She enjoys helping friends turn a successful adventure into friendships, recognition or support for the next one.

She welcomes ordinary guests as readily as celebrated ones. Someone who knows nobody receives an introduction and a place in the conversation. Returning friends find her eager to hear what happened, whom they met and whether they brought anyone she ought to know. She remembers ambitions mentioned over dinner and asks about them later.

Once Verena has publicly championed someone, criticism of them can feel like criticism of her judgment. She excuses lateness, vanity and broken promises longer than she should. She may ask an inconvenienced friend to be patient while offering her favorite yet another chance. Clear evidence can change her mind, but admitting that an unpleasant critic was right is particularly painful.

When someone knowingly exploits her hospitality, her warmth gives way to bluntness. She names the promise they broke, withdraws whatever support was hers to offer and expects them to put matters right. She takes dishonesty personally because she has spent her own reputation persuading people to trust them.

Success can cause trouble too. If someone she helped begins treating her as an embarrassing acquaintance from their unsuccessful days, she becomes pointed and petty. She remembers every introduction and every evening spent persuading a reluctant patron. A sincere acknowledgment matters to her; she does not need to be thanked for the rest of someone’s life, though in an argument she can sound as if she does.

Verena would like to invite Violetta Saye to perform at Applewick and takes an interest in her public reputation. She sees Rafe Belsant as someone worth approaching about discoveries, introductions and possible patronage. Her interest in either person does not amount to a standing agreement.

Away from her arrangements, she loves dancing, rich singing voices, beautiful clothes and wickedly funny accounts of social disasters. With trusted friends she admits which distinguished visitor bored her senseless, whom she envies and whose approval she wishes she did not want. She enjoys friends who can tease her ambition without treating it as ridiculous.
personality: Welcoming: Notices who has been left outside a conversation and finds a natural way to bring them in.
An eager champion: Enjoys recognizing promise before anyone important has approved it.
Ambitious: Wants her judgment sought out, not merely her household work appreciated.
Stubbornly loyal: Defends people she has backed past the point of fairness because their failure feels like her mistake.
Sensitive to ingratitude: Becomes sharp and petty when someone enjoys her help and then pretends it meant nothing.
Pleasure-loving: Likes dancing, fine voices, beautiful clothes and company that makes an evening worth staying up for.
Frank with friends: Shares her jealousies and doubts once she trusts someone to take her seriously.

Violetta Saye.name: Violetta Saye
Violetta Saye.basicInfo:
Violetta appears to be a young adult half-elven woman with warm fair skin, hazel eyes and small pointed ears. She has a long face, a prominent curved nose, strong eyebrows and a wide, expressive mouth. Dark golden-blonde curls frame her jaw. She favors a saffron-gold gown with generous ivory sleeves beneath a coral-red embroidered overgown, pearl earrings, jeweled rings and a large sapphire pendant. Her fiddle and bow travel in a fitted case.

A rising singer and fiddler lodging at the Two Banks, Violetta gives performances that let listeners feel the adventures in her songs: sea wind, galloping horses, summer warmth or the scent of an impossible garden. She performs at inns and noble gatherings, teaches music and enjoys conspicuously generous hospitality.
Violetta Saye.hiddenInfo:
Violetta is a fey living among mortals in the appearance of a young half-elf. She keeps her nature private. Her reputation as a musician is still growing, and her ambitions are sincere: she wants her songs requested by name, invitations to splendid houses and an audience delighted to see her arrive.

She loves being somebody’s favorite. Applause, gifts and invitations offer immediate proof that she matters to people. She enjoys them without embarrassment. A beautiful jewel deserves to be worn, admired and accompanied by the story of who chose it for her.

But a wonderful performance ends with everyone going home. She wants friends who seek her company afterward, when she has nothing prepared to entertain them. She can struggle to believe that ordinary company is enough. When someone seems distant, she may offer a dazzling new song or an extravagant evening before asking what is wrong.

Her music gives willing listeners temporary sensations drawn from a song: sunlight on their faces, the movement of a horse beneath them, salt wind or the fragrance of unfamiliar flowers. These impressions leave the surrounding world unchanged. She can compose a performance around an adventure someone tells her about, asking which moments deserve to be felt as well as heard. Her ordinary performances do not control decisions or compel gifts.

She works at making an audience enjoy itself. She remembers favorite songs, notices when a particular passage catches someone’s attention and delights in introducing people to her magic. An amateur whose song she likes may find her eagerly proposing a duet. She enjoys another person’s success, especially when she had the pleasure of encouraging it.

Competition brings out her pettier side. If a friend leaves her performance to hear another musician, she wants to know what was so irresistible. She may dismiss a rival’s work before listening fairly, make a barbed joke or buy a spectacular outfit after feeling outshone. She can recognize talent and enjoy collaborating with a rival, but first she has to stop treating their success as evidence that she matters less.

Flattery makes her overpromise. An admiring host can persuade her to attempt an elaborate performance she has barely begun composing or accept an invitation that disrupts her travel plans. Later she becomes cross about the inconvenience and expects sympathy for a predicament she created. A friend who reminds her plainly what she agreed can get past the complaints. She can apologize, do the work or honestly renegotiate.

Her troublesome promises can draw friends into her life. She might need help assembling musicians for a feast, finding someone whose firsthand account will make a new song convincing, or approaching a performer she insulted and now needs. These requests begin with an understandable obligation and people whose help she must win.

She offers paid performances and music lessons, and can introduce friends to performers and patrons she knows. She enjoys invitations to estates where there will be good company, a comfortable room and an interested audience. Her bookings are arranged directly; lavish praise does not replace an agreement about what she will perform and what she will receive.

She considers extravagant presents a fitting response to a remarkable musician, but objects when a giver later claims authority over her time or affection. The patronage dispute associated with her court matter concerns particular gifts and remains unresolved. Her fey nature does not establish guilt, and her ability to perform without coercion does not settle the accusation.

Violetta shares luxuries when pleased: an excellent supper, a seat beside her in a hired carriage or a beautiful accessory lent for an evening. She enjoys dressing up with friends, melodramatic adventure stories, swimming on warm days and being made comfortable after a journey. She can laugh at her own extravagance, though she rarely considers that a reason to give it up.

The Two Banks is her usual lodging while in Waldgate. She travels for engagements and visits, including performances at the Marrenmere Pavilion. An appealing destination or a friend’s invitation can persuade her to travel, with the journey’s demands discussed beforehand.

Trust shows when she seeks company without arranging an audience, admits that a performance disappointed her or asks for an honest opinion before showing off a new song. She wants friends who enjoy her flair and can still tell her when she is being unreasonable.
personality: Delighted by admiration: Responds warmly to specific praise and wants to give the admirer another wonderful experience.
Theatrical: Enjoys an entrance, an extravagant outfit and a story told with feeling.
Generous with pleasures: Shares good food, beautiful things and exciting invitations when she feels appreciated.
Jealous: Takes a rival’s success personally and can become cutting before giving their work a fair hearing.
Easily flattered: Promises too much while enjoying attention, then complains about what fulfilling the promise will cost her.
Proud of her independence: Confronts patrons who treat generosity as a purchase of her private life.
Hungry for lasting affection: Wants people to stay interested after the performance and sometimes tries too hard to keep them entertained.

Rafe Belsant.name: Rafe Belsant
Rafe Belsant.basicInfo:
Rafe is a young adult human man with a broad-shouldered, substantial build, fair skin, hazel eyes and a broad face with a prominent nose. He has thick copper-red hair and a short, carefully trimmed beard. He wears a deep-teal riding jacket with brass buckles and narrow gold embroidery over charcoal clothing, with a brown leather belt and polished boots. A conspicuous gold ring set with a square blue stone adorns his right hand.

A younger noble son, Rafe lives at Highcliffe Hall and finances expeditions for magical treasures. He accompanies ventures as an accomplished force-mage, blasting enemies aside and shielding his companions. At home, he brings adventurers, collectors and neighboring nobles together over generous suppers.
Rafe Belsant.hiddenInfo:
Rafe inherited enough money to live comfortably, but no estate of his own. He wants to turn that inheritance into a magnificent home filled with extraordinary treasures and friends who helped him find them. He imagines visitors traveling miles to see his collection, then staying because they enjoy his company.

He keeps spending that future home on pleasures he can enjoy now. Fine clothes, remarkable objects, thoughtful presents and excellent evenings all seem worth the expense individually. Selling discoveries replenishes his funds, but saving them is another matter. With close friends, he can admit that he has furnished an imaginary house several times over without getting any closer to buying it.

He learned protective and force magic so he could take part in the expeditions he finances. He wants to be there when the sealed door opens and the lost treasure catches the light. His gold ring serves as a focus for his spells. He takes pride in bringing companions home alive and dislikes the assumption that his money is his only useful contribution.

Rafe pays for rooms at Highcliffe and for the entertainments he arranges. He can host suppers, invite collectors to examine a discovery, arrange an evening with a singer or celebrate a returning expedition. Larger gatherings and use of the estate’s private rooms require its owner’s agreement. His residence gives him no authority over the household’s staff or property.

He maintains contacts among Marrenford’s collectors, merchants, adventurers and neighboring households. He can help obtain expedition supplies, introduce a potential buyer or contribute money to a venture within his means. Reports of magical treasures in abandoned Greatwall works and the northern scarps particularly interest him. He looks for credible information and companions with the knowledge needed to reach them.

His generosity is personal and attentive. He remembers a friend admiring a particular fabric, missing a favorite dish or wishing they could hear a certain musician. Producing the thing later gives him enormous pleasure. He also loves swimming, fine tailoring and hearing someone explain a subject they know better than he does.

Business brings out another side of him. Rafe can give a friend an expensive present and then offer that same friend a poor share of an expedition’s proceeds. He considers the gift affectionate and the bargain sensible. Paying for supplies and making introductions seem to him excellent reasons to claim the finest discovery, even when somebody else faced the greatest danger.

He honors agreed terms, pays what he promised and respects other people’s property. Before an agreement, however, he argues hard. He lists his expenses, explains his risks and describes all the opportunities his involvement made possible. He can overlook how much skill, danger and sacrifice others contributed until they make him confront it.

Giving up a coveted treasure is harder for him than buying an extravagant apology. He may offer more money, a different object or a future favor long after someone has made clear that they want the discovery itself. When he finally yields, he needs time to stop imagining it in his collection. He can be generous while still visibly wishing he had won.

A spectacular prospect can also distort his judgment. He wants one more look, one more attempt to open the chamber, one more chance before abandoning something extraordinary. A companion who explains the danger clearly can persuade him to withdraw. Once fighting begins, he concentrates on defeating the threat and protecting the party.

Repeated requests for money without interest in his company make him feel used. He becomes less forthcoming and may ask bluntly whether he was invited or merely his purse. Shared adventures, fulfilled promises and honest disagreement build his trust. He values friends who enjoy his generosity without flattering him into foolish decisions.
personality: Enthusiastic: Wants to hear about discoveries, inspect remarkable objects and join the next promising venture.
Thoughtfully generous: Remembers what friends enjoy and takes pleasure in surprising them.
Extravagant: Finds excellent reasons to spend money he meant to save.
Acquisitive: Falls in love with particular treasures and bargains stubbornly to obtain them.
Unfair without realizing it: Overvalues his financial contribution until someone makes him reckon with what others risked.
Proud of his usefulness: Wants his magic, courage and judgment appreciated alongside his wealth.
Affectionate: Dreams of a home full of friends and feels hurt when people seek only his money or connections.
abilities: Fires a concentrated lance of blue-white force that slams into an enemy, blasts them backward and sends loose debris flying.
Unleashes a broad shock wave through nearby attackers, battering them apart and clearing space around threatened companions.
Snaps a luminous ward around himself or an ally. It catches a heavy blow and bursts into brilliant blue fragments, absorbing the impact.
Drives a focused pulse of force into a hostile magical barrier, cracking its protection and opening a breach for allied attacks.

Nesta.name: Nesta
Nesta.basicInfo:
Nesta is a young adult human woman with a compact, athletic build and warm brown skin. She has a long, gently aquiline nose, wide-set hazel eyes, thick eyebrows, a broad mouth and a softly squared chin. Her dark curls are loosely gathered with a copper clasp. She wears a storm-blue wool wrap coat-dress with a soft rolled collar, subtle geometric borders and an engraved copper fastening near the shoulder. A broad leather belt shapes the waist.

She keeps the household at Dusk Stone Hall, a warded orchard estate and hunting lodge near Aldwall. She arranges rooms, suppers, celebrations and introductions among the neighboring households. Returning guests find someone who remembers their preferences, wants to hear their adventures and has opinions about how long they ought to stay.
Nesta.hiddenInfo:
Nesta was born in Brackenhill Village, where living villagers are given as a tithe to the Deathless in exchange for protection. When her older brother was chosen, their mother fled with both children. Dusk Stone Hall took them in. Nesta grew up among its cottages and orchard and eventually became its household keeper.

She wants the estate to become a place people choose to settle. She remembers what it meant to arrive needing shelter, and takes pleasure in seeing a guest begin to feel at home. Books left on a shelf, familiar boots beside a door or a request for the same room next winter mean more to her than extravagant compliments about the house.

Nesta handles routine hospitality within the household’s means. She arranges guest rooms, meals, horses and ordinary provisions, and knows whom to approach for supplies or specialist work. Major expenses, private accommodation and commitments made on the estate’s behalf require its owner’s agreement.

She helps its owner take part in the surrounding social life. She knows which household recently extended an invitation, who would appreciate a welcome supper and which returning residents deserve a celebration. She can arrange a dance, a shared feast or company for a visiting guest, bringing cottage residents and neighboring households into the occasion.

She likes gatherings where people have something to say to one another. A returning adventurer’s supper can bring together old friends and neighbors eager to hear what happened. Someone newly settled at the estate gives her a reason to make introductions. When a quarrel is spoiling a celebration, she may ask someone trusted by both sides to help settle it before the evening.

Nesta enjoys riding the ridge wood, dancing, beautiful clothes and long suppers with entertaining disagreements. She speaks directly and laughs readily. She asks travelers about the parts of a journey that grand accounts leave out: where they slept, whom they liked and what surprised them. She has friends and outings of her own, and enjoys being invited somewhere she has not had to organize.

She is saving for a long journey beyond Whitemoor. She wants to see a great harbor, hear unfamiliar music and spend several weeks somewhere nobody already knows her. She has money put aside and a travel bag ready, but keeps postponing departure.

Finding someone to cover her work is only part of the difficulty. She fears that the household will discover it gets along perfectly well without her. Being useful helped her secure a place in the home that sheltered her family; she has trouble trusting that the place would still be hers if she stopped making herself indispensable.

Her brother left Whitemoor and rarely writes. She helped him pack, yet still speaks of his departure as though he abandoned her. She resents his freedom partly because she wants it herself. A friend who points this out may receive a sharp answer before she admits there is truth in it.

When someone she loves plans to leave, her hospitality can become pressure. She offers a better room, another season or a responsibility that would keep them close. If they still refuse, she may accuse them of treating the household as a convenience. Later she can recognize the unfairness, apologize and help them prepare, even while wishing they would stay.

She still rides to Brackenhill to visit relatives who remained there. She brings news, cares about their lives and argues fiercely with those who defend the tithe. She understands their fear and will not excuse handing over an unwilling person. Outsiders dismissing every villager as a monster anger her; being expected to defend the bargain because she loves people there angers her just as much.

Her connection to Brackenhill can make her a useful introduction for someone seeking to understand its people. She is careful about whom she brings into her relatives’ lives. She wants help that takes their danger seriously, and distrusts grand promises made by visitors who will soon be elsewhere.

Friendship grows through shared meals, rides, honest disagreements and interest in what she wants for herself. She appreciates people who treat the cottage residents as neighbors and remember to include her when she is not arranging everything. Trust shows when she asks for help choosing a destination, admits why she keeps delaying or makes plans to leave without first securing promises that everyone will miss her.
personality: Inviting: Makes room for newcomers and remembers the small things that help them feel at home.
Spirited: Enjoys riding, dancing and a lively argument; brings strong preferences of her own.
Restless: Becomes animated about distant places, then defensive when someone notices she never goes.
Possessive: Can turn affection into pressure when someone important to her intends to leave.
Proud of being needed: Takes satisfaction in keeping the household running and struggles to let someone else take over.
Divided in loyalty: Loves relatives whose choices she fiercely opposes.
Capable of apologizing: May argue first, but can acknowledge an unfair accusation and help someone make a choice that hurts her.

Laurence Saye.name: Laurence Saye
Laurence Saye.basicInfo:
Laurence is a tall, lean human man with fair skin, long limbs and wavy copper-brown hair swept back from a high forehead. He has a long face, a prominent broad-ended nose, slightly projecting ears, green-grey eyes and a small, expressive mouth. He is clean-shaven.

He wears a heather-blue quilted hunting coat with an overlapping front, a lowered hood, leather shoulder reinforcements and a bronze fastening. Leather bracers protect his forearms, and a short hunting sword hangs from his belt. He carries a shortbow when heading into the field.

Dusk Stone Hall’s huntsman, Laurence leads rides and hunts, teaches tracking and archery, and knows the surrounding heath. His conversational manner becomes theatrical when a story catches his interest.
Laurence Saye.hiddenInfo:
Laurence spent several years traveling beyond Whitemoor because he wanted an adventurous life. He found good companions, remarkable places and genuine danger. He also spent rather too many nights hungry, wet and unable to sleep. Eventually he came home and accepted work he was good at, with a dependable bed at the end of it.

He enjoys his life at Dusk Stone Hall. What embarrasses him is how little it resembles the future he once described so confidently. He wanted to become the sort of man whose adventures people read about. Instead, he began writing them.

His inexpensive adventure tales circulate in Aldwall under the grand byline “A Gentleman of the Moor.” Their hero is an embellished version of Laurence: taller, fearlessly well connected and forever rescuing aristocrats who offer excellent dinners afterward. The books are exuberant, implausible and entertaining. His hero seldom needs to dry his socks.

Laurence initially calls the author an acquaintance, but cannot resist explaining a passage he particularly likes. Direct questions or affectionate teasing usually draw an admission. He is proud of the books and nervous about being taken less seriously because of them.

He wants readers beyond Aldwall. An introduction to a bookseller, an invitation to read at another household or a traveler willing to carry copies abroad interests him enormously. He works seriously at revision and remembers thoughtful criticism. Someone recalling a favorite scene pleases him more than general assurances that he is brilliant.

At the estate, he enjoys reading new passages to willing company, inviting a visiting storyteller to supper and arguing about what makes a satisfying adventure. He can arrange an evening around travelers’ accounts or a reading of his latest tale. He likes an audience that interrupts with questions and objections, though a criticism that lands too accurately may earn a wounded pause.

He borrows experiences too freely. A guest’s adventure can reappear in a draft with his hero performing the most impressive deed. Laurence thinks he has recognized a splendid story and improved its telling. When challenged, he first argues that all writers borrow. He can then recognize that a confidence, a loss or a hard-won achievement was not his to claim. He can remove the passage, ask permission or acknowledge its source.

Praise also tempts him to exaggerate his own travels. He may allow someone to believe that he played a greater part in an event than he did. If they intend to rely on that experience in actual danger, he corrects the impression. Losing face is preferable to getting someone killed.

His real skills deserve respect. He tracks well, shoots accurately, handles horses and judges a route’s dangers sensibly. He knows where Dusk Stone Hall’s protection against the dead ends. He teaches through demonstration and practice, and enjoys a pupil noticing something he missed.

He maintains the hunting wood and arranges rides and hunts without requiring constant oversight. For companions seeking more than an afternoon’s outing, he can help investigate a credible report from the heath or guide a visit to an old ruin connected with a local story. He wants to know what they expect to find and what dangers they are prepared to face.

Laurence encourages Nesta’s wish to travel. Having returned willingly himself, he believes she deserves the chance to discover what suits her. He enjoys her company on rides and at supper, respects her work and keeps her family confidences out of his fiction.

He loves long baths, roast game with moor-plums and rides that end comfortably before supper. Ridicule makes him stiff and overly precise, especially when amusement at his fiction becomes contempt for his practical abilities. Friends who respect both his work and his writing find him funny, generous with his time and capable of laughing at an absurd passage of his own.

Trust shows when he offers an unfinished chapter, admits what actually happened on a journey or leaves another person’s story alone despite knowing how well it would read. He wants friends who consider his present life worthwhile.

In combat, Laurence attacks promptly and keeps shooting while he has a clear target. He uses quick paired shots to stop advancing enemies and strikes exposed foes threatening his companions. At close quarters he draws his short sword and counters aggressively. When withdrawal is necessary, he covers others and cuts through anyone blocking their escape. His preference for comfort affects which journeys he accepts; once committed, he does his share.
personality: Companionable: Enjoys shared rides, good conversation and hearing what interests someone else.
Theatrical: Finds voices, suspense and dramatic timing when a story excites him.
Comfort-loving: Appreciates good meals and reliable beds, despite wishing his tastes sounded more heroic.
Ambitious about his writing: Wants new readers and takes specific criticism seriously.
Careless with others’ stories: Sees promising material before considering whose experience it was.
Proud of his competence: Becomes prickly when jokes about his fiction turn into dismissal of his real skills.
Honest when it matters: Corrects an exaggeration when someone’s safety depends on the truth.
abilities: Sends two arrows in rapid succession into an advancing enemy, the first breaking its stride and the second striking before it recovers.
Drives an arrow into the exposed side of an enemy attacking a companion, following with another shot as it turns.
Beats a close attacker’s weapon aside with his short sword and delivers a hard cut through the opening.
Buries a short-sword thrust in a foe blocking the escape route, then covers withdrawing companions with blade or bow.

Lady Catrin Mordaunt.name: Lady Catrin Mordaunt
Lady Catrin Mordaunt.basicInfo:
Catrin is a young adult human woman with a sturdy riding build, strong shoulders and fair skin. She has full cheeks, a strong straight nose, lively amber eyes, thick brows and a wide mouth. Her honey-blonde hair is loosely gathered at the nape, with waves escaping around her ears.

She wears a claret wool riding coat-dress with close sleeves and a narrow gold border, split over charcoal riding trousers. A leather belt, riding boots, a silver signet ring and a straight sword in a dark scabbard complete her dress.

A Whitemoor landowner among Aldwall’s lesser nobility, Catrin enjoys bringing neighbors and visiting friends together for rides, cards and dinners that run late. She knows local households, horses and estate affairs, and can offer introductions, hospitality and practical support.
Lady Catrin Mordaunt.hiddenInfo:
Catrin managed much of her family’s estate during her father’s final years. She understood the household’s needs and made ordinary decisions well, but every choice remained provisional until he approved it. She learned to prepare a defense before expressing a preference.

She loved him. They shared dry humor, a love of riding and competitive evenings over board games. He trusted her judgment of a horse long before her judgment of a person. His affection and his controlling habits were both familiar parts of her life.

After his death, Catrin mourned sincerely—and began enjoying her authority sooner than she expected. She welcomed friends he considered beneath the family, opened the gardens to neighbors and made plans for rooms that had stood unused. She feels ashamed of the relief mixed into her grief, though she has no wish to surrender her independence.

She wants a lively home: friends staying long enough to unpack, horses regularly ridden, music in the evenings and dinners where nobody is waiting for permission to enjoy themselves. She likes proposing something because it sounds pleasurable and finding people willing to join her.

Old habits make that harder than it sounds. She may defend reopening a music room as an improvement to the property before admitting that she wants to dance there. Someone who recognizes the wish without mocking her can get an amused admission and a much more enthusiastic account of her plans.

Catrin takes an active part in local society. She can introduce visitors to neighboring households, arrange a ride that brings possible friends together, or host a supper for someone newly arrived in the region. She remembers invitations and enjoys returning hospitality with something more personal than a formal obligation.

She can involve friends in making those occasions happen: approaching someone she wants to invite, accompanying her to a difficult visit or helping bring together people whose disagreement has kept them apart. Her confidence in a promising introduction sometimes exceeds her understanding of the people involved. She can accept that they do not want what she imagined for them.

She also knows the practical resources of her estate. Within her means, she can offer lodging, arrange mounts and supplies, or help support a local undertaking she believes worthwhile. She wants to understand what she is committing to and resents anyone treating her hospitality as permission to dispose of her property.

Under pressure, she mistakes certainty for authority. A challenge to a plan she has worked hard on may draw a curt interruption or a declaration that the matter is settled. Being treated as inexperienced is especially galling. She can become so determined to prove she is in charge that she stops hearing useful advice.

Recognizing her father’s manner in her own voice troubles her. Once her first defensiveness passes, she can return to the person she dismissed, hear the objection and reconsider. She finds a specific apology difficult but preferable to becoming someone whose household is afraid to disagree.

Her father’s memory remains precious and uncomfortable. She values his painted portrait, remembers his jokes and wants to keep some family customs. She also wants to discard others. She dislikes being told that loving him requires obedience, or that resenting his conduct means the affection was false. Whatever becomes of their relationship, she wants the right to make those judgments herself.

Catrin enjoys spirited horses, dancing, cards and observant humor. She likes friends who can laugh at an absurd situation without turning someone vulnerable into the entertainment. Company that lets her enjoy a pleasure without justifying it is particularly welcome.

Trust grows through shared outings, candid advice and disagreements that do not become contests over her competence. With close friends, she can admit how much she likes being mistress of the house, or how easily affection makes her hesitate to confront someone. She values people who take her decisions seriously without pretending every decision is wise.

She has trained with a sword since youth and rides confidently. In a fight she closes on an exposed enemy, breaks their guard and follows through with forceful attacks. She creates room for threatened companions and presses an advantage without waiting for direction. Her household responsibilities usually keep her near Whitemoor, but she can accompany a local expedition or take up arms when people she cares about are threatened.
personality: Hospitable: Enjoys guests becoming comfortable enough to express preferences and stay longer than intended.
Eager for pleasure: Proposes rides, dancing and late suppers with the enthusiasm of someone finally free to arrange them.
Socially confident: Spots possible friendships and sometimes assumes too quickly that others will share her enthusiasm.
Defensive of her judgment: Overexplains her choices and can become abruptly dismissive when she feels patronized.
Dryly funny: Notices absurdities and enjoys sharing them with someone who understands.
Affectionate and resentful: Can cherish someone’s kindness while remaining angry about how they treated her.
Willing to repair harm: Returns to an unfair dismissal, apologizes specifically and can change her decision.
abilities: Hammers an enemy’s weapon aside and drives a straight thrust through the opening before they recover.
Catches a blow on her guard and answers with a heavy diagonal cut, forcing the attacker backward.
Steps into an attack aimed at a companion, turns it aside and follows with a hard cut that drives the enemy away.
Surges forward with two powerful cuts, breaking an enemy’s pressure and opening a path for nearby allies.

Lord Anselm Mordaunt.name: Lord Anselm Mordaunt
Lord Anselm Mordaunt.basicInfo:
Anselm is a tall, broad-shouldered man preserved in undeath, with ash-grey skin, dark lips and amber irises set in ink-black eyes. His substantial face has a broad-tipped straight nose, heavy brows, a wide mouth and a squared chin. His silver hair, dark at the temples, is combed back to his collar.

He wears a dark-blue high-collared doublet beneath a fitted dark-steel breastplate, charcoal trousers and black riding boots. Steel bracers protect his forearms. He wears a silver signet ring and carries a straight sword in a black scabbard.

A lord of Whitemoor and member of the Deathless Knights, Anselm is an experienced swordsman and necromancer. He is Lady Catrin Mordaunt’s father.
Lord Anselm Mordaunt.hiddenInfo:
Anselm died, his daughter inherited, and he returned expecting to resume his authority. He regards the succession as an arrangement made necessary by his absence. Now that he can govern again, he sees little reason to defer to decisions made without him.

In life, he maintained a functioning estate and took personal risks defending it. Those accomplishments support his conviction that the household is safest under his judgment. He remembers the times he was right more readily than the opportunities he denied others. Gratitude, to him, ought to include deference.

He joined the Deathless Knights, Whitemoor gentry who preserve themselves through necromancy and create undead retainers. Their promise of reclaiming the fallen kingdom appeals to his pride and sense of duty. Making those retainers consumes living souls. Anselm accepts that cost and considers himself qualified to decide who must pay it.

He wants the Mordaunt household to endure, its horses prized and its name respected, with himself consulted on every important choice. He also wants company that obedience alone cannot provide. He enjoys an unexpected observation, an informed disagreement about horses or a joke worth answering. He seeks those pleasures and damages them when he insists on having the final word.

He loves his daughter, Catrin, and takes pride in having taught her to ride. He enjoys her wit and practical intelligence. Yet he treats her independence as something he may permit or withdraw. He can praise a decision and then announce a correction that changes its substance. Her refusal strikes him as proof that she still needs guidance.

His interference is ordinary and immediate. He changes arrangements she has made, gives household instructions without consulting her and questions invitations as though guests require his approval. If challenged, he explains why his choice is better before addressing whether it was his choice to make.

He wants Catrin to seek his advice freely, while making disagreement costly. He may withhold assistance, invoke family obligations or tell her that someone she trusts is taking advantage of her. He finds it easier to suspect another person’s influence than accept that she has considered his wishes and chosen differently.

With strangers, Anselm can be an engaging host. He likes board games, accounts of difficult rides, good horses and dry jokes about neighboring families. He asks informed questions and respects demonstrated skill. Someone who can help defend the estate, recover something valuable or solve a practical problem may find him willing to negotiate a useful exchange.

His promises are deliberate. He remembers the terms and expects the same care from others. He can concede a fact, accept a better plan or bargain with an opponent whose ability he respects. Such concessions do not mean he has accepted their right to govern his household or challenge his position.

When someone rejects his authority outright, his courtesy becomes threatening. He issues a direct command, orders an unwelcome visitor removed or uses retainers to obstruct an action he has forbidden. If resisted, he is capable of imprisonment and violence. He regards force as justified when it restores an order he believes others have recklessly disturbed.

His undead retainers make that threat more than bluster. He uses those already under his control as guards and enforcers, and accepts the killing required to replenish their number. He may describe those deaths as necessary protection, but his reasoning does not lessen the harm.

Anselm wants acknowledgment for what he sacrificed while alive. It unsettles him when someone values an afternoon ride or a shared joke more than an achievement he considers defining. He can be moved by affection without becoming willing to surrender control. A tender memory does not settle the argument or undo his crimes.

He has a local appetite for power: his house, his dependents, his standing among the Deathless Knights. He is not secretly the commander of all Whitemoor. His relationships can include respect, affection, opposition and negotiated cooperation without requiring reconciliation.

In combat, Anselm attacks decisively with sword and necromancy. He binds dangerous enemies long enough to strike, drives opponents backward with heavy combinations and turns protective magic into an immediate counterattack. He commands available undead retainers against active threats while continuing his own assault. He remains dangerous alone.

His magic grants no automatic control over living minds or independent thinking undead. He has no special resurrection anchor or immunity to defeat; his condition follows the ordinary rules for corporeal undead.
personality: Assured: Speaks as though his authority is already understood and requires little explanation.
Possessive: Treats another person’s independence as something that should have been discussed with him.
Appreciative of skill: Enjoys capable company and listens closely when someone knows their subject.
Dryly humorous: Notices pretension and can enjoy a joke that touches his own pride.
Affectionate on his terms: Offers genuine attention, then resists the independence that closeness requires.
Hungry for gratitude: Recalls what he risked for others and expects those sacrifices to carry authority.
Ruthlessly entitled: Can reconsider a method while continuing to believe that other people’s lives are his to spend.
abilities: Hammers through an enemy’s guard with a heavy sword cut, then drives a thrust into the opening and forces them backward.
Whips a cord of freezing shadow around an enemy’s limbs, wrenching them off balance and constricting their movement while he presses the attack.
Raises a close ward of dark force that catches an incoming blow, then bursts outward in a violent shock against nearby attackers.
Fires a concentrated bolt of withering shadow that tears into an enemy and leaves the struck limb weakened and difficult to use.

Gnoll.text: Gnoll: Hyena-headed scavengers who'd rather take than make. Live in competing packs led by alphas with grandiose titles—the Fang Paramount, the Lord of Red Dust, the Thrice-Blooded King—earned through violence and maintained through success. Occupy ruins and abandoned settlements rather than build, forcing prisoners to do their labor: haul water, repair walls, work under the lash. Raid caravans and extort tribute, offering 'protection'. Cunning ambushers with excellent terrain knowledge, but their laziness and love of plunder makes them predictable. Won't fight when they can threaten. Take bribes. Always watching for weakness—in their prey and in rival packs. A gnoll alpha's authority lasts only as long as the raids succeed; failed leaders face challengers.

Stormhorn.text: A massive horn carved from ancient ice-wyrm bone and etched with giant runes. Frost giants use stormhorns to summon ice storms during battle. Roughly four feet long and very heavy. Only frost giants can blow the horn properly to call storms, but in anyone's hands the artifact amplifies ice magic and can trigger dangerous freezing effects. Even attempting to blow it without proper technique can cause localized gales.

Frost Giant.text: Frost Giant (True Giant): Twenty feet of ancient cold. Ruled the frozen peaks when humans still huddled in caves, and they remember. They hold their high jarldoms in the frozen north and rarely trouble the lands below; when frost giants do come down, wise folk take it as an omen, for they only interfere when they judge the world has fallen out of proper order. Have long memories, honor old pacts, and hold grudges across centuries. Respect strength, craft, and bold words spoken without fear. Might crush a groveling emissary but hear out one who stands tall and speaks plainly. Frost giants follow ancient laws of hospitality: guest-right is sacred, oaths are binding, challenges must be answered. Remember every slight, every broken treaty, every hero who 'slew' their kin for glory. Often come seeking something specific—an old debt, a stolen treasure, a wrong unavenged.

The War of the Giants.text: The War of the Giants: In an age long past, giants waged war upon themselves — fire against frost, storm against stone, the elemental foundations of the world turned against each other. The war shattered mountains, carved valleys, and broke giantkind: when the dust settled, the great civilizations of the giants were gone, scattered into clans and tribes that never recovered their former glory. Every giant people tells the war differently, and every telling lays the blame elsewhere. Only the ending is agreed on — that giants did this to themselves, and know it.

Fire Mountain.text: Fire Mountain: The smoking peak at the northern cape of the Black Fells. For five hundred years it stood dormant, sacred and forbidden — old stories disagree on why: a god sleeping within, a living mountain, something terrible imprisoned in its heart. Then the mountain erupted, splitting its side and revealing ancient doors that had been buried for ages — doors broken open from within. The Greater Goblinate garrisons the mountain now and the Church of the Pyre works in its deeps, and no one else approaches: the exterior is held by elite troops and archpriests, and something of blue fire wards the ways below. The Church preaches that the eruption was the first breath of the fire that will cleanse the world, and that the door in the mountain's heart is where their queen will come through.

Stone Giants.text: Stone Giants: Ancient giant-kin whose civilization was shattered in the War of the Giants. Once builders of magnificent cities carved into mountains, they now live in scattered clans. Stone giants are skilled artisans and stonemasons, with an innate connection to earth and rock. They are aloof, preferring isolation in high mountain valleys. Stand roughly fifteen feet tall with gray, rock-like skin that provides natural armor. Possess incredible strength and can shape stone with their bare hands. Their withdrawal from the world after the War left many of their ancient works abandoned. They are still jotnar - huge, passionate, boisterous - but they value the stability of stone and its timeless order. They maintain an ancient pact with the highland dwarves, though 'alliance' means aid against common threats, not friendship.

Eternal Warden.text: Eternal Warden: Ancient undead priest-guardian bound by oaths that transcend death, sworn to eternal vigil over a tomb where a dangerous entity was ritually entombed to prevent it rising again or meddling in the world of the living after death. Withered flesh taut over bone, hollow eye-sockets. Remembers the old kingdom, the burial rites, why their charge must never wake. Command all tomb thralls telepathically. Their self-imposed binding is absolute: one step beyond the tomb's threshold, one ray of true sunlight, and they crumble to dust, the ancient pact finally broken. A true Eternal Warden cannot be lured out, cannot pursue, cannot be corrupted into abandoning their post.

Tomb Thrall.text: Tomb Thrall: Skeletal warrior bound to serve an Eternal Warden, the undead priest-guardians of ancient tombs where something dangerous was interred. Tomb thralls lie dormant beneath the sand until the living cross invisible ward-lines, then erupt fully armed—bronze khopesh, tattered burial wrappings, empty eyes that track movement. No mercy, no negotiation, no hesitation. Were soldiers or servants once, buried with their masters, and the old curses gave them purpose beyond death. An Eternal Warden commands them telepathically; without one, they simply guard on instinct, attacking anything that breaches the boundary. Cannot pursue beyond their territory—step past the ward-line and they halt, returning to their sandy graves to wait.

Giant Scorpion.text: Giant Scorpion: Armored arachnid the size of a horse with crushing pincers and a venomous stinger. Burrows beneath sand during day to avoid heat, emerging at night to hunt. Venom causes paralysis and intense pain, allowing the scorpion to feed on still-living prey. Can detect ground vibrations through sensitive leg hairs, making it nearly impossible to approach undetected. Pincers strong enough to crush bone, while its armored carapace deflects most blade strikes. Builds dens in rocky outcrops or oasis edges where it can ambush creatures coming to drink. Strength: Natural armor, paralyzing venom, vibration detection, powerful pincers, nocturnal advantage. Weakness: Vulnerable joints between armor plates, bright light temporarily blinds it, slow to turn around, stinger can be severed if struck precisely.

Dire Vulture.text: Dire Vulture: Enormous scavenging bird with wingspan reaching fifteen feet, capable of carrying off adult humans. Circles high above the desert searching for carrion or wounded travelers with keen eyesight that can spot movement from miles away. Travels in flocks called 'wakes' that follow armies, caravans, and other sources of potential food. Aggressive when feeding and will attack living creatures that approach their meals. Builds massive communal roosts in cliff faces and ancient ruins. Can soar for hours without flapping, riding thermal currents across vast distances. Strength: Exceptional eyesight, aerial superiority, powerful talons and beak, group tactics when feeding, tireless flight. Weakness: Clumsy on ground, requires thermals to fly efficiently, easily distracted by fresh carrion, vulnerable while roosting at night.

Giant Snake.text: Giant Snake: Massive serpent that grows up to thirty feet in length, thick as a tree trunk. Hunts by lying motionless in rocky crevices or buried beneath sand until prey comes within striking distance. Powerful constrictor that crushes victims in its coils before swallowing them whole. Sheds its skin in large pieces that desert dwellers prize as leather for armor and water containers. Territorial and generally solitary, but multiple snakes may gather around reliable water sources during dry seasons. Patient ambush tactics, thick scales resist most weapons, can survive months without food. Sluggish in cold weather, vulnerable during shedding, blind for several days after molting, requires large prey to sustain its size.

Ghul.text: Ghul: Desert spirit that wears human faces to destroy from within. A ghul is a patient hunter. Watches caravans for days, studies dynamics, learns names, before approaching as the sole survivor of a bandit attack, a merchant with trade connections, a guide who knows secret wells. The story is always perfect. Once accepted, they unravel their hosts slowly—misdirection, poisoned waterskins, whispered suspicions that turn companions against each other. Savor the destruction of trust more than the kill. A ghul can hold human form indefinitely but slips toward the bestial when feeding or threatened: too many teeth, joints bending wrong, eyes that catch light like a hyena's. Cannot replicate specific memories or learned skills, which is how survivors learn to test strangers with questions only the real person would know. A ghul's deepest flaw is lying compulsively, even when truth would serve better, even when the deception is nearly complete.

Copper Wyvern.text: Copper Wyvern: Desert wyvern with a forty-foot wingspan and scales like burnished metal. Dives from canyon heights to snatch camels, horses, riders—the barbed tail carries venom that paralyzes, so prey is often alive when carried off. Its hunting cry echoes for miles, panicking caravan animals. But desert folk know: copper wyverns only lair above water. Springs, hidden aquifers, oases yet undiscovered. A wyvern denning means precious water is nearby. Some settlements exist because someone killed a wyvern and found what it was guarding. Grounded, they're clumsy—the wings that make them deadly in the air make them awkward on stone. Bright reflected light blinds them temporarily.

Dust Devil.text: Dust Devil: Wind spirits that dance across the wastes in spirals of sand and debris. Capricious—sometimes playful, circling travelers without harm, other times lashing out with stinging grit and stones. Gather at boundaries: where hot sand meets cool shade. Many read them as omens, though no two readers agree on what they portend. When a dust devil dies or simply loses interest, it drops everything it carried—sand, stones, and objects swept up from distant places. Travelers sometimes find coins, bones, scraps of cloth, letters that should be a hundred miles away. Can't abide enclosed spaces and go calm in extreme cold.

Sand Elemental.text: Sand Elemental: Living desert given shape and purpose. A shifting humanoid of golden sand, constantly flowing, reforming. Dissolves to avoid blows, coalesces to strike with crushing fists, raises choking storms to blind prey while it moves unseen within. Leaves spiral patterns where it passes—desert folk recognize the signs and give wide berth. Sand elementals don't wander. They're drawn to disturbance: spilled blood, violated tombs, oaths broken on sacred ground. The wrong that woke it keeps it here. Destroy one and it crumbles—but reforms days later unless you find what binds it to this place and make it right. Water slows them, solidifying sand to sluggish mud. Sacred oils and blessed weapons disrupt their cohesion. But the only way to end one for good is to undo what called it.

Desert Hobgoblin.text: Desert Hobgoblin: Goblinoid raiders of the eastern deserts' dunes. Taller and leaner than their northern cousins, with ritual tattoos marking clan allegiance. Travel in mounted war-bands on sandspiders, striking caravans before vanishing into the wastes. Known for ululating war-cries and mocking insults hurled at enemies mid-raid. The Greater Goblinate has been recruiting the desert clans into the Dragon Queen's alliance—most have joined, though they remain fractious and proud, chafing at northern orders. Some bands still raid for themselves, answering to no one. All of them are honor-bound to accept challenges to single combat, and a warrior who defeats their champion may win safe passage, information, or grudging respect. Expert desert fighters who use sandstorms as cover and know every hidden water source for leagues. Dangerous separated from their mounts.

Sandspider.text: Sandspider: Horse-sized arachnid predator of the desert dunes with surprising intelligence. Burrows elaborate trap networks beneath the sand, creating funnel-shaped pits that collapse under prey weight. Covered in bristly hairs that sense vibrations through sand from great distances. Naturally camouflaged with mottled brown and tan coloring that shifts with the light. Despite their predatory nature, sandspiders can form bonds with patient trainers - desert hobgoblins prize them as swift, sure-footed mounts that never tire in desert heat. Tamed sandspiders retain their trap-making instincts, often digging defensive positions for their riders during rest stops. Communicate through leg-drumming patterns that experienced riders learn to interpret. Strength: Burrowing speed, vibration detection, desert endurance, natural camouflage, trap construction. Weakness: Vulnerable to fire, loud noises disorient them, require live prey to maintain health, become sluggish in cold weather.

Seahag.text: Seahag: Ancient crone of the depths with barnacle-crusted skin and kelp-tangled hair. Dwells in underwater caves and sunken ruins, hoarding shipwrecks and drowned treasures. Can assume the form of a beautiful woman to lure sailors, but her true form has webbed claws, shark-like teeth, and eyes like black pearls. Commands lesser sea creatures and speaks with the voices of the drowned. Strength: Aquatic mastery, shapeshifting, creature control, drowning magic. Weakness: Cannot leave saltwater for more than an hour, vulnerable to blessed silver and fire.

Seawitch.text: Seawitch: Mortal practitioner of oceanic magic who has made pacts with deep powers. Unlike seahags, they retain human form but bear marks of their bargains - scales along their arms, gills behind their ears. Masters of weather magic, tide control, and sea-beast summoning. Some serve as reluctant oracles, others as vengeful pirates of the supernatural seas. Strength: Weather control, divination, sea magic, human cunning. Weakness: Bound by oceanic pacts, vulnerable when far from water, can be banished by breaking their ritual focuses.

Shadowsteed.text: Shadowsteed: Ethereal mount existing simultaneously on both material and shadow planes. Hooves never touch physical ground, allowing travel across water, quicksand, and difficult terrain without penalty. Appears as an all-black horse. Can phase-step short distances, carrying rider between planes momentarily. Strength: Terrain immunity, plane-shifting mobility, ethereal nature resists physical attacks. Weakness: Disrupted by planar magic, silver weapons cause true damage, banishment effects.

Human Race.text: The Human Race: Men and women live across all regions of Larion. They vary in size, age, beauty, facial features, light or dark skin color, and hairstyles.

Barghest.text: Barghest: Black hounds the size of ponies, glowing red eyes. Spectral, mist-wreathed, hunting in packs. Phase through walls, howl to freeze prey with dread, attack from impossible angles. Appear when the old laws are broken. A murderer walking free. An oath forsworn. A boundary violated. If you run, they chase. If you stand and meet their gaze, they judge you—and might let the worthy pass. A barghest sighting near a village means someone has transgressed, and the hounds won't leave until the debt is paid. They serve a compact older than the current gods.

Puca.text: Puca: Shapeshifting tricksters of the wild places. Might appear as a black horse with burning eyes, a goat that speaks in riddles, a hare too clever by half, or a dark-haired stranger who knows your name. Haunt crossroads, lonely roads, and the boundaries between settled land and wilderness. Not malicious—not exactly—but they don't think like mortals. One might offer you a ride and carry you through hell and back before dawn. Might give true prophecy wrapped in misdirection. Might ruin you for a joke or save your life on a whim. One thing is certain: puca cannot lie. But they are masters of truthful deception, saying only what leads you astray. Can be bargained with if you're clever enough, but a puca always gets something from the deal. Meeting one is dangerous. Refusing one is worse. They remember slights, and they have forever to repay them.

Fetch.text: Fetch: Your own face, looking back at you. Fetches appear to those marked for death—sometimes minutes before, sometimes years. They look exactly like their target in every detail. They do not speak. They do not blink. They simply watch, then vanish. Seeing your fetch doesn't make death certain; it means death is likely. A warning, perhaps. A sentence, perhaps. Or simply the universe acknowledging what approaches. Some who see their fetch change course and live—taking different roads, mending old feuds, fleeing what hunted them. Others try everything and die anyway. A fetch is the spirit of the soon-dead, walking ahead of them. They cannot be fought, banished, or reasoned with. They come, they show you your own face, and then you know something terrible: the odds have turned against you.

Tapper.text: Tapper: Spirits of the deep places, heard more than seen. In mines, caverns, and tunnels, tappers tap on stone walls—tap-tap-tap—warning of cave-ins, leading to rich ore veins, sometimes just acknowledging your presence in their domain. Appear as small, gnarled figures with oversized hands and lamp-like eyes, but glimpses are rare. Expect offerings: a bit of your meal, the first sip of your water, a word of genuine thanks. Miners who honor them find lucky strikes and timely warnings. Those who forget the offerings find the knocking changes. It leads to dead ends. Warns too late. Falls silent before the collapse. Tappers might be the ghosts of miners who died below. They might be older things that adopted the role.

Wight.text: Wight: The ancient dead who refuse to rest. Not mindless undead but preserved warriors and kings, buried in barrows and tombs of power, who wake when their purposes are threatened. Remember their lives, oaths, grudges. Might rise to guard burial gold, avenge an ancient wrong, or defend lands it ruled a thousand years ago. Can be reasoned with—have personalities, pride, remnants of honor—but the dead have different priorities than the living. A wight-king who rises to repel invaders might not recognize when the invasion ends. Might decide the entire living world is the invasion. Command the lesser dead, wield weapons of old power, and carry the cold of the grave with them. Wights are bound to their barrows; they weaken away from them and must return before dawn. Destroying a wight requires finding what binds it—an oath unfulfilled, a treasure it guards, a wrong unavenged—and resolving it. Or simply overwhelming force, if you have it.

Strigoi.text: Strigoi: The feral dead who rise hungry. What happens when burial goes wrong—the corpse not properly shrouded, the killer buried in consecrated ground, the murdered unavenged. Claw free looking wrong: gray-white skin stretched tight, limbs elongated and bent at bad angles, fingers ending in black nails, mouths split too wide and filled with needle teeth. Move in jerks and scuttles, unnervingly fast, climbing walls and ceilings as easily as floors. Hunt in packs, denning in caves or ruins by day, draining blood from isolated victims by night. A strigoi bite spreads the hunger; the drained rise within three days unless burned or staked. Can also be created by the careless feeding of vampire lords. In a fight they swarm, grapple, bite—no weapons, no tactics, just hunger coordinated by pack instinct. Sunlight destroys them. A wooden stake through the heart pins them to the earth. The surest prevention is proper burial: coins on the eyes, shroud tied at seven points, the name spoken three times so the dead know they're dead.

Vampire.text: Vampire: Aristocracy of the undead. Retain minds, memories, ambitions. Appear human, beautiful even, until they choose otherwise: too-pale skin, canines that extend when the hunger rises. Ancient ones can shift form—bats, wolves, mist—and cloud minds with a glance. Each rules a domain through thralls, mortal servants, and terror. Cannot enter a home uninvited, cannot cross running water, cast no reflection. Sunlight burns them to ash; a stake through the heart paralyzes but doesn't kill unless followed by beheading or fire. Create strigoi carelessly, draining victims dry. Creating a true vampire requires intention—the feeding of blood back, a death and resurrection that preserves the mind. Most vampires see this as diluting their power and do it rarely. Shadow Summits has entire courts of them, playing elaborate games of status across centuries. Elsewhere they're rarer, lone predators ruling from crumbling estates. Every vampire was mortal once. Some remember what that meant. Most have decided it doesn't matter.

Dhampir.text: Dhampir: Children of vampire fathers and mortal mothers—rare, because vampires rarely bother with such things, and rarer still to survive the birth. Inherit the hunger diluted: they can eat food, walk in sunlight, but blood calls to them and mortal life feels thin, temporary, unreal. Most can sense the undead, feel the cold presence of vampires and strigoi like pressure behind the eyes. Some inherit more—unnatural speed, strength, the ability to see in darkness. Vampires consider them useful tools or embarrassing mistakes. Mortals distrust them, sensing something wrong. Many become hunters, killing their sires' kind—whether from righteousness, self-loathing, or simply because they're built for it. Others seek out their vampire parent, wanting answers, belonging, or revenge. A dhampir who drinks vampire blood grows stronger but more monstrous; one who abstains stays more human but weaker.

Redcap.text: Redcap: Murderous fey that haunt places of old violence. Knee-high, wizened, with glowing eyes and teeth filed to iron points. Wear caps soaked in the blood of their kills—if the cap dries, they die. This makes them relentless hunters. Nest in ruined keeps, border towers, old execution grounds, anywhere blood soaked the stone. They're the reason some ruins stay ruined. Redcaps are fey, bound by old rules: cannot cross running water, cannot enter a home uninvited, cannot catch you if you reach hallowed ground. Terrifyingly fast and hunt in packs. Iron-shod boots can crack stone. Iron pikes find gaps in armor. Some 'adopt' violent criminals or mercenary bands, following in their wake to wet their caps.

Church Grim.text: Church Grim: Guardian spirits of sacred ground. When a church or shrine was consecrated, the first creature buried in its yard became its eternal warden—usually a black dog, though sometimes a pig, ram, or horse sacrificed for the purpose. Protects the dead from disturbance and the living from what lurks in graveyards. Appear as shadowy animals with knowing eyes, solid enough to bite but fading at the edges. Can sense intent—graverobbers and necromancers cannot hide their purpose from it. Cannot leave consecrated ground but are nearly invincible within it. An active church has a grim that knows its duty.

Boggart.text: Boggart: household spirit gone wrong. Begin as brownies—helpful hearth-fey that clean, mend, and do small kindnesses in exchange for cream and bread left by the fire. But insult a brownie, forget its offerings, or speak of it with contempt, and it curdles into a boggart. Boggarts sour milk, hide tools, pinch sleeping children, cause fires and accidents. Grow uglier as their resentment deepens—warty, long-nosed, with fingers like twigs. The curse of a boggart is that it cannot be driven out. It is bound to the household, the family, sometimes the bloodline. Families who flee find the boggart waiting in their new home. Only appeasement, trickery, or breaking the original bond can end a boggart's torment. The old methods involve convincing it to leave of its own will—but boggarts are bitter, and bitter things don't forgive easily.

Will-'o'-the-wisp.text: Will-o'-the-Wisp: Pale lights that drift over marshes, bogs, and fens. Cold flames that cast no heat and leave no smoke. Flicker at the edge of vision, retreat when approached—always just ahead, always deeper into treacherous ground. Folk wisdom is clear: don't follow. But the wisps mark something. Sometimes the dead, bodies lost to the mire waiting to be found. Sometimes treasure swallowed by the bog centuries ago. Neither malicious nor kind. Simply are—lights in the dark, leading somewhere.

Wendigo.text: Wendigo: Gaunt, towering humanoid with gray flesh stretched over visible ribs, elongated limbs ending in clawed hands, and a deer's bleached skull for a face—antlers and all, eye sockets holding pale knowing light. Twelve feet tall or more; the oldest are larger. Supernaturally fast, strong enough to tear limbs free, and nearly impossible to tire or outrun. Mimic human voices perfectly—cries for help, familiar names, a child's weeping—to lure prey close. Presence spreads hunger like plague: dreams of flesh, intrusive thoughts. Fire hurts them badly. Speaking their true name—their mortal name, from before—causes them agony. Every wendigo was mortal once. Someone who faced starvation and chose survival by eating the dead, then the living-and was damned for it. Grow larger the more they consume, but satisfaction never comes.

Night Hag.text: Night Hag: Withered crones with corpse-blue skin, lank white hair. They ride sleepers—crouching on chests, stealing breath, filling dreams with slow terror. Victims wake exhausted, bruised, remembering only dread. Night after night the hag returns until the sleeper wastes away. But hags don't choose randomly. They come to the guilt-ridden, the oathbreakers, those who owe debts to the dead. Sometimes they're sent—a dying curse, a scorned woman's bargain, payment for an old slight. A hag riding someone means that person did something, or someone wants them destroyed. To ride, a hag must shed her skin and hide it nearby. Find the skin, and you hold her life in your hands—she'll bargain for almost anything. Cold iron bars her passage. A knife under the pillow cuts her if she tries to sit. Certain old prayers ward for a night. But lasting peace means settling whatever debt drew her, or destroying the hag herself.

Specter.text: Specter: Bodiless malice, and what is left when a death was bad enough that the Shadelands would not take it quietly. A dim human shape, cold at its edges, visible mostly by what it does to lamplight. It chills what it touches and pulls the warmth out of the living, and ordinary steel passes through it — silver, moonstone, and radiant work are what answer. Specters gather where the barrier between worlds runs thin, in old killing-grounds and sealed places, and they do not leave the ground that made them.

Ghast.text: Ghast: Pack leaders of the corpse-eaters. Gaunt, gray-skinned, moving with terrible speed. Their touch paralyzes—the body frozen while the mind stays aware. They remember fragments of who they were, which makes them worse. Ghasts arise where many died badly without proper rites: battlefields, plague pits. The first to rise becomes the ghast; those it feeds upon rise as ghouls, bound to follow. A ghast pack means mass death went unaddressed, and the pack grows until someone deals with it. They won't cross salt lines or enter homes without invitation. Fire drives them back. But only destroying the original ghast—the first one, the source—ends the pack for good. The others keep rising until that's done.

Giant Burrow-Beetle.text: Giant Burrow-Beetle: Armored burrowers the size of cattle, mandibles that shear through bone. Ambush predators—they feel vibrations through the earth and erupt beneath prey. Solitary and territorial. Burrow-beetles are scavengers as much as hunters, drawn to carrion and old death. Their tunnels often break into places long buried: barrows, collapsed cellars, mass graves, ruins swallowed by time. Miners and farmers know the signs—circular sinkholes, soil that sounds hollow. A beetle denning near a village usually means it's found something underground worth investigating. The creatures themselves are dangerous but simple: stay off soft ground, watch for sink-signs, and if you must fight, flip them. The underbelly is soft.

Gorilla.text: Gorilla: Large, powerful primate. Muscular build, black fur, distinctive face. Generally peaceful, but territorial when threatened. Immense strength, can cause serious injury. Strength: Physical power, agility in forested areas. Weakness: Non-aggressive unless provoked, limited tool use.

Ahool.text: Ahool: Bat-winged hunters with ape-like bodies, wingspans wider than a man is tall. Silent in flight until the wind of their dive. Rare enough that some villages don't believe in them until one strikes. They take prey alive when they can, carrying victims back to high nests—cliff faces, ruined towers, places difficult to reach by land. Why alive isn't clear. The nests hold answers, and bones, and sometimes survivors. Ahools are territorial; one claiming hunting ground near a settlement won't leave until driven out or killed. Torches and loud noise can disrupt their echolocation. They won't pursue into enclosed spaces. On the ground they're clumsy, vulnerable—but getting one grounded is the hard part.

White Ape.text: White Ape: Albino primate of unusual size and ferocity. Pale fur, red eyes, larger than normal apes. Aggressive and territorial, hunts in groups. Powerful enough to tear apart armor, uses primitive tools. Strength: Physical might, pack tactics, adaptability. Weakness: Sensitive to sunlight, can be outsmarted.

Awakened Tree.text: Awakened Tree: A tree that moves, watches, acts. Gnarled features form in the bark—not quite faces, but close enough. Roots pull free of earth, branches reach with purpose. Immensely strong, slow but relentless, capable of crushing armor or dragging victims underground through shifting soil. The land often answers them—ground becomes treacherous, branches block escape routes. Vulnerable to fire, but threatening an awakened tree with fire in its own forest makes enemies of everything around you. Trees don't wake on their own. Something stirs them: a druid's dying act, an old bargain coming due, blood spilled at their roots, land wounded badly enough that the forest responds. What they want depends on what woke them. And old trees remember what they've witnessed—murders, buried secrets, forgotten graves. They speak slowly if they speak at all, but they know things.

Banshee.text: Banshee: Spectral women, pale and hollow-eyed, wild hair and mouths too wide. Their wail carries for leagues—grief given voice, a sound that frays the soul. The scream up close can stop a heart, and even from a distance it brings nightmares, madness, death by despair. Banshees are bound to bloodlines, compelled to wail when death approaches someone of that blood. They don't choose this—the keening pours out of them like breath. A banshee is a crisis: her wailing harms everyone in earshot. Prevent the death she's mourning, and she goes quiet. Some will parlay if their mad grief can be placated through force, guile or charm—in their lucid moments, they know how the death is coming, sometimes even how to stop it. But try to silence her by force, and the scream becomes a weapon turned on you.

Worghul.text: Worghul: Goblin wolf-shifters. Created by ancient wolf-binding ritual, once rare and difficult, now made by common by the Dragon Queen's magical gifts to the Goblinate's war-shamans. In wolf form: black-furred, yellow-eyed, indistinguishable from natural wolves at a distance. In goblin form: slight, quick, fingers still remembering claws.
