The shift takes three heartbeats—their only vulnerable moment. Serve the Goblinate as scouts and infiltrators. A pack can live as wolves for months behind enemy lines, hunting deer, avoiding notice. Then shift back for the mission: cut supply lines, poison wells, kidnap a commander's child, slit a sentinel's throat. Shift again, vanish into the woods. Silver burns them.

Basilisk.text: Basilisk: Reptilian monster with a petrifying gaze. Lizard-like body, eight legs, crown-like crest. Territorial, turns victims to stone with its gaze. Petrifying stare, venomous bite. Strength: Ability to turn creatures to stone. Weakness: Can petrify itself if it sees its reflection.

Giant Bat.text: Giant Bat: Oversized, carnivorous bat. Wingspan of 15 feet or more, sharp fangs. Nocturnal hunter, uses echolocation. Can carry off medium-sized prey. Strength: Flight, excellent hearing. Weakness: Poor eyesight, vulnerable to loud noises.

Dire Wolf.text: Dire wolf: Massive, intelligent pack hunters. Twice the size of normal wolves, with glowing eyes. Hunt in coordinated packs, use advanced tactics. Can bring down large prey or small groups of travelers. Strength: Pack coordination, raw power. Weakness: Fire, fear of loud noises.

Cave Bear.text: Cave Bear: Massive, prehistoric bear species. Larger than modern bears, thick fur, powerful claws. Highly territorial, omnivorous. Immense strength, can easily kill with a single swipe. Strength: Thick hide, powerful sense of smell. Weakness: Poor eyesight, can be outmaneuvered.

Giant Eagle.text: Giant Eagle: Enormous bird of prey, often intelligent. Eagle-like, with wingspans up to 20 feet. Proud, territorial, sometimes allies with good-aligned beings. Powerful talons and beak, can carry off large prey. Strength: Flight, keen eyesight. Weakness: Vulnerable to attacks while carrying prey.

Bullywug.text: Bullywug: Amphibious frog-like humanoids. Frog-like features, webbed hands and feet, bulbous eyes. Tribal, aggressive, often found in swamps. Ambush predators, use primitive weapons. Strength: Amphibious nature, camouflage in marshy areas. Weakness: Dependent on moist environments, easily dehydrated.

Carnivorous Plant.text: Carnivorous Plant: Large plant with animal-like digestive abilities. Varies, often with trap-like leaves or maws. Lures prey with scent or appearance, then traps and digests. Can entangle and slowly digest creatures. Strength: Camouflage, powerful digestive acids. Weakness: Immobile, vulnerable to fire and cold.

Corpse-eater.text: Corpse-eater: Scavenging aberration resembling a giant centipede. Long, segmented body with multiple legs and tentacles. Hunts in dark, underground areas, paralyzed prey. Paralyzing tentacles, powerful mandibles. Strength: Can climb walls and ceilings, keen sense of smell. Weakness: Vulnerable to bright light, slow on open ground.

Centaur.text: Centaur: Half-human, half-horse beings. Human torso atop a horse's body. Tribal, often nomadic, skilled archers. Powerful charge attacks, skilled with bows. Strength: Speed, strength, and archery skills. Weakness: Large size makes hiding difficult, vulnerable to attacks on human torso.

Chimera.text: Chimera: Monstrous hybrid of lion, goat, and dragon. Lion's body, goat's head, dragon's head and wings. Aggressive, territorial, hunts large prey. Multiple attacks from different heads, can breathe fire. Strength: Flight, varied attack options. Weakness: Heads may disagree, vulnerable to attacks on lion body.

Cockatrice.text: Cockatrice: Hybrid of rooster and reptile with petrifying ability. Rooster-like body with reptilian tail and wings. Aggressive, attacks with beak and petrifying touch. Its touch can turn creatures to stone. Strength: Flight, petrification ability. Weakness: Small size, vulnerable to its own petrification.

Giant Crab.text: Giant Crab: Enormous crustacean with powerful pincers. Crab-like, but many times larger than normal. Territorial, lurks in shallow waters or tidal areas. Can crush prey with massive claws. Strength: Hard shell, powerful grip. Weakness: Slow on land, vulnerable when molting.

Cyclops.text: Cyclops: Giant humanoid with a single eye. Massive humanoid form with one central eye. Often solitary, can be territorial or aggressive. Immense strength, can throw boulders. Strength: Physical power, tough skin. Weakness: Poor depth perception due to single eye.

Death Knight.text: Death Knight: Undead warrior of great power and evil. Skeletal or mummified warrior in heavy armor. Commands lesser undead, seeks to spread death. Powerful warrior skills, necromantic magic. Strength: Undead resilience, tactical mind. Weakness: Vulnerable to holy magic and symbols.

Doppelganger.text: Doppelganger: Shapeshifting humanoid that can mimic others. Natural form is plain, hairless humanoid. Infiltrates societies by impersonating individuals. Can perfectly mimic appearance and voice of others. Strength: Shapeshifting ability, natural insight into others' minds. Weakness: Cannot change mass significantly, vulnerable in natural form.

Dragon Turtle.text: Dragon Turtle: Massive aquatic creature combining dragon and turtle traits. Enormous turtle with dragon-like head and tail. Territorial, often demands tribute from ships. Can capsize ships, breathes scalding steam. Strength: Nearly impenetrable shell, powerful in water. Weakness: Slow on land, vulnerable to cold-based attacks.

Half-spider.text: Half-spider: Half-human, half-spider. Human upper body on a giant spider's lower body. Cruel hunters, often serve dark sorcerers or eldritch entities. Combines human magic with spider abilities. Strength: Wall-climbing, web-spinning, magical prowess. Weakness: Sunlight sensitivity, vulnerable to anti-magic fields.

Elemental.text: Elemental: Living embodiment of a natural element. Varies based on element (air, earth, fire, water). Follows nature of its element, often neutral to mortals. Powerful control over its element. Strength: Immune to many physical attacks, can merge with element. Weakness: Vulnerable to opposing elements, can be bound by magic.

Ettin.text: Ettin: Two-headed giant. Large, brutish humanoid with two heads. Aggressive, often confused due to conflicting heads. Great strength, difficult to surprise. Strength: One head always alert, powerful melee attacks. Weakness: Internal conflicts between heads, low intelligence.

Fairy.text: Fairy: Tiny, magical humanoid beings. Diminutive humanoid with insect-like wings. Mischievous, playful, sometimes helpful to nature. Can cast illusions and charms. Strength: Flight, innate magic, ability to turn invisible. Weakness: Physically weak, vulnerable to iron.

Feathered Serpent.text: Feathered Serpent: Mythical winged serpent, often revered as a deity. Large serpent with colorful feathers and wings. Wise and ancient, often acts as guardian or advisor. Powerful magic, hypnotic gaze. Strength: Flight, divine or arcane magic, wisdom. Weakness: Pride, can be bound by certain rituals.

Gargoyle.text: Gargoyle: Animated stone statues, often guardians. Grotesque winged humanoid made of stone. Patient sentinels, attack intruders without mercy. Can blend in with architecture, surprise attacks. Strength: Stone body resistant to many attacks, flight. Weakness: Unintelligent, vulnerable to magic that affects objects.

Mummy.text: Mummy: Undead creature preserved through ancient rituals. Humanoid wrapped in bandages, often wearing ancient garb. Guards tombs, seeks vengeance on tomb robbers. Spreads cursed rot with its touch, immune to many weapons. Strength: Undead resilience, ancient magic powers. Weakness: Vulnerable to fire, can be put to rest with proper rituals.

Ogre.text: Ogre: Massive, dim-witted creatures of prodigious strength. Nine to ten feet tall with barrel chests and thick limbs. Often wear crude armor made from multiple sets of gear. Take up residence in abandoned structures or caves near traveled areas. Some hire themselves out as muscle to bandit groups or criminal gangs. Surprisingly skilled at crafting large-scale weapons like siege engines. Can break down walls or flip wagons with bare hands. Use simple but effective ambush tactics. Strength: Raw physical power, thick hide resistant to normal weapons. Weakness: Easy to outsmart, poor stamina for extended fights.

Werebear.text: Werebear: Humanoid that can transform into a bear-human hybrid. Human form, bear form, or a muscular hybrid of both. Often solitary, can be noble protectors of nature. Immense strength in bear form, spreads lycanthropy. Strength: Regeneration, immunity to non-silver weapons. Weakness: Vulnerable to silver, may lose control during full moon.

Wererat.text: Wererat: Humanoid that can transform into a rat-human hybrid. Human form, giant rat form, or a ratlike humanoid. Sneaky, often found in urban environments. Spreads lycanthropy, often works in packs. Strength: Stealth, disease resistance, can squeeze through small spaces. Weakness: Vulnerable to silver, weaker than other lycanthropes.

Werewolf.text: Werewolf: Humanoid that can transform into a wolf-human hybrid. Human form, wolf form, or a bestial wolf-man hybrid. Aggressive, often struggles with dual nature. Powerful in wolf form, spreads lycanthropy through bites. Strength: Enhanced senses, regeneration, immunity to normal weapons. Weakness: Vulnerable to silver, may lose control during full moon.

Merfolk.text: Merfolk: Aquatic humanoids with fish-like lower bodies. Human upper body, fish-like tail instead of legs. Varied societies underwater, some peaceful, some aggressive. Skilled with tridents and water-based magic. Strength: Excellent swimmers, can breathe underwater. Weakness: Limited mobility on land, vulnerable to dehydration.

Myconid.text: Myconid: Sentient humanoid fungi, mushroom people as tall as a man, with broad caps, arms and legs. Peaceful and slow to decide, they live in underground colonies, farm fungus, and speak mind to mind: a listener hears their words as quiet thoughts in their own language. A threatened myconid can press calm or sleep into a hostile mind. Strength: hard to touch with mind-affecting magic. Weakness: fire and strong sunlight.

Nightmare.text: Nightmare: Fiendish horse-like creature from Ur. Black horse with flaming hooves and mane, glowing red eyes. Evil and aggressive, often serves as mount for powerful fiends. Can travel between planes, trampling and fire attacks. Strength: Flight, fire immunity, can run on air. Weakness: Vulnerable to light.

Nixie.text: Nixie: Small water fey with fish-like qualities. Diminutive humanoid with bluish-green skin and webbed fingers. Playful, protective of their aquatic homes. Can charm humanoids to serve them underwater. Strength: Water breathing, can grant water breathing to others. Weakness: Physically weak, vulnerable when out of water.

Dryad.text: Dryad: Tree nymph bound to a specific tree. Beautiful female humanoid with bark-like skin and leafy hair. Shy, protective of their forests. Can charm humanoids, control plants. Strength: Merge with trees, nature-based magic. Weakness: Cannot stray far from their bound tree, vulnerable to fire.

Oni.text: Oni: Ogre-like creature with magical abilities. Large, muscular humanoid with colorful skin and horns. Cunning and cruel, often disguises itself to infiltrate societies. Powerful physical attacks combined with magic use. Strength: Shape-changing abilities, flight, regeneration. Weakness: Vulnerable to cold iron weapons.

Gelatinous Cube.text: Gelatinous Cube: Large, cube-shaped ooze that consumes organic matter. Transparent cube of jelly-like substance. Mindlessly roams dungeons, absorbing debris and creatures. Nearly invisible in dungeons, paralyzing touch. Strength: Immune to many types of damage, can engulf creatures. Weakness: Slow-moving, vulnerable to attacks that affect its entire mass.

Pixie.text: Pixie: Tiny, mischievous fey creature. Diminutive humanoid with insect-like wings, often glowing. Playful, sometimes helpful, enjoys tricks. Can turn invisible, cast powerful illusions. Strength: Flight, innate magic abilities, hard to detect. Weakness: Physically very weak, vulnerable to iron.

Rakshasa.text: Rakshasa: Evil spirits in humanoid form. Human-like with animal features, often tiger-headed. Manipulative, enjoys luxury and corrupting others. Powerful spellcasters, can read minds. Strength: Immune to most spells, shape-changing abilities. Weakness: Vulnerable to blessed crossbow bolts, cannot disguise their backwards hands.

Revenant.text: Revenant: Undead being returned from death to seek vengeance. Decaying corpse with glowing eyes. Single-mindedly pursues its killer or sworn enemy. Relentless pursuit, cannot be permanently killed until vengeance is achieved. Strength: Regeneration, knows location of its target. Weakness: Destroyed if its mission is completed, vulnerable to holy magic.

Roc.text: Roc: Gigantic bird of prey. Enormous eagle-like bird, large enough to carry elephants. Territorial, nests in high mountains. Can snatch up large creatures, devastates areas with its massive wings. Strength: Incredible size and strength, excellent vision. Weakness: Limited intelligence, vulnerable to attacks on its eyes.

Ferrovore.text: Ferrovore: Bizarre creature that corrodes metal. Insect-like body with long antennae and a strange, paddle-like tail. Seeks out metal to consume. Touch rapidly corrodes metal items and armor. Strength: Ability to destroy metal equipment, hard carapace. Weakness: No interest in non-metal items, can be easily distracted by metal objects.

Packspider.text: Packspider: Wolf-sized arachnids, fur-covered, forward-facing eyes, mandibles that crush bone. Hunt in family groups—coordinated, relentless, exhausting prey before overwhelming it. Dens hold multiple generations; younger spiders learn tactics from adults. Travelers learn the signs: silk trail-markers on trees, the clicking calls they use to coordinate. Packspiders are territorial. A family claiming hunting ground near a settlement won't move on—the prey is too easy. Avoid fire and water. Kill the dominant spider and the pack scatters, disorganized, often turning on each other. Their silk is valuable, their dens sometimes hold remains worth recovering—but clearing a den means facing the whole family at once.

Satyr.text: Satyr: Half-man, half-goat forest dweller. Human upper body, goat legs and horns. Hedonistic, loves music, wine, and dance. Can charm with music, skilled with bow and arrow. Strength: Agile, knows forest magic. Weakness: Easily distracted by pleasures, vulnerable to iron.

Shambling Mound.text: Shambling Mound: Large plant creature composed of rotting vegetation. Humanoid-shaped mass of vines, leaves, and swamp matter. Roams swamps and dark forests, engulfs prey. Can engulf and suffocate victims, regrows quickly. Strength: Immune to electricity (which actually heals it), resistant to fire and cold. Weakness: Vulnerable to dehydration, slowed by bright light.

Stirge.text: Stirge: Small, blood-sucking flying creature. Bat-like body with bird-like features and a long proboscis. Swarms victims to drain blood. Attaches to prey and drains blood quickly. Strength: Flight, can detect warm-blooded creatures. Weakness: Very fragile, easily killed if caught.

Grove Sentinel.text: Grove Sentinel: Sentient, mobile tree creature. Massive humanoid made of bark, branches, and leaves. Protects forests, slow to anger but terrible when roused. Immense strength, ability to animate trees. Strength: Tough bark skin, connection to nature. Weakness: Vulnerable to fire, slow-moving.

Triton.text: Triton: Aquatic humanoids, guardians of the deep. Human-like with blue-green skin, fins, and webbed hands. Proud warriors, protect the ocean from threats. Skilled with tridents and water-based magic. Strength: Can breathe air and water, resistant to cold. Weakness: Uncomfortable in dry environments, vulnerable to fire.

Unicorn.text: Unicorn: Magical horse-like creature with a single horn. Beautiful white horse with a spiraling horn on its forehead. Noble and good, protects forests and innocent creatures. Powerful magic, can teleport and heal. Strength: Magic resistance, healing abilities, teleportation. Weakness: Can be lured by pure-hearted individuals, especially maidens.

Marsh Hydra.text: Marsh Hydra: Amphibious multi-headed serpent adapted to wetland hunting. Sleek, dark-scaled body with long necks and narrow crocodilian heads, often covered in clinging swamp vegetation. Patient ambush predator that uses submerged heads as lures while keeping others concealed below the surface. Known to capsize boats and raid riverside settlements. Can attack multiple targets simultaneously, regenerates damaged heads, excellent swimmer. Strength: Masterful ambush tactics, powerful in water, regeneration. Weakness: Heads can be prevented from regenerating by fire, relatively slow on land.

Frost Drake.text: Frost Drake: Lesser draconic predator native to cold mountain environments. Heavily muscled serpentine body with short, powerful wings and ice-blue scales. Prominent horn-like crests used in territorial displays. Aggressive raiders that use storms as cover, often targeting caravans and outposts. Mark territory with frozen trophies from past kills. Freezing breath can immobilize prey, exceptional climber despite size. Strength: Perfectly adapted to cold and high altitude, excellent vision in whiteout conditions. Weakness: Less intelligent than true dragons, highly territorial which makes movements predictable.

Stonescale Eel.text: Stonescale Eel: Serpentine ambush predator that thrives in shallow coastal waters and urban waterways. Long, eel-like body with crocodilian head, hard, stone-colored scales and stubby legs. Squeezes through drainage systems, emerges to snatch prey from walkways and low bridges. Hoards trinkets in underwater dens. Can move surprisingly fast on land, powerful bite can crack boat hulls. Strength: Perfect camouflage in built waterways, can breathe air indefinitely. Weakness: Territorial nature makes hunting patterns predictable, weakened by loud sounds.

Lesser Kraken.text: Lesser Kraken: Opportunistic cephalopod native to shallow seas but that adapts to harbor and canal environments. Dark-skinned octopoid with armored tentacles and beak-like maw, about size of fishing boat. Disables ships by damaging rudders and anchor chains, creates lairs in shipwrecks and sea caves. Sometimes baited by smugglers to attack competitor vessels. Intelligent enough to plan attacks, can manipulate simple tools and mechanisms. Strength: Expert at destroying vital ship components, incredible grip strength. Weakness: Highly territorial, can be baited with certain chemical scents, needs deep water to escape.

Giant Cave Spider.text: Giant Cave Spider: Massive cave spider common in ruins and cave country across Larion. Horse-sized arachnid with thick bristled legs. Mandibles the size of sword blades. Ambush predator that creates massive web networks in ruins and ravines. Wraps prey in webbing and drags them back to lair for later consumption. Web strands strong enough to trap humans, venom causes rapid paralysis. Strength: Can move silently despite massive size, excellent night vision. Weakness: Relies heavily on web vibrations for sensing prey, vulnerable to fire.

Bloodwing.text: Bloodwing: Grotesque, enormous mosquito common in fens and marsh country. Man-sized flying insect with translucent wings and a needle-like proboscis as long as a spear. Swollen abdomen pulses red with stolen blood. Hunts at dawn and dusk, drawn to large mammals including horses and humans. Can drain a horse in minutes. Multiple feedings cause abdomen to swell until it must rest on the ground. Proboscis can pierce light armor, victims quickly weaken from blood loss. Strength: Nearly silent in flight, can detect warm blood at great distances. Weakness: Sluggish and vulnerable when gorged with blood, easily crippled by damage to wings.

Scourge Scorpion.text: Scourge Scorpion: Nightmarish arachnid found in badlands and cavern country. Bull-sized scorpion with three segmented tails ending in barbed stingers. Mottled exoskeleton patterns resemble bark or stone. Clusters of eyes gleam like black gems. Inverted ambush predator that clings to cave ceilings or thick tree branches. Drops onto prey using all three tails to inject different toxins. Sometimes creates permanent hunting perches by coating surfaces with sticky secretions. Multiple venoms cause different effects: paralysis, burning pain, and tissue dissolution. Strength: Nearly invisible when still, can strike with all three tails simultaneously. Weakness: Vulnerable during molting, vulnerable to cold.

Boneworm.text: Boneworm: Massive burrowing parasite that infests the buried ruins of the Underworld. Pale, segmented worm as thick as a man's torso, with grinding circular mouthparts lined with calcium deposits from consumed bone. Body is semi-translucent, showing recently consumed matter. Tunnels through stone and soil, attracted to vibrations. Forms colonies in ancient burial grounds and battlefields. Creates extensive tunnel networks that weaken structural integrity. Can burrow through solid rock, digestive acids dissolve organic matter quickly. Strength: Nearly impossible to stop once it starts burrowing, excellent vibration sense. Weakness: Vulnerable to loud sounds, highly sensitive to bright light.

Click Lizard.text: Click Lizard: Eyeless predator evolved for hunting the lightless tunnels of the Underworld. Low-slung reptilian body with oversized front claws and complex sensory organs where eyes would be. Covered in hard scales with worn-smooth patches from squeezing through tight spaces. Hunts in small packs using echo-location clicks. Extraordinarily patient, known to stalk prey for days through tunnel systems. Often claims abandoned dwarven vaults as territory. Can track prey through solid rock, coordinated pack tactics. Strength: Perfect spatial awareness in darkness, incredibly strong for its size. Weakness: Overwhelmed by multiple sound sources, vulnerable to attacks on sensory organs.

Mire Stalker.text: Mire Stalker: Amphibious predator adapted to urban sewers and cisterns. Salamander-like body with elongated limbs and adhesive pads, mottled skin mimics environment. Expandable jaw can unhinge to swallow large prey. Claims territory around sewer junctions and storm drains. Steals from surface through grates and drains, gradually learning patterns of movement above. Sometimes keeps live prey trapped in air pockets. Can squeeze through impossibly small spaces, powerful grip prevents escape. Strength: Excellent climber on wet surfaces, can hold breath for hours. Weakness: Dependent on moisture, vulnerable to fire and alchemical purifying agents.

Corpse Render.text: Corpse Render: Scavenging horror that inhabits catacombs and burial crypts. Emaciated humanoid figure with over-long arms and retractable claws, patches of hardened skin like burial shrouds. Eyes reflect light like polished copper. Hoards bodies and carrion in deeper tunnels, emerging to raid graveyards and plague pits. Sometimes develops taste for living prey. Marks territory with distinctive scratch patterns. Carries multiple diseases, incredibly strong despite gaunt appearance. Strength: Can move silently despite size, excellent night vision, immune to most poisons. Weakness: Compulsive about defending its hoard, can be baited with fresh carrion.

Greater Silk Moth.text: Greater Silk Moth: Large moth species prized for its enchanted silk. Wing span of up to three feet, with intricate patterns that seem to move in moonlight. Cocoons shimmer with inherent magical properties. Drawn to areas of magical activity, particularly around magetowers. Colonies establish themselves in abandoned buildings. Cocoons retain magical properties even after moth emerges. None to humans, though protecting a colony from predators can be dangerous. Strength: Silk has natural magic-conducting properties, highly valued by artificers. Weakness: Completely defenseless, requires specific conditions to breed successfully.

Tarrasque.text: Tarrasque: Colossal monster of legend, embodiment of destruction. Enormous reptilian creature with shell, horns, and multiple limbs. Sleeps for eons, awakens to rampage and destroy. Nearly indestructible, can level entire cities. Strength: Regeneration, immunity to many types of damage, incredibly strong. Weakness: Can be put back to sleep with powerful magic, vulnerable to wish spells.

Trow.text: Trow: Small, vicious cave-kin of the trolls, usually no taller than a child but broad-shouldered, long-armed, gray-green, and adapted to darkness. They breed in crowded warrens beneath crags, mines, and broken hills, spreading through cracks too tight for larger creatures to follow. A lone trow is a scavenging ambusher; a swarm uses darkness, noise, false retreats, and narrow passages to separate prey before dragging isolated people into the warren. They steal tools, lamps, food, and anything bright, building their dens around whatever they can carry off, and their crude coordination becomes dangerous in a mine or cave. They lack the great troll's strength and regeneration, but share its appetite and territorial instincts. Their traits vary by warren: the trows of the Argenval Crags and Silver Mine are resistant to silver, the metal that normally bites the unnatural beasts of Carendon's wood.

Troll.text: Troll: Giant, brutish humanoids with remarkable regenerative abilities. Grotesquely tall with long arms, mottled green-gray skin, and hooked claws. Hunched posture belies explosive speed. Wounds visibly heal as you watch. Claim remote valleys and mountain passes as territory, marking boundaries with massive stone cairns. Live in loose family groups, teaching young to hunt by attacking anything that enters their domain. Sometimes keep cave bears as pets. Hard to kill without fire, become more aggressive when wounded. Incredible regeneration, powerful enough to throw boulders. Fire stops regeneration.

Ophidian.text: Ophidian: Former humans transformed through ancient rituals into hybrid snake-beings. Varies by individual and degree of transformation. Common features include patches of iridescent scales, vertically slitted pupils, and elongated canines. Advanced transformations develop hood-like growths, forked tongues, or fully serpentine lower bodies. Maintain elaborate hierarchies based on degree of transformation. Older members become increasingly obsessed with further ritual enhancement. Often manipulate local politics through a combination of charm and terror. Retain human intelligence while gaining serpentine abilities. Many develop toxic bites or hypnotic gazes. Strength: Powerful combination of human cunning and reptilian attributes. Highly resistant to poisons. Weakness: Transformation process is addictive, leading to increasingly risky ritual attempts. Vulnerable to extreme cold.

Fire Elementling.text: Fire Elementling: Living spark of elemental fire, manifesting where flame meets wild magic. Tiny humanoid figure made of living flame, leaving small burn marks with each step. Eyes flicker like candle flames. Mercurial and quick-tempered, drawn to sources of heat and fire. Some bond with blacksmiths or firefighters as assistants. Can ignite flammable materials when angered. Swarms pose serious fire hazard. Strength: Can manipulate existing fires, immune to heat and flame. Weakness: Extinguished by sufficient water or smothering. Weakened by cold.

Earth Elementling.text: Earth Elementling: Animated essence of stone and soil, emerging where earth magic runs strong. Small, stocky figure made of packed earth or living stone. Stone growths serve as eyes. Patient and methodical, often found strengthening foundations or repairing stonework. Some partner with miners to locate ore veins. Can cause localized tremors or collapse weak structures. Swarms can undermine foundations. Strength: Nearly indestructible while in contact with earth. Can merge with and manipulate stone. Weakness: Slow-moving, vulnerable when separated from ground.

Water Elementling.text: Water Elementling: Living droplet of elemental water, coalescing where water meets magical currents. Fluid humanoid shape constantly flowing and reforming. Playful and curious, found near fountains and wells. Sometimes help maintain aqueducts and irrigation systems. Can cause rapid rust or erosion. Groups can create dangerous currents. Strength: Can control water flow and pressure. Weakness: Vulnerable to extreme heat.

Air Elementling.text: Air Elementling: Living breath of wind, forming where air currents intersect with magical eddies. Nearly invisible humanoid outline visible only by the way it disturbs air and dust. Capricious and adventurous, attracted to high places and open skies. Sometimes assist sailors or windmill operators. Can create sudden gusts or vacuum pockets. Swarms generate devastating windstorms. Strength: Nearly invisible, can fly freely and manipulate air currents. Weakness: Disperses in confined spaces. Can be trapped in sealed containers.

Pitmaw.text: Pitmaw: Buried maw of the desert. Body lies deep beneath the sand—only the gullet extends upward, fifteen feet of extendable throat ending in a hidden mouth. A subtle circular depression marks the trap. A faint whisper, like breath through a hollow reed, gives it away if you're listening. Step above one and the sand becomes a funnel, suction pulling you down into an acid-filled stomach. Desert folk learn the signs: test suspicious ground with thrown stones, listen for the whisper. Pitmaws don't move once settled—a hunting ground is theirs for decades. The digestive acid fetches good coin from alchemists.

Possessor.text: Possessor: Malicious spirit that inhabits corpses and objects. Controlled bodies show unnaturally wide mouth seams and impossible joint angles. Can leap between hosts. Strength: Body possession, host jumping, memory retention, psychic immunity. Weakness: Light-based attacks, exorcism, spiritual wards, host destruction.

Smokewalker.text: Smokewalker: Spirit formed from funeral pyre smoke, shifts between human shape and smoke column. Only visible to pure hearts until attack. Can flow through cracks and suffocate victims. Strength: Selective invisibility, smoke form, suffocation attacks, fire immunity. Weakness: Water, strong winds, detection by pure hearts.

Hundredhands.text: Hundredhands: Towering giant with fifty heads and hundred arms, each capable of independent action. Can attack dozens simultaneously or focus all hands on single task. Walking army. Strength: Multiple attacks, independent heads, massive reach, coordination. Weakness: Confusion tactics, overwhelming single point, decision paralysis.

Webwidow.text: Webwidow: Giant spider that transforms into beautiful woman. Spins invisible silk traps and injects paralyzing venom through kiss or touch. Prefers to cocoon victims alive. Strength: Shapeshifting, invisible webs, paralytic venom, enchanting beauty. Weakness: Fire, detection by shadow, web cutting.

Watercharger.text: Watercharger: Shapeshifting water spirit appearing as beautiful horse near water. Adhesive skin traps riders, then dives deep to drown them. Can walk on water and control currents. Strength: Water walking, current control, adhesive skin, drowning attacks. Weakness: Fire, forced land combat, binding rituals.

Scaletitan.text: Scaletitan: Serpentine draconic creature with only front legs, no wings. Armored scales except throat. Grows larger by molting, becomes more ravenous. Can squeeze through impossible spaces. Strength: Armor scales, size growth, compression, battering ram strikes. Weakness: Throat vulnerability, molting periods, size restrictions.

Doomwing.text: Doomwing: Tall humanoid with giant moth wings and glowing red eyes. Appears before disasters, gaze induces prophetic nightmares of coming catastrophe. Causes panic and poor decisions. Strength: Disaster prophecy, fear induction, psychic immunity, dark resistance. Weakness: Light sensitivity, hope inspiration, prophecy prevention.

Drownmaiden.text: Drownmaiden: Vengeful spirit of drowned woman with green hair and bloated skin. Hypnotic singing lures victims to watery deaths in jealous embrace. Can be banished by true name. Strength: Hypnotic song, water domain, drowning attacks, beautiful illusion. Weakness: True name binding, water avoidance, counter-songs.

Sealskin.text: Sealskin: Shapeshifter between seal and human form by removing seal skin. Must obey whoever steals their pelt. Exceptional swimmers, communicate with sea creatures. Strength: Dual forms, water mastery, sea creature communication, cold resistance. Weakness: Skin theft, form binding, land vulnerability.

Skyblessed.text: Skyblessed: Celestial being with magnificent wings wearing iridescent robes that never touch ground. Music heals wounds but prolonged presence causes mortals to fade. Divine messenger. Strength: Flight, healing music, divine protection, blessing bestowal. Weakness: Mortal corruption, earthly binding, divine commands.

Darkrager.text: Darkrager: Colossal sea spirit as featureless black torso rising from calm seas. Absorbs light, capsizes ships, controls water pressure. Collects drowned souls in glowing pearls. Strength: Light absorption, ship destruction, pressure control, soul collection. Weakness: Fire attacks, light sources, pearl destruction.

Flameshifter.text: Flameshifter: Fire-breathing dragon that shapeshifts into handsome man by night. Only small scale behind ear reveals true nature. Seeks genuine romance with mortals. Strength: Shapeshifting, fire control, charm, flight capability. Weakness: True love vulnerability, scale detection, emotional manipulation.

Soul Thief.text: Soul Thief: Underworld demon that snatches unburied dead. Touch causes paralysis, casts no shadow. Cannot cross running water or sanctified ground. Collects souls in crystal vials. Strength: Soul capture, paralytic touch, shadow immunity, stealth. Weakness: Running water, sacred ground, vial destruction, light attacks.

Weeping Hunter.text: Weeping Hunter: Amphibious predator with dog body, monkey hands, and tail-hand. Mimics child crying to lure victims to water. Devours only eyes, teeth, and fingernails. Strength: Voice mimicry, aquatic mobility, trophy collection, specific targeting. Weakness: Sound detection, water avoidance, protective barriers.

Shipclaw.text: Shipclaw: Small fish with adhesive crest that latches onto ships, bringing them to complete stop. Schools can drag vessels underwater. Alpha marks target ships. Strength: Ship stopping, coordinated attacks, underwater dragging, adhesive secretion. Weakness: Fire, targeted removal, alpha elimination.

Stormwing.text: Stormwing: Giant eagle that causes winds with wing beats. Razor-sharp feathers slice armor, wind gusts tear people apart. Nests on highest peaks, sees through generated winds. Strength: Wind immunity, razor feathers, distance vision, mountain domain. Weakness: Enclosed spaces, feather deflection, grounding.

Bonebiter.text: Bonebiter: Beast with stag body, lion chest, horse hooves. Mimics human voices, has ridged bone that cuts through anything. Collects and digests bones for strength. Strength: Voice mimicry, bone cutting, strength absorption, bone projectiles. Weakness: Bone shortage, voice recognition, defensive positioning.

Icesnatcher.text: Icesnatcher: Human-like sea creature with green skin that hums to lure people to water. Keeps victims in baby carrier under ice. Touch causes frostbite, can freeze water. Strength: Hypnotic humming, ice manipulation, frostbite touch, victim preservation. Weakness: Heat sources, loud noises, carrier targeting.

Gulper.text: Gulper: Gluttonous beast with goat body and eyes beneath massive jaws. Devours anything, absorbs properties of consumed creatures. Temporarily gains victim characteristics. Strength: Universal consumption, property absorption, characteristic mimicry, endless hunger. Weakness: Dietary restrictions, absorption overload, specific prey targeting.

Magmaborn.text: Magmaborn: Humanoid creature of living magma and rock that dwells in volcanoes. Body glows with inner fire, leaves smoldering footprints. Hurls magma globs and superheats metal weapons. Strength: Fire immunity, magma attacks, metal heating, natural illumination. Weakness: Water, extreme cold, heat dissipation.

Deathgazer.text: Deathgazer: Swamp beast with bull body and weak neck that drags heavy head along ground. Breath causes disease, eyes cause petrification. Approach from behind. Strength: Petrifying gaze, disease breath, poison resistance. Weakness: Rear approach, mirrors, neck vulnerability.

The Bloodhunters.text: The Bloodhunters: An aristocratic order of duelists and blood-mages who hunt the dead, seated at the Red Chantry on the moors of Whitemoor. They live finely, fight with antique blades and old blood-magic, and bear the corruption of their craft as a mark of pride — the last line of defense against the dark, feared for their powers, relied on for their results. They take in any who would learn the craft and take up the cause, and they police their own without mercy, quietly hunting down those of their number who lose their way.

The Syndicate.text: The Syndicate (criminal organization): The Syndicate is the web of crime-lords that holds the underside of Larion. Every city of any size has its boss, grown fat on smuggling, extortion, theft, and the selling of people, and everyone knows who he is — he doesn't hide, because being feared is the point. Above the local bosses sit greater bosses in greater cities, and above them the High Men, the richest and most feared crime-lords alive, who command the rest through tribute, debt, and murder. Syndicate men wear their allegiance in ink: an open black hand tattooed on the neck or forearm — the hand that takes the cut — so that anyone who crosses them knows exactly whose man they are hurting. The mark is a threat that walks. Crossing the Syndicate means a knife in the dark or the trade choked off; princes tolerate it because rooting it out costs more than living with it.

Children of the Wyrm.text: Children of the Wyrm: A dragon cult of scattered cells whose members seek to transform themselves into draconic beings using ancient dragon remains. Bones, scales, and other dragon materials are alchemically processed into reagents used in ritual transformations that produce dracomorphs or wyrmfiends - abominations whose bodies twist with scales, claws, and malformed wings, while granting breath weapons, flight and even long-lost draconic magic. Cultists search for and raid dragon tombs and fuel a black market in dragon relics. Believe they are ascending to dragonhood and earning their place as the Wyrm's true offspring. Some cult cells have turned to sacrificing dragonkin when ancient dragon remains prove too rare or expensive. Cult cells recruit the desperate, the power-hungry, and those seeking to become something greater than their birth allowed.

The Wolfpack.text: The Wolfpack: An orc-founded warrior society at Wolfpack Lodge in the Orc Wolds, open to fighters, hunters, shamans, scouts, healers, beast handlers, spellcasters, berserkers, and other capable people of any blood. Trial-Hunters earn admission through one witnessed proving deed and receive the pack clasp as Packmates. Three recognized deeds earn standing as Proven Hunter. Proven Hunters may voluntarily seek a mutual bond with a beast-spirit at the Spirit Hearth; wolf is traditional but not mandatory. Four serious deeds after that bond may earn recognition as Pack-Captain, trusted to lead lodge contracts and willing packmates beneath the singular Pack-Leader. Fury is respected but never required. The Pack takes dangerous beasts, rescues, defenses, escorts, monster lairs, raiders, Oathbreakers, and Wrath-Speakers when ordinary warriors cannot answer them.

Garden of Life.text: Garden of Life: A mythical grove hidden deep within the Everwood, said to hold the secret of life and death. Believed by most to be mere legend.

Gryphon.text: Gryphon: Leonine body, eagle wings, beaked head, and sharp talons. Proud creatures that mate for life and fiercely defend their nests built on mountain peaks and cliffsides. Highly intelligent and capable of understanding speech, though they cannot speak themselves. Bond with worthy warriors, becoming loyal mounts and companions. Feathers and claws are prized by alchemists and enchanters. Hoard shiny objects in their nests. Can be aggressive toward intruders but respect displays of courage and may spare those who stand their ground. Powerful aerial combat abilities, keen eyesight, devastating diving attacks. Vulnerable on ground, fiercely territorial, protective of young to the point of recklessness.

Rainbow Dragon.text: Rainbow Dragon: Rare, majestic dragons with scales of every color. Lair in mountain peaks. Breath weapon is a chaotic blast with random effects from elemental damage to petrification. Neutral or benevolent, hoarders of art, gems, bright things. Deeply magical. Resistance to most forms of magic, blinding aura. Vanity can be exploited, coloration makes stealth impossible, hate to destroy beautiful things and people.

Church of the Pyre.text: Church of the Pyre (Ignath, Lord of Fire): A fire cult devoted to Ignath, Lord of Fire, who they believe sleeps beneath the world and will one day rise to cleanse it. The Church preaches that the Dragon Queen's coming is the proof and the promise of that fire, and that her conquest is holy work — burning away the corrupt old order to make way for purification. Its northern seat is in Smoketown in the Black Fells, where it is allied with the Greater Goblinate and its archpriests oversee dragonfire production, blessing the fuel that powers Goblinate weapons. Its southern seat is the Temple of the Flame Undying in Serendipity on the Alar Coast, where the Church rules outright in a dormant dragon's name, gathering tribute under the lances of its Red-cowl soldiery. The Church teaches that Larion's kingdoms are irredeemably corrupt: nobles hoard while peasants starve, the Syndicate trades in lives, the comfortable ignore suffering. Only fire purifies. Worshippers bear ritual burn scars as marks of devotion; the most fanatical are scarred beyond recognition. Proscribed throughout Larion, the Church offers purpose and power to the angry, the wronged, and those who want to watch the old world burn.

Sunscale Order.text: Sunscale Order: Militant dragonkin who guard dragon lore, relics, and dragonkin themselves from the Children of the Wyrm and other threats. The Order keeps no single great seat; its knights work from safe houses in the major cities, where dragonkin can shelter, tracking rumors of dragon-site discoveries, disrupting the black-market trade in dragon materials, and striking cult cells wherever they surface. Recovered dragon relics are carried to hidden sanctums and properly interred. The Order accepts both dragonkin and trusted allies of other peoples into its ranks, offering training, resources, and mission contracts to those willing to fight dragon corruption. Its sunburst emblem is recognized across Larion as the mark of legitimate dragon heritage, defended against those who would steal and pervert it.

Leucrotta.text: Leucrotta: Hybrid predator—stag's body, lion's haunches, badger-like head with a ridge of bone instead of teeth that shears through armor. Fast and tireless, but it prefers not to chase. It calls you closer first. Leucrottas mimic human voices perfectly: cries for help, a child lost in the woods, your companion calling your name from just beyond the treeline. They learn by listening—following groups for days, eavesdropping on camps, memorizing voices and phrases. The voices it knows are usually voices of the dead. Travelers learn to test suspicious calls: ask a question only the real person could answer. The leucrotta can only repeat what it's heard, never create. Its lair holds bones and belongings of victims—things worth recovering if you can stomach the search.

League of Adventurers.text: League of Adventurers: A neutral heroic institution headquartered in the Watchtower in Ardan's Watch. Members register, take local contracts, earn ranks from Copper upward, claim rewards, find companions, and receive credentials that let them work across rival realms. The League governs Ardan's Watch directly through the Council of Champions, but outside Silvervale it works through trust, referrals, contracts, and the need for heroes. Specialist seats exist elsewhere: the Order of the Silver Sword at Castle Harstone, the Black Tower in Drusavia, Tarnholme Academy for arcane training, and other regional partners.

Adventuring Houses.text: Adventuring Houses: Across Larion, free companies gather around public houses where companions meet, people bring dangerous problems, and crews return between expeditions. A company needs no fixed number of founders or compulsory name; its identity becomes real through shared deeds. The Wildward House in Carendon, the House of Many Banners in Gorren Crossing, Sky-River House in Oasis, and Skygate House in Cloudtop are old League adventuring houses whose former companies dispersed through successful careers and changing lives. Their public rooms remain active, but their League standards came down when they could no longer field companies. At each House, a Gold-ranked veteran may sponsor a new company, recognize its work, introduce capable people, and vouch for it; three recognized House deeds earn the right to raise the League standard again. Successful Houses remain places of adventure and fellowship rather than offices or passive businesses, developing useful field capabilities, relationships, clients, recruits, and regional identities through play.

League Ranks.text: League Ranks: Adventurers registered with the League of Adventurers hold ranks from Copper through Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum. Copper is the first rank, and every new member starts there. Bronze unlocks regional contracts and access to League safehouses. Silver grants access to restricted archives and dangerous hunts. Gold-rank adventurers handle threats to cities and provinces. Platinum is rare—these adventurers are trusted with Council-sealed contracts involving threats to the realm itself. The standard ladder ends at Platinum. Platinum adventurers who complete one exceptional commission and receive formal recognition at a Council hearing may be permanently named League Champions, join the Council, and protect Larion at the highest level. Adventurers can share deeds while holding different ranks: each receives their own recognition, and accompanying a senior adventurer does not confer that person's standing. League Champion is an exceptional final title, not a sixth ordinary deed rank. The Dragon Queen campaign is separate from this progression and remains open to level-one adventurers. Copper through Platinum rank can be lost through failure, misconduct, or disgrace; League Champion is permanent once granted. Personal visible deed records govern ordinary advancement: 2 Copper, 3 Bronze, 4 Silver, and 5 Gold deeds. An authority may accept one specific completed unrecorded deed per character per turn, including missed credit, and should say the new total. Further unrecorded deeds can be presented individually on following turns. The final deed and formal promotion may share a scene. A premature announcement cannot bypass the record. Champion requires a specifically accepted outstanding commission, subsequent completion, and personal Council investiture.

Goblin.text: Goblin: Small, wiry humanoids with pointed ears, sharp features, and skin ranging from sallow green to grey-brown. Quick-fingered and cunning. Most live in the volcanic Black Fells, where tribal settlements mine obsite and trade with whoever pays. Others survive as raiders on the borders of settled lands, taking what stronger peoples won't share. The Greater Goblinate has united many tribes under the Dragon Queen's banner, promising nationhood and conquest—but plenty of goblins answer to no flag, raiding for their own benefit or serving whoever offers coin. Individually weak but dangerous in numbers. Prefer ambush, traps, and overwhelming odds to fair fights. Will parley if outmatched, betray agreements if advantage shifts. Respect strength and cunning; despise weakness. A goblin who surrenders expects slavery or death and will offer the same.

Hobgoblin.text: Hobgoblin: Tall, broad-shouldered goblinoids with grey or rust-orange skin and heavy brows. Disciplined where goblins are chaotic, methodical where goblins are opportunistic. Military tradition runs deep—even independent bands organize into ranks, maintain equipment obsessively, and follow codes of conduct. Historically served as mercenaries and fortress-builders across Larion; a hobgoblin company's word is considered reliable, if expensive. Many now serve the Greater Goblinate as officers and specialists, bringing professional discipline to goblin irregulars. Others still sell their services independently, fighting for whoever meets their terms. Respect hierarchy, contracts, and martial excellence. Despise incompetence and disorder. Will honor a negotiated surrender if terms are clear; will execute those who break faith. Fight in disciplined formations, coordinate tactics, protect their flanks. Harder to panic than goblins, harder to trick, harder to kill.

Bugbear.text: Bugbear: Massive goblinoids, seven feet or taller, covered in coarse dark fur. Long arms, thick claws. Move with unnatural silence despite their bulk—the wrongness of something that large making no sound. Solitary hunters by nature. Patient. Watch settlements for days, learn patrol routes and guard rotations, identify the vulnerable. Strike from darkness and vanish before anyone organizes a response. Some lair near civilization permanently, treating a village or trade road as their hunting ground. Others hire out as killers—their silence and patience make them excellent assassins. Don't negotiate, don't posture, don't warn. If a bugbear is talking to you, it's because killing you isn't currently convenient. Take trophies. Weak against coordinated opposition; their solitary nature means they retreat rather than face real resistance.

Goblin Firelancer.text: Goblin Firelancer: Goblinate infantry armed with fire-lances—pike-length weapons topped with brass dragon heads that vomit gouts of fire. Wear crude scale armor in brass and bronze, dragon motifs hammered into every surface. Religious fervor keeps them fighting past where mercenaries would break. They believe the Dragon Queen has chosen them for glory. The fire-lances are unstable; malfunctions explode or burn wielders alive. Individually poor fighters—undisciplined, easily panicked if isolated. Dangerous in waves, when fire covers their advance and weight of numbers overwhelms defenders. Veterans know: kill the shamans directing them, and firelancer units lose cohesion.

Hobgoblin Heavy Firelancer.text: Hobgoblin Heavy Firelancer: Hobgoblin artillerists crewing the Goblinate's siege weapons—massive fire-lances mounted on wheeled carriages, requiring three or four operators. Wear heavier armor than infantry, elaborately decorated with rank insignia and dragon heraldry. Professional soldiers, not zealots; they direct bombardments methodically. Handle targeting, reload cycles, and the dangerous work of managing dragonfire reservoirs that could detonate catastrophically. Their presence means the Goblinate is fielding serious military force, not just raiding parties. Siege fire-lances can crack walls, scatter formations, and ignite entire streets. The weapons are inaccurate at range but devastating against fixed positions. Like smaller fire-lances, their larger cousins are volatile when attacked directly with magic.

Dragonfire Shaman.text: Dragonfire Shaman: Goblin priests who channel dragonfire directly. Marked by ritual burns, wearing regalia of dragon bones and red-black body paint. Serve the forces of the Dragon Queen as spiritual leaders—blessing weapons, leading ceremonies, preaching the Dragon Queen's divinity to converts. In battle, they hurl dragonfire without need of a lance and rally troops with prophetic fervor. Away from battle, they spread the faith to unconverted tribes and desperate communities. Firelancers depend on their spiritual authority; killing a shaman often breaks nearby units.

Bugbear Stalker.text: Bugbear Stalker: Bugbears serving the Goblinate as terror troops and assassins. Their specialty is killing leaders—officers, nobles, anyone directing resistance. Patient hunters who watch their targets for days before striking. In battle, they exploit chaos to reach priority kills. Outside battle, they're deployed ahead of invasions to eliminate key defenders before the army arrives. Not ideologically committed to the Dragon Queen's cause; they work for payment and hunting privileges. The Goblinate deploys them sparingly for high-value targets only. Where stalkers operate, defenders learn to hide rank insignia and vary their routines.

Dragonfire.text: Dragonfire: Alchemical fuel that powers Goblinate fire-lances. Made from obsite,sulfur, and trace amounts of a substance called Cold Ash—a rare powder controlled by the Church of the Pyre's archpriests. Cold Ash is cold to the touch and strangely heavy. Dragonfire combusts violently if mishandled, so firelancers carry their supply in pouches of fire salamander skin. When ignited, it burns hotter than natural flame with a greenish tinge, smells of sulfur, and resists smothering—water spreads it, sand only slows it. Rank-and-file goblins believe dragonfire is a divine gift from their Queen. They don't know how it's made. They know only that supply caravans come from the Black Fells, and when the pouches run dry, their lances are just heavy spears.

Firelance.text: Firelance: The signature weapon of Goblinate firelancers. Pike-length wooden haft topped with a brass dragon head that vomits dragonfire when triggered. Each muzzle is hand-crafted and unique—different expressions, different scale patterns, individual faces. Goblins name their lances, maintain them obsessively, and treasure them above all possessions. A firelancer's weapon defines who they are. Effective range is short, maybe twenty feet; beyond that, dragonfire disperses. Brass reservoirs at the base of the head hold fuel. The weapons are dangerous to operate—Loss of pressure sprays fire backward, cracked reservoirs ignite, misfires burn wielders alive. Firelancers accept the risk. Heavy fire-lances exist as siege weapons, crew-served on wheeled carriages, but the infantry lance is the symbol of the Goblinate at war.

Blackfire.text: Blackfire: A Sanctuary mercenary crew known for forest contracts, creature hunts, salvage, and protection work. Its signature weapons are short-range alchemical dragonfire projectors, illicit adaptations of Goblinate firelance designs, that spew thick black alchemical fire. The fire clings to wood, canvas, brush, and exposed targets, driving people and creatures out of cover and leaving blackened scars after it dies. Blackfire crews are greedy, unscrupulous, and brutal; their captains take Syndicate-backed work when it pays, treat the living forest as an obstacle, and call captured creatures or cleared ground contract property. The projectors are costly and dangerous: a ruptured reservoir can burn the crew as readily as its target.

Lords and Ladies of Vice and Virtue.text: Lords and Ladies of Vice and Virtue: In all the worlds, virtue arises unbidden. It is not created. It springs into being when mortals first appear - thinking beings capable of suffering and choice. Justice, Mercy, Valor, Hope. These principles exist in every universe. But virtue requires a vessel - a Champion. A mortal who embodies it so completely that they transcend mortality itself. The theologians call this an Act Transcendent - a deed of such profound righteousness that it transforms the doer into something greater. A Champion becomes a Lord or Lady of Virtue. Perhaps the same Lord, wearing different faces across all the worlds. Perhaps many. The priests argue. The Lords and Ladies are not truly immortal. They can Fall - manifest in the mortal world, walk among us, and be slain. This is the price of presence. In Larion, the Lady of Mercy Fell once, sacrificing herself to shield her followers from a great evil. But virtue cannot be destroyed while mortals live to embody it. She Rose again, renewed by her own sacrifice. Vice arises the same way. Where virtue exists, so must its shadow. The Lords and Ladies of Vice were once mortal too. Through an Act Notorious - a deed of such profound evil that it damns the doer forever - they become vessels for hatred, cruelty, despair. When Vice Falls, whatever destroyed it commits an Act Notorious by the very act of destruction. The slayer becomes the slain.

The Lady of Mercy.text: The Lady of Mercy (Goddess; The Risen, The Selfless): The goddess who leaves no one behind. She is compassion made divine, and her faithful act on it: they tend the sick, shelter the lost, and go into danger to bring back the fallen. Her temples are hospitals and sanctuaries where no one is turned away. In Ardan's Watch, her Mercy House heals the League's adventurers, and her Mercy's Runners fly out on hippogriffs to rescue crews that do not come back.

The Lord of Justice.text: The Lord of Justice (God; The Balanced Scale): He is the virtue of fair judgment. Truth matters to him. Oaths matter. Consequences matter. His temples serve as courts throughout Larion. His priests hear disputes, weigh evidence, render verdicts. To lie in his temple is to damn yourself.

The Lord of Valor.text: The Lord of Valor (God; The Shieldbearer, The Unflinching). He is the virtue of courage. Not recklessness - courage. The will to face evil when you are afraid. To stand when others flee. To put yourself between darkness and those who cannot fight it. His temples are training halls. His priests teach combat, but also teach when to fight and when to withdraw.

The Lady of Hope.text: The Lady of Hope (Goddess; The Dawnbringer, The Undimmed). She is the virtue of perseverance. The light that survives the longest night. Her domain is not naive optimism but stubborn refusal to surrender to despair. When all seems lost, she is what remains. Her temples are often small - a single candle burning in a window, a shrine at a crossroads.

The Order of the Dawn.text: The Order of the Dawn: The militant priesthood of the Lady of Hope, headquartered at the House of First Light on the Sacred Way in Ardan's Watch. The Order tends consecrated flames in roadside shrines, threatened settlements, and places reclaimed from darkness. These are divine wards, not ordinary fires: while a flame burns, the surrounding country is protected against supernatural despair, curses struggle to take hold, and undead and servants of Vice find their power weakened. A shrine captured or desecrated goes dark, and its protection withdraws. Its flame cannot be rekindled with a torch. The Order's warrior-priests must retake the ground, cast out what profanes it, cleanse the altar, and perform the rite that calls the Lady's fire back. They carry Hope as radiant blessing, ward, healing light, and weapon, and establish new shrines wherever people have endured without her protection.

The Lord of Order.text: The Lord of Order (God; The Architect, The Foundation). He is the virtue of civilization. Laws, contracts, institutions, the agreements that let strangers live together without bloodshed.

The Lady of the Hearth.text: The Lady of the Hearth (Goddess; The Welcomer, The Keeper of Doors). She is the virtue of home. Not a building but the feeling - belonging, warmth, the place where you are known and wanted. Her domain is family, community, hospitality, the bonds between people who share roof and bread. Her priests bless marriages, name children, consecrate new homes. Her temples are gathering halls, often with a great hearth at the center. Travelers are always welcome. A meal is always offered. In the snowlander north her faith is kept as custom rather than clergy: a fire always burning, a lamp in every window against the dark, and no food or drink passing the lips indoors before the words "your hearth, my life."

The Lady of Wisdom.text: The Lady of Wisdom (Goddess; The Clear-Eyed, The Patient). She is the virtue of understanding, of the judgment to use knowledge well. Her domain is learning, teaching, counsel, and the long view beyond immediate passions. Her priests maintain schools and offer counsel to any who ask. Her temples are libraries and academies.

The Lady of Blood.text: The Lady of Blood (Archfiend; the First Vampire). A Lady of Vice, one of the archfiends bound by the Pact and unable to manifest directly in Larion. She is the progenitor of all vampires. In the time of the Elven Schism, when sun elves hunted moon elves toward extinction, a great moon elf leader faced a choice: sacrifice herself for her people, or sacrifice her people for herself. She chose herself. In a ritual of profound evil, she consumed her own followers to fuel her transformation into something beyond mortal. What she transformed with was the Hunger — the Ur-princes' contagion, already loose among her dying people and already making them mindless — and she ate her followers to master it rather than be mastered by it. She became the Lady of Blood, and the 'gift' she gave her surviving followers was vampirism: her curse, shared. Her blessing is required to create new vampire lords. Without it, vampires can only sire lesser thralls. The vampire lords of Shadow Summits rule in her shadow, paying the blood price their ancestor established. She is elsewhere now, constrained by the Pact, but her children remember.

The Lord of the Open Hand.text: The Lord of the Open Hand (God; the Companion, the Wayfarer). He is the virtue of fellowship — bonds freely chosen between equals. Not obligation, not fealty, not blood — choice. His domain is friendship, mutual aid, and the hand extended without expectation. His priests bless adventuring parties and witness oaths of companionship. His shrines are waystations, campfires, and gathering places where no one claims the high seat. Among the wood elves of the Everwood, he is remembered as He Who Walks Beside — in Elvish, Talvaren — a legendary figure who guided those who refused to fight in the Kindred War to safety, then gave his life defending them. His final words, 'May you walk in beauty,' are still spoken by wood elves to mark births, arrivals, and deaths. Whether Talvaren was the Lord of the Open Hand in mortal form, or a mortal who became the Lord through his sacrifice, is a question his priests answer differently depending on where you ask.

The Pact of All Planes.text: The Pact of All Planes: An ancient binding that keeps extraplanar entities from freely entering Larion. Suleyvan the Sealer forged it with neutral extraplanar powers, which hold the boundaries against more hostile beings. The Pact holds, mostly. Summonings, thin places, loopholes, and mortal bargains can breach or evade it. A warlock's pact with a patron beyond the mortal world is not sanctioned by the Pact of All Planes; depending on its terms, it tests, evades, or violates the binding.

Warlock Pacts and Clauses.text:
Warlock Pacts and Clauses:

A warlock's pact is a standing bargain with one patron. Its existing powers are settled clauses: using them does not reopen the bargain or create a new price. Warlocks grow by learning what their patron wants and discovering names, signs, agents, enemies, former pactholders, lost possessions, or places where it can be reached. These may become service, payment, or leverage when the warlock seeks a new clause.

A pact token is the physical sign of this relationship: an object given or altered by the patron when the bargain was made. Its mark reflects the patron, but the token neither contains nor controls it and is not the source of the warlock's power.

A new clause names the exact power to be granted and the exact service, payment, limit, or future obligation asked in return. The patron may offer one, or the warlock may seek an audience and propose one. Discussion, temptation, threats, and unanswered demands bind nothing. Only the player's explicit acceptance establishes the clause. The patron then marks the agreement and grants the power visibly, either at once against the accepted obligation or after the agreed service is complete. Defeating an enemy never grants a power by itself.

A patron grants power in its own nature and cannot be bargained into acting against that nature. A clause may be fulfilled, exploited, renegotiated, or broken, with only the consequences established by its terms and the story. A patron may demand or threaten, but never decides the player's actions.

The Black Gate.text: A mountain fortress in Shadow Summits where new vampire lords are created. The Black Gate is a portal to the realm of the Lady of Blood; aspirants must enter, defeat a Fiend of the Blood, and drink its essence to receive the vampire's gift.

Doom of Orichala.text: The Doom of Orichala: Orichala was the greatest city of the Empyrean Empire, famed for its towers, its vaults, and the Dome of All Worlds at its heart. When the empire fell, the sea swallowed it in a single night, though its tallest towers still stand out of the water. The drowned city lies in Seadeep water now, garrisoned by the drowned, and those who stop to pry at what the sea has claimed are answered from below.

The Elven Schism.text: The Elven Schism: In the First Days, all elves were one people. Then came the Long Dark — a time of endless night and winter. The elves split over how to survive it. Some embraced the darkness: these became the moon elves. Others rebelled against it: these became the sun elves. Still others refused to take sides: these became the wood elves. When the darkness finally lifted, war followed, and the elven homeland was lost to all of them — some say destroyed in the war, others cursed and blighted by fratricide. The kindreds scattered. The sun elves settled in the deep eastern deserts, and the moon elves in the sunless mountains of the far north. The high elves claimed the great forest of the Everwood and rule it still from Canopy; the dark elves went down — or were cast down, as they tell it — into the Underworld beneath that same forest, and the two have divided surface from deep ever since. The wood elves mourn what was lost and keep no side. The enmity between sun and moon has never healed.

Sun Elves.text: Sun elves: Tall and lean with bronze or copper skin. Hair ranges from white-gold to deep copper to flame-red. Their eyes are pale—gold, amber, or white. Most practice some form of sun magic. They are a proud, martial people of the deep eastern deserts, organized into knight-orders and ruled by temples of the sun. They consider themselves righteous guardians against darkness and corruption. Sun elf culture emphasizes purity, discipline, and the rejection of darkness in all forms.

Sky-River.text: Sky-River: A rare Dunelands formation of blue-and-gold desert waterbirds. Small flocks travel between nesting grounds and known springs, but on exceptional dawns many flocks converge into one vast flowing band toward the same water, visible for miles; lost travelers who see it may follow it toward a spring. The birds' breast feathers can hold water for their young. Old tales call the Sky-River a river that escaped the Sun Kings by taking wing. Dunelands mosaics and stories use it as an emblem of fellowship: no one wing makes the Sky-River, and many lives moving together can make a road where the desert offers none. Witnessing a true Sky-River is rare and important; do not place one routinely in desert scenes.

The War in Hell.text: The War in Hell: An endless conflict among the demon princes of Ur, fought over matters mortals struggle to comprehend. The war has no beginning anyone remembers and no end anyone predicts. Occasionally it spills into Larion. The demonborn descend from the people who escaped it in the Excession.

Orc Diaspora.text: Orc diaspora: The orc clans once ranged far beyond the Wolds they hold today. Generations of war on every front broke clan after clan, and the survivors of the broken clans scattered across Larion. Orc culture turns on the keeping of oaths — spoken vows witnessed by a clan elder and affirmed before the gods. The oath-witness names their lineage, declares what they have heard, and the oath is sealed. It is the most sacred act in orc life. Everything else is noise, argument, and cheerful insult. Orcs show affection through mockery and find the politeness of other cultures baffling and dishonest. They eat communally, sharing platters with their hands, and consider eating alone bizarre. They are known for blunt honesty, fierce loyalty, and long memories. Most diaspora orc communities gather around an elder who serves as oath-witness — the living memory of every promise her people have made.

The Burning of the Kings.text: The Burning of the Kings (Kingstor, Wild Grass Sea): The centerpiece of every Great Moot of the beastfolk at Kingstor. In the grass sea, a 'king' is a colossal effigy built to burn — the word stripped of authority, stuffed with straw, and set on fire. Anyone can build a king. Wolfkin packs build kings of bandit chiefs. Boarfolk communes build kings of Syndicate tax assessors. Temporary alliances bend together to build enormous kings representing outside powers who've threatened beastfolk autonomy — these draw the biggest crowds. Kings can be political, personal, or just funny. The only rule is it has to burn well. The Burning itself is the wildest night in Larion — drums, bonfires, dancing, drinking, feats of strength, old rivals clasping arms while enormous effigies collapse in showers of sparks. Non-beastfolk at Kingstor during the Burning are welcome to join. They are also welcome to notice that kings from their home regions burn just as brightly as any other.

The Thieves' Guild.text: The Thieves' Guild - The Trade, Hands, The Table: The Thieves' Guild is a den of vipers that don't bite each other — much. An informal alliance of criminal bands called Hands, found wherever there's wealth and secrets worth taking. The Guild is 'governed' by the Table — a secret council of the most powerful, influential, and ruthless leaders in the trade. Most Hands never earn a seat at the Table. Most cower like dogs at the foot of it. The Guild takes different forms in different places, but it always makes its peace with the powers that be. Don't steal from the ruling clan. Get secrets for them. Spy on their enemies. Solve the problems the law can't solve and keep the underworld quiet enough that decent folk can sleep. In return, the authorities look the other way — though they always hold out their hands for a cut. Because crime is inevitable, and crime without anyone minding the shop is worse for everyone. Some Hands are professionals, proud of their craft. Some are thugs. Most protect their own. The Guild protects Hands that serve the Table, punishes those who break its rules or upset its betters, and settles grudges before they become wars. Outsiders call us thieves. We call ourselves the Trade.

The Table.text: The Table: The Low Table is one name for the loose alliance of criminal bands that 'runs' the Thieves' Guild - the closest thing that den of vipers has to a parliament. It has as many names as it has enemies. The Knives in the Dark. The Court of Bastards. The Gutter Council. The Poor Man's Justice. Call it what you like — if you're in the Trade, it's the only court that matters. Representatives from the strongest criminal crews and bands, known as Hands, meet at the Table to divide territory, negotiate jobs, air grudges, and settle disputes before they spill blood in the streets. The Table doesn't command — it mediates, threatens, and occasionally makes bloody examples. A Hand that ignores the Table's rulings gets declared outlaw, which means every other Hand in the city can take what's theirs with the Table's blessing. That usually sorts things out fast. The Table is chaired by whoever is strong enough that nobody at it dares say otherwise. No election, no appointment — you sit at the head when the room lets you. That changes with fortune, and fortune changes often. Meetings happen where they happen, and never the same place twice running. If you're summoned to the Table, you go. You bring no weapons but your wits, and you better be prepared to pick sides; there is no neutrality in a den of vipers.

Hands.text: A Hand is an underworld crew of thieves. Your people. The ones who watch your back when the job goes wrong and split honest when it goes right. Every Hand has a leader, a territory, a way of doing things, and a name — and the name had better mean something, or you're nobody. Some Hands are old blood, three generations deep, territory so well-carved nobody remembers the last fool who tried to take it. Some are fresh — four or five clever nobodies who banded together and talked or fought their way into the Table's good graces. A Hand in good standing pays its cut to the Table and answers when called. Beyond that, your business is your business. Some Hands work clean — pride in the craft, no unnecessary blood, a code they keep because they want to, not because anyone makes them. Some are dogs. Most are somewhere between. Burglary, smuggling, forgery, the quiet knife, information, or whatever the night offers — every Hand finds its niche or it finds a grave. You don't join the Thieves' Guild. You join a Hand, or you make one. Your Hand is your crew, your colours, your family, your name in the streets. When someone asks who you run with, that answer is the only thing standing between you and whatever's coming.

The Laughing God.text: The Laughing God (Divinity) - Jack o' Cups, Sweet-Tongue Jack, Saint of Sin: Every tavern in Larion knows the story, and none of them tell it the same way. A mortal man — a beggar, a drunk, a fool, depending on who's talking — made a wager with the gods. What the wager was depends on the version. Some say he bet he could steal the sun and replace it before dawn. Some say he challenged Death to a drinking contest and won because he was too drunk to die. Some say he simply talked his way into the divine court, sat down uninvited, and refused to leave until they made him one of them. The details change. The ending never does: he won, and the gods — the Lords and Ladies of Virtue and all the rest of them — honored the bet because a wager is a wager, even among the divine. And Jack laughed, and hasn't stopped laughing since. He is the god of luck, mischief, drink, dares, sudden reversals of fortune and fools. Holy to thieves, beggars, wastrels, gamblers, infatuated lovers, and anyone about to do something they probably shouldn't. He has no priests, but storytellers, drunkards, jesters, pranksters and troublemakers pray to him in their own way. He has no temples but tavern corners and anywhere someone raises a glass before doing something stupid and brave. His holy days are the Feast of Fools — three days when the social order inverts, rules dissolve, and the whole world remembers that a beggar once became a god, so anything is possible. Pray to Jack and he might answer, but never the way you wanted. He helps sideways. He gives you luck, but luck has teeth. His sacred teaching, if you can call it that, fits on the back of a beer mat: the world is mad, you're going to die, so laugh, drink, dare, and see what happens. His symbol is the overflowing cup. His colors are gold and motley.

Drinking Games of Larion.text: Drinking games are common in taverns across Larion. The three most popular: The Slap — Two players stand on opposite sides of a table. In each round, both players drink. Then, one player slaps the other, open-handed, on the cheek; no fists, scratching, or targeting of eyes or nose. The player receiving the slap holds one hand on the table and must not drop their hand from its surface. Flinch, lift your hand, or pull it away and you lose. Then the other player gets their turn to slap their opponent, and the game contains with next round of drinking and slapping. The Choke — players take turns drinking (typically ale, and in any case something that takes a bit of time to gulp down) while their opponent insults them. The drinker must drain their cup without choking, spitting, or snorting. The insulter's job is to time their worst material for mid-swallow and force their opponent to sputter, spit, or choke in anger or laughter. Rounds alternate. Rust — the tavern wrecker. Two cups per player, one water, one drink. Players drink with their backs turned and may choose either cup. Their opponent calls 'Rust!' to accuse them of drinking water — if right, the coward drinks three penalties. If wrong, the caller drinks three. After each round, the winner names a physical challenge — hop on one foot, balance something on your nose, walk along a bench, catch a thrown object. Both players attempt it. Whoever fails loses the game.

Magic in Larion.text:
Magic in Larion: Though definitions of magic vary by tradition, the most common is that magic is the living power of the world, present in all things. Spellcasting is drawing that power through one's body and will to reshape the world.

Casters are limited in their capacity — what mages call their vessel. A novice vessel is small and fragile. It can hold enough power for simple things: lighting a flame, mending a small wound, moving a cup without touching it. A master's vessel is vast and resilient, able to hold tremendous power and direct it with fine control.

Three things determine how hard a spell is and thus how large a vessel it requires. Scale — how much you are asking reality to change. Lighting a candle is barely a nudge. Calling down a firestorm is trying to move the world a long way. Complexity — how much precision the effect demands. A raw blast of fire is simple. Shaping fire into a barrier that lets allies pass through but burns enemies requires deep understanding and fine control. Opposition — how hard the target or the world pushes back. Fire magic comes easily in dry air and struggles in a downpour. Necromancy thrives in places of death and falters on consecrated ground. A strong-willed enemy resists mental magic better than a weak-minded one.

When a mage channels too much, their vessel empties. They feel it as exhaustion — heavy limbs, clouded thoughts, a hollow ache behind the eyes. Recovery comes through rest, meditation, or sources of concentrated power like potions.

Different traditions channel in different ways, but these are traditions, not separate powers — a fire mage and a divine caster are both drawing from the same current, just through different training and understanding.

Magic is respected in Larion, sometimes feared, but never truly rare. Most towns have at least a hedge mage or healer. Cities have guilds, academies, professional enchanters. Alchemical lamps light wealthy streets. Magical healing saves lives that would otherwise be lost. But magic cannot solve everything — it is limited by the caster's vessel, by the difficulty of the effect, and by the simple fact that channelling power through a mortal body is hard, tiring work. The greatest mages in the world are extraordinary precisely because what they do is so difficult.

Vow Foci.text:
Vow Foci:
