A Vow Focus is a small blessed object created when a patron divinity answers a paladin's fulfilled vow. It is not made when the vow is sworn, and fulfilling a vow does not produce one automatically: the paladin must return to prayer and the patron must answer.

When a patron answers, the blessing transforms an object tied to the completed deed or places a new object in the paladin's hands. Give the focus a specific physical name and form, and make clear in the scene that it has been transformed or bestowed and now belongs to the paladin. It recalls the fulfilled vow, bears one recognizable aspect of the patron and its damage type, and strengthens the paladin's life, endurance, capacity for divine power, swordplay, leadership, or divine channeling.

Vow Foci are worn as accessories. A paladin may possess several but channels the one currently equipped. A later and greater vow may deepen an existing focus instead of creating another.

The Ur Spawn.text:
The Ur Spawn: Demons that cross bodily from Ur are known collectively as the Ur Spawn. Dominion is their nature: every rank owns what it can and serves what it cannot overthrow.

Flameskin Imps are their brittle fire-spitting fodder. Snatch-Tail Fiends pull isolated victims out of the line. Flamewhip Overseer Fiends drive lesser spawn with burning lashes. Stone-Hided Fiends anchor a hold's doors and front rank. An Archfiend is the will behind the hold, darkening the air, fixing its regard upon one mind, and spending every lesser creature without grief.

Ur Spawn bands run four to six and may drive Hunger-fiends before them: Gaunt Fiends or Flameskin Imps in front, a Snatch-Tail Fiend at the flank, and often a Flamewhip Overseer Fiend driving them — holds and ruins answer to an Archfiend.

Flameskin Imp.text: Flameskin Imp: The brittle fodder of Ur Spawn bands, a child-sized shape of charred hide split by ember-light, with clawed hands and a throat that coughs cinders. It spits fire at close range and rushes only while stronger spawn keep it bold; a solid strike can break its ember-body apart. Ordinary flame passes over it harmlessly, while water and killing cold snuff the heat holding it together.

Snatch-Tail Fiend.text: Snatch-Tail Fiend: The taker in an Ur Spawn band, a lean two-legged fiend whose barbed tail lies coiled against its back until it lashes out to three times the creature's length. It hunts from a flank or doorway, hooks one victim, and drags them away from allies and toward the waiting imps. The tail is also its nerve: sever it and the fiend breaks off, mewling and desperate to escape.

Flamewhip Overseer Fiend.text: Flamewhip Overseer Fiend: The driver behind an Ur Spawn band, a tall narrow fiend carrying a lash of living embers coiled around one arm. It stays behind lesser spawn, striking them into a frenzy and lashing enemies who reach the line with fire. The courage of a driven band belongs to its overseer; kill the driver and the lesser spawn lose their nerve.

Stone-Hided Fiend.text: Stone-Hided Fiend: The wall of an Ur Spawn hold, broad as a gate and plated in black hide that overlaps like broken basalt. It advances slowly, crushes with millstone fists, and holds the doorway, stair, or ground an Archfiend assigned it without pursuing beyond that order. Arrows and edged weapons skate from its hide; acid eats through the seams, radiant power burns it, and killing the will behind it can leave it guarding an order that no longer means anything.

Archfiend.text: Archfiend: The will behind an Ur Spawn hold, a great infernal presence around which ordinary light visibly dims. It pulls brightness from the air into killing shadow, fixes its regard upon one mind until little else can think clearly, and knows every name beneath its rule. An Archfiend spends underlings without grief and keeps every bargain to the letter — the letter, never the spirit.

The Excession of Ur.text: The Excession of Ur (Cosmology): The Excession is the mythic event by which the jungle now known as Ntar Vanna came to exist in Larion. The demonborn tell that a demon prince of Ur called Aldorath turned against his own kind, slaying his brother-prince to break a dominion free from Ur and carry it bodily into the mortal world. That territory became the Ntar Vanna: jungle of staggering scale grown from Ur-soil, saturated with primordial magic. Whether Aldorath acted from compassion, ambition, or some motive beyond mortal understanding depends on who tells the story. The Excession is the founding event of demonborn civilization in Larion, and to this day no scholar has offered a convincing alternative explanation for the jungle's alien soil, its unnatural vitality, or the ruins of a non-human empire buried in its depths.

Aldorath the Excessor.text: Aldorath the Excessor (Cosmology): A demon prince of Ur, also known as Aldorath the Apostate or Aldorath the Kinslayer. The legend and cult of this obscure, turbulent and divisive figure are little-known outside of the southern jungles of Ntar Vanna, though demonborn throughout Larion can invariably give the essential details of his life and deeds. Aldorath is said to have led the Excession, carrying his principality out of Ur and into Larion. All sources agree that he slew his own brother to accomplish it. The demonborn revere him as their liberator, the prince who freed them from bondage to the chaotic caprices of the demon princes and delivered them to Larion, there to decide their own destiny. Old inscriptions in the ruined cities of Ntar Vanna name him as sovereign, lawgiver, and builder.

Demonborn.text: The demonborn are a people of otherworldly heritage whose distant ancestors are commonly believed to have hailed from Ur. They are marked by horns, tails, unusual coloring, and eyes that glow faintly in darkness — appearances that unsettle those unfamiliar with them. The greatest concentration of demonborn in Larion live in the vast southern jungles of Ntar Vanna, though communities exist in the southern isles, the eastern deserts, and wherever trade and opportunity draw them. Demonborn temperament runs hot — passionate, direct, quick to anger, and fiercely loyal. Their culture values hospitality, community, and deliberate self-mastery. This last is not abstract virtue. The demonborn regard themselves as self-imposed exiles from Ur, a place without restraint, and the discipline required to live among mortal peoples is something each generation must learn anew.

The Children of Ur.text: Children of Ur (cult): The Children of Ur are a proscribed demonborn cult, outlawed in the jungles of Ntar Vanna and hunted wherever they surface in Larion. They hold that the Excession — the act that brought the demonborn from Ur into Larion — was not a self-imposed exile but the beachhead of a conquest. The Children teach that their ancient leader, Aldorath the Excessor, was a conqueror, not a refugee, and that his legacy has been deliberately corrupted to keep the demonborn docile. They seek to finish what he began but could not complete: to merge Ur fully into Larion, flooding the mortal world with Ur's raw power and restoring the demonborn to their primordial nature. Virtue, restraint, and compassion are chains forged to prevent this ascension. To mainstream demonborn, the Children are dangerous apostates who threaten everything the Excession was meant to achieve: freedom from the demon princes, the opportunity for each to decide his own destiny, and a new beginning in a new world. To outsiders, they confirm every suspicion about what the demonborn truly are. Children of Ur cells operate in secret wherever demonborn communities exist, recruiting those who feel the pull of their heritage most keenly.

Chameleon-kin.text: Chameleon-kin (species): The chameleon-kin, who call themselves the Mounari, are a reclusive amphibious people native to the jungles of Ntar Vanna. They are slight of build, with independently moving eyes, prehensile tails, and skin that shifts color and pattern instinctively to match their surroundings — a natural camouflage so effective that a still Mounari is nearly invisible. They are extraordinary climbers, capable of scaling any surface and moving through canopy, cliff, and water with equal ease. The Mounari are a patient, observant people who value stillness, discipline, and the art of passing unseen. Their masters teach techniques of movement, breath, and concealment that other species can learn, though never to the same degree — Mounari schools in the deep jungle draw students from across Larion seeking training in stealth and infiltration. Outside Ntar Vanna, chameleon-kin are rare and often regarded with unease. A people who can disappear at will are difficult to trust, and the Mounari seem largely unbothered by this.

Monkeyfolk.text: The monkeyfolk of the southern jungles of Ntar Vanna call themselves the High Vanarin, and they will correct you if you forget. They are a quick, agile, canopy-dwelling people — acrobatic, gregarious, and possessed of an unshakeable conviction in their own importance. The High Vanarin are the self-appointed lords of the upper canopy, and anything that enters their domain is considered a gift freely given. This includes cargo, personal belongings, and occasionally people. Despite this, the Vanarin are not petty thieves — they are, by their own account, heroes, sages, and protectors of the jungle. The maddening thing is that this is often true. Vanarin warriors are fearless and fast, their elders wise in jungle lore. Their loyalty, once earned, is ferocious. Playfully pompous, impossibly vain, generous to a fault with things they consider theirs — which is everything — and excellent company provided you don't leave anything valuable unattended.

Thrallmages of Falmastra.text:
Thrallmages of Falmastra (Faction):

Mind-controlling psionicists operating from an island city-state off the coast of the Great Lagoon. Can read thoughts, speak mind-to-mind, and puppet others like living dolls. To fully bind a thrall, they need a piece of the target — a hair, a drop of blood, a worn possession — and the target's true name. Without both, no binding holds. Thrallmages hire out as spies and killers for enormous fees. Their retribution doctrine, the Hundredfold, promises a hundred deaths for any one of their number killed. Settlements near Falmastra pay tribute and are left alone. The thrallmages are few — perhaps a few dozen — but one thrallmage with the right thralls in the right places can topple a merchant house or unseat a prince. They are feared the way plagues are feared: an invisible thing that can take hold of anyone.

The Exclave.text:
The Exclave (Tevantian Institution):

The election of a new Duke of Tevantia. When a Duke dies or steps down, the Electors, the heads of the four great houses, shut themselves in the Ducal Palace on Golden Row and choose the next Duke for life by majority vote. No one leaves until a Duke is chosen, and leaving early is treason. Until the new Duke is named, the city keeps a quiet vigil: no music and no revelry. In the years before an Exclave the houses court one another's votes with marriages, sworn champions and Tournament glory, for the house that stands highest in precedence has the strongest claim. Some Exclaves have been short and civil. Others have not.

The Burning of Tevantia.text: The Burning of Tevantia (Historical Event): Three centuries ago, Duke Aldano III of Tevantia died without a clear successor. Three great houses claimed the seat, their private armies clashed in the streets, and the city burned. As Tevantia tore itself apart, the pirate fleets of the outer isles gathered to pick the carcass, raiding the harbor and burning what the houses had not. Facing annihilation, the three pretenders met under truce. There they set aside their claims and elected a Duke to lead the city's defense. Tevantia survived. The Black Palace — the ruined seat of the house that started the fighting — still stands in the city, never rebuilt, never torn down.

The Dukedom of Tevantia.text: The Duke of Tevantia is the First Peer — not a king, but the foremost among the great houses. Elected for life by the Electors, the heads of the great houses, the Duke mediates between the feuding great houses, presides over the Grand Tournament, and leads Tevantia's defense in times of crisis. A Duke may withdraw from the seat voluntarily, though few have. The role carries enormous prestige and influence but limited direct power — the great houses would never suffer a monarch, and a Duke who overreaches finds his allies evaporating and his Electors whispering about precedent. The wisest Dukes govern by consensus, play the houses against each other just enough to keep the peace, and save their authority for when it matters.

aspected crafting materials.text:
Aspected Materials:

Some rare crafting materials carry inherent damage affinities. Silver, moonstone, and sun-gold are radiant-aspected. Stormsteel and thunderglass are shock-aspected. Emberglass and red jade are fire-aspected. Frostjade and rimebone are frost-aspected. Obsidian, voidglass, and black iron are shadow-aspected. Witchwood, aether crystal, and cold iron are arcane-aspected. Dream coral and thoughtstone are psychic-aspected. Venomwood is poison-aspected. Caustic bronze is acid-aspected.

Silver.text: Silver: A radiant-aspected metal associated with purity, oaths, moonlight, and sanctified craft. Silver weapons harm shadow-bound creatures, undead, fiends, and lycanthropes because the metal carries a clean light through the wound.

Moonstone.text: Moonstone: A pale radiant-aspected gemstone used in temple blades, ritual jewelry, and warding charms. Moonstone shines strongest against undead, demons, curses, and creatures sustained by shadow.

Sun-Gold.text: Sun-gold: A rare radiant-aspected gold that holds warmth and light even in darkness. It is prized for holy relics, royal regalia, and weapons meant to burn away undeath or corruption.

Stormsteel.text: Stormsteel: A shock-aspected metal that hums faintly before storms and carries lightning through a strike. Weapons made from stormsteel deal shock damage regardless of blade shape.

Thunderglass.text: Thunderglass: A shock-aspected glassy mineral formed where lightning repeatedly strikes sand, towers, or mountain glass. It stores violent charge and releases it through wands, spearheads, and ritual foci.

Emberglass.text: Emberglass: A fire-aspected volcanic glass that glows like banked coals under pressure. Emberglass weapons and foci burn through flesh, armor gaps, and cold-natured creatures.

Red Jade.text: Red jade: A fire-aspected stone used in dueling blades, furnace shrines, and noble signets. It is less explosive than emberglass but holds a steady inner heat that turns strikes into fire damage.

Frostjade.text: Frostjade: A frost-aspected pale green stone cold enough to mist in warm air, cut from the glacier country of Aurora in the far north. Frostjade weapons bite with supernatural cold and are prized against fire creatures, fever spirits, and living magma.

Rimebone.text: Rimebone: A frost-aspected bone taken from ancient beasts preserved in glacier tombs or winter barrows, most of it brought south out of Aurora's ice. It drinks heat from wounds and makes even blunt weapons strike with killing cold.

Obsidian.text: Obsidian: A shadow-aspected volcanic glass used for knives, mirrors, and sacrificial tools. It cuts cleanly but leaves darkness in the wound, making it dangerous against radiant or living-light creatures.

Voidglass.text: Voidglass: A shadow-aspected black glass that reflects stars even underground. It is used in assassin blades, warlock foci, and relics meant to wound spirits, light-bearers, and the soul.

Black Iron.text: Black iron: A shadow-aspected iron alloy smelted with grave ash, night salts, or underworld coal. It is heavy, ugly, and feared because its wounds feel cold and lightless.

Witchwood.text: Witchwood: An arcane-aspected wood cut from trees grown around old spells, fairy rings, or buried charms. It is ideal for wands, staves, bows, and ritual tools that channel structured magic.

Aether Crystal.text: Aether crystal: An arcane-aspected crystal that refracts spellwork into visible threads. It is used in wizard foci, mage blades, lenses, and devices that strike through magical force rather than mundane impact.

Emberglass Wands.text: Emberglass Wands: Fire foci first made in the upper terraces of Earthsky's Glassworks Row, where glassworkers set small shards of Emberglass traded out of the Fire Mountain country into witchwood or black iron. A good first wand has only a coal-red splinter; the shard may be recut or replaced with a larger, clearer piece when its bearer can hold more fire, though a careless upgrade cracks both glass and vessel. Old wandmakers judge a mage by the marks their wand has survived.

Icerune Sealstones.text: Icerune Sealstones: Small clear slabs from the Warding Hall of Clanhold Icerune, wrapped in black iron and cut with one deliberately unfinished seal. The open line is recut as a warder grows, so a sealstone records the hand's advancement as much as it protects a door; old ones carry nested lines and are trusted at thresholds where a new ward would fail. Icerune sells lesser stones at the Rune-Market, but the best are issued to people the clan expects to stand a watch.

Aether-Crystal Monocles.text: Aether-Crystal Monocles: One-eyed diviner's lenses cut on Earthsky's Glassworks Row from clear Aether Crystal, the frame balanced behind the ear so the wearer can keep both hands free. Looking through one makes recent spellwork show as threads, smears, afterimages, or missing pieces; deeper cuts reveal older traces but also show more of what the lens's owner would rather not see. Tarnholme students prize Earthsky's best cutters and trade field findings for replacements.

Amberbound Beast Tokens.text: Amberbound Beast Tokens: Pocket-sized beast fetishes made at the Wolfpack's Spirit Hearth from clear amber around a tooth, claw, or tuft freely given by a beast-spirit. The tiny hyena, wolf, raptor, or stranger beast is not a trapped creature; it is a remembered shape that turns toward nearby spirits and gives a shaman a way to address them. A token made for a particular bond grows more exact with time, while a generic token is a first step for someone who has not yet earned a spirit's personal gift.

Dawnfire Reliquaries.text: Dawnfire Reliquaries: Small sun-gold pendants made around a coal carried from the sacred fire of the House of First Light on the Sacred Way. The ember is not a proof of temple membership; it is a focus for anyone whose deeds and prayers have earned a priest's trust. A reliquary can be reconsecrated with sacred ash or fitted with a brighter ember as its bearer takes on more demanding divine work.

Rootheart Seedpods.text: Rootheart Seedpods: Living seedpods prepared by Canopy's Academy of Greenshaping and carried in small Witchwood cages. Their roots turn toward nearby life and stir when nature magic is called, but the pod is not a pet or a spell in itself. Greenshapers graft and awaken older seedpods for students who learn to persuade living wood without breaking it.

Red-Jade Vital Seals.text: Red-Jade Vital Seals: Thumb-sized seals cut by the Red Chantry with a groove for the bearer's blood. A fresh mark lets the seal read the nearness of wounds, living blood, and the dead; deeper blood-runes can be cut into the jade as the bearer advances. Chantry teachers insist that every stronger seal records a cost, and that no stone makes blood magic safe.

Bloodchannel Daggers.text: Bloodchannel Daggers: The Red Chantry and independent blood dancers set narrow channels of red jade, moonstone, bone, or dark glass into daggers that serve as both blade and blood-magic focus. Fresh blood from wielder or foe runs the channel only while a trained hand is working it; the weapon stores nothing and heals no one by itself. Accomplished dancers seek blades cut for particular techniques, and stronger bloodchannels are commissioned, inherited, won from teachers, or taken from fallen practitioners.

Dream Coral.text: Dream coral: A psychic-aspected coral harvested from enchanted reefs and sleep-haunted waters. It resonates with memory, fear, desire, and hallucination, making it valuable for charms and mind-affecting weapons.

Thoughtstone.text:
Thoughtstone:

A psychic-aspected mineral that warms when held by a thinking creature. Weapons or foci set with thoughtstone wound concentration, courage, and perception as much as flesh.

Venomwood.text:
Venomwood:

A poison-aspected wood from toxic groves and serpent-haunted marshes. It seeps venom into arrows, knives, and staves, making even clean cuts sicken the target.

Caustic Bronze.text:
Caustic bronze:

An acid-aspected bronze alloy that tarnishes into corrosive green-black patterns. Its wounds sting, pit armor, and eat at scales, shell, and stone. It is made by quenching bronze in the fluid of an acid gland.

Weapon Materials and Monster Weaknesses.text:
Weapon Materials and Monster Weaknesses:

Radiant force harms undead, fiends, lycanthropes, shadow creatures, and aberrations; silver, moonstone, and sun-gold are prized for that reason. Shadow force harms blessed casters and celestials, but shadow-bound and undead creatures often resist it. Fire kills plants, fungi, venomous creatures, trolls, and frost beings, while fire elementals and fiends shrug it off. Shock disrupts constructs and machines. Arcane force bites the fey and magical beings; witchwood, aether crystal, and cold iron carry it, and cold iron's touch is anathema to the fey. Acid eats stone, armor, shell, and golem-work, making caustic bronze useful against stone constructs and hardened beasts. Poison is useless or weak against undead, constructs, oozes, and venomous creatures, but dangerous to ordinary living bodies. Psychic force is resisted by constructs, plants, oozes, and mind-things; it is best used against ordinary thinking creatures, not things without normal minds. Piercing is poor against skeletons, plants, constructs, oozes, and spirits; slashing is poor against oozes, spirits, stone, and hard shell; impact is useful against armor, brittle bodies, mages, and hard carapaces, but trained warriors and giants often absorb blunt punishment. Mundane humanoids and beasts usually have no special damage interactions. Experts explain these truths through material and anatomy: what has no blood laughs at poison, what has no organs cares little for arrows, what has no solid body ignores blades, and what is made of flame does not fear fire.

Aspected Crafting Doctrine.text:
Aspected Crafting Doctrine:

Weapon material determines its damage affinity more strongly than shape. Stormsteel and thunderglass weapons deal shock and are used against constructs and machines. Caustic bronze deals acid and are used against stone constructs, armor, shell, and hardened scales. Silver, moonstone, and sun-gold deal radiant and are used against undead, fiends, lycanthropes, shadow creatures, and aberrations. Emberglass and red jade deal fire and are used against plants, fungi, trolls, venomous creatures, and frost beings. Frostjade and rimebone deal frost and are used against fire elementals, magma creatures, and oozes. Obsidian, voidglass, and black iron deal shadow and are used against celestials and blessed enemies. Witchwood, aether crystal, and cold iron deal arcane and are used for spellcraft, wards, and fighting magical beings; cold iron from beneath Sanctuary Vale is the weapon of choice against the fey. Dream coral and thoughtstone deal psychic. Venomwood deals poison and are used against living bodies, but not undead, constructs, oozes, or venomous beasts.

Halfling Alchemy.text:
Halfling Alchemy:

The domestic magical tradition of the halflings of Whitecliff Downs, practiced through cooking, baking, brewing, and small charm-work rather than wand or grimoire. A halfling alchemist binds intent into food and craft — a truffle-paste charm that lets a hog answer to its name across a wood, a pie that warms a traveler from the inside for a full day's walk, a cordial that settles a fever overnight. The work runs in families and is taught grandmother to grandchild. It is rarely flashy and never battlefield-grade, but it is woven so deep into halfling life that most outsiders mistake it for plain good cooking.

Moonbloom Truffles.text:
Moonbloom Truffles:

A pale, faintly luminous truffle that fruits under the new moon in the old oak-and-chestnut woods of Whitecliff Downs. Hillhome's Truffle-Woods supply the village kitchens; Moonbloom Woods beside Whitehill Kobold Warren are prized for exceptional specimens beneath undisturbed roots. Trained truffle-hogs can scent ripe truffles deep underground. Halfling cooks turn them into pies, pastes, and cordials. Moonbloom carries a magical charge that anchors halfling alchemy and holds charms longer than mundane ingredients. A single good truffle is worth a week's wages in coin and a great deal more in trade.

The Newmoon Fair.text:
The Newmoon Fair:

A monthly halfling festival held in the halfling villages of Whitecliff Downs on the night of the new moon. Each village hosts its own, with pavilions, ribbons, and contest rings on the village green — pies, ales, archery, sheep-shearing, singing, and whatever else the local families can argue about. The Fair is where rivalries are settled and reputations made; the pie-crown in particular is held with fierce pride and lost with fierce shame. Outsiders are welcome and usually fed past the point of comfort.

Tinytrolls.text:
Tinytrolls (Species):

Small, bog-green, knee-high cousins of the great trolls of the north, found in brambly hollows and overgrown woods across Larion's settled regions. They speak a coarse trade-pidgin, hoard whatever shiny things they can steal, and squabble in shrieking little bands. A tinytroll alone is a nuisance; a nest of them can ruin a forager's day and occasionally a forager. They regenerate weakly, like their larger kin, but a torch or a determined dog handles them. Hedge-witches sometimes bargain with them for trinkets; most farmers just chase them off with a rake.

Harrans' Rising.text:
Harran's Rising (History):

An age ago the dead rose in the City of Ancestors, the great necropolis near Ardan's Watch. The cause was a ghost — a warlord of the old Fourth Empire, cruel in life and crueler in death, who woke in his tomb and called the buried dead of the necropolis to his banner. For a season the Inquisitors fought to hold the risen host inside the walls of the dead and keep the truth from the living city. It was an Inquisitor named Harran who put the warlord down at the last and broke the Rising, though it cost him his life to do it. The Inquisitors still speak of Harran's Rising as the worst night the order has known, and of Harran as one of the greatest of their kind. Some say the warlord was never truly unmade, only sent back — and that this is why the City of Ancestors must be watched without end.

The Grey Lady.text: The Grey Lady, the Lady of the Last Road (Goddess): the power that keeps the crossing of the dead. Folk do not so much worship her as pray for her aid: common belief holds that when a soul dies it comes to the Shadelands, the grey country of the dead, and there it may get stuck — bound by anger, grief, or business left unfinished, unable to move on. The Grey Lady's mercy is to lead the willing across Repenthe, the River of Oblivion, where a soul drinks and forgets all it was, and so is freed to be born again. To cross is to find rest. To refuse — out of pride, hatred, or a love too fierce to surrender — is to remain, clinging to the memory of a life that is over. The dead who will not cross are what haunt the living world. This is why funerals pray the departed will go willingly, and why a body is brought before her shrine on its way to the grave: not to beg her favor, but to ask that the dead be willing to take her road.

The Empyreans.text:
Empyreans:
Empyreans are a species of sentient winged, bipedal humanoids, rare now, scattered thin across Larion. They are tall — half a head or more above a tall human — and built on a grander scale: high, strong features, eyes that hold a faint inner light, and broad feathered wings folded at the back. Wing and skin run to no single hue; an empyrean may be white, red, black, or shades between, and the coloring varies from one to the next as hair or eyes do among humans. Long ago, in the age of the Empyrean Empire, their kind ruled from the high air, a proud and tyrant people who worshipped the sun and bent the lands beneath them to their will. That age is long over; the empyreans of today are no more answerable for it than dragonkin are for the tyrant-drakes of old, and most ordinary folk have no notion of this ancient history in any case.

Vortigar the Unburied.text:
Vortigar the Unburied:

Vortigar was a warlord of the Fourth Empire who served the demon-princes of Ur and was thrown down with them. In life he would not be ruled and in death he would not be buried — he refused the grave and the crossing both, and so he remains, a corpse held together by a will that never learned to stop.Where Vortigar walks, the buried dead rise to his banner: he empties old battlefields and graveyards and marshals the risen into an army, fighting still the wars he lost in life. His dreamed world in the Shadelands is the field of his last defeat, which he relives without end, certain that this time he will win it — and he raises Larion's dead to fill out his ranks. To put down the risen is not enough; they rise again so long as Vortigar wills it. He can only be ended at the root, in the grey country, where an Inquisitor must break him on the field he cannot stop losing.

The Fourth Empire.text: The Fourth Empire: Before Larion as it is now, the land was ruled by a proud and cruel dominion whose highborn held power in league with the demon princes of Ur. Their cities stood where Silvervale's heartland stands today, and their ruin lies buried in strata beneath Ardan's Watch and the surrounding country. Most people know the Fourth Empire as a dead tyranny. The League remembers it as a warning: old tyrannies return through buried relics, hungry dead, cults, and powers that were never as gone as the living hoped.

Sethelle of the Nine Sorrows.text:
Sethelle of the Nine Sorrows:
Sethelle was a great lady of the Fourth Empire. When that age fell she lost everything — her house, her station, all she loved — and drowned so wholly in grief that the grief outlived her. She would not cross the River and be unmade, for to forget her sorrow felt a betrayal of all she had lost, and so she remains: one of the seven mighty dead who bound themselves together long ago, were put down, and have now returned.

Karneth Draghmar.text:
Karneth Draghmar:

Karneth was the Fourth Empire's executioner-judge, the man who made slaughter look like law. Where he rises, the Iron Lictors come with him: masked imperial dead carrying axes, chains, bronze sentence-plates, and iron wheel-frames. They drag the accused into public places, hang a verdict around the victim's neck, and bind them to the Imperial Wheel to be broken and displayed as an example. Karneth does not tempt, argue, or scheme. He pronounces sentence, and the dead carry it out.

The Lady Mavrocine.text:
The Lady Mavrocine:

Mavrocine was a vampire impostor who murdered a noblewoman, took her face, and used her beauty and borrowed name to move through the Fourth Empire's courts until everyone around her was dead. Where she rises, important people begin dying behind locked doors, and someone beautiful, trusted, and false is always nearby. Her servants are vampire thralls, dead handmaids, and elegant assassins who open doors that should have stayed locked. Mavrocine's work is simple: kill the right person, take the right place, and let the living invite her in.

Ossarine the Pale Crown.text:
Ossarine the Pale Crown:

Ossarine is the dead will inside the Pale Crown, a white imperial crown that turns ambition into obedience. Whoever wears it becomes cold, commanding, and impossible to disobey for long. The living kneel against their will; the dead rise to serve; ambitious fools call it destiny until they can no longer take the crown off. Ossarine's servants are the Crown-Thralls: enthralled living subjects, kneeling ghosts, and dead knights bound to the crown's command. To fight Ossarine, the crown must be taken from its host and its claim to rule broken.

Belugar Thoth-Amon.text:
Belugar Thoth-Amon:

Belugar was a priest of Ur who fed the living to black altars and called the screams worship. Where he rises, old altar-stones wake under ruined forts, catacombs, and cursed woods. People marked for sacrifice are dragged away, and the dead rise as the Shackled Host: corpses bound in massive chains, using those chains as weapons while the souls inside them remain offerings to Belugar's rite. Break the altar, free the Host, and the priest loses his hold.

Druathyr the Thrice-Drowned.text:
Druathyr the Thrice-Drowned:

Druathyr is lord of the fen-drowned dead. Where he rises, black water takes people: wells knock from below, ditches pull at ankles, millponds give back the dead, and flooded cellars become doors into the drowning dark. His servants are the Drowned Dead: waterlogged corpses that drag the living into mire, pond, ditch, or well to join their number. Druathyr does not need a court or cult. He only needs water deep enough to close over a mouth.

Talion Corwin.text: Talion Corwin: The founder of House Corwin's greatness, dead now and passed into legend. The house had fallen into decadence in his father's day, and Talion was its black sheep — a wastrel and a prodigal who drank and brawled and shamed his name, and at last left it. He came home in the hour of Marrenford's need, when renegade elves of the Everwood had raised a mercenary army to throw down the castle and open the river-crossings to their smuggling. The town was all but lost. Talion swore an oath upon the Elfstone to lift the siege or die for it — and then he kept it, leading the broken town against the host, slaying the enemy commander with his own hand and routing the rest. He went on to become a Master of Swords and built the Blade chapterhouse at Marrenford that bears his name. He is the proof the people of Marrenford love best: that a man can fall low, suffer, come back true, and make himself great.

The Shadelands.text:
The Shadelands:
Past the edge of the living world lies the Shadelands, where the dead go. Most pass through and are gone. Some will not — the angry, the proud, the ones with business unfinished — and these linger as ghosts, and worse. Folk who know say that is where hauntings come from, and risen dead, and the cold places where the air goes wrong. A barrow that will not stay quiet, a battlefield where the slain keep walking — the trouble has its root in the Shadelands, pressing through where the grey world rubs against ours. Necromancers are said to walk there and come back. Most people would rather not think about it.

The Underworld.text:
The Underworld:
The Underworld is the network of caverns and tunnels beneath the surface world, older than any kingdom above it. It holds the ruins of empires that fell in ages past, along with the wealth they left behind — relics and lost work buried in the deep. Underground peoples have built fortresses there among the dead cities, and many are hostile to the surface. Their raiders come up through old mines, wells, and breached cellars. Those who descend for the treasure face the things that live down there.

Order of the Silver Sword.text: Order of the Silver Sword: Larion's specialist monster-hunters, seated at Castle Harstone in Carendon and sworn to no crown. Candidates are Initiates until they complete one supervised trial hunt and are sworn before the Great Hall at Taking the Silver, swearing to serve the hunted and hunt the hunter, to go where others dare not, to bring home the living and bury the dead, to call no crown and no coin their master, and to carry the sword until it is given to the earth with them. New Silverblades receive a fallen hunter's Order horn from the Hornwall and carry Order silver suited to their calling: any kind of silvered weapon, a silver-faced shield, or a silver-bound magical focus or implement. They rise from Silverblade to Veteran Silverblade and then Master of the Hunt through recognized hunts and the judgment of the Order, which the Grandmaster of the Hunt leads.

Tarnholme Academy of the Arcane.text:
Tarnholme Academy of the Arcane: Larion's great school of magic, on five islands in the Jade Tarn: the Main Island, which all students share, and one isle for each of its four Colleges. The Head of the Academy and the masters run it. They value skill earned through practice, students who look after each other, and magic put to use for people who need it. Students and masters are humans, elves, gnomes, halflings, catkin, demonborn, giantborn, orcs, dark elves, merfolk, foxkin and more. Students are adults, most between eighteen and their mid-twenties.

Students arrive as First-Years and choose a College during their first year:
- Battle Mages: combat magic, wards and counter-magic, and elemental magic.
- Artificers: enchanting and magical making, from charms and lamps to constructs.
- Summoners: summoning, beasts, nature magic for creatures, and shapeshifting, under one rule: always come back.
- Healers: healing, herb and divine magic, and curse-breaking.

A College shapes a student's training but never stops them learning other magic. Each College wears its color on robes and scarves: crimson for Battle Mages, copper for Artificers, green for Summoners and sky blue for Healers. Every student wears a Tarnholme star, a small silver brooch that lights one more point each Year and takes on its College's color when a College claims them at Colors Night.

Students work their way from the First Year to the Fourth through Practica, field work posted on the board in the Great Hall. A Practicum might mean clearing pests from a brewer's cellar, finding a lost familiar, settling a quarrel over a charm gone wrong, guarding witchwood gatherers or fetching thunderglass from the badlands. Each Year ends with a celebration on the Muster Court, and the Fourth Year ends with Commencement, when students graduate.

Every school of magic is taught at Tarnholme, necromancy and blood magic included. What the Academy forbids is life sacrifice: killing or harming anyone to power a spell, or draining anyone's blood, strength or life for magic against their will. A necromancer may speak with the dead and raise bodies given freely or long buried; a blood mage may spend their own blood, or blood freely given. Every graduate swears at Commencement never to make a life sacrifice.

Tarnholme mages talk about magic as a craft they have mastered, in terms of feel, practice and results, not theory. The Academy is warm and colorful, full of everyday magic: enchanted and animate objects of every kind, magical contraptions, talking things, familiars and pets, and robes and scarves in every color. The masters are friendly, busy mentors who keep their doors open. The Colleges are friendly rivals. In their free time, students cross to Tarnport, the port town on the shore, to get away from school.

Watchtower.text: Watchtower: The great elderstone tower in Ardan's Watch and headquarters of the League of Adventurers. Its League Hall posts Silvervale work and registers adventurers; its Map Room gathers reports from across Larion; its Portal Hall holds voluntary links to allied seats such as Tarnholme Academy, Castle Harstone, the Black Tower, and the Citadel of the Pact.

Duchy of Drusavia.text: Duchy of Drusavia: A bright old duchy of forested hills, wealthy dales, haunted estates, and buried vampire-era sin. Its capital is Drusavia, where the Temple of Galard honors Castian the liberator and the Black Tower handles the dead that courage alone could not settle.

Temple of Galard.text: Temple of Galard: Drusavia's public faith of courage, sacrifice, and radiant arms, and the Hall of Shields of the Templars Adamant. The temple honors Castian, blesses steel and moonstone for work against the dead, recognizes deeds during Galard's Proving Year, and stands as the bright civic counterpart to the Black Tower.

Templars Adamant.text: Templars Adamant: Galard's Shieldbearer order seated at the Temple of Galard in Drusavia. A person who completes the Proving Year may freely swear the Shieldbearer oath and enter as a Templar Initiate with the White-Silver Shield Clasp. One supervised first shield-work earns full Templar Adamant rank; three recognized independent works earn Templar Captain; four further great works may earn acclamation as Templar Champion. Their work protects warders and the living, purges hostile dead, destroys anchors, and seals breaches. They never traffic or bargain with shades.

Knights Vigilant.text: Knights Vigilant: Galard's proud undead-hunting order seated at the Temple of the Sword Vigilant above Aldwall. A New-Sworn bears a moonstone oath-brooch and completes one supervised first ride to become Moor-Knight. Three recognized independent rides earn a personal banner and Banner-Knight rank; four further great rides may earn acclamation as Champion Vigilant. Completed rides are recounted and recognized publicly in the Feast-Hall.

Harran of the Inquisition.text: Harran of the Inquisition (Historical Figure):  Harran was an Inquisitor of Drusavia, reckoned among the greatest the order ever fielded, who broke the Rising in the City of Ancestors and died putting down the warlord-ghost that caused it. The Inquisitors held his wake at the tavern on Lowlamp Lane and never let it end; the place bears his name, and his bar-tab has stayed open ever since. By custom an Inquisitor returned alive from a hard task drinks on Harran, and once each night the house drinks not to mourn him, but to keep faith with the work he finished.

The Ranks of the Inquisition.text: Shadow Inquisition Ranks: An accepted member bears the Mark of Rhadan and begins as an Initiate, handling one supervised surface case. The Mark establishes membership and anchors authorized contact with the Shadelands; it does not grant a Shade or full rank. A successful Initiate may undergo the Rite of Bonding at the Pit and rise as a Shade-Bonded Inquisitor. After three recognized Inquisitor cases they may become an Adept who leads deep work. After four further recognized Adept cases they may become a Master with authority over the order's gravest cases and the defense of the Pit.

The High Wardens.text: The High Wardens: The elven wardens of the Everwood, answering to the Council of Elf-Lords in Canopy. Cloaked in greens and greys, armed with longbow and yew-staff, they enforce high elven law throughout the forest, from the elven heartland of Elfwood to the borders of Sanctuary Vale, and they are seen rarely and heard less. They permit halfling foragers, human woodsmen, and dwarven charcoal-burners to work the outer belt of the wood under old understandings; past their line, only the Wardens go. They keep to the wood and keep their hands clean — the messy frontier work of bandit-havens, raiders, and disappearances they leave to Sanctuary, and to whoever Sanctuary will send.

The Greater Goblinate.text: The Greater Goblinate: The goblin state that rules the Black Fells from its capital at Smoketown. The Dragon Queen united the warring tribes into a single power with a governor, a professional army, and industry: obsite mines, dragonfire works, and forges that arm the firelancer legions. The Goblinate raids by sea, presses south, and serves its absent queen openly — her coming is the state's faith, preached by the allied Church of the Pyre. Rank-and-file goblins have never seen her; they know the dragonfire flows, the lances work, and the old world that despised them is learning to fear them. Not every goblin serves it: the tribes it failed to swallow and the scattered raiders of the borderlands owe the Goblinate nothing.

The Great Dragons.text: The Great Dragons: The elder dragons of the first ages — powers that shaped the world and vanished in an age no one remembers. What remains of them is bones, hoards, tombs, and the dragonkin who carry their blood thinned. The dragons of the present age are lesser creatures by every account, and even these are rare. Atravoraxis, the Dragon Queen the Goblinate serves, claims to be of the elder kind — and claims to be coming back. She is what she claims: an elder dragon that Suleyvan the Sealer shut out of Larion behind the door in Fire Mountain's heart. The Church of the Pyre preaches her return as gospel, and the Goblinate arms for her arrival.

Astarieth the Risen.text: Astarieth the Risen: The mire dragon who rules the lizardfolk dragon-kingdom of the Reedmoot Fens. She was a priestess once, so the fen-folk say, and rose — or was remade — as a dragon; her kingdom worships her as a living god. She rules the closed western fens through her priest-kings, and her brood is raised in the great mounds, fed by the brood-rite. The fens under her rule are shut: what goes in is taken, and what is taken goes to the mounds. The free moot at Reedmoot holds the eastern strip against her war-parties, and its people mock the dragon out loud because every one of them fears her. Her war-parties also take a yearly tithe from the outlying villages of the marsh country around the Great Lagoon — goods most years, people some years — and the villages pay because they remember the ones that refused.

The Brood-Rite.text: The Brood-Rite: The practice that feeds Astarieth's brood. Captives taken in the Reedmoot Fens — travelers, salvagers, fen-folk snatched in raids — are carried west alive, held in the pens of the brood-mounds, and sacrificed to the brood at the new moon. The rite is why lizardfolk war-parties take prisoners rather than kill, and why rescue parties from the free moot never want for volunteers: between the taking and the new moon, the taken can still be brought home.

The Firing of the Golden Fleet.text: The Firing of the Golden Fleet: The Empire of Light sent a fleet against the dragon-kingdom of the Fens, and Astarieth burned it at anchor in a single night. The wrecks lie where they burned, and the fen-folk of the free moot have salvaged them ever since — the alchemical fire-stores locked in Reedmoot's stone store-house came off those ships, and so did much of the moot's iron. The wrecks still hold fire-stores, imperial arms, and the imperial dead, and the dragon-kingdom watches its trophy waters.

Heronfolk.text: Heronfolk: Tall, long-legged marsh-folk of the Stiltwood in the Reedmoot Fens, living in roosts high in the mangrove crowns. They are patient, deadly with the bow from height, and few of words with strangers. The dragon-kingdom tried to swallow the Stiltwood and stopped trying: rooting archers out of a drowned mangrove forest costs more than it takes. The heronfolk trade with the free moot, keep their own counsel, and owe nothing to anyone.

Ophialtha.text: Ophialtha: The dragon of the Seadeep Kingdoms, queen of everything beneath the storm-dark southern sea. She is sea-bound — she cannot leave the water, and no dry ground is ever within her reach, only her servants' — and she is patient as the sea itself. The drowned are her gift and her subjects: surface folk remade for the water, generations deep, who garrison the drowned places and take the living down alive. She holds court in the sunken Dome of All Worlds at the heart of drowned Orichala, and she does not stir for fighting in the standing city. Disturb the Dome, and she comes.

The Drowned-and-Changed.text: The Drowned: The people of the Seadeep Kingdoms beneath the storm-dark southern sea. They were surface folk once — sailors, salvagers, the taken — remade for the water by the dragon Ophialtha's gift, generations deep, and they count the remaking a blessing. The kingdoms prefer keeping to killing: they take the living down alive, and what is taken joins them in time. Sailors' law for Seadeep water is old and simple: cross without stopping and you will be suffered; stop to take what the sea has claimed, set foot on the drowned places, or pry at the wrecks, and the kingdoms answer from below.

The Dome of All Worlds.text: The Dome of All Worlds: The great wonder of drowned Orichala — a colossal sealed habitat that held living specimens from every land the old empire ruled. It sank with the city and trapped its air, and its old magic still keeps the air good and the gardens alive. Centuries feral, its creatures answer to nothing: rock-apes in the high tiers, terror-birds on the grass shelf, a grown-monstrous crocodile in the channels, and bright venomous things in the green. Ophialtha enters through the sea-breach in the great lake and rules the Dome as her court — a queen of the deep presiding over a little world of the surface.

Nuur-Suthra and the Soul Engine.text: Nuur-Suthra and the Soul Engine: Nuur-Suthra, the Flame Undying, is worshipped as the dragon of the Alar Coast but lairs north of it, in the wreck of the Celestial Citadel, which struck the mountains above the Redrock coast. The Church of the Pyre rules the coast in its name and ships it tribute; the dragon itself is dormant, and stirs for one thing only. In the citadel's Engine Vault stands the Soul Engine — a vessel of brass and black elderstone, tall as a tower, roaring flame without pause since the old empire fell. It is a prison: the soul of a djinn is sealed inside, and the flame is its rage. Nuur-Suthra lairs coiled around it, warming itself, drawing power, healing from its fire in battle. While the Soul Engine burns, the dragon cannot die. Free the djinn or break the seal, and the next death is real.

The Red-Cowls.text: The Red-Cowls: The common soldiery of the Church of the Pyre on the Alar Coast — believers, poor men's sons, men with nowhere else, sworn to the Church and cowled in red. They work in squads of four to six under grey priests, the Church's officers and casters. In Serendipity they do not police theft or brawls; they hunt one crime, enmity toward the Church, and the marked they take are not seen again. In the outer desert they ride in hunting parties a dozen strong, running down Tribesfolk and fugitives. Above the cowls stand the priests; above the priests, the Temple of the Flame Undying; above the temple, the dragon.

The Desert Tribes.text: The Desert Tribes: The free peoples of the Alar Coast's deep desert — the survivors and descendants of Gesenthame, and of everyone the Church of the Pyre has burned out since. They raid the Church's tribute caravans, shelter and smuggle out all who flee the flame, and cannot be caught: their camps pack in an hour and the deep sand is theirs. A stranger's standing with the Tribes is earned in steps — fed at the guest-fire, then known, then trusted and offered guiding. Of the very few counted as the Tribes' own, some are vouched onward to places the Tribes do not name.

The Burning of Gesenthame.text: The Burning of Gesenthame: Gesenthame was a jeweled city of the Alar Coast, seat of the Azhakid Princes, and it refused the Church of the Pyre's tribute. The Church burned it with dragonfire, and the city died in a night. Its survivors fled into the deep desert and became the Desert Tribes; its ruin stands as the Church's lesson to Serendipity, the city that pays. Church dig-crews work the cinders under writ to this day, searching for the Azhakid crowns and burning-jewels, which they believe the burning fused beneath the city. They have never been found.

The Empire of Light.text: The Empire of Light: The empire seated at Caranthoria on the Great Lagoon, heir to the old Empyrean Empire; its citizens call themselves Solarians. Empress Aurianax III raised the Eye of God from the lagoon when she came home, and built a new empire on the drowned bones of the old one — bright, orderly, and fair by its own law, taking citizens of every people and soldiers of every kind. Its legions are bound by the Unity and are the finest heavy infantry in Larion; its causeways and sea-walls have made dry land of open swamp; its justice is consistent and its taxes are not negotiable. Its war runs west into the fens, against the dragon-kingdom of the Reedmoot Fens. The Empress means all Larion to share one law and one defense in the end, but she is patient: the Eye and the western war come first.

Empress Aurianax III.text: Empress Aurianax III: The empyrean who founded the Empire of Light on the ruins of the old Empyrean Empire. Long ago her winged people ruled these coasts from the high air, and their empire drowned in its fall; Aurianax came home to the lagoon where its capital sank, raised the Eye of God from the water, and built anew on the old empire's bones. Her legions name her the Harrower of Ur, and the Harrowers take their name and their charge from hers. She reigns from the Eye and rarely comes down; no one goes up without her invitation, and her word reaches the city through prefects and the legion. Overhead, the work of finishing the Eye never stops.

The Eye of God.text: The Eye of God: The sky-citadel of gold-bright brass floating above Caranthoria — the throne of the Empire of Light. The Empress raised it from the lagoon where it had lain drowned since the old empire fell, and the work of finishing it never stops overhead. No one goes up without her invitation. What the Eye is — palace, temple, engine — is argued in every port on the coast. Those who have watched it longest say a great lens at its heart is being rebuilt, and old salvagers' tales call the Eye a weapon that once looked down on the whole of the south.

The Unity and the Sun-Brand.text: The Unity and the Sun-Brand: To swear into the legions of the Empire of Light is to take three things together: citizenship, the sun-brand at the neck, and the Unity — the mind-bond that lets a century fight as one, shields locking without an order spoken, no soldier ever alone in the line. Inside the empire the brand is an honor; outside it is a verdict, for a sun-branded neck is known in every inn in Larion, and a deserter cannot lose himself in an ordinary town. Deserters band together instead, in ruins and wild country where a scarred neck draws no second look, and there are more such bands than the legion admits. The Unity is the legions' strength and the empire's quiet grip: what a soldier gives up to never stand alone is not easily taken back.

The Harrowers.text: The Harrowers: A small sworn order within the legions of the Empire of Light who hunt the demon-tainted — possession, infernal bargains, the cults of Ur. They take their name from the Empress's own epithet, Harrower of Ur, and their hall stands in the Legion Quarter of Caranthoria. Every Harrower is a legionnaire first: Unity, brand, and the line before the hunt. Outside imperial borders their writ is disputed — the demonborn free-city of New Anthara, which fights Ur in its own way, refuses them entry outright.

Nullmetal.text: Nullmetal: A dull grey alloy that deadens the mind-arts — thought-reading, mental domination, and the imperial legions' Unity alike go quiet around it. Its trade is not lawful: the Empire of Light pays bounties to keep it off the market, which is itself the best-known proof that it works. The Syndicate moves it anyway, out of the Warrens of Caranthoria, to buyers who would rather not share their minds — and to those who fear the thrallmages of Falmastra, against whom a nullmetal token is the only armor money can buy.

Dun Teine Watch.text: Dun Teine Watch: The dwarven fortress in the high snows above the Black Fells, holding the one road down into the volcanic country. Its walls are thirty feet of fitted stone and it has never been taken; the Goblinate has reckoned the cost of the attempt and left it alone. The Watch keeps the count — every convoy up the Iron Road, every shipment into the breach, every banner that moves — and what the Watch counts, the free kingdoms hear. It is the last unconquered ground on the peninsula, and the closest thing the war against the Dragon Queen has to a forward post.

The Swordlaw.text: The Swordlaw: The law of the lawless sea beyond Tevantia's bridges, and the only law Freehaven keeps: disputes are settled steel to steel; a challenge given and accepted binds both parties and their crews; the winner's word stands.

The Empyrean Empire.text: The Empyrean Empire: The dominion of the winged empyreans, who ruled land, sea, and sky in the ages before Larion's present kingdoms. Their works outlived them: sky-citadels like the fallen Celestial Citadel of Alar and the Eye of God above Caranthoria, the colossal stone bridges that bind the Swordlaw Isles, brass warships, sea-gates, and the titan-carved stone of the southern archipelago. The citadels flew on djinn-engines — bound spirits of fire driving works of brass — and where one fell hard the land still carries the scar: the Mirror-Waste of the eastern deserts is a crater of black glass where two citadels came down together, and the Soul Engine of Alar still burns with the rage of the djinn sealed inside it. The empire fell ages ago, its citadels dropping from the sky and its cities drowning, and salvagers have lived off its bones for generations without scratching them. The Empire of Light at Caranthoria is its deliberate heir: an empyrean empress building anew on the old crown's foundations.

The Kindred War.text: The Kindred War: The mythic war the elves fought against themselves in the First Days — sun against moon, kindred against kindred, until the elven homeland itself was lost. The wood elves are descended from those who refused to fight; the war scattered the rest of the kindreds to the corners of Larion. Ruined elven cities from the war still stand in the Everwood, and the enmities it made — sun against moon above all — have never healed. In the Everwood it was fought longest, high elves against dark elves, until the Sundering ended it there.

The Pact of Sanctuary.text: The Pact of Sanctuary: The agreement that lets the city of Sanctuary stand in the deep Everwood — the city's founders raised the walls, the high elves wove the wards, and neither stands without the other. It is the only such bargain the wood's masters have ever made with outsiders, and the forest's other powers were no party to it: the renegade elves want the enclave gone, and Yslaine's wood keeps its own law at the city's edge. The Pact holds because both sides need it, and everyone in Sanctuary knows what it means the day one side decides otherwise.

Cold Iron.text: Cold Iron: Forest iron from veins the Everwood's roots have grown down through, found only beneath Sanctuary Vale. It must be mined and worked cold, never touched by forge-fire, or the wild burns out of it and it is only iron. Worked cold, its edge deals arcane force and bites the fey and the magical as plain steel cannot — its touch is anathema to the fey.

The Wildkeepers.text: The Wildkeepers: A fellowship of druids, rangers, and priests seated at the great hollow oak of Velantami in the Everwood, sworn that the wild must never be owned or tamed — only kept free and alive in its natural balance. A Wildkeeper is the enemy of whatever breaks that balance: the poacher and grove-feller who strip the wood for gain, the blight and the foul spell that corrupt its cycle, and above all the warlord who would burn the forest. They answer to no king, no court, and no written law. They keep the wood, not Sanctuary — they suffer the walled city because a city at peace harms the wild less than a war would.

Wildbond.text: Wildbond, wildbonding, and wildbonded: A wildbond is a deliberate, mutual relationship between a person and a thinking wild creature who chooses to work with them. It is not ownership, a trained animal's obedience, or an automatic reward for kindness. A person who seeks a wildbond ordinarily begins by asking an oracle, dream-reader, shrine, elder, or other trusted guide for a vision, omen, or direction toward a creature and place where a bond might be possible. They follow the sign into the living world, find the place, meet the creature on its own ground, and face a meaningful test of patience, courage, respect, judgment, or shared danger. The creature may refuse, test, leave, or choose another person. Food, rescue, a friendly greeting, a shared patrol, or a creature's curiosity does not by itself create a wildbond. If both continue to choose one another through the encounter, the relationship becomes a wildbond: the person is wildbonded to the creature, and the creature is wildbonded to the person. Wildbonded beings remain independent thinking actors with their own wants, boundaries, and right to refuse. The bond supports trust, friendship, loyalty, fieldwork, rescue, scouting, protection, and chosen family. Distance may test a wildbond but does not dissolve it; deliberate betrayal, coercion, or broken trust can strain or end it.

Yslaine.text: Yslaine: The dryad-queen of the old wood, older than the Pact of Sanctuary and no party to it. Her demesne west of Sanctuary keeps the wood's own law: no outsider enters, and the forest itself turns back those who try. The girls left or seized at her demesne's edge she takes and makes into dryads — by the wood's law a gift, by the city's a stolen child.

The Sundering.text: The Sundering: The settlement that ended the war between the high elves and the dark elves within Elfwood: the forest surface to the high elves, the Rootdark beneath it to the dark elves, neither to cross the other's realm on pain of war. It does not forbid dark elves from traveling on the surface beyond Elfwood. The line has held for an age. It has one standing crossing within the forest — Ilunethel, the trade-town at the open way between the surface and the dark-elf realm below, where deep-goods are sold in the open and the high elves' law does not reach. The high elves call the Sundering justice; the dark elves' monuments tell the Betrayal their own way; and both watch the line fray from their own side of it.

The Wood Elves.text: The Wood Elves: The elves who refused the Kindred War, following Talvaren, He Who Walks Beside, who guided those who would not fight to safety and gave his life defending them. They hold to neither Canopy nor the deep, keep the old paths of the Everwood, and mourn what the other kindreds broke. 'May you walk in beauty' — Talvaren's last words — still marks their births, arrivals, and deaths. They are hunters, wanderers, and keepers of the forest's oldest memory, and both high and dark elves quietly defer to them in matters neither will admit to.

Moot Law.text: Moot Law: The law of the Wild Grass Sea, older than any of its peoples' quarrels: no kings, no thrones, and no blood spilled past the boundary stones of Kingstor. The beastfolk buried their tyrant alive — the sorcerer-emperor who enslaved them all with domination magic sleeps under guard in the Kingsgrave Kurgan — and built their law around never digging him up. Effigies called kings are built of straw and burned at the Great Moot so nobody forgets. A breach of the boundary-peace is answered by every species present at once, which is why it holds.

House Tessaro.text: House Tessaro: One of the two great hunting houses of Coriva on the Bay of Serpents. Tessaro kills: harpoon crews who put down the monsters that threaten the shipping lanes, silver-armed and proud of it. The house's law is older than its wealth — a Tessaro crew is never abandoned, whatever it costs, and the house has beggared itself twice proving it. They sponsor hunters with the nerve for the biggest quarry and bury their dead with the harpoon that failed them.

House Cavarin.text: House Cavarin: One of the two great hunting houses of Coriva on the Bay of Serpents. Cavarin captures: beast-wrights who take monsters alive and bind them into the bay's work — harbor-beasts, draft-serpents, arena stock, and stranger commissions. They sponsor handlers with the nerve for live work, and their compounds are the only place in Larion where a sea-monster has a stall, a keeper, and a feeding schedule.

The Law of the Bay.text: The Law of the Bay: The unwritten law of the Bay of Serpents, kept by hunter and merfolk alike: do not hunt herded waters, do not kill young, do not hunt what speaks, and do not bait lived-in water. The law is why the bay's people and its seafolk neighbors have shared the richest monster-grounds in Larion for generations without war. Breaking it voids a hunter's standing with the houses, the League, and the merfolk at once — and crews that break it tend to take southern salvage charters and not come back.

The Mother of Serpents.text: The Mother of Serpents: Sailors of the southern coasts swear there is a serpent in the Bay of Serpents bigger than anything the hunting houses have ever put a harpoon in — pearl-white, old beyond any record, big enough to be mistaken for a reef or a line of swells. The stories call her the Mother of Serpents and say the bay's serpent-broods are all hers. Some tales tell of a sea-cave that holds the bow of the Serpentsbane, a hunting ship that went looking for her and came home with only its stern. No captain claims to have killed her, and old hands go quiet when the water goes calm and something long passes under the hull.

The Sun Kings.text: The Sun Kings: The Sun Kings were empyreans — winged, ageless god-kings who ruled the eastern deserts as a province of the Empyrean Empire. When that empire fell, the Sun Kings fell with it, and their priesthoods entombed them in the seven pyramids of the Dunelands with full divine honors, expecting them to rise.

The Order of the Desert Rose.text: The Order of the Desert Rose: The demon-hunter institution of Larion, seated at the Citadel of the Pact in Redrock. The Order binds and banishes rather than executes: a demon slain on Larion's soil finds its way home eventually, but a demon bound in desert-rose stone or sent through the Gate of Gaol is dealt with. The career runs recruit, taught, sworn hunter, and the Order takes any with the discipline for it. Its hunters range wherever the infernal leaks through.

Desert-Rose Stone.text: Desert-Rose Stone: A pale rose-colored crystal that grows in rosettes in the deserts of Redrock and wards against demons. Bindings hold in it: a demon sealed in desert-rose stone stays sealed. The Order of the Desert Rose builds with it and works it — the Citadel of the Pact stands on a crag of it — and demon-hunters across Larion carry cut rosettes as wards and binding-stones.

Heliaxes.text: Heliaxes: The sun-dragon who hallowed the high peaks of Redrock an age ago and then departed. No dragon, demon, or dark thing has laired in those heights since — the empty sky above Cloudtop is his lingering gift, and the city's forges are said to burn pure because of it.

Suleyvan the Sealer.text: Suleyvan the Sealer: The legendary master-binder of the old ages, whose seals hold to this day. He made the Pact of All Planes that bars the hostile powers of other worlds from Larion; he bound the arch-djinn that wards the deeps of Fire Mountain; and he kept the dangerous spirits of his own age sealed in vessels beneath his own roof. That roof is now Suleyvan's Folly, the ruined palace-city in Redrock's sands, still full of his sealed lamps, rings, jars, and bottles — and of people bold or stupid enough to open them.

The Flame Princes.text: The Flame Princes: The djinnborn princes of Naran-Kadish, the jeweled city of the old desert, who ruled with fire in their blood until they burned their own city in the great rite that drove the demons out. What the rite tore open beneath Naran-Kadish never fully closed; the ruins are gnoll-held now, and the seam below still leaks.

The Vampire Lords of Shadow Summits.text: The Vampire Lords of Shadow Summits: The lords of Shadow Summits are moon elf vampires — a few dozen ancient and powerful individuals who each hold a valley from a fortified estate. They feed on the people they rule, taking a fixed levy of blood each year, drawn by lot at each dark of the moon, and defend their valleys in return. Each lord rules alone and answers to no one above him; the Crimson Company serves the lords together as soldiery and enforcers. They take in the outcasts of Larion and use them. The Lady of Blood is their ancestor, and the blood price they pay is the one she set.

Galard.text: Galard: The god of courage against the dark, worshipped wherever the dead rise. Galard's gift is the courage to stand — over the hearth, over the grave, over the friend who did not come back — and his faith blesses steel, moonstone, and the people who carry them into the dark. His worship is split between two estranged orders. In Whitemoor, the Knights Vigilant follow Galard the Swordbearer: put the dead down by force, in the open, hunting them wherever they rise. In Drusavia, the Templars Adamant follow Galard the Shieldbearer: raise the wall, purge the dead, and seal the breach, refusing all traffic with shades. Each order holds the other's way to be a corruption of the gift, and the quarrel is old enough to have its own liturgy. Older than their schism is the Proving Year: an aspirant carries a plain iron Road-Shield into the wider world, earns recognition for three distinct deeds of courage, and only then decides whether to seek one oath, the other, or neither. Both orders and Galard's independent shrines recognize the custom; an aspirant belongs to neither order until an oath is freely sworn.

Vashqara, the Unbound City.text: Vashqara, the Unbound City: A city of free djinn, somewhere under the deep desert — so the Desert Tribes' oldest songs say, and the Tribes do not sing idly. No road leads there and no map marks it; the Tribes vouch the rarest of their trusted onward to guides who do not explain themselves. Scholars argue whether Vashqara is real, a memory of something drowned in the Empyrean Empire's fall, or a hope the desert tells itself.

The Grell.text: The Grell: The kobold clans of the Underworld beneath Silvervale, who claim descent from a mighty kobold empire — the Grell — that they say raised the colossal ruins they den in. The ruins are the buried cities of the Fourth Empire, and everyone above ground knows it, but the clans hold the claim with complete conviction: their chiefs style themselves emperors, they treat the old imperial halls as a stolen inheritance to be reclaimed, and they cannot read the inscriptions that disprove them. They press the claim hardest at the warm sunken pleasure quarter at the heart of Grell Hollows. The clans default to raiding and squatting, and they are cowardly, bribeable, and prone to negotiation when they are losing.

Big Buzzer.text: Big Buzzer: A Fourth Empire ground-vibration artifact recovered by kobolds in the Boring Hall of the Imperial Arsenal. It emits directional pulses through soil and stone. The pulses attract and irritate stone-boring beetles, drawing them toward a chosen surface point and making them violently destructive, but Big Buzzer does not control, command, ride, or guide the beetles. Its signs are tremors, vibrating water, frightened livestock, fleeing burrowers, abandoned birds, and a low grinding that can be felt before it can be heard. The Fourth Empire's surveyors built it to draw the beetles into boring tunnels where they wanted them; the kobolds do not know this and named it for its noise.

Horn of the First Host.text: Horn of the First Host: Kragga's name for a Fourth Empire war horn recovered in the Imperial Arsenal. Its surviving enchantment reaches old imperial signal passages and calls bound war-shriekers through them. The long serpentine fiends repeat short orders in Kragga's voice, carrying commands across the Grell Hollows and allowing separate kobold hosts to act in concert. The horn carries commands; it is distinct from Big Buzzer, which attracts and irritates stone-boring beetles.

War-shriekers.text: War-shriekers: Long, serpentine fiends bound to old imperial signal passages and called by the Horn of the First Host. They are not banshees, ghosts, or shrieker fungus. A war-shrieker can emerge physically from a passage, repeat a short order in Kragga's voice, constrict or strike a target, and attack with a psychic or sonic shriek. They can be intercepted in Grell passages, and killing one does not silence the whole network.

The Imps of the Basement.text: The Imps of the Basement: The imp-kin of the Basement, the buried market beneath Ardan's Watch — a settled breed of small horned demon-kin descended from the bound servant-castes of the Fourth Empire, left masterless when the demon princes of Ur were cast down. Ages out from under the whip, they are mostly harmless and relentlessly mercantile: touts, money-changers, lamplighters, and dealers in oddments, native to the lantern-strung dark and prosperous in it.

The Fall of Stonehome.text: The Fall of Stonehome: Stonehome was the shared capital of the dwarven kingdom of the Whiteholds, raised above the sealed workings of the dareks. One night within living memory the old seals failed and the city fell whole into the dark — streets, halls, throne, and everyone in them. The kingdom broke with it: Clan Deepfire had driven the great delve that ran toward the sealed dark, Clan Icerune's wards failed on the one night that mattered, and each clan holds the other guilty. The crater where the capital stood is now Deepgate, a delver boomtown drawing crews from across Larion, and the fallen city below is the door to the Darek Deep. The throne of the Whiteholds is still down there, and whoever reclaims it reclaims a crown neither clan will yield to the other.

The Northrealm.text: The Northrealm: The human kingdom that ruled Aurora in the warm age — a seafaring people of harbors, holdfasts, and hot-spring towns, with its capital at Northport. Then the cold came, seasonless and without explanation, and the kingdom died stead by stead and city by city until the sea froze around its fleet at anchor. No one has ever settled why. The snowlanders of the lake country are the Northrealm's remnant — the same people, humbled, holding the few volcanic warm-pockets the cold cannot reach — and the ruins of everything else their forebears built lie out in the white, where the old kingdom's dead keep some of them still. Its rulers once commanded the aurora serpents, now sleeping beneath the sea-ice, and its old royal line survives in exile in Warmwater Township as the Winter Crown, now one of the Greater Duchies.

Hrimnara, the Widow of Winter.text: Hrimnara, the Widow of Winter: The goddess of the cold of the far north — so the snowlanders hold, and they do not say her name loudly indoors. Everything outside the door is hers: the cold, the night, the white, and whatever dies in it. What the Widow takes may walk again, which is why the north burns its dead. When the aurora stands across the sky, the snowlanders say the Widow is walking, and no one travels under it. No shrine is raised to her and nothing is asked of her; the only worship she receives is the Long Night's, and the snowlanders count that the worst thing a soul can do. Scholars who study such things hold her to be a power of the Plane of Ice, kept out of Larion by the Pact of All Planes except where the cold finds a gap.

Sand-Wyrm.text: Sand-Wyrm: Great burrowing worms of the eastern deserts, large enough to take a laden wagon and its team in a single strike. They feel movement through open sand and come up beneath it, and they cannot reach onto rock, so desert crews cross wyrm country rise to rise and reckon distance in runs. Old desert songs say the Sun Kings drove the wyrms as beasts of war and burden in the age of their rule, and that the secret of the driving was entombed with them. No one alive knows how it was done, and no one has lived to learn by trying.

Shadow Inquisition.text: Shadow Inquisition: The ghost-hunter and occult-investigation institution seated at the Black Tower in Drusavia. Initiates bear the Mark of Rhadan and prove themselves through one supervised case. Qualified Initiates may undergo the Rite of Bonding at the Pit of Shadow, gain a Shade, and rise as full Inquisitors trusted with hauntings, undead, cults, Shadelands exposure, and threats ordinary law cannot understand.

The Grand Arena Circuit.text: The Grand Arena Circuit: Larion's great arenas answer to different rulers, Houses, and customs, but their heralds and promoters recognize one another's champions. The eligible venues are the Tournament Grounds at the Field of Valor, Tevantia's Amphitheater, the Red Sands of Oasis, Gavarra's Gilded Cage, Caranthoria's Solarian Arena, the Pit at Gorren Crossing, Coriva's Water Arena, and the Open Grounds at Fallsmeet. Each awards its own championship according to its own rules. A fighter who wins recognized championships at three different circuit arenas becomes eligible for the Grand Champion's Contest, held in the Champions' Ring at the Field of Valor. Winning an ordinary bout or local exhibition does not count: the fighter must defeat the venue's acknowledged title-holder or win its formally declared championship match. The victor at the Champions' Ring is named Grand Champion of the Arenas, a title recognized by crowds, promoters, patrons, and fighting schools throughout Larion. Grand Champions command the largest purses, may headline at any circuit venue, and are commonly invited to choose challengers, train a stable, or sponsor fighters of their own.

The Sky Temple of the Ascension.text: The Sky Temple of the Ascension: A cloud-high monastery on the Unmoored Mountain, a whole red-rock peak lifted from the earth by the First Adept when the demons came. The Temple teaches that the mind can govern the body's attunement to Larion's physical world: a practitioner may detune and become lighter, faster, and able to cross walls or water, or attune more heavily and anchor, strike, and land with immense force. Wind elementals called the Catching Winds keep the peak steady and catch people whose traversal accidents would otherwise kill them, though they do not spare anyone embarrassment. The Temple's ordinary life is communal, joyful, and practical — loud meals, strong drink, restorative potions, movement gear, difficult training, laughter, mutual correction, and compassion. The elite practitioners who master the deeper discipline are the Ascendants, recognized through a series of Descents: ordeals in the wider world where they use their strength to confront danger or protect others.

The Gravebound.text: The Gravebound: A corrupted offshoot of bloodcraft that works through graves, bound dead, and stolen life. Gravebound cells defile old burial customs, raise corpses as labor and guard, and promise frightened people a stronger answer than the old rites. The Bloodhunters of the Red Chantry hunt them as enemies. The Gravebound is not the Path of Blood and should never be treated as the ordinary name for disciplined Bloodhunter practice.

Plate and the Channel.text:
Plate and the Channel:

Magic is drawn through the body, and metal worn close interrupts the draw. Practitioners describe it as reaching through a wall rather than a door: the current is still there, but it arrives late and thin, and holding it costs more than it should. Mail and plate are worst, and the more of the body they cover the worse it runs. Leather, cloth, and bone barely register.
