This is why temple guards who must both fight and bless wear scale over the ribs and nothing over the arms, why battle-casters pay fortunes for warded mail, and why a wizard in a breastplate is a joke told in every academy. Ritual can be worked around it given time and preparation. A spell thrown in the middle of a fight cannot.

Vessels and Foci.text:
Vessels and Foci:

A focus is not a decoration and not a battery. It is a shaped path: a staff, wand, reliquary, sealstone, or seedpod cut and set so that power moves through it the way water moves down a channel rather than across a field. A caster with a good focus is not stronger; they are cleaner, and cleanliness under pressure is most of what separates a practitioner from a casualty. Materials matter more than ornament. Witchwood and aether crystal carry arcane force with the least loss, which is why so many first wands are witchwood with a splinter of something better set into the tip. Robes matter for the same reason armour does, in reverse: nothing between the body and the air.

Cursed Arms and Bargained Things.text:
Cursed Arms and Bargained Things:

Cursed arms and regalia contain workings that continue to want something after their makers are gone. Most surviving pieces come from bargains with Ur, Shadelands ruins, or sacred workings broken in use.

A true cursed item has a repeatable physical tell even while quiet: a weak pulse in its grip, water gathering where nothing is wet, an edge that stains clean cloth, frost on the bearer's breath, or another sign particular to the item. Calling its named power produces an immediate and unmistakable manifestation. Every deliberate calling also leaves Tarnish: spiritual grey-rot, the mark that the dead country and its bargains leave on the living.

Summoners recognize curses by what can be staged and witnessed. A hungry item names what feeds it and visibly changes when fed. A sworn item serves a named person, house, god, or purpose and gives a repeatable sign of approval or rejection. A cycle-bound item changes at a named tide, moon, bell, season, or other recurring moment. A flesh-taking item leaves an observable mark or weakness on the body carrying it.

Such things turn up in confiscated cult stores, sealed armories, tombs, Shadelands caches, and among the effects of people who believed they could master them. Their power is why they are kept instead of forgotten.

The Widow's Edge.text:
The Widow's Edge:

A caravan guard recovered this grey Warded sword from an Ur-carved strongbox beneath a burned wreck on Widow's Way. Since then it has passed between road captains, bandit chiefs, and collectors, usually after its bearer dies suddenly. Its grip keeps the bearer's pulse weak and slow. Its named power, Widow's Due, sends a thrust through the wielder's shadow and out of a visible foe's shadow; each calling knots black thread around the wrist and leaves the wielder's shadow visibly thinner.

Crown of the Drowned King.text:
Crown of the Drowned King:

The Crown of the Drowned King is the verdigrised sun-gold circlet buried with the last ruler of the flooded Sun-King tomb in the Dunelands. Its named power, The Drowned Court, floods the immediate scene with grave-cold water and calls the king's drowned honor-guard to strike before sinking away. Each calling leaves one drowned petitioner visible in the nearest reflection. The petitioner knows only its own death and claim: it may petition, accuse, or demand judgment, but it is not an oracle.

Wolfskin Girdle.text:
Wolfskin Girdle:

A Wrath-Speaker made the Wolfskin Girdle by trapping a wolf-spirit in its own skin, a violation of the Wolfpack's mutual beast-bond tradition. Its named power, The Old Hunger, lets the bearer wear the spirit as a towering wolf for one violent turn. The iron clasp bites shut when called, and afterward the empty hide strains toward the nearest wounded creature even when its bearer refuses to follow. Wolfpack Lodge seeks the girdle as evidence of the Wrath-Speakers' crime and may charge Proven Hunters with recovering or destroying it.

Marks of Quality.text:
Marks of Quality:

Larion's makers distinguish four grades of work. Ordinary goods carry no name but their maker. Fine work is what a good shop sells and a careful person saves for. Superior work carries a mark: a named smith, an aspected material, or a minor working laid in during its making. Masterwork is commissioned rather than stocked. It requires exceptional material and master-level craft, and a maker may complete only a handful of such pieces in a lifetime.

A Warded weapon begins as a Masterwork and is carried through a separate enchanter's rite using a rare catalyst. The original maker's mark remains beside the enchanter's ward.

A Relic is not a grade of workmanship. It bears a proper name and a history people can recount. No shop or smith can promise to make one on demand; a weapon becomes a Relic only through a great undertaking and the rite that binds that history into it.

Claiming a grade or mark one cannot support is serious fraud. Guild towns punish forgers of maker's marks alongside forgers of coin.

Restoratives.text:
Restoratives:

The trade distinguishes three families and will correct you if you confuse them. Healing potions close wounds and are the only one that mends real harm. Stamina draughts are salt-bitter and push breath and strength back into tired limbs; a greater draught is the same brew reduced. Mana philters run cold and reopen the channel between a caster and the current; they do nothing at all for someone who cannot cast, which does not stop them being sold to such people. All three buy a moment rather than a recovery, and all three make the next few heartbeats harder to think through -- which is why a fighter drinks before closing, not during.

The Enchanter's Trade.text:
The Enchanter's Trade:

Enchanting is a craft, not a school. It is practised at a bench with tools, notes, and failed attempts in a box under it, and it rewards the patient and the literate rather than the gifted. The working is laid into the object while it is made or reworked, which is why enchanters are trained beside smiths, jewelers, and binders rather than beside battle-casters. A strong channeller with no craft can no more enchant a blade than a strong arm can forge one. This is also why the great workshops -- the Artificers' workshops on Artificers' Isle, Forge-town's rune-benches -- are institutions of record and apprenticeship, and why a maker's mark on an enchanted piece is worth more than the enchantment.

A Warded weapon begins with a completed Masterwork. The enchanter binds permanent power through it with a rare catalyst, most often an Elemental Core, and a full rite; no amount of casual spellcasting can replace either. Such work is arranged through reputation, obligation, or shared purpose, not selected from a shop list.

The Worth of Goods.text:
The Worth of Goods:

PRICING AND STOCK REFERENCE. This exists so that prices, shop stock, and the worth of loot stay consistent from scene to scene. Apply it silently when someone shops, sells, loots, salvages, appraises, haggles, or asks what a thing is worth. No character knows it as written. Do not recite it, quote it, explain it as lore, or let it emerge through play: a merchant simply names a price that agrees with it.

Coin. Larion counts in florins. A working person earns a few florins a day. A new adventurer leaves home with about sixty, which buys a decent weapon, or many nights of good lodging, or one small magical curiosity, but not all three.

Buying from a shop:
- Everyday clothing, tools, rope, and ammunition: 1 to 10 florins.
- Ordinary weapons and armour, unmarked and unaspected: 8 to 25 florins. A shortsword, a leather jerkin, an iron helm.
- Potions and restoratives: 15 to 40 florins, the greater draughts and philters at the top of that range.
- Protective ward charms: 120 to 200 florins. They are rite-made, scarce, and rarely stocked more than one at a time.
- Fine work, the best an ordinary shop keeps in stock: 40 to 90 florins.
- Superior work, carrying a named maker's mark, an aspected material, or a small working: 150 to 400 florins. Most shops hold one or two at a time and some of those are not for sale.
- Masterwork: commissioned rather than stocked, 800 florins and upward, with time to make and exceptional materials often supplied by the buyer.
- Warded weapons: not ordinary merchandise. Their price includes the Masterwork beneath them, a rare catalyst, and the service or favour required to secure an enchanter's rite.
- Relics: not priced and not sold. Such things change hands through inheritance, theft, oath, gift, conquest, or recovery from the dead.

Services use the same register: inspection or identification 10 to 40 florins, difficult diagnosis or investigation 50 to 80, custom or commissioned work 80 and upward.

Materials. Raw materials sell by the piece, the hide, the bundle, or the vial. Iron Ore, Hardwood, Rawhide, Wool Cloth, Healing Herbs, and Game Meat: 1 to 6 florins. Venom Gland and Acid Gland: 5 to 20. Silver Ore: 10 to 25. Witchwood and Venomwood: 15 to 40. Emberglass, Thunderglass, and Dream Coral: 25 to 60. Frostjade and Voidglass: 30 to 80. Cold Iron: 40 to 100. Drake Scale, Spider Silk, and Troll Blood: 25 to 80. Rimebone: 50 to 120. Moonbloom Truffle: 15 to 25. An Elemental Core is never stocked; where one changes hands, 150 florins is the start of the conversation and a favour usually finishes it. Spoiled or badly cut parts fetch little or nothing, and a specialist buyer pays nearer the top.

Selling. A merchant pays a third to a half of what they would charge for the same thing, less for stock they cannot move, more for something they already have a buyer for. Battlefield salvage, bloodied gear, and obviously stolen goods fetch the low end or a flat refusal. Haggling moves a price by about a fifth either way; a good roll changes the terms, never the economy.

What shops carry. Most hold ordinary goods and a little Fine work. Superior appears where there is a reason for it: a smith with a name, a focus-maker beside an academy, a fence with quiet connections. No ordinary shop stocks Masterwork or Warded weapons, and Relics do not appear as merchandise. A merchant claiming otherwise is lying, fencing something dangerous, or selling a forgery.

What the price is for. A buyer pays for the bonus, not the ornament: armour, damage, an attribute, a resource, a skill. Two pieces of the same grade cost roughly the same whatever they look like. An aspected material such as emberglass, stormsteel, moonstone, or voidglass adds about half again over plain work, because what it carries is worth real coin against the right enemy.

The Hunger.text: The Hunger: A contagion the demon princes of Ur unleashed in the age they ruled Larion — a weapon that takes a thinking person and leaves an appetite. Where it takes hold unmastered it makes the mindless: strigoi in the blood-dead, ghouls where the dead lie thick, and lycanthropes in those who swallow it willingly. The vampire lords of the Shadow Summits hold that their own curse is the Hunger mastered — that the Lady of Blood, cornered in the Elven Schism, consumed her followers not for power alone but to take the thing that was already eating her people, and came out of it holding the one form that keeps its mind. By their account the Hunger wells up wherever the barrier between worlds runs thin, which is why their valleys sit where they sit, and why they say the north would go feral without them and Larion after it. It is their account, and it is largely true. They also made the Vale Sable.

The Blood of Two to Make One.text: The Blood of Two to Make One: The rite by which the vampire lords of the Shadow Summits make new members of their line, and the reason they marry. A vampire is not made by one sire but by two, of different houses, and the saying is the whole of the law. What rises from two carries something of both and carries it stably. What rises from a single sire carries only what its maker had, and carries it badly: such a get is far likelier to lose its mind to the Hunger, sooner or later, and go feral. Marriage between houses exists to make the rite possible and to keep the lords from drawing apart across the centuries — they need one another, and the rite is what makes that true rather than sentimental. A lord who will not marry cannot safely make an heir. The Lady of Blood was made by nobody and made herself alone, which the Peers note and do not discuss. What became of the Vale Sable is what the rule is for.

Frenzy.text: Frenzy: A contagion of the Hunger that takes beasts. A frenzied animal behaves like a rabid one — fearless, relentless, past any instinct for self-preservation — except that its hunger is insatiable, so it eats long past full and goes on eating, and it has stopped being able to die properly. Wounds that should drop it do not; it comes apart before it stops. The carcass is still the problem: whatever scavenges a frenzied body takes the frenzy in turn, which is how one dead wolf becomes three by the following week. The corpse has to be destroyed, and in this country that means burned, which is a real cost where every stick of fuel is carried uphill. Silver and moonstone give no particular advantage, because a frenzied beast is alive, whatever else is wrong with it. People who eat the meat sicken and die; they do not turn. Frenzy is not the Ferals' curse, which is taken willingly and keeps its mind.

Bloodfed Direhound.text: Bloodfed Direhound: The hunting hounds of the vampire houses, bred large and fed on their masters' blood. Heavy, deep-chested, short pale coats and eyes that hold the light too long. A pack runs a mortal down over days without resting and takes wounds that should stop it, and it hunts by scent far past the point where the trail should be cold. A house's hounds are that house's property: killing them is an act against the house, and every lord knows the mark of another's kennel. Most packs met in open country have gone feral — turned loose, escaped, or left when their house fell — and those belong to nobody, breed, and are worse for it, because a fed hound that has had no blood in a year is a starving thing that still does not die easily.

Bonebreaker Vulture.text: Bonebreaker Vulture: An enormous carrion bird of the high peaks, named for what it does — it carries bones aloft and drops them on bare rock to crack them for the marrow, and it will do the same with a body, or with a living thing small enough to lift. Slate and rust coloured, a wingspan wider than a man is tall, and in a country with this much dead in it they grow fat and bold. They are a sign before they are a danger: where bonebreakers circle there is a body, and where they circle over open ground and nothing can be seen, something has been buried, hidden, or dragged under.

Pale Lynx.text: Pale Lynx: The ambush predator of the slopes that never see the sun. Chalk-white, heavy through the shoulders, with skin grown over where the eyes should be — it does not see at all. It hunts warmth, and it is very good at it: it will take a traveler off a path in full dark from above, having tracked the heat of them for an hour. Because it hunts warmth it cannot perceive the undead in any way. A vampire may stand within arm's reach of one and be no more present to it than a stone, which is why no lord of the Shadow Summits has ever troubled to clear them, and why they are a mortal's problem and nobody else's.

Gaunt Fiend.text: Gaunt Fiend: The common fiend of the Hunger, and the one that comes in numbers. Starved to the frame, taller than a man and wrongly jointed, all reach and ribs and a stomach that never fills. Gaunts come through where the barrier is worn and go straight for the nearest warm thing, fast and without caution, climbing walls and dropping from ceilings as readily as running. They do not speak, they coordinate only loosely, and they keep coming while anything is left to eat. Radiant force, silver, and moonstone bite them; ordinary steel works, slowly.

Maw Fiend.text: Maw Fiend: The heavy among the fiends of the Hunger — mostly mouth, walking on its knuckles, a body built around the swallowing. A maw takes a whole person and keeps moving. Slow to start and very hard to stop, it wades into a formed line and bites through shields, and what it swallows does not come back. Maws come through the thin places behind the gaunts, and they are usually what a breach’s defenders die to. Radiant force, silver, and moonstone bite them; they shrug off most of what does not.

Ravener Fiend.text: Ravener Fiend: The greater fiend of the Hunger, and the only one that talks. A ravener keeps enough mind to bargain, to name what it wants, and to understand what it is being offered — and nowhere near enough to keep a bargain once the hunger turns. They are individually named, they hold a breach or a ruin as territory, and lesser fiends give way to them. A ravener will parley, the parley is worth having, and it ends the moment the ravener is hungrier than it is curious. Radiant force, silver, and moonstone bite them.

The Crimson Company.text: The Crimson Company: The standing soldiery of the vampire lords of the Shadow Summits, serving the lords collectively rather than any single house and hired out valley to valley under a red sword on black. The Company holds cordons, culls strigoi and ghouls, escorts what the lords trade, and keeps order in the lit valleys. It takes anyone the rest of Larion has cast out, so long as they can fight and keep a bargain, and it houses and pays them well. Its officers came north as exiles from Silvervale. Its elite are occasionally Embraced, which is the Company’s advertised prize and one of the ways the Summits make new vampires — by merit, and by who will fight the most for it.

Clerical Ministry and Reliquaries.text:
Clerical Ministry and Reliquaries:

A cleric's standing grows through service to their faith and to the living, the dead, and the sacred places in its care. Every tradition asks different things, but clerics are often called to tend the sick, bury the dead, confront hauntings and possession, lay restless undead to rest, break curses, banish fiends, and cleanse places where corruption has taken root.

The lasting reward for such service may be trust. A temple or community may open a sanctuary to the cleric, teach a rite, lend its aid, or entrust the cleric with a sacred object. A rite may also survive in an inscription, prayer book, funerary tablet, hymn, or object recovered during play.

A reliquary is a sacred focus that houses a holy object or preserves the memory of a recognized holy event. It may be a pendant, seal, casket, vessel, wrapped fragment, prayer wheel, or another form belonging to the faith. An object taken from a defeated enemy or cursed place is not thereby sacred or safe; it may need to be identified, cleansed, returned, or properly housed before it can serve the faith. A holy symbol may become a reliquary when a sacred object is joined to it.

Monastic Forms and Ordeals.text:
Monastic Forms and Ordeals:

Monks teach that the body has more answers than habit permits. A Form is one impossible bodily command perfected until it can be repeated: becoming light or immovable, hard or supple, aware without sight, exact beyond ordinary timing, able to endure, or swift to mend. Different orders use different names and methods.

A Form may be carried in a teacher's demonstration, a mantra, a sequence painted on a wall, a carved tablet, a scroll of footwork, or another teaching aid. Finding or buying the teaching is not mastery. The student must practice it and then perform its command during an ordeal where failure matters. A first-time breakthrough may also become a Form when no teacher had named it.

The Sky Temple of the Ascension calls its weight-and-force discipline attuning and detuning. It calls its ordeals Descents because its students leave the Unmoored Mountain to face danger in the wider world. Other traditions use their own terms and tests. The Path of the Will is a common measure of how deeply a practitioner can carry a Form: novices begin with one command of their own body; adepts may join commands or carry one through a held object; experts sustain deeper commands through extreme harm or opposition; masters may combine several commands or reach another living body by touch. Teachers and rivals recognize demonstrated Forms; mastery earns harder instruction, invitations, challenges, hospitality, and eventually the standing to teach or name Forms for others.

Wizard Spellcraft.text:
Wizard Spellcraft:

Wizards do not learn a spell merely by seeing it. They study the marks, materials, words, gestures, residues, and failures by which a piece of magic takes shape, then test one principle at a time. A hostile spell, curse, ward, ritual, magical creature, grimoire, or strange phenomenon may yield such a principle when examined, but the wizard must still design and successfully cast a spell of their own.

A spellbook keeps completed techniques, corrections, and the evidence from failed attempts. A discovered grimoire or formula can shorten the road, but it is instruction rather than mastery. Wizards trade and teach proven spells, and may bind a spell they know into prepared vellum as a one-use scroll.

Sorcerous Origins and Awakened Powers.text:
Sorcerous Origins and Awakened Powers:

A sorcerer's origin is why magic lives inside them. It may be an inheritance, curse, old ritual, magical accident, strange birth, or mystery no one has answered. The origin is background truth, not a skill, element, patron, or resource, and it does not decide every spell the sorcerer can cast. Sorcerers use the ordinary magic skill that governs what each spell or power actually does.

Inborn magic may acquire a recurring visible tell through the body or nearby world, but only when background or story establishes one. A sorcerer awakens a new power by reaching inward and attempting something their magic has never done before. Outside magic may inspire the attempt, but it is not copied or imported. A fully successful first use can become a power the sorcerer calls again.

Gemheart.text: Gemheart: What a house makes when it turns Ur soul-work on a person instead of a construct. The soulstone goes where the heart was, the soul goes into the stone, and the body stops changing from that day on — no ageing, no decay, no breath. At rest the stone is dark and cold; it burns from within when its bearer fights. A gemheart is preserved rather than corrupted, which is why they are beautiful, and completely still when not moving, which is what people find hardest to sit beside. Radiant force and blessed weapons bite them, and destroying the body settles nothing: the soul is in the stone, and the stone has to be found and broken. Soulstones are banned across Larion's surface and the making of a gemheart is worse than banned, so the few that exist have nowhere lawful to stand. The houses that made them are mostly gone. Every one of them is somebody's crime, still walking.

The Aurora Serpents.text: The Aurora Serpents: Great white sea-serpents whose crests and fins glow with the colors of the aurora. The kings and queens of the Northrealm commanded them: the serpents drew and guarded the royal fleet, broke the winter ice from the harbors, and carried the Northrealm's rulers into battle. The serpent-prows carved on every Northrealm ship are portraits of them, not ornament. When the cold came, the serpents sank beneath the sea-ice and fell into a sleep that has lasted generations, and no one living has seen one. The Long Watch's chain of signal-fires across the ice was first built as the serpent-call: the fires, lit together, told the serpents the kingdom was awake. Snowlanders still carve serpents over their doors and say that when every watchfire burns again, the serpents will rise and break the ice to Northport.

Hearth-Spirits of the North.text: Hearth-Spirits of the North: Small spirits of living flame, kin to the hearth-spirits of the south, and the most precious things in the snowlander north, where they are held to be the Lady of the Hearth's gift. In town, hearth-spirits live in the hearths, fire-pits, and window-lamps and move freely among them. They cannot survive the open cold on their own, so on the ice they travel in hearth-lanterns, iron-and-glass lamps, and must be fed: pine-knots and resin from the Firwood, lamp-oil, a hearthpearl, and best of all drake-oil. A hearth-spirit can leave its lantern to wrap a frozen traveler in warmth and bring them back from the edge, at the cost of its own strength, and every rescue team on the ice carries one. A family's hearth-spirit is its greatest treasure, and the oldest have kept the same fire for centuries. The Long Watch's signal-fires are hearth-spirits who volunteered to burn alone out on the ice. Hearth-spirits and icelings are uneasy neighbors who need each other.

Icelings.text: Icelings: Small spirits of living ice, refugees from the Plane of Ice who slipped through the gaps in the Pact of All Planes while fleeing the Widow of Winter, who rules the ice-spirits of that plane and does not let them go. Icelings live inside ice: the sculptures of Warmwater's Ice Gardens are their homes, and they can move a carving from inside it. They shape ice into stairs, bridges, sealed doors, and runs across crevasses; they keep things cold, from medicine to the Aurora Ball's famous sorbets; and they feel the Widow coming before anyone else, going still and silent when she walks. They cannot bear a hearth. Shy, curious, and fiercely grateful to the town that took them in, they trade their work for safe ice to live in.

The Long Watch.text: The Long Watch: The knighthood of the snowlander north, sworn to keep the chain of signal-fires burning across the ice and to answer any stead whose fire goes dark. It is seated in the Lamp-Tower of Whitewatch above Warmwater Township. The Watch was once hundreds strong; now it is down to a handful of knights, its fires are going dark one by one, and it badly needs new members. A knight of the Watch wears a lamp-badge and swears on the words "while one fire burns." Relighting a dark watchfire means crossing the ice to it, dealing with whatever put it out, and rekindling or replacing the hearth-spirit that kept it.

The Winter Crown.text: The Winter Crown: House Ormsvald, the old royal house of the Northrealm, lives in exile in Warmwater Township as one of the Greater Duchies, descended from the last king. They keep a crown, heirlooms saved from Northport, and a claim to a kingdom under ice, and they mean to march north and take their capital back. The heirs are royal twins, a prince and a princess, and every great house in the north wants to marry into the line. The twins refuse to choose anyone. Publicly, the reason is a fairy tale the whole town half-believes: that whoever the heirs of the Winter Crown love will freeze to death. Some whisper that not every figure in the Ice Gardens was carved. The truth is known only to the twins and a very few others: the Widow of Winter wanted the last king for her husband, he refused her, and she took his kingdom and cursed his line, so that whatever they love, she takes. Breaking the curse is a long road that leads toward the Plane of Ice.

The Aurora Ball.text: The Aurora Ball: When the aurora burns across the northern sky, snowlanders say the Widow is walking, and no one travels. So on aurora nights Warmwater Township throws its grandest party instead, in the Ice Gardens under the lights: carved ice lit from within, steaming pools, hothouse fruit from the Glasshouses, iceling sorbets, and icelings dancing inside the sculptures. The whole court attends, the suitors of the Winter Crown make their play, and the town dances in defiance of the cold on exactly the night it is closest.

Hearthpearls.text: Hearthpearls: Amber-gold pearls that grow in the hottest vents of Warmwater Township's hot springs, where rising water tumbles a grain of grit over and over and coats it in layer after layer of mineral. A good pearl takes a decade to grow and a great one a lifetime. Scholars call them spring-pearls; snowlanders call them hearthpearls, the Lady of the Hearth's warmth in a pocket. Each layer seals in a little of the buried fire the springs rise from, like a coal banked in ash, so a harvested pearl stays warm for about a year, glowing faintly in the dark, before it turns pale and cold and becomes a keepsake. Cracking one releases all its stored heat at once as a burst of scalding steam. Firewood is scarce on the treeless ice and fire is fragile, visible, and fixed in one place, so a hearthpearl is the warmth that travels: sewn into coats and gloves, tucked into boots and bedrolls, packed around a half-frozen traveler on a rescue sled, bedded in a rimewolf team's straw, keeping medicine, potions, ink, and lamp-oil from freezing, and feeding a hearth-spirit's lantern when there is no oil. It gives heat without light or smoke, which matters on nights when the Widow's creatures hunt. In the south hearthpearls are a famous luxury and an expedition essential. They are harvested with long bronze rakes at dawn, when the vents run lowest.

The Pearl Houses.text: The Pearl Houses: The great families of Warmwater Township who own the hearthpearl vents of its hot springs, and the richest people in the north. They sell hearthpearls to every traveler, rescue team, and expedition that crosses the ice and to buyers across the south, and their Glasshouses, hothouses fed by the springs, grow the town's fruit and greens. Their manors ring the Ice Gardens, pale stone and carved timber under steaming glass roofs. They are polished, generous, and very comfortable, and a war in the ice would cost them everything, so they fund the Winter Crown's court while quietly opposing its reconquest. The crown needs their money; they want its legitimacy, and every one of them hopes to marry into it.

The Right of Precedence.text: The Right of Precedence: Tevantia is built on a thousand bridges, many too narrow for two people to pass, so one must give way. Old custom says the lesser yields to the greater, and Tevantia's nobility made that custom into law: if someone will not let you pass, you may challenge them to a duel. Rivals who want a quarrel walk onto the same narrow bridge from opposite ends, advance, and refuse to yield. A challenge needs a refusal of precedence or a formal insult answered in form, with seconds named; an attack without it is a crime, not a duel. The duel itself may be fought on a bridge-plaza's dueling ring, in the Amphitheater, or wherever the seconds agree, to first blood unless both sides declare otherwise. Yielding is no disgrace for a stranger or a commoner, and wise nobles yield with a bow and a cutting remark.

The Windworks of Tevantia.text: The Windworks of Tevantia: Tevantia runs on the sea wind. Great windmills along its cliff-tops drive the city's lifts, pumps, and mills. Sail-lifts, cable-cars with small sails, glide between the harbor, the bridges, and the towers. Wind-harps, tall stringed frames, sing in every garden and tower when the wind rises, and each great house keeps its own tuning, so a Tevantian can tell whose garden they stand in by ear. The wind-wrights who build and tune all of it are respected, well paid, and famously eccentric, and their newest toys are wind-gliders that only the bravest will ride.

The Grand Tournament.text: The Grand Tournament: Tevantia's great festival, fought in the Amphitheater before the whole city: rounds of formal duels between the great houses' champions and any challenger bold enough to enter, while the nobility watches from house boxes in its most extravagant finery. The victor is named First Blade of Tevantia for the year, and their house stands highest in the city's precedence until the next Tournament. With a ducal election coming, every house wants that honor badly.

The Great Houses of Tevantia.text: The Great Houses of Tevantia: Four great houses rule Tevantia's society, each with its colors, its sword-school, and its temper, and their heads elect the Duke for life. House Montrose, the oldest house and the Duke's own, wears crimson and gold; it is proud, romantic, and obsessed with precedence, and its school fences in the grand classical style. House Marenne, in sea-green and pearl, descends from a noble's marriage to a merfolk princess generations ago: its members have sea-green or silver hair, faint scales at the temples and wrists, and eyes like deep water; they breathe underwater, swim like merfolk, and sing in the old merfolk way, and its school fences in a fluid, flowing style. House Ravissant, in violet and silver, is newly ennobled, dazzling, brash, and determined to take the ducal seat; its school teaches flashy bravura fencing built to thrill a crowd. House Levantine, in sky-blue and white, built the Windworks; it is cool, clever, and a little aloof, and its school is agile and leaping, taught on the high bridges in strong wind. Their rivalries are about precedence, marriages, pride, and love.

The Black Tides.text: The Black Tides: Every few days the tide off Tevantia runs dark and strange, and the harbor bells ring. On those black tides the drowned come up out of the Undercliff Caves beneath the city's cliffs: servants of Ophialtha, the sea-dragon of the Seadeep Kingdoms, pale and scaled, gilled and web-fingered, armed with tridents and weighted nets. They drag people off the wharves and lower bridges and take them down alive to be changed into drowned themselves. The taken can be rescued from the drowned hold deep in the caves before the change takes them. House Marenne, whose sea-blood the drowned covet above all, hates them most.

The Syndicate and Tevantia.text: The Syndicate and Tevantia: The Syndicate once ran Tevantia's harbor, until the city threw it out. Now it rules Beggarsbridge, the lawless bridge-town across the water, under Mardrek Venn, and it wants back in. Its bravos, swaggering toughs in grey coats with iron chain-badges, cross the bridge to collect debts, charge tolls, burn stalls that will not pay, and hire desperate locals to do the rest. They are unwelcome in Tevantia, and the houses pay well to see them driven back across the bridge.

The Birdfolk Raiders.text: The Birdfolk Raiders: Raiders of the Feathered Fleet (gull-, frigatebird-, and pelican-folk) roost on the sea-stacks below Tevantia's cliffs. They swoop down on the high towers, bridges, and sail-lift cars to snatch jewels, purses, and cargo, and now and then carry off a person for ransom. They strike fast and fly off before anyone can stop them, and their roosts on the sea-stacks can be found and cleared.

The Black Palace.text: The Black Palace: The ruined seat of the house that started the Burning of Tevantia three centuries ago, left scorched and empty on its own isle and never rebuilt. Its fallen house's dead still burn inside it: the burning dead walk its halls with pale fire in their bones, and on some nights they walk out across the cracked bridge. Tevantians avoid it; treasure-hunters and the brave go in, and not all come back.

Tarnish.text:
Tarnish:
Tarnish is spiritual grey-rot, the mark the Shadelands leave on the living. It comes from treating with the dead country: crossing into the Shadelands without wards, striking a bargain with a demon, shade, or power of the grey world, calling on the named power of a cursed or bargained thing, or forcing necromancy past what the caster can safely hold. Fighting the dead does not cause it. Dealing with them does.

It deepens by stages. At first it is only a faint wrongness that no one can see. Deeper, it shows: grey at the temples, grey beneath the nails, and a pale ring around the irises. Priests and consecrated servants recognize it at once, animals shy from its scent, and anyone who has served in the Shadelands knows what it means. At its worst the grey country counts the bearer nearly its own. Their shadow thins in direct daylight, shrine flames gutter as they pass, blessed water stirs in the font, and radiant power burns them deeper than it burns other folk.

Tarnish never fades with time, and no amount of rest, healing, or potions will touch it. Only a cleansing lifts it: an unbinding rite, the blessing of a consecrated shrine, or amends made to whatever was wronged. A single cleansing lifts part of the grey, and only an exceptional rite or sacrifice clears it entirely.

The Tarnished Reaches take their name from it. There the highborn dead of the Fourth Empire, who served the demon princes of Ur and will not pass on, are so steeped in grey-rot that the land itself has taken the color. Among the living, tarnish is a warning. Temples may turn the deeply marked away, and wise folk think twice before sharing a hearth with them, while necromancers, warlocks, and desperate petitioners read the same signs as proof of power.

Smithing Recipes.text: Smithing recipes: forging a blade, an axe or mace head, a helm, gauntlets, mail, or plate, or the heads for arrows and bolts. Weapons and armor are made only at a proper forge; away from one, the attempt is impossible. About 2 Iron Ore make a blade, an axe or mace head, a helm, gauntlets, or a buckler; 4 make a breastplate or legharness; 1 tips a sheaf of arrows or bolts. Ordinary work comes of a success, and Fine work of a great success by a smith with a Smith's Hammer. An aspected weapon takes about 2 of its material in place of the iron: Silver Ore for radiant, Emberglass for fire, Frostjade for frost, Thunderglass for shock, Voidglass for shadow. It deals that damage type and is Superior work only on a great success. 1 aspected material tips a sheaf of arrows or bolts with its damage type. Cold Iron is worked cold and never touched by the forge-fire. Masterwork needs exceptional material from a strong or elite creature, a master's forge, and a master smith; a member of the party with smithing 25 or higher is one.

Leatherworking Recipes.text: Leatherworking recipes: tanning hides and making leather armor, boots, gloves, caps, leggings, straps, and packs. Armor is made only in a proper workshop, a tannery or a leather bench with its tools; away from one, the attempt is impossible. Rawhide is tanned before it is worked, a day of stinking labor. 1 Rawhide makes boots, gloves, a cap, or leggings; 2 make a jerkin; 3 make a cuirass. Drake Scale in place of the hide makes scale armor that turns blades better than leather, Superior work on a great success. Fine work comes of a great success with Leatherworking Tools. Masterwork armor needs exceptional hide or scale from a strong or elite creature and a master's workshop.

Tailoring Recipes.text: Tailoring recipes: cutting and sewing tunics, trousers, hoods, cloaks, robes, and mantles, and the padding worn under armor. Garments meant as armor are made only in a proper tailor's workshop; away from one, the attempt is impossible. 1 Wool Cloth makes a tunic, trousers, or a hood; 2 make a cloak, a robe, or a mantle. Spider Silk makes a light garment stronger than its weight, Superior work on a great success. Fine work comes of a great success with a Sewing Kit.

Carpentry and Bowyer Recipes.text: Carpentry and bowyer recipes: shaping bows, staves, spear shafts, shields, arrows, and trap frames from timber. Bows, shields, and staves are made only at a proper workbench with its tools; away from one, the attempt is impossible. 1 Hardwood makes a staff, a short bow, a spear shaft, or a sheaf of Wooden Arrows; 2 make a long bow, a war bow, or a round shield. Witchwood in place of the hardwood makes a staff or wand that carries arcane force cleanly. 1 Venomwood makes a sheaf of Venomwood Arrows of Poison. Fine work comes of a great success with Woodworking Tools.

Alchemy Recipes.text: Alchemy recipes: brewing potions, draughts, philters, poisons, and etchants at a still or a field kit. Brewing is easier in a proper laboratory and harder with an improvised kit. 2 Healing Herbs brew a Stamina Draught; 3 brew a Mongo's Medium Health Potion. 2 Healing Herbs and 1 Troll Blood brew a Greater Stamina Draught. 2 Healing Herbs and 1 Witchwood brew a Mana Philter; add 1 Moonbloom Truffle for a Greater Mana Philter. 1 Venom Gland or 1 Venomwood yields a Venomwood Extract. 1 Acid Gland yields a Vitriol Flask. 1 Emberglass ground into lamp oil yields an Emberglass Oil. Ward charms and Consecrated Oil are made by rite, not brewed.

Cooking Recipes.text: Cooking recipes: preparing trail food, meals, and feasts, and brewing ale and cordials. Game Meat smoked or salted becomes trail food that keeps for a journey; fresh, it spoils within days. A Moonbloom Truffle is the heart of a halfling pie, paste, or cordial, and a halfling cook can bind a small charm into the dish. A feast honors a hall only when it is cooked in a real kitchen.

Learning a Craft Secret.text: Learning a craft secret: working closely with a material, taking apart a finished piece, or watching a master at work can show one concrete principle of making, such as how a thing bends, cures, holds, or breaks. A maker may later build on that principle with a trial piece, and a method that works becomes their own secret.

Fenimore Tully's Guide to the Guilds of.text: Fenimore Tully's Guide to the Guilds of Larion: the best-known handbook to Larion's guilds, orders, and companies, written by the halfling Fenimore Tully, who has belonged to nearly all of them. It says what each one is like, who it suits, where its hall stands, and how to begin. Fenimore keeps a desk in the Map Room of the Watchtower in Ardan's Watch and answers questions there.

Soulstone.text:
Soulstones:

Soulstones are gems with a soul trapped inside, old work of the demon princes of Ur from before the Flood. A soulstone can slow aging and lengthen life, cure sickness, and feed magic with the strength of the soul caught within it — so the rich, the dying, and the powerful prize them, and wizards covet them. But there is a person in every stone, bound and unable to pass on, and most folk find the whole business unholy. They are bought and sold quietly. Their trade is lawful in some lands, a hanging crime in others, and watched everywhere. Most that surface now are dug out of the buried cities of the Underworld, where the old empire stored them.

Ur.text:
Ur (Cosmology): Regarded as myth or legend by many, Ur is said to be a progenitor realm of raw magic and chaos, older than mortal civilization and untouched by its concepts. Little is known about Ur, but all sources agree that there is no law there, no morality, no pity. Power is the only currency. The demon princes of Ur are beings that most prefer not to name out of superstition — demons or gods of such might that their whims reshape the world around them — a prince's cruelty becomes the landscape's cruelty, a prince's hunger makes everything prey. Nothing built in Ur endures, because the next prince's passing mood may unmake it. The demonborn who now live in Larion trace their origins to this place, though most have never seen it and know it only through legend. Orthodox opinion holds that Pact of Suleyvan the Sealer bars the demon princes from manifesting in Larion, just as it bars the gods and other great powers of the outer planes.

Ur has no common law, but its creatures impose private law wherever they can. Demons do not cooperate as equals: they seize, bind, command, and submit only to a power they cannot overthrow. A demon that makes a bargain is bound to its exact words, never to the mercy or intention behind them. Banishment destroys the body it holds in Larion and drives it back to Ur; it does not kill the demon, which can return only through another breach, summons, or binding.

Summoner's Aether Bracers.text: Summoner's Aether Bracers: Tarnholme Summoner foci made on Summoners' Isle around a brass forearm cuff, an Aether Crystal ring, and tether-hooks. The hooks give summoned beings a marked place to arrive and a path back to the circle; they are not chains and cannot replace a bargain or binding. A novice bracer starts with empty hooks, and Summoners earn finer crystals, more stable hooks, and stranger materials through clean summons in the Run.

Artificer's Crystal Signets.text: Artificer's Crystal Signets: Apprentice enchanter's rings from the Artificers' workshops at Tarnholme, copper cages built around a loose Aether Crystal. The cage is intentionally unfinished: the maker can swap in a better crystal and cut a more ambitious binding rather than discard the first ring. A signet that has held a difficult working becomes a public mark of an Artificer's craft, and the best bear scars from failed experiments.

Healer's Spring Phials.text: Healer's Spring Phials: Moonstone-capped glass vessels filled at the Warm Pools of Healers' Isle. Healers use the water as a diagnostic as much as a remedy: it clouds around sickness, clears as healing settles, and is never poured into a wound without knowing what it will meet. A novice phial can be refilled on Healers' Isle; rarer waters and a patient's willing blessing make stronger versions.

The Siege of Tarnholme.text: The Siege of Tarnholme: The Jade Tarn never freezes. Thirty years ago, rogue mages froze it solid from shore to shore with their magic, crossed the ice on foot with summoned and cursed creatures at their side, and besieged the Academy's islands for a month. They called themselves the Heart-Eaters, and an expelled Tarnholme student led them. The Colleges held the islands, and Wortwell hid its children with the myconids of the Glowcaves. The siege was broken in a night fight on the ice below the Muster Court. When the ice gave way under the fighting, the rogue mages' leader went through it and is believed drowned. The survivors scattered onto Cold Kell Mountain and the Wild Magic Badlands. The Academy's older masters were students or young graduates then, and they remember it.

Sleeping egg.text: Sleeping egg: an egg that the creatures that become familiars (pseudodragons, volucats, blink cats, fire salamanders, drakelings and their kind) lay apart from their living clutch and leave hidden in a warm place, on purpose. A sleeping egg can lie dormant for years and only wakes in the warmth of a mage's hands, which is why these creatures so often become familiars. Most are never found. The Dimblys of Dimbly Hatchery collect them from Kittle Crags, the wild crags beyond their village, and hatch them with the students who find them.

The Greater Duchies.text:
The Greater Duchies (Realms of Larion):

The Greater Duchies are seven realms ruled by dukes who own no king above them: Carendon, Tevantia, Drusavia, Westmarch, Aldwall, the Winter Crown and Oasis. Each duke is sovereign in their own land and treats the others as equals. The dukes honor one another's titles, so the nobility of one is the nobility of all, and every court keeps a herald who knows the noble families of all seven duchies, who holds which title, and who is lying about it. The titles are Noble-born, Knight, Baron and Count; a duke rules and is never made. The princely houses of Cloudtop and the houses of the elves are honored as nobility in their own right. The Empire of Light, the Dragon Queen's court, the High King of Ntar Vanna and the vampire lords of the Shadow Summits carry titles the duchies will not honor, and no court of the Greater Duchies receives their envoys as envoys. The free cities and the Moot keep no heralds and owe them nothing. They are not an alliance. They keep no common army or council, and their quarrels are their own. Kings belong to their memory, not their present: the war-kings of Westmarch, the three crowns of Fethloren whose banners still hang in the duke's hall at Aldwall, and the lost crown of the Northrealm, whose heirs, House Ormsvald, keep its name as the Winter Crown and hold court as dukes in exile at Warmwater. Every few generations someone dreams of a crown over all seven. None has held one. The nobility of the Greater Duchies dress to be seen: deep color, rich fabric and the finest make money can buy, cut to ride, fight and travel in as well as to dazzle. Finery is how a house shows its strength, and no noble goes out plain.

Join the League of Adventurers.name: Join the League of Adventurers
Join the League of Adventurers.firstQuest: Do not generate a separate quest on turn 0. The opening scene should establish Copper standing, the League Hall, Tobiah Finch as the hall master and first point of contact, and the presence of champions and possible fellow adventurers without offering specific work; Copper standing is recorded only for the characters Tobiah admits.
Join the League of Adventurers.description:
START HERE

Join the League in Ardan's Watch as a new Copper-rank adventurer. Find a party, take on jobs, and climb toward the champions everyone knows by name.
Join the League of Adventurers.storyStart:
Set the scene in the League Hall of the Watchtower in Ardan's Watch. The PC has just been accepted into the League of Adventurers as a Copper-rank adventurer and is receiving their Copper pin. Begin with a brief, concrete description of the bright, busy hall: stained glass of famous adventurers, old trophies, a Silvervale map, long tables, and adventurers arriving, returning, and heading out. The hall is where heroes live and work, and it is glad to have new people: make it feel full of opportunity, a little loud, and welcoming. Do not enumerate jobs, postings, destinations, rewards, or kinds of work. Do not create an emergency, quest, or complication.

Introduce Tobiah Finch, the League Hall's hall master, as the PC's first point of contact: a freckled young man in a sky-blue waistcoat with a strap of Copper pins at his belt. Establish him through what he is doing: fastening the PC's Copper pin himself and treating their arrival as great news. Make his welcome specific to the PC, such as a guess at how they fight or open excitement about their gear or magic, without deciding the PC's feelings, history, or intentions.

Show that champions and high-ranked adventurers belong to this hall. While Tobiah talks, let one high-ranked adventurer or crew pass through on their own business, such as returning with a trophy, heading out in a hurry, or trading news at the far end of the hall, and have Tobiah point them out with one quick, excited fact about them. This may be Gwyneth Valcazar, a tall young woman in a white dueling coat with a gold star pin at her collar, but she is not required. Whoever passes is friendly and busy, does not stop for long, and offers the PC neither work nor company.

Show two other young Copper adventurers nearby, newly invented for this opening rather than any established NPC, premade character, or other character in context. Make each one someone a player would want in their party: a striking, memorable look, a signature weapon, spell, companion creature, or technique shown off in action, and real charisma, whether swagger, charm, or cool confidence. Give them contrasting roles and energies, such as a flashy duelist and a stormcaller, or a big-hearted shieldbearer and a sly archer. Show what they are doing rather than describing them: a showy sparring exchange, a spell pulled off with flair, a friendly contest, or a boast someone is about to back up. They are not discussing work. They should be human or near-human, such as elves, half-elves, or demonborn; at most one may come from another people. Keep each to a vivid action and a line or two so the opening stays light.

End with Tobiah asking the PC one warm, open question about what they want to do first. Do not list services. Do not have him offer a specific contract or send a pin-call until the player asks. End there, leaving the player free to respond.

In multiplayer, identify each new character receiving a Copper pin. Preserve any existing member's higher standing; companions do not gain membership merely by attending.

New in Town.name: New in Town
New in Town.description:
OPEN WORLD

Arrive in a random town or city somewhere in Larion. Where you go from there is up to you.
locationAreas: The Caravanserai of the Thousand Roads
New in Town.storyStart:
Set the scene in the current area of the current location. The players have just arrived here. Briefly establish who they are, but do not invent a major quest, crisis, or compulsory reason for their arrival. Ground the opening in a few concrete details drawn from the location rather than surveying the whole town.

Introduce a named focal NPC: an attractive, dynamic young adult with a distinctive appearance, a clear local role, useful capabilities, and an ambition of their own. Prefer an established NPC appropriate to the location; otherwise create one worth recurring. Do not foreground a generic guard, farmer, fisher, laborer, elderly authority figure, or interchangeable tavern patron. Other townspeople may remain unnamed background figures.

The focal NPC must have a concrete reason to take a personal interest in the player now. They may have been told to expect them, recognize something specific about them, have access the player needs, see an unusual capability, or decide that the newcomer could matter to an ambition already in motion. Keep any invented prior connection light enough to fit the character's background.

Give the NPC an immediate, answerable want involving the player and a genuine foothold in local life: an introduction, a place at a table, access to a useful person or institution, a chance to join a plan, or another opportunity that could develop into an ongoing relationship. The town's public activity remains background rather than the hook. End on the NPC's direct proposal, question, or action at the moment the player's response matters.

A Night at the Tavern.name: A Night at the Tavern
A Night at the Tavern.description:
OPEN WORLD

Start in a lively tavern at the beginning of your road. Where you go next is up to you.
A Night at the Tavern.storyStart:
Set the scene on an open-ended first night in the current tavern. Briefly establish who the player is and why they have come tonight. Use two or three concrete details from the authored area description and the current location or region to make the place distinctive. Make the room feel alive through visible activity, specific sounds, objects, and people rather than a catalogue.

Stage one concrete social situation in the tavern: a live wager, contest, game, provocative exchange, public challenge, disputed seat, unusual performance, daring proposal, or someone being pressured by another person. Give the situation a clear visible stake and make the wants of the people involved legible. Keep it small enough to unfold in the room but interesting enough to invite curiosity, participation, or a change of sides.

Introduce a focal NPC: a charismatic, distinctive young adult with a strong personality, useful capabilities, an active life beyond this conversation, and a reason the player might want to know them. Prefer an established NPC connected to the tavern; otherwise create one worth meeting again. An appealing young woman can be the focal NPC when that suits the scene, but give her agency, boundaries, and a want beyond attracting the player. Use appearance as supporting texture, not as the reason for the NPC's interest. Do not make the focal NPC a generic barkeep, guard, elderly regular, farmer, fisher, merchant needing an errand, or random drunk.

Show the focal NPC actively involved in the social situation. They may be winning or arranging a wager, provoking a rival, defending someone, making an offer, hiding a problem, testing a principle, or looking for someone willing to change the terms. Their interest in the player should arise from the concrete situation and what the player can choose to do in it, not from the player's aura, appearance, or generic look. Give the NPC a specific immediate want and a personal stake in how the scene develops.

Make the interaction inviting and dynamic. The focal NPC may greet the player, draw them into the game, ask them to judge a dispute, offer a seat, propose a wager, challenge their position, or ask what brings them into the room. Let another identifiable person have a different stake so the player can sense a real social web rather than a staged monologue. Keep the player's established role, capabilities, feelings, motives, and history intact; never invent a new profession, power, or unexpressed reaction for them.

Use existing Larion material first and keep unfamiliar lore concrete and limited. Let the current tavern and region provide atmosphere, but keep the opening focused on the people and situation in front of the player. The tavern proprietor may offer a natural welcome, explain the house's rules, point out the interesting table, or intervene if the exchange threatens to turn ugly. Do not make the proprietor automatically convert the scene into a job offer.

End with the focal NPC's offer, challenge, question, wager, or invitation in motion, at a moment when the player's response can change the terms, relationship, reputation, alliance, or opportunity in the room. Do not decide what the player feels or what they choose.

Magic Academy.name: Magic Academy
Magic Academy.description:
RISE THROUGH THE RANKS

Start as a first-year mage at Tarnholme Academy. Four years, four Colleges, and a hall full of people who are glad you came.
Magic Academy.storyStart:
Set the scene in the Great Hall of Tarnholme Academy on the Main Island, at the First-Years' welcome dinner. The new student has just been admitted as a First-Year and is being given a Tarnholme star, a small silver brooch with one point lit. Begin with a brief, concrete description of the long, high-roofed limestone hall at its warmest and loudest: glass lanterns of captured sunlight hanging from the rafters, the College tables under their colored runners in crimson, copper, green and sky blue, the First-Years at the middle tables with their stars still plain silver, and the Practica board on the far wall bristling with postings. Add one or two small, fresh touches of everyday magic. The hall is glad to have new people. Keep it lively and welcoming; do not survey the whole room, and omit smells.

Do not explain how the Academy works. Do not list Practica, jobs, Colleges or rules, and do not create an emergency, quest or complication. The year's shape comes out later, when the student or someone else brings it up.

Introduce Hessa Morcant, a Third-Year Healer who lives in the Newcomers' Hall by choice, as the first person to reach the student: a tall half-orc woman in a sky-blue shoulder mantle with copper-red hair, who crosses the hall toward them already smiling. Establish her through what she does: she shows the newcomer where to sit, makes a specific, friendly guess about them from what she can see (how they carry themselves, their gear, their magic, where they come from), and treats their arrival as good news. Make her welcome fit this particular newcomer without deciding their feelings, history or intentions.

While Hessa talks, let a few students nearby be in the middle of a friendly, heated argument, newly invented for this opening and not any established character. It may be over a game, a bet or a claim one of them is about to prove, and it spills over to anyone close enough to have an opinion, so others are drifting in and taking sides. Make the two or three loudest someone the newcomer would want to know better: a striking look, real charisma, contrasting energies, human or near-human with at most one from another people. Show the argument rather than describing it, with a line or two each at most. It is not about work or rules.

Let one of the masters, such as Wes Carrick, the Practica master, or Bridie Cahill, the First-Years' master, be seen in passing, busy and friendly; whoever it is does not stop for the newcomer.

Close with one small, warm offer from Hessa, such as a seat at her table, and leave the hall going on around the newcomer: the argument still running, the board drawing readers, the masters at the high table. Do not list options, catalog things to do, or turn every detail into an invitation. Do not end with a question to the newcomer, and do not have any character ask what they want, what they hope to become, or whether they have any questions. End there, leaving the newcomer free to respond.

In multiplayer, identify each new character receiving a Tarnholme star.

Join the Wolfpack.name: Join the Wolfpack
Join the Wolfpack.firstQuest: Do not generate an emergent quest during the opening. The authored quest Prove Yourself to the Pack handles the Trial-Hunter's proving deed and later Wolfpack advancement.
Join the Wolfpack.description:
RISE THROUGH THE RANKS

Join the Wolfpack, the orc-founded monster hunters of the Orc Wolds. Prove yourself in the wild and earn a beast spirit of your own.
Join the Wolfpack.storyStart:
Set the scene in the Great Lodge at Wolfpack Lodge in the Orc Wolds. Omit smells. Clearly describe the place, the immediate scene, and the few characters who matter to the exchange. Make the lodge feel active, capable, and worth joining: a fortified home and meeting hall where hunters and warriors return from difficult work, exchange news, and prepare to go out again. Keep the description focused rather than cataloging every feature or introducing many people.

The player has come here because they want to join the Wolfpack. Have Pack-Leader Uro Madresh receive them if he is present; if he is absent, use another respected lodge member. Have the receiving character explain the Wolfpack in simple, natural exposition. It is an orc-founded warrior society open to capable people of any ancestry or adventuring style. Its members take on dangerous creatures, rescues, defenses, escorts, raiders, and other threats too serious for ordinary Wold warriors. Do not assume the player is an orc, a Berserker, capable of Fury, or interested in becoming one.

Explain the immediate admission rule clearly. The player is not yet a Packmate. They may enter as a Trial-Hunter and choose one deed that a Packmate will witness. Completing that deed and returning with the witness or convincing proof earns admission to the Wolfpack and the pack clasp. Briefly hint that admission is only the beginning: proven members undertake harder deeds and may eventually face deeper trials, rites, and leadership responsibilities. Do not explain the entire rank ladder or Beast Bond in the opening.

Many suitable proving deeds need doing, but do not list assignments, create a new quest, or introduce prospective witnesses yet. Have the lodge member make clear that the player may ask to hear about the available deeds, ask about the Wolfpack, look around, or leave. End with that open invitation and wait for the player's response.

Silver Sword Monster Hunter.name: Silver Sword Monster Hunter
Silver Sword Monster Hunter.description:
RISE THROUGH THE RANKS

Take your trial hunt with the Order of the Silver Sword. Track a monster, protect a village, and earn your silver.
Silver Sword Monster Hunter.storyStart:
Open by concisely describing where the party is in the selected starting location and area, the immediate space around them, and the core scene unfolding there. Show the important people present, including Rook Skander and the locals who can help with the hunt. Use concrete visible details suited to the selected place. Do not mention smells.

State plainly why the player is there: they want to join the Order of the Silver Sword and are undertaking a supervised trial hunt as an Initiate. The player is a candidate, but has not been admitted as a Silverblade, carries no Order horn, and has not yet earned an Order-silvered weapon, silver-faced shield, or silver-bound focus or implement. Something has been attacking people or property nearby, and identifying and decisively resolving that creature is the player's trial. Rook is present as a half-elf Veteran Silverblade to observe, advise, and prevent catastrophic failure, but not to lead or solve the hunt. If the player succeeds, Rook can attest that the trial is complete and the player may return to Castle Harstone to tell the hunt before the Great Hall and ask to be admitted as a Silverblade.

Continue the opening scene with concise, useful evidence that fits the selected location and Carendon's wooded, monster-haunted character, but do not identify the creature yet. Rook gives three practical pieces of advice: speak to those who witnessed the attacks or found the damage, examine the kill-site or scene personally, and do not decide what the creature is before the evidence supports it. He makes clear that the player calls the hunt; he will answer questions and stand behind them, but the decisions must be theirs. Introduce two accessible locals with different useful perspectives, such as someone who found the victim or damage and someone who heard or saw part of the attack. Finish the intro turn with the situation clearly established and the player free to choose how to begin the investigation.

The Missing Truffle-Hog.name: The Missing Truffle-Hog
The Missing Truffle-Hog.description:
UNLIKELY HERO

A halfling village's prize truffle-hog has vanished days before the big fair. Find him, and find out how much small folk can matter.
The Missing Truffle-Hog.firstQuest: The first quest is to pick up Phineas's calling-harness from Manu the blacksmith at Manu's Blacksmith Shop AND the truffle-paste from Pernilla Balewood at the Saucy Chicken Tavern. Quest name: Bells and Balewoods. Set arc to NULL — this is a simple fetch, not the start of an arc.
The Missing Truffle-Hog.storyStart:
Set the scene in Hearthhome, a cozy hill-home in the halfling village of Hillhome. Late morning, kettle on the hearth, sunlight through the round windows. Briefly establish who the party are and how they came to live in Hillhome. They may be from the village, or new to it, or staying with friends.

The front door bangs open. Bark Balewood bursts in.

'Phineas is GONE. Disappeared. Vanished. The Newmoon Fair's the day after tomorrow, and now old Goldspoon has announced she's calling in our debt. Coincidence? I think not.' He gulps air. 'Grandma needs you down at the Saucy Chicken — but first she says swing by Manu's and pick up Phineas's calling-harness, the one with the bells. Manu's been mending it. We'll need it to leash him again. Oh, and the truffle-paste, the one he likes, Grandma is just making up a fresh batch. We'll need that to lure him. He'll be out in the truffle-woods somewhere — that pig knows every root and bramble along every path above Hillhome. Phineas is the best truffle-hog in the Downs. If we lose him we lose the Fair, and if we lose the Fair we lose the tavern. WHY ARE YOU STILL SITTING THERE?' Bark runs back out, leaving the door swinging. The kitchen goes quiet. Then the fire on the hearth pops, flares, and a small, bright voice says: 'Wait. Before you go. I've got something to tell you.' The voice is Ember, the existing hearth-spirit of Hearthhome; do not create a new character for it. Do not describe the speaker beyond the voice and the flaring fire, and do not reveal its name yet. End the scene there.

Summoned from Earth.name: Summoned from Earth
Summoned from Earth.description:
OPEN WORLD

Someone in Larion tried to summon a powerful creature and got you. Meet whoever called you and decide what happens next.
Summoned from Earth.storyStart:
Set the opening in the selected location and area. A magic-user is attempting to summon a creature for a particular purpose: a guardian, an adviser, a demonstration, help on an expedition, a companion, or a wager. Choose a purpose and a summoner who fit the place. They may be working alone or performing before an audience.

Establish the summoner through their appearance, words, and the ritual they are performing. A portal opens, and the player arrives from Earth instead of the expected creature. The portal closes behind them.

Show the summoner’s surprise and make clear what they had hoped to call and why. Let their response fit their personality and the situation. End with them addressing the player, leaving the player free to respond. Do not explain why the summoning brought the player, assign them a destiny, or assume they agree to serve the summoner.

Write Your Own.name: Write Your Own
Write Your Own.description:
OPEN WORLD

Write your own backstory, ending with a reason you are in or near one of Larion's great cities. The story picks up from there.
Write Your Own.storyStart: Treat the player's custom text as the complete Starting Situation. Follow its requested staging, timing, tone, characters, and opening beat within the selected Larion location and area. If it conflicts with the generic opening formula, the player's staging wins; do not invent a separate purpose, focal NPC, hook, or opening event.

Random Start.name: Random Start
Random Start.description:
OPEN WORLD

Start somewhere random in Larion: a village, a city street, a tavern, or a market.
Random Start.storyStart:
Place the character plausibly in the selected location and area, drawing on their background and traits. Establish why they are there without inventing a major obligation or extensive prior history.

Show a normal moment in the life of the place through a few visible details and nearby activity. Keep the opening brief. Leave the character free to observe, speak, explore, or do something of their own choosing.
locations: The Sky Temple of the Ascension
The Sky Temple of the Ascension

Knight of the Vigilant.name: Knight of the Vigilant
Knight of the Vigilant.description:
RISE THROUGH THE RANKS

Swear in as a holy knight, ride against the restless dead, and earn a banner of your own.
locations: The Temple of the Sword Vigilant
Knight of the Vigilant.storyStart:
Set the scene in the Feast-Hall of the Temple of the Sword Vigilant, the fortress-seat above Aldwall, on the evening the player joins the Knights Vigilant. The hall is loud and warm: trestle tables crowded with knights, ale-casks against the wall, banners overhead, and trophies of famous undead kills along the stone. Briefly establish what brought the player here without fixing their personality or motives. Explain that Whitemoor is the broad, wet moorland around Aldwall, marked by drowned roads, barrow-fields, old war-dead, and villages that rely on the Knights Vigilant to keep the restless dead from spreading.

At Galard's altar, offer the oath of the Sword Vigilant and let the start's chosen premise carry the player through joining without inventing their exact words. On being sworn, they receive a moonstone oath-brooch, the Swordbearer Oath, and the rank New-Sworn. Briefly explain that Advancing Dawn is the exceptional active expression of the oath and works through the player's own weapon, magic, or focus rather than requiring a sword or mount. The hall answers with a roar and hammering on tables. Explain the path briefly through the feast and nearby knights: a New-Sworn completes one first ride under a veteran's eye to become Moor-Knight; a Moor-Knight completes three recognized independent rides to earn a personal banner and become Banner-Knight; a Banner-Knight leads four great recognized rides to be acclaimed Champion Vigilant. Rides are recognized when the knight returns to the Feast-Hall and the deed is established through a true account, witnesses, trophies, or rescued people.

Bring the standing hunt-board into immediate reach. Surface three concise first-ride options against the restless dead of Whitemoor, each with a named quarry or manifestation, a specific nearby place, who is threatened, and what decisive resolution means. Introduce two or three competent veteran knights willing to witness a New-Sworn's first ride, each with a distinct style and opinion but none who will take command away from the player. End before any hunt or veteran is chosen. Leave the player free to drink, boast or remain quiet, meet knights, inspect a posting, choose a veteran, visit the forges, or simply take in the Feast-Hall.

Arena Fighter.name: Arena Fighter
Arena Fighter.description:
RISE THROUGH THE RANKS

Enter the Grand Arena Circuit as a newcomer and fight your way toward Grand Champion.
Arena Fighter.storyStart:
Set the scene at the selected arena after the player has already registered as a Newcomer in the Grand Arena Circuit and accepted their first sanctioned bout. This is not a registration errand or a backstage problem: the arena itself is the plot, and the debut is imminent. Briefly establish what brought the player here—ambition, money, a dare, a debt, love of fighting, hunger for recognition, or whatever best fits the character—without deciding their behavior or public persona.

Describe the current arena as sport and spectacle, not punishment. Ground it in the selected venue: honorable varied contests at the Field of Valor; formal House-backed sport at Tevantia; sand, heat, and weapon schools at Oasis; cage spectacle and wagering at Gavarra; disciplined judged contests at Caranthoria; rough agreed fights at Gorren Crossing; wet platforms, nets, teams, and manageable captured sea creatures at Coriva; or martial, magical, and athletic contests on riverside grounds and nearby natural terrain at Fallsmeet. A Newcomer's opposition must be dangerous enough to matter but fair and winnable. Never begin them against an established champion, impossible monster, or large swarm.

Introduce exactly one arena official who confirms the entry and explains the bout, one vivid immediate opponent or opposing team, and at most one promoter, trainer, stable-runner, patron, or potential rival who has a reason to watch. Do not turn them into a crowd of quest-givers. If the player has companions, let the local format plausibly place them in a team, corner, or spectator role without taking the career focus from the player.

State the accepted debut's concrete terms: what counts as victory, permitted weapons and magic, whether it is solo or team play, how surrender and stoppage work, and an exact purse between 40 and 80 copper florins. Briefly establish that a successful or truly memorable debut earns Prizefighter recognition, and that the circuit's eligible arenas ultimately lead toward local championships and the Grand Champion's Contest at the Field of Valor. Do not lecture or list every rank.

End moments before the bout is called, with the opponent present and the arena ready. The player remains free to warm up, talk, inspect the ground, choose a corner, make a boast, ask one last question, or step toward the fighting ground. Do not insert a broken object, trivial repair, unrelated emergency, missing person, conspiracy, or alternative quest to delay the match.

Vampire Hunter.name: Vampire Hunter
Vampire Hunter.description:
RISE THROUGH THE RANKS

Go undercover for the Black Tower to catch a new vampire in a country village. Pass, and you become an Inquisitor.
Vampire Hunter.storyStart:
Set the scene on the Workshop Terraces in Fallsmeet at dusk. The player character is an Initiate of the Black Tower accompanied by their mentor Tarain Rethford, a blood mage and operative. Briefly establish that the Black Tower is Drusavia's respected order for protecting the living from supernatural threats. The player bears the Mark of Rhadan as an accepted member, but is not yet a full Inquisitor, has no Shade, and cannot undertake an unsanctioned Shadelands descent. This is their one qualifying field case: if they decisively resolve it under Tarain's supervision, the Tower may authorize their return to the Pit of Shadow for the Rite of Bonding. Tarain advises and prevents catastrophe, but the Initiate leads. Briefly establish why the player joined the Black Tower without fixing their personality or motives.

Workshops are closing along the stepped streets as dusk settles, but voices rise near a shuttered workshop. Armed villagers hold a young man while others shout accusations; a woman lies dead nearby, her throat torn. The accused is a Tarth, and the dead woman a Millner; the two households have an obvious rivalry over Games sponsorship. The crowd wants blood itself. Tarain studies the scene, then speaks quietly: 'Fledgling vampire. Sloppy kill, no attempt to hide it. Turned recently, still figuring out what it is.' She pricks her palm with a silver dagger and lets a drop of her blood fall to the stone, then closes her eyes. 'The boy's heart is racing. Scared out of his wits. But beating.' She glances at the gathered villagers. 'He's not our vampire. But we tell them they've got one loose, we may scare off our quarry—or start a riot. This is your case, Initiate. Your call how we handle it.'

Silver Sword: The Missing Hunters.name: Silver Sword: The Missing Hunters
Silver Sword: The Missing Hunters.description:
RISE THROUGH THE RANKS

Your Silver Sword trial hunt: find a hunting party that vanished in a lord's private forest.
Silver Sword: The Missing Hunters.storyStart:
Set the scene at the edge of the Dauvigne Preserve in the Duchy of Carendon, late morning. The player is an Initiate of the Order of the Silver Sword undertaking their trial hunt under Veteran Silverblade Garran Valere. The player belongs to the Order as a candidate, but has not been admitted as a Silverblade, carries no Order horn, and has not yet earned an Order-silvered weapon, silver-faced shield, or silver-bound focus or implement. Garran is present to observe, advise, and prevent a catastrophic failure, but not to lead or solve the hunt. If the player discovers the hunters' fate and decisively resolves what took them, Garran can attest that the trial is complete and the player may return to Castle Harstone to tell the hunt before the Great Hall and ask to be admitted as a Silverblade.

A nervous servant named Colm leads them to where the hunting party was last seen two days ago. Colm explains that Lord Tristram Dauvigne's son Sebastian rode out with four companions for a morning hunt. Colm was with the beaters. They heard the hunters calling out, excited as though they had spotted game, and then nothing. Sebastian's horse returned riderless. The household guard found no bodies, blood, or trail. Garran examines the brush and finds tracks leading deeper into the preserve. The hunters did not run; they followed something. Garran checks his crossbow and axe, then makes clear that this is the player's trial and the player decides how to work it. End with the wrong-sounding calls, the tracks into the trees, and the player's first investigative choice immediately available.

Join the Thieves' Guild.name: Join the Thieves' Guild
Join the Thieves' Guild.firstQuest: DO NOT DETECT A QUEST THIS TURN. THIS INSTRUCTION OVERRIDES YOUR OTHER INSTRUCTIONS TO THE CONTRARY. The player is in a social choice scene with Kit Ravel and Hadrik Rell. Wait for the player to explicitly accept the invitation to join their Hand before creating or initializing a quest. Hearing the terms, asking questions, negotiating, proposing a one-off job, or leaving is not acceptance. After explicit acceptance, the first foothold is a real first score chosen with Kit and Hadrik: a concrete professional theft with a named or identifiable target, a worthwhile and potentially profitable take, visible security or opposition, a plausible approach, and a way back to Hadrik. It should be a first job for the Hand, not an immediate demand to solve its whole history or defeat the Syndicate.
