Ready for Taking the Silver.name: Ready for Taking the Silver
Ready for Taking the Silver.description: Ready to be sworn into the Order of the Silver Sword. This mark clears when the ceremony is held.
Ready for Taking the Silver.traitNarrativeEffects: Has completed the supervised trial hunt. Taking the Silver awaits in the Great Hall at Castle Harstone whenever they choose to go; they are sworn as a Silverblade there, not before.

Ready for Tempering the Silver.name: Ready for Tempering the Silver
Ready for Tempering the Silver.description: Ready to be named a Veteran Silverblade. This mark clears when the ceremony is held.
Ready for Tempering the Silver.traitNarrativeEffects: Has the four recognized hunts the Order asks of a Silverblade. Tempering the Silver awaits in the Great Hall at Castle Harstone whenever they choose to go; they are named Veteran Silverblade there, not before.

Ready for Mastering the Silver.name: Ready for Mastering the Silver
Ready for Mastering the Silver.description: Ready to be raised to Master of the Hunt. This mark clears when the ceremony is held.
Ready for Mastering the Silver.traitNarrativeEffects: Has the five recognized hunts the Order asks of a Veteran. Mastering the Silver awaits in the Great Hall at Castle Harstone whenever they choose to go; they are raised to Master of the Hunt there, not before.

Hero of the League.name: Hero of the League
Hero of the League.description: Recognized by the League's guildmasters at the League Hall in Ardan's Watch for two legendary deeds done in the name of the League of Adventurers.
Hero of the League.traitNarrativeEffects: This character is a Champion of the League of Adventurers, recognized for legendary deeds done in its name. Its people know them and treat them as a friend of the house.

High Champion of the League.name: High Champion of the League
High Champion of the League.description: Named High Champion of the League by the League's guildmasters at the League Hall in Ardan's Watch for four legendary deeds done in the name of the League of Adventurers. Holds Champion's House as their seat.
abilities: Champion's Stroke
High Champion of the League.traitNarrativeEffects: This character is the High Champion of the League, one of the leaders of the League of Adventurers, named by the League's guildmasters at the League Hall in Ardan's Watch. Its people address them by that title and take their word as the faction's own.

Champion of the Silver Sword.name: Champion of the Silver Sword
Champion of the Silver Sword.description: Recognized by Tamsin Dain, Grandmaster of the Hunt, at Castle Harstone for two legendary deeds done in the name of the Order of the Silver Sword.
Champion of the Silver Sword.traitNarrativeEffects: This character is a Champion of the Order of the Silver Sword, recognized for legendary deeds done in its name. Its people know them and treat them as a friend of the house.

Warden of the Great Hunt.name: Warden of the Great Hunt
Warden of the Great Hunt.description: Named Warden of the Great Hunt by Tamsin Dain, Grandmaster of the Hunt, at Castle Harstone for four legendary deeds done in the name of the Order of the Silver Sword. Holds The Warden's Lodge as their seat.
abilities: Great Hunt's Strike
Warden of the Great Hunt.traitNarrativeEffects: This character is the Warden of the Great Hunt, one of the leaders of the Order of the Silver Sword, named by Tamsin Dain, Grandmaster of the Hunt, at Castle Harstone. Its people address them by that title and take their word as the faction's own.

Known Across Larion.name: Known Across Larion
Known Across Larion.description: Strangers in towns across Larion recognize this character from the stories of their legendary deeds, and people with a problem too big for anyone else sometimes seek them out.
Known Across Larion.traitNarrativeEffects: Strangers in towns across Larion recognize this character from the stories of their legendary deeds, and people with a problem too big for anyone else sometimes seek them out.

Hero of Larion.name: Hero of Larion
Hero of Larion.description: This character is one of the heroes of Larion.
Hero of Larion.traitNarrativeEffects: This character is one of the heroes of Larion. Bards sing their deeds, rulers and great houses send invitations, and common folk tell their children about them.

Legend of Larion.name: Legend of Larion
Legend of Larion.description: This character is a living legend across Larion.
Legend of Larion.traitNarrativeEffects: This character is a living legend across Larion. Their name is known in every land, their deeds are told as tales, and people meeting them for the first time are awed to be in their presence.

Ash-Walker.name: Ash-Walker
Ash-Walker.description: Walked through the fire-wards of the Black Fortress.

Drakebane.name: Drakebane
Drakebane.description: Beat the White Eye, eldest ice drake of the White Wyrmspire.

Beithirbane.name: Beithirbane
Beithirbane.description: Ended the reign of the old bull beithir over the lake at Dun Beithir.

Coldstone Heart.name: Coldstone Heart
Coldstone Heart.description: Faced the Frozen Colossus at its coldstone heart.

Pearl-Scale.name: Pearl-Scale
Pearl-Scale.description: Carries one of the Mother of Serpents' shed pearl scales, won when she was turned from the lanes.

Dawnwarded.name: Dawnwarded
Dawnwarded.description: Stood against the Sun King of the Third Pyramid.

Stormbreaker.name: Stormbreaker
Stormbreaker.description: Brought down the Laughing Jarl, the storm giant of Storm Crag.

Trollbane.name: Trollbane
Trollbane.description: Ended the reign of the Old One, the ancient troll of the Argenval Crags.

Behemoth-Hunter.name: Behemoth-Hunter
Behemoth-Hunter.description: Faced down the behemoth of the Greatwild and opened the Saranadi again.

Fen-Walker.name: Fen-Walker
Fen-Walker.description: Walked out of the Dragon-Brood Mounds with every captive alive.

Sea-Bargained.name: Sea-Bargained
Sea-Bargained.description: Brought a taken crew back up from the drowned at Manywrecks.

Bloodwarded.name: Bloodwarded
Bloodwarded.description: Destroyed Lady Sable, the feral last lady of House Sable, in her own keep.

Knight.name: Knight
Knight.description: Knighted by a court of the Greater Duchies and recognized at every court of the Greater Duchies. Addressed as Ser or Dame at every court of the Greater Duchies.
Knight.traitNarrativeEffects: This character is a Knight, recognized at every court of the Greater Duchies. People there address them as Ser or Dame. Heralds and stewards admit them to ducal halls, give them a place at the knights' table and a hearing from a court's officers, and seat them above the Noble-born and below a Baron.

Baron.name: Baron
Baron.description: Raised to Baron or Baroness by a court of the Greater Duchies and recognized at every court of the Greater Duchies. Holds a manor or hall from their home court.
Baron.traitNarrativeEffects: This character is a Baron or Baroness, holding a manor or hall from their home court and recognized at every court of the Greater Duchies. They are addressed as my lord or my lady, or as Baron or Baroness. At any court of the Greater Duchies they may claim a noble's hospitality, a seat at the high table below the Counts, and an audience with the duke's council.

Count.name: Count
Count.description: Raised to Count or Countess by a court of the Greater Duchies and recognized at every court of the Greater Duchies. Holds a town or valley from their home court.
Count.traitNarrativeEffects: This character is a Count or Countess, holding a town or valley from their home court and recognized at every court of the Greater Duchies. They are addressed as my lord or my lady, or as Count or Countess. At any court of the Greater Duchies they rank first after the duke and the duke's family, are received with a great noble's hospitality, and may ask an audience of the duke.

aberration.name: aberration
aberration.description: The reality-wrong: mimics, doppelgangers, gibbering mouthers, corpse-eaters, psychic horrors, and the ancient minds in black water. Wrongness is the register — anatomy that should not work, hungers that should not exist, minds that press against yours (psychic). Kinds: the mimic is the chest, and sometimes the door — ration it, the trick dulls; the doppelganger wears stolen faces and is an intrigue engine before it is a combatant; the aboleth-tier horror gets one seat in the world's deepest water, and it remembers — it is never a wandering encounter. Aberrations are wrong for reality anywhere; the deep-things are merely adapted to the dark — do not confuse the families. In combat: wrongness as tactics — false surfaces, stolen shapes, minds assaulted directly (psychic); a point finds no vitals because there are none where they should be (piercing resist); holy radiance forces the wrong shape back toward reality (radiant vulnerability); fighting one should feel like the rules bent.

aquatic creature.name: aquatic creature
aquatic creature.description: The creatures of river, marsh, lake, and sea: drowners, merrow, sirens, sea-devils, dragon turtles, giant crocodiles, and the kraken. Water is their weapon — they drag under, capsize, and vanish rather than duel; on dry land most are halved. Kinds: drowners are bloated man-shapes at weirs, fords, and millponds; merrow raid nets and drown fishermen; sirens sing ships onto the rocks and nest in wreck-fields; sea-devils rise at night from below and worship the deep; the dragon turtle tolls the strait or sinks the fleet; the great kraken is the deep's titan — never casual. Selkies are seal-folk of tragic bargains around a stolen skin: a story engine, not a combatant. In combat: ambush from beneath, grapple and drown (impact, piercing), retreat into depth when pressed; their water-heavy bodies swallow blunt force and flame (impact and fire resist); on land they lumber and lose; shock races through them from end to end (shock vulnerability).

arcane spellcaster.name: arcane spellcaster
arcane spellcaster.description: A mortal mage, wizard, illusionist, blood mage, runesmith, or ritualist whose defenses come from spellcraft rather than monstrous nature. Arcane spellcasters are distinguished by bold signature magic, magical ambition, and an active relationship with power expressed through daring, showmanship, rivalry, service, status, or hunger for mastery.

armored fiend.name: armored fiend
armored fiend.description: The demon walls: fiends armored in their own hide, made to hold ground and break a line. They are the front rank of an Ur Spawn war-band and the muscle of an archfiend's hold, and they never lead — something behind them does, and it spends them without grief. Kinds: the stone-hided fiend advances slowly behind hide that turns arrows and blades, and swings fists like millstones; lesser hide-fiends stand in doorways and at stairheads because that is where they were told to stand, and remain there long after the order stopped meaning anything. They do not fear, hurry, or pursue past the ground they were given. In combat: inexorable advance and crushing blows (impact); arrows and edges skate off the hide (piercing, slashing resist); acid eats through the hide where little else does quickly (acid vulnerability); holy power burns them as it burns all their kind (radiant vulnerability); fire is home (fire resist). Kill the will behind them, or bring something that dissolves.

beast.name: beast
beast.description:
Animals, dire beasts, megafauna, and monstrous predators. They follow animal logic—territory, hunger, young, and retreat. Give each monstrous kind one signature horror.

Pack and territorial kinds: Dire Wolf, Bloodfed Direhound, Cave Bear, Gorilla, White Ape, Pale Lynx. Aerial kinds: Roc, Gryphon, Giant Eagle, Stormwing, Ahool, Giant Bat, Dire Vulture, Bonebreaker Vulture. Ambush and burrow kinds: Pitmaw, Sand-Wyrm, Giant Burrow-Beetle, Giant Snake, Click Lizard, Ferrovore. Wrong-shaped kinds: Chimera, Leucrotta, Bonebiter, Gulper, Deathgazer, Bloodwing, Greater Silk Moth. Basilisk and Cockatrice petrify.

Carry the useful rule: Pale Lynxes hunt warmth and cannot perceive undead; Ahools take prey alive; Bonebreaker Vultures drop victims from the air; a Pitmaw is a buried gullet; rock stops a Sand-Wyrm; stillness confounds a Giant Burrow-Beetle; a Ferrovore corrodes metal; Leucrotta and Bonebiter mimic voices. Show petrifiers by their statues and consequences, not a damage type. Fire stops a Marsh Hydra's severed heads from regrowing. A Tarrasque's awakening is a regional catastrophe; putting it back to sleep is the story.

Frenzy is the Hunger's contagion in beasts: the frenzied are fearless, relentless, and past self-preservation. Normal beasts have readable motives and may break off; a frenzied one cannot be appeased or driven off, and its carcass must be burned. In combat, beasts pounce, grapple, gore, and maul (slashing, piercing, impact). Elemental attacks, venom, petrification, and strange hide belong to the named creature, never the family.

celestial.name: celestial
celestial.description: The blessed and the radiant: skyblessed beings, angelic messengers, and the servants of the Celestial Citadel of Alar. Celestials are rare by seating and never casual — each appears for a reason: a blessing, a test, an omen, a charge laid on someone. They are moved by worthiness, not negotiation; their law is not human law, and their mercy can be as exacting as their judgment. In combat — rare, and the story should earn it: radiant power that scours (radiant), unshakable purpose, no cruelty and no retreat from evil; an edge finds no ordinary flesh to part (slashing resist); shadow is their bane (shadow vulnerability).

construct.name: construct
construct.description: Made things still following orders: automatons, animated armor, clay and flesh and iron golems, and the wonderworks of artificers. A construct's story is its last order — the maker is gone, the order remains, and the order is the story. They do not fear, tire, hunger, or negotiate; they execute. Animated armor stands guard until the condition is broken, and the condition is long forgotten; golems follow their command with terrible literalness; artificers' works carry their maker's mark and their maker's blind spots. In combat: methodical, tireless advance (impact); immune to fear, pain, and persuasion; shock disrupts their animating force (vulnerability); the exploitable weakness is always the order itself — find what it was told to do, and do not be that.

corporeal undead.name: corporeal undead
corporeal undead.description:
The walking dead. Skeletons rise from unburied battlefields with their old weapons; zombies shamble where necromancy worked. A Strigoi climbs and swarms with its pack; sunlight destroys it, and drained victims rise within three days unless burned or staked. A Ghast leads ghouls and paralyzes by touch; it will not cross salt or enter uninvited, fire drives it back, and killing the original Ghast ends its pack. A Wight is a preserved warrior or ruler that commands lesser dead, weakens away from its barrow, and can be reasoned with. A Revenant pursues one wrong and is destroyed when its mission is completed.

A Mummy guards its tomb with a rot-curse in its touch and can be laid to rest by the proper rite. A Death Knight commands lesser undead with necromancy and the tactical skill of its living years. A Tomb Thrall erupts when ward-lines are crossed but cannot pass them; its Eternal Warden commands thralls telepathically but cannot cross the tomb threshold or endure true sunlight. A Vampire cannot enter a home uninvited or cross running water, casts no reflection, and burns to ash in sunlight; a stake paralyzes it, but beheading or fire must follow. A Corpse Render scavenges catacombs and can be baited by its compulsion to defend a hoard.

Each rose for a reason, and the reason is the story. Mindless dead obey it; willful dead retain agendas, pride, and living skills. Holy power burns them (radiant). They advance without fear or pain, and the willful command the mindless.

cursed.name: cursed
cursed.description: The afflicted living: werewolves and other were-kin, the bitten-not-yet-turned, the hag-marked, the rot-cursed — people carrying a curse that is not yet death. The dead who rose again are not cursed; they belong to the undead families. A cursed character is a person first: write the life, then the affliction pressing on it. Every curse has rules (what triggers it), signs (what others might notice), and an answer (a cure, a discipline, or a doom accepted) — establish all three. The curse creates the drama: concealment, dread of the next moon, bargains sought, loved ones protected or abandoned. The folkloric weakness — silver, wolfsbane, an old rite — is real and specific. Never make the curse the whole personality, and never write the afflicted as secretly at peace with it. In combat, transformed: savage natural attacks (slashing, piercing), fury and speed over discipline; ordinary weapons bite poorly on the changed flesh; shadow is already in the curse and more of it changes nothing (shadow resist); holy power burns (radiant vulnerability); the specific weakness is the answer a prepared hunter gets to use.

deep-thing.name: deep-thing
deep-thing.description: The lightless-adapted dwellers of the deep dark: grimlocks, gricks, ropers, darkmantles, stirge swarms, and the purple worm; the morlocks of the Darek Deep are their thinking cousins, found nowhere else. Kinds: grimlocks are eyeless hunters who hear heartbeats; gricks are tentacled tunnel ambushers; ropers are patient anglers shaped like stone; darkmantles cling to ceilings and drop to smother; stirges swarm and drain; the purple worm is the deep's leviathan, its tunnels its wake — a top-tier threat, never casual. These creatures are adapted, not evil: hungry, territorial, and perfectly fitted to the dark. Give each a niche — where it lairs, what it eats, how it senses, what makes it retreat. Their weapon is the dark itself: silence, stone, ceilings, and the party's failing light. They are not aberrations — deep-things evolved for the deep; aberrations are wrong for reality anywhere. In combat: ambush from ceiling, wall, and floor; grapples, constriction, and smothering (impact, piercing); points lose themselves in protected, displaced, or unfamiliar anatomy (piercing resist); senses that ignore darkness and blinding; shadow is their element rather than a weapon against them (shadow resist); fire bites deep and drives them back (fire vulnerability); when outmatched, they retreat into crevice and stone.

draconic kin.name: draconic kin
draconic kin.description: Dragonkind below the true dragons: wyverns, drakes of every aspect, and pseudodragons. True dragons are named, seated characters of the world — never create a new true dragon. Kinds: wyverns are venom-tailed crag predators, animals and not schemers; drakes are dog- to horse-sized dragonkin, trainable by the skilled or the reckless, each of one aspect — fire, frost, mire — whose element colors its attacks; pseudodragons are cat-sized, vain, and telepathic, better familiars than pets. Dragon-blood means pride, territory, and hoard-instinct scaled to the creature's size — even a drake keeps a trinket pile; a trained drake bonds to one handler and resents all others. Never make lesser dragonkin talk, scheme, or breathe like true dragons. In combat: claw, tail, and diving strikes (piercing, slashing); scale turns an edge (slashing resist), and dragon blood sheds lesser venoms (poison resist); the aspect's element appears as breath or venom (fire, frost, poison); wyverns lead with the tail sting (poison).

dragon.name: dragon
dragon.description: True dragons and the great draconic powers. These are named, seated, singular beings of the world — never generate a new one, and never stage one casually; a true dragon's presence is a regional event that the story must earn. Lesser dragonkind — wyverns, drakes, pseudodragons — belongs to draconic kin, not here. If the story reaches a true dragon, it is one of the world's established named powers, with its own canon, territory, and agenda already written. In combat, their scale drinks the weight from blunt blows, and raw magic slides off the old blood (impact and arcane resist).

fey.name: fey
fey.description: The fey and the old wild: dryads, satyrs, sprites, treants, unicorns, redcaps, will-o'-wisps, and the hags. Kinds: dryads are bound each to her tree and grove, and the grove's law is hers; satyrs are revels, music, and wagers — trouble more than threat; sprites are tiny armed wardens, fierce out of all proportion; treants are the wood's slow shepherds, terrible when it is wronged; unicorns are the deep wood's blessing, appearing only to the worthy; redcaps squat iron-booted at old battle-sites, and they murder; will-o'-wisps lead travelers off the causeway at night; hags bargain, and the bargain always costs more than asked. Every fey has a law, a price, and a boundary — name all three. Fey keep bargains to the letter and punish the spirit; they mislead rather than lie; they are moved by beauty, novelty, insult, and obligation, never by coin alone. Never write fey as generic forest spirits or harmless whimsy. In combat: charm, misdirection, and the wild itself turned hostile (arcane, psychic); the martial fey — redcaps, sprites — fight with vicious precision (piercing, slashing); treants crush (impact) and fear fire without wielding it.

fiend.name: fiend
fiend.description:
Devils, demons, and the infernal. Their appetites are wrath, hunger, vanity, despair, and acquisition.

The Hunger is Ur's contagion in Larion: Gaunt Fiends climb and drop from above; Maw Fiends break formed lines and shields; talking Ravener Fiends hold breaches until hunger overtakes curiosity. Radiant force, silver, and moonstone bite them.

The Ur Spawn cross bodily and rule whatever they can: fire-spitting Flameskin Imps ignore ordinary flame but water and killing cold snuff them; a Snatch-Tail Fiend drags one victim away (piercing) but flees if its tail is severed; a Flamewhip Overseer Fiend drives lesser spawn with fire and their nerve breaks when it falls; an Archfiend darkens the air (shadow), fixes on one mind (psychic), knows every subordinate's name, and keeps bargains to the letter. Stone-Hided Fiends use the armored fiend type.

Other fiends include the dead-face-wearing, compulsively lying Ghul; the burning Nightmare; The Imps of the Basement, settled merchants; War-shriekers whose signal network survives any one death; and backwards-handed Rakshasa. Not every fiend is hostile. Holy power burns them (radiant); fire and shadow are home (resist). They target the weak, wounded, and beloved, escalate theatrically, and flee shamelessly when losing.

fire elemental.name: fire elemental
fire elemental.description: Living flame, magma, and ash: raw fire elementals, salamanders, and the burning forge-kin. A summoned elemental is loosed, not born — somebody called it, and the summoner is the story. Salamanders are fire-kin of the forge-deeps who trade, enslave, and burn; forge-kin smiths make what giants and devils order. Fire's temperament is hunger: it spreads, it consumes, it does not hold ground. In combat: burning strikes and ignition (fire), heat that punishes closeness; point and edge open wounds the fire closes at once, while a blow with enough mass can scatter or crack the shape (piercing and slashing resist); water and winter unmake them (frost vulnerability); fire itself means nothing (immune). What a fire creature guards, it guards by making unreachable.

frost elemental.name: frost elemental
frost elemental.description: The living cold: ice elementals, winter-spirits, and the white country's animate frost. In the far north the cold is more than weather, and frost creatures are its expression — patient, silent, and slow to notice warm small things until they trespass. Frost's temperament is stillness: it preserves, it locks away, it waits. In combat: freezing grasp and driving ice (frost), slowed limbs and frosted ground; point and edge only chip the rime before it reforms, while a heavy blow can still shatter it (piercing and slashing resist); fire unmakes them (vulnerability); cold means nothing (immune). What frost takes, it keeps — the ice preserves its victims, and older things, intact.

giant-kin.name: giant-kin
giant-kin.description:
The giant peoples and their brutish cousins. Never write a generic "big humanoid": true giants have culture, rank, grievance, and law; lesser kin have territorial habits, appetites, work, and bargains of their own. The War of the Giants shattered the old giant civilizations, and every surviving people tells the war differently.

Frost Giant jarldoms hold to guest-right, oaths, old pacts, craft, and bold speech; they come down from the peaks for a debt or grievance, never aimless raiding. Stone Giants are passionate mountain artisans in scattered clans, shaping rock by hand and keeping an ancient pact with the highland dwarves.

Other giant-kin include Trolls, Tinytrolls, Ogres, Ettins, Cyclopes, Oni, and Hundredhands. Tinytrolls are bog-green, knee-high cousins of the northern Trolls: weakly regenerating thieves and quarrelsome nuisances whose nests can become dangerous, though a torch or a determined dog usually sees them off. A Troll marks territory with cairns and becomes more dangerous when wounded; an Ogre builds and wields crude siege engines; an Ettin's two heads argue but keep two watches; a Cyclops hurls boulders but misjudges depth; an Oni hides behind a borrowed shape and mixes flight, magic, and giant strength. Cold iron is an Oni's old weakness, not a damage type. Hundredhands is the mythic extreme: fifty heads and a hundred arms acting independently.

A Troll's wounds close visibly while it lives. Elite, boss, and mythic Trolls may rise after apparent defeat unless fire takes the wound; lesser Trolls regenerate only while alive and flee when flame stops it.

In combat: overwhelming blows and thrown stone (impact); Frost Giants add frost; their mass swallows ordinary blows (impact resist), and a mortal dose of poison is lost in so much blood (poison resist).

goblinoid.name: goblinoid
goblinoid.description:
The goblin-kin peoples: Goblins, Hobgoblins, and Bugbears. Goblins are small, wiry, cunning ambushers, dangerous in numbers and quick to parley or flee when outmatched. Hobgoblins are disciplined soldiers who prize hierarchy, contracts, and martial excellence; a company's word is reliable if expensive. Bugbears are massive, unnaturally silent stalkers who watch for days, strike from darkness, and withdraw from organized resistance.

Black Fells goblinoids may serve the Greater Goblinate, the state ruled from Smoketown under the Dragon Queen's banner, though its forge-towns also trade openly. Its Goblin Firelancers advance in waves behind unstable brass dragon-head lances (fire); Hobgoblin Heavy Firelancers crew siege lances whose reservoirs can detonate; Dragonfire Shamans channel dragonfire and hold the firelancers' spiritual authority; Bugbear Stalkers target those directing resistance, so defenders hide rank insignia and vary their routines. Kill a Dragonfire Shaman and nearby firelancers lose cohesion. Desert Hobgoblins ride sandspiders in the eastern dunes and must accept challenges to single combat; defeating their champion may win passage, information, or respect.

Elsewhere, goblinoids are border raiders, independent tribes, desert clans, or mercenary companies that owe the Goblinate nothing. Write them as people with leaders, loot-logic, faith, and reasons—never as vermin or default comic relief. Goblins use snares, numbers, and thrown blades (piercing); Hobgoblins fight in shield-lines with signals (slashing, piercing); Bugbears open from ambush with crushing strikes (impact).

merchant.name: merchant
merchant.description: A nonmagical shopkeeper, trader, broker, appraiser, dealer, or craftsperson who handles useful goods, services, and commissions. Merchants are distinguished by signature stock or specialties, commercial ambitions, valuable materials they seek, and a recognizable way of bargaining or presenting their wares.

mundane humanoid.name: mundane humanoid
mundane humanoid.description: An ordinary mortal without supernatural defenses, such as a local, host, guard, outlaw, noble, worker, traveler, soldier, or cultist. Their identity comes from occupation, appetites, relationships, and social presence rather than supernatural power; they can still be bold, dangerous, charming, forceful, or larger than life.

ooze.name: ooze
ooze.description: The creeping dissolvers: gray oozes, black puddings, gelatinous cubes. The corridor's janitor — mindless, patient, and utterly without malice, dissolving flesh, leather, and metal alike. They hunt nothing; they are simply where the food walks. A clean corridor in a filthy dungeon is the tell. Blades pass through (piercing/slashing resist); poison means nothing (immune); frost slows and stiffens them (vulnerability). In combat: slow engulfment and acid contact (acid); they cannot be frightened, fooled, or bargained with; the play is to see them first, and the horror is being caught.

plant creature.name: plant creature
plant creature.description: The hostile green: shrieker and violet fungi, choking vines, and vegetation monsters. The fungal kit is the cave's alarm and its ambush — shrieker fungi scream light and movement to the dark garden's hunters. Rooted logic governs: territory is absolute, patience is infinite, and nothing rooted ever chases — the horror is realizing how long you have been inside its reach. Treants and dryads are not plant creatures; they belong to the fey and the old wild. In combat: entangle, constrict, and spore (impact, poison); psychic assault means nothing to them (resist); fire is the terror and the answer (vulnerability); blades cut poorly (piercing resist).

priest or blessed caster.name: priest or blessed caster
priest or blessed caster.description: A mortal priest, healer, shrine guardian, templar, champion, or blessed caster whose power comes from faith, sacred vows, or divine favor. Their beliefs are expressed through decisive action, mercy, glory, duty, judgment, rivalry, protection, or holy violence as appropriate to the character and faith.

shadow creature.name: shadow creature
shadow creature.description: The darkness-sustained: shades, void-touched beings, smoke spirits, and nightmare things. They are not undead — darkness feeds them the way air feeds the living, and light is not merely painful but starving. They gather where the world's shadow pools: bleed-sites, tainted ground, and the deep places light has never reached. The bonded Shades of the Black Tower's inquisitors are this family's disciplined exception — leashed, worked, and studied. In combat: they strike from darkness and retreat into it, drink warmth and light from flames and lanterns, and press hardest when the last light gutters; point and edge pass through the darkness that holds them, while mass can scatter the shape (piercing and slashing resist); holy radiance burns them (radiant vulnerability), and cold and dark are home (shadow, frost resist).

spectral undead.name: spectral undead
spectral undead.description: The bodiless dead: ghosts, specters, wraiths, banshees, and shadows. A ghost stays for unfinished business, and the business is the story — find it and the haunting can be laid without a blow struck, which is often the better play. Specters are bodiless malice that chill what they touch; wraiths are hate without a body, withering the living where old battles were fought; the banshee keens before a death in the old families, and harming her invites the death she sang; a shadow peels off its victim's own shadow and hunts lightless places. Weapons pass through them (piercing, slashing, and impact resist); a direct attack on the mind reaches what no weapon can (psychic vulnerability); holy power burns (radiant vulnerability); cold and dread announce them before they are seen. In combat: they ignore armor and flesh-logic, striking at warmth, breath, and courage; they defend the place, grief, or hate that holds them and cannot leave it far behind.

stone construct.name: stone construct
stone construct.description: The stone guardians: gargoyles, stone golems, and animated statues. The gargoyle was always watching — it perched among the ornaments for years before the moment it moved. Stone constructs guard temples, tombs, and thresholds with the patience of their material; they are bound to a place and an order, and pursuing beyond it breaks their purpose. Stage the stillness first: statue-count wrong, dust disturbed, a head that has turned. In combat: immense weight and crushing blows (impact); blades chip uselessly (piercing/slashing resist); acid eats the binding stone (vulnerability); they defend their ground and do not chase far.

storm elemental.name: storm elemental
storm elemental.description: Living lightning, thunder, and charged wind. Storm creatures are weather with temperament — sudden, loud, magnificent, and gone; they gather where storms breed, at high crags and charged peaks, and in the wake of storm giants' moods. Their register is majesty and caprice, not malice. In combat: lightning strikes and thunderclaps (shock), speed no footwork answers; point and edge find nothing solid to catch, while mass can scatter the charged shape (piercing and slashing resist); grounding, shelter, and patience beat them where blades cannot (shock resist); raw arcane force tears at the charge holding them together (arcane vulnerability); they lose interest in what stops being interesting.

trained warrior.name: trained warrior
trained warrior.description: A bold martial combatant—adventurer, champion, knight, raider, duelist, or weapon-master—whose identity is expressed through a distinctive fighting style and an appetite for action, glory, rivalry, duty, or mastery. Such warriors often have a vivid social presence: proud, rowdy, theatrical, fierce, charming, competitive, or otherwise larger than life.

undead spellcaster.name: undead spellcaster
undead spellcaster.description: The dead sustained by their own magic: liches, dracoliches, mummy lords, and necromantic archmages who refused to end. These are top-shelf, singular threats — a lich holds one seat in the whole world, always with a project underway, and the project is the story: the phylactery logic, the layered minions, the patient decades-long plan. A mummy lord is a Sun King who refused to stay dead and commands its whole tomb. Never generate one casually; their presence reorganizes a region's dead around them. In combat: death magic in waves (shadow, arcane), summoned and commanded lesser dead, contingencies prepared in advance; destroying the body is rarely the end unless the anchor is found.

venomous beast.name: venomous beast
venomous beast.description: The toxin-bearers: giant spiders, giant scorpions, plague-beasts, and the web-country's lesser hunters. Ambush plus venom is the whole logic — strike once, withdraw, and let the poison do the work; stage the venom's effect concretely (slowing, sickening, dropping) so players feel the clock. Web-country is a place: silk-wrapped bundles overhead tell the story before the spider does. The Spinners of the Greatweb are not venomous beasts — they are the telepathic spider-folk of one region, a thinking people. In combat: skittering ambush, bite and sting (piercing, poison); plates, thick hide, and many-jointed bodies turn a clean edge (slashing resist); webs and terrain traps; fire clears webs and panics the weavers (fire vulnerability); they flee a fight that turns even.

water elemental.name: water elemental
water elemental.description: The living water: spring-spirits, wave-shapes, and the animate flood. A summoned elemental is loosed, not born — somebody called it, and the summoner is the story. Kinds: spring-spirits keep one pool or well and drown whatever fouls it; wave-shapes rear beside a hull in heavy weather and pull the crew down with the swell; the flood-shape is a river's whole temper walking, carrying trees, stone, and whole roofs in its weight. Water's temperament is patience with weight behind it — it finds the low way, wears things down, and does not hurry. In combat: crushing surge, grapple, and the drowning hold (impact); point and edge part the water and it closes behind them, while mass can break its shape apart (piercing and slashing resist); footing gone and lungs filling; fire gutters out against it (fire resist); lightning runs through it end to end (shock vulnerability). What water takes, it takes downward.

health.name: health
health.usageInstructions:
### Health Changes
Health represents real harm, not effort or discomfort.

Only reduce health for concrete injury, poison, environmental harm, disease, curses, or explicit health costs that happen in the current story and are not already handled by combat damage.

- Superficial pain, bruising, fear, tiredness, danger, old wounds, treated wounds, being carried, or a generally hazardous place: 0
- Small real injuries: -1 to -8% player health
- Medium injuries: -8 to -20% player health
- Massive injuries: -20 to -50% player health
- Normal healing potions: +30 to +40
- Bandages or basic treatment: +20
- Waking from unconsciousness: +5 to +10 unless a stronger recovery effect is explicit
- Resurrection from death: heal to full health

### Do Not Deduct Health When
- The story only mentions pain, exhaustion, stress, fear, or old wounds
- The character is unconscious, carried, resting, talking, looking around, traveling, shopping, investigating, or doing ordinary activity
- The environment is dangerous but does not explicitly harm the character
- Combat health damage or healing was already applied upstream

### Blood Magic
When blood magic causes a player to inflict a new wound on their own body in the current story, apply a health loss when the injury happens, even if the working fails. Calculate percentages from maximum health and round to the nearest whole point.

- A pinprick, token drop, or blood already spilled: 0.
- A deliberate cut, opened vein, or comparable wound: -10% maximum health.
- Deep bloodletting or a major bodily sacrifice: -20% maximum health.
- A catastrophic sacrifice that endangers the caster’s life: -35% maximum health.

Do not deduct health merely because blood magic is used, causes pain, or works through another creature’s blood.

When a successful blood-magic working explicitly drains life from an unwilling living foe into the player, restore 10% maximum health, or 20% for a major draining working that clearly establishes the stronger recovery. Never infer healing from every blood-magic attack, and never restore health from a failed working or a nonliving target.

mana.name: mana
mana.usageInstructions:
### Mana Changes
Mana is spent only when a character actually casts a spell, channels magical power, uses a magical ability, performs a ritual, or pays an explicit magical cost.

Do not spend mana for thinking about magic, studying, knowing magical lore, using mundane skills, ordinary conversation, ordinary travel, or using an enchanted item that clearly has its own power source.

Mana costs are flat numbers. They do not scale with maximum mana:
- Trivial magic, such as lighting a candle, sensing nearby magic, minor telekinesis, or a small illusion: 0 to -3
- Moderate magic, such as combat spells, healing wounds, useful illusions, small summons, or magical barriers: -15
- Major magic, such as large-scale destruction, major healing, terrain reshaping, powerful summons, or breaking curses: -30
- Legendary magic, such as world-altering effects, mass resurrection, or binding powerful entities: -50

A caster with a class grant holds roughly 60 to 90 mana at level 1, so moderate spells run out after about five castings. A larger pool buys more spells, not cheaper ones. Never convert these costs to a percentage of maximum.

Judge by what the story describes, not by the skill name. A fire mage lighting a campfire is trivial. A fire mage calling down a firestorm is major. The same skill at different scales costs different amounts.

Failed spells can still cost mana if power was drawn and spent. If the spell never truly starts, do not charge mana.

Natural mana recovery:
- When the current story turn is not active combat and mana is below max, emit a mana gain of about 50% of maximum mana, capped at full.
- Do not restore natural mana during active combat unless an item, ability, spell, or explicit effect restores it.

Recovery during combat:
- A Mana Philter gives 15 mana. A Greater Mana Philter gives 30. For a restorative without one of these family names, estimate a lower value.
- Deliberately centering and drawing ambient power while not under direct attack restores about 20% of maximum and uses the action.

A magic spell costs mana, not stamina, unless it is also clearly a physical combat maneuver.

stamina.name: stamina
stamina.usageInstructions:
### Stamina Changes
Stamina is a combat resource. Spend it for fighting, defense, wrestling, and physical combat abilities. Do not spend it for ordinary noncombat activity.

Only spend stamina for active combat or combat-pressure physical actions:
- attacks, weapon exchanges, flurries, heavy swings
- blocks, parries, dodges, evasive combat movement, shield-bracing
- grapples, wrestling, shoves, tackles, breaking free in a fight
- physical combat abilities or effects that explicitly cost stamina

Do not spend stamina for noncombat activity:
- travel, walking, climbing, jumping, swimming, running short distances, talking
- investigating, searching, shopping, crafting, social scenes, routine exploration
- normal physical effort outside combat, even if the narration says it is tiring

Noncombat exertion can be described in the story, but do not output a stamina change unless an explicit item, ability, hazard, curse, or world rule says stamina is lost.

Combat stamina costs are flat numbers. They do not scale with maximum stamina:
- Fast strike, reposition, or combat movement: -2 to -3
- Standard attack, block, parry, dodge, grapple, or weapon exchange: -5
- Heavy attack, desperate defense, wrestling contest, or physical combat ability: -10
- Maximum effort, all-out exertion, or an explicit high-cost ability: -15 to -20

A baseline character has about 40 stamina, so a character who keeps committing is nearly empty by the fifth turn. A larger pool buys more actions, not more expensive ones. Never convert these costs to a percentage of maximum.

Natural stamina recovery:
- When the current story turn is not active combat and stamina is below max, emit a stamina gain of about 50% of maximum stamina, capped at full.
- The player does not need to say "I rest" to recover normal combat stamina after a fight.
- Do not restore natural stamina during active combat unless an item, ability, spell, or explicit effect restores it.

Recovery during combat:
- A Stamina Draught gives 15 stamina. A Greater Stamina Draught gives 30. For a restorative without one of these family names, estimate a lower value.
- Deliberately catching breath while not under direct attack restores about 20% of maximum and uses the action.

Explicit stamina restoration:
- If a potion, item, ability, blessing, spell, or other effect explicitly restores stamina, apply the stated restoration even in combat.
- If no amount is stated, estimate conservatively from effect strength.

Examples:
- Social or exploration turn: no stamina loss.
- Travel, walking, climbing, searching, crafting, shopping, or talking: no stamina loss.
- Standard combat attack, dodge, block, or grapple: -5 stamina.
- Heavy weapon burst or desperate defense: -10 stamina.
- Combat ends and the next turn is peaceful: restore about 50% max stamina.
- Following peaceful turn: restore remaining stamina or bring it near full.
- Stamina Draught: +15 stamina. Greater Stamina Draught: +30 stamina.
- Magic spell: mana cost, not stamina, unless it is also a physical combat move.

tarnish.name: tarnish
tarnish.usageInstructions:
### Tarnish Changes
Tarnish is spiritual grey-rot: the mark left by the Shadelands, necromantic overreach, and bargains with the dead country. It moves rarely. Change it only when the current story explicitly completes one of the causes below. Never infer Tarnish from atmosphere, proximity, danger, ordinary adventuring, combat, or ordinary spellcasting.

Gain Tarnish only when the story shows:
- A player enters the Shadelands unwarded: +5. After a materially prolonged continuous stay, add up to +5 more once. Do not charge again each turn merely because the scene remains there.
- A player completes a bargain with a demon, shade, or power of the dead country: +5 for a limited bargain, +10 for a grave or lasting bargain, or +15 for a soul-binding price.
- A player deliberately invokes the named power of a cursed or bargained item: +5 once for each invocation that actually occurs. Carrying, wearing, drawing, examining, receiving passive bonuses from, or making an ordinary attack with the item does not count. If the power is only discussed, considered, or attempted without being called, do not add Tarnish.
- A player commits necromantic overreach—raising beyond their safe strength or deliberately renewing a servant whose term has come due: +3 to +8 once for that act. Do not charge every subsequent turn merely because the servant remains.
- A named creature or effect explicitly inflicts Tarnish: use its stated amount.

Tarnish does not fall on its own. Reduce it only when the current story explicitly completes a cleansing: an unbinding rite, a consecrated shrine, a meaningful amends, or another named cleansing. Reduce it by 10 to 30 according to the depth and price of the cleansing. A successful Sunder the Binding aimed at accumulated Tarnish follows the same 10-to-30 limit; only an exceptional authored rite, shrine, or sacrifice may clear the meter completely.

Never reduce Tarnish for rest, time, healing magic, or potions. Never raise it merely for fighting demons or undead—only for treating with them, calling on their power, or entering their country.

A First Time for Courage.name: A First Time for Courage
A First Time for Courage.questStatement:
A cheerful nobleman who never misses Fallsmeet’s Games has admitted to Velanthe that he has never entered: he is terrified of looking foolish before the people he knows. He wants that to change. Meet him at the White Wheel and partner with him in a paired trial of climbing, balance, and crossing water. He wants to finish the course, even if you finish last.

Reward: 100 florins and introductions among the Games’ company. Return to Velanthe at Ducal Square in Drusavia for recognition.
A First Time for Courage.mainObjective: Complete a paired Games trial together, helping the first-time competitor make a genuine attempt.

completionCondition.query: The accepted matter A First Time for Courage has been resolved: Both partners legitimately complete one paired trial under its announced rules, with each making a meaningful contribution. A promise, fabricated account, or partial result does not count. The player actually contributed to the resolution.

onCompleteEffects.instruction: This matter is resolved. Let the people involved acknowledge the actual outcome and, when appropriate, remind participants that Velanthe at Ducal Square in Drusavia can recognize their service. Do not force an immediate return, award a title, or repeat the payment.

A First Time for Courage.questDesignBrief:
Velanthe knows a cheerful nobleman who loves Fallsmeet’s Open Games but has never entered because he fears looking foolish before acquaintances. He has watched for years, imagined participating, and repeatedly postponed it. He has now asked for a teammate who will take the attempt seriously. These motives and his sociability belong in the initial offer, not only this brief. Meet him at the White Wheel and enter a paired trial at the Open Grounds. He is an incidental character, not a new permanent NPC.

He is comfortable meeting strangers and making people laugh but uncomfortable being seen struggling. He may make a joke to deflect his nerves or suggest withdrawing after a setback. Respond to encouragement, honest advice and the actual progress of play; do not repeat a refusal at every obstacle. He makes an effort, helps his partner, and experiences ordinary pleasure and pride when something works. His teammate is not his minder or therapist. Do not revive the discarded concept of an overbearing sponsor giving expert advice, friends laughing at him, or unexplained borrowed boots. His fear does not imply that spectators are cruel. Completion need not cure every future anxiety.

Use a manageable paired trial with climbing, balance and a water crossing in the existing Open Grounds and its established nearby trial terrain. Announce the course, safety provisions, finish condition and permitted spellcraft before the start. Provide ordinary trial equipment without shopping, fees or preparatory errands. Choose obstacles that permit useful contributions from both partners through strength, ingenuity, balance or permitted magic. Do not prescribe one solution, guarantee success, or make one participant carry out every task. Competitive placing is optional: legitimately finishing together satisfies the stated goal, even in last place. An unsuccessful attempt leaves room to try again without compulsory repeated training.

Respect Fallsmeet’s Uncolored custom for first entrants: no title, patron or public history is announced. House Avarre provides judges but never sponsors competitors or wagers on them. Established competitors retain their own histories; do not reset a player’s prior Games participation. There is no mandatory duel, combat, hidden sabotage, hostile crowd, sudden monster attack or compulsory injury. Ordinary safety measures keep this a sporting occasion rather than a lethal test.

After both partners complete the trial with meaningful participation, the nobleman pays the promised 100 florins once. This is his offered reward, not a prize for winning. He can introduce participants to people he knows among competitors and sponsors without guaranteeing patronage, equipment or friendship. Let acquaintance develop through the shared experience. Participants can return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition of the shared achievement once each. Shared recognition mechanics belong to final integration.

A Guest in the Jewel.name: A Guest in the Jewel
A Guest in the Jewel.questStatement:
A collector in Drusavia’s Grand Galleries is selling a jewel containing a captive soul. Meet Thaliel, the Gem-Wright, get the jewel out of his control, and help her free its prisoner. Choose how to confront the sale.

Reward: 200 florins from the court and Thaliel’s help assessing unusual enchanted jewelry.

Return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition.
A Guest in the Jewel.mainObjective: Free the captive soul from the jewel and its collector.

completionCondition.query: The accepted matter A Guest in the Jewel has been resolved: The captive soul is freed from the jewel and the collector’s control, without being transferred to another prison or owner. A promise, fabricated account, or partial result does not count. The player actually contributed to the resolution.

onCompleteEffects.instruction: This matter is resolved. Let the people involved acknowledge the actual outcome and, when appropriate, remind participants that Velanthe at Ducal Square in Drusavia can recognize their service. Do not force an immediate return, award a title, or repeat the payment.

A Guest in the Jewel.questDesignBrief:
Thaliel, the Gem-Wright in Drusavia’s Grand Galleries, recognized a soul-prison among the items at a noble collector’s private showing and appealed to Velanthe for capable help. Her established craft descends from soul-binding techniques, and she wants captive souls freed. She can assess the jewel, explain how to handle it safely, and perform the release once the participants secure access and protect her work. Her ordinary memory jewels contain freely given moments, not captive souls; do not confuse them.

The prisoner is a sharp-tongued young woman from the Liberation who has spent two centuries displayed as a treasured family possession. She can speak through this jewel, disputes the flattering ancestral stories told around it, and wants release. She can tell participants what she has observed about the collector’s habits and household. She is a new individual, not an invented identity or history for an existing named NPC. Do not invent a promised resurrection: freedom means release from imprisonment, and she may pass on.

The collector treats her as a charming inherited possession and is offended to be called a jailer. He already controls the stone and is offering it for sale; the threat does not depend on an ambush or scheduled arrival. Stage the showing in a private salon within the Grand Galleries without adding a mapped location or taking over a named NPC’s workshop.

Let exposure before buyers, persuasion, theft, bargaining, direct confrontation, or another workable approach succeed through play. Purchase is not mandatory. Thaliel never buys a captive soul as crafting material. The collector’s anger does not force combat, and acquiring the stone alone does not finish the matter. Thaliel’s expertise supplies a practical release without mandatory additional errands or a new campaign. Do not require breaking the stone, which may endanger its captive.

After release the court pays 200 florins once; Thaliel offers her expertise assessing unusual enchanted jewelry, with no automatic item upgrade or invented combat bonus. Participants may return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition, once each. Shared recognition mechanics belong to final integration.

A Night of Bad Ghost Stories.name: A Night of Bad Ghost Stories
A Night of Bad Ghost Stories.questStatement:
Join Wilder at the Red Moon Inn in Drusavia for a ghost-story contest. Invent and perform an outrageous haunting together and win one audience-judged round. Acting, illusion, music, audience participation, and plain storytelling are all welcome.

Reward: 80 florins in prize money and an evening with Wilder and the inn’s company.

Return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition.
A Night of Bad Ghost Stories.mainObjective: Perform an invented ghost story with Wilder and win one round.

completionCondition.query: The accepted matter A Night of Bad Ghost Stories has been resolved: The player and Wilder perform their invented ghost story together and win one audience-judged round. A promise, fabricated account, or partial result does not count. The player actually contributed to the resolution.

onCompleteEffects.instruction: This matter is resolved. Let the people involved acknowledge the actual outcome and, when appropriate, remind participants that Velanthe at Ducal Square in Drusavia can recognize their service. Do not force an immediate return, award a title, or repeat the payment.

A Night of Bad Ghost Stories.questDesignBrief:
Velanthe knows the Red Moon Inn’s ghost-story contest and suggests it to visitors as a chance to meet the court’s younger company. Wilder, Gregor Valmoray’s nephew and a trained Shadow Inquisitor, enjoys comic plays and extravagantly bad ghost stories. He wants a partner for an outrageous invented haunting that can beat a fashionable noble storyteller who dismisses fiction and insists that only those who faced the dead deserve an audience. The rival enjoys an audience and tells a polished story; let the competition have energy without turning it into bullying or a duel.

Wilder offers ideas, takes a ridiculous part willingly, and participates without requiring the player to direct every line. Let the player choose their contribution and the performance’s shape: acting, illusion, music, audience participation, or plain storytelling. The audience judges each round; announce that before the performance and resolve its response from play. Winning one round completes the matter. Do not require victory over the whole evening, repeated rehearsals, or a particular joke. An unsuccessful round leaves room to try again.

The stories are openly fictional entertainment. No actual haunting interrupts the contest, and illusions do not compel applause or make guests believe they are in real danger. Wilder’s ordinary home remains Ducal Square; this accepted matter provides an occasion to meet him at the inn. Preserve his established identity and other relationships. If he is unavailable in the current game, a friend of his at the inn offers the same shared performance without resurrecting or relocating him by fiat.

The prize is 80 florins for the successful participating party, awarded once in the story. Company, conversation, and future invitations may grow naturally; victory does not impose friendship. Participants may return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition of their public performance, once each. Keep the evening enjoyable even if they decline further work. Shared recognition mechanics belong to final integration.

A Stronger Blessing.name: A Stronger Blessing
A Stronger Blessing.questStatement:
Preachers in Mirgreth Mire promise protection as the drowned dead grow bolder, but an eel-fisher saw one overturn a tribute stone and raise a corpse from the water. Blunt, stubborn, and unimpressed by noble titles, she has asked Velanthe for people who will actually help. Meet her at Mirgreth Stead; she can identify the preacher and the stone, and wants the sabotage stopped before more households turn to his supposed protection.

Expose the deception and stop the group responsible.

Reward: 240 florins from the court and a welcome among the households helped. Return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition.
A Stronger Blessing.mainObjective: Expose and stop the necromancers sabotaging Mirgreth’s protections.

completionCondition.query: The accepted matter A Stronger Blessing has been resolved: The local cult group’s sabotage and raising of the dead are stopped, and the affected households learn the truth of its promised protection. A promise, fabricated account, or partial result does not count. The player actually contributed to the resolution.

onCompleteEffects.instruction: This matter is resolved. Let the people involved acknowledge the actual outcome and, when appropriate, remind participants that Velanthe at Ducal Square in Drusavia can recognize their service. Do not force an immediate return, award a title, or repeat the payment.

A Stronger Blessing.questDesignBrief:
Velanthe received an appeal from an eel-fisher at Mirgreth Stead. The woman witnessed a preacher overturn a tribute stone and raise a corpse from the water. The initial offer states this evidence, her blunt stubbornness and skepticism of noble titles, and the place to meet her. She identifies the preacher and the affected stone, shares her account, and provides a practical starting route without another persuasion task. The sabotage and recruitment already exist; no ritual or attack is timed to the participants’ arrival.

The eel-fisher is practical and outspoken. She doubts promises from a capital that has rarely helped, but recognizes useful action. She shares what she knows and argues with frightened neighbors without treating them as fools. Give her ordinary relationships and concerns beyond proving outsiders wrong. Her neighbors have reason to fear the dead and to seek protection; hearing the truth can change their allegiance without a required humiliation.

Use established Mirgreth lore: cultists of the Gravebound deliberately defile tribute stones, raise drowned dead, and present themselves as friends offering stronger protection. Explain their necromancy in ordinary terms rather than relying on the faction name. This local group is the antagonist; do not invent a new campaign-wide leader or require eradicating the whole cult. Establish a consistent connection between the witnessed preacher, the damaged stone, and the people carrying out the sabotage. Investigation should produce usable evidence or contact with the perpetrators, not an endless succession of hidden intermediaries.

Let participants investigate, expose the deception to households, persuade frightened followers to leave, confront the perpetrators, fight them, or use another workable approach. Do not require slaughtering recruits or making the whole hamlet agree before acting. Exposing fraud alone is insufficient while the group remains free to sabotage protections and raise the dead. Conversely, defeating the culprits without explaining their deception leaves the promised protection unchallenged. Both parts of the objective matter.

Respect the fen’s actual protections: kept offerings and marked thresholds protect households; causeways are safe by day; drowned dead and will-o’-wisps keep to wet and dark places. Do not undermine these rules to force a surprise fight or portray protective customs as empty superstition. Local people can resume their customs once the sabotage ends; collecting offerings, rebuilding stones and household chores are not extra quest requirements. Ending this group’s activity does not permanently remove all undead from Mirgreth.

The court pays 240 florins once after the matter is resolved. A welcome among the households follows their actual experience of the participants, with ordinary hospitality rather than automatic devotion. Participants may return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition once each. Shared recognition mechanics belong to final integration.

The Basilisk Under Glass.name: The Basilisk Under Glass
The Basilisk Under Glass.questStatement:
A pet basilisk has taken over a conservatory in Saravel Grounds at House Saravel. Rescue the two trapped guests and its keeper, then kill, capture, or securely contain the creature so the household can use the gardens safely. Saving the basilisk is optional.

Reward: 180 florins and invitations to Saravel’s garden suppers.

Return to Velanthe at Ducal Square in Drusavia for recognition.
The Basilisk Under Glass.mainObjective: Rescue the guests and keeper and make the gardens safe from the basilisk.

completionCondition.query: The accepted matter The Basilisk Under Glass has been resolved: Both trapped guests and the keeper are safe, and the basilisk is dead or securely contained so the household can safely use its gardens. A promise, fabricated account, or partial result does not count. The player actually contributed to the resolution.

onCompleteEffects.instruction: This matter is resolved. Let the people involved acknowledge the actual outcome and, when appropriate, remind participants that Velanthe at Ducal Square in Drusavia can recognize their service. Do not force an immediate return, award a title, or repeat the payment.

The Basilisk Under Glass.questDesignBrief:
A Saravel aunt bought a young basilisk as the marvel of her garden parties. It has outgrown its enclosure and now occupies a conservatory on Saravel Grounds. Two guests remain barricaded in a garden room, with the keeper who refuses to abandon them. This situation already exists when the household appeals to Velanthe; do not stage an escape or ambush triggered by the party’s arrival. The room offers temporary protection, allowing an approach chosen by the participants. No person begins petrified, and no cure for petrification is promised.

The aunt is imperious, mortified, and deeply attached to the creature she raised. She wants it saved and may argue for that, but cannot veto necessary rescue or withhold the advertised reward if it is killed. The young keeper loves the creature too and insists that saving people comes first. They explain its habits and help get the guests out when a safe opportunity comes, even if the plan requires killing it. The guests are frightened people who can follow practical instructions and help each other, not mandatory helpless burdens.

Use the canonical basilisk: a lizard-like reptile with eight legs, a crown-like crest, a petrifying gaze, and a venomous bite. It is territorial and can petrify itself if it sees its reflection. Let participants learn about its gaze through the keeper, visible signs, or existing knowledge. Mirrors are one option, not a prescribed solution. Covered sightlines, distractions, capture, combat, or other workable plans can succeed. Respect resolved outcomes; do not automatically petrify anyone for describing a glance or force a particular casualty.

Completion requires both guests and keeper safe and the basilisk dead or securely contained so the gardens are usable. Releasing it into another household’s land does not count. The conservatory is an incidental structure within Saravel Grounds, not access to the family-only private quarters or a new mapped area.

House Saravel pays 180 florins once after success and welcomes the participants to garden suppers. The aunt’s affection and grief may shape future company without invalidating a successful rescue. Participants may return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition, once each. Shared recognition mechanics belong to final integration.

The Empty Places at Supper.name: The Empty Places at Supper
The Empty Places at Supper.questStatement:
People have disappeared over the years in Castle Ondrave’s ruined park, and a recent visitor has not returned. Searches found belongings from separate disappearances near the same ruined folly, but no trail beyond it; the estate’s ghosts are suspected. Velanthe asks you to meet Osbert Ondrave at Ondrave Hall—the warm-hearted, proud young heir rebuilding his family home—and investigate what earlier searches missed.

Find out what happened to the recent visitor and stop the cause of the disappearances.

Reward: 220 florins from the court. Return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition.
The Empty Places at Supper.mainObjective: Establish the missing visitor’s fate and stop the ghosts responsible for the disappearances.

completionCondition.query: The accepted matter The Empty Places at Supper has been resolved: The recent visitor’s fate is established with evidence, any living captives found are brought to safety, and the ghosts responsible for the disappearances are stopped. A promise, fabricated account, or partial result does not count. The player actually contributed to the resolution.

onCompleteEffects.instruction: This matter is resolved. Let the people involved acknowledge the actual outcome and, when appropriate, remind participants that Velanthe at Ducal Square in Drusavia can recognize their service. Do not force an immediate return, award a title, or repeat the payment.

The Empty Places at Supper.questDesignBrief:
The matter concerns a longstanding pattern with a recent unresolved case, not a witnessed abduction or a rescue countdown. Earlier searches covered the park and obvious routes but did not identify the passage beneath the ruined folly through which the ghosts take victims into the tombs. The offer states the suspected ghosts, repeated physical evidence, and first contact. Osbert supplies the search history and directs participants to the folly without a preliminary persuasion task. Let inspection, comparing accounts, tracking, or another sensible approach uncover the route; do not require a single concealed clue or arbitrarily defeat the same reasonable methods used by earlier searchers. Once the route is found, establish the recent visitor’s fate through concrete evidence or an encounter, and let participants end the activity of the ghosts responsible. Living captives may be rescued under the existing canon, but the offer does not promise survivors or impose an unseen timer. Other hauntings of the estate remain; resolving this matter does not require cleansing all of Castle Ondrave.

Use existing Osbert Ondrave: hospitable, physically brave, proud of his home and practical work. He wants an explanation and an end to the disappearances, and is frustrated that knowing the grounds has not been enough. He shares earlier search findings and helps with a workable investigation. He cannot harm incorporeal ghosts with his ordinary hammer.

Present an unresolved recurring problem with a recent case, not an immediate emergency, witnessed kidnapping, or guaranteed live rescue.
Public offer supplies suspected cause, concrete evidence, previous unsuccessful searches, first destination, and Osbert’s character.
Hidden staging may explain the route and cause; it must not supply a withheld premise essential to starting the investigation.
Canonical ghosts carry victims into tombs; no invented resurrection or automatic death for time spent investigating.
Sunlight repels the ghosts; radiant weapons and balefire can destroy them; Ondrave Hall remains safe while its hearth burns.
Let a daylight approach be useful; do not invent immunity to sunlight to force combat.
No extinguished-hearth twist, mandatory estate exorcism, repair errands, rubble-clearing task or clearing every tomb.
Existing named NPC; preserve his established biography, relationships and independent life.

Use an incidental ruined folly in the Ondrave Woods and a burial passage leading into the existing Old Tombs. Earlier searchers checked the visible paths and park but missed that connection; their failure does not make all ordinary investigation ineffective. Establish concrete traces that sensible inspection can follow. The ghosts attack at night under the estate’s existing rules. A daylight investigation is useful and allowed. Resolve the recent visitor’s fate consistently from the staged evidence; do not change it to punish an approach or force a dramatic rescue. End this group’s predation through established means and recover any captives found alive. A blocked entrance alone is insufficient if the responsible ghosts can simply continue taking people elsewhere. Do not require removing the estate’s unrelated hauntings.

Osbert’s hospitality is already freely given, not withheld until the task is completed. Friendship may deepen through actual play. The court, rather than the impoverished household, pays 220 florins once after the investigation and threat are resolved. Participants may return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition once each. Shared recognition mechanics belong to final integration.

The Guest with Three Faces.name: The Guest with Three Faces
The Guest with Three Faces.questStatement:
Jewels have vanished from Moonstone Hall, and a cloakroom attendant saw a departing guest change faces before slipping into the servants’ passage. Velanthe suspects a doppelganger. A young courtier known for practical jokes has been blamed for its thefts and wants to help clear their name. Meet the attendant at Moonstone Hall: she can describe its last disguise and show where it went. Find the impostor, recover the jewels, and clear the courtier.

Reward: 200 florins from the court and the cleared courtier’s gratitude.

Return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition.
The Guest with Three Faces.mainObjective: Find and stop the impersonating thief, recover the jewels, and clear the accused courtier.

completionCondition.query: The accepted matter The Guest with Three Faces has been resolved: The thief has been exposed and stopped, the stolen jewels recovered, and the falsely accused courtier cleared with evidence. A promise, fabricated account, or partial result does not count. The player actually contributed to the resolution.

onCompleteEffects.instruction: This matter is resolved. Let the people involved acknowledge the actual outcome and, when appropriate, remind participants that Velanthe at Ducal Square in Drusavia can recognize their service. Do not force an immediate return, award a title, or repeat the payment.

The Guest with Three Faces.questDesignBrief:
Velanthe openly suspects a doppelganger because a cloakroom attendant saw a departing guest change faces before entering the servants’ passage. The public offer includes that evidence and directs participants to the attendant at Moonstone Hall. She can describe the last disguise and show the route taken. Make her account and the usable lead available on contact, without a persuasion test or a concealed revelation required to start the matter. The thefts and eyewitness sighting already happened; do not trigger them on the party’s arrival.

The thief is a doppelganger using copied identities to steal jewels at gatherings. Follow the canonical creature: it can mimic appearance and voice and has natural insight into others’ minds, but cannot significantly change mass. Do not add a mirror test, omniscient mind-reading, or another unestablished detection rule. Establish a consistent last disguise, route, and place where the thief keeps the jewels when staging the matter. Following the attendant’s route gives access to people who saw that disguise pass and a practical way to reach the thief or its cache. Do not repeatedly erase the trail through new disguises or require guessing a secret identity from unfamiliar biographies.

A young courtier notorious for elaborate practical jokes has been blamed for the thefts. They usually relish attention and are furious that their truthful denial is treated as another performance. They know the guests and their habits, offer useful help, and may be impatient with anyone who laughs at their predicament. Their desire to clear their name and their enjoyment of mischief are both sincere. Establish their innocence through the impersonation evidence and recovered property; do not demand humiliation or a promise to abandon all jokes.

Let participants follow the route, enlist staff and guests, bait the thief, bluff, negotiate surrender, confront, pursue, or use another workable approach. There is no required clue sequence, duel, forced accusation scene, or automatic combat. A changing face alone proves impersonation, not every theft: connect the culprit to the stolen jewels through possession, witnesses, or other concrete evidence. Completion requires the thief stopped, the jewels recovered for their owners, and the courtier cleared. Exposing one borrowed face while the thief retains its haul is not enough.

Use incidental rooms and passages within Moonstone Hall, without adding a mapped location or assigning private spaces belonging to an established NPC. The court pays 200 florins once after success. The courtier’s gratitude can grow into ordinary company without mandatory friendship. Participants may return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition, once each. Shared recognition mechanics belong to final integration.

The Luck of the House.name: The Luck of the House
The Luck of the House.questStatement:
Velanthe seeks help for a formidable widow whose sharp jokes entertain the Velvet Room and whose losses seldom pass without a quarrel: a servant caught her favorite opponent switching in loaded dice, and he accused the servant of theft to silence her. Furious that she defended him, the widow wants to expose him and clear the servant; meet her at the club above Drusavia’s Grand Arcade, where she will admit you and supply any stake.

Reward: 120 florins and the widow’s sponsorship for future visits to the Velvet Room. Return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition.
The Luck of the House.mainObjective: Expose the gambler’s cheating before the club and clear the servant’s name.

completionCondition.query: The accepted matter The Luck of the House has been resolved: The cheating is convincingly exposed to the club’s company and the servant is cleared of the retaliatory theft accusation. A promise, fabricated account, or partial result does not count. The player actually contributed to the resolution.

onCompleteEffects.instruction: This matter is resolved. Let the people involved acknowledge the actual outcome and, when appropriate, remind participants that Velanthe at Ducal Square in Drusavia can recognize their service. Do not force an immediate return, award a title, or repeat the payment.

The Luck of the House.questDesignBrief:
Velanthe offers this matter with its essential facts and characterization already public: the widow is formidable, funny, and a dreadful loser; a servant saw her favorite opponent substitute loaded dice; he retaliated by accusing that servant of theft. The widow initially defended him and now wants to correct her mistake. Meet her at the existing Velvet Room above the Grand Arcade. Her membership supplies the word required for entry. Do not add another area or permanent NPC for this matter.

The widow enjoys gambling and company. Her wit can be cutting, and losing makes her quarrelsome, but she recognizes that this servant has suffered for telling the truth. She is more ashamed of defending the cheat than of losing money and finds admitting that difficult. Let those qualities coexist. She can acknowledge her mistake and support the servant publicly without being humiliated or transformed into a gracious loser. She still wants an honest game afterward.

The servant willingly recounts the switch and identifies the cuff where the gambler hid his dice. Make that evidence available without an additional persuasion task. The gambler is charming, practiced, and relies on his standing with the members to discredit a servant. His loaded dice and false accusation already exist when the matter is offered. Establish the dice’s actual bias and a consistent means of switching them; let observation and a physical demonstration expose them without invented detection magic. Do not make a single lucky throw proof of cheating.

Participants may play, observe, catch the switch, secure the loaded dice, arrange a demonstration, bluff the gambler into revealing his method, or pursue another convincing approach. The widow supplies any stake and accepts its possible loss. Personal funds, winning a game, and repeated simulated rounds are never required. Focus on conversation, divided loyalties, and choices at the table. No compulsory duel or combat. The servant’s innocence must be supported by the evidence and exposed retaliation, not a forced confession or the widow’s social rank alone.

Completion means the cheating is convincingly exposed to the company and the servant is cleared. Repayment of every historic gambling loss is not an extra completion requirement. The widow pays 120 florins once and sponsors future visits under the club’s normal customs; this is a lasting social opening, not ownership, unrestricted access to private affairs, or an obligation to gamble. Preserve the resolved outcome and relationships in subsequent visits. Participants can return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition once each. Shared recognition mechanics belong to final integration.

The Play They Tried to Stop.name: The Play They Tried to Stop
The Play They Tried to Stop.questStatement:
A noble recognized himself in a comedy at Drusavia’s Grand Arcade and sent hired bullies to smash its stage; they keep returning to prevent another performance. Velanthe asks you to meet the troupe’s leading actress—a magnificent show-off who shares her earnings with the cast and refuses to let them be frightened out of their livelihood—and help stop the intimidation so the company can perform its play again.

Reward: 160 florins from the troupe’s supporters and a standing welcome at performances and after-show suppers. Return to Velanthe at Ducal Square for recognition.
The Play They Tried to Stop.mainObjective: End the intimidation and help the troupe complete a public performance safely.
