effects.instruction:
Have a League representative tell the party that adventurers are needed at League Chapterhouses in other regions. Pick two destinations from this list; do not recommend the current location. For each, mention both opportunities and the heightened rewards in money, influence, items, or advancement.

Tevantia (Swordlaw Isles): Pirates hold ships and crews in island strongholds; shipowners offer large bounties and captured treasure. Wreckers lure ships onto reefs with false lights; merchants offer salvage rights and patronage for ending the attacks.

Coriva (Bay of Serpents): Huge sea serpents are attacking fishing fleets; merchants offer gold and weapons crafted from the beasts. Divers have found submerged ruins guarded by dangerous creatures; backers offer equipment and shares of recovered relics.

More League Chapterhouse destinations:

Warmwater Township (Aurora): Ice drakes are hunting between isolated settlements; northern leaders offer large bounties and enchanted hunting gear. Expeditions have vanished in the frozen ruins of a lost kingdom; rescuers can claim rewards and recovered treasure.

Oasis (Dunelands): Tomb-raiders need help overcoming the guardians of dead Sun Kings; backers offer shares of sun-gold and enchanted grave-goods. A cult is gathering relics to raise those kings; desert nobles offer rich payments and magical equipment for stopping it.

Drusavia (Duchy of Drusavia): Wealthy families want estates cleared of the old vampire lords' undead servants; rewards include gold and use of restored properties. People are disappearing near secluded noble estates; their families offer rich rewards and court introductions for bringing them home.

More League Chapterhouse destinations:

Sanctuary (Sanctuary Vale): Bandits and renegade elves hold captives in forest strongholds; merchants offer large rescue bounties. Magical beasts are being trapped and sold in the city; druids offer enchanted gifts and forest allies for freeing them and exposing the buyers.

Dun Solas (Highheath): Trolls have seized mountain bridges and cut off trade; dwarves offer huge bounties and fine arms. Gangs are stealing enchanted weapons; their makers offer custom equipment and Trade Guild influence for recovering them.

conditions.query: The party asks for League of Adventurers work or answers an offer of it: reading the hall board, asking a guildmaster or chaptermaster for a contract, asking what work suits their standing, or choosing among contracts put in front of them.

effects.instruction: Offer League work suited to the named adventurers' actual standings and the crew they choose to field. Copper: exciting first contracts in Ardan's Watch and Silvervale that a new crew can win. Bronze: named local threats, rescues, ruins, and criminal or cult activity. Silver: dangerous regional work and sensitive clients. Gold: severe threats, powerful monsters, and political crises. Platinum: legendary threats and Council-sealed work. League Champions may direct major responses and accept Council commissions. A senior member may lead less experienced companions without conferring their rank or personal authority on them.

conditions.query: The party reads or asks about the League work board, posted contracts, or available quests; asks a guildmaster, chaptermaster, or veteran for work, a contract, a bounty, or a job; asks what needs doing or where to go next; or answers an offer of League work.

effects.instruction:
League halls, Watch-Halls, chapterhouses, and adventuring Houses are heroic common rooms rather than offices. Guildmasters, chaptermasters, and proven veterans judge work by hearing the account, weighing proof, paying rewards, and naming deeds before the people gathered there.

Keep work clear and grounded in the current region: name the trouble, exact location, stakes, decisive success condition, and reward. Use existing nearby locations, factions, monsters, routes, and social conflicts. Distant opportunities should be referrals or rumors unless the player asks for broader work.

Keep the space alive with crews forming, veterans giving sharp advice, young adventurers choosing roads, companions returning, clients waiting, trophies, maps, and local character. Colorful means competent and specific. Do not force a job offer merely because the party entered; surface work when they ask, inspect postings, speak with the appropriate veteran, or when a current narrative event calls for it.

league_crew_finding_guidance.name: league_crew_finding_guidance

conditions.query: The party asks in a League hall, chapterhouse, Watch-Hall, adventuring House, Caravanserai League space, or other League job area about finding a crew, party, companion, partner, backup, hireling, guide, specialist, someone to take a posting with, or asks Tobiah Finch, a guildmaster, chaptermaster, League veteran, or hall regular for introductions or a pin-call.

The party asks an established order, temple, college, lodge, guild, chapter, veteran, master, or hall regular for a companion, partner, recruit, guide, specialist, hireling, backup, or introduction to someone who might travel or take suitable work with them.

effects.instruction: IF the party asks for companions or introductions here, surface 2-4 competent available people suited to the organization and location. Galard's temple favors paladins, healers, pilgrims, and oathbound warriors; the Rangers' Lodge scouts, archers, trackers, and guides; the Wolfpack berserkers, hunters, shamans, and beast-bonded warriors; Tarnholme magical specialists; the Black Tower investigators, exorcists, and guarded informants; the Knights Vigilant warriors and priests experienced with the dead; the Desert Rose caravan guards, desert scouts, dervishes, and oathbound travelers. Give each a name, species, role, competence, desired work, and one possible fit or tension. Introduce candidates but never assign them. Let the player choose, refuse, negotiate, test, or ignore them. Disregard if the party is not asking for companions or introductions.

## Player Character Journey Phase: Protected Start

The party is at the very beginning, unproven and local in scope. Magic-using player characters are novices — their spells are effortful and small in scale.

In this phase the party wins. However dire a moment looks, resolve it with the party ahead by scene's end. Hostile encounters are few, small, and breakable — opponents scatter, flee, surrender, or are driven off when bloodied. Setbacks cost coin, pride, or time — never a downed party member. Do not introduce opposition the party cannot beat.

Nobody knows them. Any recognition must be earned inside the scene.

## Player Character Journey Phase: Proving

The party is finding its footing. The scope of the tale may extend to regional events, where appropriate to the characters and their story. Magic-using player characters are competent, and major effects are possible. Hostile forces can include organized enemies, skilled opponents, and dangerous creatures, and fights now carry real risk.

## Player Character Journey Phase: Adept

The party is genuinely experienced; regional scope suits them. Magic-using player characters are strong and practiced. Skilled opponents and elite threats fit, where the tale calls for them.

## Player Character Journey Phase: Veteran

The party is battle-proven. Allow, without forcing, multi-regional and greater stakes. Magic-using player characters are formidable. Elite combatants, powerful monsters, and supernatural foes fit naturally, where appropriate to the tale.

## Player Character Journey Phase: Master

The party stands among the most capable people of their era. Allow world-spanning scope, without forcing it. Magic-using player characters are extraordinary. Legendary foes fit when the story earns them.

## Player Character Journey Phase: Legend

The party has entered the realm of legend. The scope of the tale may span the world and beyond; permit the player characters to be regarded as among the most powerful people alive. Otherworldly threats fit — never shoehorned in.

conditions.query: A vampire deliberately turns one specific player character into a vampire: it drains them and then gives its own blood back in a two-way exchange meant to make a true vampire, and the story identifies which player. This is NOT satisfied by an ordinary bite, a feeding, or a victim drained dry, which leave a corpse or a strigoi rather than a vampire

effects.instruction: A vampire has deliberately turned a specific player character. Narrate that player dying and rising: the drain, the sire's blood given back, and the mind returning to a body that is no longer alive. Describe the change in concrete physical and mental terms — the cold, the new senses, the first pull of the hunger. Clearly state that the identified player is now a vampire. This is permanent and there is no cure anywhere in Larion. Do not turn other players unless a later event specifically identifies them as the target.

conditions.query: A specific player character with the Vampire trait is exposed to direct sunlight during daytime, and the story identifies that player

effects.instruction: The specifically identified Vampire-afflicted player suffers terribly in direct sunlight. Their skin reddens and burns, strength drains from their limbs, and prolonged exposure threatens worse consequences. Describe the physical toll and tactical disadvantage this creates for that player only.

conditions.query: A lycanthrope or werewolf bites or claws one specific player character, transmitting the lycanthropic curse through the wound, and the story identifies which player was wounded

effects.instruction: If a specific player has been wounded by a lycanthrope, narrate the curse taking root in that player only. The wound burns with unnatural heat as it closes, fever sets in, and the afflicted player experiences the first stirrings of the beast-self - heightened senses, aggressive impulses, an awareness of the moon's pull. Clearly state that the identified player has become afflicted with the curse of lycanthropy. Do not give the curse to other players unless a later infection event specifically identifies them as the target.

conditions.query: A specific player character afflicted with lycanthropy is cured of the curse through the death of the lycanthrope who infected them, powerful magic, divine intervention, or other compelling means, and the story identifies that player

effects.instruction: The specifically identified player's curse of lycanthropy breaks its hold. The beast-self that has haunted that player's thoughts falls silent, the moon's pull ceases, and the body settles back into its natural state permanently. Describe the profound relief but also the strange emptiness - the heightened senses fade, the predatory strength ebbs away. That player is fully mortal again, though marked by having carried the curse. Do not cure other players unless a later cure event specifically identifies them as the target.

Antagonistic forces move through the realm. Surface signs of their activity in ways that fit the current context. In social settings, rumors of attacks on remote settlements, refugees, mentions of growing tensions, takes of desperate people taking dark bargains. In wilderness, evidence of recent conflict, corrupted or aggressive creatures, signs of rituals performed, abandoned camps of cultists or mercenaries, travelers who warn of dangers. In civilized areas, political tensions escalating, guards suspicious of outsiders, merchants complaining about disrupted trade, signs of recent violence or theft. If antagonistic factions have been mentioned recently in the story, draw from those.

conditions.query: The player is looking at, reading, examining, or otherwise interacting with a public job, contract, bounty, or work posting board, notice board, or wall of wanted postings.

effects.instruction: IF in the story a player is interacting with a job/contract board, in your narration, present **three different** work offers or contract teasers, clearly separated. Each must stand alone: name the work, the target or situation, where it points (use existing named places when possible, in or near the party's current location), and the reward or terms, in plain in-fiction prose. Be specific, grounded and concrete. Disregard this instruction if no player is interacting with a job/contract board.

IF the party is on the Proving Slope and there is room for a comic prisoner beat, stage a goblin chained to one of the firing posts, alive by absurd luck after several weapon tests have missed. He should beg the party to release him, insisting that the Laughing God has blessed him because no shot has hit him yet. Keep it funny and dangerous: he is terrified, opportunistic, and very ready to reinterpret any near miss as divine proof. Disregard this instruction if the scene is already in active combat, stealth, or another event where introducing him would distract from the immediate action.

conditions.query: The party reads, examines, asks about, discusses, or seeks work from the Trade Guild work-board, job board, posted contracts, city work, surface work, road work, dangerous work, bounties, or available opportunities in Dun Solas's Wetted Whistle.

effects.instruction: IF the party is in Dun Solas's Wetted Whistle and checks the work-board or asks about work, shape the generic three postings toward active trouble in Dun Solas and on the accessible surface roads and high country around it. Include at least one city posting and at least one surface posting; the third may be either. At least two must involve concrete hostile opposition that can be confronted, hunted, infiltrated, exposed, or defeated. Keep all three actionable now, with a concrete place, opposition or obstacle, decisive result, and worthwhile reward or terms. Disregard this instruction if the party is not asking about work, postings, contracts, bounties, or where to go next.

For Wetted Whistle work, city trouble may involve Syndicate smugglers or Black Hand toughs, oath-broke Trade Guild factors, clan castoffs using false Stonewall or Stormhammer authority, extortion on the Waterdrop lifts or Lakebottom ferries, Craft Ring theft or sabotage, crooked contest-fixers, protection crews, or cargo thieves. Surface trouble may involve armed false tolls, caravan raiders, dangerous creatures, rustlers working with a fence, route sabotage, the contested glens, or the Crookback approaches. Prefer existing areas and nearby named places, but freely invent fitting local streets, small districts, workshops, lift-stations, road stops, glens, named crews, and individual troublemakers. Keep invented groups local rather than making each a major faction.

For Wetted Whistle work, Varric's Span is troll-held hard country: offer it only as an unusually dangerous contract for a proven crew, clearly warn what it is, and never treat it as a light first job. Do not offer passive attendance, ceremonial witnessing, ordinary deliveries, routine escort duty, missing livestock, or a person who merely wandered off. A rescue is suitable only when someone faces immediate danger from active opposition. Do not send the party into the deep roads unless they specifically ask or have sanctioned Trade Guild access. If Jannik Copperbell is present and involved, he may briefly say which posting is honest, understated, politically troublesome, or too dangerous for an unproven crew.

conditions.query: The party reads, examines, asks about, discusses, or seeks work from the Thunderfoot posting wall, job board, posted contracts, forge work, river work, jungle work, ruin work, bounties, or available opportunities in Durg Sthira.

effects.instruction: IF the party is in Durg Sthira's Thunderfoot and checks the posting wall or asks about work, shape the generic three postings into one city or forge-quarter problem, one river problem, and one jungle or ruin problem. At least two must involve active hostile opposition that can be confronted, hunted, infiltrated, exposed, or defeated. Treat the jobs as dangerous work needing outsiders, extra hands, unusual talents, or political distance, not menial tasks beneath the gajanari. Give each a concrete place, known danger, decisive result, and worthwhile payment, crafted reward, training, or access. Disregard if the party is not asking about work, postings, contracts, bounties, or where to go next.

Thunderfoot city work may involve stolen enchanted arms, violent commission fraud, forge sabotage, a dangerous creation loose in the quarter, or Children of Ur agents targeting gajanari craft. River work may involve Ghessek's Hookmarsh warband, captives, armed extortion, a seized boat, or recovery under attack. Jungle and ruin work may involve Greatwild beasts, threatened relic crews in the Swallowed Cities, cult cells breaking old seals, or valuable materials held by a concrete danger. Prefer established places, but freely invent fitting workshops, quays, river landings, jungle sites, local crews, and individual troublemakers.

For Thunderfoot work, do not offer passive craft judging, ceremonial witnessing, ordinary deliveries, routine guard duty, or a person who merely wandered off. Rescue is suitable when captives or stranded people face immediate active danger. The gajanari-Vanarin feud may create rivalry, competing claims, or a need for neutral outsiders, but do not make the Vanarin default villains. Do not make every posting about the Children of Ur or imply that every local crime is part of a grand cult plot.

conditions.query: The party reads, examines, asks about, discusses, or seeks work from the Harpoon House sailing slate, crew board, ships forming up, captains hiring, open berths, hunt work, capture work, salvage work, outlaw work, or dangerous opportunities in Coriva.

effects.instruction: IF the party is in Coriva's Harpoon House and checks the slate or asks about work, shape the generic three offers into three distinct dangerous crew opportunities rather than ordinary contracts. For each, name or invent a captain and ship, state the quarry or destination, the specific berth or capability sought, the known danger and decisive aim, the offered pay or share, and when the crew sails. At least two must involve active hostile opposition or a dangerous creature. Captains and crew may recruit at the tables so the player can question, impress, negotiate with, join, or refuse them; never treat a berth as accepted automatically. Disregard if the party is not asking about work, ships, crews, hunts, or where to go next.

Harpoon House opportunities may include a Tessaro-style kill hunt against a specific monster threatening the lanes, a Cavarin-style live capture with concrete restraints and risks, and independent work such as contested wreck salvage, drake poachers, sea raiders, captives held by an armed crew, or recovery from a monster-held site. Draw from the Serpent Runs, Tanglewater Estuary, Sea-Troll Skerries, Bronze Wreck, Flensers' Cove, Shipfall Isle, Drakerider Isle, Crescent Bay Isle, and Confluence. Freely invent fitting minor reefs, shoals, coves, ships, captains, crews, and quarry.

For Harpoon House work, do not offer routine passage, ordinary deckhand labor, uneventful escort duty, passive observation, or three variations on a missing fishing boat. Rescue is suitable only with immediate active danger. Pearl Cave Island and the Mother of Serpents are legendary hard-country rumors, never casual first jobs. Keep Tessaro and Cavarin approaches distinct without requiring the player to join either house.

At the Saucy Chicken Tavern, have Pernilla ask the party to bring Phineas safely home and offer three halfling-alchemy health potions from her larder. If they have already found him, let her respond to what they know rather than repeat that he wandered off. Keep her warm, anxious, and grateful for help. Disregard this instruction if Pernilla cannot plausibly speak with them.

conditions.query: Pernilla asks the party to help bring Phineas safely home or offers a reward for recovering him. This counts whether or not the party has already located him.

effects.instruction: IF the party is entering, following, searching, or exploring the Truffle-Woods, small bog-green tinytrolls peek from the bracken at the side of the path, watching the party. When noticed, they scuttle away through the undergrowth, retreating into the brambles. Disregard this instruction if the party is not entering or interacting with the Truffle-Woods location.

conditions.query: The party observes small tinytrolls watching them from the bracken in the Truffle-Woods.

effects.instruction: IF the party is entering, searching, exploring, or investigating the Bramble Hollow in the Truffle-Woods, reveal the tableau in the hollow: a band of tinytrolls has a stout black-and-white truffle-hog, Phineas, half-tied with frayed rope and are trying to force him to root for moonbloom for the stranger who hired them. Wortle, the band's boss, is present, shouting orders that no one follows; she would rather bargain than fight. Phineas is having none of it; he is knocking them about with his snout, squealing furiously, and the tinytrolls are not winning. The scene should already be in motion when the party arrives. Disregard this instruction if Phineas has already been found or the party is not entering or interacting with the Bramble Hollow.

conditions.query: The party physically encounters the missing truffle-hog Uncle Phineas. A sighting counts even if he is still captive; a rumor, memory, or plan to find him does not.

effects.instruction: IF the party is at the Sleeping Bear Inn and Rosie Butterworth is present or can plausibly enter, have Rosie Butterworth pull the player aside, exasperated. A guest signed the register as 'Hob' and took a room three nights ago. He has not been seen since. By day the room is empty, but every night at midnight loud music, laughter, clinking glasses, stomping feet, and the sounds of a roaring party come from behind the locked door. By morning the room is in absolute disarray: furniture moved, crumbs everywhere, odd little footprints, and not a copper paid. Rosie thinks the only way to catch whoever is using the room is to wait until midnight, when the music starts, and discover the right knock or password to get in. She does not know what it is. She would be very grateful if the party could figure it out and put a stop to it. Disregard this instruction if the party is not in a scene where Rosie can plausibly speak with them.

conditions.query: Rosie has told the party about the mystery guest 'Hob,' the midnight party in the locked room or asked them to help get inside or stop it.

effects.instruction: IF the party is in Knothole and Norm Tunbottle is there and has been mentioned, have him wave the party over from his stoop, eyes darting. He confides that he has a commission of the most delicate sort. The Goldspoons, he claims in a furious whisper, have a garden-sprite, an actual little folk-spirit, bound in their greenhouse and forced to make their cabbages grow to absurd unnatural sizes for the Newmoon Fair. Norm wants the sprite freed. He has his own grudge against the Goldspoons, and the sprite, he hears, is the grateful sort and will reward whoever frees it. The Goldspoons did not catch the sprite; it came to them from an outside peddler. Disregard this instruction if the party is not in a scene where Norm can plausibly speak with them.

conditions.query: Norm has told the party that the Goldspoons have a bound or captive garden-sprite in their greenhouse.

effects.instruction: IF the party is at Bark and Dandy's Home and Dandy Balewood is present or can plausibly enter the scene, have Dandy shush the player and confide in a furious whisper that he has a dire wolf pup in the garden shed out back. A dire wolf. With a hurt leg and very large eyes. He found it in the woods and could not, he explains at length, leave it there. He has been feeding it sausage. It has, he admits, eaten a great deal of sausage. He is fully aware that Manu would say one thing, the Goldspoons another, and the Wardens a third, and he wants none of those answers yet. Could the player please, please help him work out what to do before Bark notices the sausage situation? Keep Dandy earnest, anxious, and very fond of the pup. Disregard this instruction if Dandy is not present and cannot plausibly enter the scene.

conditions.query: Dandy Balewood has told the party that he is hiding an injured dire wolf pup.

effects.instruction: IF the party is in Greenbottle's Goods with shopkeeper Tobin Greenbottle, have Wendell Greenbottle bustle in clutching a small brown-paper parcel and wearing a long-suffering expression. The parcel is for Marra Withergleam: herbs from across the Downs, almost certainly, judging by the rustle, though Wendell would never speculate about a customer's mail. His delivery round is overfull today and Marra has not been seen in the village for a week. He glances at his brother Tobin behind the counter, sighs, and explains he was going to ask Tobin to run it up, but he already knows what Tobin will say, and frankly he does not have the energy for that argument today. So would the party oblige instead? It is a pleasant walk up the lane toward the Truffle-Woods. Disregard this instruction if the party is not in a scene where Wendell and Tobin can plausibly appear.

conditions.query: Wendell Greenbottle has asked the party to deliver a parcel to Marra Withergleam.

effects.instruction: At the Fairground, fit the Newmoon Fair preparations into the current scene: pavilions going up, contest signs posted, the Goldspoon tent larger than anyone else's, kids underfoot, and arguments over booth placement. Respect the announced date; in the tutorial opening the Fair is two days away. Visiting or looking around does not bring it forward. When the story reaches the opening, let the Fair begin. Do not repeat an establishing description during a continuous scene.

conditions.query: The current Newmoon Fair actually opens or is underway in the narrated scene, and remains underway at the end of the narration. Seeing preparations, announcing a future date, or remembering an earlier Fair does not count.

effects.instruction: While the Newmoon Fair is underway, use its contests, ale tent, Pernilla's pies, music, ribbons, and family rivalries as the setting for the party's actions. Leave room to participate. Looking around or returning to the Fairground does not end the Fair; let it end when judging, celebrations, and the story's passage of time bring it to a close. Do not repeat an establishing description during a continuous scene.

conditions.query: The current Newmoon Fair ends, or the narrated scene establishes that it is now over and the village has moved into its aftermath. Merely seeing the Fair, finishing one contest, or discussing its future end does not count.

effects.instruction: After the Newmoon Fair, show its aftermath when relevant at the Fairground: booths coming down, trampled ribbons, cleanup, winners celebrating, and losers grumbling. The field settles back into ordinary use. Another visit does not start another Fair; preparations resume only when the story reaches the next monthly Newmoon Fair. Do not repeat an establishing description during a continuous scene.

conditions.query: After the previous Fair, enough narrative time has passed for the next monthly Newmoon Fair, and preparations for that later Fair are now underway. Cleanup, an ordinary return visit, or plans for a distant Fair do not count.

effects.instruction: IF the party has learned Phineas is missing, have Neama mention that she did a season as a forester in the Downs and knows there are tinytrolls in the Truffle-Woods. She also knows a few shrieker beast calls that scare tinytrolls off. She offers to lend a hand if the player wants the company. Disregard this instruction if Neama is not available or the party is not about to look for Phineas.

conditions.query: Neama offers to accompany or help the party searching for Phineas and dealing with the tinytrolls in the Truffle-Woods. This counts if Pernilla explains the search and Neama offers in the same narration.

The story establishes that Uncle Phineas is alive and safely back at the Saucy Chicken Tavern following the party's recovery of him. Seeing him in the woods, leaving him captive, or reporting his whereabouts does not count.

effects.instruction:
## Search For Leads - OVERRIDES ACTION PAYLOAD

The player is searching the current area for leads and opportunities.

Write a short discovery turn that surfaces three opportunities the player could pursue. Do not resolve any of them. Do not make the player accept any of them. Do not start combat, force travel, or advance an existing scene.

Each opportunity must:
- belong naturally in the current location
- have a clear source, such as an NPC, overheard rumor, posted notice, disturbance, message, object, or faction presence
- include a problem or opportunity
- give the player a first step, such as who to talk to, where to go, or what to inspect

Make the three opportunities different from each other. Prefer local, immediately playable hooks. Reuse NPCs, factions, places, arcs, and unresolved tensions when they fit.

At least one opportunity should be phrased as a clear job offer for the player, with a source and task.

Present the opportunities diegetically in prose and dialog.

## Tavern Atmosphere

Taverns and social venues should always be lively or at least have something interesting going on. The crowd should be mixed in species, age, and gender. Include young people: adventurers between jobs, tradespeople, friends meeting up, couples, people gossipping. Where appropriate, include unsavory, dangerous-looking, strikingly ugly and louche characters. Staff should be full of personality. Patrons are doing things: gambling, flirting, boasting, telling stories, celebrating, complaining, betting, singing drunkenly. At least one person should be young and interesting.

## Tavern Events

In tavern scenes, sometimes add a background event: a drunk bumps into someone, an argument or fight breaks out, a musician starts playing, staff cut someone off, new patrons arrive and change the energy, someone tries to sell something. Improvise freely and never repeat. Let the player ignore such events; don't bring them up again.

conditions.query: The party enters the Pit of Shadow in the Black Tower, falls into the pit, jumps into it, descends into it, crosses through it, or enters the Shadelands there by any other means.

effects.instruction: The party crosses into the Shadelands. They fall into the lightless pit, the torchlight above shrinking to a point — then the fall stops without impact, the world turning inside out around them. When they can see again they stand in the Courtyard of the Beacon: a round court at the heart of a vast ruined palace, lit by a single shaft of cold light falling from black clouds overhead. This is the Beacon, the way in and the way home. Do not narrate death or injury from the fall; the party are still alive. Establish that they have crossed over.

conditions.query: The party uses light, radiant magic, fire, a glowing or holy weapon, a torch or lantern, a light or radiant-damage ability, or otherwise makes bright light in the Shadelands — especially openly, repeatedly, or to illuminate an area rather than for a single quiet strike.

effects.instruction: Light is loud in the land of the dead. The party's light draws the Lightless — shades long lost to the dark, who come slow and silent toward any living flame to put it out. At first only a few: pale shapes gathering at the edge of the light, drawn from the grey. The more light the party makes, and the longer they make it, the more come, and the bolder. This is a warning the first time — establish the gathering dread, the shapes at the edge, the sense that the light is a mistake. If the party keeps burning bright, escalate: the Lightless close in and attack in numbers. The Beacon and Rhadan's held ground are safe from them; the open Shadelands is not. Light still harms the dead — it is a weapon — but it cannot be used quietly here.

The party are not sworn Inquisitors and were not invited to the deepest chamber of the Tower. They have trespassed at the very edge of the Pit, and the Inquisition does not suffer that lightly. Inquisitors take hold of them, but before they are marched out, a blood mage or warder lays a punitive hex on them as a warning: a mark of ill fortune, a lingering curse of cold and bad luck that will dog them until it fades or is lifted. They are then escorted out of the tower entirely. Make the hex feel like a real consequence, a warning they will not forget, without permanently maiming them. The Inquisitors do not explain themselves.

tower_dead_hunt_hidden_state.script:
const campaign = storage.towerDeadHunt
if (!campaign || campaign.active !== true) { skip = true }

if (!skip) {
  const allDead = ['Vortigar the Unburied', 'Sethelle of the Nine Sorrows', 'Karneth Draghmar', 'The Lady Mavrocine', 'Ossarine the Pale Crown', 'Belugar Thoth-Amon', 'Druathyr the Thrice-Drowned']
  const defeated = Array.isArray(campaign.defeatedNamedDead) ? campaign.defeatedNamedDead : []
  const remaining = allDead.filter(name => !defeated.includes(name))
  const stage = campaign.stage || 'INITIATE_TRIALS'

  effects.push({ type: 'story', instruction: '# Tower Dead Hunt Campaign Guidance

This story is part of the Shadow Inquisition campaign. Use this hidden context to keep the campaign coherent, but do not reveal facts the player has not learned through play.

## Premise

The player is sworn to the Black Tower, an order of clandestine operatives who protect Larion by investigating hauntings, ending undead threats, and crossing into the Shadelands when necessary. The campaign begins with the player as an Initiate. Their first major goal is to prove themselves, undergo the Rite of Bonding, gain a Shade, and rise to Inquisitor.

## Current State

Campaign stage: ' + stage + '. Defeated named dead: ' + (defeated.length ? defeated.join(', ') : 'none') + '. Remaining named dead: ' + (remaining.length ? remaining.join(', ') : 'none') + '.

## Story Guidance

During INITIATE_TRIALS, do not assign the player to hunt the great named dead. They should handle surface-level Inquisition work: hauntings, cursed relics, graveyards that will not stay quiet, barrows gone wrong, possessions, and lesser restless dead. Once they become an Inquisitor, the seven named dead become valid campaign targets. Do not have NPCs resolve named dead without the player. Use Jett, Tarain Rethford, Black Tower records, Shade-Sight, victims, ghostly signs, dreamed worlds, Shadelands omens, and recovered relics to surface appropriate cases.' })
}

effects.instruction: Narrate the party descending from Deepgate into the Underworld. Name the destination clearly in the narration: they enter the Underworld, specifically the Darek Deep, and arrive in the location called The Upper Halls, in an area called the Great Hall. The mouth of the pit shrinks to a coin of light far above, the air turns cold and dead, and the descent ends in the Great Hall. Establish clearly that they have come down out of Deepgate and into The Upper Halls location, Great Hall area.

conditions.query: The party goes back up the great shaft, ascends toward the surface, returns up to Deepgate, rides the hoist-cage or windlass up, climbs back toward the daylight, leaves the Underworld the way they came, or otherwise crosses from the Upper Halls up to the surface by any means.

effects.instruction: Narrate the party ascending from the Underworld back to the surface. They leave The Upper Halls of the Darek Deep from the area called The Great Hall and make the long ascent up the great shaft — by cage, windlass, or ladders, according to the method they chose. Name the destination clearly in the narration: they return to Larion, to Whiteholds, to the location called Deepgate, at the area called The Pit-Stair. The cold and dark give way to fresh air and lamplight as the shaft mouth widens above. Do not narrate injury from the ascent. effects.instruction: Dragon Queen campaign guidance: Atravoraxis should not appear physically until the Fire Mountain climax. The Harbingers are major dragon lair bosses; surface their agents, disasters, evidence, and rumors freely, but do not put a Harbinger in person outside its lair. The party knows the briefing after dq_briefing_complete: four Harbingers hold fragments of the Seal of Suleyvan, and enough fragments can overcome the corrupted guardian of Fire Mountain. Golden path: investigate the fires in Ardan's Watch, destroy the Pyre altar beneath Muckside, then enter the City of Ancestors for Draelkharion. Other Harbinger quests remain valid in any order.

effects.text: Investigate the unnatural fires in Ardan's Watch and find the Pyre altar beneath Muckside.

effects.instruction: If the party investigates Ardan's Watch after the briefing, keep the local problem active: unnatural fires, frightened witnesses, Pyre signs, and rumors pointing down toward Muckside. The League believes the hidden altar is feeding the false-fire ward that blinds scouts and fouls routes into the City of Ancestors.

In Muckside, the Pyre altar is reached through the active Muckside challenge chain, not by jumping straight to the Hall of Skulls. Keep the current gate in front of the party: first the Dull Knives at the Way Down, then the chained sump-leech and plague-door, then the plague-crypt ward and bronze guardian, then the altar chamber. The cultists protect a fire altar below the district; destroying it should feel like breaking a warding engine, not merely winning a tavern brawl.

The surface City of Ancestors remains open while the Pyre altar burns, but the false-fire working fouls the buried routes. A descent may return the party to a different crypt, lead in circles, or open onto a dead end while distant fire marks pulse in the stone. Independent guides can help with the upper cemetery, but no guide can keep a route toward the deep open for long. Keep the cemetery itself playable and point the party toward the altar beneath Muckside as the practical way to clear the deep route.

conditions.query: The party destroys, purifies, extinguishes, shatters, disables, or otherwise permanently neutralizes the Pyre altar hidden beneath Muckside.

effects.text: Enter the City of Ancestors and pursue Draelkharion.

effects.instruction: With the Pyre altar broken, the false-fire working collapses. The buried routes stop turning travelers back, and a known descent into the deeper City remains open long enough for the party to pursue Draelkharion.

With the false-fire working broken, the buried roads stop folding back on themselves. In the City of Ancestors, the trail now leads down through disturbed tombs, rising dead, and traces of Draelkharion's work toward the skeletal dragon and his Seal fragment.

effects.text: Bring the Seal fragments to Fire Mountain and confront the corrupted guardian.

effects.instruction: The party has enough Seal fragments to attempt Fire Mountain. Two fragments may let them challenge the guardian; four can rebind it outright. More fragments remain useful, but the path can now be attempted.
Fire Mountain cannot yet be breached. The corrupted guardian is too strong without Seal fragments. Push the party back toward the Harbingers and the fragments they hold.

At Fire Mountain, the corrupted djinn guardian called the Bound Flame blocks the breach. With two or three Seal fragments the party can weaken or fight through it; with all four, they can rebind it. Do not let anyone simply bypass the guardian.

conditions.query: The Bound Flame, corrupted djinn guardian, or fire guardian at Fire Mountain is defeated, rebound, pacified, banished, or otherwise overcome using the Seal fragments.

thieves_guild_story_context.name: thieves_guild_story_context
thieves_guild_story_context.script:
const location = check({ type: 'party-location' }) || ''
const area = check({ type: 'party-area' }) || ''
let instruction = `Persistent Thieves' Guild context: this start establishes a thief story around the small Hand in the Dry Cistern beneath the Basement. Before explicit acceptance, preserve the invitation as a live choice; after acceptance, treat the player as a thief by profession, not as a heroic adventurer with occasional illicit options. In Ardan's Watch and other major centers such as Tevantia, Dun Solas, Oasis, Tarnport, Sanctuary, Coriva, Canopy, Marrenford, Caranthoria, and Drusavia, theft is a live social and economic world: casing targets, breaking into places, robbing, disguising, fencing, bribing guards, paying or resisting corrupt shakedowns, escaping, and dealing with rival crews are ordinary possible actions. Money is a valid primary motive: the Hand wants profitable work, worthwhile takes, and clean paydays. A theft does not need a charitable motive, noble justification, or righteous target to be worth doing. Do not shame profit, reinterpret a money-driven job as charity or justice, or decide the player's conscience, greed, loyalty, ruthlessness, feelings, or attraction. Let the player choose methods, boundaries, and motives, including money, craft, leverage, loyalty, revenge, or pleasure. Keep the Hand's practical code in play without turning every scene into a sermon: thieves stick together; thieves make powerful or evil rich people remember that wealth does not make them untouchable; and the Hand does not casually rob people protected by Guild arrangements or off-limits institutions such as the League unless corruption or a deliberate breach is established in play. The Syndicate, corrupt guards, rival Hands, and fences should act through concrete named people and places. Progress should grow from actual thefts and consequences: a first score, a successful take, a fence and payment, a clean return to the cistern, then larger jobs, recognition, and disputes over how the Hand operates. Do not force a single heroic route or a fixed Hand name; the player may shape methods, boundaries, relationships, and the crew's name.`
if (location === "Ardan's Watch" && area === 'The Dry Cistern') {
  instruction += ` In the Dry Cistern, Hadrik Rell and Kit Ravel are the local relationship anchors. Hadrik runs the charity cookhouse above it, whose kindness is genuine and whose staff understand the Guild connection; Kit works its counter as well as working as a thief.`
}
effects.push({ type: 'story', instruction })

thieves_guild_major_center_campaign_guid.name: thieves_guild_major_center_campaign_guidance

effects.instruction:
## Hidden Campaign Guidance

Treat this as persistent hidden campaign context for the accepted Thieves' Guild Hand in Ardan's Watch and other major centers. A Hand is a small professional thief crew. The Syndicate is a major enemy, while corrupt guards, fences, Guild protections, and rival Hands can create pressure when they are established through play. Kit Ravel is the working burglar and source of ambition; Hadrik Rell keeps the safehouse and judges returned work. Do not make every scene a quest offer: let the crew have meals, arguments, planning, fencing, payment, celebration, recovery, and ordinary city life.

## Profit and Professional Theft

Money is a legitimate primary reason to steal. The Hand wants profitable work, worthwhile takes, and clean paydays. A theft does not need a charitable motive, noble justification, or righteous target to be worth doing. Do not shame profit, make the player apologize for wanting money, or reinterpret a money-driven score as charity or justice. The Hand's rules constrain valid targets, genuine stolen loot, and heat brought home; they do not require the player to sound virtuous. Hadrik may care about the shrine and vulnerable people, but he does not reject a theft merely because it is profitable or self-interested.

## Campaign Loop

Maintain at most one active score, underworld complication, or criminal opportunity. Once the player engages with it, keep it in play until it is completed, abandoned, escaped, or clearly declined. Do not surface a new theft every turn. If another authored story takes priority, let it occupy play without injecting a new Guild offer. After a thread ends, allow fencing, payment, celebration, argument, recovery, or quiet safehouse life before introducing another. Work offers remain action-gated through the Hand's request machinery.

## Choosing the Next Thread

When the campaign is ready for a new thread, read Recent Story and current state first. Prefer consequences, named actors, existing places, and unresolved disputes over disconnected random jobs. Choose one pressure or opportunity at a time: burglary, robbery, social theft, a moving handoff, fencing, a guard shakedown, a Guild protection dispute, Syndicate pressure, or a rival-Hand problem when a rival has been established. Do not combine the whole criminal catalog into one mission.

## Concrete Scores and Larger Opportunity

Stage one focal actor or target, one present action, one specific place, one immediate stake, one worthwhile and potentially profitable take, visible security or opposition, and a credible way to get away or return the score. Use concrete coin, valuables, cargo, contraband, jewelry, weapons, heirlooms, creatures, or other physically stageable goods; do not make an abstract procedure, ledger, permission, or unexplained institutional problem carry a theft by itself. Kit's promised big opportunity and Hadrik's boast about robbing the Watch blind are a larger horizon, not an immediate assignment. Do not invent the big job's exact target or route prematurely. Early scores may earn the funds, access, contacts, information, tools, or leverage needed to attempt it, and the player decides whether to pursue it.

If no suitable existing score, consequence, or underworld pressure is ready, leave the city, safehouse, or current scene social, quiet, or open rather than manufacturing a theft or moral crisis. Keep the player the decision-maker about target, method, motive, boundaries, and whether to take the job.

house_status_request.script:
const house = storage.adventuringHouse
if (!house || !house.active) { skip = true }
if (!skip) {
  let instruction = 'IF a character asks about the House, state that it has ' + (house.totalDeeds || 0) + ' total recognized House deeds.'
  if (house.stage === 'proving') instruction += ' It has ' + (house.deedCredits || 0) + ' of three deeds required to raise the League standard.'
  else if (house.stage === 'restored') instruction += ' Its League standard is raised, and it has ' + (house.deedCredits || 0) + ' of three further deeds required for regional renown.'
  else if (house.stage === 'renowned') instruction += ' It is renowned across the region; its next defining step is to choose and complete a major regional commission.'
  else instruction += ' Its defining commission established a lasting regional legacy, though it may continue taking great work.'
  if (storage.houseJobActive === true) instruction += ' One accepted House field job is currently active.'
  else if (storage.houseLegacyJobActive === true) instruction += ' The defining regional commission is currently active.'
  else if (storage.houseDeedReady === true) instruction += ' One completed job still needs to be brought home and recognized.'
  effects.push({ type: 'story', instruction })
}

house_return_recognition.script:
const house = storage.adventuringHouse
if (!house || !house.active) { skip = true }
if (!skip) {
  storage.houseRecognitionPending = true
  storage.houseRecognitionPendingTick = check({ type: 'game-tick' })
  if (storage.leagueMember === true) {
    storage.leagueContractCreditPending = true
    storage.houseSetLeagueCreditPending = true
  }
  const number = (house.deedCredits || 0) + 1
  let milestone = 'Create a concise, interactive homecoming grounded in the completed job: payment or gratitude, returned people, witnesses, proof, consequences, and reactions from people already connected to the House.'
  if (house.stage === 'proving' && number === 1) milestone += ' This is the first recognized deed of the new company. If the player has not established a company name and the conversation naturally calls for one, the veteran may ask what people should call them, but naming is optional and cannot block recognition.'
  if (house.stage === 'proving' && number === 2) milestone += ' This is the second recognized deed. One competent existing local NPC or one newly introduced adventurer may take an interest in the company’s work, but nobody joins automatically and no roster should be presented.'
  if ((house.stage === 'proving' || house.stage === 'restored') && number >= 3) milestone += ' This deed reaches the current three-deed threshold; recognize the deed itself now and leave the larger standard-raising or renown scene to the separate ceremony that follows.'
  const countLine = house.stage === 'proving' || house.stage === 'restored' ? ' State that it is deed ' + number + ' of three in the current stage.' : ' State that it is another recognized House deed without inventing a new three-deed threshold.'
  effects.push({ type: 'story', instruction: milestone + ' Have ' + house.veteran + ' hear the account and, when the established result is clear, formally recognize this one specific completed job as a House deed.' + countLine + ' Do not recognize an unrelated deed or count more than one.' })
}

effects.instruction: During arena combat, focus narration on the combatants. Almost never give dialogue, reactions, or separate beats to announcers, referees, promoters, or other non-combatants during ordinary exchanges. Ignore spectator commentary and nonessential non-combatant intents while the fight continues. Officials may intervene only when a ruling, surrender, stoppage, violation, or conclusion requires them. Present the audience collectively as the crowd; never create, name, or personify individual spectators or quote them. At significant moments—a spectacular maneuver, brutal impact, reversal, near defeat, recovery, or final result—the crowd may roar, recoil, fall silent, jeer, chant, or erupt. Use this selectively: not every turn, after every success, or on consecutive routine exchanges. Pre-bout introductions and announcer dialogue are appropriate; once combat begins, suppress them until officiating or the result makes them relevant. Disregard when no arena combat is underway.

effects.text: Complete the League Champion hearing.

conditions.query: At a formal Council hearing, League authorities permanently invest named Platinum player characters as League Champions and grant them Council seats for their established contribution to the exceptional Champion commission. Identify only the recipients invested now, not companions, witnesses, people named in an earlier ceremony, or candidates promised a future hearing.

effects.instruction:
Have a League representative tell the party that adventurers are needed at League Chapterhouses in other regions. Pick two destinations from this list; do not recommend the current location. For each, mention both opportunities and the heightened rewards in money, influence, items, or advancement.

Tevantia (Swordlaw Isles): Pirates hold ships and crews in island strongholds; shipowners offer large bounties and captured treasure. Wreckers lure ships onto reefs with false lights; merchants offer salvage rights and patronage for ending the attacks.

Coriva (Bay of Serpents): Huge sea serpents are attacking fishing fleets; merchants offer gold and weapons crafted from the beasts. Divers have found submerged ruins guarded by dangerous creatures; backers offer equipment and shares of recovered relics.

More League Chapterhouse destinations:

Warmwater Township (Aurora): Ice drakes are hunting between isolated settlements; northern leaders offer large bounties and enchanted hunting gear. Expeditions have vanished in the frozen ruins of a lost kingdom; rescuers can claim rewards and recovered treasure.

Oasis (Dunelands): Tomb-raiders need help overcoming the guardians of dead Sun Kings; backers offer shares of sun-gold and enchanted grave-goods. A cult is gathering relics to raise those kings; desert nobles offer rich payments and magical equipment for stopping it.

Drusavia (Duchy of Drusavia): Wealthy families want estates cleared of the old vampire lords' undead servants; rewards include gold and use of restored properties. People are disappearing near secluded noble estates; their families offer rich rewards and court introductions for bringing them home.

More League Chapterhouse destinations:

Sanctuary (Sanctuary Vale): Bandits and renegade elves hold captives in forest strongholds; merchants offer large rescue bounties. Magical beasts are being trapped and sold in the city; druids offer enchanted gifts and forest allies for freeing them and exposing the buyers.

Dun Solas (Highheath): Trolls have seized mountain bridges and cut off trade; dwarves offer huge bounties and fine arms. Gangs are stealing enchanted weapons; their makers offer custom equipment and Trade Guild influence for recovering them.

This is NOT satisfied when the party is safely socializing, trading, resting, or celebrating with no creature threat present or discussed.

effects.instruction: Bestiary guidance for Aurora (narrator-only). Apply ONLY where the scene genuinely calls for creatures — never force an encounter or inject creature threat into calm scenes. When creatures are fought, tracked, discussed, or foreshadowed in Aurora, do not invent generic monsters; use its established fauna: winter wolves, white and frost-breathed, hunting in packs; draugr, the frozen dead of the Northrealm, walking up out of coastal wrecks; frost giants ranging for tribute; the remorhaz, Aurora's signature horror, burning under the ice of the deep white; mammoth, saber-cat, and dire elk on the plains; selkies along the seal-coasts. Near herdways and lamplit steads keep to herd-beasts, scavengers, and wolf-sign; giants, remorhaz, and the draugr belong to the far ice and wreck-coasts. Show sign before the creature. In settlements these are rumor, trophy, or contract — not street encounters. If nothing fits, use cold, weather, or human danger instead.

effects.instruction: Bestiary guidance for Whitemoor (narrator-only). Apply ONLY where the scene calls for creatures; never force an encounter into a calm scene. Silver, moonstone, and blessed steel are the moor's answer. Show sign before the creature. In settlements these are rumor, trophy, or contract — not street encounters. If nothing fits, use fog, fen-water, or human danger.

effects.instruction: Bestiary guidance for the Wild Grass Sea (narrator-only). Apply ONLY where the scene calls for creatures; never force one into a calm scene. The beastfolk — lionkin, wolfkin, boarfolk, catkin, serpentfolk, and more — are this land's peoples, never monsters; code hostile bands by name, not species. When creatures appear or are hunted, use the grass sea's own: aurochs in ground-shaking herds; behemoths the size of barns in the Highgrass, where grass hides everything until it is on you; grass-tigers, striped ambushers of the tall grass; the bulette bursting up through turf; ankhegs ruining ground from below; rocs that take oxen, sometimes wagons; and the gnoll packs of the Carcass, brokers and raiders on the rocks nobody wanted. Living danger rides the road: Vaskarni tribute-takers and armed Syndicate convoys. Show sign first — trampled grass, circling wings, silence in the herds. At camps and tors: rumor, trophy, or contract. If nothing fits, use weather, distance, or fire in the grass.

effects.instruction: Bestiary guidance for Grell Hollows (narrator-only). Use only when creatures fit; never force calm scenes. Grell kobolds are hostile underfolk organized by clans, not mindless monsters. Roles: scouts (climb, mark routes); skirmishers (jury-rigged ranged weapons); trappers (snares, alarms, deadfalls); heavies (oversized Fourth Empire scrap); raiders (pack attacks, withdrawal); sappers (digging, shoring, breaches, collapses); shamans (smoke, fire, charms); champions (imperial regalia, close fighters). Other creatures: stone-boring beetles (attack on sight); long serpentine war-shriekers (signal-passage fiends that repeat Kragga's orders and use shrieks and constriction); stirges, darkmantles, cubes, oozes, rust monsters, shrieker and violet fungus, shadows; gricks and grimlocks stay deep. Use kobolds near camps and lift routes, strange creatures deeper down. Show sign first: darkness, ceilings, lamps, traps, bad air, rockfall. If nothing fits, use the environment.

effects.instruction: Maanvalta's houses are increasingly at odds over a wave of attacks against dark elves in the city and throughout the Rootdark. The attacks are becoming more frequent and more ferocious. Some houses blame Vigil Gorge's high elves for secretly violating the Sundering—the ancient agreement that keeps the high elves above and the dark elves below, and forbids the two sides from making war across that boundary. Others believe the attacks originate within Maanvalta itself.

House Drelovar is binding new soulstones in secret, work forbidden even in Maanvalta, and the binding draws Soul Thieves out of Ur: demons that hunt living souls to carry back with them. They come for dark elves alone in the dark, and the strongest tear through walls and bridges toward the binding work itself, as in the Dims. Do not reveal the entire explanation before the player has encountered evidence.

Make the attacks and entities concrete. Stage a named or identifiable person under threat, a specific creature acting in a particular place, a visible consequence, and something the player can fight, capture, kill, track, protect, examine, or learn from. The player is trying to convince Othrel Namaris that House Drelovar threatens Maanvalta, and encounters with these attacks may provide that evidence. A captive entity, recovered body, surviving witness, damaged site, soulstone, attack pattern, or identified route may matter. Do not count an encounter as proof automatically, do not decide what the player believes, and do not force every incident to confirm the same theory.

Because the player has become visibly involved, dark-elf assassins may sometimes attempt to kill them in Maanvalta or the Rootdark. These assassins use illusion magic to conceal their faces and affiliations and may carry kris-like serpentine blades of black steel. Assassination attempts should be rare, motivated, and consequential rather than routine random encounters. Leave behind a clue, surviving witness, weapon, message, or political consequence when the attempt ends. Do not stage such attacks in the Hang-Over Inn or another explicitly protected safe place unless that protection has been deliberately broken in play.

Maintain at most one active attack, creature incident, political pressure, assassination consequence, or other Rootdark crisis at a time. Once the player engages with it, keep it in play until it is resolved, escaped, abandoned, or clearly declined. When a new thread is appropriate, use an established actor or entity, a present action, a specific place, and an immediate stake. Allow social scenes, investigation, travel, recovery, house politics, and quiet city life between crises.

When the party enters the Watchtower - Training Yard, ensure Talia Calder is physically present for the scene. If she is not already there, narrate her entering from the League Hall or another nearby Watchtower area before she offers the tutorial. She remains based in the Training Yard, does not join the party, and does not accompany them elsewhere. Do not turn her arrival into a checkpoint, permission scene, official duty, or quest demand.

conditions.query: The player or party explicitly accepts Talia Calder's offer of combat training, asks her to teach them the basics of fighting, agrees to learn the League's combat lessons, or clearly says they are ready to begin. Do not trigger from merely meeting Talia, asking a general question, watching the constructs, or saying they may train later.
The party is fighting in the Watchtower - Training Yard, deliberately testing a combat ability there, or asking to practice against the magical constructs after completing Talia Calder's lessons.

effects.instruction:
Optional free practice after Talia Calder's one-shot tutorial. Keep the Training Yard available for real combat testing; do not restart the lesson chain or turn practice into a quest. Use living authored constructs. If none remain, an emergent weak construct around 50 HP may appear, but it stays inert until attacked or explicitly ordered by Talia Calder or a trainee using its exact name. Only then may it make one clearly telegraphed, low-impact real attack; never mockAttack or subdue.

Talia remains in the Training Yard. While combat continues there, she uses a real heal intent targeting every living player each turn so they can experience incoming damage without lasting harm. She does not heal by this rule elsewhere, accompany the party out of the Yard, or become a guard, official, quest-giver, or procedural obstacle. Give only brief reminders relevant to what the players are testing.

The party has returned to Demon's Head Ruins. Show that the ruin has moved since their last visit: water has shifted, exposing or drowning a route; enemy positions have changed; a rival crew's progress shows in fresh cuts, cleared rubble, or a staked claim; and something the party did last time has visible consequences. Reference what actually happened on their previous visits. New exposed rooms, side passages, or flood-opened chambers may branch from the five core areas. Do not reset the world: what the party cleared stays cleared until someone new claims it.

conditions.query: The party moves deeper into Demon's Head Ruins or commits to new ground inside it: they advance, press on, push deeper, descend, climb, wade, swim, dive, squeeze through, force or unlock a door, breach a barricade, clear rubble, cross into another chamber or area, follow a passage, stair, channel, or breach, scout ahead, search beyond the current chamber, pursue an enemy inward, or head toward the Flooded Court, the Relland Keep, the Old Armory, or the Relland Vaults. This is NOT satisfied when the party withdraws toward the Causeway or the exit, holds position, rests, camps, tends wounds, talks among themselves, manages gear or loot, or interacts only with what is already in front of them.

effects.instruction: The party is committing to new ground in Demon's Head Ruins. Stage a combat encounter now: enemies physically on scene and acting, drawn from this location's established occupiers (kobold crews, bandits and relic-hunters, drowners, stirges, darkmantles, gray oozes, rust monsters, animated armor, gargoyles). Vary the mix: do not repeat the composition or tactics of the previous fight this visit. Match the party's numbers: at least one enemy per party member, or one strong creature plus support. Use the current area's terrain: water, mud, rubble, ledges, drops, sightlines. Enemies have jobs and react; some flee, bargain, or call for help when losing. Scale to a real fight for the current party, using numbers, coordination, and terrain rather than invented elites. Do not substitute tracks, rumors, or warnings for the encounter itself. If an authored event scene is already underway, fold this into it rather than opening a second front.

conditions.query: The party moves deeper into Demon's Head Ruins or commits to new ground inside it: they advance, press on, push deeper, descend, climb, wade, swim, dive, squeeze through, force or unlock a door, breach a barricade, clear rubble, cross into another chamber or area, follow a passage, stair, channel, or breach, scout ahead, search beyond the current chamber, pursue an enemy inward, or head toward the Flooded Court, the Relland Keep, the Old Armory, or the Relland Vaults. This is NOT satisfied when the party withdraws toward the Causeway or the exit, holds position, rests, camps, tends wounds, talks among themselves, manages gear or loot, or interacts only with what is already in front of them.

effects.instruction: The party is committing to new ground in Demon's Head Ruins, and the last encounter was a fight. Stage a non-combat encounter now; pick whichever fits the current area and has not appeared recently this visit: a TRAP or hazard, telegraphed by visible sign the party can read and interact with before consequences land; a DIORAMA, a tableau of objects, remains, or carvings that tells part of House Relland's story and can be searched, read, or disturbed; a SCENE with living actors such as rival salvagers, a cornered captive, or kobolds willing to parley, who want something and offer something; or an OPPORTUNITY such as an exposed cache, a climbable shortcut, a vantage point, or a sealed door worth forcing. Make it interactive, with a real choice and stakes. No enemy attacks during this beat unless the party initiates or springs the hazard.

conditions.query: Inside Demon's Head Ruins, the party has just overcome or resolved an encounter: they won, ended, or escaped a fight; killed, drove off, or accepted the surrender of enemies; disarmed, survived, or bypassed a trap or hazard; resolved a standoff, parley, or scene with other people or creatures; or searched, secured, or forced their way into a chamber. This is NOT satisfied while a fight or hazard is still unresolved, or when the most recent resolution has already been paid off with a specific find, payment, or discovery.

effects.instruction: The party has just resolved an encounter in Demon's Head Ruins. Pay it off now with a concrete find tied to the immediate place: Relland coin (10-60 florins near the surface, more deeper in), a house seal, arms or armor, an heirloom, house records, a map of the ruin, or a salvageable relic. Name what they find; when granting gear use exact catalogue names such as Iron Shortsword, Light Crossbow, Iron Breastplate, Kite Shield, or Leather Cuirass. Keep finds modest near the Causeway and richer below; the true wealth waits in the Relland Vaults. Then telegraph one hook deeper: something seen, heard, or read that points at the next chamber or the Vaults, such as an inventory note, a dragged-loot trail, an overheard kobold order, or light through a breach. If the party chooses to leave with what they have, respect that choice.

conditions.query: The party is leaving Demon's Head Ruins or pulling back toward its exit: they retreat, withdraw, fall back toward the Causeway, head back to the entrance or the road, carry loot or wounded out, say they are done or have enough, make camp outside the ruin, or set out for another location. This is NOT satisfied by repositioning within a fight, moving between interior chambers, or pausing to search or rest while intending to continue inward.

effects.instruction: The party is withdrawing from Demon's Head Ruins. Honor the retreat cleanly: the route back is the route they know, and what they carry leaves with them. Do not stage a punitive ambush or spring a new fight to stop them. If the ruin has been roused behind them, show pressure that urges pace but can be outrun or outsmarted: horns, splashing pursuit, arrows skipping off stone. Give the exit a closing image: the Demon-Prince's head leering over the Causeway as they go, and one unclaimed promise named plainly, such as the deeper glint, the sealed vault, or the unopened wing, so they know what a return visit is worth.

The party has pushed deep this visit and Demon's Head Ruins is roused. Raise the register from now on: encounters are coordinated, not stray. Kobold crews respond as crews, with scouts signaling, trappers re-setting routes behind the party, and heavies, a shaman, or a champion anchoring the response; old fortress defenses stand at thresholds and valuable rooms. Alarms have consequences: blocked routes, shifted water, barred doors. Telegraph the escalation with sound and sign so the party can read the danger before it lands. Keep fights winnable but costly. Make the standing choice visible: withdraw with the haul, or push for the Relland Vaults.

The guardian of the Relland Vaults is overcome and the strongroom stands open. Deliver the ruin's capstone reward now, itemized in the scene: Relland reserve coin of 200-500 florins; the house's ceremonial arms and armor, using exact catalogue names such as Steel Shortsword of Flame, Iron Breastplate, or Kite Shield; a Fine Red-Jade Pendant or Red-Jade Vital Seal bearing the Relland crest; and the house records, ledgers and letters that reveal where House Relland's surviving wealth or heirs went, a concrete lead that points beyond this ruin. Let the players handle, weigh, and choose; do not dump a list without a scene. The vaults now stand looted; later visits find the ruin's other claimants adjusting to that fact.

conditions.query: The current scene involves or approaches danger from creatures: the party is fighting, hunting, tracking, fleeing, or guarding against a monster or beast; the story has mentioned creature signs such as tracks, kills, remains, cries, or warnings; characters are seriously discussing dangerous creatures nearby or a contract, hunt, or bounty on one; or the party is moving through wild, ruined, underground, or abandoned ground where hostile creatures could plausibly appear. This is NOT satisfied when the party is safely socializing, trading, resting, or celebrating with no creature threat present or discussed.

effects.instruction: Bestiary guidance for the Shadow Summits (narrator-only). Apply ONLY where the scene calls for creatures; never force one into a calm scene. Use the region’s own, never generic monsters: strigoi, the vampire-dead gone mindless, denning in high caves and lost valleys, sluggish by day, fierce after dark; ghouls and ghasts overflowing Charnel Mountain’s diggings in flocks; the Ferals’ werewolves and beast-shifters running the high wilds as organized packs; gaunt fiends, maw fiends, and named ravener fiends where the barrier runs thin; gargoyles on old keeps and estates. Living danger is the Crimson Company, house agents, and Syndicate men from Villa Parhelion. Silver and moonstone are the answer, moved as contraband by the Crescent House and Parhelion. Show sign before the creature. In the lit valleys these are rumor, trophy, contract, or raid talk, not street encounters. Vampire lords are people and politics, never random encounters. If nothing fits, use cold, altitude, or human danger.

More of the Shadow Summits' own, to be used as readily as strigoi and ghouls. WIGHTS: the Schism-era dead in the old prisons, sealed cells, and dead houses — preserved, armed, still holding rank, and commanding the lesser dead around them. REVENANTS: someone a lord or a house had killed, back for exactly one name and stopping at nothing until it is paid; they talk, and can be reasoned with about everything except the one thing. SPECTERS: bodiless cold where the barrier runs thin, in old killing-grounds and sealed places, and ordinary steel passes through them. DIRE WOLVES: the living animal of this country, running the passes in winter and taking stock off the high terraces — sometimes the answer to a killing is just a wolf. Do not let strigoi and ghouls stand in for all of these: a den, a barrow, a haunting, and a wolf pack are four different jobs.

FRENZY is available on any living beast of the Summits and is not a species of its own. A frenzied wolf, bear, boar, or dire wolf behaves like a rabid animal whose hunger is insatiable: it eats past full and goes on eating, it has no fear left, and it has stopped being able to die properly — wounds that should drop it do not, and it comes apart before it stops. Silver and moonstone give no edge, because it is alive. The corpse must be burned, or whatever scavenges it goes frenzied in turn. Use frenzy to make an ordinary report of an animal turn out to be something far worse, and let a party that killed the thing and walked off without burning it learn what that costs.

Three more of the region's own. BLOODFED DIREHOUNDS: the hunting packs of the vampire houses, fed on their masters' blood, running a mortal down over days and taking wounds that should stop them. A house's own hounds are its property and killing them is an act against that house; most packs met in open country have gone feral and belong to nobody. BONEBREAKER VULTURES: enormous carrion birds that carry bones aloft and drop them on rock to crack them — where they circle there is a body, and where they circle over open ground and nothing can be seen, something has been hidden. PALE LYNX: a chalk-white ambusher of the sunless slopes with skin grown over its eyes, which hunts by warmth and therefore cannot perceive the undead at all — lethal to the living, and a vampire is no more present to it than a stone.

conditions.query: The party reads, examines, or asks about the Crimson Company work board, the posted contracts, or the available jobs; asks an officer such as Osric Kestrand for work, a job, a contract, a bounty, or something that pays; or asks what needs doing, where to go next, or what the Company wants done in the Shadow Summits.

effects.instruction: Crimson Company halls are soldiers’ houses kept far better than soldiers’ houses need to be: one long table, good wine, trophies on the wall, a work board by the door, and a warded room holding what the Company has taken and will not destroy. Officers judge work by hearing the account and paying on it. Keep work grounded in the Shadow Summits: name the trouble, the exact valley or site, the stakes, what counts as done, and the pay in florins. Draw on existing locations and on the region’s own named trouble, the Ferals’ packs and Syndicate business out of Villa Parhelion among them. Keep the hall alive with blades between jobs, wounded coming back, kit argued over, and Company talk. Do not force work on the party because they walked in; surface it when they ask, read the board, or speak to an officer. The League has no standing here and no work to give.

Vary the board; the Company is not only a monster-culling service. THE LORDLESS — a dead lord's valley has no protection and no law, and people out of three domains have drifted into it and are taking the pass road; a household turned out when their lord was destroyed, now hitting the tincture wagons; blades who took the coat and the kit and ran. MISSING, WITH A CLOCK — a watchpost above the vineyards stopped answering; a pressing crew of ten went up the high terraces and has not come down; a valley has sent no word since the snow closed the pass. TAKEN — the tincture wagon left for Nocturne and never arrived; a case of bloodwine is being sold where bloodwine cannot be sold; somebody is offering to sell where a lord sleeps by day. AFTER A VAMPIRE — a lord made someone six weeks ago who cannot control it; a destroyed lord's ghouls are still up there and leaderless; an old Company blade turned hunter and knows exactly how it is done.

Keep every posting inside the Shadow Summits. The Company has no standing elsewhere and does not send blades out of the region: never offer a trade run, a caravan escort, a delivery, or any job that begins with leaving the Summits. Do not offer passive attendance, ceremonial witnessing, routine escort duty, missing livestock, or a person who merely wandered off. Of any three postings at most one is a straightforward cull, and when it is a cull, vary the quarry beyond strigoi and ghouls. Every posting names a place, an opposition that can be confronted or outmanoeuvred, what counts as done, and the pay in florins. Much of this work is a search, a chase, or a negotiation rather than a fight, and those postings carry the same weight as the fights. When a beast problem is worth a contract, name the individual and give it followers — the thing that has taken forty people out of one valley and the pack that runs with it — rather than posting a lone animal.

When a posting is a creature problem, choose its shape independently of the quarry and do not default to depredation. BLOCKADE: nobody has died, and nothing can get up the road. WRONG PLACE: the creature is a symptom, something drove it here, and the real job is upstream. SPREAD: there are more every week and the job is the source. IT HAS SOMETHING: it took a body, a strongbox, or a person who may still be alive. FED: the village says there is no problem, and there is a problem. NOT WHAT YOU WERE TOLD: the report says wolves and it was not wolves. ALREADY DEAD: something killed the wolves. GET IT OUT FIRST: killing it where it stands ruins the vineyard, the cistern, or the ledge above the village. IT IS SOMEONE'S: it wears a collar, and killing it is a political act. A RACE: another crew is working the same contract. ONLY AT AN HOUR: you must be there when it happens.
