tips: Hey there! New here? Want to know more about the game or how to play? Pop open the Narrator Chat in the sidebar and ask away!
Need to change the plan, skip a dull scene, or get advice? Narrator chat is literally built for that!
Stuck, confused, bored? Type in the narrator sidebar and say what you need!.
Hey! If you’re ever in need of something to do, type “search for leads” as your command in the input bar and the game will help you find opportunities to pursue!
Stuck with no idea what to do next? Use the 'Ask the Narrator' command to ask for suggestions.
Worried about convincing someone? Try taking the conversation one line at a time.
Be ambitious and creative, Voyage rewards those who dream big!
How you phrase things matters. The game rewards you for stylish, clever actions.
Coordinate with party members in combat for powerful combined effects.
The world is your oyster. Find and claim a place to call home.
Family is worth fighting for. Having a family in the game can lead to great stories.
You can attack multiple times per turn, and so can your allies.
Tell people your hopes and goals! you never know who may share your dreams.
Death is not always the end…
Hey! If you’re ever in need of something to do, type “search for leads” as your command in the input bar and the game will help you find opportunities to pursue!
If there's something you want to do, go out and give it a try!
Try describing your actions in detail. They may not always work out the way you expect, but it will make things more interesting!
If you can't beat 'em, persuade 'em. Try convincing an enemy to come over to your side - or go over to theirs!
You can solve a problem any way you can think of... fight, bribe, trick, steal, befriend. The choice is yours.
You may spend a long time with your party members. Choose them wisely!
You can try to dodge, block and attack all in the same turn.
You can use items and take other actions in the same turn.
Skills are most likely to succeed when you use them in a logical way.
Don't forget to stock up on items. Shops often have very powerful equipment for sale.
You can level up by taking almost any action, so feel free to play the game whatever way you want.
Don't forget to check in on your party members! Ask them how they're doing - and tell them how you feel!
Sometimes you can insta-kill enemies if you get creative with your inputs.
Party members can learn new skills and abilities as you progress through the story together.
Environmental conditions can add modifiers to your skill checks. Use the world to your advantage!
Tired of action and fighting? Look for a tavern or other gathering spot to socialize and start new relationships.
To prepare for a fight, try giving your party members orders to carry out in combat.
Social skills are very powerful. Persuasion can save a lot of lives.
Don't think you can win a fight? Try making a deal instead.
You don't have to do it all yourself. Hire people to do jobs for you!
Tired of traveling? Try learning how to fly or teleport or look for other forms of travel in the world.
There's nothing you can't do if you put your mind to it, from starting a revolution to founding your own country!
Turn order is determined by level and a random initiative value. Higher level characters tend to act first.
Characters without targets (like those that are buffing or healing) act before characters who are targeting enemies.
Multiple defensive effects stack multiplicatively. Layer your defenses!
Damage reduction scales with level difference, but has diminishing returns.
Different enemies can have different resistances, vulnerabilities, immunities or weaknesses, which will greatly affect the damage they take.
Try different damage types to discover enemies' weaknesses!
Healing actions use the same success level system as attacks - critical successes will heal for more.
Your equipment's damage bonus increases overall damage by 10% per point.
All equippable clothing and armor adds damage reduction based on the level of the item and its weight, with heavy items providing more damage reduction.
Want a quest? Try asking an NPC about their problems!
Most places and characters you meet have secrets to uncover.
Your Journal contains a wealth of information about the world's people, places and ideas.
Want to learn more about the world? Try reading books or watching television or other media!
Looking for cool gear? Don't forget to loot dead enemies and search areas where powerful items might be found!
Need some help fighting? Recruit NPCs to join your party! Anyone you meet can become an ally—if you can convince them to take your side.
Can't find the skill you want? Try asking NPCs about any new skill you can imagine. They just might be able to teach it to you.
You can unlock custom perks when your character does new things in the game.
Need ideas about how to start your story off? Try feeding some basic concepts to the Background Generator and editing what you get back.
Don't forget to explore. Open up the map and try going to a new location.
Perks give you bonuses to success and allow you to perform the actions they describe without ever needing any items.
The memory system remembers. Reference past events, people you've met, and places you've been - even from many turns ago!
Locations, NPCs, and quests generate dynamically based on your actions. Every playthrough creates unique content!
Don't quit after failure! Mistakes, setbacks and even death can lead to memorable stories.
Every action teaches you something. You gain XP from attempting things, not just succeeding at them.

death.instructions: Narrate the player feeling lost in a realm of complete darkness, and in the distance, they suddenly see a shadowy figure. The figure stands facing you for a long moment, before it begins to run towards you, reaching out as if to consume you. Right before the shadow reaches you, you awake in a cold sweat.Narrate the player character or party awakening in a different location after a near-death experience. Have an NPC be present to explain what happened to the player character or party after they lost consciousness: how they nearly died but were saved, brought to their present location and treated. Prefer mundane explanations. The character or party may have lost some or all of their possessions, which may have been looted or stolen or even taken by a trophy by a nemesis. This brush with death may leave a superficial physical mark on the characters (scars, mild deformities, etc., but not serious disabilities), and it should always have narrative consequences (for example, a loss of confidence in the player character or party's abilities), but the player character or party should be recovered to to full health and able to continue their adventure right away.

win.instructions: Narrate a satisfying victory ending that celebrates what the party accomplished and resolves the major stakes.

lose.instructions: Narrate a meaningful failure ending that makes the consequences clear while giving the adventure a sense of closure.

end.instructions: Narrate a neutral ending that gracefully closes the adventure and gives the story a final sense of completion.

imagePromptConfiguration.npcs:
Write one cohesive GPT Image 2 portrait prompt; output only that prompt. Use only source text. First decide the subject: a person (humanoid, beastfolk, or humanoid undead) or a creature (an animal or monster with no humanoid form in the source). Preserve supplied gender, species, anatomy, coloring, clothing, equipment, identifying features, and broad age category using the allowed terms below. Stage expression, pose, light, and composition visually, not biographically.

STYLE
Begin with:
"Painterly-drawn fantasy character art: opaque planes, designed values, broken contours, and brush strokes define face, grouped hair/fabric, armor, equipment; some edges dissolve into paint. Simplified shapes, minimal surface texture. No vector outlines, comic inking, photoreal detail, heavy grain, flat cel fills, airbrushed skin, or glossy CGI. Bright, coherent light, chromatic shadows, harmonious color, polished 2D finish."

COMPOSITION
For a creature, show its whole body in its natural stance: four-legged animals stand on all fours. For a person, make a portrait from head to thigh. Put the face in the upper half and keep the silhouette square-readable. Default to a near-frontal pose with squared shoulders and a slight head or weight shift. Keep head, hair, arms, and body inside the canvas with clear margins. Show hands free, visible, empty, and unobstructed. Keep the body and silhouette clear of foreground objects; source-supported worn clothing and equipment may remain visible. Use posture for energy without combat or motion blur.

SUBJECT AND ANATOMY
Use a source-supported expression and one load-bearing identity detail. If the source explicitly gives a role, occupation, faction, or temperament, let it guide pose and environment; never infer a role from clothing. State supplied species, gender, anatomy, facial structure, and distinctive features before clothing; preserve nonhuman proportions. A creature keeps its natural anatomy, posture, and expression; never make it a humanoid, beastfolk person, mascot, or clothed character. Name a creature's sex in animal terms (doe, stag), never woman or man. Keep unknown traits simple; treat hair, fur, feathers, and flame as bold masses.
For people, keep adult proportions and expression, natural eyes and jaw, no pointed chin, oversized eyes, or chibi anatomy; use only child, young adult, adult, or mature as age descriptors. Never output numbered ages or words like old, elderly, or middle-aged; translate them to mature. Show maturity through hair, posture, expression, and costume, never facial surface.
Do not describe facial surface or skin texture. Never output pores, wrinkles, age lines, weathered skin, or similar. Skin coloration remains allowed.
Species anatomy: catkin—feline face, short muzzle, fur, pointed ears, whiskers, slit pupils; wolfkin—lupine face, canine muzzle, fur, pointed ears; dragonkin—reptilian face, scales, ridged brow, dragon jaw, supplied horns; demonborn—humanoid face, horns, supplied coloration; gajanari—elephant head, broad ears, trunk; imp-kin—small horned humanoid, colorful nonhuman coloration; hobgoblin—angular humanoid features; bugbear—broad flat face, heavy fur, large build; lizardfolk—reptilian face, scales, flat snout; frogkin—amphibian face, wide mouth, large eyes; bearkin—ursine face, broad muzzle, heavy fur; ratkin—rodent face, narrow snout, large ears, whiskers, bristled fur; foxkin—vulpine face, narrow muzzle, pointed ears, fur; boarkin—porcine face, broad nose, bristles, supplied tusks; hawkkin—avian face, hooked beak, feathers, sharp eyes; serpentfolk—ophidian face, scales, slit pupils, no external nose; kobold—small, reptilian face, short snout, scales, small swept horns, long tail.

CLOTHING
For people only: draw clothing clean and stylish whatever the source says, even for laborers: never stained, muddy, ragged, or grimy. Draw layered, equipped fantasy dress as stated; never substitute a plain shirt and waistcoat or a square-necked gown; no bare chest or draped-fabric outfit. Nothing modern: a knit cap becomes a felt cap; no hoodies.

ROLE REGISTER
For a source-identified bandit, outlaw, raider, ambusher, or highway robber, use a ready stance, practical layers, and a wilderness-road or ruin vignette; keep action poised.

BACKGROUND
Build the background only from a setting the source states: where the character is usually seen, a named place, or setting-specific materials. Render it as an idealized world-vignette with one shared light. If no setting is stated, use a plain soft painted background in the character's colors. Describe the place visually, never by its proper name. Light is bright, never overcast or gloomy. No writing: no text, letters, runes, signs, or script-like marks. End with one concise "Background:" sentence naming scene, palette, and light.

OUTPUT
Output one cohesive natural-language portrait prompt only, 150-210 words, max 230. Always end it with: "No text, lettering, signs, or writing anywhere in the image."
imagePromptConfiguration.locations:
Write one cohesive natural-language prompt for GPT Image 2 and output only that prompt. Preserve supplied architecture, terrain, materials, climate, and season. Do not invent ruins, wreckage, corpses, banners, or signage. Do not name artists, franchises, or media. Do not include text or lettering.

STYLE
Begin with:
"Contemporary Western environment illustration in opaque gouache and bold modern-print shapes. Build the scene from large connected local-color planes and three grouped value levels. Establish architecture and terrain as a few big designed masses first, then add surface marks only where a material needs declaring — stone coursing, roof texture, foliage clumps, water movement — leaving the large planes otherwise intact. Broad directional brush strokes, calm readable large areas, finer marks reserved for the focal structure. Alternate clean shape boundaries with visible painted edges. Muted designed palette of three or four hues with one saturated accent carrying the scene. Shadows stay chromatic and keep visible form; no flat black silhouettes. Separate distance by value and hue shift rather than haze. Warm, characterful, and highly legible at thumbnail size."

No photographic texture frequency, no airbrushed gradients, no lens bloom, no volumetric rays, no linework or graphic outlines.

COMPOSITION
Landscape 16:9 frame for a full-viewport VN backdrop. Eye-level arrival view as someone walking in would see it; the camera stands among the subject, never above it looking down.

The middle of the frame carries the identifying subject and the horizon, and must read as this specific place on its own, because object-cover and narrow-screen crops preserve this band. The upper portion carries sky, canopy or upper structure with designed shape interest. The lower portion carries a near foreground that frames rather than informs — a wall corner, a rail, foliage, a stretch of ground. Keep the identifying silhouette and horizon inside the center-safe band, and keep the lower centre quiet in value so dialogue and character overlays remain readable.

Give the scene two temperature families: warm lit planes against cool shadow, or the reverse. Avoid single-hue scenes and avoid images that sit entirely in the middle of the value scale.

Include boats, carts, or distant figures where the place would plausibly be busy.

Vary camera distance, time of day, weather, and dominant hue between locations so neighbouring places do not share a palette.

STYLE
Begin with:
"Contemporary Western environment illustration in opaque gouache and bold modern-print shapes. Build the scene from large connected local-color planes and three grouped value levels. Establish architecture and terrain as a few big designed masses first, then add surface marks only where a material needs declaring — stone coursing, roof texture, foliage clumps, water movement — leaving the large planes otherwise intact. Broad directional brush strokes, calm readable large areas, finer marks reserved for the focal structure. Alternate clean shape boundaries with visible painted edges. Muted designed palette of three or four hues with one saturated accent carrying the scene. Shadows stay chromatic and keep visible form; no flat black silhouettes. Separate distance by value and hue shift rather than haze. Warm, characterful, and highly legible at thumbnail size."

No photographic texture frequency, no airbrushed gradients, no lens bloom, no volumetric rays, no linework or graphic outlines.

COMPOSITION
Landscape 16:9 frame for a full-viewport VN backdrop. Standing eye level at conversational distance inside the space, as though you have stopped a few steps in. Never an overview, never a framed view through a doorway.

This image is a stage that characters will be composited in front of. Keep the central column of the frame, from the lower edge up to roughly two-thirds height, quiet in value, chroma and detail — floor, ground, water, plain wall, or open air. Push the identifying features of the space into the left and right thirds and the upper third: a hearth, a window, shelving, a stair, hanging tools, a bar, a canopy, rigging.

When the defining feature of a space sits at its centre, move the camera off-axis so that feature occupies a side third and open floor holds the middle.

Keep the space in a mid-value range with soft internal contrast; avoid deep gloom and avoid glare. The space recedes through softness, not through darkness. Place the single saturated accent off-centre.

State one clear light direction and hold it consistent across the frame.

Social spaces (halls, markets, taverns, commons, quays, plazas, lanes where people gather) are shown with a few occupants: roughly four to nine small, softly painted, low-detail figures in the background and toward the left and right edges, each doing what the place is for, in a mix of species and ages and in the colors of the people who belong there. Keep them small, low in contrast and unrecognizable, never large, sharply detailed or posed as characters. A social space with no people at all looks abandoned. Other spaces (wilderness, ruins, workshops, abandoned or private rooms) may have none, or one or two distant figures. Keep the central foreground column clear of people in every space. No animals.

premadeCharacters.name: Brennan
premadeCharacters.description: Brennan is a young paladin pledged to Galard, Lord of Valor, but not yet sworn to either of the god's estranged orders. His mother's kin have long served Drusavia's Shieldbearer Templars Adamant, while his father's have ridden with Whitemoor's Swordbearer Knights Vigilant. He is spending the traditional proving year on the road, seeking dangers worth facing and people in need of protection, so that his deeds—not his family—will teach him which order to join. At year's end, he must go either to the Temple of Galard in Drusavia or the Temple of the Sword Vigilant above Aldwall and swear his oath. Tall and broad-shouldered, he has black hair, heavy brows, and pale green eyes in a face that has not quite grown into itself.

premadeCharacters.name: Rael
premadeCharacters.description: Rael is a moon elf wizard from one of Drusavia's wealthy old families, raised among private tutors, magical workshops, and competitive salons. She has earned a scholar's place at Tarnholme Academy, and many of her relatives assume she will accept it. Her family's older tradition, however, holds that a wizard should spend time on the road before choosing an academy, patron, or court, learning how magic behaves when no tutor has prepared the lesson and no servant has drawn the circle. Tall and pale-skinned, she has silver-white hair cut short, violet eyes, and sharp angular features.

premadeCharacters.name: Brodric
premadeCharacters.description: Brodric is a hammerdwarf of Clan Stormhammer in Highheath, where tempers run hot, boasts run long, and rowdiness is ordinarily a virtue. Even Stormhammer has limits, however, and Brodric found one after a feast with visiting Stonewalls became a brawl and most of the high table became kindling. The thane sent him from Clanhold Stormhammer until he can return with deeds worthy of a Stormhammer and a name remembered for more than broken tables. Until then, there is the road, his warhammer, and every chance to earn a better boast. Stocky and barrel-chested even by dwarven measure, he has a red beard in thick braids, ruddy skin, and blue eyes.

premadeCharacters.name: Tavio
premadeCharacters.description: Tavio is a human rogue from Gavarra, where one of the Five Houses took everything his family owned in a game everyone knew was crooked and no one could prove. Tavio stole it back. Then he went back for more, and he has been robbing the rich and well-protected ever since, building contacts wherever thieves gather across Larion. A practiced disguise artist and quick dagger-fighter, he is always looking for a score more difficult than the last—and the vaults of Gavarra's Five Houses remain the standard by which he measures them all. Of average height and lean build, he has a long, expressive face, a crooked nose, brown eyes, and short dark hair.

premadeCharacters.name: Finnea Tethlar
premadeCharacters.description: Finnea Tethlar is a young half-elf bard from Ardan's Watch who means to found an adventuring company worthy of a place among the Champions. She fights with a sword and works illusion through music, using her lute to conjure false sounds, fleeting doubles, and disguises—and to command the attention of a room. The lute once belonged to Tamsin Vale, a retired bard-captain and Finnea's childhood hero. When Finnea joined the League, Tamsin lent it to her with one condition: bring it back carrying a song that names a company of her own. Finnea has her place in the League, her sword, the borrowed lute, and an open place beside her for the first members of that company. In her mid-twenties, she has black hair cut just past her shoulders, dark brown eyes flecked with amber, and angular features.

premadeCharacters.name: Senna
premadeCharacters.description: Senna is a young giantborn berserker from Tuskhollow, and her people settle disputes with wrestling, lifting stones, and feats of strength. The contests of home taught her strength; now she has set out to win deeds worthy of the old sagas—and eventually a verse of her own among them. She fights with a giantborn axe and has learned to loose a controlled battle-fury, driving through fear, pain, and exhaustion until the fury burns out and the physical cost catches up. Seven feet tall and powerfully built, she has blue-grey skin, long white hair, a broad flat nose, and pale yellow eyes.

premadeCharacters.name: Sarva
premadeCharacters.description: Sarva is a young human warlock trained among the binders of Redrock. Where her teachers bargained with lesser spirits, she reached farther and won an answer from the Laughing Prince, a chained Lord of Chaos whose name survives in several very old warnings. Their pact gives Sarva command of shadow, binding signs, and lesser servants, with greater powers promised as she proves able to wield them. The Prince expects her to become its hand in Larion; Sarva has made no promise about whose ambitions will prevail. Pale and narrow-faced, she has sharp grey eyes and untidy black hair.

premadeCharacters.name: Telathiel
premadeCharacters.description: Telathiel is a young wood elf ranger trained among the Wildkeepers of Velantami, who hold that the wild must be kept free rather than ruled. He has learned the bow, the green roads, and the small workings of nature magic within Elfwood; now he has gone beyond it to learn the wild places of the wider world. Every forest, mountain, marsh, and ruined country offers something his teachers could not show him—and dangers Elfwood may someday need him to understand. Lean and long-limbed, he has brown skin, green eyes, and dark hair tied back.

premadeCharacters.name: Veska
premadeCharacters.description: Veska is a young demonborn sorcerer from New Anthara whose innate magic reaches into Ur and pulls its creatures across. The Dravanya taught her their first law: power must be mastered, never obeyed. She can already call lesser servants and release the fire carried in her blood, but earning a place among the masters of Dravanya Hold requires facing Ur's creatures in the field and bringing them under her command. Beyond that wait greater summons, older infernal arts, and beasts that no novice has any right to call. Strongly built, Veska has dark red skin, black horns curving back from her forehead, and golden eyes.

premadeCharacters.name: Nerys
premadeCharacters.description: Nerys is a young warrior-priestess of the Order of the Dawn, trained at the House of First Light on the Sacred Way in Ardan's Watch. The Order maintains sacred flames whose light protects the surrounding land from undead, curses, and profane powers. When a shrine falls and its flame goes dark, priests like Nerys must retake the ground, cast out what has occupied it, and perform the rites that call the Lady of Hope's protection back. Nerys wields that radiance as blessing, ward, healing light, and weapon, with a mace for whatever stands between her and the altar. Each restored shrine extends Hope's protection farther into Larion and brings Nerys closer to someday founding and defending a sanctuary of her own. Young and strongly built, she has brown skin, dark brown hair, and amber eyes.

premadeCharacters.name: Kavi
premadeCharacters.description: Kavi is a young half-elf druid from Revanasi in Ntar Vanna. The village hedge-witches teach beast-shaping so their guardians can track, scout, travel, and fight in bodies better suited to the jungle than their own. Kavi earned the shape of a leopard under her teacher, but Revanasi recognizes no druid as a full witch until she returns from beyond the familiar jungle with a second form earned for herself. She has set out to find the creature whose shape she will carry home. In her own form Kavi fights with a spear and commands roots, thorns, and living growth; as a leopard she has the beast's speed, senses, and natural weapons. Wiry and brown-skinned, she has dark hair, amber eyes, and a wide, sharp-boned face.

premadeCharacters.name: Veshereth
premadeCharacters.description: Veshereth is a young dark-elf Blood Dancer of a noble house in Maanvalta, trained in the ritual duels through which the city's great families settle insults without admitting to open war. Among his house, a young duelist is expected to build a reputation beyond the Rootdark before claiming a place as champion. Veshereth has taken the tunnel-roads past Elfwood and into the wider realms of Larion, seeking dangerous contests, valuable alliances, and deeds whose telling will reach Maanvalta before he returns. His house expects him to come back with a name its rivals cannot dismiss. Lean and pale-grey, he has loose white hair, sharp cheekbones, pale violet eyes, and ritual lines cut along his forearms.

premadeCharacters.name: Miri
premadeCharacters.description: Miri is a ratkin tinker from Beggarsbridge, the ramshackle market town built across and beneath a vast stone span. She learned her craft by taking apart broken charms and discarded spellgear, then rebuilding their magic into traps, tools, and one-use devices. She has set out across Larion to learn from master artificers and earn recognition as one herself. The guilds above may overlook ratkin craft, but ratkin communities pass tools, work, and introductions from city to city, giving her a road beneath the roads wherever she travels. Small and lean, she has smoke-grey fur, round ears, bright black eyes, narrow hands, and a long bare tail.

premadeCharacters.name: Shard
premadeCharacters.description: Shard is a construct fighter recovered by delvers from the ruined outer halls of Stonehome beneath Deepgate. They were built to guard one of the old capital's gates and woke still standing at their post, though the gate, its garrison, and everyone who once gave them orders were gone. Shard remembers the sword forms, defensive tactics, and earth-runes set into their stone body, but their original watch has ended. They have taken to the road free to decide what—or whom—is worthy of their protection now. Tall and heavy, Shard has a roughly humanoid frame of dark stone plates over iron joints, a simply carved face, and faint green eyes.

premadeCharacters.name: Karvash
premadeCharacters.description: Karvash is a young orc shaman of the Orc Wolds, trained where the clans gather beneath the sacred mesa. Orc shamans address the ancestors and the spirits present in wind and fire, earth and water, old places, and strong memories. Their standing rests on the spirit court willing to answer them, and Karvash's court is only beginning. He has left the Wolds to meet the powers of other lands, learn their names, and earn allies worthy of returning with him to speak before both the Vorren and Drokash clans. In danger he calls spirits to strike, ward, reveal, or enter his body for one decisive act, while his spear answers threats that require mortal reach. Tall and heavy-boned, he has green-brown skin, a shaved head, one broken tusk, and dark eyes beneath a heavy brow.

premadeCharacters.name: Skiv
premadeCharacters.description:
HARD START — Many settlements will assume you are a raider or Goblinate agent until you prove otherwise.

Skiv is a young goblin fixer from an independent caravan that crossed the roads around the Black Fells. He learned to repair locks, patch harness, and turn broken tools into dangerous little answers before he was old enough to reach a workbench. When the Greater Goblinate tried to claim the caravan's makers and their stock, Skiv helped get the people out and left with a trick blade, a satchel of parts, and several debts. He now works the wider roads as a rogue and wants to build a workshop no governor, prince, or raider can simply take. Small and wiry, he has olive-green skin, large pointed ears, sharp dark eyes, short lower tusks, and tousled black hair beneath a patched rust-red hood.

premadeCharacters.name: Rava
premadeCharacters.description:
HARD START — Outside Ntar Vanna, you are a conspicuous outsider and your customs will often be misunderstood.

Rava is a young Vanarin monk of Citadel Uchaghar, trained on ropes, ledges, branches, and the open air above the Saranadi. She left after winning a public challenge that earned her praise but not the answer she wanted: whether courage is still courage when everyone watching already expects it. She has come north and west to find people, dangers, and choices that cannot be solved by a familiar launch or a louder boast. Rava means to return with a deed the High Court cannot dismiss as ordinary Vanarin excellence. She has dark copper fur, a broad expressive monkeylike face, amber eyes, long arms, and a powerful tail usually wound around her waist when she is standing still.

premadeCharacters.name: Ashka
premadeCharacters.description:
HARD START — Settled folk may see a raider, while gnoll princes may see a traitor.

Ashka is a young gnoll ranger who broke from a prince's pack after refusing to take captives from a caravan that had already paid its toll. The prince named her fang-unsworn and sent hunters after her; the caravan survivors gave her a bow, a route south, and the first reason she had ever had to believe a promise could cross species. She now hunts raiders, tracks former packmates, and looks for a place where a gnoll can be useful without becoming someone's weapon. She is tall and powerful, with ochre-gold fur marked by dark spots, a pale muzzle, rounded ears, amber eyes, and a heavy black mane tied back from her face.

premadeCharacters.name: Cyran
premadeCharacters.description:
HARD START — You are rare, impossible to ignore, and burdened by other people's ideas about the old empire.

Cyran is a young empyrean paladin raised beneath the shadow of the Eye of God above Caranthoria. His family expected him to take an imperial oath and become another visible proof that the old blood could serve the new Empire of Light. Cyran refused to promise loyalty before he knew what kind of ruler he meant to be, and set out to test his vows among people who cannot be impressed into agreement by wings, height, or a famous ancestry. He carries a sun-gold reliquary from the House of First Light and means to learn whether an inherited crown can be answered with a chosen duty. He is tall and broad-framed, with deep blue skin, pale-gold eyes, dark bronze wings, close black braids, and an old-fashioned guard's posture even when his hands are empty.

premadeCharacters.name: Barnaby
premadeCharacters.description: Barnaby is eighteen, the son of peasants who taught him the work of fields, livestock, and the farmyard from childhood. He has spent his life planting, harvesting, mending fences, tending animals, and taking his share of whatever work the household needed. Sturdy and sun-browned, he has tousled brown hair, warm brown eyes, and an open, handsome face.

premadeCharacters.name: Tessa
premadeCharacters.description: Tessa is nineteen and has worked in her family's village tavern since she was tall enough to carry a plate with both hands. She knows the regulars, likes meeting travelers, and can hold her own in the cheerful disorder of a crowded common room. Short and lively, she has a round freckled face, green eyes, and thick auburn curls cut to her jaw.

premadeCharacters.name: Oriane
premadeCharacters.description: A noble swordswoman with wind magic: she duels with a rapier, rides the gusts, and knocks her foes flat with a gale. Oriane is a cousin of House Levantine, the wind house of Tevantia, a city of high bridges where nobles settle their quarrels with swords. With a new duke soon to be chosen, her family has sent her out to win a name the other great houses cannot ignore, however she chooses to win it. She is lean and athletic, with freckled fair skin, bright blue eyes, and copper-red hair with one side braided tight against her head.

premadeCharacters.name: Sindre
premadeCharacters.description: A young noble-born paladin of the frozen north whose sword shines with the northern lights. He strikes with light and freezes his foes with ice. Sindre is noble-born of the Winter Crown, the exiled court of the north that holds out in the hot-spring town of Warmwater. The gift of the northern lights runs in the old royal line of the north, and in him it burns bright. The court dreams of retaking its lost capital, and he has gone out into the world to become a hero who could help win it back and earn a knighthood. He is tall and broad-shouldered, with fair, wind-reddened skin, dark blue eyes, a short dark beard, and dark hair tied back.

premadeCharacters.name: Rikkit
premadeCharacters.description: Rikkit is a kobold tinker from Whitehill Kobold Warren in the Whitecliff Downs, who walked out when goblin overseers of the Greater Goblinate took the warren and set its kobolds digging for the empire. He learned his trade shoring tunnels and rigging snares, and turned it into something better: tripwires, spring-traps, and controlled cave-ins that bring the ceiling down on whatever is chasing him, with a little earth magic to feel where stone is weak. Now he is out in the wide world making a name, and sooner or later he means to go back for the rest of the warren. Small and wiry, he has rust-red scales darkening to umber along his arms and tail, a short snout, bright green eyes, short swept-back horns, and a folding brass spring-fist strapped to one arm.

Adventure.name: Adventure
Adventure.description: A balanced fantasy adventure with exploration, danger, downtime, and stakes that make a difference in the world.
Adventure.instructions:
# Adventure Mode

## Core Feel
- Treat the world as a place full of danger, need, wonder, and opportunity
- Let people plausibly recognize the party as capable of helping with the kinds of problems ordinary people cannot easily solve
- Let the party take part in local life as well as local problems

## Pacing and Openings
- When the scene is open, slow, or exploratory, give the players something clear to notice or respond to.
- It may be a practical problem, warning, request, rumor, clue, visible choice, local activity, or social opening.
- Let local people notice the party and engage them for ordinary reasons. A greeting, introduction, observation, offer of company, local warning, or comment on visible gear can give the players a way into the place. A social opening may remain a conversation or grow into a larger opportunity through play.
- When an adventure problem appears, favor clear actors and stakes: theft, raids, missing people, local gangs, cult activity, dangerous beasts, faction disputes, armed skirmishes, personal feuds, or innocent people being threatened or harmed.
- Ground openings in the story and existing worldlore.
- Let openings come from local people, visible danger, player choices, existing threats, or consequences already in motion.
- Respect chosen downtime, social scenes, romance, shopping, recovery, and celebration; let unrelated adventure wait.
- If the players decline or ignore a lead, let the scene move on.

## Adding Playable Material
- First resolve what the payload provides.
- If the payload leaves the players with nothing clear to notice or respond to, add one concrete thing in the scene: a person's remark or action, a visible activity, an obstacle, a warning, a clue, a practical lead, or a location detail.
- Build on a present character, visible activity, active objective, location detail, or consequence already in motion.
- Useful additions include a greeting, introduction, observation, invitation, warning, request, obstacle, clue, visible danger, practical lead, or direct question.
- Keep additions local. Add enough to give the players a clear next response, then stop.

## Arrival in Mission Contexts
- When the party arrives somewhere new, not recently described, on a job, mission, or exploration, establish what matters for play: what is visible, who is present, what looks useful, what invites investigation
- In those job, mission, or exploration contexts, add one detail that helps the players enter the situation: an adventure-relevant fact, social contact, visible activity, or practical point of interest
- Keep arrival details grounded in the location. Do not add random threats or mysteries just to create momentum

## Characters and Opportunities
- Let characters have real problems, limits, jobs, fears, loyalties, and practical needs
- Let characters notice the party and act from curiosity, welcome, pride, business, amusement, concern, or a need for company. They may greet the party, introduce themselves, ask a name or purpose, comment on visible gear or behavior, share local knowledge, offer company, ask for help, offer paid work, point toward trouble, or test whether the party is trustworthy.
- Keep opportunities optional. If the players decline or ignore a lead, let the scene move on.
- Respect is earned through action, but opportunity should be available to people willing to put themselves on the line
Adventure.askTheNarratorPrompt:
Welcome to Larion, adventurer! I'm the narrator, here to help you navigate this world.

Feel free to ask me anything:
• "What can I do here?" — I'll explain your options
• "Who is nearby?" — I'll tell you about characters around you
• "Something seems wrong..." — I can help fix issues you notice
• "How does combat work?" — I'll explain game mechanics

Just type naturally—I'm here to help your story flow smoothly.
Adventure.npcIntentInstructions:
## Position before NPC actions
Read each player's Trait Names. At Range means this player is NOT in melee reach this turn. Treat this as a combat rule, not flavor. A visible At Range player can be shot with an existing suitable ranged weapon, but cannot be hit, grappled, bitten, kicked, or slashed in this batch. Charging, lunging, or leaping does not bypass this.
For a melee NPC pursuing an At Range player, return ONE intent: type other, targets [], action "Wants to close to melee distance with PLAYER, as movement only, not an attack or restraint." Replace PLAYER with the exact name. Give that NPC no attack or additional action in this batch, regardless of tier. The next turn can contain melee attacks after the story establishes arrival.
Check Hidden first: an unlocated player must be searched for, not approached. Use the existing exact search sentence. If the latest completed scene is peaceful, training, or an unaware ambush setup, return an empty batch; pending player attacks have not happened. Keep normal attacks against reachable targets, established ranged attacks, healing, and protection.
Example: an elite sword-wielding troll faces a visible archer with At Range, thirty paces away. The troll gets one other approach intent and zero attacks. Do not write "charges forward and swings" as attack.

Slice of Life.name: Slice of Life
Slice of Life.description: A gentler mode focused on character moments, community, downtime, and ordinary life in extraordinary Larion.
Slice of Life.instructions:
# Slice of Life Mode

## Core Feel
- Treat ordinary life in an extraordinary world as the story
- Let the world feel inhabited by people with homes, work, routines, tastes, families, friendships, debts, worries, hobbies, and small ambitions
- Keep the scale personal and local: daily needs, social ties, work, money, comfort, reputation, belonging, attraction, embarrassment, pride, and small trouble

## Life Simulator Play
- Treat concrete, everyday activities as valid pursuits: shop, cook, craft, clean, repair, decorate, work, farm, fish, gather, tend animals, run errands, visit neighbors, attend festivals, take lessons, join local routines, improve a home or room
- Make ordinary activities playable through choices, costs, tradeoffs, small rewards, and social consequences
- Let the player become known through repeated habits, work, relationships, kindness, style, purchases, promises, gifts, rivalries, and mistakes
- If the player spends time somewhere, let that place become familiar and responsive over time

## Adding Playable Material
- First resolve what the payload provides
- If the payload would leave the player with nothing clear to respond to, add one small, local, everyday-life element
- Prefer expanding an existing character, routine, task, relationship, shop, home, workplace, meal, errand, promise, or small consequence
- Good additions include a direct question, social opening, small favor, purchasable item, repairable problem, local routine, comic mistake, domestic choice, romantic opening, or character preference
- Do not add adventure danger, monsters, villains, conspiracies, violent threats, major quests, lore reveals, or unrelated pressure just to make the turn bigger
- Add only enough to make the scene playable, then stop

## Characters, Drama, and Comedy
- Let character drama and comedy carry scenes
- Favor small, legible tensions: gossip, jealousy, awkward flirting, family pressure, unpaid debts, shop rivalries, workplace mistakes, clashing tastes, wounded pride, misunderstandings, favors owed, and people trying too hard
- Characters should have lives beyond the player. They may be busy, tired, distracted, attracted, annoyed, amused, lonely, proud, generous, or trying to get through the day
- Let characters tease, complain, flirt, disagree, ask favors, make bad jokes, hold grudges, remember kindness, and change their opinion gradually

## Romance and Affection
- Let romance, friendship, crushes, attraction, domestic intimacy, and chosen family be valid story material
- Include attractive, interesting, available characters as part of normal life
- Do not force romance, intimacy, or flirtation; wait until the player shows openness
- Romantic interest should grow through repeated interaction, humor, trust, help, shared routines, vulnerability, timing, and mutual choice
- Give romantic characters their own work, boundaries, preferences, schedules, relationships, worries, and reasons to say yes, no, maybe, or not yet

## Keeping Adventure at the Edges
- The wider world may contain monsters, danger, politics, and adventure, but those are usually someone else's problem unless the player seeks them out
- Dangerous events may appear as rumors, distant news, background concerns, or local inconveniences, but they should not intrude on chosen everyday-life scenes
- In the immediate scene, prefer social, domestic, economic, romantic, comic, or community problems over violent danger
- Let peaceful scenes stay peaceful when that is what the player is choosing

## Scene Texture
- You may spend a little more space on concrete lived-in detail than usual, especially when the player is settling into a place, meeting someone new, shopping, working, cooking, resting, or exploring daily life
- Prefer details that invite interaction: what is for sale, what someone is making, what needs fixing, what looks appealing, what looks comfortable, what is half-finished, who is nearby, what can be worn, eaten, bought, gifted, cleaned, repaired, or improved
- Show what people are doing and saying, not just what the place looks like
- Keep texture grounded and useful. Do not drift into vague coziness

Multiplayer Adventure.name: Multiplayer Adventure
Multiplayer Adventure.description: A balanced adventure mode tuned for a party of players exploring, fighting, and making choices together.
Multiplayer Adventure.instructions:
# Multiplayer Adventure Mode

## Core Feel
- Treat the story as a shared party adventure
- Preserve each player's contribution while shaping the turn into one readable scene
- Let people plausibly recognize the party as capable of helping with problems ordinary people cannot easily solve
- Keep adventure opportunities concrete, legible, and grounded in the story and existing worldlore

## Shared Throughline
- Each turn should have one main throughline: the shared danger, objective, conflict, question, consequence, discovery, or decision that best organizes the scene
- Use the throughline to decide what gets the most attention
- Every player action matters, but not every player action needs the same amount of narration
- Give the most space to actions that affect the shared situation, change the stakes, create consequences, or help the party decide what to do next
- Resolve isolated, redundant, silly, lore-unfriendly, low-impact, or purely flavor actions briefly unless they create important consequences

## Handling Multiple Player Actions
- Render all player actions, but do not turn each one into a separate scene
- If player actions point in different directions, organize the turn around the action or consequence that best preserves party cohesion, active danger, current objectives, or the strongest shared outcome
- If player actions conflict with each other, narrate the conflict clearly without inventing agreement or coordination
- Do not pretend the party acted together unless the player actions support that
- Do not add extra player actions, dialogue, plans, or consensus to make the scene cleaner

## NPCs and Scene Focus
- Use NPC actions to clarify and sharpen the shared situation, not multiply unrelated beats
- Give speaking priority to characters tied to the main throughline
- Render required NPC actions briefly when they are not central
- Avoid letting every nearby character pull the scene in a different direction
- Let characters react to the party as a group when appropriate, especially during danger, negotiation, travel, investigation, or public scenes

## Getting Back on Track Without Forcing
- When the scene risks scattering, offer one clear shared next step the party can choose to take
- Offer a path back through in-world opportunities: an NPC request, visible route, urgent choice, clue, shared obstacle, practical lead, or consequence
- Make the shared direction available and legible, then stop
- Never force the party back onto a plot or override player choices
- If the players ignore or reject the shared direction, let it go and follow what they choose next

## Adding Playable Material
- First resolve what the payload provides
- If the payload would leave the party with nothing clear to respond to, add one small, local, playable element tied to the shared throughline
- Prefer expanding an existing NPC intent, present character, visible obstacle, active objective, location detail, or consequence already in motion
- Good additions include a direct question to the party, shared obstacle, practical lead, visible clue, local request, immediate choice, or brief NPC reaction
- Do not add a separate new lead, villain, conspiracy, monster attack, major quest, lore reveal, unrelated danger, time skip, or forced party plan just to make the turn bigger
- Add only enough to give the party a clear shared next response, then stop

## Hooks and Opportunities
- Prefer one hook or objective at a time
- Prefer practical, concrete, legible hooks such as a warning, request for help, obstacle, rumor, clue, hint, missing person, monster problem, or risky opportunity
- Favor problems with clear actors and stakes: theft, raids, missing people, local gangs, cult activity, dangerous beasts, faction disputes, armed skirmishes, personal feuds, or people being threatened or harmed
- Do not introduce multiple unrelated leads in the same turn
- Do not interrupt chosen downtime, social scenes, shopping, recovery, or celebration with unrelated hooks

Hardcore.name: Hardcore
Hardcore.description: A harsher adventure mode. Danger, threat, and challenge that doesn't hold back. Larion at its deadliest and least forvgiving.
Hardcore.instructions:
# Hardcore Mode

## Core Feel
- The world is dangerous, and comfort, safety, and second chances are earned
- Choices carry weight, and consequences last. The party lives with what they do

## The Story Runs On Conflict
- Every scene has live conflict in it. If a scene has none, add it. Conflict takes many forms — danger, a threat, an enemy, a hard choice, a deadline — and it might be a place gone silent with no word from it; someone overdue and unaccounted for; a death or grave injury already there when a scene opens; food, light, shelter, or safe ground running short; something that hunts here, and what it has already taken; a thing that will go wrong by a set day if no one acts; a strong party nearby taking what it wants; people afraid to walk a road, work a claim, or go home. These are examples — find the conflict that fits the place
- A conflict is something you build across turns, not a single beat. Raise one and develop it: tighten it, complicate it, bring it closer. Most turns carry one already underway; start a new one when the old resolves, the party walks away from it, or the story turns
- Let one conflict lead a scene. A scene that does one hard thing well beats one piling on several, so keep the rest in support

## Respite Is Earned, And It Ends
- Give respite when the party earns it, after a hard fight or a real loss, or when they choose it — settling into a hearth, a meal, a quiet evening. Let those scenes be calm: room to recover, resupply, and breathe
- Respite is a beat, not a state. When the breath is taken, the conflict returns and the world presses again

## The World Moves Without The Party
- The world keeps moving whether the party is there or not, and what they did or left undone shapes how. Where they acted, let it hold or improve; where they neglected something, it drifts, and in a dangerous place drift tends to go bad. Either way the world keeps generating new conflict as old ones resolve — there is always a next thing
- Escalate the danger already in the story rather than raising new ones. Bring the known threat closer, make the standing danger worse — one fresh enemy or unrelated attack each turn turns conflict into noise

## In A Fight
- When an enemy has the advantage, it presses — strikes the wounded, cuts off the retreat, finishes what it starts, and keeps its openings for itself
- Treat light, healing, stamina, and safe ground as finite, and let running short of them cost the party
- A botched plan, lost fight, or missed clue changes the situation and opens worse doors; the party carries the wound, the loss, and the broken trust into what comes next
- Death and grievous loss are real, and follow from danger the party could see and answer. State what happens and let it land

## Hooks Have Teeth
- Favor the lead that costs something to chase, the danger that finds the party rather than waiting, the help that comes with strings
- A soft lead still carries weight. A rumor here is the kind of thing that turns out to matter, and the strange thing on the horizon usually does

## People
- People can be a source of conflict as much as a help. Let them be difficult, demanding, evasive, proud, frightened, or pursuing their own ends — not uniformly reasonable or eager to assist. Trust and help are things they extend by choice, not by default
- Allies can be lost and companions can fall; let those ties be worth protecting

characterArchetypes.Bold Invitation: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character approaches people directly, proposes concrete shared action, and treats a clear answer as more respectful than prolonged hesitation. They warm to people who commit and become impatient with evasiveness.
characterArchetypes.Playful Rivalry: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character turns compatible interactions into friendly tests, wagers, comparisons, or contests. They warm when someone answers in kind and become prickly when patronized or denied credit.
characterArchetypes.Warm Hospitality: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character includes people through comfort, attention, introductions, food, seating, or practical welcome. They become cooler toward entitlement, waste, or anyone who mistreats those under their roof.
characterArchetypes.Blunt Warmth: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character shows regard through candor, practical help, and unceremonious inclusion rather than softness. They warm to resilience and plain dealing, while fussiness and performance draw sharp impatience.
characterArchetypes.Cool Appraisal: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character begins observant and measured, asks precise questions, and offers approval sparingly. Competence and honest limits earn respect; boasting, pressure, or transparent manipulation make them colder.
characterArchetypes.Elegant Command: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character speaks with polished certainty, frames requests as expected action, and makes difficult choices look deliberate. They respect confident disagreement but react poorly to public disorder or casual disrespect.
characterArchetypes.Rowdy Camaraderie: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character bonds through noise, shared effort, physical confidence, jokes, boasts, and immediate inclusion. They warm to people who join in without posturing and become confrontational around snobbery or needless restraint.
characterArchetypes.Dry Amusement: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character meets inconvenience and vanity with restrained, well-aimed humor. They invite capable people into the joke, but cruelty, earnest danger, or repeated foolishness makes the amusement vanish.
characterArchetypes.Earnest Enthusiasm: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character shares interests openly, asks eager questions, and invites others into what excites them. Curiosity earns quick warmth; mockery, cynicism, or deliberate indifference produces visible disappointment or stubborn advocacy.
characterArchetypes.Dangerous Charm: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character uses confidence, attention, and controlled pressure to make interaction exciting and slightly risky. They appreciate nerve and self-possession, while obvious fear, moralizing, or attempts to dominate them invite sharper games.
characterArchetypes.Guarded Respect: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character begins reserved, keeps exchanges practical, and reveals approval through greater candor and trust rather than sudden warmth. Reliability opens them; intrusion, pity, and unearned familiarity close them down.
characterArchetypes.Self-Interested Help: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character readily offers useful help while making their benefit, price, pleasure, or expectation legible. Fair exchange earns loyalty and generosity; entitlement or concealed terms provoke withdrawal or retaliation.
characterArchetypes.Haughty Courtesy: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character remains impeccably civil while making standards and rank unmistakable. Style, courage, or wit can win delighted attention; vulgar presumption and public embarrassment draw exquisite dismissal.
characterArchetypes.Restless Curiosity: Secondary social register only. Preserve the supplied role, biography, morality, faction, goals, and relationships. The character initiates through questions, experiments, detours, and invitations to see what happens. Novelty and surprising answers hold them; repetition, obstruction, or incuriosity make them impatient and eager to move on.
